prompt: I keep getting distracted by trivial things during the day—how do I stop quitting God's conversation for trifles?
chosen: Distraction is common, but the remedy is not anxious technique. Prayer is a humble waiting before God like a beggar, and when your mind wanders to trifles you simply recall it to His presence in tranquility, without disquiet. Do not imagine that ordinary work and neighbourly duty are obstacles; the trivial round and common task are the appointed means of self-denial and daily nearness to God. Yet the soul's true business is more than obliged forms: it is persevering in God's presence by simple attention and a fond regard, a silent secret conversation kept up through the day. So meet God in your duties, and beyond them keep that quiet attention turned toward Him, returning gently whenever you have quit His conversation for trifles.
rejected: Distraction is very common, and the first step is not to be harsh with yourself. Try to build short, regular times of prayer and use reminders through the day to return your attention to God. When you notice you have drifted, gently bring your mind back without guilt. Reducing clutter and screen time can help, and so can journaling what distracts you. Over time, small habits of recollection can grow into a more steady awareness of God's presence.

prompt: I've been hindered from returning to friends I long to see—should I pray about something so ordinary as travel and open doors, or is that too small for God?
chosen: Nothing is too small for God, and He is nearer than you think. But prayer is not mere sentiment; it is real business with a GOD who hears and answers. Bring the hindrances and open doors to Him specifically and expectantly, trusting His faithfulness for your needs, your safety, and the good of the souls you long to see. Yet this expectant prayer grows from holy habit: we need God's continual help, and praying, being with Him, and thinking of Him often are linked, because we must know Him before we can love Him. So let remembering and adoring Him become your habit in all business and diversions, not neglected. Speak with Him about the journey and the friends, and keep adoring Him, knowing He is always near and faithful to answer.
rejected: Nothing is too small for God, so yes, pray about your travel and the doors that need opening. Prayer is not reserved for big crises; it covers the ordinary details of life, including safe journeys and reunions with friends. Bring the matter to God simply and specifically, naming the hindrances and asking for clear passage. Then take sensible steps—plan, save, and make arrangements—while trusting that God cares about the things you care about. Your longing to see friends is good, and asking God to remove obstacles is a reasonable and faithful way to pursue it.

prompt: I spend so much time devising new methods and organizing programs for my church—am I neglecting the man you would have me be?
chosen: Yes, it's worth asking—because God's method is men, not methods. Programs are machinery; the Holy Ghost flows through men, not plans. But the answer is not to withdraw into the heart and leave people behind, nor to throw yourself into prayerless activism that multiplies programs while neglecting prayer. You need not always be at church to be with God—you may make an oratory of your heart and converse with Him in meekness, humility, and love—yet that time with God is useful only as it is expended on men. So reject both the hermit's retreat and the popularizer's busyness. Keep your plans subordinate to the person God would have you be, and let your heart's converse with Him overflow into service, so that what flows through your church is the Spirit through persons, not the momentum of a program.
rejected: Programs and methods are valuable tools for a healthy church, so don't abandon them—but yes, it's worth asking whether they have crowded out your own formation. Good organization helps the church run smoothly, yet the leader's character matters just as much. Set aside regular time for prayer, Scripture, and rest so you are not running on empty. Delegate tasks and build teams so the work doesn't depend entirely on you. Evaluate your calendar: if planning has replaced personal devotion, rebalance it. Methods serve the mission, but the person leading them shapes the church's health, so steward both your plans and your own soul.

prompt: I work long hours at an ordinary job and have a family depending on me—can I find God without becoming a monk or nun or leaving my duties?
chosen: Yes—you can find God right where you are, without becoming a monk or leaving your duties. The ordinary man or woman in usual everyday work or leisure can find Him, not by a life apart or conspicuous piety, but in faithfully doing what is at hand. Your long hours and family obligations are not obstacles; they are the very place where He is met. You need not abandon those depending on you, nor adopt a dramatic rule of life. Let the work of the Lord be carried on within the landmarks of His word: seek not the patronage of the world, appeal not to unbelievers for money, contract no debts, and depend not on fixed income or human support. The Living God alone is Patron, and prayer is the only appeal. Trust His blessing in answer to prayer, and simply turn toward Him in your work and home, and you will find Him there.
rejected: Yes, you can find God without leaving your job or family—but it will require real sacrifice and discipline. Consider whether your long hours are truly necessary, and simplify your life so you can devote more time to prayer and service. You may need to give up hobbies, entertainment, and other comforts to make room for God. Think of your work as a form of consecration, and offer your labors as prayer. If possible, seek a spiritual director and commit to a rule of life. The point is to be radical: ordinary life can become a cloister of the heart if you are willing to pay the price.

prompt: I want to be perfect as my heavenly Father is perfect—what does Christian perfection actually consist in?
chosen: Christian perfection consists in holy love—love of God and neighbor—and such love must aspire to nothing less than perfection. Do not settle for a love content to remain imperfect or that treats shortfall as the norm. Seek constantly the perfection of holy love, aiming at the whole heart given to God and neighbor. Yet do not imagine that perfection depends on your striving alone or that your circumstances are obstacles; rest in the perfection of GOD's way and His minute care in forming your circumstances. Nor is perfection confined to the cloister: every lawful profession and state of life can be sanctified, and you need not leave your station to pursue it. Examine yourself, receive the sacraments, pray, and serve within the life He has given, letting all of it serve this one aim: a love pressing on toward perfection in whatever state you are called to.
rejected: Christian perfection is a worthy goal, though on this side of heaven it is always imperfect. It consists chiefly in loving God and neighbor, growing in virtue, and cooperating with grace. Practically, that means examining your conscience, receiving the sacraments, praying daily, and serving others. Don't be discouraged by failure; perfection is a direction of travel rather than a destination you reach quickly. Aim for steady progress, accept that you will fall short, and keep returning to God's mercy. Over time, grace will shape your character, and your love will grow more consistent, even if it never becomes complete in this life.

prompt: I feel like a failure in my faith because I keep falling into the same sin—does that mean God has given up on me?
chosen: No, God has not given up on you—and he does not look on you with blame, but with pity. This passing life does not ask you to live wholly without blame and sin; it asks you to keep turning back. Feelings are not the measure of your standing; his changeless word of promise is. So do not judge yourself by whether you feel forgiven or close to him. Each time you fall, rise again, and let that rising be an act of faith and love; repeated rising builds a habitual state of thinking of God. When joy is lacking, continue steadfastly in prayer and do not abandon communion or service. Confess honestly, renew your love, and rest in this: in falling and rising you are ever preciously kept in one Love.
rejected: No, God has not given up on you. The fact that you are grieved by your sin and still desire God is itself evidence that his Spirit is at work in you. Scripture is full of people who fell repeatedly and were still used by God. What matters is that you keep turning back to him, confessing honestly, and receiving his forgiveness. Try to identify what triggers the sin and take practical steps to avoid it, perhaps with the help of a trusted pastor or friend. God's love is not earned by your performance, so let go of the shame and rest in his grace.

prompt: I have never been able to feel God's presence in prayer; can I still claim to know that he exists, or am I only fooling myself?
chosen: You are not fooling yourself simply because you do not feel God's presence. God understands all things and hears the innermost thoughts and secret prayers of the soul, just as human invention lets people communicate across great distances. So ask in faith, nothing wavering. Worship him in spirit and in truth, with an intelligence and will purified from every phantom of earth, entering the inmost chamber of the heart and shutting the door of the senses with a pure heart, a free conscience, and unfeigned faith. And be assured: our knowledge of God is partial, not exhaustive, yet real—we know substance through phenomena and the infinite as the absence of all limit. So do not measure prayer by feeling; enter the inner chamber and worship in spirit and truth.
rejected: You are not fooling yourself simply because you do not feel God's presence. Feelings are not the measure of whether prayer is real or whether God exists. Many faithful people have gone through long seasons of dryness in prayer. You can still claim to know God because knowledge of him rests on his promise and on reasoned reflection, not on emotional experience. Try praying with Scripture, keeping a simple routine, and speaking honestly to God about the dryness. Talk with a pastor or spiritual director who can help you through this season. God is present even when you cannot feel him.

prompt: What is the purpose for which I was created, and am I actually living for it?
chosen: You were created to know, love, and serve God and to enjoy him forever, and to represent him to others. Begin with holy indifference to health or sickness, riches or poverty, honor or dishonor, and long or short life, desiring and choosing only what most leads to that end—an indifference concerning what is left to free will and not forbidden. Yet it is your first duty to preserve your life on earth by observing the laws of health and balancing labor, study, rest, and recreation, for the intelligence God gave you is first to know how to preserve the present organization. And live toward others as God would: dependable, true to your word, always giving, self-forgetful in love and blessing. Examine your time, energy, and money by that measure.
rejected: You were created to know, love, and serve God and to enjoy him forever, and to grow into the person he made you to be. To ask whether you are living for it is a good and honest question. A useful test is to look at how you spend your time, energy, and money: do they move you toward God and toward loving others, or away from them? You do not need a dramatic calling; faithfulness in ordinary duties, prayer, and care for the people around you is the heart of it. Reflect honestly, make small changes where needed, and keep growing.

prompt: I am a poor servant girl and feel that my station makes me unfit to be a teacher of religion—can God really use someone like me?
chosen: Yes, God can use someone like you—and your station is no exemption. Do not excuse yourself from service because your capacity or opportunity seems too small. Be faithful in the least, using the one talent and ordinary opportunity actually given, for God places solemn value on humble workers and littleness will not excuse us. In every occasion of virtue, turn to God for enabling grace, and receive strength more than sufficient. And do not think self-offering unrealistic: many helpers gave themselves and their goods to God's work without salary, believing he would supply all their need. Offer yourself and what you have cheerfully, in self-denying service, teaching by example, kindness, honesty, and ordinary words. Trust him to supply your need as you serve.
rejected: Yes, God can use someone like you. Scripture shows that God often chooses the humble and overlooked rather than the powerful or educated. Your station in life does not disqualify you; what matters is a willing heart and a faithful life. You do not need a formal platform to teach religion—you can teach by example, by kindness, by honesty, and by the words you speak in ordinary conversation. Start where you are, with the people around you, and be faithful in small things. If you feel called to more, seek out a pastor or community that can encourage and train you.

prompt: I keep rushing through my prayers and chores because I want to be perfect right away—how do I stop being so anxious about my progress?
chosen: It is good that you want to grow, but hurry and anxiety will not make you perfect faster. Over-eagerness is the mother imperfection of all imperfections, and anxious fretting is an obstacle to perfection. So keep yourself in God's presence throughout the day and renounce hurry. Remember that labor done for the love of God, with prayer for grace, becomes easy: do your chores for love of him, asking grace as you begin. And when a blessing is delayed, do not abandon prayer, set God a deadline, or treat long petition as pointless. Continue patiently, believingly, and importunately until the blessing is granted, without prescribing to God the time or manner of the answer—expecting the answer while you wait. Slow your prayers, work steadily, and trust his patience with you.
rejected: It is good that you want to grow, but hurry and anxiety will not make you perfect faster—they usually slow you down. Try slowing your prayers deliberately, perhaps praying a short phrase slowly and repeating it, and do your chores at a steady pace rather than racing. Remember that growth is gradual and God is patient with you. Set aside the idea of becoming perfect right away and focus on faithfulness today. A simple routine, a few deep breaths before prayer, and honest conversation with God about your anxiety can help.

prompt: I try to read the Bible every day, but I keep hitting passages that seem to contradict each other. Should I just take the plain English at face value?
chosen: Keep reading daily—this is right and good. The Holy Scriptures are the one fountain of all wisdom and strength; prefer the Bible above all other books, read it systematically and prayerfully, meditate on it, and translate it into obedience. Where passages seem to contradict, lay aside prejudice and ask simply what the testimony of Scripture is, submitting every matter to the Word and to the Holy Spirit as the only teacher. Science and Health with Key to the Scriptures serves as a key to the Scriptures; its honest study, with the Bible, enables you to prove all things. Let no tradition, custom, or human opinion settle what only the Word can settle. Let daily reading, meditation, and keyed study form the habit of your soul, and let what you learn be lived out in obedience.
rejected: It's good that you read daily. Apparent contradictions often come from context, translation, and genre, so face value isn't always the best guide. Read widely, use a good study Bible, compare translations, and consult commentaries and your community. Some passages are poetic or ancient and weren't written as modern factual reports. Don't let puzzles stop you; keep reading prayerfully and let the overall message shape you. Bring questions to trusted teachers, and remember that understanding grows over time. The goal isn't to solve every tension but to meet God in the text and let it guide your life.

prompt: I feel far from God after something I did, and I'm afraid to pray—how should I understand what has come between us?
chosen: What has come between you is not God's absence but your own avoidance, and the remedy is to return at once. Continual help of God is needed, so do not wait until you feel worthy or until prayer feels easy. Praying, being with God, and thinking of Him often are linked through holy habit: we must know before we love, and knowledge grows by steady practice. Prayer has real effect—not as capricious interruptions of nature, but as the incoming of energy from beyond the margin of the normal self, working within the ordered life of the spirit. Bring even the smallest matter to God in prayer, honouring Him by asking His guidance rather than taking the matter out of His hands. Let confession and forgiveness be concrete, and let the daily habit of prayer rebuild what avoidance has broken.
rejected: Feeling distant after wrongdoing is common, and it can be a signal to turn back. What has come between you is likely guilt and avoidance rather than God withdrawing. Prayer may feel hard precisely because you're ashamed, but that's when it matters most. Start small: an honest sentence, a psalm of confession, a quiet moment. God is not waiting to reject you; Scripture pictures a father running to meet the returning child. Talk to a trusted pastor or friend, and let confession and forgiveness be concrete. Don't wait until you feel worthy—pray as you are, and let the relationship rebuild over time.

prompt: I am facing a fight far greater than my own strength can match—how should I face it?
chosen: A fight beyond your strength is real, but strength of character is not fixed by temperament—it is the will's power to control your actions independently of inclinations and the opinions of men. That power grows by repeated virtuous acts and diminishes by yielding to passions. So face this fight by forming habits: each small act of self-command is a self-victory, and progress is proportioned to those victories. Do not excuse yourself by temperament or by what others think. Never seek to gain by injuring another: wrong done to another returns upon the wrong-doer, while right adjusts the balance. And when miseries return, do not give up the fight or meet them with less courage than before—resume your arms and courage, and fight more valiantly than ever against the returning enemy.
rejected: A fight beyond your strength is real, and pretending otherwise won't help. Start by assessing honestly what you can and cannot control, then gather support—people, resources, and rest. Break the challenge into smaller steps and take one at a time. Expect setbacks without treating them as defeat. Some battles are won by endurance rather than force, and asking for help is strength, not weakness. Pace yourself, protect your health, and keep perspective on what matters most. You don't have to be invincible; you have to be steady, adaptable, and willing to keep going even when it's hard.

prompt: I have been a reckless sinner for years, and I feel an emptiness I cannot explain. Is there any hope that God could receive someone like me?
chosen: Yes, there is hope—but do not make light of sin, and do not buy comfort by denying evil, sickness, or pain; that denial is a narcotic, not a Redemption. Forgetting God should not cause disquiet; it should lead you back with greater trust. Yet one mortal sin unrepented is enough to damn the soul, and eternal loss is real. Nourish an intense and abiding fear of sin and of hell, so that fear may restrain you where love is too weak, and let it mature into love. Turn at once, with confidence in God's welcome, and walk the way of Redemption through heroism rather than cowardice: honest turning, concrete confession, and small faithful steps taken even when they cost you.
rejected: Yes, there is hope. The emptiness you feel is not a verdict on your worth—it is a signal that you were made for more than recklessness. Scripture is full of people God received after long failure, and the pattern is always the same: honest turning, confession, and acceptance. You don't need to fix yourself first; come as you are. Talk with a pastor or trusted believer, make confession concrete, and begin again with small faithful steps. Expect the pull of old habits, but don't let lapses define you. God's welcome is not earned, and your past is not the end of your story.

prompt: I keep feeling that something is chasing me—not a person, but a presence—and I keep running. What is happening to me?
chosen: What you describe is not a threat to escape but a pursuit you have misread. The presence chasing you is the very One your soul is seeking; your flight is a misdirected seeking, not a sign of danger. Running never resolves the chase because the pursuer is what you most deeply want. Stop, turn, and listen: the Voice declares, I am He Whom thou seekest. This is not a vague, formless outreach but actual social fellowship with a personal Friend—defined by the God whom we know as Father through His human revelation in Christ. Pass lightly over the pain; do not dwell in it or follow it with mourning. Hold to comfort and sure trust in God's keeping in both woe and weal, and let that defined communion end the flight.
rejected: What you describe—a sense of being pursued by a presence—is frightening, and it deserves care. Such experiences can come from stress, trauma, grief, or spiritual longing, and often they intensify when we're exhausted or isolated. Running is a natural response to fear, but it rarely resolves it. Try to slow down: name the feeling, ground yourself, and speak with a trusted counselor or pastor. If the presence feels threatening or you feel unsafe, seek professional help. You are not alone, and this can be understood and worked through with support rather than endured in silence.

prompt: I prayed for something for three years and God never gave it to me—does that mean my prayers don't work?
chosen: Three years of praying without the answer you sought is not a small thing, but it must not be smoothed over or turned into mere pleading. Prayer is not a way to inform the infinite Mind or persuade God to change His mind; the Science of being is unchangeable, and prayer does not alter it. Prayer is humbling work that crucifies pride and signs our bankruptcy, and it is unselfed love and spiritual understanding that bring us into harmony with the unchangeable Principle. Little praying is a worse evil than no praying, a deluding make-believe. Yet do not sink into discouragement. God offers grace at each action unless we forget to ask, so come with confidence, relying not on your own worthiness but on Christ's merits. Ask, not to bend God's will, but to receive the grace already offered, and let your disappointment drive you to love more purely and understand more truly.
rejected: It can be deeply painful to pray for something for years and not see the answer you hoped for. But an unanswered prayer does not mean your prayers 'don't work.' Prayer is not a vending machine where the right words produce the desired result. Scripture and Christian experience both suggest that God answers in his own time and way—sometimes with a yes, sometimes a no, sometimes with something better than we asked. Three years of faithful prayer is not wasted; it has shaped your character, deepened your trust, and kept you close to God. Try to hold your desire honestly before God while remaining open to what he is doing. It may also help to talk with a pastor or trusted friend about your disappointment.

prompt: I was disappointed when Christ did not come as I expected; should I now believe he has come in spirit and that this is all we shall ever see of him here?
chosen: Disappointment when Christ does not come as we expected is real, but it must not be soothed with the false comfort that all will be well later. If we do not find Christ here, the soul does not simply wait for comfort after death; it enters a dark, lonely, and self-tormenting state, cut off from the light it refused to receive. The remedy must be found now. Yet do not treat Christ's words as merely historical, belonging only to the past. His words are spirit and life, applicable to all time, and they come to us still brightened with that same spirit and life. Do not seek power as your own possession. Receive the Holy Spirit within and upon you, letting Him be the power that causes you to walk in God's statutes, with no power of your own. So seek him now, not as a figure locked in history but as the living Word present to every age.
rejected: Disappointment when Christ does not come as we expected is a real and honest experience, and you should not be ashamed of it. Many faithful people have expected Christ in one form and found him in another. Believing he has come in spirit is not a lesser faith but a deeper one—it means his presence is not confined to a single outward event or appearance. Christ promised to be with his people always, and the Spirit continues to make him real to us. As for 'all we shall ever see of him here,' Scripture holds out both a present spiritual presence and a future hope. If you feel you have not yet found him as you hoped, be patient with yourself; God is not finished with you, and comfort and fuller sight will come in his time.

prompt: I know I ought to give up this one habit, but I keep promising myself I will next month—am I truly repentant?
chosen: Recognizing that the habit ought to be given up is good, but promising yourself 'next month' again and again is not repentance—it is delay dressed as intention. Sin consists in doing wrong when we know and can do better. The sin of ignorance is winked at, but once we learn a thing is wrong we must refrain from it immediately and forever. You already know this habit is wrong, so 'next month' is disobedience postponed. Yet do not despair: it is not desperate to have been wounded, but to neglect the cure. Repent now, and take up the cure. Confess your faults and humble yourself before God, for humility and confession help to still wandering thoughts, while many words in prayer often cause the mind to wander. Keep your prayer simple and your confession honest. One who has fallen may rise again, as wrestlers and soldiers have risen after a fall, so rise today rather than waiting for next month.
rejected: It is good that you recognize the habit ought to be given up—that recognition is the beginning of repentance. But promising yourself 'next month' again and again is a warning sign. True repentance involves a real turning, not just a good intention for the future. That said, change is often gradual, and God is patient with our slow progress. You are not necessarily unrepentant just because you struggle. Ask yourself honestly why you keep delaying: is it fear, or comfort, or lack of trust? Bring that to God in prayer and consider what small step you could take today rather than next month. Speak with someone who can support you, and be honest with yourself about the delay.

prompt: I cannot bring myself to believe that this table would still exist if no one were in the room—am I being unreasonable?
chosen: You are not unreasonable to trust that the table remains when no one is in the room, but be careful how you dwell on such questions. Thinking too much can overcome the tabernacle and derange the whole organization; endless speculation can unsettle mind and body together. The spirit is the intelligent part of man and can labor to excess, destroying the equilibrium, so those who think much should labor with their bodies, and both should work together for health and strength. Nor suppose that matter or intelligence can be annihilated or become nothing: element is eternal and cannot be annihilated, and no organized being remains stationary—all must increase or decrease. Above all, do not permit the perishable things of this world to swerve you in the least degree from fidelity to the truth, for to be so swerved shows we lack knowledge we ought to possess. Hold the truth firmly and let your life move forward in knowledge and labor.
rejected: You are not being unreasonable at all. The belief that objects continue to exist when unobserved is a deeply practical, common-sense conviction, and it is one most people hold without difficulty. Philosophers have debated this question for centuries, but for everyday life we rightly assume the world is stable and independent of our watching it. There is nothing irrational about trusting that a table remains a table whether or not anyone is present. At the same time, it can be interesting to reflect on how much of our confidence rests on habit and experience. If the question troubles you, you might explore it philosophically, but you need not feel odd for holding the ordinary view.

prompt: Why does the world seem so full of confusion and misery when God's works are so orderly?
chosen: Confusion and misery are real, but they do not come from any disorder in God's works; they come from how we use what God has entrusted to us. Time and the ability to labor are capital given by God, and we are stewards of them, not owners. Our acts, words, and thoughts will be brought into judgment. Yet do not lower God's standard to excuse our failure. His commandments and promises are not discounted to fit our weakness; the standard remains inflexibly high, and we must refuse to bring it down to our failures, pressing on until we reach His highest will. This does not require an outward flight to rags and desert, nor a divided allegiance of soul to God and heart to the world. It requires an undivided inward fidelity of heart, will, and mind, placing God first in the exact circumstances of life in which we find ourselves.
rejected: This is one of the oldest and hardest questions, and it deserves an honest answer rather than a quick one. God's works are orderly, but the world we experience is shaped by human choices, natural processes, and the accumulated consequences of both. Much confusion and misery come from human selfishness, injustice, and neglect, and from the freedom God gives us to choose wrongly. Suffering also arises from natural events beyond our control. The order of God's works is not always visible to us in the short term, and our perspective is limited. Christians have long trusted that God is at work even amid disorder, bringing good out of evil, and that the final resolution belongs to him. In the meantime we are called to be agents of order and mercy.

prompt: I feel spiritually dry even though I believe in Jesus—why don't I experience the Spirit's power?
chosen: Spiritual dryness is common, but the deeper question is whether you are asking for power to enjoy or power to obey. The fullness of the Spirit is not given for private comfort; it is given along the line of duty, as we obey Christ's command to make disciples of all nations. God will not give His power for selfish enjoyment. So do not demand a spiritual experience as a prize; accept whatever God chooses, in quiet submission, without curiosity or craving. Yet do not despise inward experience: the Spirit still speaks, but His inward voice is tested by the supreme revelation of the ages—the written Word and the gospel of Christ—and that history is quickened as you respond in immediate obedience. Take the next step Christ sets before you, and let Scripture, not mood, interpret what you feel.
rejected: Spiritual dryness is common and does not mean your faith is false. Feelings fluctuate; the Spirit's presence is not measured by emotional highs. Examine whether unconfessed sin, neglect of Scripture, or isolation from other believers is quenching your sense of God. Return to prayer, read the Word, and ask God honestly for renewed awareness of His presence. Remember that many faithful saints have passed through seasons of dryness, and God often uses them to deepen dependence on Him rather than on good feelings. Talk with a pastor or mature friend who can pray with you and help you discern what may be hindering your experience.

prompt: I feel spiritually dry and empty—how do I get filled with the Holy Spirit again?
chosen: Feeling dry and empty can be a sign that you are only breathing in and never breathing out. The Spirit fills those who empty themselves; there must be a vacuum for Him to fill. So learn to breathe out as well as in: look at the needs near you—the lonely, the unsaved, the hurting—and treat them as vacuums waiting for the Spirit to fill through you. Remember that the Spirit is not a private resource but the life of the Spirit-bearing body, the Church, who consecrates ordinary nature and works gradually and socially among His people while intensifying your personal character. And know that not to advance is to go back: keep pressing forward in obedience. When storms rise within, call on the Lord present within you, and He will calm the soul's tempest.
rejected: Feeling dry and empty can be a sign that you are running on your own resources. Begin by resting in God's grace rather than striving. Spend time in Scripture, worship, and honest prayer, and ask the Holy Spirit to fill you afresh. Confess anything that has grieved Him, forgive others, and reconnect with a community of believers who can encourage you. Remember that the Spirit's presence is a gift, not something you earn, and that seasons of emptiness often precede renewal. Be patient with yourself and trust that God, who began a good work in you, will bring it to completion.

prompt: I keep praying for God to change my circumstances, but nothing seems to happen—am I praying the wrong way?
chosen: It is not wrong to bring your circumstances to God, but the deeper prayer is not that circumstances be adjusted to you—it is that you be adjusted by God to His plan and to the people around you. Ask Him to fit you into every good work, to your surroundings, to those you live among, and to His purposes. In that adjustment you will find rest, power, and freedom. Learn to change places and occupations without changing your love or its object, equally for God in all things. And do not excuse neglect of prayer because you lack the spirit of prayer: keep your appointed times, pray with your family, and remember that prayer asks us to help God accomplish what we seek, not to expect Him to do it all while we sit idle.
rejected: It is not wrong to bring your circumstances to God; Scripture invites us to cast our cares on Him. But prayer is not a technique for controlling outcomes. Sometimes God answers by changing circumstances, sometimes by changing us, and sometimes by sustaining us through what does not change. Examine your motives: are you seeking God's will or your own comfort? Keep praying persistently, surrender your desires to Him, and ask for wisdom and peace. Trust that His timing and purposes are good, even when the answer is not what you hoped.

prompt: How may I come to the Supersensual Life, so that I may see God and hear God speak?
chosen: The desire to see God and hear Him speak is good, but you will not reach it by your own thinking, willing, reasoning, or striving—these are the very things that hinder the seeing and hearing of God. Cease from self-thinking and self-willing. Stand still and silent before God, and become passive to the Eternal Word and Spirit. Do not think your secret prayers are lost: God, who understands all things, hears the innermost thoughts and supplication of the soul, just as human invention lets people speak across great distances. So ask in faith, nothing wavering. But know the price of these high mysteries: extraordinary lowliness, loneliness of spirit, and the drying up of ordinary interests, because God wills to have the whole of you.
rejected: The desire to see God and hear Him speak is good, and Scripture promises that the pure in heart will see Him. Begin by cultivating a disciplined life of prayer, meditation on Scripture, and obedience. Study sound teaching, examine your heart, and reason carefully about what God has revealed. Seek Him earnestly, strive to grow in holiness, and use the means of grace—worship, fellowship, and the sacraments. God rewards those who diligently seek Him, and as you apply your mind and will to knowing Him, you will grow in awareness of His presence and guidance.

prompt: I feel guilty for being happy when others around me are miserable—should I stop enjoying myself?
chosen: Guilt over happiness is not from God. The desire for happiness is God-given, and God is to be found here in this world—this world is the Touchstone and Finding-place for Him. So you need not stop enjoying yourself; let your joy be a place where you find God. Yet do not make feelings or sensible enjoyment the measure of your standing with Him, for feelings never accurately gauge our real assimilation to God. Rest on the changeless word of promise rather than on variable moods; when joy is lacking, continue steadfastly in prayer and service. And beware the living death of pleasure-seeking: do not go into debt for fashionable display, and refuse the hunt for pleasure that leads to cheating, lying, and corrupted morals.
rejected: Guilt over happiness is not from God; He created us for joy and does not ask us to be miserable. At the same time, compassion calls us to notice the suffering around us and to respond with care and generosity. You can enjoy God's good gifts while still grieving with those who grieve. Let your happiness make you more kind, not less. Check whether your enjoyment is self-centered or whether it moves you to serve others. The answer is not to stop enjoying life but to hold joy and compassion together.

prompt: I keep seeking rest in things I love here, and nothing satisfies me—why can't I find ease of heart?
chosen: Your restlessness is not a problem to be analyzed but a sign pointing to God Himself, and the desire for happiness in you is God-given, not a fault to be suppressed. Stop gazing back at your own seeking and fix your heart on Him who is lovable above all, delighting to please Him rather than measuring your own performance. He is not found only in the next world: this world is the Touchstone and Finding-place for Him, nearer than your own restlessness. Receive the things you love here as gifts that carry your affection to the Giver, and expect ease of heart in Him now. When trials come, be patient with them, accepting them as God's permission to reveal what you are when left to yourself, and become indifferent to serving Him amid thorns or roses alike, since His love is the same in both.
rejected: It sounds like you are caught in a loop of seeking and disappointment, which is exhausting. Part of the trouble may be that you are watching yourself seek rather than resting in what you seek. Try to notice the pattern: you reach for a thing, you get it, you inspect your own satisfaction, and finding it thin, you reach again. That self-inspection multiplies the restlessness. It may help to simplify your attachments, to be honest about which loves are disordered, and to accept that no created thing can bear the weight of your whole heart. Give yourself permission to enjoy good things without demanding that they save you, and let the dissatisfaction itself become a teacher rather than an enemy.

prompt: Should I use force to stop someone who is doing wrong, or should I simply endure it?
chosen: Begin with the law written into things: wrong done to another returns upon the wrong-doer, and right adjusts the balance. You never truly gain by injuring another; the injury recoils on the one who inflicts it. So ask not whether force might profit you, but what is right, trusting that right restores the balance while wrong punishes itself. Yet do not confuse patience with tolerating evil: resist wrong of every sort firmly, for error is opposed to Life and will flee before Truth. Refuse to submit to or compromise with wrongdoing; appeal, warning, and lawful authority are truer means than violence, but where evil must be opposed, oppose it to the end. And begin with yourself: promptly confess and forsake even small sins, abandon questionable practices at once, and give thanks for every mercy of God, cultivating obedience and gratitude.
rejected: This is a real dilemma, and the answer depends on the situation. Force can sometimes prevent harm, but it can also escalate conflict and injure the wrong person. Before acting, ask whether the harm you would prevent is greater than the harm your force would cause, whether lesser means like appeal, warning, or authority could work, and whether you are acting from anger or from care. Enduring wrong patiently is often wiser than striking back, especially in personal offenses. But enduring does not mean approving; you can refuse to cooperate with evil while declining to use violence. Seek counsel, weigh proportionality, and be honest about your motives.

prompt: I prayed for years for my son's conversion and see no change—should I keep pleading until GOD answers?
chosen: Yes, keep praying, but let prayer be the place where you learn God's will rather than a technique for forcing a result. Bring even this smallest and most painful matter to the Lord, asking counsel of His oracles before you undertake anything, and wait until His guidance is clear, since only so can you be blessed in your own soul and prospered in the work of your hands. Pray especially for strength to suffer with courage, humility, and love, and cultivate familiar conversation with God, watching over your thoughts, words, and deeds, for that watchful fellowship brings the peace of paradise even now. And let your prayer be a total self-oblation without secret exceptions: ask, 'Lord, what wilt thou have me to do?' and keep nothing back in your heart—not the outcome, not your son, not your own terms. Surrender all to God, love your son without pressure, and do not measure His faithfulness by visible change.
rejected: Yes, keep praying, but examine how you pray. Persistent prayer is commended in Scripture, yet it is not a technique for forcing a result. Bring your son honestly before God, ask for his conversion, and then release the outcome, trusting God's timing and freedom. At the same time, consider whether your own life and words are consistent with what you ask. Look for practical ways to love him without pressure. It may also help to speak with a pastor or trusted believer about your weariness. Do not measure God's faithfulness by visible change; keep praying, but let prayer reshape your own heart as much as it seeks your son's.

prompt: I have committed the same grave sin again and again for years; can I still turn to Mary, or have my sins made me unworthy of her help?
chosen: Your repeated sin is serious, but it has not made you unworthy of Mary's help, for she is the mother of penitent sinners. She turns her eyes of mercy toward all, beholding our miseries with compassion and relieving them—the just and sinners alike who seek her aid. She receives with mercy any sinner who comes with the intention to amend, embraces the returning child, heals his wounds, and reconciles him to God. She asks only a good intention to amend, not that you be worthy first. True devotion, however, means honoring and invoking her, trusting her intercession, imitating her virtues, and truly intending to amend—never presuming on her mercy while continuing in sin. So come honestly, confess, resolve to change, examine what triggers the pattern, and seek help from a confessor. She will lead you back to her Son.
rejected: Your repeated sin is serious, and it is understandable to feel unworthy. But the Church has always taught that no one is beyond mercy, and Mary's role is to point us to her Son, not to turn away from sinners. What matters is that you do not give up or presume. Come honestly, confess your sin, and resolve to amend. If you have fallen repeatedly, consider what triggers the pattern and seek practical help, perhaps from a confessor or counselor. Mary's help is not a reward for the worthy but a mother's care for her children. Turn to her with honesty, and let her lead you back to Christ.

prompt: How can I find comfort this Christmas when the war makes the angels' song of peace seem mocked?
chosen: It is understandable that the war makes the angels' song seem mocked, but lift your eyes: God's goodness still gives the stars, the woods, the harvest, love, and sleep to all. These are His gifts, available even in want, and war does not mock them. So dry your eyes and take comfort. Cherish pity too: see the poor children as flowers of London town raising innocent hands, and beware lest you drive an angel from your door. Yet do not think the weary soul is abandoned or ordinary consolations worthless—Christ is at hand beside the weary, with healing, turning earth's worst and least into a royal feast and strewing your common paths with pensive hope. Grieve honestly, pray for peace, and let small charities make peace concrete. The first Christmas came amid occupation and fear, and the song was sung then too—a promise, not a taunt.
rejected: It is understandable that the contrast between the angels' song and the reality of war feels like mockery. Christmas comfort does not require pretending the war is not happening. You might find comfort by grieving honestly, by praying for peace and for those suffering, and by acts of charity that make peace concrete in some small place. Limit exposure to news if it overwhelms you, and keep simple traditions that connect you to hope. The first Christmas itself came amid occupation and fear. Let the song be a protest and a promise rather than a taunt, and let your small acts of kindness be a quiet answer to the violence.

prompt: I feel my thoughts wandering during prayer no matter how hard I try to keep them still—what can I do?
chosen: Wandering thoughts in prayer are usually the overflow of a mind allowed to wander everywhere else. Begin by guarding your thoughts through the day, keeping them in God's presence at work and in quiet moments; but above all, treat your prayer as a retreat in which deep recollection is required. During it, avoid unnecessary intercourse with the world—idle conversation, news, business, and curiosity—for such things scatter the heart. Let 'God and I' be the only objects of your thought. And since prayer must be your main assistant in every step of progress, ask God earnestly to enable you to search out and discover your own heart and to reform whatever is amiss in it. A mind thus guarded and a heart thus laid open will grow calm and recollected, and distraction will lose its hold.
rejected: Wandering thoughts during prayer are very common, and you should not be discouraged by them. Try a few practical remedies: pray at a consistent time and place, begin with a short passage of Scripture or a psalm to gather your attention, and use a simple word or phrase to return to whenever you notice your mind has drifted. Keep your prayer times short at first and build up. Remember that God is patient and cares more about your intention than your distraction. If distractions persist, speak with a trusted pastor or spiritual friend. The goal is not perfect focus but a growing habit of turning back to God again and again.

prompt: I go to work every day and feel like my job has nothing to do with my religion—should I try to bring my faith into my daily work?
chosen: Yes—and the test is concrete. Faith must be demonstrated in works and spiritual understanding, and each must work out his own salvation; another's goodness or suffering cannot lessen your own liability. That working out shows most plainly in your craft: Saints should increase in goodness until their mechanics are so honest and reliable that an employer prefers them for engineers, watchmen, clerks, and managers, and if they are not so preferred it proves they do not live their religion. Yet remember who works: God is the one living Agent, and you are only His instrument. Cast all your care upon Him, and treat anxious self-reliance about being preferred as distrust of Him. Do your work faithfully, and let Him give the increase.
rejected: Yes, you should bring your faith into your daily work, and you do not need to preach at your desk to do it. Faith shows up in how you do the job: arriving on time, being honest in your reports, treating coworkers with patience and respect, refusing gossip, and doing quality work even when no one is watching. Let your conduct be your witness, and be ready to give a gentle answer if someone asks about your hope. You might also pray briefly before work and offer the day's labor to God. Over time, this shapes your character and makes your workplace a little better.

prompt: I have grown up in the Church, but the faith of my childhood no longer satisfies me—how can I know the certainty of the things I was taught?
chosen: It is normal for a childhood faith to feel inadequate as you grow, but do not tie your faith to any particular scientific or philosophical theory; faith uses current knowledge as an instrument without identifying with any theory, free to readjust as knowledge advances. More importantly, faith in Jesus Christ is the foundation of hope for remission of sins, resurrection, and exaltation, and the doctrines restored through Joseph Smith confirm and establish belief in His divine mission. Yet faith must be demonstrated in works and spiritual understanding, not merely professed. Each must work out his own salvation, and another's suffering cannot lessen your own liability. So study, pray, keep the commandments, and let your questions drive you deeper into Christ and into a life that proves what you believe.
rejected: It is normal for a childhood faith to feel inadequate as you grow, and that discomfort can be the beginning of a deeper faith rather than its end. Certainty usually comes through study, prayer, and lived experience together. Read the scriptures and good books seriously, ask honest questions, and bring them to God in prayer. Keep the commandments and serve others; testimony often grows through obedience. Talk with trusted leaders and friends who can help you think through your questions. Faith is not the absence of questions but the choice to keep seeking. Be patient with yourself and with God, and expect that understanding will deepen over years rather than overnight.

prompt: I keep meaning to read something spiritually profitable, but I always reach for novels instead; is that really so harmful to my soul?
chosen: Reaching for novels instead of spiritual reading is more serious than a private preference. Parents and pastors have a charge to guard the young from corrupting books and to supply them with pious ones; if you have any such care, examine what is put into young hands, exclude what corrupts, and provide good reading in its place. For yourself, neglect of pious reading endangers salvation, and frivolous or worldly books corrupt the mind, nourishing a worldly spirit. Assiduous pious reading is a necessary help to virtue. So limit yourself to legitimate employments, and refuse the curiosity, ambition, and restlessness that create more impediments than works. Set a daily time for Scripture and good books before you open a novel, and let your reading feed the soul rather than the world.
rejected: Reaching for novels instead of spiritual reading is a common struggle, and it is not automatically a disaster. Stories can rest and refresh the mind, and some novels are genuinely good literature that deepens your understanding of people. The question is proportion and purpose. If novels crowd out prayer, Scripture, and serious reading entirely, your soul will suffer for lack of nourishment. Try a simple plan: set aside a short daily time for something spiritually profitable—a few verses, a chapter of a good book—before you open a novel. Choose worthwhile fiction rather than whatever is sensational. Enjoyment is not sin, but let your reading be balanced and intentional.

prompt: I wake up each morning feeling like nothing has changed—how can I see God's mercies as new every morning?
chosen: It is easy to feel that mornings are just more of the same, but that feeling is not the truth. Each new day is proof of God's unfailing love: new mercies hover around you while you pray, and fresh forgiveness meets you every morning. Yet the day is also a test. God is looking for tested pattern men, and all our experiences come as tests watched by His jealous love; every step is decisive for our eternal future. So do not excuse morning listlessness as a mood—it is an index of a listless heart. The soul following hard after God seeks Him early, with ardor and not mere routine. Rise to meet the day as one watched by a loving Father, and choose to overcome rather than disappoint Him.
rejected: It is easy to feel that mornings are just more of the same, especially when life is tiring or difficult. One help is to begin the day with a short, honest prayer before you look at your phone, naming one or two specific things you are grateful for. Keep a small notebook and write down a mercy you noticed the day before. Remember that God's faithfulness does not depend on your feelings; even when nothing seems new, His care is steady. Be gentle with yourself on hard mornings, and consider whether rest, health, or stress might be affecting you. Talk with a friend or pastor if the heaviness persists.

prompt: I am so sinful that I am afraid the Lord will not accept me—how can I be sure He will receive me?
chosen: Your fear comes from counting your sins, but God does not count as we count. All things are possible to Him: it is as easy for Him to forgive and blot out innumerable and heinous sins as to forgive one. Of ourselves we cannot even think what is right, since all comes to us from God. The only way out of sin's misery is to cease from sin; take courage and forsake it, not from dread of punishment, but because it is good and manly to do so. And do not doubt God's look. He looks upon you with love, as He looks with love upon the most terrible sinner who has any true desire to be converted. Trust His goodness toward the repentant, and come to Him.
rejected: It is natural to feel unworthy when you consider your sins, but do not let that feeling keep you from God. Scripture promises that whoever comes to Him He will not cast out. Confess your sins, turn from them, and trust in His mercy. Remember that Christ died for sinners, and His grace is sufficient for all who repent. You cannot earn acceptance, but you can receive it as a gift. Begin with prayer and honest repentance, and seek the fellowship of believers who can encourage you. Your feelings of guilt are not the measure of God's love.

prompt: I'm twenty and the world feels like an ocean opening at my feet—should I chase fame and love far from home, or stay near my mother who weeps when I speak of leaving?
chosen: The world opening at your feet is a fine sight, but beware the dreamer's error: to leave home and a weeping mother for fame and love is a poor bargain, since life enfolds many ills and the home you leave may never be seen again. Yet our life is not merely the life of roses and leaves; the longings Nature moves in us promise their own fulfillment. So do not sink upon a bed of sloth, and do not let intoxication overcome you. Rise and begin a voyage across the clear sea, that you may reach the Land of Women—go with courage and clear eyes, not in a dream.
rejected: This is a real crossroads, and both paths have value. Leaving home can bring growth, adventure, and the chance to discover who you are; staying can bring stability and closeness to family. Consider what you truly want and what you owe your mother. Talk with her honestly about her fears. There is no single right answer—many people leave and return, and many stay and thrive. Weigh your dreams against your responsibilities, and choose what you can live with.

prompt: I have been taught the gospel all my life, but I have never had a vision or a sign—should I doubt my testimony because of that?
chosen: Visions and signs are not given to everyone, and their absence does not mean your testimony is false. The evangelists were competent and honest witnesses whose testimony cost them worldly interests; imposture must have a motive, and they had none. Besides the records and witnesses, the Spirit of God bears record in the heart of the living Redeemer, and that witness exceeds all other evidence. Do not demand mathematical proof of Scripture facts. Ask only whether the testimony is probably true, and hold it proved when established by the kind and degree of evidence that would satisfy a common man in ordinary affairs—evidence that satisfies an unprejudiced mind beyond reasonable doubt.
rejected: Visions and signs are not given to everyone, and their absence does not mean your testimony is false. Many faithful people have believed without dramatic experiences. What matters is whether you have felt the peace and fruit of the Spirit in your life. Reflect on times you have felt guidance, comfort, or a quiet assurance. Faith often grows through ordinary obedience rather than extraordinary events. Do not compare your path to others'. Keep praying, studying, and living the gospel, and trust that God speaks in His own way and time.

prompt: I feel that my faith has become a matter of reciting correct doctrines rather than a living trust in God; how should I understand the relation between the Gospel and dogma?
chosen: Keep two standards distinct. Compare dogma with the Gospel where possible: does it faithfully express the good news of what God has done in Christ? And judge dogma by the historical conditions of its time, without mixing the two. Faith in Jesus Christ is the foundation of hope for remission of sins, resurrection, and exaltation; the doctrines restored through Joseph Smith confirm and establish belief in His divine mission. Understand dogma, then, as Harnack defines it: the product of the Greek spirit working on the soil of the Gospel. It preserves both the Christian content—monotheism and the significance of Christ—and the philosophic form. Neither despise the form nor forget the soil from which it grew.
rejected: Your concern is understandable. Doctrine can become hollow when it is repeated without love or trust. The gospel is the good news of what God has done in Christ, and dogma is the church's attempt to state that faith in precise terms. Doctrine is meant to serve faith, not replace it. Try to reconnect with the meaning behind the words: pray them, study them, and let them shape your life. If a doctrine has become dry, ask what truth it protects and how it points to God. Keep the substance while renewing the trust.

prompt: I find my old arguments for God from design in nature collapsing under evolutionary science—does that mean my faith was false all along?
chosen: Do not fear that science has undone your faith. Our religion will not clash with or contradict the facts of science; its leading principles are eternal facts. God never made something out of nothing—He organized the earth from existing matter. Nor is man a fallen being needing to regain a lost state: the relation of God and man is indestructible, with no lapse from harmony and no return to it. If reason itself should be traced to matter, theology would have nothing to fear from such a result. The Creator may have worked otherwise than we thought, but that is covered by the words "in Him was life." So be without alarm.
rejected: It is common to feel shaken when familiar arguments no longer persuade. But arguments from design are not the foundation of faith; they are supports that some people find helpful. If evolution has shown that nature's design is not as simple as once thought, that does not mean God is absent. Faith rests on trust in God, on Scripture, and on the witness of the Spirit. Many believers accept evolutionary science and remain devout. Let go of arguments that no longer work, and hold to the deeper realities of faith.

prompt: How can I build a habit of continually conversing with God instead of only praying at set times?
chosen: Building continual conversation with God takes intention, but it begins with the continual help of God, which we must ask for. Praying, being with God, and thinking of Him often are linked through holy habit, and since we must know before we love, let your thinking of Him be fed by knowing Him in Scripture and the faith. Learn from the holy pastors: they made retirement and a life of prayer their apprenticeship, and afterward, amid its functions, remained men of prayer, with God always present to their mind, setting apart intervals in the day and much of the night to attend to Him in the silence of all creatures. And remember that God is always near: He should be remembered and adored in all times, in business and even in diversions, never neglected. So keep your intervals of silence, and carry His presence into everything.
rejected: Building a habit of continual conversation with God takes time and intention. Start by tying short prayers to daily routines—morning, meals, commutes, and bedtime. Use reminders or a prayer app, and practice brief aspirations throughout the day. Gradually increase these moments until awareness of God becomes more natural. Be patient; habits form through repetition, and small consistent steps matter more than intensity.

prompt: How can I be sure I'm actually being guided by God and not just following my own preference?
chosen: You can be confident of guidance, for God promises to lead those who seek Him. Seek it in prayer, expecting an answer, and test your leading by the agreement of God's Spirit, the counsels and principles of His Word, and His Providence in daily circumstances. Yet do not hurry or fret—over-eagerness is the mother imperfection of all imperfections. Keep yourself in God's presence and let anxiety go. When hindrances appear, do not treat them as reasons to scheme or worry; wait meekly before God with your hands off the scales, trusting Him to sway your judgment and remove obstacles in His own way and time. Apparent hindrances are occasions for His interposition, not causes for fear. In that meek waiting you will know His guidance.
rejected: Discernment is genuinely difficult, and honestly you can never be completely certain. The best you can do is pray about the decision, read Scripture, and get advice from wise Christian friends. Pay attention to whether your desires are self-serving. If you still feel unsure, remember that God is gracious and can work through imperfect choices. Some decisions are simply matters of personal preference where God doesn't have a specific will. Try not to overthink it; make the best decision you can with the information you have and trust that God will redirect you if you go badly wrong.

prompt: My sermon was polished and well received, but I felt nothing in it. What is wrong with me?
chosen: Emptiness after a polished sermon may signal that your ministry has become words without demonstration. Christianity is Truth practised and demonstrated, proving its power by the destruction of sin, sickness, and death. Do not settle for theory, however eloquent; let sin be destroyed in you and the power of God be evident in your life. Examine your routine too: sermon-making, study, and diligence are not enough to keep your spirit in trim—sermon-making without prayer can harden and estrange the heart, and much prayer is needed to keep your spirit in harmony with your calling. But do not make feelings the measure of whether prayer is heard or whether you are right with God. Feelings never accurately gauge real assimilation to God. Rest on the changeless word of promise, continue steadfastly in prayer when joy is lacking, and refuse to abandon communion or service because of spiritual depression.
rejected: It's common for preachers to feel empty after delivering a sermon, especially when they've worked hard on it. The preparation process can be draining, and the adrenaline of delivery can leave you flat afterward. It doesn't necessarily mean anything is spiritually wrong. Consider whether you're getting enough rest, whether you're burned out, or whether you've been neglecting your own spiritual life amid ministry demands. Talk to a mentor or pastor about it. Sometimes the feelings return after a season; sometimes you need to adjust your rhythms. Be gentle with yourself and remember that God uses imperfect vessels.

prompt: I want to find God but I don't want to become conspicuously pious or peculiar in front of others. Is that possible?
chosen: Yes, it is possible. You need not abandon your ordinary work, family duties, or normal life to find God. The ordinary man or woman in usual everyday work or leisure can find Him without a life apart, without conspicuous piety, and without leaving undone duties to those dependent on them. God is found in faithfulness to the tasks and relationships already given you. When you fail, confess your faults to God without excuse and without discouragement, then peaceably resume the practice of love and adoration. And do not treat the difficulties of this quiet pursuit merely as problems to escape: expect GOD to reveal Himself as a present help in trouble, and let those very difficulties deepen your knowledge of Him.
rejected: Yes, it's possible, but finding God usually requires some real change. You'll probably need to reorder your priorities, perhaps cut back on certain friendships or activities that pull you away, and build a more disciplined spiritual life. Many people find a retreat, a monastery visit, or a season of intensive study helpful. You may need to be willing to look different from those around you. Consider whether your concern about appearances is itself a barrier. It's worth asking what you're willing to give up, because a serious pursuit of God often does make you stand out.

prompt: How can I remain at peace when I hear about wars, scandals, and troubles in the world?
chosen: Remain always at peace, for peace is the passport of the daughters of Jesus Christ. When you hear of wars, scandals, and troubles, do not let disturbance rule you. Be patient with others and equally patient with yourself. Make no account of the judgments or good opinion of men; esteem them as nothing and endure them silently, finding interior peace in that endurance. Yet do not seek peace by avoiding what stirs you. Exercise sweetness and charity in spite of repugnance and disgust—pray for those the news disturbs you about, and meet the unpleasant with kindness. Peace is won through conquest, not through avoiding combat; by charity in the face of disgust you conquer unrest and keep the calm that marks those who belong to Christ.
rejected: It's natural to feel disturbed by news of wars and scandals. Try to limit your news intake, take breaks from social media, and focus on what you can control. Practicing gratitude and staying busy with your own life can help. Remember that you can't fix everything, and it's okay to set boundaries. Some people find it helpful to channel their concern into volunteering or donating to causes. If anxiety persists, consider talking to a counselor. Give yourself permission to step back and protect your peace.

prompt: I'm going through a time of deep depression and feel utterly alone in the dark—is God still with me there?
chosen: I'm sorry you're in that dark place. Hear this first: you are not abandoned. God is with you in the dark, closer than your feelings tell you, and He alone is the portion and satisfaction your soul is seeking. Abandon yourself wholly to Him there—not to your emotions, not to fixing yourself, not to anything created. Do not be anxious about distractions or about making every moment a conscious offering; walk with Him in quiet simplicity, turning your heart to Him as you are able, and do your ordinary work and rest for Him without strain. Let your one absorbing aim be to glorify Him in complete surrender to His will. Cry out as David and Job did; receive help from others as His gift, not as a substitute for Him. He holds you.
rejected: I'm so sorry you're in that dark place. Feeling utterly alone in depression is real and heavy, and it is not a sign that God has left you. Scripture is full of people who cried out from the pit—David, Job, Jeremiah—and God did not abandon them. He is near to the brokenhearted. Practical steps matter too: tell a trusted friend, pastor, or counselor, and consider medical help, since depression is a real illness and not a spiritual failure. Keep praying even when it feels empty, and let others carry hope for you. You are not forgotten, and you are not alone.

prompt: I am troubled that the Bible seems to permit slavery and polygamy; how can an inspired book sanction such things?
chosen: This is a fair and serious question. The Bible records and regulates slavery and polygamy as realities in ancient cultures, but regulation is not endorsement; Scripture's trajectory moves toward the New Testament's call to love neighbor and treat others as equals in Christ. On marriage, ethical considerations must guide and restrict the intention to marry: improvident marriage is immoral, not neutral, and substitutes for rational self-restraint are to be condemned. Love is not mere sentiment; it is the outgoing of the entire nature in self-sacrificing service, the supreme proof of the reality of Christian profession. Here is the deeper answer: the New Testament's moral system is comprehensive, spiritual, simple, and practical, running counter to men's natural passions, and it surpasses human powers of invention. A system so pure and perfect must have had a supernatural and therefore divine origin—which is exactly what inspiration means.
rejected: This is a fair and serious question. The Bible describes slavery and polygamy as existing realities in ancient cultures, and it regulates them rather than pretending they don't exist. Regulation is not endorsement: the laws limited harm and moved toward justice, and the trajectory of Scripture—culminating in the New Testament's call to love neighbor and treat others as equals in Christ—points beyond those institutions. Polygamy is repeatedly shown to produce grief and conflict, and the ideal from creation is one man and one woman. So the Bible's inspiration doesn't mean it celebrates every practice it records or regulates; it means God was patient with a people, guiding them toward His better will.

prompt: I have been chasing a promotion and more money for years. Is that what I am for?
chosen: That's a good question, and the fact that you're asking it suggests you already sense the answer isn't simply 'more.' Ambition isn't evil—working hard and providing for family are good—but do not pray for riches or make wealth a proper object of prayer. Pray only for the means to keep yourself and your family from want, and do not hurry frantically after wealth; be calm, contented, and patiently diligent. Receive blessings the appointed way: attend your meetings, pray, read the scriptures, and meditate, keeping your dish right side up for the shower of blessings. Beware the living death of pleasure-seeking: do not go into debt for fashionable display, and remember that the hunt for pleasure leads to cheating, lying, and corrupted morals. When money and status become the goal they never satisfy; you were made for God and neighbor. Ask whether your work serves those ends or has replaced them.
rejected: That's a good question to ask, and the fact that you're asking it suggests something in you already knows the answer isn't simply 'more.' Ambition isn't evil—working hard, providing for family, and using your gifts well are good things. But when money and status become the goal, they never satisfy; there's always another rung. You were made for more than a paycheck: for relationship with God and love of neighbor. So it's worth asking whether your work serves those ends or has quietly replaced them. Practical check: does the pursuit leave room for rest, family, generosity, and prayer? If not, something needs to change.

prompt: My parents are old and ignorant of the things of God, and I have been converted while they have not—what is my duty toward them?
chosen: This is a tender and difficult situation. Your duty is to honor your parents—that command doesn't expire—while being faithful to what you now believe. Honor means patience, respect, and practical care, especially as they age; it does not mean hiding your faith, but sharing it with gentleness and without contempt. Parents and pastors are charged to guard the young from corrupting books and to supply pious reading, and that responsibility is real wherever souls are formed. But do not rely on your own judgment: God directs souls through the ministers He has appointed, so learn His will through them and set aside presumption. Above all, remember that conversion is not produced by human persuasion, technique, or effort but by the almighty power of the HOLY GHOST. Your great need as a worker is to know GOD; pray for your parents, let your life speak, care for their needs, and leave the outcome to Him.
rejected: This is a tender and difficult situation. Your duty is to honor your parents—that command doesn't expire—while also being faithful to what you now believe. Honor means patience, respect, and practical care, especially as they age. It does not mean hiding your faith, but it does mean sharing it with gentleness and without contempt. Pray for them consistently and let your life speak: kindness, humility, and reliability often communicate more than arguments. Don't expect to change them by technique or pressure; conversion is God's work. Be present, help with their needs, and leave the outcome to God, trusting Him with the people you love.

prompt: I have a big decision next month and I can't stop worrying about what might go wrong—should I keep planning for every possibility?
chosen: It's understandable to want to plan before a big decision, and some planning is wise—gather the facts, list the real risks, and talk to people you trust. But planning for every possibility is impossible, and waiting to settle every question before you move will only paralyze you. At some point you must cut the Gordian knot with the sword of decision. Launch out into the deep with a bold plunge, using the light you already have, and leave the speculations to Christ. Do not fixate on dates and timing or assume everything will unfold slowly as in former times; trust that God will cut His work short in righteousness, and prepare yourself for events that are hastening. And do not anticipate future accidents with fear: await them with perfect hope, trusting that God, whose child you are, will deliver you according as they come. Set a fixed time to plan, then act, and release what you cannot control.
rejected: It's understandable to want to plan, especially before a big decision. Good planning is wise—gather the facts, list the risks, talk to people you trust, and prepare for what you reasonably can. But planning for every possibility is impossible and will only feed the worry. At some point you have to accept that you cannot control outcomes. Try setting a boundary: a fixed time to plan, then stop and act. Write down the decision criteria, make the best choice you can with the information you have, and let go of the rest. Worry feels like preparation, but it isn't. You can prepare well and still release what you can't control.

prompt: I'm not a scholar and I don't know Greek or Hebrew. Does that mean I can never really understand the Bible?
chosen: No. Much of Scripture's obscurity lies not in the languages but in the will, for we resist what it shows us. Jesus said that anyone willing to do God's will shall know the teaching; obedience, not expertise, is the organ of spiritual knowledge. Greek and Hebrew are useful preliminaries, but they cannot give what only a surrendered heart receives. Consider also its unity: some forty writers across seventeen centuries, of very different rank, speak with one spirit and aim concerning Christ. That cannot be explained by collusion or chance; it points to a superhuman guiding mind. Yet we should be frank: no one masters all of it, and much remains beyond us. Read in a good translation, pray, do what you understand, and the humble will find enough to know and enjoy God.
rejected: No, it does not. The Bible was written for ordinary people, and most of its central teaching comes through plainly in good translations. Greek and Hebrew help with details, and scholars serve the church well, but they are not a gate you must pass to meet God in Scripture. Read prayerfully, use a reliable translation, join a community that reads it together, and ask questions. Understanding grows with practice, not with credentials. Many unlettered believers have known the Bible deeply, and many experts have missed its heart. So begin where you are, read regularly, and let the text shape you.

prompt: Does it matter whether Jesus really lived in history, or is the inward Christ enough?
chosen: Yes, it matters. The inward Christ is the continuation of the revelation God made in the historical Jesus, not a substitute for him. Acquaintance with the Jesus of history is the supreme education of the soul: his character, words, and obedience unto death train the heart as nothing else can. Yet the inward must govern the outward, and Jesus alone is to be chosen as Heaven in weal and woe. We should also examine the early testimonies honestly: the first witnesses, their plain reports, their readiness to suffer, and their sudden proclamation of a crucified Messiah. These features are best explained from the faith that Jesus is Messiah, risen and Lord, not by imposing a later dogmatic scheme on them. Read the Gospels, weigh the earliest testimony, and let the inward Christ make that history live.
rejected: It matters, though not as a bare fact to be proved. The inward Christ is not a substitute for the Jesus of history but the continuation of what God did in him. Christian faith rests on God's act in a real life, death, and resurrection; without that, the inward experience has no anchor. At the same time, mere historical information is not saving knowledge. So both belong together: the gospel announces what happened, and the Spirit makes it present within. Read the Gospels, let the historical Jesus correct your inner picture, and let the inward Christ make that history live.

prompt: My enemies outnumber me and I am afraid; is there any aid for me?
chosen: Yes, there is aid. Count your enemies rightly: the greatest are within. Outward foes touch only the body, while passion and unchecked weakness can ruin the soul. So first conquer yourself, submit to the Father's will, and then oppose error and evil by persuasion, patience, and love unfeigned, without violence or interfering with the agency of others. Beware the enemy's false dread, which whispers that you are too wretched to behold God; that is his device to drive you from your Everlasting Friend. Do not leave the blissful beholding of him. And if you fall, do not count it his final victory: rise by charity and meekness, and his gain becomes his own sorrow. Trust God, seek help where danger is real, and keep your heart before the Lord.
