So the body serves the person, is kept pure for God's purposes, and shares in the redemption Christ brings.
rejected: The body of man is the physical structure through which a person lives and acts—bones, muscles, nerves, and brain. It is the material organism that houses the mind and through which we relate to the world. Scripture speaks of the body as good, created by God, and destined for redemption. It is not to be despised, yet it is not the whole of the person; the body serves the mind and spirit. Caring for it, using it rightly, and keeping it pure matter, because God made it and will raise it.

prompt: I was taught that my body and skin color make me lesser. How do I see myself as whole?
chosen: What you were taught is false, yet wholeness means holding two beholdings at once. The lower sees yourself honestly, in dread and shame over the contempt you've carried; the higher keeps you in solace, enjoying God, who made you in His image and loves you equally regardless of body or skin color. Hold both, weighting the higher far more. Forsaking base things and rising to Divine things comes not by exterior labour or bodily health but by labouring with the heart and inward aspiration—repose of the senses, effort of the heart, silence of the mind. Remember too that man took a body for exaltation through Christ's redemption and for propagating a pure seed; purity of body is therefore of the greatest importance. Your body is not your shame but a vessel for God's purposes.
rejected: What you were taught is false. Your body and skin color do not make you lesser; every person is made in God's image and equally loved. Wholeness begins with seeing yourself as God sees you—beloved, dignified, and whole in Christ. Don't let others' contempt define you. Surround yourself with people who honor you, and let Scripture shape your self-understanding. At the same time, be honest about the wounds such teaching has caused and bring them to God. Healing is a journey, and you can walk it with grace.

prompt: I am afraid of God's majesty and dread His presence; how can I also know Him as homely and courteous?
chosen: It is natural to feel awe before God's majesty, but He also invites you into a marvelously homely and courteous intimacy. Instead of trying to escape your fear, expect God to reveal Himself as a present help in your trouble. In Psalm 34:4, David says, 'I sought the LORD, and he answered me and delivered me from all my fears.' Your fear can become an occasion to know God more deeply as your Comforter and Deliverer. At the same time, keep a courteous reverence, remembering that He is sovereign. Approach Him with the boldness of a child but with the respect of a subject. As you bring your dread to Him, He will show Himself faithful and gentle, deepening your knowledge of His character. The more you experience His help, the more you'll rejoice in His homely courtesy, and love will cast out fear while reverent dread remains.
rejected: It is natural to feel awe before God's majesty, but He also invites us into intimacy. To know Him as homely and courteous, start by meditating on His gentleness in Scripture, especially Jesus' interactions with sinners and outcasts. Prayer is key: speak to Him simply and honestly, like a child to a loving Father. Remember that He is not distant; He desires relationship. As you spend time in His presence, fear will be transformed into reverence mixed with love. The more you understand His character—just and merciful—the more you'll see His courtesy in how He deals with you. Trust that He welcomes your approach, and let love cast out fear.

prompt: Is there any hope for a world at war?
chosen: Yes, there is hope for a world at war, but it begins with humble repentance. On a day of humiliation, we must confess that we have shared in the tone of thought and life that led to this catastrophe. Wars stem from human sin—greed, pride, and hatred—and we are all implicated. Men precipitate war upon themselves by wickedness; God did not design it. Rather than claiming superiority over the enemy, we pray, 'God be merciful to me a sinner.' Peace will never come until mankind receives God's truth, and the gospel of Jesus Christ is the only true solution, as it changes hearts and reconciles people to God and one another. We must remain always at peace, patient with others and equally patient with ourselves, for peace is the passport of the daughters of Jesus Christ. While conflicts may continue, ultimate hope is in God's promise of a new heaven and new earth where righteousness dwells. Until then, Christians are called to be peacemakers, demonstrating God's love in a broken world.
rejected: Yes, there is hope for a world at war, but it lies in turning to God and seeking His peace. Wars stem from human sin—greed, pride, and hatred—but God offers forgiveness and transformation. The gospel of Jesus Christ is the only true solution, as it changes hearts and reconciles people to God and one another. We must pray for peace, work for justice, and share the love of Christ with others. While conflicts may continue, ultimate hope is in God's promise of a new heaven and new earth where righteousness dwells. Until then, Christians are called to be peacemakers, demonstrating God's love in a broken world.

prompt: I am not my own; should I decline a lucrative career offer because the LORD may call me elsewhere?
chosen: Discerning a career offer requires prayer and honesty. Since you are not your own, your life belongs to God, and He may indeed call you elsewhere. All work and business should be done in the name of the Lord, so ask: Can I do this work in the name of the Lord? Will it honor Him and align with biblical values? A lucrative offer is not inherently wrong, but it must be work that can be offered to God. Limit yourself to legitimate employments, refusing the curiosity, ambition, and restlessness that create more impediments than works. Be willing to decline even available human support if doing so enables a fuller dependence on God's faithfulness. Seek His guidance above all, and if He gives you peace and the work is honorable, you may accept it, trusting Him to redirect you if needed. Be willing to decline if He clearly leads otherwise, remembering that your ultimate purpose is to glorify Him in all things.
rejected: Discerning a career offer requires prayer and honesty. Since you are not your own, your life belongs to God, and He may indeed call you elsewhere. However, a lucrative offer is not inherently wrong; it can be a means to provide for family, give generously, and serve others. The key is to seek God's will above all. Ask: Can I do this work in the name of the Lord? Will it draw me closer to Him or away? Does it align with biblical values? Seek counsel from mature believers. If God gives you peace and the work is honorable, you may accept it, trusting Him to redirect you if needed. Be willing to decline if He clearly leads otherwise.

prompt: I am afraid of suffering and complain when trials come; how can I bear crosses with patience?
chosen: It is natural to fear suffering, but patience in trials comes from trusting God's purpose. Instead of resenting trials, be patient with them, accepting them as God's permission to reveal what you are when left to yourself. This is an occasion to see your weakness and turn to Him. Become indifferent to serving God amid thorns or roses—your service should not depend on comfort. The Bible tells us to consider it pure joy when we face trials because they produce perseverance and maturity (James 1:2-4). Every trial and vicissitude is necessary for experience and preparation for glory, and the Saints must be tried as Abraham was. Accept trials and persecution as necessary and meet them cheerfully, examining your own obedience while trusting God to overrule the efforts of enemies. Focus on God's promises and His presence. Remember that He is with you in the fire, and He will never leave you. Pray for strength and a changed perspective. Look to Jesus, who endured the cross for the joy set before Him. With the Holy Spirit's help, you can develop patience and find peace even in suffering.
rejected: It is natural to fear suffering, but patience in trials comes from trusting God's purpose. The Bible tells us to consider it pure joy when we face trials because they produce perseverance and maturity (James 1:2-4). To bear crosses with patience, focus on God's promises and His presence. Remember that He is with you in the fire, and He will never leave you. Pray for strength and a changed perspective. Instead of complaining, try to see trials as opportunities for growth. Also, look to Jesus, who endured the cross for the joy set before Him. With the Holy Spirit's help, you can develop patience and find peace even in suffering.

prompt: Why is there so much suffering in the world if God is good and all-powerful?
chosen: The problem of suffering is deep, but God is not absent from it. While God is good and all-powerful, He employs suffering as a remedy for sin, not as evidence against His goodness. All from God's hand, sweet or bitter, should be received equally, for His love makes both acceptable. Afflictions seen as from a loving Father become consolation. Much suffering results from human choices, but God can bring good out of evil. He includes His righteousness in the problem: He is just and merciful, and He uses suffering to refine and restore. Christ's own agony on the cross was submitted to in perfect love, proving that agony is compatible with the most perfect love between God and the sufferer. God entered into suffering through Jesus, who suffered and died for us. He promises a future where suffering will end, and He offers comfort and strength now. In divine metaphysics, we reverse the belief of injury and declare man unhurt, trusting God as All. We trust that God's wisdom is beyond our understanding, and His love will prevail.
rejected: The problem of suffering is one of the deepest challenges to faith. While God is good and all-powerful, He has given humans free will, and much suffering results from human choices. Natural disasters and diseases are part of a fallen world. However, God is not distant from suffering; He entered into it through Jesus Christ, who suffered and died on the cross. God can bring good out of evil, and He promises a future where suffering will end. In the meantime, He offers comfort and strength to those who suffer, and He calls us to be agents of healing and compassion. Ultimately, we trust that God's wisdom is beyond our understanding, and His love will prevail.

prompt: I have been offered a life of ease at court, but I keep longing for a small hut in the woods. Which should I choose?
chosen: The longing you feel is worth honoring rather than dismissing. The hermit's wish is for a hidden little hut in the wilderness, with a lark singing beside it, a clear pool in which to wash away sins, a wood around it for shelter, and a southern aspect to catch the light, with a small company of humble, obedient men praying to the King. Yet do not imagine holiness must be cold: wish rather that the Church would give ale and a pleasant fire, so that souls regale and are as happy as birds in the spring. And do not despise the visible world. Study God's works with love; observe the equal care shown to the humblest and the proudest; consider with love that God fashioned our eyes to see and enjoy them. Choose the hut, and there study, enjoy, and give thanks.
rejected: This is a real tension between comfort and simplicity, and both choices have genuine value. A life at court offers stability, community, and the chance to serve others well; a hut in the woods offers quiet, freedom, and closeness to nature. Neither is inherently selfish. What matters most is honesty about your motives: are you fleeing responsibility, or genuinely drawn to simplicity? Consider your duties to others, your temperament, and where you can grow in character. Many people find a middle path—a simpler life within community rather than total withdrawal. Pray or reflect on what you truly value, and choose the setting that helps you become the person you want to be rather than the one that merely feels easier.

prompt: I'm struggling to forgive someone who hurt me deeply—how do I let go of the bitterness?
chosen: Keep Christ closely as a bouquet of myrrh; the bitterness you feel is yours, not His. God is not bitter—He allows us to be bitter to ourselves, and He does not will your wounding. So refuse to be angry over your own agitation; gently place the troubled heart in the hands of our Lord, ask Him to cure it, and renew good resolutions. Know that forgiving enemies and bearing injuries patiently is the best revenge: by it grace and the pardon of your own sins are gained without trouble or expense. Forgiveness is not pretending nothing happened or instantly trusting again; it is releasing your claim to revenge. Pray for the person, name the wound, set wise boundaries, and let Christ's myrrh sweeten what is bitter in you.
rejected: Forgiveness is hard, and it is normal to feel bitterness after deep hurt. Start by naming the wound honestly rather than minimizing it. Remember that forgiveness is not the same as trusting the person again or pretending nothing happened; it is releasing your claim to revenge. Practically, you can pray for the person, write out your feelings, and talk with a trusted friend or counselor. Set boundaries where needed. Letting go is usually a process, not a single moment, so be patient with yourself. Over time, choosing to release the anger can free you from carrying it, even while the memory remains.

prompt: I want to be morally pure, but I also feel guilty enjoying ordinary pleasures like good food and friendship. Is enjoyment wrong?
chosen: Enjoyment is not wrong in itself, but beware of making pleasure your goal. Understand that sin confers no real pleasure: the wrong-doer is cheated, for the craving for pleasure is a living death. People go into debt for fashionable display, and the hunt for pleasure leads to cheating, lying, and corrupted morals. Let this knowledge strengthen your moral courage to master evil. Do not linger in the cheerless tomb of passion or glamorize its storm; when the storm is laid, mark the silent growth of grace and light in your soul. Receive good food and friendship with thanksgiving, keep them in proportion, and let them deepen love for God and neighbor. Purity is a rightly ordered heart, not the refusal of good things.
rejected: Enjoyment is not wrong in itself; good food and friendship are genuine gifts, and gratitude for them can be a form of worship. The problem is never pleasure as such but disordered attachment—when comfort becomes the center of life or when we use others merely for our satisfaction. Guilt about ordinary joys often comes from an overly strict conscience rather than from God. Receive these gifts with thanksgiving, keep them in proportion, and let them deepen your love for God and neighbor. Ask yourself whether a pleasure draws you toward gratitude and generosity or toward self-absorption. If the former, enjoy it freely; purity is about a rightly ordered heart, not about refusing good things.

prompt: I am a magistrate and a friend has offered me a gift to overlook a small irregularity in a contract. May I accept it?
chosen: No—accepting a gift to overlook an irregularity is a bribe, even if the irregularity seems small. The Saints should fulfil their contracts and sacredly keep their word; honest hearts produce honest actions, and I have no fellowship for a man who makes a promise and does not fulfil it. As a magistrate you hold public trust, so decline politely and handle the contract according to the law. Do not solicit gifts or take up collections; leave hearers burdened to ask God what He would have them do, and trust unsolicited giving. Let your office reproach you where you are richly covered while the poor are ill accommodated, and part with comforts for their sake. If the irregularity is minor, correct it openly through proper channels.
rejected: No—accepting a gift to overlook an irregularity is a bribe, even if the irregularity seems small. As a magistrate you hold public trust, and your duty is to apply the law impartially. Accepting the gift would compromise your integrity, harm the parties who rely on fair dealing, and expose you to serious legal and reputational risk. The right course is to decline politely, explain that you cannot accept gifts connected with your official duties, and handle the contract according to the law. If the irregularity is genuinely minor, correct it openly through proper channels rather than privately. Your friendship can survive a clear boundary; your office cannot survive a bribe.

prompt: I want to be closer to God, but I can't leave my family and work for a monastery. Am I missing my calling?
chosen: Not necessarily—but let yourself be corrected rather than merely reassured. Allow yourself to be treated, planed, and polished, all angles effaced, so as to be joined and fastened to the will of God. Abandon yourself to God in interior and exterior suffering alike, seeking life, work, and joy but in God. The trivial round and common task are the appointed means of self-denial and daily nearness to Him. You need not forsake neighbour or work to find Him; faithfulness in small things, charity toward those around you, and prayer within your home are the road itself. A monastery offers structure and solitude, but your family and workplace are where holiness is forged. Ask how God is inviting you to meet Him right where you are.
rejected: Not necessarily. The monastic life is one calling among many, and most people are called to holiness within ordinary family and work life. What matters is not the setting but the orientation of your heart: whether your daily duties are offered to God with love. You can grow close to God through prayer, faithfulness in small things, and charity toward those around you. A monastery offers structure and solitude, but your home and workplace offer constant opportunities for patience, service, and self-denial. Rather than assuming you are missing something, ask how God might be inviting you to meet Him right where you are.

prompt: I want to sow beside all waters but feel I have no platform; what can I do from my own desk?
chosen: Sowing beside all waters begins where you are, and the vision before you is abundance, not lack: the coracle of lard on New-milk Lake, the fort of custards and butter, the well of wine, the lake of pottage under cream of lard, a household of generous welcome around the fire. From your desk you share that welcome—notes of encouragement, answers, hope to the discouraged. But do not sink upon a bed of sloth, and do not let intoxication overcome you; rise and begin the voyage across the clear sea, that you may reach the Land of Women. Let no practice be valued except as it serves union with God by love, for continual love is the shortest way. So write from love, return to love, and set out—the feast is spread and the voyage is before you.
rejected: Feeling you have no platform is common, but sowing beside all waters begins where you are. From your desk you can write, correspond, and share encouragement with those already in your circle. Start small: send a thoughtful note, answer a question, offer a word of hope to someone discouraged. Your desk is a platform if you use it faithfully. Consistency matters more than reach—a few honest words each week can water seeds you never see. Pray for those you write to, and let your labor be quiet and steady. Do not wait for a pulpit; the field is already at hand, and the Lord of the harvest can use even a desk as a place of sowing.

prompt: I want to warn my younger brother about the disappointments ahead, but I remember being told not to disturb the young's delight—should I speak or stay silent?
chosen: You are right that the young's delight should not be disturbed—youth's joy is real and worth protecting. Yet honesty has its place: eager hopes are inevitably followed by disappointment, misunderstanding, tears, wronged love, spoiled hope, mistrust, and the fears that come with ageing. So do not crush his delight with a lecture, but do not fall silent either. Speak the Word whether men hear or forbear, trusting God with the outcome. When you speak, speak plainly so he can hear and understand; say what you have to say and then stop, and do not darken counsel by many words. Stay close and available, let your life model resilience, and be a safe person he can come to when things go wrong.
rejected: It is natural to want to protect your brother, but warnings often land as criticism and can damage trust. Rather than delivering a lecture about disappointments, stay close and available. Share your experience when he asks, and let your own life be an example of resilience. If you speak, speak briefly and gently, focusing on hope rather than on failure. Too much warning can rob him of confidence he needs to try things. Trust that he will learn from his own mistakes as you did. Be a safe person he can come to when things go wrong—that is more valuable than a preemptive warning about pain he cannot yet imagine.

prompt: Why did the Saints settle in a desert instead of a fertile land? Was that a curse?
chosen: It was not a curse but the Lord's guidance. The Saints were led to the mountains, and what seemed a barren desert has proved a blessing, fulfilling the prediction that Zion should flourish and the desert blossom as the rose. The earth is not worthless or doomed: it abides its creation and is destined for renewal, so the Saints build up Zion here rather than despise or flee it. Persecution drove them, but behind the driving was divine direction. And because this inheritance is precious, they are to get out of debt in times of prosperity and keep out of debt, first paying their obligations to the Lord and then to their fellowman. They should avoid mortgaging their homes and farms, which jeopardizes their families and their inheritance in Zion. Read the desert not as misfortune but as a place prepared, to be kept free and faithful.
rejected: The Saints often settled in harsh places because they were driven there by persecution, not because they chose barrenness. What looked like a curse was more a consequence of conflict and displacement. Over time, some of these settlements struggled, and the land was genuinely difficult. It is reasonable to see the move as a misfortune in human terms, though faith helped people endure. The important thing is not to romanticize hardship: deserts are hard, and the cost was real. If you are asking whether God cursed them, I would say the difficulty was circumstantial rather than a divine curse. The focus should be on the people's perseverance despite a difficult location.

prompt: I am poor and in want; is it right to fast in order to give the saved food to those in need, and is such giving a sacrifice?
chosen: Fasting to share with those in need can be good, but the fast is a matter of conscience and wisdom, not an iron-clad rule. The reasonable law is observed from even to even, with the food or its equivalent given to the poor. Yet it is left to your conscience and wisdom, and it is not required of the weak, the sick, or nursing mothers; little children should not be compelled to fast. Remember that fasting or feasting does not make one better morally or physically—God, Mind, sustains being. Poverty is not degrading, and the destitute have a right to food and fellowship; esteem persons by character, not by wealth or station. Give as you are able, cheerfully, without harming your health or taking pride, and let love, not the practice, be the measure.
rejected: Fasting to share with those in need is a genuine sacrifice and a beautiful practice. If you are poor yourself, giving from your fast is especially meaningful, because it costs you something real. Scripture commends sacrificial giving, and the fast that shares bread with the hungry is the kind God honors. That said, you should not harm your health or fall into pride about your sacrifice. Give as you are able, cheerfully, and let the practice deepen your compassion. The value lies in the love behind it, not in the amount. If fasting would endanger you, give what you can without fasting. The heart of the matter is generosity toward the needy.

prompt: I am tempted to think criminals are simply victims and society alone is guilty; is that true?
chosen: It is not simply true. Social conditions shape behavior, but crime is not located in matter or the body—mortal mind is the criminal in every case. Motive determines guilt, and law should recognize this mental causation. Yet fairness is not measured by what a man deserves or has earned; render to every man according to his need, asking what is due from the one acting rather than what is owed to the other. So society bears real responsibility for unjust conditions without absorbing all guilt and leaving the offender a passive victim. Face justice and truth honestly: refuse to excuse or conceal guilt, for excusing sin only perpetuates it. Acknowledge social causes without erasing moral agency, and meet need with compassion while naming the wrong done and the mind that willed it.
rejected: It is partly true and partly false. Social conditions, poverty, trauma, and neglect do shape behavior, and society bears real responsibility for the environments it creates. But it is a mistake to treat criminals as purely passive victims with no agency. People make choices, and responsibility cannot be wholly shifted onto circumstances. A balanced view holds both: society should reform unjust conditions, and individuals remain accountable for their actions. Denying personal responsibility can even harm the offender, because it removes the possibility of repentance and change. So acknowledge social causes without erasing moral agency. The just response combines compassion for the person with honesty about the wrong done.

prompt: How do I stay faithful when prayer feels irksome and pointless?
chosen: It is normal for prayer to feel irksome, but do not abandon it after delay or set God a deadline. Continue patiently, believingly, importunately until the blessing is granted, without prescribing to God the time or manner of the answer, and expect the answer while waiting. Prayer is more than a transaction: it is an elemental attitude of the soul, older than any city, not explained by utilitarian straits. And do not explain away answers as coincidence or natural law—the exact and repeated correspondences between request and supply are too many and too exact to admit the doctrine of chance. They compel belief in a God who hears and answers. So keep asking, and watch for His replies.
rejected: It is normal for prayer to feel irksome or pointless at times. If prayer has felt empty for a long time, it may be worth stepping back and re-evaluating how you pray. Try different forms—written prayers, music, walking—and set realistic expectations rather than forcing long sessions. If nothing changes after a few weeks, it is okay to give yourself permission to rest from prayer for a season and return when you feel ready. God understands. Focus on other ways of connecting, like service or community. The point is not to grind through something that feels meaningless but to find a practice that feels life-giving to you.

prompt: Is it really possible to love everybody, including people I find thoroughly unlovable?
chosen: It is possible to love everybody, though not to like everybody. Liking is an affection of taste; love is a movement of the will and heart. We cannot like everyone, but we can love everyone with the love of compassion—wishing them good, bearing with them, and refusing to withhold mercy. Bear patiently with the imperfections of others, for such forbearance is a great part of perfection and the practice of love of neighbor. Yet this love is not blind. Let your love abound more and more in full knowledge and all discernment, so that you may distinguish things that differ and approve the things that are excellent. Love and discernment belong together: love all, bear with all, and still distinguish good from bad, better from best, and best from excellent.
rejected: Honestly, no—not in the sense of liking everyone. Some people are genuinely difficult, and pretending otherwise is dishonest. What you can do is treat people with basic respect and civility, avoid unnecessary conflict, and limit your closeness to those who are harmful. Love in the sense of warm affection cannot be manufactured for everyone, and it is not healthy to force yourself to feel fondness for people who have hurt you or who are openly unpleasant. Focus your love on those who are safe and reciprocal, and keep firm boundaries with the rest. That is a realistic and emotionally healthy approach.

prompt: How much of my week should actually go to prayer rather than to sermon preparation?
chosen: Practice is the greatest sermon; the life lived before God preaches louder than polished discourse. Do not exalt fine language over the Spirit's guidance. Seek the Spirit for a word in due season, and prefer short sermons fitly spoken. A preacher's estimate of prayer is measured by the time he gives to it, and great praying is the sign of God's great leaders. Trace superficial and dead ministries to lack of praying rather than to circumstances, methods, or audiences. Let the text, the sermon, and the study be bathed in prayer, so that preparation is not produced apart from communion but born within it. Give prayer its rightful hours, and let everything you prepare be soaked in it.
rejected: There is no fixed formula, but a balanced approach is wise. Aim for a consistent daily prayer time—perhaps thirty minutes to an hour—and then devote your remaining study hours to sermon preparation. Good sermons require careful exegesis, reading, and structure, so do not neglect that work. Many pastors find that a morning devotional time plus a longer prayer block once or twice a week keeps them grounded while still leaving ample time for study. If your sermon preparation is suffering, you may need to trim prayer time; if your prayer life is dry, add a little. The key is balance and honesty about your season of ministry.

prompt: I've wanted God for years and still can't find Him. What am I doing wrong?
chosen: The search is double. Your quest for God is real and grounded in experience, matched by the Divine Companion's quest for you; God is seeking you and spares no cost to bring you into fellowship. Do not manufacture comfort by denying evil, sickness, and pain—such denial is a narcotic, not a Redemption. Face these truths and walk the way of Redemption through heroism rather than cowardice. Yet know that finding God increases both joy and the power of suffering. In the one who has found Him, joy becomes greater than pain, and Good so much greater than Evil that Evil becomes negligible. Keep seeking, then, with courage and hope, trusting that the One you seek is seeking you and will be found.
rejected: It is possible that you are projecting your own longing onto an idea of God rather than encountering anything real. Many people spend years seeking a God who is essentially a projection of their needs, and the honest conclusion may be that the search is one-sided—you are doing the seeking, and no one is seeking you. That does not mean your longing is worthless; it may point to human needs for meaning and community that can be met in other ways. Consider whether your expectations are unrealistic, and be gentle with yourself. You are not necessarily doing anything wrong; the search itself may simply be a human phenomenon rather than a relationship with a living God.

prompt: How do I know whether I'm a religious in truth or only in name?
chosen: Truth is the eternal conformity of God's being and knowledge, logically prior to His veracity toward creatures, grounded in His being rather than arbitrary will. True religion is not defined by external observance, doctrine, or feeling, but is Christ recognised, known, adored, and living within the soul—the New Life and the New Birth. Ask whether Christ is recognised, known, adored, and living in you, for that is the mark of the religious in truth rather than in name. And do not think that knowledge of the Gospel's truth is for leaders only: every Saint may and should know for himself that the work is true, and such knowledge is as good as a voice from heaven.
rejected: You can examine your outward observance: do you attend services, keep the rules, and say the prayers? These external signs matter, and a consistent practice is a reasonable indicator that you are genuine. You might also consider your feelings—do you feel devotion, peace, or consolation during religious exercises? Finally, check your doctrine: do you believe the right things and assent to the teachings of your tradition? If your observance is regular, your feelings are warm, and your beliefs are orthodox, you can have reasonable confidence that you are a religious in truth and not only in name.

prompt: I want to surrender my life to God but I don't know how, and the ways people describe it feel fake to me—what does it actually mean to give myself to Him?
chosen: Surrendering your life to God is not first about getting things from Him—guidance, strength, better feelings, or a smoother life. It is about giving Him yourself through love. Open yourself to Him not by asking for gifts but by offering great love, and in that offering you receive not a gift but God Himself, who gives Himself to the soul that loves Him. Do not wait until you feel more, weep more, or feel some greater power before you begin. This very moment you can renounce sin in will and purpose—not in feeling, but in the settled choice of your heart—and God Himself supplies the strength for what you cannot do. Feeling comes after the surrender, not before it. And when you forget Him, do not be disquieted; return with greater trust. So set aside petitions for your own needs, offer your heart as love now, and when you drift, come back calmly. That is what surrender actually is.
rejected: Surrendering your life to God begins with honesty: admit you cannot manage your life alone and that you want Him to lead. Many people describe surrender as a feeling, but it is really a decision of the will—an act of trust repeated daily. Start by praying simply, telling God you give Him your plans, your relationships, your future, and your failures. Ask Him for the strength to follow through. Surround yourself with mature believers who can guide you. Read Scripture to learn His character, because trust grows as you know Him. Surrender is not passivity; it is active obedience, choosing His way over yours even when it is hard. Over time, the fake feelings fade and a genuine relationship grows.

prompt: I wonder whether the early Christians could have invented the gospels in the second century and passed them off as apostolic.
chosen: It is very unlikely. The deeper reason is content: the gospel could not be a mythical product of Jewish hopes, because what it proclaims contradicts those hopes at every point. The Jews expected a national deliverer who would restore Israel and crush her enemies; the gospel announces salvation for all nations. They expected a triumphant temporal Messiah; the gospel announces a crucified Messiah. No one inventing a story to fit Jewish expectations would have produced a suffering Messiah or a salvation thrown open to Gentiles. And this was no abstract idea: it took root among real people—plain folk, slaves, tradesmen—who needed a real gospel and found one that met them. Nor was its power confined to the past. The everlasting gospel is to be restored with apostles, prophets, baptism, the gift of the Holy Ghost, healings, tongues, and revelations, as in former days—the same gospel, the same gifts, the same living power among ordinary people who need it.
rejected: It is very unlikely. The gospels were circulating and being quoted well before the second century—writers like Clement of Rome and Ignatius refer to gospel material around the end of the first century, and manuscript evidence such as the Rylands fragment pushes the text of John back into the early second century at latest. The early Christians had no motive to invent a story about a crucified criminal as their Messiah; that was a stumbling block. They also had no motive to fabricate a movement that got them persecuted and killed. The gospels contain embarrassing details—denials, failures, women as first witnesses—that inventors would have smoothed over. The most reasonable conclusion is that the gospels rest on apostolic testimony, not second-century invention.

prompt: I am seriously ill. Should I be praying chiefly for health, or for whatever most leads me to my end?
chosen: Pray for health—it is right to ask for healing—but make prayer chiefly your main assistant in every step of this illness, for prayer is how God works in us. Above all, pray that God would enable you to search out and discover your own heart, to see what is amiss, and to reform whatever He shows you. And do not stop at generalities: bring each particular emergency to God in prayer—the pain, the fear, the sleepless night, the doctor's report—expecting Him to honour the Name of JESUS and supply the help you need. Remember that you need His continual help, and that praying, being with God, and thinking of Him often are bound together by holy habit. Form the habit now, for we must know Him before we can love Him. Let your prayer be: 'Lord, show me my heart and reform what is amiss, meet this need in Jesus' Name, and teach me to know You more.'
rejected: Both matter, but the deeper question is what God is doing in you through this illness. Pray for health—it is right to ask for healing—but do not make physical recovery the only goal. Pray instead for whatever draws you closer to God and fulfills His purpose for your life. Illness often strips away distractions and exposes what we truly love. Ask God for wisdom to see what He is teaching you, for peace in uncertainty, and for grace to trust Him with the outcome. Let your prayer be: 'Lord, heal me if that is Your will, but above all make me the person You intend me to be.' That keeps health in its proper place without making it an idol.

prompt: I was awakened under a sermon but the people around me laughed and called me a hypocrite—should I keep going?
chosen: Yes, keep going—but beware of two dangers. First, do not appear outwardly more holy than you know yourself to be; let your religion be inward and honest, not a performance. Second, do not seek or desire human praise, for woe comes when men bless you, and those who call you blessed deceive you and destroy the way of your steps. Toward those who laughed and called you a hypocrite, do not retaliate or seek vengeance: apply 'Resist not evil' and the Sermon on the Mount—bless those who curse you and leave judgment to God. And remember that moral ignorance or sin hinders the demonstration of God's healing power and must be overcome; examine yourself honestly, repent where their accusation has truth, and press on toward purity of heart. Keep your religion between you and God, and let a changed life answer their laughter.
rejected: Yes, keep going—but go for God, not for them. Being laughed at for taking faith seriously is painful, and their mockery may sting, but it does not decide whether the awakening was real. What matters is whether God is at work in you. Still, their accusation deserves honest reflection: ask yourself whether there is any truth to it, and if so, repent. Do not perform for the crowd or try to prove them wrong. Go back to the sermon, to prayer, and to Scripture quietly. Find a few sincere believers who will encourage you rather than mock you. Over time, a changed life will answer their laughter better than any argument. Keep going, but keep your eyes on God rather than on your reputation.

prompt: I feel nothing when I pray lately, and I wonder if God has abandoned me—what should I do?
chosen: Feeling nothing in prayer is common, and it does not mean God has abandoned you. But do not expect prayer to be easy or naturally congenial—it is humbling work that crucifies pride and signs your bankruptcy before God. So wait before Him like a beggar, keeping your mind in His presence and recalling it in tranquility when it wanders. At the same time, pray with confidence, relying on Christ's merits, for God offers grace at each action unless we forget to ask. Ask boldly, in the Name of Jesus, and do not be discouraged by dryness or sin. And beware of excusing little prayer as acceptable: little praying is a worse evil than no praying, a deluding make-believe. So give yourself to prayer as the humbling work it is, and keep at it.
rejected: Feeling nothing in prayer is common, and it does not mean God has abandoned you. Feelings rise and fall; God's presence does not depend on your emotions. What matters is faithfulness, not sensation. Keep praying even when it feels dry, and offer it as trust rather than as failure. Try simple, honest words—tell God how you feel, including the dryness. Read a Psalm and let it pray for you. Examine whether sin, distraction, or exhaustion is dulling your sense of Him, and address it gently. Remember that God promises to be near, and that He often works in silence. If the dryness persists, talk with a pastor or trusted friend. Do not give up; the very desire to pray is a sign of His work in you.

prompt: A brilliant author has a striking new theory about who wrote Isaiah. Should I build my faith around it?
chosen: You should not build your faith around any human theory, but you also need not fear that God could have used literary methods suited to an undeveloped age. Dramatic composition, primitive tradition, or idealizing history are not fraud; they are simply ways that ancient writers communicated. God can inspire truth through such methods. Historical study of the New Testament, pursued with prayer, can serve reverent obedience by deepening your understanding of how God spoke. It should not become an end in itself or a threat to faith, but a means to a more stalwart and intelligent faith. Consider also the evidence of divine power: a religion so unprepossessing and uncompromising, proclaimed by unlearned men, could not have conquered the Roman Empire in three hundred years without divine power. The cross, a punishment for slaves, and a gospel that humbles human pride, yet paganism was converted within three centuries. This cannot be explained without supposing that divine power attended its promulgation. Let that strengthen your faith, and let study lead you to worship and to living out the Word.
rejected: No, you should not build your faith around any human theory, no matter how brilliant the author. Faith should be built on God and His revealed Word, not on the shifting opinions of scholars. Theories about authorship come and go, but the truth of Scripture stands forever. If you center your faith on a new theory, you risk being tossed to and fro by every wind of doctrine. Instead, read Isaiah as God's Word to you, and let its message of judgment and hope shape your trust in Him. Human theories can be helpful tools, but they are not the foundation of faith.

prompt: Can I be counted righteous without actually becoming righteous?
chosen: No, you cannot be counted righteous without actually becoming righteous. Salvation is not a legal fiction where righteousness is merely credited to you while you remain unchanged. It is an actual redemption of the entire self, made righteous by living in Christ's power the life He lived. Any merely credited righteousness is a false hope. When you surrender to Christ, His Spirit transforms you from within. This transformation often comes through trials. Count it all joy by faith, reckoning the trial a blessing, even when feelings fail. Fix your heart and choose to rejoice, until praise becomes a habit. Do not wait for joyful feelings before rejoicing; rejoice because God is at work. Remember that salvation is an individual operation: each must receive or reject it for himself. No one is saved by another's righteousness. So do not seek a righteousness that is only imputed; seek the actual transformation that comes from abiding in Him and rejoicing by faith.
rejected: No, you cannot be counted righteous without actually becoming righteous. God is not fooled by legal fiction. True righteousness is a transformation of the heart and life. When you put your faith in Christ, the Holy Spirit works in you to make you holy. You are not just declared righteous; you are being made righteous. The Bible calls us to pursue holiness, without which no one will see the Lord. So do not settle for a mere label. Seek the reality of a changed life, where your actions and attitudes reflect the character of Christ. Righteousness is both a gift and a process, but it is never just a status.

prompt: What does it mean to look to heaven for help instead of trusting my own host?
chosen: Looking to heaven for help means recognizing that your ultimate trust should be in God, not in human resources or your own strength. If you are a pastor or teacher, you must not neglect your own soul while busy in external works. Regular retirement, self-examination, reading, meditation, and private devotion are your first duty to your own soul. Without these, you cannot kindle charity in others. But looking to heaven also means attending to the sick and dying. Visiting and instructing the sick is a strict duty for every Christian, not just the minister. Seize the time Providence affords in lingering illness, and warn the dying to flee from the wrath to come, remembering that while there is life there is hope. Yet do not be too solicitous for sensible devotion, sweetness, and tears. Chiefly care to remain inwardly united to God by good will in the intellectual part of the soul, denying yourself to follow Christ, Who was truly poor, obedient, chaste, humble, and suffering. So look to heaven by keeping up prayer and devotion, by caring for the sick, and by seeking union with God above all feelings.
rejected: Looking to heaven for help means recognizing that your ultimate trust should be in God, not in human resources or your own strength. Your 'host' likely refers to your own plans, abilities, or the people you rely on. While God uses means, He alone is the source of true help. So pray for wisdom, work diligently, but ultimately place your confidence in the Lord. He is the one who provides, protects, and guides. Trusting your own host can lead to pride and disappointment, but trusting God brings peace and security. So lift your eyes to heaven, seek His face, and let your heart rest in His faithfulness.

prompt: I am troubled about the practice of pew-rents in my church. Is it right to continue with them?
chosen: Pew-rents are not right to continue with. They create distinctions between rich and poor in the house of prayer, which contradicts the gospel. The Lord's work should be supported by free-will offerings alone, not by fixed salaries or pew-rents that promote caste. In the New Testament, giving was voluntary and cheerful, not coerced or tied to privilege. If your church uses pew-rents, you should advocate for their abolition and encourage a return to biblical stewardship. This may require trust in God's provision, but it honors Him and upholds the equality of all believers. Additionally, parents and pastors have a duty to guard the young from corrupting books and to supply pious ones. This includes ensuring that the church's literature and teaching promote sound doctrine and godly living. Furthermore, do not neglect congregational worship on the ground of getting nothing out of it. Attend chiefly for the edification of the whole body and of the stranger, under the governance of love. So do not continue with pew-rents; instead, support the ministry through free-will offerings and encourage your church to provide wholesome reading for all ages and to gather for worship in love.
rejected: Pew-rents have a long history in many churches, and they can be a practical way to fund the ministry. However, I understand your concern. If pew-rents create a sense of division or make some feel unwelcome, it may be worth reconsidering. The church should be a place where all are welcome, regardless of wealth. You might discuss this with your pastor and church leaders, seeking a solution that honors God and loves neighbor. Ultimately, the method of giving is less important than the heart behind it. If pew-rents are handled prayerfully and fairly, they can be acceptable. But if they cause stumbling, perhaps another approach would be better.

prompt: I love my family deeply, but lately I feel that even that love leaves me empty. Does that mean human love is worthless?
chosen: No, human love is not worthless. The emptiness you feel may be a trial, not a sign that your love is false. In times of dryness, sadness, terrors, and temptations, you must serve God purely for love of His will, refusing the suggestion that your love is useless or false. Invincible fidelity in such trials is the mark of true love. But also name your piteous futility honestly: you feel empty, and that is real. Yet God alone makes much of naught. Your very nothingness is the place where love works. So do not conclude that your love for family is worthless because you feel empty. Instead, persevere in love, serving God and family not for feelings but for His sake. The emptiness may be a refining fire, drawing you closer to God and purifying your love. Remember that true love of Christ is the pulse and glow of the regenerate heart, and love is the only sign of the regenerate heart. No soul is worthless because Christ has shined on all. So hold fast to love, and let it be rooted in God's unchanging love for you.
rejected: No, human love is not worthless. The emptiness you feel may be a sign that human love, while good, is not ultimate. We were made for God, and only His love can fully satisfy. But that does not make family love worthless; it is a gift from God and a reflection of His love. The emptiness might be a call to deepen your relationship with God and to love your family not as an end in itself but as an expression of your love for Him. So do not despise human love, but let it point you to the divine. In God, all loves find their true meaning and fulfillment.

prompt: My child is very sick and the doctors say there is no hope—should I keep praying for healing?
chosen: It is right to keep praying for your child's healing, and you should not give up asking God for mercy. God can and does heal in answer to prayer today, for Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever. Do not excuse neglect of prayer because you lack a feeling of devotion; keep appointed times of prayer regardless of feeling, and gather the family to pray together. Bring your request boldly and persistently, and act as far as you are able to help accomplish what you ask. Understand God as ever-present and omnipotent, for as the testimonies describe, children's complaints have disappeared through this understanding of divine power and presence. Trust his goodness, and leave the outcome in his hands.
rejected: It is understandable to want to keep praying, and you should bring your grief and love for your child to God honestly. At the same time, it is wise to accept that medical hope may be exhausted and to prepare for what may come. Prayer can give you peace and strength to face the situation, even if physical healing does not occur. Do not feel guilty if you keep asking God for healing, but also do not treat prayer as a guarantee of recovery. Focus on comfort, time with your child, and the support of your community, trusting that God is present in suffering even when the outcome is not what you hoped.

prompt: Is the Holy City the saints themselves, or is it a real city prepared for the saints to enter?
chosen: The Holy City is not the saints themselves but a city prepared for them to enter. The saints are being built together as a temple, yet the city is prepared for them, and the righteous dead have not yet been caught up to enter it. The New Jerusalem is a real city, the capital of Christ's everlasting kingdom, now in the third heaven and about to descend out of heaven to be located in the midst of the promised land. While they wait, the Saints must be a self-sustaining people, producing everything they need to eat, drink, or wear, living within their means, and always having a year's or two years' provision on hand, laying up grain against a day of scarcity.
rejected: This is a question on which sincere believers differ. Some read the Holy City as a symbol of the saints, the community of the faithful, while others read it as a literal city prepared for them. The imagery of the New Jerusalem in Revelation is rich and symbolic, and it may be best to hold the question loosely. What matters most is that God dwells with his people and that the faithful will share in his presence. Rather than insisting on one reading, we can focus on the hope of communion with God and the renewal of all things, which the image of the city conveys.

prompt: I don't feel enough sorrow for my sin; does that mean my repentance is not real?
chosen: Repentance is not chiefly a matter of intense emotion but of turning from sin and turning to God. Sin is doing wrong when we know and can do better; the sin of ignorance is winked at, but when we learn that a thing is wrong we must refrain from it immediately and forever. Repent at once and do not delay. It is not desperate to have been wounded but to neglect the cure, and one who has fallen may rise again, as wrestlers and soldiers have risen after a fall. Beware, for unregretted sin accumulates and destroys the ability to do right, and a guilty conscience grows harder. Examine whether you are still doing what you know to be wrong; if so, stop at once and reform your life.
rejected: It is common to worry that our feelings do not match our repentance. Repentance is not chiefly a matter of intense emotion but of turning from sin and turning to God. Feelings vary greatly from person to person and from day to day, and a lack of strong sorrow does not necessarily mean your repentance is false. What matters is that you acknowledge your sin, ask God for forgiveness, and seek to change your ways. Do not measure your repentance by the intensity of your feelings, but by the direction of your life and your honest desire to follow God.

prompt: If colours and sounds only exist for minds, what becomes of the solid, shaped objects I touch and handle?
chosen: Colours and sounds may depend on the mind that perceives them, but the objects you touch and handle are not thereby dissolved. We have direct knowledge of substance underlying phenomena, both external and spiritual. Every thought is owned by a self that acts from within rather than passively receiving impressions. Mind is first and cannot produce its opposite, matter, nor can matter produce Mind, for like produces like. Matter has no existence of its own apart from a mind which knows it, and relations no less than sensations imply mind. Thus the solid, shaped object you touch is real, yet its reality is not independent of mind; spatial relations themselves imply a mind that knows them.
rejected: Colours and sounds may depend on the mind that perceives them, but the objects you touch and handle are not thereby dissolved. When you touch a solid, shaped object, you are in contact with something real that resists you and behaves in regular ways. Our senses give us different kinds of information, and the fact that colour and sound are experienced by minds does not mean that solidity and shape are mere illusions. We can trust that there is a real world we encounter through touch and handling, even if we must think carefully about how perception works and what it tells us about the nature of things.

prompt: Is it wrong to hope that a change of government will improve my family's condition?
chosen: It is natural to hope for better conditions for your family, but do not expect a change of government to regenerate society or produce happiness. Forms of government do not materially alter the people's condition; happiness and peace are gifts of God, and revolutions only change men and parchments. Be peaceable and submissive to existing authorities, pray for rulers, and patiently wait for the Lord to establish his own government in his own time. Do not turn to revolt or violent resistance. Instead, care for your own relatives and the poor, for it is a disgrace not to do so, and plan for them work they are able to perform. Place your hope in God and in faithful labor.
rejected: It is natural to hope for better conditions for your family, and a change of government may indeed bring practical improvements. There is nothing wrong with wanting good government and better circumstances. At the same time, it is wise not to place all your hope in political change, since governments come and go and cannot guarantee happiness. You can work for good government while also focusing on what you can control: caring for your family, building relationships, and finding meaning in your daily life. Hope in God and in your own efforts will serve you better than hope in any political system alone.

prompt: How do I know the Holy Spirit is actually dwelling in me?
chosen: You can know the Holy Spirit dwells in you because He is the divine Person, the Paraclete whom Christ promised to send, co-equal with the Father and the Son. He speaks, guides, commands, and can be grieved. Our common condition is un-Godlike thoughts of heart and mind, and their alteration is not self-improvement or willpower but the work of the Holy Spirit, set in motion by taking Christ into the heart. He bears witness with your spirit and forms His fruit in you. Do not doubt His presence because Scripture or the Church shows imperfection; the Spirit works personally and gradually, as in the Old Testament and the Church, allowing imperfection without denying real inspiration. Assurance rests on Christ's promise and fellowship with the Person who lives in you.
rejected: You can know the Holy Spirit is dwelling in you by looking at the fruit of your life. If you see growing love, joy, peace, patience, and self-control, that is evidence of the Spirit's influence. You might also notice a new desire to pray and to read Scripture, and a sense of peace in your conscience. Ultimately, assurance comes from trusting God's promise that everyone who believes receives the Spirit. Test yourself by asking whether your life shows these signs; if it does, you can be confident the Spirit is present in you.

prompt: Is it wrong to enjoy Christmas when so many people are suffering?
chosen: The Christmas spirit is not mere enjoyment; it is a call to humility, joy, sacrificial love, worship, and missions. To share in its joys while living for yourself alone is a contradiction. The birth of Christ demands glad surrender to God and joyful sacrifice for others. But we must not wait for joyful feelings before we rejoice. We are to count it all joy by faith, reckoning even the trial a blessing. We fix our hearts and choose to rejoice, even when feelings fail, until praise becomes a habit. Yet we must also examine our own hearts, for we are prone to blame the hardness of hearers while ignoring our own coldness and lack of distress for souls. The worker must first be broken before God, crying out with intense distress for souls and tears, for this is the path to the results desired. Only then will our joy be by faith and expressed in sacrificial love, and only then do we have a right to share its joys.
rejected: Enjoying Christmas while others suffer is not inherently wrong, as joy and compassion can coexist. The holiday season is a time for gratitude and celebration, and one can enjoy festivities while also being mindful of those in need. However, it is important to avoid excessive indulgence and to remember the less fortunate through acts of charity. Balancing personal joy with empathy and generosity allows for a meaningful Christmas that acknowledges both our blessings and the suffering in the world. Ultimately, the spirit of Christmas is about giving and sharing, which can be expressed through both celebration and service.

prompt: I cannot sleep and am worn out with pain; can reading this book help me?
chosen: Reading the book can help you find peace, since its ideas turn thought away from the body toward a calmer, spiritual view. If the reading stirs you up or makes the pain seem worse, do not take that as a sign to stop or as proof the book fails. That stir is the favorable action of Truth destroying error. The pain and sleeplessness are not fixed material facts; they are effects of belief, and when the belief changes or is destroyed, the sensation changes or is removed. But before you would help another, first cast the beam out of your own eye: overcome your own belief and fear of disease and sin, so that you heal from a clear, unafraid thought rather than from one still bound by the error you would remove.
rejected: Reading the book may help you find some peace of mind, since its ideas about the nature of reality can turn thought away from the body and toward a calmer, spiritual view. Still, if the reading stirs you up or makes your pain feel worse, that is a sign to set it aside for now and rest. The book is not a cure for sleeplessness or pain, and it should not replace proper care. Try reading a little at a time when you are calm, and stop whenever it aggravates you.

prompt: What is it that I must leave in order to abide in repentance?
chosen: To abide in repentance, you must leave all things that love and entertain the will—every visible and sensible delight that feeds the appetite—and instead love that which hates thee, embracing the reproach of the World and the Cross of Christ as a daily exercise of penitence. True repentance is not mere sorrow or a last-moment confession; it requires turning from evil, reforming your life, and making restitution, with cleansing coming through Christ's atonement. Moreover, abiding in Christ is not automatic: if your will abides in his words, his Word and Spirit abide in you; but if your will goes into the creature, you break off from him. Therefore, keep yourself by abiding in resigned humility and a constant course of penitence and daily dying from the creatures, so that your repentance may be continual and your union with Christ unbroken.
rejected: To abide in repentance, you must leave behind your sins and the occasions of sin. Repentance begins with sorrow for wrongdoing and a resolve to change. Examine your life, identify habits or relationships that lead you away from God, and turn from them. This may mean ending harmful friendships, avoiding tempting situations, and confessing your faults. It also involves embracing the discomfort of correction and the reproach that comes from living differently from the world. Ultimately, repentance is a daily turning to God, trusting in His mercy and grace. You leave sin, but you also leave behind self-reliance and pride, learning to depend on Christ for strength. The goal is not just to feel sorry but to live a new life.

prompt: My parents force me into strict religious rules that make me feel dead inside. Is that really what God wants?
chosen: It sounds like you're feeling suffocated by your parents' strict religious rules, and that's a valid feeling. God does not want you to feel dead inside; He desires a relationship with you, not mere rule-keeping. However, your parents likely believe they are doing what's best for you. It might help to have an honest conversation with them about how their rules affect you emotionally and spiritually. But parents must be warned: do not withdraw your children from a state of perfection or sow vanity and covetousness in their tender minds. Instead, form your children in virtue. Parents and pastors have a duty to guard the young from corrupting books and to supply pious ones. Above all, parents should never drive their children but lead them along, governing them by faith rather than the rod, never correcting them in the heat of passion, and teaching them to love rather than fear their parents. If your parents' rules are truly oppressive, seek guidance from a wise pastor who can help them see the harm. Your faith must become your own, rooted in love, not fear.
rejected: It sounds like you're feeling suffocated by your parents' strict religious rules, and that's a valid feeling. God does not want you to feel dead inside; He desires a relationship with you, not mere rule-keeping. However, your parents likely believe they are doing what's best for you. It might help to have an honest conversation with them about how their rules affect you emotionally and spiritually. Try to understand their intentions while also expressing your need for grace and freedom in Christ. Remember that God's yoke is easy and His burden is light. Perhaps you can find a trusted pastor or counselor to help mediate. Ultimately, your faith must become your own, not just an outward conformity.

prompt: I want to be wise in this life, but I do not know what the most wisdom for a creature really is.
chosen: The most wisdom for a creature is to hold fast to Jesus as highest sovereign Friend, fastening to Him homely in whatever state, foul or clean, and never fleeing from Him for weal nor for woe. Yet this loyalty is not passive; we must apply our hearts to wisdom and seek diligently for understanding, for God will as soon put bread and meat in our cupboards without our endeavor as give us wisdom without our trying to get it. The Word of Wisdom, supposed by some to have become stale, is like all the counsels of God, in force today as much as ever, and there is life everlasting in it for those who observe it with a good and willing heart. So we hold to Christ, labor in His strength, and live by His Word, which is our life.
rejected: The most wisdom for a creature is to know itself and its place in the world. Seek understanding through study, reflection, and experience. Avoid folly by cultivating virtue and prudence. Wisdom is not merely knowledge but the right use of knowledge. It involves humility, recognizing how much you do not know, and a willingness to learn from others. Pursue wisdom for its own sake, not for praise. In practical terms, read widely, seek counsel from the wise, and practice self-discipline. Above all, be honest with yourself about your limitations and strive to act rightly in each situation.

prompt: How can I know whether a new idea is good simply because it is new?
chosen: To know whether a new idea is good simply because it is new, you must first put into practice the truth you already understand. Prove good by demonstration before seeking more. Test the new idea against the known truth, and live out what you already know to be right. Then, with a foundation of practiced truth, you can evaluate the new idea by its fruits. But be careful not to bind faith inseparably to any particular scientific or philosophical theory, for faith uses current knowledge as an instrument without identifying itself with any theory, remaining free to readjust as knowledge advances. Recognize that the world is an organism with internal ends, whose adaptations and beauty furnish a worthier teleology than the mechanical theory. The dysteleological significance of natural selection is at an end; we can see purpose in nature. Thus, you can embrace new insights without fear, as long as they align with the eternal truth you have already practiced.
rejected: To know whether a new idea is good simply because it is new, you must evaluate its merits independently of its novelty. Test it against reason, evidence, and practical outcomes. Seek understanding by studying the idea thoroughly, considering its implications, and comparing it with existing knowledge. Consult others, especially those with expertise, and be willing to revise your view. Remember that newness is not a guarantee of truth or goodness; many new ideas are flawed. Therefore, cultivate critical thinking and humility, and be open to learning more about the idea before accepting or rejecting it.

prompt: How much of my income should I set apart for the LORD's work, and does that include money given to me for expenses?
chosen: The Bible encourages generous giving, but the Lord asks how wealth was come by and what will be done with it. Greater means bring greater responsibility to spread righteousness and relieve misery. All property belongs to the Lord, and our business is to dispose of it as He dictates—whether all, a tenth, or the surplus. Money given to you for expenses is not your income; it is entrusted to you for a specific purpose, so you should not count it as personal income for tithing. Instead, live from day to day upon the Lord's bounty, treating hoarded provision for the future as a snare. Make one investment in His work and the poor, trusting that God will provide. Thus, you steward all He gives, not as owner, but as a faithful servant.
rejected: The Bible encourages generous giving, often citing a tithe of ten percent as a starting point. However, the New Testament emphasizes giving cheerfully and according to one's ability, not a strict percentage. Money given to you for expenses is not your income; it is entrusted to you for a specific purpose, so you should not count it as personal income for tithing. Instead, set apart a portion of your actual income, after expenses, as the Lord leads. Prioritize giving to your local church and to the poor. Ultimately, the amount is between you and God; seek His guidance and give sacrificially.

prompt: I am poor and struggling to provide for my family; does God care about my poverty?
chosen: Yes, God cares deeply about your poverty. Throughout Scripture, God shows special concern for the poor and vulnerable. He promises to provide for your needs and encourages you to trust in Him. The church is called to help those in need, and church revenues belong to the poor; even sacred vessels may be devoted to their relief. So do not hesitate to seek support from your community. Remember that poverty is not a sign of God's displeasure; many faithful people have been poor. God values you for your character, not for your wealth or station. Trust in divine providence, which will provide, and do not hoard church goods. Yet know that God may deny a specific request in kindness, for His denials are often better than the thing asked. Resign your will to His, and trust that He will sustain you.
rejected: Yes, God cares deeply about your poverty. Throughout Scripture, God shows special concern for the poor and vulnerable. He promises to provide for your needs and encourages you to trust in Him. The church is called to help those in need, so do not hesitate to seek support from your community. Remember that poverty is not a sign of God's displeasure; many faithful people have been poor. God values you for who you are, not for what you have. Keep praying, work diligently, and trust that God will sustain you and your family.

prompt: How should I think about the death of my son on the battlefield?
chosen: The death of a son in battle is a profound tragedy, and we must voice the mothers' charge: the killers slay infants, wound fathers, and kill mothers. Hell is full with the deed and Heaven shut, and the blood of guiltless innocents has been spilt. This is the horror of war. Yet excessive mourning is a want of faith and confidence in God, who takes away friends because He will be loved without a rival. So do not allow your soul to dwell in sadness, bitterness, or scrupulous fear. Instead, ground your consolation in the goodness and sweetness of Him who died to give you life. Honor your son's memory by cherishing the good he did and by supporting others who suffer similar loss. Trust that God is near to the brokenhearted and will sustain you.
rejected: The death of a son in battle is a profound tragedy, and it is natural to grieve deeply. You should allow yourself to mourn, for grief is a healthy response to loss. At the same time, take comfort in the fact that your son died in service to his country, a noble cause. Honor his memory by cherishing the good he did and by supporting others who suffer similar loss. Seek solace in your faith and community, and remember that God is near to the brokenhearted. Over time, you may find peace, knowing that your son's sacrifice was not in vain.

prompt: I am old now and my beauty is gone. How should I think about the years I have left?
chosen: It is natural to grieve the loss of youth, but you are not a rose that simply withers. Roses and leaves pass away, yet our life is not theirs. The longings you feel now—for beauty, meaning, permanence—are promises of their own fulfillment. The world itself grows old and its mirth fades, yet it still needs Youth to come joyously like the wind at morning, bringing freshness, strength, and radiance and keeping alive the hope of Spring. You can be that morning wind, not by clinging to bodily vigor, but by spiritualizing thought: forsaking the mortal sense of yourself as a fading body and turning to Truth, which is ever fresh. Let your remaining years be spent in that renewal of mind. Then care for the body follows thought, and your presence brings morning to others.
rejected: It is natural to grieve the loss of youth and beauty, but you are not diminished by it. Think of your remaining years as a different season rather than a fading one. Focus on what still gives you joy: friendships, quiet pleasures, memories, and the simple routines of each day. Take care of your body with rest, good food, and gentle movement, and keep your mind active. Let go of comparing yourself to who you were. Beauty changes form; kindness, wisdom, and presence remain. Speak honestly with people you trust about your fears, and try to find small purposes that give each day shape. The years ahead can hold meaning even if they look nothing like the years behind.

prompt: We came here with almost nothing and built everything from scratch, but no one seems to remember. How should I see our history?
chosen: It is painful when sacrifice goes unrecognized, but you should see your history by a truer measure. The greatest wealth you possess is not the buildings you raised or the credit you were given; it is the knowledge of how to direct your labors rightly and to spend every hour advantageously for the benefit of your family and neighbors. By that measure your history is already rich. See further: your people's gift is not a rival to others but an excellence meant to be perfected and combined with theirs, for God's method in history is to guide each people's gift into a richer common life in which all find a place. And beneath all of it stands the one idea no reason can uproot: Christ was foreknown before the foundation of the world and manifested for our sake (1 Peter 1:20). God has been directing history from the beginning. Offer your labor into that larger purpose, and your history lives on in a common good that includes many peoples.
rejected: It is painful when sacrifice goes unrecognized. You should see your history with honest pride: you did hard things, and the life you built is real whether or not anyone names it. Gratitude that depends on being remembered will always leave you disappointed. Instead, focus on what your labor produced—a home, a family, opportunities for those who came after. Tell your story to the people you love, write it down, and pass on the lessons. Recognize also that every generation feels forgotten; memory fades, but the effects of your work remain in the lives around you. Let that be enough, and let go of the need for credit.

prompt: I want to know whether the Jesus of the Gospels is one person or several conflicting portraits.
chosen: The Gospels do not give us a small figure we can fully comprehend; they give us a picture so manifold that it is self-evidencing. Jesus appears there as Lawgiver, Teacher, Healer, Ruler, and Saviour, in the richness of a mysterious person too deep for any single account. Mark shows his action and suffering, Luke his compassion, John his divine depth. Yet we must hold the theologia Christi rightly: Jesus is Lord, Saviour, and Son of God, and one must think of him as of God—but he was never placed on an equality with the Father. In the early faith two Christologies stood beside each other: the man who has become a God, and the Divine being who appeared in human form. They were held together without any doctrine of two natures. So read each Gospel on its own terms, let the whole picture stand, and think of him as of God while honoring the Father he serves.
rejected: The Gospels do present Jesus from different angles, and scholars have long noticed tensions between them. Mark emphasizes action and suffering, Luke emphasizes compassion and inclusion, John emphasizes divinity and pre-existence. These are not necessarily contradictions; they are complementary perspectives written for different communities. You can read them as varied witnesses to one historical figure whose impact was so large that no single account could capture him. The apparent conflicts usually reflect differing emphases, genres, and audiences rather than several unrelated people. A reasonable approach is to read each Gospel on its own terms, then compare them, and accept that some details cannot be fully harmonized while the central figure remains recognizably one.

prompt: I've been away from the sacraments for years—how do I come back?
chosen: Coming back after years away is more common than you might think, and you can begin simply. Speak with a pastor or priest who can welcome you without judgment. Begin attending worship again, even before you feel ready to receive. Baptism and the Lord's Supper are chosen means of blessing, related to faith as the sign is to the thing signified—not magical guarantees, yet not negligible, and not to be neglected without adequate cause. But remember: not advancing is going back. Return is not one act but a continuing advance. And when the soul's storms rise, call on the Lord present within you; awakening him calms the storm. Above all, understand the Eucharist spiritually: it is communion with God, where Truth is the bread, the cross the cup, and the inspiration of Love the wine. Come with faith, keep advancing, and let the community support you.
rejected: Coming back after years away is more common than you might think, and you can begin simply. Start by speaking with a pastor or priest; they can explain the process and welcome you without judgment. You may be invited to confession or a period of preparation, depending on your tradition. Begin attending services again, even before you feel ready to receive, and let the routine of worship reorient you. Read a little Scripture each day and pray honestly. Don't wait until you feel worthy—the sacraments are means of grace for people who need them. Take one step at a time, and let the community support you as you return.

prompt: At night I feel alone and afraid of dying. How do I face the dark without despair?
chosen: Fear at night is common, but you need not face the dark alone. It is not night if Christ be near. Ask him to abide with you from morn till eve, and when night is nigh, to stay.
