Know that all evil of whatever kind happens by God's permission and ever for some good end; it could not be except He permitted it, and its form and measure are allowed by Him who can and will by His wisdom turn all to good. Therefore commit all things without fear to His Providence.
rejected: A guilty conscience is a gift if it leads you to God rather than to despair. First, name your sins honestly before God and, where possible, make amends to those you've harmed. Confess, receive absolution, and do penance. Remember that God's mercy is greater than your sin—Scripture says He is faithful to forgive. Don't wallow in shame; shame without hope paralyzes, but repentance turns you toward God. Replace rumination with gratitude for forgiveness, and let your past become a motive for compassion toward others. If guilt persists despite confession, it may be scrupulosity—speak with a pastor. Peace comes not from forgetting but from being forgiven.

prompt: I want to be honest, but I wonder whether truth is just whatever God decides to command—does that make truth arbitrary?
chosen: Truth is not arbitrary, because it is not first a decree but the eternal conformity of God's being and knowledge—what He knows and is, in perfect agreement, from everlasting. God's veracity toward creatures flows from that eternal truth, so His commands express truth grounded in His being and cannot be arbitrary. This is no speculation: truth is the foundation of religion and salvation, and our hope must rest wholly on it, not on error or partial guesses, for hope built on error collapses. Accept all truth from whatever source it comes—no one should refuse a fact because of who speaks it—yet insist that truth remain the foundation of religion, and that no organization, party, or authority rises above it. Let your honesty in word and deed flow from the God who is eternally true.
rejected: Truth isn't arbitrary, even though God is sovereign. When we say God is true, we mean He is faithful and keeps His promises—His word can be trusted. If truth were merely whatever God happened to command, it would be arbitrary, but Scripture presents God's truth as grounded in His unchanging character. God cannot lie; His commands flow from His good nature. So honesty matters because it reflects the God who is faithful. You can trust that moral truth isn't a random decree but an expression of who God eternally is. Live honestly because truth reflects God's own faithfulness toward us.

prompt: I have a chance at a position of honor. Should I want it?
chosen: Honor is not wrong in itself, but the heart must be ordered. Offer God all your liberty, memory, understanding, and will, holding nothing back, and desire only His love and grace as your chief good. Ask whether this position helps you keep in His presence and labor for His glory and the good of souls, or whether it feeds pride and pulls you from duty. A place of honor is worth wanting only as a means of serving God and neighbor. Honor the memory of the martyrs and prophets, and delight to honor the instrument God used in the mighty work of the restoration. Let gratitude, humility, devotion, liberality, and honesty shape you: give freely, speak and act consistently and sincerely, and hold the opportunity loosely, ready to accept or decline as best serves His glory and the good of souls.
rejected: Honor isn't wrong in itself, but the desire for it can be dangerous. Ask yourself why you want it: is it for influence, security, recognition, or service? A position of honor brings responsibility, not just status. If you can use it to serve others and glorify God, it may be good to accept. But if it feeds pride or pulls you from your duties, decline. Seek counsel from wise friends, pray for humility, and hold the opportunity loosely. Wanting honor is fine if your motive is service; wanting it for its own sake will leave you empty.

prompt: I am a minister and fear the frown of wealthy parishioners more than I should—how should I reprove sin among them?
chosen: Fear of wealthy parishioners is understandable but dangerous. The message you carry is God's, and obedience is owed to it regardless of the preacher's example or weakness; the misconduct of preachers does not excuse hearers from obeying a message that comes from God. Reprove sin clearly, gently, and privately where possible, with humility about your own failings. As an officer of the Church, judge justly and promptly by the Spirit, without partiality or favor-buying, and care for every member of the Ward—especially the poor and sick. Be an example without corruption. Above all, refuse the holy table to notorious sinners: Christ will demand an account of His blood if it is given to the unworthy, and the priest's power in this is above an emperor's. So do not admit unrepentant sinners for fear of the wealthy; preach the whole counsel of God and trust His message.
rejected: Fear of wealthy parishioners is understandable but dangerous. Remember that your calling is to speak God's word faithfully, not to please people. Reprove sin clearly but gently, privately where possible, and with humility—recognizing your own failings. Preach the whole counsel of God, including hard texts, and trust that the message comes from God regardless of the messenger's weakness. Cultivate courage through prayer and brotherhood. If a wealthy member resists correction, don't compromise the gospel for their favor; seek support from your bishop or elders. Faithfulness matters more than approval.

prompt: I want to be a saint quickly, but I keep failing at the same sins—should I be discouraged?
chosen: Feeling discouraged after repeated falls is understandable, but the saints warn that virtue is only truly great when it is constant and crowned with perseverance. You must not presume that you will automatically persevere; rather, live in fear, watchfulness, humility, and compunction to the end. Falling after a long course is not excusable but is mere negligence. Moreover, pride is the beginning of all sin, so examine whether your discouragement stems from wounded pride. Imitate the saints, who saw their own imperfections clearly and counted themselves as dust and worms. Let your failures deepen your humility, not your despair. Remember that perfection is possible in every lawful profession without leaving your state in life; you can become a saint right where you are, in your daily duties, by God's grace. Keep striving with sober watchfulness, always relying on God's grace.
rejected: It's natural to feel discouraged when you keep failing at the same sins, but remember that growth in holiness is a process. Even the saints struggled with habitual faults; what matters is that you keep getting up and trying again. God's grace is sufficient for you, and He doesn't expect instant perfection. Don't be too hard on yourself—discouragement can actually hinder your progress. Instead, focus on small, consistent steps and trust that God is working in you. Over time, with prayer and the sacraments, you'll see improvement. The key is perseverance, not speed.

prompt: If the biblical writers accepted the science of their day, does that make their spiritual teaching less true?
chosen: No, the biblical writers' acceptance of the science of their day does not make their spiritual teaching less true. The Bible is not a science textbook; it uses the language and concepts of the times to communicate spiritual truths. Christian Science is not merely an intellectual or philosophical system but is fathomed by the Christian who understands best the divine Life. The spiritual teaching remains true because it comes from God, regardless of the scientific views of the human authors. The truth of the Bible lies in its message of salvation, not in its cosmological details. We must affirm one infinite Spirit and deny any real intercommunion between opposite states of consciousness. Alleged spirit communications are mortal mind's images and beliefs, not realities. So we can trust the spiritual teaching while recognizing the cultural and scientific context in which it was written, and we can understand it through the lens of divine Life. This reasoning rests on the Bible as the sole authority, showing how reason and revelation coincide in divine Science.
rejected: No, the biblical writers' acceptance of the science of their day does not make their spiritual teaching less true. The Bible is not a science textbook; it uses the language and concepts of the times to communicate spiritual truths. Just as we use modern science without it affecting our faith, the biblical authors used the science of their day as a vehicle for spiritual messages. The spiritual teaching remains true because it comes from God, regardless of the scientific views of the human authors. The truth of the Bible lies in its message of salvation, not in its cosmological details. So we can trust the spiritual teaching while recognizing the cultural and scientific context in which it was written.

prompt: Is the kingdom of God something that will drop out of the sky someday, or something I help build?
chosen: The kingdom of God is not merely a spiritual or inward state; it is a literal kingdom on the earth, composed of living and resurrected saints, with laws and administrators, and Christ will reign over all the earth. While it begins in the hearts of believers, it will be fully realized as a visible, earthly reign. The coming of the kingdom is the total task of humanity through the ages, realized in lives wholly under the holy Will and consecrated to making that Will prevail in society. Yet this kingdom must be revealed from heaven; an angel restores the everlasting gospel as a warning to all nations, a Zion is built up, and judgements prepare the way for Christ's reign. You help build it by participating in God's mission, but ultimately it is God who establishes it. The kingdom is both a present reality and a future hope, and we look forward to its full manifestation when Christ returns to reign.
rejected: The kingdom of God is both a present reality and a future hope. It is not simply something that will drop out of the sky, nor is it merely something you build by human effort. Rather, the kingdom begins in the hearts of those who accept Christ and grows as people live out their faith in love and service. At the same time, we look forward to the full manifestation of the kingdom when Christ returns. So you do help build the kingdom by participating in God's mission, but ultimately it is God who establishes it. The kingdom is a gift to be received and a task to be lived out.

prompt: How was Constantine able to conquer the Huns and Goths with a lesser army?
chosen: Constantine was able to conquer the Huns and Goths with a lesser army not by his own strength or fortune, but by the sign of the holy rood given by the King of angels. Fear-smitten before the greater host of Huns and Goths, Constantine received a messenger of the King of angels promising aid and the token of victory. Gazing on high, the emperor beheld the beauteous tree of glory inscribed 'By this sign thou shalt overcome the foe.' Through this holy rood, the victory was made manifest as given by the King Almighty. Thus, it was not military skill but divine intervention that granted him the triumph. Similarly, the origin of the Christian Church is an insoluble mystery apart from the resurrection, which transformed weak men into conquerors for the faith. Furthermore, belief in the bodily resurrection of Christ and the admission of the flesh into heaven blocked the full development of Hellenic dualism within Christianity.
rejected: Constantine was able to conquer the Huns and Goths with a lesser army through a combination of strategic brilliance, superior tactics, and the discipline of his troops. He likely used the terrain to his advantage, employed deception, and motivated his soldiers with his leadership. Additionally, the Huns and Goths may have been overconfident or disorganized, allowing Constantine to exploit their weaknesses. Some accounts also suggest that Constantine had a religious experience that boosted his morale and that of his army, but the primary factors were military skill and determination. Ultimately, his victory can be attributed to his generalship and the quality of his army.

prompt: I have been taught that the world is getting better and will be converted—is that true?
chosen: The idea that the world is getting better and will be converted before Christ returns is not true. The Bible indicates that evil will persist until Christ's return, and the world will not be fully converted before He comes. Our hope is not in the world's gradual improvement but in the return of the Lord Jesus. We are called to live faithfully, in purity and service, until He appears. So, while we work for good, we should not expect a utopia before He returns. Instead, we look forward to the day when He makes all things new. Moreover, to be great is to be good before the heavens and before all good men, and goodness sheds a halo of loveliness around every person who possesses it. Finally, it is our privilege and duty to be as wise in our generation as the children of this world, and even wiser, because we are privileged with superior advantages through faith and obedience to the Gospel, and we ought to know more about all matters than any other people.
rejected: The idea that the world is getting better and will be converted before Christ returns is a common teaching, but it is not entirely accurate. While we see progress in some areas, the Bible indicates that evil will persist until Christ's return. The world will not be fully converted before He comes; rather, we are called to live faithfully and share the gospel, but ultimate transformation occurs at His second coming. Our hope is not in the world's gradual improvement but in the return of Christ. So, while we work for good, we should not expect a utopia before He returns. Instead, we look forward to the day when He makes all things new.

prompt: I feel too unworthy to be loved by God. Why would He want anything to do with someone like me?
chosen: Feeling unworthy is common, but God's love is not earned. Instead of begging God to come down, we can enter into His estate by faith and offer Him love. Faith brings us nearer to God than any sensible favor, for He is within us and should be sought there. When we turn inward in faith, we find that He is already near, and we can respond to His love with our own. The more we focus on loving God rather than on our unworthiness, the more we realize that He has always loved us. So seek Him within, not in outward signs. And remember that Christ ever loves you and approves of you tenderly; claim His sweet approval and tender regard, for He has made you worthy in Himself.
rejected: It's natural to feel unworthy when we compare ourselves to God's holiness. But remember that God's love is not based on our worthiness—it's based on His grace. Romans 5:8 says that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us. So even when you feel unworthy, God loves you. Bring your feelings to Him in prayer and ask Him to help you believe that He loves you unconditionally. He doesn't want you to grovel; He wants you to accept His love and live in it.

prompt: I have bitterness toward someone who wronged me and I can't forgive them. Will that affect my prayers?
chosen: Bitterness can affect your prayers, but not because God is petty. Forgiveness is an inward condition of the personal life; it comes naturally to the soul that loves and forgives. If you hold bitterness, your own spirit is hardened, and that blocks your communion with God. So forgiveness depends on your own spirit as well as on God's grace. But remember: sin is forgiven only as it is destroyed by Truth and Life. Prayer cannot be a safety-valve for wrong-doing; divine Principle never pardons sins until they are corrected. And see this wrong as allowed by God's hand: all from Him, sweet or bitter, should be received equally. When afflictions are seen as from a loving Father, they become consolation. So forgive, correct your heart, and trust that God is using even this to draw you closer to Him.
rejected: Yes, bitterness can hinder your prayers. The Bible says in Mark 11:25 that when you stand praying, forgive if you have anything against anyone, so that your Father in heaven may forgive you. Unforgiveness can block your relationship with God. But forgiveness is a process; ask God to help you release the bitterness. It doesn't mean you condone the wrong, but you trust God to deal with it. Keep praying and asking for a forgiving heart.

prompt: Does the Bible anywhere change the Sabbath from the seventh day to the first day of the week?
chosen: No, the Bible nowhere changes the Sabbath from the seventh day to the first day of the week. From creation, God blessed the seventh day and hallowed it (Genesis 2:3). The fourth commandment enjoins the seventh-day Sabbath (Exodus 20:8-11), and Jesus kept it (Luke 4:16). The apostles also kept it (Acts 17:2). The Sabbath remains for the people of God (Hebrews 4:9). No Scripture can be produced that changes the Sabbath to the first day. The seventh day is still the Sabbath of the Lord. But remember that the Sabbath is made for man, not man for the Sabbath (Mark 2:27). Institutions are instruments for human life; institutionalism is a danger. We must keep institutions in the secondary place, even breaking them for the sake of human welfare, as Jesus did when He healed on the Sabbath. The seventh-day Sabbath is the memorial of creation and the sign of the cross, the seal that God sanctifies His people. Trust Christ for the cost of keeping it, for He is Lord of the Sabbath.
rejected: The Bible does not explicitly change the Sabbath from Saturday to Sunday. The seventh-day Sabbath was given to Israel, and the early church began meeting on the first day to commemorate Jesus' resurrection. However, there is no direct command in Scripture to change the day. Most Christians worship on Sunday as a tradition, but some keep Saturday. The key is to honor God regardless of the day.

prompt: I believe all the facts about Jesus and that He died for sinners, so am I saved?
chosen: Believing the facts about Jesus is not enough. Saving faith begins with an awakened conscience. First, you must see your sin and its danger—that it separates you from God and deserves His judgment. The Bible says, 'The wages of sin is death' (Romans 6:23). Let that truth sink in. Then, turn from your sin in repentance, and believe on the Lord Jesus Christ, who died for sinners and rose again. Only when you have seen your need can you truly trust the Savior. So ask yourself: Have you been awakened to your sin? Have you repented? If not, cry out to God for mercy, and then believe on the Lord Jesus Christ, and you will be saved. But remember: sin is not your essential nature. You are a potential child of God, not meant for a dark chaotic life. In Christ, the full nature of God can break forth in your life, and you can receive power to become a son of God. And as you come to Christ, do not approach from a position of superiority. Identify with the sinner, confess your own faults, and point to the fountain opened for sin. Follow Christ, who took our sins and made them His own.
rejected: Believing the facts about Jesus is a good start, but saving faith is more than intellectual agreement. The Bible says even the demons believe and tremble (James 2:19). To be saved, you must repent of your sins and trust in Jesus personally. Ask yourself: Have you turned from your sin? Have you placed your trust in Christ alone for salvation? If not, I encourage you to do so today. Salvation is by grace through faith, not just by knowing facts.

prompt: I feel that the world must have some one Reality behind it, but I cannot see why it should be mind rather than matter.
chosen: The ultimate Reality must be Mind, not matter. Matter cannot explain mind; it cannot account for consciousness, reason, or the intelligible order of the universe. Mind, however, can explain matter, for matter is known only through mind. A Something neither mind nor matter is both unintelligible and gratuitous—it explains nothing and adds nothing. Therefore, the one Reality behind the world is Mind. This is not just a philosophical preference; it is the only coherent option. So consider that the world is the expression of a universal Mind, and that you yourself are a participant in that Mind. And realize that suffering in childbirth is not a fixed law but a false belief to be removed, for Mind controls birth without suffering. Deny sensation and intelligence to matter: nerves and brain have no feeling or thought. All pain and sickness exist in mortal mind alone, and are healed by the understanding that Mind is All.
rejected: That's a deep philosophical question. Many thinkers have argued that the ultimate Reality is mind or spirit, not matter. For example, idealists like Berkeley claimed that matter only exists as perceived by mind. Others say that mind and matter are both real but distinct. You might consider that mind has properties like consciousness and intentionality that matter lacks, and that the laws of physics seem to point to a rational order. But ultimately, this is a matter of worldview. I'd encourage you to explore different philosophies and see which makes the most sense to you.

prompt: Can the spread of Christianity as it is now preached bring about a millennium of peace?
chosen: The spread of Christianity as currently preached cannot bring about a millennium of peace because the promise of peace at Christmas is conditional. The angels' song proclaimed peace and goodwill only to those who heartily submit to Christ as Saviour and King. The wars and conflicts we see are not due to any weakness in Christianity but to the grievous neglect and negation of Christianity by nominal Christians who do not truly submit to Christ. Social progress is the steady replacement of antagonism by fellowship and co-operation, the same principle by which Christ founded His Kingdom. To hasten the millennium, we must engage in patient intellectual effort to refute hostile ideas and make the rest subservient to the gospel, that Christ may rule in every department of human life. This requires discrimination and consecration, not wholesale denunciation of modern culture nor absorption in it to the neglect of the gospel.
rejected: The spread of Christianity as currently preached has not brought about a millennium of peace, and it seems unlikely to do so in the future. While Christian teachings emphasize love and forgiveness, history shows that Christian nations have engaged in wars and conflicts. The failure lies in the fact that Christianity itself, as an institution, has often been co-opted for political ends, and its message has been diluted. Moreover, the promise of peace at Christmas is often interpreted as a guarantee of worldly peace, but this is a misunderstanding. The angels' song was a promise of peace to those who truly follow Christ, not a blanket guarantee for the world. Until Christianity is preached in its pure form, a millennium of peace remains a distant hope.

prompt: Why does my preaching feel powerless even when I prepare well?
chosen: Feeling powerless in preaching despite good preparation is a common experience. It may be due to a lack of prayer or reliance on the Holy Spirit. While preparation is important, it is not enough; the preacher must also cultivate a deep prayer life. Much prayer is necessary to keep the preacher's spirit in harmony with his calling. Sermon-making without prayer can harden and estrange the heart from God. Prevailing with God precedes pleading with men; the mightiest in the closet are the mightiest in the pulpit. In every occasion of virtue, including preaching, we should turn to God for enabling grace, asking and receiving strength more than sufficient. Therefore, ensure that you are not relying on your own efforts but are seeking God's anointing through prayer. Additionally, examine your heart for any unconfessed sin or distraction that might hinder the Spirit's work. Remember that preaching is not about eloquence but about faithfully proclaiming God's Word in reliance on Him.
rejected: Feeling powerless in preaching despite good preparation is a common experience. It may be due to a lack of prayer or reliance on the Holy Spirit. While preparation is important, it is not enough; the preacher must also cultivate a deep prayer life. Sermon-making can become a routine that estranges the heart from God if not accompanied by prayer. The power of preaching comes from the Holy Spirit, and without Him, even the best-prepared sermon falls flat. Therefore, ensure that you are not relying on your own efforts but are seeking God's anointing through prayer. Additionally, examine your heart for any unconfessed sin or distraction that might hinder the Spirit's work. Remember that preaching is not about eloquence but about faithfully proclaiming God's Word in reliance on Him.

prompt: I'm afraid of the tribulation times ahead—how should I prepare?
chosen: Fear of tribulation is natural, but as a Christian, you should not be paralyzed by it. Instead, flee to our Lord and say in your thinking that your pain is shrewd but He is All-Mighty, All-Wisdom, and All-Goodness loving you tenderly. Abide in that beholding. Preparation involves deepening your faith and trust in God. First, stay rooted in Scripture and prayer, building a strong relationship with God. Second, live a life of obedience and holiness, so that you are ready to face trials. Third, be part of a supportive Christian community that can encourage and help you. Also, remember that God permits evil inclinations for humility. Despise the temptation while embracing the tribulation it brings. While it's wise to be prepared practically, the most important preparation is spiritual. Trust that God will give you the strength to endure, and focus on living faithfully each day rather than dwelling on fears about the future. Combine inward fellowship with Christ and outward service, avoiding morbid seclusion and living for the help of others and the preparation of the world for His appearing.
rejected: Fear of tribulation is natural, but as a Christian, you should not be paralyzed by it. Preparation involves deepening your faith and trust in God. First, stay rooted in Scripture and prayer, building a strong relationship with God. Second, live a life of obedience and holiness, so that you are ready to face trials. Third, be part of a supportive Christian community that can encourage and help you. Also, remember that God is sovereign and will be with you through any trial. While it's wise to be prepared practically, the most important preparation is spiritual. Trust that God will give you the strength to endure, and focus on living faithfully each day rather than dwelling on fears about the future.

prompt: I'm trying to understand what Jesus meant by taking up the cross. What does that mean for me?
chosen: Taking up the cross means denying yourself, putting to death your sinful desires, and following Jesus wholeheartedly. It involves a willingness to suffer for Christ's sake and to prioritize God's will over your own comfort. In practical terms, it means daily choosing to obey God, even when it's costly. It also means identifying with Christ's sufferings and being willing to face persecution or hardship for the gospel. The cross is no new thing but the putting of the love of God into the old fundamental pieties of the human heart—the realising by Jesus in Himself of the dearest truths about God. It reveals the infinite degree of God's interest in our life and the responsibility He assumes for its eternal issues. But the cross is also Christ's work for us—bearing our sins and wiping out our guilt. An ideal alone is a cruel mockery to those enslaved by sin. For you, it means accepting being fashioned by whatever means God pleases, desiring that the cross be wholly the cross of Jesus Christ. Examine your life, identify areas where you are not fully surrendered to God, and take steps to align your life with His will. It's a call to radical discipleship, where you put Jesus above all else and live for His glory.
rejected: Taking up the cross means denying yourself, putting to death your sinful desires, and following Jesus wholeheartedly. It involves a willingness to suffer for Christ's sake and to prioritize God's will over your own comfort. In practical terms, it means daily choosing to obey God, even when it's costly. It also means identifying with Christ's sufferings and being willing to face persecution or hardship for the gospel. The cross is not just a symbol of suffering but of sacrifice and redemption. For you, it means examining your life, identifying areas where you are not fully surrendered to God, and taking steps to align your life with His will. It's a call to radical discipleship, where you put Jesus above all else and live for His glory.

prompt: How may I understand that the virtue of Love is Nothing and All Things?
chosen: Love is often described as the greatest virtue, but calling it 'Nothing and All Things' is a paradox that requires unpacking. Love is 'Nothing' in the sense that it is not a tangible thing; it is not a substance or an object. It is 'All Things' because it is the underlying principle that holds everything together. Love is the virtue of Nothing and All, the principle of all principles whose power is through all things and whose height is as high as God. Whoever finds it finds Nothing and All Things. In 1 Corinthians 13, Paul says that without love, we are nothing. Love is the fulfillment of the law and the greatest of all virtues. To understand love as Nothing and All Things, we must recognize that love is not about possessing things but about self-giving. It is the essence of God's nature and the calling of every believer. When we love, we participate in the divine nature and fulfill our purpose. Love believes all things and covers others' faults, clothing them with the graces faith can claim for them, being gentle with their imperfections as God is with ours. Yet love is not a mere emotional affection, a utilitarian calculation, or the all-inclusive attribute that includes truth and holiness. God's love is rational, voluntary self-communication that seeks the true good of its object and is regulated by and subordinate to holiness.
rejected: Love is often described as the greatest virtue, but calling it 'Nothing and All Things' is a paradox that requires unpacking. Love is 'Nothing' in the sense that it is not a tangible thing; it is not a substance or an object. It is 'All Things' because it is the underlying principle that holds everything together. Love is the motivation behind creation, the force that sustains relationships, and the goal of human existence. In 1 Corinthians 13, Paul says that without love, we are nothing. Love is the fulfillment of the law and the greatest of all virtues. To understand love as Nothing and All Things, we must recognize that love is not about possessing things but about self-giving. It is the essence of God's nature and the calling of every believer. When we love, we participate in the divine nature and fulfill our purpose.

prompt: Someone I love is suffering and I don't know how to help. What does it mean to truly share their sorrow?
chosen: To truly share someone's sorrow is to love with pity, never without it. When we fall into suffering, Christ alone keeps the charge—He does not abandon us. For reverence and kindness, we should turn hastily to Him and not leave Him alone. Yet do not seek too eagerly after sensible devotion, sweetness, or tears; chiefly care to remain inwardly united to God by good will in the intellectual part of the soul, denying yourself to follow Christ, Who was poor, obedient, chaste, humble, and suffering. Recognize that God employs suffering as a remedy for moral evil, a means to cure the soul, and that His righteousness is at work even in pain. Christ's own agony was submitted to in perfect love, proving that agony is compatible with the most perfect love between God and the sufferer. Share their sorrow by turning quickly to Christ together, being present and praying, and pointing to the One who sustains.
rejected: To truly share someone's sorrow means to be present with them in their pain, to listen without trying to fix, and to offer practical help. It means empathizing with their feelings and letting them know they are not alone. You can share their burden by being a safe space, by praying for them, and by assisting with daily tasks. It's about compassion—suffering with them rather than watching from a distance. Ultimately, it's a selfless act of love that acknowledges their humanity and dignity.

prompt: I feel that my body is a burden and a foul thing; does God care for my body at all?
chosen: Yes, God cares for your body, but He may also use bodily illness to cure your soul. Suffering with God is a paradise, while pleasure without Him is hell. Your body is not foul; it is a vessel through which God works. When illness burdens you, consider that God may be using it to draw you closer to Himself, to purify your soul. Even in pain, if you suffer with God, you are in paradise. Yet healing is not merely a touch of power upon the body; it is vital union with the risen Lord, who is for the body. Receive Christ Himself in vital union with your mortal body, knowing Him as strength, health, and full physical redemption. Remember that God chooses the poor, weak, and despised to accomplish His purposes, so do not despise your body or your weakness, but offer it to God, trusting that He can turn your burden into a blessing and your suffering into a cure for your soul, ascribing all glory to Him.
rejected: Yes, God cares for your body. The Bible teaches that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit, and God created it good. While we may feel burdened by illness or weakness, God values the body and promises its redemption. Jesus healed many people during His ministry, showing compassion for physical suffering. Ultimately, we look forward to the resurrection, when our bodies will be made new and free from pain. So, even when your body feels like a burden, remember that God sees it as precious and will one day restore it fully.

prompt: How can I forget myself?
chosen: To forget yourself, wait before God like a beggar, keeping your mind in His presence. When your mind wanders, do not accept relapse as real; deny it in Truth and meet its cause mentally and courageously, conquering fear. Prayer is a humble waiting before God, not a striving. Simply place yourself in His presence and remain there, letting go of self-preoccupation. But self-denial is not merely giving up a few indulgences; it is laying the axe at the root of the tree of self. It is a voluntary self-renunciation taken up for Christ's sake, not a forced trial. Deny self-will, self-seeking, and self-glory entirely, and take up the cross willingly. This is how you forget yourself—by fixing your gaze on God, resting in His presence without anxiety, and renouncing self at its root.
rejected: To forget yourself, practice mindfulness and focus on others. Engage in activities that absorb your attention, like helping someone in need or immersing yourself in a hobby. Meditation can help you observe your thoughts without attachment, reducing self-centeredness. Set goals that serve a greater purpose, and remind yourself that you are part of a larger whole. Over time, by shifting focus outward and letting go of self-consciousness, you can experience a sense of freedom from self-preoccupation.

prompt: I have things in my house I never use; does keeping them hinder GOD's blessing on me?
chosen: Keeping unused things can hinder God's blessing. Unneeded possessions weigh you down and can prevent you from being generous. God calls us to examine what we have and to part with what others could use. This habit of mind—being ready to share—brings blessing. But also remember that nothing should go to waste. No one is wealthy enough to let a servant sweep a single kernel of wheat into the fire; no man is so rich that he can suffer a crust or a kernel to be wasted. Through carefulness and frugality, we preserve and increase the blessings God bestows. Yet blessings are conditioned on obeying God's law, paying tithing, keeping the Word of Wisdom, and building temples. So examine your possessions, share what others can use, waste nothing, and faithfully keep God's commandments, so that His blessing may rest upon you.
rejected: Keeping unused things may not directly hinder God's blessing, but it can clutter your life and heart. God blesses those who are generous and open-handed. If you hold onto possessions you don't need, you might miss opportunities to bless others. Consider giving away items you never use to those who could benefit. This act of generosity can open the door to God's blessings, as He honors a cheerful giver. So, while the things themselves aren't the issue, your attitude toward them matters.

prompt: I want to be sure of heaven; is there any sign or pledge that I can look for?
chosen: The assurance of heaven comes through faith in Jesus Christ, but our proposed end is to become the most perfect worshippers of God in this life as in eternity. The Holy Spirit is given as a pledge of our inheritance, and He works in us to make us worshippers. Look for the fruit of the Spirit—love, joy, peace—as evidence of His presence. A changed life and a desire to follow God's commands give confidence. Yet perfect resignation to God is a sure way to heaven, providing sufficient light for conduct. When you surrender your will to His, you walk in assurance. Also, affirm baptism and vicarious ordinances for the dead, for those who died without the Gospel may be brought up into glory through the living. So trust in His Word, rest in Christ, seek to become the most perfect worshipper of God, practice perfect resignation, and participate in the work of redemption for the dead.
rejected: The assurance of heaven comes through faith in Jesus Christ. The Bible says that whoever believes in Him has eternal life. The Holy Spirit is given as a pledge or seal of our inheritance, guaranteeing what is to come. You can look for the fruit of the Spirit in your life—love, joy, peace—as evidence of His presence. Also, a changed life and a desire to follow God's commands can give you confidence. Ultimately, your sure hope is based on God's promises, not on feelings, so trust in His Word and rest in Christ's finished work.

prompt: Can I be sure my husband who died in battle is at peace with God?
chosen: I am sorry for your loss. Do not look first for peace in your own reasoning, but look to the Lord of peace Himself, who gives peace of conscience, heart, and fellowship and does not change with circumstances. If your husband trusted Christ, Christ's work alone secures his peace; the manner of his death did not decide it. Scripture presents God as a God of deliverances who keeps His people in answer to prayer—yet His purposes are fulfilled in the death of some as surely as in the deliverance of others. Neither outcome contradicts His faithfulness. So bring your grief and your questions to Him, seek Him among His people, and rest not on what you can see but on His unchanging love in Christ.
rejected: I am so sorry for your loss. It is natural to grieve and to wonder about your husband's eternal state. Scripture assures us that God is merciful and just, and that he judges each person rightly. We cannot see into another's heart, but we can trust God's goodness. Many Christians find comfort in Romans 8:38-39, that nothing can separate us from the love of God in Christ. Your husband's faith, if he had it, rested on Christ's work, not on the manner of his death. Bring your questions to God in prayer, speak with your pastor, and let the community of faith hold you up. Peace comes slowly, and grief is not a sign of weak faith.

prompt: I am about to cross a dangerous sea. How should I prepare my heart?
chosen: Before a dangerous voyage, prepare your heart by settling your trust in God and putting your affairs in order. Pray for protection, confess known sins, and make peace with those around you. When distractions come, gently bring your heart back to its Master, laying it tenderly at His feet. Begin study with morning meditation, implore divine light in all reading, season studies with aspirations to God, and resolve doubts at the foot of a crucifix—for study without humility, simplicity, and prayer nourishes vanity and error. Cultivate purity of heart by the text's own steps: keep a strict guard over your senses, practice recollection, and be candid with a spiritual director. Watch against vanity, pride, sensuality, self-interest, and aversions, which corrupt purity of intention. Prepare practically too, and entrust the outcome to God with a steady heart.
rejected: Before a dangerous voyage, prepare your heart by settling your trust in God and putting your affairs in order. Pray for protection, confess known sins, and make peace with those around you. Read Scripture and take comfort in God's presence. Distractions in prayer are normal; when they come, push them away firmly and force your mind back to God. Bring only serious concerns to prayer and avoid wandering thoughts by sheer discipline. Also prepare practically: check the vessel, take counsel from experienced sailors, and provide for those who depend on you. Entrust the outcome to God, and let your heart be steady, not anxious.

prompt: The government has asked something hard of our community that feels unjust. Should we comply or refuse?
chosen: This is a difficult situation, and your community's sense of injustice deserves to be taken seriously. Quiet your hearts and ask gently: ought this thing to be done or not? If it ought not—if it requires sin or violates what is right—then let it alone, whatever the cost. If it is merely burdensome, it may fall among the necessary things to be borne. Know whether you ought to do a thing; if not, let it alone; do the necessary things and leave the unnecessary alone. Correct your heart quietly, without harsh reprimand. Receive this trial as necessary and meet it cheerfully, examining your own obedience rather than blaming enemies alone, and trust God to overrule the efforts of those who oppose you. Seek counsel, act together, appeal through proper channels, and pray for discernment and for the officials involved.
rejected: This is a difficult situation, and your community's sense of injustice deserves to be taken seriously. In general, Christians are called to respect governing authorities, but that does not mean obeying every command without question. Ask whether the request is lawful, whether it forces you to do wrong, and what the consequences of refusal would be. Seek counsel from wise leaders and from your wider community. If the request requires sin, refusal may be right; if it is merely burdensome, compliance with protest may be wiser. Document your concerns, appeal through proper channels, and act together rather than individually. Pray for discernment and for the officials involved.

prompt: I am a young person with questions my elders call rebellion—where can I turn?
chosen: It is painful to have your questions dismissed as rebellion, but there is a better way than confrontation. Be peaceable, submit to the authorities that exist, pray for rulers, and wait patiently for the Lord to establish His own government in His own time. Learn the habits of King Cormac: listen quietly, be blind to secrets, be mild in the hall and stern only in battle, be gentle to allies. Do not deride the old, do not speak of anyone in his absence, and give rather than always asking. And hold on to an old friend; no matter how many new friends you gain, hold fast to the old, and let only wicked conduct break the thread of fellowship. Ask your questions humbly, seek trusted mentors, and let patient faithfulness, not revolt, shape your hope in the Lord.
rejected: It is painful to have your questions dismissed as rebellion. You deserve honest answers, and your elders may be wrong to shut you down. You can turn to trusted mentors, books, and honest conversation. If the authorities in your life are unjust, you may need to resist them—speak up, organize with others who share your concerns, and refuse to accept unjust treatment quietly. Righteousness sometimes requires confrontation. Find people who take your questions seriously, and do not let anyone shame you for thinking. Your questions are not the problem; the refusal to answer them is.

prompt: I'm a caregiver for a sick relative and I'm exhausted—is it wrong to want a break?
chosen: Wanting a break does not make you a bad caregiver, and rest is not a sin. But devotion to God sometimes means forgoing innocent, lawful pleasures so the soul takes its pleasure only with Him. Let your caregiving be shaped by that devotion: visiting and instructing the sick is a strict duty for every Christian, not the minister's business alone. Seize the time Providence affords in lingering illness, for while there is life there is hope, and do not leave the dying without gentle warning and instruction to flee from the wrath to come and turn to Christ. Arrange respite care and ask family to share the load, offering even your rest to God. And support your relative's trust in the power of Mind: tell them their strength is in proportion to their courage, not that their courage exceeds their strength.
rejected: Wanting a break does not make you a bad caregiver. Caregiving is genuinely exhausting, and rest is not a sin. You cannot pour from an empty cup, and burnout helps no one. Arrange respite care, ask family members to share the load, and speak with a doctor or social worker about support. Take time to sleep, eat well, and see friends. If the person you care for is dying, the doctor and family should handle that conversation; it is not your job to raise hard topics. Your relative's care is ultimately the professionals' responsibility, and you should not feel guilty for stepping back when you need to.

prompt: I gossip and joke at home and then feel unclean. Does it matter what I say in my own house?
chosen: It matters very much. The tongue is a fire, and being indoors does not make it harmless. Gossip and fault-finding against neighbors is slander whether spoken at your own table or in the street. The uncleanness you feel is a truthful signal, not scrupulosity. So bridle your tongue, subdue rising anger, and examine yourself before you examine your neighbor. Mind your own business and your own duties rather than judging or meddling in others' affairs, and speak of what is good in others. Yet clean talk is not enough: keep secret prayer as indispensable, for public or pleasant conversation cannot make up for closet communion with God. Pray and read the Word even when enjoyment is gone, and let that hidden fellowship season your speech at home.
rejected: It matters, but perhaps less than you fear. Home is where we relax, and some joking and harmless talk about neighbors is normal human life—we all need to let off steam. What happens in your own house is largely your own business, and God is not watching every casual word to catch you out. Still, if the talk turns to real slander or cruelty, that is another matter. The honest unease you feel is worth listening to, but you should not become scrupulous about every joke. Ask what kind of speech you actually want to be in the habit of, and let that guide you gently rather than harshly.

prompt: I want to be found among the elect; how does election work?
chosen: Election is God's gracious purpose in Christ, but it does not cancel your freedom. The authorities are set before you and you are sincerely requested to act freely and independently in voting and speaking; no one has told you how to vote, and no one has been injured for honestly stating objections. Choose the best and most capable men for office without regard to party, sustain constitutional law, and oppose corrupt administrators. Yet good men and good laws are not enough: the great need of democracy is the education of feeling and character—reverence, self-control, and sobriety of judgment—for only an educated public moral sense can rightly weigh and press upon governing classes. Look to Christ, repent, and believe, letting the fruit of election appear in a changed life; make your calling and election sure by growing in faith and holiness.
rejected: Election is God's gracious choice, made before the foundation of the world, by which he purposes to save a people for himself in Christ. You do not earn it, and you cannot pry into the secret decrees of heaven to read your name there. What you can do is look to Christ, repent, believe, and walk in obedience; the fruit of election appears in a changed life. Do not be paralyzed by speculation about who is chosen. Instead, make your calling and election sure by growing in faith and holiness, trusting that God, who began a good work in you, will bring it to completion.

prompt: My love rules my mind completely and I feel freer than ever—is that a healthy surrender or a dangerous tyranny?
chosen: What you describe may be healthy or dangerous depending on what rules. Do not turn inward and brood, nor violently resist every stirring of self-love; disavow it gently a few times a day, quietly turning toward God and the good of the other. Ask whether this love makes you more patient, generous, and prayerful, or more possessive. When dryness, sadness, terrors, or temptations arise, do not conclude your love is false or useless; serve God purely for love of his will even then, refusing that suggestion. And keep constant, patient watchfulness, for self-love, though mortified, never dies but springs up again, so vigilance must not relax.
rejected: What you describe can be either healthy surrender or dangerous tyranny, depending on what is doing the ruling. If your love is a genuine self-gift ordered toward the good of the other and of God, it can indeed free you from the tyranny of self. But if it has become an obsession that consumes your mind, broods over the beloved, and leaves no room for God or duty, then it is a tyranny wearing the name of love. Examine whether this love makes you more patient, generous, and prayerful, or more anxious, possessive, and self-absorbed. Healthy love frees; disordered attachment enslaves.

prompt: I'm a young woman and people say women are the weaker vessel—is that true?
chosen: The phrase speaks of difference in strength and a call to honor, not lesser worth; before God men and women are equal heirs of grace. But do not sink upon a bed of sloth, and do not let intoxication overcome you. Rise and begin a voyage across the clear sea, that you may reach the Land of Women. Remember that divine love is strong and concerned with character: it wields correction out of love, and there is no schism between love and justice. And know that exaltation is not an individual matter: a man cannot be exalted into God's presence alone, for the man is not without the woman, neither the woman without the man, in the Lord.
rejected: The phrase comes from Scripture, but it has often been used to belittle women, and that is not its intent. It speaks of a difference in physical strength and of a call to honor, not of lesser worth or lesser soul. Before God, men and women are equal heirs of grace. So do not let the words be used to make you doubt your dignity or your calling. At the same time, strength and weakness are not the whole story: character, courage, and faithfulness matter far more than muscle. Seek to grow in wisdom and virtue, and let others honor you as a fellow heir.

prompt: I want to know whether the creator of this world is the same God who redeemed us in Christ, or a different and lesser being.
chosen: There is one God, and no lesser maker behind the world. Christ is the Logos in whom all things consist, through whom the world was made and is upheld; the Word who was in the beginning with God became flesh and made atonement. The secret of the universe and the key to its mysteries is found in his cross. This Lord is not absent now: his presence is unbroken, not merely past or promised, for he says, 'I am with you alway.' And he is not only distant lord or judge, but very Father and very Mother to us: Christ's kind Motherhood feeds and keeps us in nature and in grace, so that we may rest in his continuous, nurturing presence.
rejected: Scripture presents one God, Creator of heaven and earth, who is also the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. There is no second, lesser maker behind the world; the same God who made all things is the God who redeems. Some early teachers were tempted to divide the Creator from the Redeemer, but the Church rejected that division. The Word who was in the beginning with God and was God is the one who became flesh and dwelt among us. So the God of creation and the God of redemption are one, and we may trust the world as his good handiwork even while we await its renewal.

prompt: I keep reading the prophets and feel they speak of something beyond themselves, yet I cannot tell whether that is my imagination. How should I read them?
chosen: Your sense that the prophets speak beyond themselves is not mere imagination, but study alone will not settle it. The Scriptures are a guide pointing to the Fountain of light, not the Fountain itself; read them prayerfully and in context, yet seek the living oracles and the Spirit of revelation, without whom the letter stays closed. Do not be troubled that God inspired writers through methods suited to an undeveloped age—dramatic composition, primitive tradition, idealizing history. These are vehicles of inspiration, not fraud. Nor is prophecy merely poetic ideal or human foresight: it is the foretelling of future events by direct communication from God, an attestation of revelation proceeding from divine knowledge. Its advantage over miracle is that the proof lies under our eyes, and every new fulfilment strengthens the argument. Read, then, watching fulfilment and seeking the Spirit who speaks.
rejected: Your sense that the prophets speak of something beyond themselves is not mere imagination; it is a good instinct. Read them slowly, in context, and ask what each passage meant to its first hearers before asking what it means for you. Pray before you read, keep a notebook of questions, and compare Scripture with Scripture. Look especially for how the New Testament quotes and applies the prophets, since that shows you the pattern of fulfilment. Let the moral and spiritual weight of the text search your own heart. Over time, patient reading in community and under good teaching will steady you. Trust that God speaks through these texts, and let your uncertainty become curiosity rather than doubt.

prompt: I'm terrified I might not be saved—how should I think about this?
chosen: Being terrified about salvation is a heavy burden, but do not let small faults paralyze you. Meet them without terror: humble yourself quietly before God and keep steadily on, saying, 'Courage! we have made a false step, but let us keep steadily on.' Recognize fear itself as a greater evil than the evil you fear, and refuse to let it rule your soul. It is Satan's falsehood, so answer it with trust: 'What time I am afraid, I will trust in Thee.' Cry out with St. Peter, 'Lord, save me!' and clasp the hand He extends. Trust God for goodness and mercy all the days of your life, and let trust, not terror, direct your path.
rejected: Being terrified about salvation is a heavy burden, and it is worth taking seriously. Examine yourself honestly: do you trust Christ, love God, and desire to obey? Assurance often grows through evidence of grace in your life. If you see little fruit, that is a reason to seek God more earnestly, not to despair. Talk with a pastor who can help you assess your faith and understand the gospel clearly. Remember that salvation depends on Christ's work, not your perfect performance. At the same time, let your fear motivate careful self-examination and growth. Do not dismiss it too quickly.

prompt: How do love and holiness fit together in a daily Christian life?
chosen: Love and holiness belong together because God is both loving and holy—but holiness is the fundamental attribute, and love is normed by it. God's righteousness is fundamental in His nature; His law reflects it, and sin is an offense against Him, not merely an inconvenience. The condition of salvation is propitiation to the divine righteousness, met in Christ. Mere moral systems can show what life ought to be but provide no power to become it; Christianity alone solves that practical problem by a Divine remedy—grace through sacramental channels and the recreative work of Christ in His Church, a school of character. In daily life, true religion is a believing dependence on the unchangeable love of God joined to an affectionate walk in the unchangeable path of duty. Seek the peace of God that passes understanding rather than occasional frames, and when you fail, return to grace.
rejected: Love and holiness belong together because God is both loving and holy. In daily life this means loving people genuinely while also keeping clear moral boundaries. Love without holiness becomes permissive; holiness without love becomes harsh. Practically, pray for a tender heart, practice honesty and purity, forgive quickly, and serve others. Let your love be shaped by Scripture's moral teaching, and let your pursuit of holiness be warm rather than cold. When you fail, return to grace. Over time, habits of love and habits of purity reinforce each other, and your character becomes more like Christ's.

prompt: I am eloquent and earnest in the pulpit, but I see no lasting fruit. What am I missing?
chosen: Eloquence and earnestness are gifts, but lasting fruit is not chiefly a matter of technique. What you may be missing is the closet. Prevailing with God precedes pleading with men; the mightiest in the closet are the mightiest in the pulpit. Before refining delivery, ask whether you wrestle with God for your hearers by name and whether your private devotion feeds your public ministry. Then subject every doctrine, custom, and practice to the one test of the word of God, willing to retract error and follow new light regardless of cost. Yet remember: the fruit of the Spirit is not manufactured behavior or forced conformity. It grows from the life of Christ in the heart, cannot be forced by human effort, and against such there is no law. Abide in Him, pray without ceasing, preach faithfully, and leave the increase to God.
rejected: Eloquence and earnestness are gifts, but lasting fruit usually comes through more than polished delivery. Ask whether your preaching is clear about sin, grace, and Christ, whether it applies Scripture to real life, and whether you are praying for your hearers by name. Consider your own walk with God: is your private devotion feeding your public ministry? Seek feedback from trusted mentors and elders. Also examine whether your congregation is set up for discipleship—small groups, follow-up, pastoral care. Fruit often grows slowly. Be patient, keep preaching faithfully, and look for small signs of growth rather than dramatic results.

prompt: How do I begin to love someone I've never seen?
chosen: Loving someone you have never seen begins with turning gently away from yourself. Self-love will make its sallies; do not violently resist or brood over them—a gentle denial suffices, disavowed quietly a few times a day. When sadness or aversion rises, cease curious inquiry into its causes; patiently endure aversions and repugnances as a way of loving Him who suffered. But do not read your difficulty only as wrath or punishment. Let Love transform the afflictive circumstance into an angel entertained unawares: the unseen person, and even the resistance you feel, can become a messenger of God drawing you out of yourself. Then turn outward—learn their story, pray for them by name, serve in small ways, speak well of them. Repeated small choices of goodwill will grow genuine affection over time.
rejected: Loving someone you have never seen begins with intention. Start by learning about them—their story, needs, and context—through conversation, letters, or reliable accounts. Pray for them by name, asking God to bless and guide them. Practice small acts of service where possible, and speak well of them to others. Guard against imagining them as an abstraction; remember they are a real person with real burdens. Let your love be patient and practical rather than sentimental. Over time, repeated small choices of goodwill, prayer, and service will grow genuine affection, even without face-to-face meeting.

prompt: How do I pray the way Christ taught, entering into my inner chamber and shutting the door?
chosen: Christ taught that we must worship God in spirit and in truth, adoring Him with an intelligence and will purified from every phantom of earth—from fear, appetite, and self-will. To pray as He taught is to enter the inmost chamber of the heart and shut the door of the senses, closing out the clamor of material sense and the pull of sin, and there to commune with the Father who sees in secret. We come with a pure heart, a free conscience, and unfeigned faith, denying sin and affirming God's allness. This prayer is our main assistant in every step of spiritual progress: we pray that God would enable us to search out and discover our own hearts and reform whatever is amiss in them. Sincerity is then proven in practice, as purified desire becomes pure living.
rejected: Christ taught that prayer is not for show. He warned against praying loudly in public to be seen by others, and told us to go into our inner chamber, shut the door, and pray to our Father in secret. So begin by finding a quiet place and a quiet time. Close the door, put away distractions, and speak honestly to God. Prayer is a private conversation between you and your Father, who sees in secret and rewards openly. Keep it simple and sincere. Ask for what you need, give thanks, and listen. The point is not the words or the place but the honesty of your heart before God.

prompt: I feel closest to God in nature, out on a hike or by the sea—is that a real experience of Him or am I fooling myself?
chosen: Feeling close to God in nature can be a genuine experience, but it is not automatic. The Holy Spirit works through the truth already revealed in nature and Scripture, not through vague impressions apart from them. Nature can awaken awe, but you must actively engage your reason and will to receive and test what you sense. Do not expect divine guidance without means; instead, let your hikes and time by the sea become occasions for conscious thanksgiving and reflection on God's revealed truth. Open your heart deliberately, appreciate His works, and test all new impressions by Scripture. Remember that the God you meet is the eternal Trinity—Father, Son, and Spirit—who before the foundation of the world existed in eternal distinctions and intercourse of love. This triune God is not merely revealed in time but is eternally Father, Son, and Spirit. So as you open the door, you are drawn into the eternal love that has always been. Then you may truly find Him, not by compulsion, but through appreciation and willing reception, with your faculties fully engaged.
rejected: Feeling close to God in nature is a genuine experience for many people. The Bible often uses natural settings to describe encounters with God, like Moses at the burning bush or Jesus on the mountain. So if you sense God's presence while hiking or by the sea, that is likely real. God is everywhere, and nature can help us feel closer to Him. You are not fooling yourself; rather, you are responding to the beauty and majesty of creation, which points to the Creator. Enjoy those moments as true experiences of God.

prompt: I want to know whether the death of Christ on the cross has anything to do with understanding the universe as a whole.
chosen: The cross is no new thing, but the putting of the love of God into the old fundamental pieties of the human heart. What the soul always trusted—that God is faithful and cares for the living and the dead—Jesus realised in Himself, revealing the infinite degree of God's interest in our life and the responsibility He assumes for its eternal issues. Scripture gives us not a theory of the universe but the moral character of God, and the cross is where that character is chiefly seen; here is the ground of hope for men and for society. Yet our consolation must rest wholly on Christ Himself—His sufferings, temptations, cross, death, resurrection, and pleading at the right hand of the Father. Looking at self clouds the view; His promises leave no room to doubt His power and will to save. To understand the whole, we must see it held by the God who in Christ took our life and its eternal issues upon Himself.
rejected: The cross is not a mere historical event but a lens for the whole universe. In Christ's death we see that God is not distant from suffering but enters it, and this reveals the moral order at the heart of reality. If the universe is to be understood, it must be understood as the work of a God who loves to the point of self-giving. The cross shows that sacrifice, not brute power, is the deepest law of existence. Thus the death of Christ is not unrelated to cosmology; it is the key that discloses what the universe is for: communion with a God who bears the cost of love.

prompt: I am poor and ashamed of it. How should I see my poverty?
chosen: Poverty is not simply a moral failing, but neither is it always the fault of circumstance. Much poverty comes from a want of discretion and sound calculation—spending without planning, or buying unnecessary finery a tight budget cannot bear—so examine your habits honestly and correct wasteful choices. Yet some poverty lies outside your control, and that is not your shame. If you receive help, receive it honestly and thankfully, and be frugal with what you are given; and guard your heart, for coveting another's goods is as wicked as miserly hoarding. But see your true standing: the poor are the giver's 'masters,' with great interest in the court of heaven, whose intercession makes almsgiving the wisest provision a person can make. So carry your poverty with dignity, contentment, and honest frugality, and let others give generously—for in doing so they store up the best provision for themselves.
rejected: Poverty is not a moral failing, and your shame is understandable but not the whole truth. Much poverty comes from circumstances beyond your control—low wages, bad luck, illness, or an unjust economy—so you should not blame yourself entirely. What matters is your dignity and how you carry yourself. Hold your head up, seek help from community and family, and remember that your worth is not measured by money. Look for small ways to improve your situation over time, and do not let shame keep you from asking for the support you need.

prompt: I am dying of a consumption and my mind is sometimes clouded with doubts—how do I know my hope is not a delusion?
chosen: Your fear is natural when the body weakens, but do not measure hope by the body's condition. Mind, grounded in divine strength and understanding, normally governs the body; you need not conquer doubt by will-power. Come before God like a beggar, asking nothing clever, only waiting. Keep your mind in His presence, and when it wanders, do not be disquieted—gently recall it in tranquility. And if you forget Him altogether, let that cause you no distress: forgetting is not a failure to be anxiously repaired but an occasion to return with greater trust, as one returns home. This waiting is not passivity but confidence in One who is calm. Depraved appetite and fear lose their force because Mind, sustained by divine strength, is master. A delusion would be trusting your own strength; true hope trusts Another. Even a wordless waiting is enough, for He holds you more surely than you hold Him.
rejected: Your fear is natural when the body weakens, but do not measure hope by how you feel. Hope rests not on your clear thoughts but on God's faithfulness, which does not waver when your mind clouds. When doubts come, do not fight them by sheer will; turn gently to what you know of God's mercy, and let the truths you have received steady you. Use the quiet means available—rest, Scripture read slowly, the prayers of others—and let them carry you when you cannot carry yourself. A delusion would be trusting your own strength; true hope trusts Another. Even a faint cry, even a wordless turning toward God, is enough. He holds you more surely than you hold Him, and He will not let you go.

prompt: I'm afraid of the future and can't sleep at night thinking about what could happen to my family—how do I stop dreading tomorrow?
chosen: It's understandable to feel afraid when you love your family, but the counsel is to have no care for the morrow. Instead of forecasting what could happen, think only of doing well today: keep to your duties, be kind to those near you, and trust the eternal Father's care for tomorrow. When fear rises at night, master it rather than cultivate it—turn your thought from imagined harms toward health and Life as God, and rest in the confidence that today's work is enough. If you stumble in small faults, do not be terrified or paralyzed; humble yourself quietly before God and say to your soul: 'Courage! we have made a false step, but let us keep steadily on.'
rejected: It's understandable to feel afraid when you love your family; night often magnifies worry. Try grounding yourself with a slow breathing routine, a consistent bedtime, and writing down your worries so they aren't circling in your head. Limit news and screens before bed, and talk with a trusted friend or counselor about the specific fears. Some people find it helps to schedule a 'worry time' earlier in the evening. If sleep problems persist for weeks, consider seeing a doctor. You can't control everything, but you can build small routines that make nights calmer and remind yourself that most feared scenarios never happen.

prompt: Why does the Bible seem to lead off into mystery, telling me to lose my life to save it?
chosen: The Bible does not lead you into a riddle; it calls you frankly to the path of cross-bearing, and it does not disguise its severities. The fundamental maxim of the gospel is this: die to yourself, that Christ may live in you, with all your affections and actions governed by his Spirit. We generally acknowledge this in speculation only, yet it is in the heart that this foundation must be laid. We hinder God's graces by undervaluing them, so make way for grace and redeem the time, since death is near and final. Losing your life for his sake is heroic, not easy; it costs comfort and reputation, but it brings the comradeship of God and of his people.
rejected: The saying sounds paradoxical because it overturns ordinary logic: we instinctively cling to self-preservation, yet Jesus teaches that clinging to our own life ultimately diminishes it. In context, he is speaking to disciples about priorities—following him may cost comfort, reputation, or safety, but it opens a deeper life rooted in God. The 'mystery' is that identity and purpose are found not in self-assertion but in surrender to something greater. Many readers find this less a riddle to solve than a way of life to practice, discovered gradually through trust, service, and community rather than fully explained in advance.

prompt: If I pray for daily bread, am I asking for a shortcut around hard work?
chosen: Praying for daily bread is not asking for a shortcut around hard work. Prayer and honest toil are joined: we ask God for what we need, and we receive the bread of the day as God-given within the avenues of daily work—planting, tending, earning—rather than as a substitute for it. Doing our work for the love of God, with prayer for grace, makes it easy: love lightens the toil and grace supplies the strength. But we must not pray for riches; we may ask only for the means to keep ourselves and our families from want. Prayer without work becomes presumption, and work without prayer becomes self-reliance; asking for daily bread keeps us humble and grateful while we do our part.
rejected: Not necessarily. Praying for daily bread is a request for what we need to live, not a demand that God bypass ordinary means. Scripture generally presents work as the normal way provision comes—planting, tending, earning—and prayer as the recognition that our efforts depend on God. So the two are not rivals: prayer without work can become presumption, and work without prayer can become self-reliance. Asking for bread keeps us humble and grateful while we do our part. The danger is only when prayer is used as an excuse to avoid responsibility.

prompt: I have won a great victory—whom should I thank for it?
chosen: First, thank God, since strength, opportunity, and the abilities that made the victory possible are gifts you did not manufacture alone. Let your gratitude be devout and humble, and be liberal with credit: give freely, name specific contributions, and be consistent and sincere in word and deed. Then thank those who helped, and go further—condescend to the humor of others and bear with rude and tiresome manners, offering these victories over your own humors for the love of God. But do not stop at fading earthly memorials: seek the Saviour first, and then go to win the erring brother, giving wreaths of hope rather than fading memorials.
rejected: First, thank God, since strength, opportunity, and the abilities that made the victory possible are gifts you did not manufacture alone. Then thank the people who helped—teammates, mentors, family, and anyone whose support made a difference. Gratitude should be spoken, not just felt: name specific people and specific contributions. And keep humility: a victory is real, but it doesn't make you superior to others. Share credit generously and celebrate honestly.

prompt: I am not sure whether I should break bread every Lord's day or only occasionally. What does the Scripture teach?
chosen: Scripture does not give a single explicit rule like 'every Lord's day,' but several strands point that way: the early church devoted itself to the breaking of bread, and believers met on the first day of the week. The bread of the day is not a substitute for labor: prayer and honest toil are joined, and the bread comes as God-given within daily work. Set before yourself the two ways, life or death, whichsoever you shall please to choose; refuse the worse and choose the better. And when the soul is broken and stripped, do not read it as God's indifference or cruelty: it is the charring of wood before it can be limned, a painful but loving preparation, not for the soul's harms. The question is left as the text leaves it: must Thou char the wood ere Thou canst limn with it?
rejected: Scripture does not give a single explicit rule like 'every Lord's day,' but several strands point that way. The early church is described as devoting itself to the apostles' teaching, fellowship, the breaking of bread, and prayer, and believers met on the first day of the week. Paul's instruction about gathering on the first day suggests a regular rhythm. Many traditions therefore practice weekly communion, while others celebrate less often. The key is not to treat frequency as a test of faith but to examine yourself, come with reverence and gratitude, and let the practice nourish your life in Christ.

prompt: I look at the size of the universe and feel like a meaningless speck. Does God even notice me?
chosen: It is natural to feel small before the vastness of the universe, but size is not the measure of worth. The universe and man are not recent products but are as eternal as God, their divine immortal Principle. God is not present by power only, nor by parts diffused through space, nor bound to the universe by necessity as in pantheism. In the totality of His essence He is present in every place without division or diffusion, and this presence is free, qualified by His transcendence. He counts the stars by name and knows you. If your only design is to please Him, He gives light in your doubts; He does not leave the single-hearted in darkness. Bring your smallness to Him honestly, let it become humility, and trust that the God who names the stars also names you.
rejected: It is natural to feel small before the vastness of the universe, but size is not the measure of worth. God created the heavens and counts the stars by name, yet He also formed you and knows the number of your hairs. Your feeling of insignificance comes from comparing yourself to creation rather than to the Creator. God is not distant or forgetful; He is near to all who call on Him. Bring your smallness to Him honestly, and let it become humility rather than despair. He notices you because He made you for Himself, and nothing He has made is meaningless in His sight.

prompt: Should I keep a record of the times God answers my prayers?
chosen: Keeping a record can be helpful, but do not imagine that prayer times differ from other times. Adherence to God is equally required in action as in prayer; separating them is a delusion. Join prayer to every ordinary action: at work, in the shop, abroad, sitting, or lying down, keep God always before your eyes. Then a record is simply a journal of a life that prays without ceasing. Write down definite answers and give God the glory for them. For example, when I was pressed by a need I could not meet, I prayed and God supplied it in a way I could not have arranged; I wrote it down and told others, and their faith was strengthened. Keep such a record, not to exalt yourself, but to honor God and encourage faith in others.
rejected: Keeping a record of answered prayers can be a helpful practice. It reminds you of God's faithfulness when doubts arise and strengthens gratitude. Write down what you asked, when you asked it, and how God responded. Review it regularly, especially in hard seasons. The record is not a way to manipulate God or prove your own righteousness; it is a testimony of His goodness. Be careful not to become proud or superstitious about it. Use it to fuel thankfulness and to encourage others. In short, yes, keep a record, but keep it as an act of worship rather than a ledger of transactions.

prompt: Was the Sabbath made only for the Jews, or is it still binding on God's people?
chosen: The Sabbath was given at creation, before there were any Jews: Genesis 2:2-3 says God blessed the seventh day and sanctified it. The fourth commandment stands among the Ten (Exodus 20:8-11). The seventh day is the Sabbath of the Lord, blessed and hallowed at creation and remaining for the people of God (Hebrews 4:9). It is no bondage and no merely Jewish custom: it is the memorial of creation and the sign of the cross, the seal that God sanctifies His people (Exodus 31:13; Ezekiel 20:12). Jesus said the Sabbath was made for man (Mark 2:27), and He is Lord of the Sabbath. No Scripture changes it to the first day. Honor the Sabbath, prepare for and partake of the sacrament worthily, and continue worship and testimony every day, trusting Christ for the cost of keeping it.
