prompt: I have suffered a great loss and feel my grief is unbearable; can anyone understand a sorrow like mine?
chosen: Your sorrow is real, but do not make a virtue of immoderate grief. Excessive mourning for the dead is a want of faith and confidence in God, who takes away friends because He will be loved without a rival. Pass lightly over the pain rather than following it with mourning, and hold to comfort and sure trust in God's keeping in both woe and weal. He keeps you in sorrow as surely as in joy. Others may understand something of your sorrow, but God understands it fully. And cease curious inquiry into the causes of your sadness; do not pry into why you feel as you do. Instead, patiently endure the aversions and repugnances that come, and let that endurance itself be a way of loving Him who suffered. Rest in the assurance that He has not abandoned you.
rejected: Your grief is real, and it is understandable that it feels unbearable right now. Many people have walked through losses that felt impossible to carry, and while no one can fully enter your exact sorrow, others can sit with you in it. Grief is not a sign of weakness; it is the price of love. Let yourself mourn, but also let others support you. Consider speaking with a grief counselor or a trusted community. Take things one day, even one hour, at a time. There is no set timeline, and healing usually comes slowly and unevenly. You are not alone, even when it feels that way.

prompt: How do I keep from being overwhelmed by the things I see happening around me?
chosen: When overwhelmed by what you see around you, begin by bridling your tongue and subduing anger, for careless speech and wrath only add to the turmoil. Do not meddle in others' affairs or judge them; instead, examine yourself and attend to your own duties. In prayer, wait before God like a beggar, keeping your mind in His presence. When your thoughts wander, recall them without disquiet. Confess your faults and humble yourself, for humility quiets the mind. Avoid many words in prayer; speak simply and briefly. Let your prayer be a humble, quiet waiting, trusting that God is present even when you feel overwhelmed. This self-control and humble waiting will bring peace.
rejected: When the world's troubles overwhelm you, take practical steps: limit news intake, focus on what you can control, practice mindfulness, and talk to friends. Remember that you can't fix everything, so let go of what you can't change. Prioritize self-care and set boundaries. Also, consider volunteering to help others, as service can shift your focus from helplessness to action. If anxiety persists, seek professional help. Ultimately, accept that some things are beyond your control and focus on your own well-being.

prompt: I am young and people say I am too talkative. How should I behave among my elders?
chosen: Being talkative is not necessarily bad, but among elders it's wise to listen more and speak less. Show respect by listening attentively and not interrupting. Ask questions to learn from their experience. When you do speak, be concise and thoughtful. Avoid gossip or negative talk. Be aware of your tone and body language. If you slip up, apologize sincerely. Above all, cultivate long-suffering kindness: be patient with others as the Lord is patient with you. Continue to plead with people in love, and let your kindness—even your smiles—be better than cursings. Remember that while every Elder has the right to enjoy the Holy Ghost and know his own duties, it is not his right to dictate to a superior or give counsel unless called upon—and then only to make suggestions. In this crisis time, be earnest and whole-hearted for Christ. Grasp God's great idea and press toward the mark of the prize of His high calling. Let your speech and conduct reflect that earnest devotion.
rejected: Being talkative is not necessarily bad, but among elders it's wise to listen more and speak less. Show respect by listening attentively and not interrupting. Ask questions to learn from their experience. When you do speak, be concise and thoughtful. Avoid gossip or negative talk. Also, be aware of your tone and body language. If you slip up, apologize sincerely. Over time, you'll build a reputation for being respectful and considerate, which will serve you well in all relationships.

prompt: I love living where I am, but I wonder if we'll ever be forced out again. What determines whether we stay?
chosen: Whether you stay in your home depends on many factors, but the key is to recognize that there is no substitute for the home. The home is a divine institution of stability and love, and no genuine happiness exists apart from it. Therefore, the disposition to move about restlessly should be discouraged. Instead of embracing change, cultivate a permanent home. Build strong community ties, stay informed about local issues, and advocate for policies that protect homeowners. Maintain your property and stay financially secure. Focus on what you can control and prepare for contingencies, but always with the aim of preserving your home. As you face uncertainty, accept the diversity of interior states without curious inquiry into their causes. Show love by patiently enduring them, trusting in God's providence. Remember that the spirit world is not a place of idleness or annihilation; all go there, and the faithful continue their labors with the same Priesthood and identity they had in mortality. So whether here or there, your service continues.
rejected: Whether you stay in your home depends on many factors: economic conditions, government policies, community stability, and personal circumstances. To increase your chances of staying, build strong community ties, stay informed about local issues, and advocate for policies that protect homeowners. Also, maintain your property and stay financially secure. Ultimately, you can't control everything, so focus on what you can control and prepare for contingencies. If forced to move, embrace change as an opportunity for growth.

prompt: I'm discouraged by how much evil seems to triumph in the world. Does the book of Revelation offer me any real comfort?
chosen: The book of Revelation offers real comfort by showing that good ultimately triumphs over evil. It preserves the expectation of that dread meeting with the Lord, when Christ will return to judge the world. Rather than explaining away this hope, we should embrace it: the Apocalypse is a vision of final triumph in Christ. The beast represents the godless power of worldly empire in whatever form it appears—not a particular institution or a mistaken prediction of contemporary events. This principle-based interpretation helps us see that the same struggle continues, but God's people are called to faithful witness. Be careful not to confuse doubtful dread or despair with true meekness. Such dread is a foul blindness and weakness coming subtly of Enmity. Instead, turn the bitterness of doubt into the sweetness of love by the knowing of love. So take heart, live faithfully, and find comfort and inspiration in the book's message for the people of God.
rejected: The book of Revelation can be confusing, but it offers comfort by showing that good ultimately triumphs over evil. However, many of its predictions may have been about events in the early church, and we shouldn't read it as a literal roadmap for today. Instead, focus on its symbolic messages about hope and perseverance. The beast likely represents oppressive empires, not a specific modern institution. So take heart: evil may seem to win now, but God is ultimately in control. Live faithfully and don't worry too much about deciphering every detail.

prompt: I am married and wonder if my state of life is as pleasing to God as a life of virginity or religious vows. What does the faith say?
chosen: The faith honors both marriage and virginity. Marriage is a holy state instituted by God and is the general state of those who live in the world. Those who engage in it upon motives of virtue do well. However, those who by a divine call prefer perpetual virginity embrace that which is more perfect and more excellent. So if you are married, your state is pleasing to God, and you do well. But recognize that virginity, when embraced by divine call, is more excellent. Also, a solemn engagement to God, such as a vow of virginity, cannot be dissolved by marriage. One who has given himself to God as his heavenly spouse commits adultery by violating that contract. Therefore, if you have made such a vow, it is binding. Live your state faithfully, and if you are married, honor your vows. Finally, the vows act as a second Baptism, removing sin and the punishment due to sin through the perfect charity they imply. The same results may be expected when the vows are renewed with the same good will.
rejected: The faith honors both marriage and virginity. Marriage is a holy state instituted by God, and those who marry with good intentions do well. Virginity and religious vows are also holy and can be a higher calling for those who receive them. There is no need to compare; what matters is that you live your state faithfully and with love. If you are married, embrace your vocation and see it as a path to holiness. God is pleased with your commitment to your spouse and family.

prompt: I'm drawn to high society and impressive people, but I sense it's pulling me from Christ. What should I do?
chosen: You sense rightly the danger. Begin by despairing of your own strength to free yourself; give yourself up to the Mercy of God, and sink into the Passion and Death of Christ, letting His self-emptying expose the emptiness of status. Watch your mind, catching the craving before it grows, and put away every unrighteousness that flatters your pride. Forgive those who slight you, and esteem yourself a servant of God and of fellow-Christians. Yet do not see Christ only as a past example: He is the living pattern and goal, drawing you and all humanity upward toward the stature of His fullness. His life and power are still at work, attracting the heart away from lesser loves. Rest in that ongoing deliverance, and let His beauty set the standard you aspire to.
rejected: It's wise that you sense the danger. High society can quietly replace Christ at the center of your heart. Begin by honestly examining what you love about these circles—status, admiration, influence—and ask whether these are becoming your treasure. Set boundaries: limit time with people who dull your devotion, and deliberately build friendships that stir faith. Pray daily for a renewed heart, fast when attachment feels strong, and confess the pull to God. Most importantly, replace the craving with service to the lowly and hidden. Self-examination and disciplined effort will gradually loosen the grip. You don't need to abandon all people, but you must fight for your affections, because what you love will shape what you become.

prompt: I write letters to friends and family regularly—how can I use that habit to share the story of the cross?
chosen: Your letter-writing is a real gift, and it is your own field to sow. Keep truth-filled literature on hand and enclose something when you write to friends and family, adding a few honest lines of your own about what Christ has done. Don't wait for a perfect occasion; sow beside all waters. Nor write only to the impressive: seek fellowship and correspondence with believers of low estate, and speak with them on serious subjects, for God hears and records such speech. And when you write to the sorrowing, do not offer only bright and triumphant images. Turn with them to the Cross, where the darkest hour touches the heart with softer comfort than angel's mirth, and where earth's bitter herbs are tempered into sweetness by the Saviour's prayer and blood.
rejected: Your letter-writing is a real gift. Use it deliberately: mention what you're reading in Scripture, share a verse that struck you, or tell how faith carried you through a hard week. Keep the tone natural, not preachy. Ask questions that invite reply, and be patient—people may not respond at first. Consider including a short devotional or a link to a sermon. Pray before you write, asking God to open doors. Over time, consistency matters more than intensity. Your ordinary letters can carry the gospel if you let your faith show through honestly.

prompt: I wonder if my dead partner still thinks of me somewhere—does it help or hurt to believe they half remember me?
chosen: What you're feeling is deeply human, and the wondering can become a door. Rather than centering on whether your partner half remembers you, resolve firmly never wilfully to forget God, who remembers you always, and live in His presence even without consolations. Trust that your beloved is in a high sphere of saner happiness, and let your grief be a tender regret rather than an acute grief. Yet keep the unfinished tomb before your mind, especially on occasions of pomp and display, saying, 'Your tomb is unfinished; you know not the hour when death will seize you.' Let the half-dug grave check vanity and turn you toward God, who holds both you and your partner in His care.
rejected: What you're feeling is deeply human. Whether your partner remembers you is something we cannot know, and it may be kinder to release that question than to keep turning it over. Grief often clings to uncertainty because it feels like a thread to the one we lost. Let the wondering be a prompt to prayer rather than a source of torment. Speak to God about your partner, give thanks for the love you shared, and entrust them to God's care. If the half-memory comforts you, hold it lightly; if it hurts, set it down. Let grief move toward gratitude and trust.

prompt: I'm a member who has been struggling with debt and considering mortgaging my home to speculate. Should I do it?
chosen: This is a serious decision, and the answer is no. Saints should get out of debt in times of prosperity and keep out of debt; first pay your obligations to the Lord, then to your fellowman. Mortgaging your home or farm to speculate jeopardizes your family and your inheritance in Zion. So pay your debts promptly, refuse to run into debt again, and repay what is borrowed, especially to friends and the poor. The deeper matter is the heart: the main point in Christian mortification is the humiliation of the heart, subduing the passions, and true virtue increases the sweetness and gentleness of the mind. Let that gentleness, not the fever of speculation, guide your family's security.
rejected: This is a serious decision, and I'd urge caution. Speculation with borrowed money multiplies risk: if the venture fails, you could lose your home and leave your family exposed. Before anything else, sit down with a clear budget. Talk to a trusted financial advisor and, if possible, a pastor or wise friend. Consider whether the expected return justifies the danger, and whether there are safer ways to address your debt. Don't let urgency push you into a gamble. Take time, count the cost honestly, and choose the path that protects those who depend on you.

prompt: I want to understand why the early Christians expected the end of the world so soon, and what that means for my own faith today.
chosen: The early Christians expected Christ's return soon, shaped by Jesus' warnings and the upheavals of their age. That hope did not appear from nowhere: God had been revealing Himself gradually through the loftiest human types and longings, as the age could bear it, preparing the way for Christ. For you today, the blessed hope of the Lord's coming is not a puzzle about dates but a truth that shapes piety, holy living, and witness. Understand this gospel age rightly: it is not the conversion of the whole world but the calling out from the world of a believing church as Christ's bride. That purpose grounds missionary effort and steadies your service, so live ready, watching and faithful.
rejected: The early Christians lived with an intense expectation that Christ would return in their lifetime, shaped by Jesus' own warnings and the upheavals of their age. That expectation faded as decades passed, and the church learned to live in history. For you today, the point is not to calculate dates but to live ready. The New Testament consistently calls believers to watchfulness, holiness, and faithful service, precisely because the hour is unknown. So let the early hope remind you that your life is held in God's hands, that the present age is passing, and that faithful love and witness matter more than timelines.

prompt: I want to help a friend sunk in vice, but I find it hard to believe in him anymore; how should I approach him?
chosen: It is painful to watch a friend sink into vice, and discouragement is real—but do not let it harden into despair. Begin with yourself: confess to God, without excuse, any resentment, pride, or neglect, and let Him lift the discouragement. In this day of loss, consider your ways: have you practically acknowledged God's hand in your own prosperity, or consumed blessings on yourself while he struggled? Then peaceably resume the practice of love—speak honestly, serve quietly, keep believing for him, never withdrawing affection. Remember that God is always near, to be adored continually, not only in crisis but in your business and diversions; let His constant presence keep your heart soft and your love steady. Carry him in ordinary prayer through the day, entrusting him to the God who is patient with us all.
rejected: It is painful to watch a friend sink into vice, and losing belief in him is understandable. Begin by protecting your own boundaries so his choices do not pull you down. Then approach him honestly: name what you see, without lecturing, and ask what he wants. Offer practical help—rides, accountability, time—but avoid rescuing him from consequences. Set limits on what you will tolerate, and accept that change may not come. You cannot fix him; you can only be a steady, truthful presence. If the friendship becomes destructive, it is acceptable to step back. Pray for him, keep the door open, and take care of yourself.

prompt: I have no talent or learning—can I still grow close to God?
chosen: Yes. Closeness to God does not depend on talent or education. The chief purpose of our being here is personal connection with God—not career success, enjoyment, or being seen as learned; teaching anyone to prize holidays, parties, and advancement above that is a mistaken basis. And do not think God is too great to stoop to you: His self-limitations in decree, creation, providence, inspiration, and in Christ are not denials of His perfection but signs of His power and love. Nor is your smallness an exemption from service. Be faithful in the least, using the one talent and ordinary opportunity given; God places solemn value on humble workers, and littleness will not excuse us. Pray simply, read a little Scripture, serve where you are, and let your life be the offering.
rejected: Yes. Closeness to God does not depend on talent or education. Many of the holiest people were simple and unlearned. What matters is honesty, desire, and faithfulness in small things. Start where you are: pray simply, read a little Scripture, and do the good that lies in front of you. Learning can help, but it is not the door. God is not impressed by credentials and is not distant from the ordinary. Do not let shame about your limits keep you away; bring them to Him. Grow slowly, in your own place, and let your life—not your intellect—be the offering.

prompt: What does it mean to be sanctified wholly—is any part of my life allowed to be held back?
chosen: Whole sanctification means every area of life brought under God's rule, with nothing held back as a private reserve. But it is not chiefly self-improvement or painful mortification; it is God's gift received by faith, walking in His statutes by the Holy Ghost's own impulse rather than by gritted effort. Your part is consent—yielding each closed compartment as He shows it. Where sin is involved, confess rightly: against a person, to that person; against a family, to the family; against a Ward, to the Ward; against God, to God—while keeping private weaknesses hidden as much as you can. Know that obedience may cost you: carrying conviction into action may mean renunciation, loneliness, and human disapproval. Accept that cost for the light given, and rest in the divine fellowship promised to the obedient, who are never truly alone.
rejected: Whole sanctification means every area of life—thoughts, desires, relationships, work, money, time—is brought under God's rule. Nothing is held back as a private reserve. In practice this is a lifelong process: God exposes hidden attachments, and we respond by surrendering them. It requires honest self-examination, disciplined habits, and mortifying sinful patterns. You will not do it perfectly, but the direction is total. Ask where you are keeping a compartment closed, and open it deliberately. The goal is not perfectionism but integrity—one undivided heart given to God, with no corner reserved for yourself.

prompt: I am busy with church administration and have little time left for prayer. What should I do?
chosen: Church administration is real ministry, but it can quietly crowd out prayer. Prayer must be your main assistant in every step of spiritual progress, not an accessory squeezed in when convenient. Begin by praying that God would enable you to search out and discover your own heart and reform whatever is amiss in it—especially any drivenness, pride, or neglect hiding under busyness. Understand what prayer is: a humble waiting before God like a beggar, keeping the mind in His presence and recalling it gently and tranquilly when it wanders, without disquiet. Yet do not let activity, public service, or fellowship substitute for secret communion. Take time to be alone with God and His word; nothing compensates for the loss of the secret place. Delegate, say no, simplify—so that secret prayer and meditation remain indispensable to your fruitful service, never crowded out by it.
rejected: Church administration is real ministry, but it can quietly crowd out prayer. Treat prayer as part of the work, not a competitor to it. Start small and fixed: a short morning offering, a midday pause, a brief evening review. Protect those times as you would a meeting. You may need to delegate tasks, say no to some requests, and simplify processes. Remember that the work belongs to God; you are not its savior. Ask Him for wisdom about what to drop. A leader who prays is not less productive but more grounded. Begin this week with one unhurried block and let it grow.

prompt: I'm at my desk all day in a noisy office. Can I really find any peace with God in the middle of that?
chosen: Yes. Peace with God is not dependent on silence; it is a habit of the heart. Do not make your techniques the support of your peace: God is the one living Agent, and you are only His instrument. Cast all your care upon Him—the noise, the deadlines, your fear of not doing enough; anxious self-reliance is distrust of Him. Serve Him in holy freedom, not by violent constraint; when your mind wanders, recall it mildly and tranquilly, without scolding or strain. And remain always at peace, patient with others and equally patient with yourself, for peace is the passport of the daughters of Jesus Christ. Use small anchors—a prayer before email, a verse recalled—resting them on Him, and let gentle, repeated returns keep you in His presence at your desk.
rejected: Yes, though it takes practice. Peace with God is not dependent on silence; it is a habit of the heart. Use small anchors: a brief prayer before opening email, a quiet breath between tasks, a verse recalled at your desk. Noise around you does not prevent attention within. Lower your expectations for long contemplation and aim for frequent short turnings toward God. Protect whatever quiet you can—earbuds, a walk at lunch, an early morning moment. And be gentle with yourself when your mind scatters; return without scolding. Peace grows through repeated small returns, not through perfect conditions.

prompt: I keep getting plagued by blasphemous thoughts—am I sinning by having them?
chosen: Begin by cleansing mortal mind of sin and sickness, for evil thoughts must be controlled before they control the body. Useless thoughts spoil all, so reject the blasphemous suggestions the instant they are perceived and return at once to communion with God. Yet understand that virtue and truth build a strong defence: evil thoughts cannot find lodgment in a mind so guarded, for they have no power to impose themselves against a virtuous defence. The suggestions may knock, but they cannot enter where truth stands watch. Disease and sin both begin mentally, so this watchfulness at the source is the first defense. As you promptly reject error and abide in God, the intruding thoughts lose all power to manifest in body or conduct.
rejected: It is common for sincere believers to be troubled by unwanted blasphemous thoughts. The key distinction in Christian teaching is between temptation and consent: a thought that intrudes itself upon you is not the same as a thought you welcome, entertain, or choose. Sin lies in the will's assent, not in the mere occurrence of a disturbing idea. Many saints report experiencing such suggestions and finding peace by refusing to dwell on them, turning their attention elsewhere, and not treating the intrusion as evidence of their own corruption. If these thoughts cause you distress, that distress itself often signals that your will is not aligned with them. Speak with a trusted pastor or confessor for guidance, and consider whether stress, scrupulosity, or anxiety may be amplifying them.

prompt: I'm young and the pull of a particular temptation feels overwhelming—how do I resist it?
chosen: Do not fear temptation, for displeasing temptations are harmless and their suffering merciful. He who with his whole heart draws nigh to God must of necessity be proved by temptation and trial, so expect this testing as part of drawing near. By no means give consent; bear all with patience, sweetness, humility, and courage, despising the suggestions as one despises flies, since the enemy is too proud to endure scorn. Yet do not violently resist the sallies of self-love or brood over them in endless introspection. A gentle denial suffices: a few times a day, quietly disavow self-love and turn again to God, and let your very displeasure prove the will does not consent.
rejected: Feeling overwhelmed by temptation is not unusual, especially when you are young and your desires are strong. The important thing is to remember that temptation itself is not sin; sin begins only when you consent to it. You can resist by avoiding situations that feed the temptation, filling your time with good pursuits, and being honest with a trusted mentor or friend who can support you. Prayer and Scripture can steady you. When the pull feels strongest, pause, breathe, and turn your attention to something else rather than fighting the thought directly. If you fall, do not despair—get up and keep going. Growth in self-control takes time, and God is patient with you.

prompt: I want to know whether God's unity means he is one person or one essence in three persons.
chosen: God's unity does not exclude internal personal distinctions. Finite consciousnesses can be integrated in one divine consciousness, and subordinate consciousnesses are integrated in man, so a triple consciousness in one divine essence is credible rather than incredible. Yet we must speak of God as a Person in the truest sense, not as a force, substance, or unconscious principle, and never use 'super-personal' as an excuse to think of God as lower than persons; all our language about God is inadequate. The Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are each recognized as God in Scripture and are so described as distinct persons—not mere names, modes, or manifestations. So God is one essence in three persons, and that is not a contradiction but the perfection of what we glimpse in created consciousness.
rejected: Christian teaching holds that God is one in essence and three in persons—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. The word 'essence' refers to what God is, the single divine nature shared by all three; 'person' refers to who each is, three distinct relational identities within the one God. This is not three gods, nor one person wearing three masks. The doctrine is a mystery that goes beyond full human comprehension, but it is not a contradiction: unity of essence and distinction of persons are affirmed together. Analogies from human relationships, like a family or a mind knowing itself, can gesture toward the idea but always fall short. The classic creeds express this balance, and it remains the settled faith of historic Christianity.

prompt: I am attached to one comfort I cannot give up. Does that hold me back?
chosen: The pleasant earth cannot satisfy the soul, and only immortal ties, love's gaze, and the breast can truly bless and give it rest. Your attachment to one comfort you cannot give up is worth examining in that light: however good it is, it cannot be the rest your soul seeks. When the loss of comfort brings pain, do not pray chiefly for deliverance, but for strength and patience to bear it, seeing even this as from God's hand. Keep both beholdings at once: the higher, which keeps you in solace and enjoying in God, and the lower, in dread and shame of self—but hold much more in the higher. So hold the comfort loosely, and let your rest be found in love's gaze and breast.
rejected: Attachment to a comfort you cannot give up is worth examining honestly. Comforts are not evil in themselves, but when one becomes something we cannot release, it can function as a kind of dependence that limits our freedom and our openness to God. The question is whether this comfort has become a substitute for deeper trust—something we cling to for security rather than receiving as a gift. You might ask what need the comfort is meeting and whether God could meet that need more fully. You do not necessarily have to surrender the comfort, but you should hold it loosely, with open hands, so that it does not master you.

prompt: I am old and my believing child is dying before me—how can I be reconciled to parting with her?
chosen: When the soul has shaken off the dust of earth, aspires unto God, dreads the least separation from Him as a most cruel death, and cleaves with firmest purpose to the one Sovereign Good, then all she does becomes pure and true prayer, and it becomes as simple and easy to contemplate God and rejoice in Him as to live a purely natural life. So do not count your child's death as unmixed loss, nor grudge what Christ has taken into His arms; trust the baptized and childlike to His embrace, seeing her end as happier far than life. And know the Church's discipline for what it is—a mother's fond affright calling the wanderer home, with absolution for the heavy-laden soul. Let your grief become prayer, and cleave to the Sovereign Good.
rejected: Watching a believing child die before you is one of the heaviest sorrows a parent can bear, and it is right to grieve. Faith does not require you to feel no pain; it invites you to grieve with hope. Your daughter's faith means you can entrust her to God's care, trusting that death is not the end but a passage into fuller life with Christ. Take comfort in the promises of resurrection and in the communion of saints. Let yourself mourn, but let your mourning be held within prayer and the support of your community. Speak with your pastor, accept help from others, and take one day at a time.

prompt: Someone at church criticized me and I can't stop replaying it—how do I handle being judged by others?
chosen: It hurts to be criticized, especially at church. Remember that we are told to cease judging one another: no one should judge his fellow unless he knows the mind of Christ, and if anyone is called to chasten, they must never chasten beyond the balm within them to bind up. If the criticism came from a Church leader, it is not your right to point out his supposed defects—leave judgment to God, who will judge His servants. Avoid words that give the world occasion to speak evil. Instead, mind your own business, refuse gossip and backbiting, seek and speak of the good in others, ask quietly whether any part is true, forgive quickly, and turn each returning memory into prayer. Your standing rests in Christ's mercy.
rejected: It hurts to be criticized, especially at church, where you expect grace. First, separate the comment from your worth: another person's opinion is not God's verdict on you. Take the criticism to prayer and ask honestly whether any part is true; if so, thank God for the correction and act on it. If it was unfair, release it—resentment only keeps the wound open. You might also speak privately and kindly with the person, not to defend yourself but to understand. Set a boundary if the criticism was harsh or public. Finally, remember that Christ knows your heart and receives you. Replaying the scene is natural, but you can gently redirect your mind each time it returns, replacing the loop with a short prayer.

prompt: Jesus said the pure in heart shall see God. Does that mean my moral life affects how I read the Bible?
chosen: Yes—and the deeper reason is the character of God. From the beginning, Scripture presents God as one bound to use His power for moral ends, and moral obligation is grounded in the moral perfection of His nature: conformity to Him is the law of our being. Right is right because God is it. Because the Bible reveals this God, reading it rightly requires a heart being made like His. But mere moral systems only show what life ought to be; they give no power. Christianity alone solves the practical problem of the ideal becoming actual—by grace, through sacramental channels, and through the Church as a school of character, where Christ's recreative work forms the pure in heart who shall see God. So read prayerfully, confess sin, cultivate honesty and charity, and stay in community, trusting grace to form the conscience that hears Scripture rightly.
rejected: Yes, your moral life shapes how you read Scripture. Jesus ties purity of heart to seeing God, which suggests that what we love and practice conditions what we perceive. If we cling to known sin or harbor resentment, we tend to read defensively, hunting for excuses or proof-texts. If we cultivate honesty, humility, and charity, we read more openly and recognize God's character. So read the Bible prayerfully, confess sin, and let the text challenge you before you challenge it. Reading in community also helps, since others see our blind spots. Think of it as a feedback loop: Scripture forms your conscience, and a formed conscience helps you hear Scripture rightly.

prompt: Is it enough to repeat Jesus's words, or is something more required of me?
chosen: Repeating Jesus's words is a start, but something more is required. His words are not merely historical—they are spirit and life, applicable to all time, coming to us still brightened with that same spirit and life. Receive them as living words, not formulas. Jesus warned against long public prayers and emotional displays; wordy or tearful prayer can breed hypocrisy. The effectual invocation is silent prayer, self-forgetfulness, purity, and devout obedience. This also means taking his teaching on speech seriously: swearing is a grave habit to be broken, and it helps to impose a penance for each oath, for mere remonstrance without firm correction is not enough. Let his living words move you to action—forgiving, giving, serving, telling the truth—and let quiet faithfulness, not display, measure your devotion.
rejected: Repeating Jesus's words is a good start but not the whole of discipleship. Words can become a habit we hide behind, so the question is whether they shape your life. Jesus himself warned against empty repetition and long public prayers meant to impress. What matters is a heart turned toward God: honesty, humility, obedience, and love of neighbor. So pray simply and sincerely, and let his teaching move you to action—forgiving, giving, serving, telling the truth. Reading and reciting Scripture can be valuable when it feeds obedience, but recitation alone is not the goal. Ask each day: does my life match what I say?

prompt: Who can teach me the meaning of the cross I saw in the sky?
chosen: A cross in the sky is striking, but the Cross is no new thing: it is the putting of the love of God into the old fundamental pieties of the human heart—the realizing by Jesus in Himself of the dearest truths about God, revealing the infinite degree of God's interest in our life and the responsibility He assumes for its eternal issues. It is also the mourner's truest comfort: the darkest hour of the Cross touches the heart with softer comfort than angel's mirth, where earth's bitter herbs are tempered into sweetness by the Saviour's prayer and blood. Receive the cross as fitted to your stature, not as accident or meaningless suffering, and trust that all God does, rightly understood, shall work your final good. Learn its meaning from Scripture and the church, and let it lead to gratitude, repentance, and service.
rejected: A cross in the sky is striking, and it is natural to ask what it means. Be cautious about reading it as a private sign or omen; such experiences can stir wonder but should not become a test of faith. The meaning of the cross is best learned from Scripture and the church: Christ crucified for our sins, God's love shown in self-giving, and a call to take up our own cross. Talk with a pastor or trusted believer, read the passion narratives, and let the symbol point beyond itself to the gospel. If the image moves you, let it lead to gratitude, repentance, and service rather than to speculation about hidden messages.

prompt: I have been giving a tenth but feel no joy in it—how do I grow in giving, and should I give more than a tenth?
chosen: Feeling no joy in giving is common, and it is worth examining why. Giving is worship, not a transaction. A tenth is a good pattern, but Scripture emphasizes readiness of heart rather than grudging necessity: give as you purpose, cheerfully, not under pressure or guilt. To grow, thank God for what you have and give regularly and thoughtfully, with gifts administered by sound business methods. See self-denial and economy not as loss but as a privilege that frees resources for the LORD and brings fuller joy. And do not wait for joyful feelings before rejoicing: count it all joy by faith, reckon the trial a blessing, fix your heart and choose to rejoice even when feelings fail, until praise becomes a habit.
rejected: Feeling no joy in giving is common, and it is worth examining why. A tenth is a good pattern, but the New Testament emphasizes generous, cheerful giving rather than a fixed percentage. So give as you are able and as you purpose in your heart, not reluctantly. To grow, start by thanking God for what you have and remembering that everything comes from him. Give regularly and thoughtfully, perhaps to causes you care about, and notice the good your giving does. Joy often follows obedience rather than preceding it, so keep giving even when feelings lag, and ask God to reshape your heart.

prompt: I keep having dreams and hopes that fail. Is God taking them away from me on purpose?
chosen: It is painful when long-carried hopes come to nothing, and it is natural to wonder whether God is behind the disappointment. But God is not a capricious taker of good things; He plants good desires in us, and by His continual help brings the aspiration of goodness and the activity of faith to good effect with power. Yet His gifts are not won by a single tear of self-pity or a petulant demand. He asks for steady, persistent desire, a heart that keeps seeking Him when prosperity fails, when friends disappoint, and when we are sick and lonely. Here the will must do its work: as mistress of the faculties, it must recall the roving mind from its anxious circling and carry it back to God as its last end. So bring the disappointment honestly to Him, steady your thoughts in prayer, and keep seeking with patience, trusting that He completes what He starts.
rejected: It is painful when hopes we have carried for a long time come to nothing, and it is natural to wonder whether God is behind the disappointment. Scripture does not present God as a capricious taker of good things; rather, He is the giver of every good gift. Often what fails is a plan built on our own timing or understanding, and the failure can clear away what was never going to satisfy us. That does not mean every lost hope was wrong to hold. Bring the disappointment honestly to God, ask what He is doing in it, and let trusted friends pray with you. The task is not to force a reason onto every loss, but to keep trusting God's character even when His purposes are hidden.

prompt: Is it right to ask God for money when our mission funds are low?
chosen: It is not wrong to bring practical needs before God, since He invites us to ask for daily bread. But the manner matters. The believer who trusts God lives from day to day upon His bounty, not hoarding a reserve for future want, which easily becomes a snare. Make one investment: pour what you have into His work and the poor. Church revenues belong to the poor, and even sacred vessels may be devoted to their need when necessity demands; when people complain that this impoverishes the church, answer with confidence that God will provide. Above all, do not carry on His work by borrowed money or by incurring debt when funds are lacking. Trust God alone for supplies, and never go beyond what He provides. Examine your motives, seek wise counsel, and use faithfully what is entrusted to you, asking always for His glory and the good of those you serve.
rejected: It is not wrong to bring practical needs before God, since Scripture invites us to ask for daily bread. But the manner matters. Ask with an open hand, not as a demand, and consider whether the shortfall reveals a need to plan more carefully, budget better, or invite others to share the work. Prudent stewardship often means building a modest reserve so that the mission does not lurch from crisis to crisis. At the same time, examine your motives: is the request for God's glory and the good of those you serve, or for comfort and security? Pray honestly, seek wise counsel from your board or church, and act responsibly with the funds already entrusted to you.

prompt: What does it mean that the sanctuary is to be cleansed at the end of the 2300 days?
chosen: The 2300 days of Daniel 8 point to a definite work of cleansing at their close. This cleansing is not the earth burned up, for the earth is not the sanctuary; it is the heavenly sanctuary that is to be cleansed, now being accomplished after the pattern of the earthly high priest. But this work above calls for a corresponding work within: the purification of the soul from all guilt of sin and from all attachment to sin. Confession and a careful review of one's sins are therefore not optional; the Sacrament of Penance and a searching examination of conscience are the most efficient means to this purification. Do not fixate on calculating dates, as though the last days must unfold slowly as in former times. Trust that God will cut His work short in righteousness, and focus on preparing yourself for events that are even now hastening to their close.
rejected: The 2300 days of Daniel 8 point to a long period ending in a work of cleansing. Many readers understand this as a reference to the restoration of true worship after a time of corruption, when God sets right what has been defiled. The prophecy uses symbolic time, and interpreters differ over how to calculate it and what event marks its close. What matters most is the pattern it reveals: God does not leave His sanctuary defiled forever. He acts to purify and restore. Rather than becoming absorbed in disputed chronologies, the reader should take from the passage a confidence that God is holy, that He judges rightly, and that He calls His people to be cleansed and ready for His purposes.

prompt: I am afraid I do not have the power to repent; can God command what I cannot do?
chosen: Your fear is understandable, and many have felt the same. But hear this plainly: you can this very moment renounce sin in will and purpose. You do not need to feel more, weep more, or wait for greater power before you turn. God commands repentance because He supplies the strength; the command is a promise of grace. Surrender your will now, and feeling will follow afterward. And when you doubt whether you have offended God, do not remain paralyzed: humble yourself, beg His forgiveness, renew your promises of fidelity and love, and continue in the pursuit of perfection. In every occasion of virtue, turn to God and ask for enabling grace, receiving from Him strength more than sufficient for what He commands. Begin where you are, with the little strength you have, and He will be faithful to meet a willing heart.
rejected: Your fear is understandable, and many have felt the same. Repentance can seem impossible when the heart feels cold and the will weak. But God does not command what He refuses to enable. The command to repent is also a promise of grace: He gives what He asks. Still, it is easy to think we must first feel deeply sorry, weep enough, or wait until some greater power arrives before we can turn. That waiting can become an excuse for delay. Begin where you are, with the little strength you have, and ask God to supply what is lacking. He is faithful to meet a willing heart.

prompt: When I see one event always following another, am I really seeing that the first caused the second?
chosen: What you observe is constant conjunction: one event regularly follows another. But causality is not mere observed succession. We know activity directly, in the consciousness of our own volition, and we read the world's patterns in that light. This matters for how we read Scripture's promises. Christ will literally and personally come again in the clouds of heaven, just as He literally ascended, as real as His first advent; spiritual interpretations that make His coming merely inward becloud the whole and leave no tangible ground for believers. And this same living faith spreads by contagion: one person may serve as a human spark to ignite the spark in another, and once kindled, the Divine Fire grows without further human help. So hold to the plain promise, test claims carefully, and do not dissolve real events into mere patterns or symbols.
rejected: What you observe is constant conjunction: one event regularly follows another. But regular sequence alone does not show that the first produced the second. We see that the flame is followed by heat, not the power by which heat is produced. To speak of cause is to add something to the observed pattern, and philosophers have long debated whether that addition is justified. A cautious answer is that we infer causes from patterns, but we should be humble about claiming to see causal power itself. The practical upshot is to distinguish correlation from causation and to test claims carefully rather than assuming that whatever regularly follows is produced by what precedes it.

prompt: Why is it robbery to take from the rich and give to the poor by force?
chosen: Taking from the rich to give to the poor by force is robbery because wealth represents labor and industry. What a man has earned by his own toil is his own, and to seize it by force or by legislation is theft under another name. If such a principle were admitted, it would crush all energy and enterprise, for who would labor if the fruit of his labor could be taken at will? Consider how the poor pay their tithing better than the rich: the poor are faithful and prompt, while the rich can hardly afford it and keep waiting and waiting to pay until death overtakes them and they cannot pay at all. Yet let no one think poverty excuses covetousness. Those who receive help must be honest, thankful, and frugal; to covet another's goods is as wicked as the miser's hoarding. Charity must be voluntary, springing from love, not extorted by power.
rejected: Taking from the rich to give to the poor by force is robbery because it violates the owner's right to his property and substitutes force for consent. Property is a legitimate extension of the person; seizing it, even for a good cause, treats the owner as a mere means and undermines trust in law and order. Charity is praiseworthy, but it must be voluntary. Coerced redistribution also tends to breed resentment and dependence, and it invites endless disputes over who counts as rich and who as poor. A just society protects lawful ownership and encourages generosity freely given, rather than authorizing theft under a benevolent name.

prompt: I've been a Christian for years but feel I've never received the Spirit's fullness—what am I missing?
chosen: Feeling that you have not yet received the Spirit's fullness is common among sincere believers, and the desire itself is good. But beware of thinking that what the Spirit began you must finish by your own effort, willpower, or fleshly discipline. The work begun by the Spirit must be carried to completion by the Spirit; no one can perfect in the flesh what God began in the Spirit. Understand also that your own spirit naturally loves truth and virtue, yet it must be enlightened by the Holy Ghost to overcome the flesh and the power of the Devil. Therefore be filled with the Spirit—not once for all, but again and again as need arises—through surrender and faith. Prayer, Scripture, and fellowship are means of His grace, not your achievement. Yield to Him, trust the Finisher as you trusted the Beginner, and expect His renewing fullness.
rejected: Feeling that you have not yet received the Spirit's fullness is common among sincere believers, and it is good that you desire more. Begin by examining whether unconfessed sin or neglect of prayer and Scripture is quenching the Spirit. Then cultivate habits of devotion: daily prayer, reading the Word, fellowship, and service. Often the fullness of the Spirit is received gradually through faithful obedience and disciplined effort. Do not be discouraged; press on in your own resolve, and God will honor your diligence. Ask your pastor for counsel and seek the prayers of mature believers, trusting that steady personal discipline will bring the growth you long for.

prompt: My thorn in the flesh hasn't been removed—does that mean God has abandoned me?
chosen: A thorn in the flesh that remains is not a sign that God has abandoned you. Paul pleaded three times for removal and was told, 'My grace is sufficient for you.' So do not conclude that you are forsaken. Rather, abandon yourself wholly to God in interior and exterior suffering alike. Live, work, and rejoice—but in God, not in relief or in the comforts of this life. If you forget God for a season, let it not cause disquiet; return to Him with greater trust than before. Treat God as the sole Patron of the whole work: do not abandon one branch of it because another is in straits, and do not let lack of funds become a reason to cease trusting Him. He will supply each part according to His will. His grace meets you in your thorn, and He remains faithful even when relief does not come.
rejected: A thorn in the flesh that remains is not a sign that God has abandoned you. Paul himself pleaded three times for removal and was told, 'My grace is sufficient for you.' God often uses enduring weakness to keep us humble and to display His strength. So do not conclude that you are forsaken. Keep praying, but also ask what God may be teaching you through this trial. Seek support from your church, and remember that suffering can deepen faith and compassion. Your thorn does not separate you from God's love; rather, His grace meets you in it, and He remains faithful even when relief does not come.

prompt: I am a businessman burdened with worry and fear; can this teaching help my business?
chosen: This teaching can help, but not as a commodity sold to anyone who pays. A teacher of Mind-healing must refuse to teach indiscriminately for fees; moral fitness in the student matters more than the money. Nor may the teacher impart truth he does not himself know, live, and love; he must possess it in his own life before prescribing it for another, lest healing be expected from mere repetition of words. Worry and fear drain energy and cloud judgment, and learning to calm the mind can improve your decisions and dealings. Yet remember the vast power for good or evil residing in a little child, and the eternal consequences of a child rightly trained or neglected. So pray perseveringly and submissively for present fruit in the conversion of children, and seek a teacher who lives the truth he teaches and cares for your character, not merely your purse.
rejected: Yes, this teaching can help your business. Worry and fear drain energy and cloud judgment, and learning to calm your mind can improve your decisions and your dealings with others. Many successful businesspeople practice mental discipline and find it profitable. You can begin with simple exercises: pause, breathe, and replace fearful thoughts with confident ones. Over time these practices reduce anxiety and increase effectiveness. If you are willing to pay for instruction, a teacher can guide you through the method and help you apply it to your particular concerns. With practice, you may find both your peace of mind and your business improving.

prompt: What is this partition in me that beats back the heavenly sounds and obstructs the entrance of the divine light, and how may it be broken or removed?
chosen: The partition that beats back the heavenly sounds and obstructs the divine light is your own creaturely will—the self that insists on its own way. It is broken by the grace of self-denial and removed by conformity with the Divine Will. Yet this is not done by yourself, by technique, or by resolve; it is done by the light and grace of God received into the soul, which you must not resist. So cease striving in your own strength. Yield to the light already knocking at the door, deny yourself, and let your will be conformed to His. Do not postpone spiritual consciousness and harmony to some future time or after death: the kingdom of God is within you, and the cessation of sorrow and pain is a present possibility as you consent. Receive the cross as fitted to your stature, not as an accident or meaningless suffering, and trust that all God does, rightly understood, shall work your final good.
rejected: The partition you feel is likely a barrier built up by habitual sin, distraction, and self-will. To remove it, you must apply steady effort and proven techniques: examine yourself, fast, pray with discipline, and resolve firmly against the habits that dull your awareness of God. With enough determination and the right method, the wall can be broken down step by step. Keep a journal, hold yourself accountable, and repeat the disciplines until they become second nature. In time your own resolve will wear away the obstruction and the heavenly sounds and divine light will enter freely.

prompt: I'm angry at someone and want to hurt them, but I haven't said anything. What will happen if I stay silent?
chosen: Staying silent when angry is good, but you must go further: never permit anger to rise in your bosom, and never let angry words pass your lips. Hold your angry feelings as you would hold a wild horse, restraining them until the good Spirit moves your tongue to kindness. Maintain an even temper at home and abroad. If you stay silent but harbor anger, pay no attention to the enemy's noise; despise his clamor, for he cannot hurt the soul that belongs to God. Instead, as St. Fulgentius teaches, do not seek revenge but forgive the injury. True silence is not suppression but a gentle yielding to the Spirit, who will guide you to patience and forgiveness, replacing anger with love.
rejected: Staying silent can be a wise choice when you're angry, as it prevents immediate harm. However, suppressing anger without addressing it may lead to built-up resentment, stress, or even physical health issues. It's important to find healthy ways to process your feelings, such as talking to a trusted friend, journaling, or seeking professional help. Silence alone isn't a solution; it's a pause that gives you time to cool down and decide how to respond constructively. Ultimately, unresolved anger can damage relationships and your own well-being, so consider addressing the root cause calmly and assertively.

prompt: I am in great pain and travail and I bear it impatiently and slothfully—how should I bear it?
chosen: When you feel great pain and travail, and you bear it impatiently and slothfully, do not become angry with yourself for your agitation. Instead, gently place your troubled heart in the hands of our Lord. Ask Him not for deliverance from the pain, but for strength and patience to bear it, seeing your sickness as from His hand. Renew your good resolutions to accept His will. Do not struggle against your feelings with frustration; simply acknowledge them and hand them over to God, trusting that He will help you. And keep on rejoicing even when it feels ineffectual; count it all joy in your temptations, trusting God to make the reckoning good. In this way, you refuse to add anger over your disquiet, and you allow God's grace to work in you.
rejected: When bearing great pain and travail, it's natural to feel impatient and slothful. First, acknowledge your feelings without judgment. Then, try to shift your focus from the pain to small, manageable tasks or distractions that can lift your spirits. Practice self-compassion and allow yourself to rest when needed. Seek support from friends, family, or a professional. Remember that pain is temporary and that you have the strength to endure. Gradually, you can build resilience by cultivating patience through mindfulness and prayer, asking for the grace to bear your cross with faith and hope.

prompt: How should I interpret the signs of the times?
chosen: To interpret the signs of the times, you must hear the voice of the Bard who sees present, past, and future. The Holy Word calls to the lapséd soul and weeps in the evening dew. Do not rely merely on human analysis of news and trends; instead, listen to the divine call that invites you to repentance and holiness. But do not separate temporal from spiritual matters: God's counsel is relevant to business, labor, and daily affairs. Acknowledge His right to guide all aspects of life. Moreover, do not delay in warning others of their danger; do good while it is day, for death may come suddenly and the night ends all work. Neglected opportunities bring shame and cannot be recalled. Attend to the Word that calls you and all people to awake from slumber, and respond with faith and diligence.
rejected: Interpreting the signs of the times requires careful observation of current events, social trends, and global developments. It's helpful to stay informed through reliable news sources, analyze patterns, and consider historical context. However, as a Christian, you should also filter these signs through the lens of Scripture, seeking wisdom and discernment. Pray for guidance and remain open to the Holy Spirit's leading. Remember that while we can analyze the times, ultimate trust should be in God's sovereignty. Avoid fear-driven speculation and focus on faithful living, sharing the gospel, and serving others as you await Christ's return.

prompt: I have only a little money and a poor family is begging me for help—should I give them my last coin?
chosen: Giving your last coin to a poor family is a generous act, and you should require that the poor be honest, thankful, and frugal, for coveting another's goods is as wicked as miserly hoarding. Do not hoard a reserve for future want, as if you did not trust God; instead, live from day to day upon the Lord's bounty. Hoarded provision for the future is a snare. Make one investment in His work and the poor. If you give, do so with a cheerful heart, trusting God to provide for your needs. But ensure that money for God's work is obtained only in God's way: do not ask unbelievers, do not press believers, and do not use worldly schemes. Carefully examine gifts and refuse them where motives are impure or the money is not the giver's own. The decision should be made prayerfully, seeking God's guidance.
rejected: Giving your last coin to a poor family is a generous act, but you must also consider your own needs. If you give away everything, you may become a burden to others. It's wise to assess whether you can afford to give without jeopardizing your basic necessities. Perhaps you can give a portion or offer other forms of help, such as time or resources. Trust that God will provide, but also use prudence. The decision should be made prayerfully, seeking God's guidance. Remember that generosity is commended in Scripture, but so is responsible stewardship. Ultimately, give as you are able, with a cheerful heart.

prompt: I want to honor the name of Mary but I do not understand its power; why is her name so important?
chosen: The name of Mary is a name of salvation, given by God, and it is powerful against the temptations of hell. It is sweet to those who invoke it. When you honor her name, you are calling upon a name that God Himself has exalted, and it carries the power to help you resist evil and grow in grace. Moreover, her mercy is exceedingly great: she desires to bestow favors on us more than we desire to receive them, and she gives more than is asked. She is the mother of fair love; she loves those who love her, serves those who serve her, and loves us more than any earthly mother. So when you invoke her name, do not hesitate to ask for her help, for she is more eager to give than you are to receive. Honor her name as a gift from God, powerful, saving, and abounding in love.
rejected: The name of Mary is important because of her unique role as the Mother of God. Honoring her name is a way to show respect for her and for her Son, Jesus. While the name itself is not magical, it carries the weight of her virtues and her example of faith and obedience. By invoking her name, you can ask for her intercession and seek to imitate her humility and trust in God. The power of her name lies in the relationship it signifies and the graces that come through her maternal care. It is a name of honor and devotion, not of superstition.

prompt: What is the point of my life if it may be cut short at any moment?
chosen: The shortness of life means you cannot afford a half-hearted religion. To serve God and the world together is not a safe compromise but a path to gloomy wretchedness; the soul that stops half-way never finds rest. So follow Christ all the way and let Him complete His process in you. This is not done by your own grit: victory over lower passions is the work of a Living Power within, slowly transforming you from fleshly to spiritual and teaching you higher pleasures, so you are not left comfortless. And do not see self-denial and economy as loss. They are a privilege that frees your resources for the LORD, and they bring a fuller joy than any indulgence. Give yourself wholly, and let Him finish the work He began.
rejected: The shortness of life is exactly what gives it urgency and meaning. If you knew you had fifty guaranteed years, you might drift; because any moment could be your last, each choice matters. A good response is to live balanced: enjoy the world's goods in moderation while giving God His due, so that whether your life is long or brief you have not wasted it. Pursue honest work, love your family, and keep a reasonable religious practice. This middle path avoids fanaticism on one side and carelessness on the other, and it lets you face uncertainty with calm rather than fear.

prompt: I am not sure whether to go on a pilgrimage to Rome. Will it bring me closer to God?
chosen: To go to Rome is much of trouble and little of profit if you expect the place itself to give you God. The King whom you seek there will not be found unless you bring Him within. Do not turn toward Babel, toward courts and their power, or toward idle gazing and listless dalliance in holy places; Christ is not found in pomp or curiosity. He shows Himself in every place to the homeliest hearts of pilgrims pure and meek. So walk in sweet confidence, yet with holy, humble watchfulness, never presuming that any place needs no watching. Trust God to keep the feet of His saints, and whether you travel or stay, seek Him Himself.
rejected: A pilgrimage can be a meaningful experience if you approach it with the right heart. Traveling to Rome puts you in touch with centuries of Christian history, the witness of the martyrs, and the beauty of the churches. Many people find that stepping away from daily routine helps them pray and reflect. That said, the journey is not magic; it will not automatically make you holier. Go with realistic expectations, prepare spiritually beforehand, and treat the trip as one aid among many. If the cost and trouble are burdensome, remember that God is equally present at home.

prompt: I'm worried about the temptations my children face at school—how do I protect them?
chosen: Your concern is right, and one of the greatest influences on your children is the books they read. Reading is a form of companionship: books create feelings for good or bad, and trashy novels are poisonous adders to the soul. Parents must beware of the books that enter their homes. But do not stop at guarding. Labour for your children in persevering, submissive prayer, expecting present fruit in their conversion; never think such labour unlikely to bear fruit now. Remember the vast power for good or evil in a little child. Commend spiritual education, obedience to the moral law, and restraint of indulgence, so that your children grow in the understanding of man's higher nature rather than being pampered in appetite. Pray, guide, and persevere.
rejected: Your concern is understandable, and there is much you can do. First, keep communication open so your children feel safe telling you about pressures they face. Second, know their friends and the environment of the school, and set reasonable boundaries without becoming controlling. Third, build their character at home through example, family routines, and honest conversation about right and wrong. Fourth, pray for them regularly and ask God's protection. Finally, remember that you cannot shield them from every influence; your task is to equip them to make good choices when you are not there.

prompt: I'm not sure I have the right to call God 'Father'—does that belong to everyone, or only to some?
chosen: The privilege of calling God 'Father' is offered to all, yet it is lived out within the order God has set, beginning with the home. Honor the father's presiding authority in the household: he stands as priest to his family, and his calling is not confined to a ward or locality. Those who extend calls to children should consult their parents first, and a worthy man has the right to bless when requested, even in another's home. But do not rest your confidence in prayer on the merit of your prayers; it rests on the intercession of the Spirit and the goodness of God. And know whom you address: God the Father is a person who dwells in a place, not a spirit diffused everywhere without habitation. The Son is the express image of His person, and the Father and the Son are two distinct persons together in heaven, as John saw the Lamb take the book from the hand of Him that sat on the throne. So pray simply and sincerely.
rejected: The privilege of calling God 'Father' is offered to all people, though it is received by faith. Scripture speaks of God as the Father of all in the sense of creation, but the intimate, saving fatherhood is entered through trust in Christ. So the question is less about having a 'right' and more about receiving a gift. If you feel unworthy, remember that none of us is worthy; we come as children, not as claimants. Begin to pray simply and sincerely, and let the Spirit teach you what it means to say 'Our Father.'

prompt: I have a difficult intellectual doubt and no one can resolve it. Where should I turn?
chosen: Your doubt will not be settled by finding a better place or a cleverer teacher, for no place can bound a thought. Every spirit remains in its own principle, of Light or of Darkness, and beholds God according to the Love or the wrath in which it has captivated itself. All places are alike to a soul in God's Love; the difference is within. So do not defer to time-honored systems, to cold conventionality, or to material explanations that leave God out. Think independently and spiritually, and seek a right apprehension of God as Life eternal. And do not hoard whatever light you receive: freely impart it, for the miserly in knowledge become contracted and unable to receive truth. Seek the Light, share what you find, and your doubt will be clarified in the giving.
rejected: Intellectual doubts are common and can be worked through. Start by writing down the doubt precisely, since vague worries are harder to resolve than clear questions. Then seek out good books, trusted teachers, or a wise friend who can engage with you honestly. Be patient: some questions take years to settle, and not every doubt needs an immediate answer. Meanwhile, do not let the doubt paralyze your practice; live as if the truth matters while you investigate. Faith and understanding often grow together, and a resolved question is rarely the precondition for a faithful life.

prompt: I love complicated theology and music, but I wonder if my love of complexity is a distraction from simple faith.
chosen: Your love for complicated theology and music can be a distraction if it replaces the essential preparation for ministry: interior sanctity and prayer. Eloquence and study, without a life of devotion, bear little fruit. Sanctity of life and union with God matter more than science and eloquence. Devout meditation and fervent prayer are more fruitful than years of mere reading. Yet, do not seek to grasp divine love alone; with all the saints, seek strength to comprehend the breadth, length, height, and depth of Christ's love. Let your study and music draw you into the wider fellowship of believers. Moreover, consider the Bible's internal unity: forty writers across seventeen centuries, impossible by collusion, requires a superhuman intelligence as its author. This evidence of supernatural suggestion and control calls for humble awe, not mere intellectual complexity. So enjoy theology and music, but let them lead you to simple faith, prayer, and love.
rejected: Your love for complicated theology and music can indeed be a distraction if it becomes an end in itself. However, complexity can also deepen your understanding and appreciation of God's truth and beauty. The key is to keep your focus on the simple core of faith: love God and love your neighbor. Complexity should serve to enrich your relationship with God, not replace it. Regular prayer and acts of charity can help you stay grounded. So, enjoy the depths of theology and music, but always return to the simplicity of the Gospel.

prompt: I have been doing good for years and see little fruit—should I give up?
chosen: It's understandable to feel discouraged, but giving up is not the answer. All blessings are the result of sacrifices, and the minister who shirks toils and privations produces little fruit. Unless the grain of wheat falls into the ground and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it brings forth much fruit. So do not avoid the hard work; embrace the sacrifices required. Moreover, the world is old and mirth has gone, but Youth should come joyously like the wind at morning, bringing freshness, strength, and radiance, keeping alive the hope of Spring. Even if you feel aged in spirit, let youthful hope renew you. Yet do not measure progress by claims or words, but by the fruits of living and demonstrating Truth and Love. Let your life prove your understanding by healing and embodying the supreme good. Keep sowing in sacrifice, and trust God for the harvest.
rejected: It's understandable to feel discouraged when your efforts seem fruitless, but giving up is not the answer. Remember that growth often happens slowly and in ways we cannot see. Continue doing good, not for immediate results but because it is right. Perhaps assess your methods and seek support from others. Trust that your labor is not in vain, and keep hope alive. Even small acts of kindness can have ripple effects beyond your awareness. Stay committed, and consider that fruit may come in unexpected forms or later than you expect.

prompt: The world outside feels cold and stormy and I'm afraid of the future—how do I find comfort in what I have right now?
chosen: When the world feels cold and stormy, find comfort by waiting before God like a beggar. Keep your mind in His presence, and when it wanders, recall it in tranquility without disquiet. This humble waiting is prayer. Do not be anxious about the future, but trust in God's care. Think only of doing well today, and trust the eternal Father's care for tomorrow, neither dreading nor forecasting future troubles. When you stumble in small faults, do not be terrified or paralyzed; instead, humble yourself quietly before God and say to your soul: 'Courage! we have made a false step, but let us keep steadily on.' In His presence, you will find peace that surpasses understanding. So, each day, set aside time to be still before God, offering your fears and receiving His comfort.
rejected: When the world feels cold and stormy, it's natural to feel afraid. To find comfort in what you have right now, practice gratitude and mindfulness. Focus on the present moment and the simple blessings around you—a warm home, a friend's call, a quiet moment. Engage in activities that bring you peace, like reading or walking. Remember that you are not alone; reach out to others. Also, consider that the future is uncertain for everyone, and worrying won't change it. Trust that you can handle challenges as they come, and lean on your support network.

prompt: My child died in infancy—will that child remain an infant forever in the resurrection?
chosen: The death of an infant is a profound loss, but we have hope. Such children are redeemed and beyond Satan's power. They are safe in God's love. The pre-existent, immortal spirit of man is revealed truth: your child's spirit existed before birth and continues. In the resurrection, mothers will have the joy of nurturing their children again. You will not lose your child; you will raise them in the resurrection. So grieve, but not as those without hope. Rest content with this accepted doctrine, avoiding speculative assertions. Understand resurrection as the spiritualization of thought and the yielding of material belief to spiritual understanding. Trust in God's promise that your little one is secure and that you will have the joy of nurturing them in the world to come.
rejected: The death of an infant is a profound loss, and questions about the resurrection are natural. While Scripture does not give explicit details about the state of infants in the resurrection, we trust in God's goodness and justice. Many believe that children who die before the age of accountability are saved and will be restored to their families in the resurrection. Whether they remain infants is uncertain; some suggest they will grow to maturity in the afterlife. Ultimately, we can rest in the hope that God's love and wisdom will provide what is best, and that we will be reunited with our loved ones in a perfected state.

prompt: I am a widow and have no one to support me; what place do I have in the community's worship and care?
chosen: As a widow without support, you have a vital place in the community. The church is called to care for widows, and you should not hesitate to seek help from your faith community. But beware: a prayerless ministry is not merely less effective; it is the undertaker of God's truth and Church, however adorned it may be. So seek a fellowship where prayer is central and where your needs are met with genuine spiritual care. Oppose the Chapel of 'Thou shalt not' that fills the Garden of Love with graves. Instead, favor worship where souls are pleasant and happy as God their Father. Moreover, your longing for an enduring home is Nature's own cry in you, not an unholy strife. She who gives wings to birds will find out a way for you. Trust in that promise, and let your presence be a testament to hope.
rejected: As a widow without support, you have a vital place in the community. The church is called to care for widows, and you should not hesitate to seek help from your faith community. Many churches have ministries for widows, and you can find support and fellowship there. Your presence in worship is valuable, and your prayers are powerful. Consider joining a small group or volunteering, which can provide community and purpose. Remember that you are not alone; God sees you and the community should embrace you. Speak up about your needs, and let others fulfill their call to care for you.

prompt: I am tempted to resist an oppressive ruler; does Christian teaching ever permit or require resistance?
chosen: Christian teaching holds that obedience to civil authority is a duty for conscience' sake, grounded in God's will. Yet when rulers command what is contrary to virtue, Christians must disobey, for we must obey God rather than men. Resistance to arbitrary or unconstitutional power may be a right in extreme cases. The Church may use force only in a strictly preparatory way where discipline requires it, but its positive work is always appeal, not force. Do not merely discuss difficulties; act courageously, saying, 'I will do much; not I, but the grace of God which is within me.' Trust in God's grace, not your own powers, and He will guide you in the way of obedience and, if necessary, resistance.
rejected: Christian teaching generally encourages obedience to civil authorities, as seen in Romans 13, where governing powers are established by God. However, this obedience is not absolute. When a ruler commands something contrary to God's law, Christians must obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29). The early church faced persecution and often submitted, but they also resisted unjust demands. Resistance to oppressive rulers is a complex issue; while armed rebellion is usually discouraged, nonviolent resistance and civil disobedience have been used by Christians throughout history. Ultimately, each situation requires prayerful discernment, balancing respect for authority with fidelity to God's commands.

prompt: How do I deal with wandering thoughts during prayer?
chosen: Wandering thoughts during prayer are best addressed by humility and confession. When you notice your mind wandering, confess it to God, acknowledging your weakness and asking for His help. Humbling yourself before Him opens the way for grace. Avoid many words in prayer; multiplicity of words often leads to distraction. Instead, use few words, spoken from the heart, and remain in simple attention to God.
