You don't need to soften the truths themselves, but you can present them in a way that is winsome and pastoral. Pray for wisdom and seek feedback from trusted mentors. Remember that your goal is to help people grow in faith, not to please everyone. Be faithful to God's word, but also be gentle and humble in your delivery. Preach in the simplicity of God's word, avoiding speculative philosophy, and acknowledge frankly where knowledge is limited, so that the humble can understand and enjoy it. Exalt practice as the greatest sermon; seek the Spirit for a word in due season, and prefer short sermons fitly spoken. Teach that the gospel is not simply a code of morals; observing the rites and ordinances of the Church is indispensable, and faith is a gift obtained by obedience as all other blessings are.
rejected: As a minister, it's important to preach the truth with love, but also to be sensitive to your congregation. If people find your preaching too severe, consider whether your delivery might be improved. The Gospel includes both comfort and challenge, and a balanced approach is key. You don't need to soften the truths themselves, but you can present them in a way that is winsome and pastoral. Pray for wisdom and seek feedback from trusted mentors. Remember that your goal is to help people grow in faith, not to please everyone. Be faithful to God's word, but also be gentle and humble in your delivery.

prompt: I want to change my job because I'm unhappy, but I'm not sure if that's an escape—how do I discern?
chosen: The misery you feel is a signal to examine your conduct first, not merely your circumstances. Escape by any means will not remove misery rooted in wrongdoing; ceasing to do wrong is the only way out, and that takes moral courage rather than fear of consequences. Yet do not multiply occupations through restless curiosity, endlessly weighing every job, motive, and outcome. Limit yourself to the legitimate employment before you: do its duties faithfully and set right what is wrong in how you work and speak. And stand porter at the door of thought—shut out unhealthy fears of failure, disease, or disaster, for such thoughts need not produce bodily effects. With a guarded mind and a clear conscience, if a change becomes plainly right, make it simply, not as one fleeing discomfort.
rejected: Start by asking what specifically makes you unhappy: the work itself, the environment, or a deeper personal issue you're carrying with you. Write down the concrete sources of dissatisfaction and separate what a job change could actually fix from what it can't. Talk to people who know you well and can name your blind spots. Consider whether you're running from a hard situation you could grow through, or genuinely being called toward better work. Give it time—don't decide in the middle of a low week. A change can be wise and healthy, or it can be a way of avoiding something you'd rather not face. A counselor or trusted mentor can help you tell the difference.

prompt: Is mystical experience a reliable way to know God?
chosen: Mystical experience is not a reliable foundation on its own. The Holy Spirit works through the truth already revealed in nature and Scripture, received with active mind and will, and every impression is tested by that truth. Spiritual knowledge is not intellectual attainment; wisdom lies in the full knowledge of God through fellowship, open to the unlearned as much as the scholar, so neither despise nor idolise natural knowledge and culture. Above all, do not try to establish God's goodness from facts of nature or history, nor reduce moral judgements to feelings or subjective approval. Our knowledge of God's character rests solely in the moral consciousness: true moral judgements are self-evident deliverances of Reason, and in them we read God's own judgements. Tested by this standard, mystical experience may deepen devotion, but it is not the ground of knowing God.
rejected: Mystical experience can be genuine and deeply meaningful, but as a sole foundation for knowing God it is unreliable. Experiences are interpreted through our own psychology and culture, and they can be mistaken, exaggerated, or even manufactured. The wiser approach is to treat such experiences as confirming and enriching a knowledge of God that rests on something steadier: Scripture, the witness of the community of faith, and the moral life. Test private impressions against what has been revealed and against the fruit they produce—love, humility, patience. An experience that makes you more loving and grounded is likely trustworthy; one that makes you proud, isolated, or erratic should be questioned. So mysticism can help, but it needs testing.

prompt: How can God need anything from me if he is perfect and complete?
chosen: God needs nothing from you, for He is perfect and complete; yet His way is perfect, and His minute care forms the very circumstances in which you stand. Do not question His wisdom or suppose His ordering is a mistake. What looks like a need in Him is His will to be your all: giving the all for the all means renouncing everything that is not God and living as if only God and the soul existed. But this is no passive dependence. Fight your own battles with confidence and personal effort, knowing yourself and cherishing good character, while acknowledging your constant dependence on God. He asks nothing because He lacks, but because His perfect wisdom appoints your place and calls you to Himself.
rejected: God does not need anything from you in the sense of lacking something. He is complete and self-sufficient. But He created you with real freedom and real responsibility, and He desires your love, trust, and cooperation—not because He is incomplete, but because love and relationship are what He made you for. Think of it less as God having a need and more as God inviting you into a partnership. Your choices matter to Him and shape your own life and the lives of others. So the question isn't really about God's deficiency but about your calling. He doesn't need you, yet He chooses to work with you, and that is a gift rather than a demand.

prompt: How should I seek something holy that has been hidden for many years?
chosen: Approach worship expecting what God has promised: peace, security against evil, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit. The saints testify that those who expect these shall find them; where they seem absent, the lack is in our not expecting, not in God's giving. So seek the hidden holy thing with confident expectation, not resignation—and do not console yourself that if it is not found here, all will be well after death. Without finding Christ here, the soul enters a dark, lonely, self-tormenting state; the remedy must be found now. Nourish fervent devotion by assiduous holy reading and meditation from your tender years, following Timothy's example, and let that steady practice carry your expectant search.
rejected: Begin by clarifying what you mean by the holy thing that has been hidden—an old calling, a lost practice, a truth you set aside. Then approach it patiently. Seek it through prayer, through Scripture, and through wise counsel from people who know the tradition well. Don't expect instant results; hidden things often take time to recover. Be honest about why it was lost, and be willing to do the patient work of study and practice. Community matters here—don't seek alone. Keep your expectations modest and steady, and let the search itself shape you. If it remains hidden, accept that some things are not given in this life, and trust that God's timing is good.

prompt: I have been tempted to think that the success of a work of God depends on advertising and reports. How should I regard such means?
chosen: Do not measure the success of a work of God by advertising, reports, numbers, or visible results. Success is faithfulness to His word and the witness borne to His faithfulness; numerical and financial measures are not the measure of God's blessing. Prize quality above quantity of service: the main purpose is to please God and to do well, not to do much. And insist that God's work be done according to God's mind, separate from the world. Establishments that mix the world and the church, however well advertised, lead away from the Word. Let every report and every means serve faithfulness to what God has spoken, and refuse whatever would blend His work with the world's ways.
rejected: Advertising and reports are tools, not the measure of a work of God. It's natural to want people to know about good work, and communication can help others connect with it. But be careful not to let metrics become the goal. Ask whether the work is faithful to what God has called it to be, whether people are actually being served, and whether the message is honest. Reports can encourage supporters and attract resources, which is legitimate, but they can also tempt you to inflate results or chase visibility. Use these means soberly, keep them subordinate to the work itself, and regularly check your motives. Success in God's eyes is faithfulness, not publicity.

prompt: I have tried to lose myself in pleasure and excitement, but the emptiness comes back. Why?
chosen: The emptiness returns because no worldly pursuit can permanently satisfy the inner void. Romance, family, business, pleasure, and art are good in their measure, but taken as the final answer they leave the same ache behind. Notice what the excitement actually gives: a brief glow that dulls the senses and leaves you duller than before. There is a higher joy that sharpens rather than numbs, a spiritual sense of good that makes the soul more alive. When you taste it, the old intoxication loses its appeal—not from fear of punishment, but because you see it as the poor substitute it is. Yet do not conclude from dryness, sadness, terrors, or the enemy's uproar that your love is false or useless. Such trials are not evidence against you; they are the ground on which fidelity proves invincible. Serve God purely for love of His will, even when consolation is gone, and refuse the suggestion that your love is wasted. Only the finding of God is a permanent success.
rejected: The emptiness returns because pleasure and excitement are not designed to fill the soul; they only distract it for a time. You were made for something deeper than sensation, and every thrill fades because it cannot reach the center of who you are. This is not a flaw in you but a signal: the ache is pointing beyond itself. Rather than chasing another excitement, pause and ask what your heart is actually seeking. Many have found that the void is a space meant for God, and that when He fills it, the restless cycle of pleasure and letdown finally quiets.

prompt: I was criticized by someone who said I don't live as I preach. How do I change?
chosen: Being told you don't live as you preach is painful, but it can be a gift. Here is the plain counsel: turn to God, listen, and change one thing. First, don't defend yourself. Ask God for enabling grace, for you cannot close the gap between your words and your life by your own strength; receive the strength he gives, more than sufficient for every occasion of virtue. Then go to the person who criticized you, thank them, and ask what they saw. Listen without arguing. Pick one concrete area where your conduct doesn't match your message and begin changing it this week in God's strength. But go further: learn to intercede for the people who hear you. Prayer for them is a necessary school of preaching; without it, no amount of homiletics, genius, or polished delivery can make you a preacher. Let the criticism drive you to God and to prayer for others, not to self-justification.
rejected: Being told you don't live as you preach is painful, but it can be a genuine gift. First, resist the urge to defend yourself. Ask God to search your heart and show you where the gap between your words and your life actually is. Then go to the person who criticized you, thank them for their honesty, and ask what specifically they saw. Don't argue; listen. Take one concrete area where you know your conduct doesn't match your message and begin changing it this week, with accountability from someone you trust. Real change comes through humility, honest self-examination, prayer, and steady obedience over time. Remember that integrity is built in small, repeated choices, not in a single dramatic resolution. Let the criticism drive you to God rather than to self-justification.

prompt: Is God the Father a person with a shape and a habitation, or is he only a spirit everywhere at once?
chosen: Scripture teaches that God is spirit, yet it also presents the Father as a person who dwells in a place and has a form. The Son is the express image of the Father's person, and John's vision shows two distinct persons together in heaven: the Lamb takes the book from the hand of him who sits on the throne. The Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are each recognized as God in Scripture and described as distinct persons, not mere names, modes, or manifestations. Yet God's nature is undivided, and there is but one God. A plurality of gods is self-contradictory, because each would limit the other and so be finite rather than God. The divine persons share one undivided essence, so their unity is numerical, not merely integral.
rejected: Scripture speaks of God as spirit, and Jesus told the Samaritan woman that God is a Spirit and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth. This means God is not confined to a physical location or a bodily form; he is present everywhere at once. Since God is omnipresent, it is a mistake to think of the Father as having a shape or a dwelling place. He fills heaven and earth, and no temple or throne can contain him. Therefore the Father should be understood as pure spirit, unlimited by space, rather than as a person located in one place with a body.

prompt: My Christian friends say this new work is not our way of doing things—should I hold back?
chosen: Your friends are giving you the counsel of old friendship, and that counsel deserves honor. It is good to hold on to an old friend and never let him go; no matter how many new friends one gains, one should hold fast to the old, and only wicked conduct breaks the thread of fellowship. Yet this work, if it is truly of God, is not your achievement but GOD's own work through His servant, done in obedience to Him and for the glory of His Name. Do not try to prepare your own good works or rely on your own strength. Receive the good works God has prepared for you as garments made to order, and go forward in His all-sufficiency even while you feel weak and helpless. Keep faith with your old friends, test all things by Scripture, and trust the One who sends you to finish what He began.
rejected: Your friends are right to be cautious, but caution should not become a cage. New work is not automatically wrong just because it is unfamiliar; the question is whether it is faithful to Scripture and fruitful for the gospel. Weigh their counsel seriously, since they know you and your tradition. Yet the deciding factor is not whether a method is old or new, but whether it honors Christ and serves people. If the work is sound in doctrine and motive, you need not hold back merely because it is different. Pray, seek wise counsel, and go forward with humility rather than fear.

prompt: I feel uneasy speaking of God as a force or a 'something not ourselves'—is that a lower way of thinking than calling Him a Person?
chosen: Your unease is well-founded. Speaking of God as a mere force or 'something not ourselves' is a lower way of thinking, for it falls short of the personal language Scripture uses: God knows, wills, loves, speaks, and hears. He is not an impersonal energy but a living Person. Yet all our language about God is inadequate—not because God is less than personal, but because He is infinitely more personal than we can conceive. When we say God is 'super-personal,' we mean eminently personal, the very source and perfection of personhood. Moreover, God is not contingent or dependent on anything outside Himself. He is a se, having the ground of His existence in Himself. His existence is necessary, not contingent, and His being precedes His willing. He could not cease to be, nor is His essence a product of His will. Finally, when the divine Spirit comes into the awakened human spirit, He does not suppress or displace the human person. Rather, the Spirit is appropriated into our spirit, becoming the life of a new moral personality. The finite is not supplanted by the infinite; it is perfected and indwelt by Him. Thus, calling God a Person is the truest way we can speak, even while acknowledging that our concepts cannot fully contain Him.
rejected: It is understandable to feel uneasy with impersonal language for God. Calling God a force or 'something not ourselves' can seem vague and less than personal. Yet all our language about God is inadequate. Still, personhood is the highest category we have, and Scripture speaks of God as personal—knowing, willing, loving. So while we must remember that God transcends our concepts, calling Him a Person is not lower but higher than calling Him a force. The danger is to think of 'super-personal' as less than personal, which would be a mistake. God is personal in the truest sense, even if infinitely beyond our understanding.

prompt: What am I, and what happens to me when I die?
chosen: You are a human being, formed in the image of God, with reason, conscience, and a capacity to love. Death is not the end of who you are; it is a door to a higher state, and your identity is preserved, not erased. For the righteous, death is not something to mourn hopelessly—it is a passage into fuller life, and the body itself is raised again. Mortality is not truly real as such: being is immortal and inseparable from Deity, so what appears as death is a transition, not a destruction. Yet this transition is also a judgment: we are judged according to the deeds done in the body and the thoughts and intents of the heart, and death leaves us as judgment finds us. So live now with a conscience awake, trusting that the person God has made and loved is kept and will be restored.
rejected: You are a human being, a creature of body and soul, made with reason, conscience, and a capacity to love. Your worth comes from being made in the image of God. As for death, it is the separation of soul from body—the end of earthly life. From a purely natural view, the body returns to dust and the soul goes to God for judgment. Many people find this frightening because it seems like an ending, a loss of everything we are. But this life is not the whole story, and death is not simply a wall we hit. Reflecting on mortality can help us live more honestly now.

prompt: How can I be sure God has accepted me when I can't see Jesus at the Father's right hand?
chosen: Assurance does not depend on seeing Jesus with your eyes; it rests on trusting God's promise and the witness of the Spirit within. But the test 'Would Jesus have done this?' is not a casual tool: it must be grounded in careful study of Scripture and an established habit of inward intimacy with Jesus, from which the answer comes instantaneously from within. Remember who it is you trust. God the Father is a person who dwells in a place, not a spirit diffused everywhere without habitation; the Son is the express image of his person, and the Father and the Son are two distinct persons together in heaven—as John saw the Lamb take the book from the hand of him that sat on the throne. And do not presume that vague sincerity suffices: without finding Christ here, the soul enters a dark, lonely, self-tormenting state after death. The remedy must be found now.
rejected: Assurance does not depend on seeing Jesus with your eyes. It rests on trusting God's promise and on the witness of the Spirit within you. One practical help is to ask, in any situation, whether Jesus would have done this—and to let that question guide your choices. Over time, as you see his character reflected in your life, your confidence grows. You cannot see the Father's right hand, but you can see the fruit of his grace in your conduct. If you are sincerely seeking God, you can trust that he receives you, even when sight fails.

prompt: I've never really thought about the evangelization of the lost world—does that affect my spiritual life?
chosen: Yes, it does affect your spiritual life—more than you may realize. Personal salvation is the beginning, not the whole. The wider aim is to comply with God's Will and to raise the consciousness of the world. Union with God is not the absorption or disappearance of the self, nor a fusion in which you cease to be a distinct person; it is a love-union on a higher spiritual level, in which your will consciously cooperates with the divine will while your individuality is preserved—with its rights and its joy. And the fulness of the Spirit is given along the line of duty and obedience to world evangelization. The promised power lies along the line of duty; God will not give His power for selfish enjoyment. We receive the Spirit in fulness only as we obey Christ's command and step out into His plans for the world.
rejected: Yes, it does affect your spiritual life, though perhaps not in the way you expect. The Christian life is not only about your own growth; it is also about participating in God's mission to the world. When you ignore the lost world, your spiritual life can become narrow and self-focused. Engaging with evangelization—through prayer, giving, or going—broadens your vision and deepens your love. It reminds you that you are part of a larger body. So even if you never go overseas, you can support the work and pray for the nations. Your spiritual life will be richer for it.

prompt: I'm struggling with grief over someone who died. Can they still reach me somehow?
chosen: I'm sorry for your loss. Grief is human, but excessive mourning for the dead is a want of faith; God takes away friends because he will be loved without a rival. Yet the right response is not coldness: your grief should be a tender regret rather than acute grief, trusting that your beloved is in a high sphere of saner happiness. Death is not the end of who they are—it is a door to a higher state, and their identity is preserved, not erased; the body itself is raised again in the resurrection. So do not seek signs or messages from the dead; that is not the path of peace. Rather, bring your sorrow honestly to God, lean on community, and let tender remembrance, not anguish, shape your heart.
rejected: I'm sorry for your loss. Grief is a natural and deeply human response to losing someone we love, and it is not wrong to feel it. As for whether they can reach you—most traditions are cautious about claims of contact from the dead, and it is usually wiser not to seek signs or messages. What you can do is honor their memory, lean on community, and bring your sorrow honestly to God. Grief takes time, and there is no set timetable. Be gentle with yourself, and let others support you as you mourn.

prompt: If I should in all things walk contrary to other people, must I not be in a very unquiet and sad state, and be accounted a madman?
chosen: Walking contrary to others does not automatically mean misery or madness. Do not be astonished or cast down when you find evil inclinations within or opposition without; God permits them to make you humble. But do not seek peace by avoiding combat: peace comes through conquest, not evasion. Exercise sweetness and charity even amid repugnance and disgust. And learn not to be troubled in tribulations, afflictions, and injuries, not to be incensed against those who inflict them, nor to entertain resentment. Sincerely believe yourself worthy of all injuries, contempt, and scorn, desiring rather to be abhorred as filthy mire than to possess the delights of earth or be honoured and exalted by men. If your contrariety is born of pride it will leave you unquiet; if it is conscience, you may be accounted strange but need not be sad. Seek humility, and do not confuse stubbornness with faithfulness.
rejected: Walking contrary to others does not automatically mean misery or madness. Sometimes a person must stand apart for conscience's sake, and that can bring loneliness and misunderstanding. But you should examine yourself: is this contrariety born of pride, or of genuine conviction? If it is pride, it will indeed leave you unquiet. If it is conscience, you may still be accounted strange, but you need not be sad. Seek humility, listen to wise counsel, and do not confuse stubbornness with faithfulness. Peace comes from a clear conscience, not from universal agreement.

prompt: My church feels cold and unwelcoming, but the tavern feels warm and human. Am I wrong to prefer it?
chosen: You are not wrong to notice the difference, and I wish the Church would give ale and a pleasant fire, so that souls regale and are as happy as birds in the spring. Yet the coldness you feel is not merely the fault of priests or institutions; it comes from the tepid love for a dimly known Lord in each member's heart. When each heart worships the beloved Christ, the Church gains what is lacking. But remember, one need not be always at church to be with God; you may make an oratory of your heart for familiar conversation with Him in meekness, humility, and love. So do not give up on the church, but cultivate that inner oratory, and let your love for Christ warm both your heart and your church.
rejected: You are not wrong to notice the difference. Many churches can feel cold and unwelcoming, while a tavern often offers warmth and human connection. The longing for community and acceptance is natural. However, the church is not just a building or a social club; it is meant to be a place where God's love is shared. If your church feels cold, consider whether you can help make it warmer. But also be cautious: the tavern's warmth may be superficial, while the church's coldness may be a call to deeper faith. Ultimately, seek God's presence and community wherever it can be found, but don't give up on the church too quickly.

prompt: I want to love my neighbor as myself, but I find it hard to love myself at all—how should I love the soul while hating the sin?
chosen: Loving your neighbor as yourself begins with understanding that you are made in God's image. To love the soul while hating the sin, you must distinguish between the divine ground given to you from the Love of God and your own self-hood. Love the divine ground in yourself and in others, but hate the evil self-hood wherein evil cleaves to you. For Love hates all Egoity and self-hood, which is the root of Hell. Remember that self-love is the enemy through which the devil attacks us, so the crucifixion of the old man and perfect disengagement of the heart by universal self-denial is absolutely necessary before a soul can ascend the mountain of God. When the soul is inflamed with the love of Christ, it becomes indifferent to honors and disgrace, to sufferings and pleasures, and free from the approach of irregular passions. Then you can extend that same grace to others, loving the soul while hating the sin.
rejected: Loving your neighbor as yourself begins with understanding that you are made in God's image. Even if you struggle to love yourself, remember that God loves you unconditionally. To love the soul while hating the sin, you must separate the person from their actions. Hate the sin because it harms, but love the sinner because they are God's creation. Similarly, for yourself, acknowledge your faults but don't let them define you. Practice self-compassion and seek God's grace to see yourself as He sees you. Then you can extend that same grace to others. It's a journey; start by accepting God's love and letting it flow through you.

prompt: What is the treasure I should lay up?
chosen: The treasure you should lay up is not found in any Somewhat, image, opinion, affection, or natural fervour. Rather, it is found only by the soul going out of Somewhat into Nothing, where it may say, 'I have nothing, I can do nothing, I am nothing,' and so give glory to the Eternal Being. But this requires taking up the vow to espy God in all and deny self in all, counting the cost. For if you seek God only in pleasant things, you will miss Him in the common and the dull. Yet the dullest walk, when walked with God, is lit with wisdom. And like the hermit, you may wish for a hidden little hut in the wilderness, a lark beside it, a clear pool to wash away sins, a wood around it, a southern aspect, and a few humble and obedient men praying to the King. For in such simplicity, the soul finds its treasure in God alone.
rejected: The treasure you should lay up is the kingdom of God within you. Seek first His righteousness and all things will be added. Store up good works, acts of love, and a pure heart. These are treasures that neither moth nor rust destroys. Invest in your relationship with God through prayer, scripture, and service to others. Material wealth is temporary, but spiritual riches last for eternity. Let your treasure be the love of God and the love of neighbor, and you will find true fulfillment.

prompt: Our mission society is in debt; should I resign rather than be connected with borrowed money?
chosen: Whether to resign from a mission society in debt is a personal decision, but debt itself is not sinful; however, running into debt without prospect of repayment is not wise. The society should urge prompt payment of debts, refuse to run into debt again, and recognize the duty of repaying what is borrowed, especially from friends and the poor. But remember that sin is not merely a debt or a legal penalty; it is a personal condition of will and habit that spoils and enslaves the whole personality and casts a shadow on God's face. Salvation is not merely relief from penalty but deliverance into a life of holy will. Moreover, the Saints should fulfil their contracts and sacredly keep their word, for honest hearts produce honest actions. A promise-breaker is not to be fellowshipped. So as you consider your connection with the society, seek not just financial integrity but also the transformation of hearts and practices. If the society is borrowing without a plan to repay, that is concerning. Seek wise counsel and act according to your conscience and God's leading.
rejected: Whether to resign from a mission society in debt is a personal decision. Debt itself is not sinful, but mismanagement or lack of transparency can be. If the society is borrowing without a plan to repay, that is concerning. You should prayerfully consider whether staying allows you to help steer toward financial responsibility or whether resigning is a better witness. However, abandoning the society in its time of need might not be the best course. Seek wise counsel from trusted believers and examine the society's practices. Ultimately, act according to your conscience and God's leading, prioritizing integrity and the gospel's advance.

prompt: I want to be at peace with God but I feel like an enemy of his; who can make peace for me?
chosen: You feel like an enemy of God, but the good news is that men precipitate war upon themselves by wickedness; God did not design it. Peace will never come until mankind receives God's truth, and that truth is the gospel of Jesus Christ. Through His death and resurrection, Jesus reconciled us to God. Your feelings of enmity are real, but they are not the final truth. Put your faith in Christ, confess your sins, and receive God's forgiveness. Peace with God is not something you achieve; it is a gift received by grace. And as you receive it, remain always at peace, patient with others and equally patient with yourself, since peace is the passport of the daughters of Jesus Christ. But do not think that prayer alone is a substitute for self-defense and preparation. We must take every precaution and strive to help the Lord, being as willing to fight our own battles as to have Him fight them. So draw near to God in prayer, read Scripture, and take up the whole armor of God, and His peace will guard your heart.
rejected: You feel like an enemy of God, but the good news is that God Himself has made peace through Jesus Christ. Through His death and resurrection, Jesus reconciled us to God. Your feelings of enmity are real, but they are not the final truth. Put your faith in Christ, confess your sins, and receive God's forgiveness. Peace with God is not something you achieve; it is a gift received by grace. Draw near to God in prayer and read Scripture to reassure your heart of His love. As you rest in Christ's finished work, the Holy Spirit will witness to your spirit that you are a child of God, and His peace will guard your heart.

prompt: Can a soldier who sheds blood in battle be following Christ?
chosen: A soldier can follow Christ, and his sacrifice can share in Christ's own spirit. Christ resisted unto blood, striving against sin, and the soldier who at lawful command defends the right at the cost of his life acts in that same spirit, sharing the holy war of right against wrong. His courage and duty are taken up into faith: he trusts in Christ, obeys Him, and lets His mercy, purity, and self-sacrifice color his service. He fights lawfully and gently, never from cruelty or hatred, and is prepared to meet Christ as Saviour and Judge. Such sacrifice must be made only for righteousness and truth. Under trial he does not complain or despair but waits patiently upon the Lord, taking whatever befalls from His hands as intended for the highest good, and plays the part of a valiant soldier in the Spirit of Christ, co-operating with His grace.
rejected: Yes, a soldier can be following Christ while serving in battle. Military service requires courage, discipline, and loyalty, and these are genuine virtues. A soldier who defends his country and protects the innocent is performing a necessary duty, and shedding blood in a just war is not the same as murder. Christians have served in armies for centuries, and the Church has long recognized that some wars are justified. What matters is that the soldier acts lawfully, avoids cruelty, and serves a just cause rather than personal gain. So a soldier's courage and sense of duty can be honorable, and there is no contradiction between military service and Christian faith.

prompt: My brother has left the world to become a hermit, and I miss him. Should I try to bring him back?
chosen: It is natural to miss a brother, and your grief shows real love. He has entered this life solely to serve God and Mary and to save his soul, and one who takes up such a confraternity must not forsake its appointed days for worldly affairs. Do not treat his solitude as a failure or demand perfect human sympathy: each heart's bitterness is its own, and God alone knows us fully. Accept his hidden solitude as Heaven's will and trust God with your secret throbbings. Yet prayer is not mere passive reception. It is a mutual correspondence in which you bring yourself, give as well as receive; your missing him means His missing you. Rest in the Lord, love him in prayer without pressure, and do not turn him back toward the world.
rejected: It is natural to miss a brother who has withdrawn from the world, and your grief shows real love. But before trying to bring him back, consider what he is seeking. A hermit's life is chosen for prayer, silence, and closeness to God, and it may be his genuine calling rather than an escape. You could write to him, visit if allowed, and express your affection without pressure. If his choice is sincere and stable, trying to pull him back could harm both of you. Respect his vocation, keep the relationship warm through letters and prayer, and trust that God is at work in his solitude.

prompt: I have been hoarding gold in a chest for years. What does that do to my soul?
chosen: Hoarding gold in a chest for years does real damage to your soul. Keeping riches unused brings leanness of soul and darkness of mind: the heart shrinks around what it clutches, and the mind grows dim to God and neighbor. Every dollar and every ability is meant to be put out to use for the good of the community. Watch also against spiritual pickpockets and leakage; hold fast what you have, and store up each day's treasures of grace in the savings bank of eternity. And consider Elene, who decked the rood with gold and gems, adorned it with precious stones, and sealed it with locks in a casket of silver. That rood dwells there as a solace for the ill of any disease, affliction, or sorrow, so that men straightway find aid and divine grace through that holy form. Let your gold serve such lasting good.
rejected: Hoarding gold in a chest for years can quietly shape your soul. On one hand, saving is prudent and provides security for the future; there is nothing wrong with being careful with money. But if the hoard becomes an end in itself, it can breed anxiety, secrecy, and a habit of measuring life by possessions. You may find yourself trusting the chest more than God, and generosity can wither. It would be wise to ask why you are storing so much, whether you have real needs ahead, and whether some of it could relieve others' needs. Keep saving reasonably, but let your security rest in God rather than in gold.

prompt: I've been taught that close friendships and family ties compete with devotion to God. Should I distance myself from the people I love?
chosen: You should not simply distance yourself from people you love, but understand what they are for. Particular devotions—friendships, family ties, religious practices—are means to an end, and that end is God; when the soul is with God, its end, these means may be laid aside. Yet do not rely on sensible favors or warm feelings, even from loved ones, as though they brought you nearer to God. Faith brings us nearer to Him than any sensible consolation, and He is within us, so He should be sought there. And remember that God is always near: He should be thought of and adored continually, even in business and diversions, never neglected. Enjoy your loved ones as gifts, hold them lightly, and let every tie turn you inward to the God who is always present.
rejected: You should not simply distance yourself from people you love. Close friendships and family ties are among the greatest goods of human life, and Scripture itself speaks of love for neighbor and family. What matters is order: God first, then the people He has given you. If a relationship becomes an idol that pulls you from prayer, honesty, and worship, it needs correction. But withdrawing from loved ones out of fear of competition usually harms both you and them. Instead, let your love for God deepen your love for others. Keep your devotions, be honest about your limits, and enjoy your relationships as gifts rather than rivals.

prompt: I read about saints who did extreme penances and strange feats; am I obliged to imitate them?
chosen: You are not obliged to imitate every extreme penance or strange feat, but do not dismiss the saints. Their example is a perpetual and moving sermon, and the sight of their relics is a strong incentive to virtue. What moves us is the love of God, self-denial, and service behind their feats, not the exact outward form. Pride is the beginning, end, and cause of all sin, so imitate the saints in humility, seeing your own imperfections and counting yourself dust and worms. Yet hold all revealed principles in balance, not elevating one as a hobby while dimming others. Give first place to the fundamental doctrines of the fatherhood of God, the atonement, and the restoration. Let the saints' example stir you to virtue in your own state of life, seek wise counsel, and honor their relics as reminders of the holiness to which you are called.
rejected: You are not obliged to imitate every extreme penance or strange feat you read about in the lives of the saints. Such stories arose in particular times and cultures, and many of those practices were suited to individual callings rather than to everyone. What matters is the virtue behind them—love of God, self-denial, and service—not the exact outward form. Imitating dramatic feats without the same calling or guidance can harm your health and lead to pride. Instead, look for the ordinary ways your own state of life invites you to grow in virtue, and seek wise counsel. The saints' example can inspire you, but it is not a rulebook of required feats.

prompt: I'm young and already suffering so much—why would God let this happen to someone who has barely lived?
chosen: Your pain is real, and the first thing to do with it is to hand it to God—but do not imagine one tear or one desperate prayer settles everything. God asks for steady, persistent desire, not a single cry. Keep turning to Him day after day, in consolation and in dryness, and do not seek Him only when prosperity fails, friends disappoint, or you are sick and lonely. Abandon yourself to Him in this suffering, interior and exterior, and seek life, work, and joy in Him alone. Know that God is nearer in sickness than in health; do not put your chief trust in medicine, for remedies succeed only as He permits. Trust belongs in Him, who holds you even when you feel nothing. He honors those who keep asking, seeking, and knocking.
rejected: I'm so sorry you're carrying this much pain at such a young age. Suffering is not a sign that God has abandoned you or that you did something wrong. Many faithful people have asked your exact question, and Scripture makes room for lament. Practically, it may help to name your grief honestly in prayer, lean on trusted people, and get support for your health. Your life still has meaning even now, and God is not distant from pain—He is near to the brokenhearted. Take it one day at a time, and let others help carry the weight with you.

prompt: I want to know how to keep the Sabbath rightly; can we keep it at all?
chosen: Yes, the Sabbath can and should be kept. Scripture is plain: the seventh day is the Sabbath of the Lord, blessed and hallowed at creation and remaining for the people of God. No verse can be produced changing it to the first day of the week. Set the day apart as holy: attend to its worship and duties, refrain from ordinary labor and pleasure, and set a faithful example on that day. Prepare beforehand for the sacrament and partake of it worthily, examining yourself and coming with reverence rather than carelessly. Yet do not confine worship and testimony to one day—let prayer, gratitude, and witness continue every day. Guard the Sabbath, prepare for its meetings, and let its devotion overflow into all your days.
rejected: Yes, you can keep the Sabbath. Many Christians treat Sunday as a day of rest and worship, setting aside ordinary work and gathering with others. Practically, keep the day distinct: attend worship, avoid unnecessary labor, spend time in prayer and with family, and let the day be refreshing rather than burdensome. The Sabbath was made for people, not people for the Sabbath, so the point is rest and devotion rather than rigid rule-keeping. Start small, be consistent, and let your practice be shaped by gratitude rather than guilt.

prompt: I long for something beyond this life and feel guilty about it—is that longing holy or just escapism?
chosen: That longing is not escapism if it is turned toward God Himself. Cease from petitioning for your own needs and gifts, and let your one desire be to receive God Himself, opening yourself by offering great love rather than grasping. If you doubt you have offended God, do not remain paralyzed—humble yourself, beg His forgiveness, renew your promises of fidelity and love, and begin again. When aridity comes and your heart feels nothing, do not sink into sadness or cease laboring; labor independently of the heart, joyously amid holy occupations, practicing holy abjection and humility. The soul that longs for what lies beyond this life is being drawn to the Giver, not merely to gifts. Let that longing become an offering, and continue in the pursuit of perfection.
rejected: That longing is not necessarily escapism. Scripture itself speaks of longing for a better country and for God's presence, so a desire for what lies beyond this life can be holy. The test is direction: escapism avoids present responsibilities and relationships, while holy longing deepens love for God and others here and now. Ask yourself whether the longing makes you more patient, loving, and faithful, or whether it pulls you away from what God has given you to do. Bring the feeling to God honestly, and let it shape how you live today rather than replacing today.

prompt: I see so much war and strife in the world—did God will this?
chosen: War and strife are not God's design. Men precipitate war upon themselves by their own wickedness—greed, pride, and hatred—and God did not will it; human agency, not God's purpose, brought the evil. Nor will peace ever come by human effort alone; peace will never come until mankind receives God's truth and the gospel of Jesus Christ. Yet do not let the troubles you see loom larger than God's promises. God foresaw the wars of men and will overrule their results for good; take His promises and comfortings largely and your troubles lightly. So do not charge God with the evil you see. Pray for peace, work for justice, carry the gospel, and take comfort mightily, for God has not abandoned the world He made.
rejected: War and strife are a heavy thing to witness, and it is natural to ask where God is in it. Scripture does not present God as delighting in bloodshed; it presents Him as grieved by human wickedness and as a God of peace. Much of the world's conflict comes from human choices—greed, pride, fear, and injustice—rather than from God's desire. At the same time, God is not absent; He works to bring good out of evil and calls His people to be peacemakers. The honest answer is that God permits what He does not delight in, and He calls us to pray and work for peace.

prompt: I am uncertain whether the Apostles appointed our bishops and presbyters, and whether that gives them authority over us.
chosen: This question is answered by submitting to the authority of the prophets and apostles speaking through the Bible, not by private judgment. Scripture shows the apostles appointing men to oversee the churches, and that ministry stands in apostolic order; to submit to it is perfect freedom, for it is submission to Christ who sent them. Apostles must know for themselves, as eye and ear witnesses of Christ's divine mission, not merely believe by report; they act under the Presidency, and when the Presidency is removed the Twelve are next in authority until a new one is organized. Yet remember that Scripture, though more trustworthy than individual reason or the creeds of the church, is not the ultimate authority. The only ultimate authority is Christ Himself, who teaches us by His Spirit and leads His church progressively to distinguish the essential from the non-essential.
rejected: This is a fair question, and Christians have answered it differently. Historically, the early church did understand its bishops and presbyters as standing in a line of ministry traced to the apostles, and many traditions still teach that. Others see church leadership as a practical arrangement rather than a direct apostolic appointment. What matters most is that leaders serve the gospel and the flock rather than lord it over them. Examine the Scriptural witness, consider your own tradition, and weigh the fruit of the ministry. Authority, wherever it is claimed, should be exercised with humility and accountability.

prompt: I look at the beauty and order of the world and wonder whether it is designed, or whether it is only accident. Does it matter what I conclude?
chosen: It matters, and the answer is nearer than a hereafter. The world is not a machine to be explained away by accident; natural selection's dysteleological significance is at an end, and the world can be seen as an organism with internal ends, whose adaptations and beauty furnish a worthier teleology than the mechanical theory. But the truest wisdom is not brilliance in argument—it is the art of comfort, with softest step and gentlest tone. And that comfort is not deferred: the true sense of being and its eternal perfection appear now, in the beauty and order before you. Conclude that design is real and present, and let gratitude, gentleness, and quiet responsibility be your response.
rejected: It matters, but perhaps less than you fear. Science explains the world's order through natural selection and physical law, and many conclude that apparent design is an illusion produced by accident plus time. On that view, the question of design is settled negatively, and what remains is to decide how to live without cosmic purpose. You could still choose to treat beauty as valuable and to act kindly, but the conclusion does shape your outlook: accident tends toward resignation or self-made meaning, while design invites gratitude and responsibility. So yes, it matters—mainly for how you hold your own life, not for whether the world really is ordered, since that is a matter of evidence rather than preference.

prompt: How do I deal with people who oppose or contradict me?
chosen: Begin by distinguishing disagreement from hostility, but remember that the great majority of difficulties between brethren arise from misunderstanding rather than malice. Reconcile forthwith, and before judging, look at the design of the heart. Contradiction from friends is especially hard to bear, yet endure it, bear with it, and finally love it as a dear contradiction. Ask what is true in the objection and respond to the argument rather than the ego. Above all, do not mistake fierce contention about the kingdom of Christ, or slandering and persecuting others for religion, for zeal. Those who do so have not yet known Christ; such pride about opinions is an image of Self that helps forward the Kingdom of Darkness. Seek understanding, hold firmness without resentment, and let love, not victory, be the goal.
rejected: Start by distinguishing disagreement from hostility. When someone opposes you, separate the substance of their objection from the tone; ask what is true in it, and respond to the argument rather than the person. Stay calm, avoid defending your ego, and state your view clearly without needing to win. Set boundaries where behavior is abusive, but do not confuse firmness with resentment. Seek understanding first: repeat back what they mean, ask questions, and look for common ground. If the issue is trivial, let it go; if it matters, pursue it patiently and in private where possible. The goal is not agreement but respectful, honest relationship.

prompt: I have good desires but never seem to bring them to good effect—what am I missing?
chosen: You are not missing a technique so much as the recognition that God inspires good desires and by His continual help brings them to good effect, fulfilling aspiration and faithful activity with power. Name the desire, define one concrete next step, set a time, and remove friction—but as cooperation with grace, not self-generated effort. Allow no repose or slipping back in the spiritual ascent; go forward like a mountain-climber until the goal is reached, since desires turning aside after lower objects lose themselves in byways and countless distractions, while withdrawing into the one unchangeable Good deepens recollection. Yet do not demand to attain perfection in a day; that demand only brings useless disquiet. Tend toward it patiently, pray over each intention, review weekly, and rely on the power that completes what He begins.
rejected: You are probably missing a workable bridge between intention and action. Good desires stay abstract unless you convert them into specific, small, scheduled commitments. Name the desire, define one concrete next step, set a time, and remove friction. Anticipate obstacles and plan a response. Track progress and review weekly. Also examine whether your desires are genuinely yours or borrowed from others; vague or conflicting aims dilute effort. Finally, accept that effect often lags behind desire, and that consistency matters more than intensity. Start small, act today, and let results teach you rather than waiting for motivation to arrive fully formed.

prompt: I am a layperson with money to give but little time to pray. Does my giving substitute for prayer?
chosen: No, giving does not substitute for prayer, and the deeper issue is honesty rather than scheduling. Prayer is humbling work: it crucifies pride and signs our bankruptcy before God. To excuse little praying as acceptable is a deluding make-believe—little praying is a worse evil than no praying, because it quiets the conscience while leaving the soul unexercised. Do not treat brief prayer as self-sufficient, nor fit it into leftover time. Time is essential to private communion with God, and much time alone with Him is the secret of prevailing prayer; the short prayers that prevail owe their efficiency to long seasons with God. Give the best of your time and strength to prayer. Let the closet come first, and let study and activity come second, freshened by the closet.
rejected: No, giving does not substitute for prayer; they are different goods, and generosity is genuinely valuable. But if you have little time, treat prayer as something you can do briefly and regularly rather than as an all-or-nothing obligation. A few minutes of honest prayer each day, offered before work or at night, can sustain your giving and keep it from becoming mere transaction. Consider whether your giving is also an expression of love for God and neighbor, not only a financial habit. Set a modest, realistic rhythm, protect it, and let your generosity flow from that relationship rather than replace it.

prompt: How do I know what God wants me to do in a specific situation?
chosen: Begin with prayer for wisdom, recognizing that God inspires good desires and by His continual help brings them to good effect, fulfilling with power the aspiration of goodness and the activity of faith. Gather the facts, test your motives, consult Scripture and wise counsel—but as cooperation with grace, not self-reliant analysis. Do not demand that circumstances and people be adjusted to you; be adjusted in every good work—to your surroundings, to those around you, and to God's plan—and find rest, power, and freedom in that adjustment. If you doubt whether you have offended God, do not stay paralyzed: humble yourself, beg His forgiveness, renew your promises of fidelity and love, and continue in the pursuit of perfection. Clarity grows as you take faithful steps and rely on the power that completes what He begins.
rejected: Use a clear process. First, pray for wisdom and honesty. Second, gather the facts: what is actually at stake, who is affected, what options exist. Third, test your motives—are you seeking your own comfort or the good of others? Fourth, consult Scripture and wise counsel. Fifth, weigh consequences and your responsibilities. Sixth, act, and review what happens. Look for the option that best fits your gifts, your duties, and the needs in front of you. God often guides through ordinary means—prayer, counsel, circumstances, and conscience—rather than through dramatic signs, so expect clarity to grow as you take faithful steps.

prompt: I feel like my religious observance and outward practices are empty—what am I missing if I keep all the externals but feel no spirit within?
chosen: You are right to sense that something is missing. The externals—religious observance, outward signs of abnegation, even the holiness of profession—profit nothing without the spirit of humility and truth, in which Christ dwells in the heart by faith and love. The kingdom of God is within you. Do not seek spiritual experiences as achievements or with curiosity; accept them only as God chooses, without praying for or secretly desiring them. Submit totally, without questioning, fear, or curiosity. You cannot serve both God and mammon: Spirit and matter cannot both be trusted. Expel material beliefs and serve God alone. What you are missing is Christ Himself, dwelling in you by faith and love. Humility strips away self-reliance; truth exposes pretence. Seek Him within, not in outward things, and let your heart be wholly surrendered to His indwelling presence.
rejected: You are not alone; many faithful people go through dry seasons. The externals—Mass, prayers, devotions—are means, not ends. What you may be missing is a living relationship with Christ, nurtured by humility and truth. Without humility, practices become performance; without truth, they become superstition. Christ dwells in the heart by faith and love, and the kingdom of God is within you. So rather than abandoning your practices, let them become expressions of an inner surrender. Ask yourself: Am I seeking God Himself, or the comfort of routine? Invite the Holy Spirit to purify your motives. The emptiness you feel may be God's invitation to deeper conversion, to let go of self-reliance and rest in His grace.

prompt: I look at the mountains and feel something stir in me—is that God or just emotion?
chosen: That stirring could be a genuine awareness of God's presence, but do not approach it casually. The divine presence is both beneficent and terrible, filling the soul with wondering, trembling adoration. Keep always in mind that God is present, sees and hears all things, and penetrates the heart. By this remembrance guard against anger and dissolute mirth. When you look at the mountains, remember that the same God who made them is holy and awesome. Yet His dealings with the soul are a tender mystery of Infinite Love forcing itself upon an unwilling creature, taking only to restore. Even the soul's gloom may be the shade of His outstretched hand. Let joy and holy fear blend in your heart. Test the experience: Does it lead you to worship, humility, and love? Thank God for the moment, but don't rely on it alone. Seek Him in prayer, Scripture, and community. Let the mountains remind you of His greatness, and let your faith rest on His Word, not on passing sensations.
rejected: That stirring could be a genuine awareness of God's presence in creation, or it could be simply natural emotion. The Bible says creation declares God's glory, so awe at mountains can point to Him. But emotions are fickle. Test the experience: Does it lead you to worship, humility, and love? Does it align with Scripture? God often uses nature to awaken us, but He wants a relationship deeper than feelings. Thank God for the moment, but don't rely on it alone. Seek Him in prayer, Scripture, and community. Let the mountains remind you of His majesty, but let your faith rest on His Word, not on passing sensations.

prompt: I wonder whether the idea of an absolutely perfect Being really implies that such a Being exists, or whether I am only defining a word.
chosen: The question of whether an absolutely perfect Being exists is a classic philosophical problem. The ontological argument claims that if we can conceive of a perfect Being, it must exist, because existence is a perfection. But critics say existence is not a property, and we may merely be defining a word. However, the argument points to something deeper: our longing for perfection suggests we are made for more than this world. Remember that your spirit existed before you came here, exists after death, and will be reunited with the body in the resurrection; both body and spirit are needed for a perfect man. This eternal perspective grounds your longing. Aspire constantly to the perfection of holy love, seeking nothing less than perfection in that love. Yet sanctification requires discovering and rooting out habitual disorders, guarding the senses, living in recollection, opening your interior to a spiritual director, and aiming at God's will rather than at multiplying external works. While reason alone may not compel assent, it can open us to the possibility of God. Ultimately, belief in God is a matter of faith and relationship, not just logical deduction. You might explore the arguments, but also consider the witness of those who have encountered the divine.
rejected: The question of whether an absolutely perfect Being exists is a classic philosophical problem. The ontological argument claims that if we can conceive of a perfect Being, it must exist, because existence is a perfection. But critics say existence is not a property, and we may merely be defining a word. However, the argument points to something deeper: our longing for perfection suggests we are made for more than this world. While reason alone may not compel assent, it can open us to the possibility of God. Ultimately, belief in God is a matter of faith and relationship, not just logical deduction. You might explore the arguments, but also consider the witness of those who have encountered the divine.

prompt: I keep committing the same small sins. Do they really matter?
chosen: Yes, they matter greatly. Every sin, even the smallest, is an insult to God, measured by His infinite greatness compared with your littleness. Unregretted sin accumulates and destroys the ability to do right. Even small sins, if unrepented, harden the heart and dull the conscience, making it easier to fall into greater sins. The Bible warns that whoever is unfaithful in little things will be unfaithful in much. You must not ignore them. True repentance means turning from evil, reforming your life, and making restitution where possible. Bring them to God in confession, ask for strength to overcome them, and strive to grow in virtue. Do not let them become habits. God's grace is available, and cleansing comes through Christ's atonement. Take seriously even the smallest sins, for they can separate you from God if left unaddressed. Avoid sin at any sacrifice, for it is the greatest of evils.
rejected: Yes, they matter. Even small sins can become habits that dull your conscience and distance you from God. The Bible says that whoever is faithful in little things is faithful in much. Repeated small sins can lead to greater ones and hinder your spiritual growth. They may seem insignificant, but they grieve the Holy Spirit and affect your relationship with God. However, God's grace is greater. Don't be discouraged; instead, bring them to God in confession and ask for strength to overcome them. Focus on growing in virtue and rely on His help. Remember, God loves you and wants you to grow in holiness.

prompt: I have neglected visiting the sick because I thought it was only the minister's duty—am I wrong?
chosen: Yes, you are wrong. Visiting and instructing the sick is a strict duty for every Christian, not only the minister. Jesus said, 'I was sick and you visited me.' While the administration by anointing and laying on of hands is an authoritative ordinance, too sacred to be repeated loosely—after the blessing is pronounced, time should be given to prayer and thanksgiving rather than unwarranted repetition—this does not excuse you from your duty. Seize the time Providence affords in lingering illness. Warn the dying to flee from the wrath to come, remembering that while there is life there is hope. In all things, be peaceable, submit to existing authorities, pray for rulers, and wait patiently for the Lord to establish His own government in His own time. Ask God for wisdom and compassion to serve the sick faithfully.
rejected: Yes, you are wrong. Visiting the sick is not only the minister's duty; it is a Christian duty for all believers. Jesus said, 'I was sick and you visited me.' Caring for the sick is a way to serve Christ Himself. While ministers have a special role in anointing and prayer, every Christian is called to show compassion and practical help. Neglecting this duty means missing an opportunity to serve Jesus. You can visit, pray with, and assist the sick in various ways. Don't leave it only to the minister. Ask God to give you a heart of compassion and look for opportunities to serve the sick in your community.

prompt: My temper flares up before I can stop it, and then I'm angry at myself for being angry—what should I do?
chosen: The double anger you describe is a sign that you are still measuring yourself against others and against your own image of how you should be. Learn first not to be troubled in tribulations, afflictions, and injuries, and not to be incensed against those who inflict them. When the heat rises, bridle your tongue and refuse resentment; say nothing until your spirit is quieted. Then examine yourself honestly, attending to your own duties rather than judging others. Do not be angry that you were agitated—gently place the troubled heart in the hands of our Lord and ask Him to cure it, renewing your good resolutions. Sincerely believe yourself worthy of all injuries, contempt, and scorn, desiring rather to be abhorred as filthy mire than to possess the delights of earth or be honoured and exalted by men. In that lowliness the flare loses its fuel.
rejected: That double anger is exhausting, and it's worth naming: first the flare, then the self-directed frustration at having flared at all. A useful first step is to slow the sequence down. Notice the physical signals—jaw tightening, heat in the chest—and give yourself a brief pause before speaking. Some people find it helps to name the feeling silently: 'I'm angry right now.' That small gap can keep a sharp word from escaping. It's also worth looking at what tends to set you off; patterns often reveal unmet needs or old wounds. Be patient with yourself. Getting angry about being angry just adds a second layer of suffering. Treat the first flare as information rather than failure, and treat the second as a habit you can gently unlearn over time.

prompt: I've been faithful in doing good for years but I don't feel any special insight. Does obedience really lead to understanding?
chosen: It's understandable to feel discouraged, but obedience is not a transaction whose results are uncertain. Obedience to God's commandments is an eternal principle: there will never be a time in time or eternity when obedience to God's commandments is not obligatory. It is the means of keeping in touch with God, and only in this way can we consummate our mission and obtain eternal life. The blessings are conditioned on obeying God's law—paying tithing, keeping the Word of Wisdom, and building temples. Yet do not live outside the sense of God's love. Keep yourself in His love by constant trust and constant obedience, and the hard things become easy, and sorrow is silver-lined with hope. Understanding grows along that path rather than before it.
rejected: It's understandable to feel discouraged when years of faithfulness don't seem to produce the insight you hoped for. But it's worth questioning the assumption that obedience is mainly a means to a feeling or a reward. Obedience is better understood as a way of life, not a transaction that guarantees a particular experience. Understanding often grows slowly and quietly, and it may look different from what you expected—patience, steadiness, and a clearer sense of what matters. It can also help to talk with trusted people about what you're noticing. Feelings are unreliable measures of growth. Keep doing good because it is good, and hold lightly the expectation that insight should arrive on a schedule.

prompt: What does it mean that the Spirit doesn't erase me but becomes the life of a new me?
chosen: It means the Spirit's work is not about deleting your personality or replacing you with someone else. The divine Spirit is appropriated into the awakened human spirit, becoming the life of a new moral personality; your gifts are not abolished but taken up into a new governing principle. Yet the fulness of the Spirit is given along the line of duty and obedience to world evangelization—God will not give His power for selfish enjoyment. So let the soul be converted and become as a child, turning itself again to God out of whom it proceeded, forsaking all its own imaging and lust and self-made centres, and so coming to the Divine Vision again. The new me is not a possession but a homecoming, animated from within and directed outward in obedience.
rejected: It means the Spirit's work is not about deleting your personality or replacing you with someone else. Rather, the Spirit takes up residence in your awakened human spirit and becomes the animating life of a new moral personality. Your memories, temperament, and gifts are not abolished; they are reoriented and purified. Think of it as the difference between a lamp being extinguished and a lamp being lit—the same vessel, but now filled with light. The 'new me' is continuous with the old, yet governed by a new principle. Growth in this life is gradual, and the Spirit shapes character through ordinary faithfulness rather than dramatic displacement.

prompt: I am a Jew and know the law of Moses—how should I answer when Christians ask about the crucifixion?
chosen: Answer honestly and with respect. Explain what the law of Moses means to you, and note that a crucified Messiah sits uneasily with expectations of a triumphant deliverer. When Christians speak of the crucifixion as a sacrifice that pardons sinners who merely ask, or as appeasing divine wrath, gently press back: the efficacy of that death lies in the practical affection and goodness it demonstrated, not in automatic pardon nor in placating an angry God. If 'Jewish Christianity' comes up, reserve it for Christians who maintained Jewish national and political forms and literal Mosaic observance as essential, or claimed a Jewish prerogative, contrasted with the universalistic Christian religion. And do not read the death as mere tragedy: where a testament is, there must be the death of the testator; the blood of martyrs is the seed of the Church; and Joseph and Hyrum showed the greatest love by laying down their lives for their friends.
rejected: Answer honestly and with respect for both traditions. You can explain what the law of Moses means to you and how a crucified Messiah sits uneasily with expectations of a triumphant deliverer. Many Christians read the crucifixion as a sacrifice for sin; you may say that from a Jewish standpoint the Torah provides its own means of atonement and repentance, and that a death on a tree carries its own scriptural weight. Ask what they mean by 'crucifixion'—atonement, martyrdom, or something else—since Christians differ. Keep the conversation about texts and meanings rather than about who is right. It's fine to say you don't have a settled answer; honesty and curiosity serve better than a rehearsed reply.

prompt: I want to know the secret of a holy and useful life. Where do I begin?
chosen: Begin with prayer. Prayer on the knees, both secret and in the companionship of believers, is the one great central secret of holy living and serving—the corner-stone on which all life-work is built, and the first resort in every crisis great or small. Do not separate the Spirit's work from the Church: the Spirit is the life of the Spirit-bearing body, consecrating nature and working gradually and socially while intensifying personal character. And do not settle for a bare minimum of knowledge. Seek to be filled with the mature knowledge of God's will in all wisdom and spiritual understanding, for that is the secret of true living. Pray with others as well as alone, serve somewhere specific and unglamorous, and keep company with honest people who will tell you the truth. Start this week with prayer and one act of service.
rejected: Begin with small, concrete habits. Set aside a regular time each day for reflection or prayer, however brief, and protect it. Read widely—Scripture, good books, and the lives of people you admire—and notice what they did rather than only what they said. Serve somewhere specific and unglamorous; usefulness grows through faithfulness in small duties. Keep company with people who are honest and kind, and let them tell you the truth about yourself. Expect slow progress and setbacks, and treat them as information rather than verdicts. Finally, clarify what you mean by 'holy' and 'useful'—the answers will shape your priorities. Start this week with one habit and one act of service.

prompt: I am terrified that God's love will demand everything from me and leave me with nothing. Is that what love is?
chosen: Your fear is real, but it must not set the terms of the question, because perfect love casts out fear. God does not look on you as a threat to be managed; He looks on you with love, as He looks with love on the most terrible sinner who has any true desire to be converted. Do not imagine yourself beyond His merciful regard. Love is not a demand that strips you bare; it is the living God drawing you to Himself, and every surrender He asks is a way of giving you more of Him. He does not wish to harm you but to do you great good, so love Him fervently and without servile fear. Meet this trial as a place where faith grows stronger and love grows purer, trusting His goodness toward you.
rejected: Your fear is understandable, because love does ask a great deal. Scripture says we must take up our cross and follow Christ, and that whoever loses his life for his sake will find it. But notice that this is not a transaction that leaves you empty. God does not ask you to surrender good things so that He can keep them from you; He asks you to trust Him with them. The saints who gave everything testify to receiving far more than they gave. So bring your fear honestly to God. Ask Him to show you what love really is, and ask for courage to trust Him. Love is not chiefly about what you must give up; it is about the One to whom you give it.

prompt: How do I find the fulness of the Holy Spirit in my life?
chosen: Seek the fullness of the Holy Spirit by remaining in the body where He dwells. The Spirit is not an impersonal influence or emanation but a divine Person, the Paraclete sent by Christ, co-equal with the Son, who speaks, guides, commands, and can be grieved. He is the life of the Spirit-bearing body, the Church, consecrating nature rather than bypassing it—working through Scripture, sacraments, prayer, and fellowship. He works gradually and personally, so do not be scandalized by imperfection in the Old Testament or in the Church; such imperfection does not disprove His real inspiration and presence. Pray for Him, read Scripture with an open heart, worship, obey, and confess sin. Expect Him to form character in you over time—love, joy, peace, self-control. Keep asking, and trust that He will fill those who hunger for Him.
rejected: Seek the fullness of the Holy Spirit by cultivating a personal relationship with Him. Pray for Him, ask Him to fill you, and read Scripture with an open heart. Practice the presence of God through worship, silence, and obedience to what you sense He is prompting. Avoid grieving Him by sin, and keep short accounts through confession. Many find it helpful to seek Him apart from church structures, since the Spirit blows where He wills and is not confined to institutions. Expect Him to work in your heart and character, producing love, joy, peace, and self-control. Be patient, keep asking, and trust that He will fill those who hunger for Him.

prompt: Are the Father and the Son the same person, or two persons together in heaven?
chosen: The Father and the Son are two distinct persons together in heaven. God the Father is not a mere spirit diffused everywhere without a habitation; He is a person who dwells in a place, and the Son is the express image of His person. This is why John saw the Lamb take the book from the hand of Him who sat on the throne—two persons, one enthroned and one approaching. Scripture recognizes the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit each as God, and describes them as distinct persons who are not mere names, modes, or manifestations. Yet there is one Fatherhood of God and one brotherhood of man, and there is but one Mind, as the testimonies declare. So when you pray, you pray to the Father through the Son in the Spirit.
rejected: The Father and the Son are not the same person. They are distinct persons who are both fully God, together with the Holy Spirit. This is the doctrine of the Trinity: one God in three persons. The Father is not the Son, and the Son is not the Father; each is a distinct person, yet they share one divine essence. In heaven, the Son is at the right hand of the Father, interceding for us, and the Father is the one who sent the Son. So when you pray, you pray to the Father through the Son in the Spirit. The three are not three gods but one God, and the distinctions among them are real, not merely names or appearances.

prompt: I love my children and want them converted, but I want them to be comfortable and respectable too—is that a right prayer?
chosen: It is natural to want your children converted and also comfortable and respectable, but remember that conversion is the work of the almighty power of the HOLY GHOST, not of human persuasion, technique, or effort. Your great need as a worker is to know GOD. So bring even the smallest matters concerning your children to the Lord, taking no step without asking counsel of the oracles of God and seeking guidance in believing prayer, learning His will before undertaking anything and waiting until His guidance is clear. Pray for their conversion with dependence on the Spirit, and seek for them hearts comforted in the full sense—strengthened, courageous, and consoled—not merely pleasant circumstances. Only so can you be blessed in your own soul and prospered in the work of your hands.
rejected: It is natural to want your children converted and also comfortable and respectable, and there is nothing wrong with desiring good things for them. God cares about the whole person, so you can pray for their salvation and for their wellbeing. At the same time, be careful not to let comfort and respectability become more important than conversion. Pray honestly, trust God with the outcomes, and do what you can to point them toward Him. Use good judgment and common sense in parenting, and don't overthink every small decision—sometimes you just have to act and trust God with the results.

prompt: How can I know anything about God's character from looking at nature, which seems so cruel and full of suffering?
chosen: Nature can teach us something about God, but it also mirrors our own condition. The more truly a man knows his own misery, the more fully he beholds the majesty of God; and the more vile he is in his own eyes for the sake of God, truth, and justice, the more worthy of esteem he is in God's eyes. So strive to look on yourself as utterly contemptible. Yet remember that God, in His promises to hear our prayers, is desirous to bestow Himself upon us; if we ask anything beneath Him, we put an affront upon Him and hurt ourselves by preferring to Him a creature which He framed. Worldly pains and pleasures are not comparable to spiritual ones, so be careful for nothing and fear nothing, desiring only not to offend God. Beyond nature, look to Christ, who reveals God's character most fully.
rejected: Nature can teach us something about God, but it is a limited and ambiguous teacher. Its beauty and order point to a Creator, yet its cruelty and suffering raise real questions.
