The Bible acknowledges this tension and points us beyond nature to Christ, who reveals God's character most fully. So while nature can stir wonder and gratitude, it should not be our primary source for knowing God. Look to Scripture and to Jesus, who shows us a God who suffers with us and promises to make all things new. Nature's cruelty is a sign of a broken world, not a revelation of God's heart.

prompt: Did my spirit exist before I was born, and will it live after death?
chosen: Your question touches the difference between mortal belief and immortal understanding. Belief is mortal—it shifts, doubts, and dies with the body—but Mind is immortal, and it is Mind that understands. Yet this does not make the human spirit a passing thing. Man's spirit existed before he came here; it exists after death; and it will be reunited with the body in the resurrection, for both are needed for a perfect man. Mortal belief speculates; spiritual understanding knows the spirit's eternal nature. But do not rest in understanding as a private comfort. The fulness of the Spirit is given along the line of duty and obedience to world evangelization: God will not give His power for selfish enjoyment. We receive the Spirit in fulness only as we obey Christ's command and step out into His plans for the world. So let your hope in the spirit's eternity move you to obedient service, where the promised power is found.
rejected: This is one of the oldest questions people ask, and different traditions answer it differently. Many religious traditions teach that the soul is created at conception or birth, while others hold that it pre-exists. From a Christian perspective, Scripture speaks of God knowing us before we were formed in the womb, which suggests our identity is rooted in God's eternal purpose. As for death, most Christian teaching affirms that the spirit survives the body and awaits resurrection. Practically, the question matters less than how we live now: trust God, love neighbors, and live faithfully. If you want certainty about the afterlife, prayer and study of Scripture can bring peace, but ultimately these things rest in God's hands.

prompt: What is the unforgivable sin, and could I have committed it?
chosen: The unforgivable sin is generally understood as blasphemy against the Holy Spirit—a deliberate, persistent rejection of God's truth and grace. But do not treat any sin lightly. Unrepented sin accumulates; each act left unregretted hardens the heart and destroys the ability to do right, and a guilty conscience grows heavier the longer it is ignored. Learn too that sin confers no real pleasure: what seems enjoyment is a false appetite that promises and does not pay, and this knowledge strengthens moral courage to master evil. Yet do not think forgiveness means that sin is merely overlooked while the belief in it continues. Forgiveness is the destruction of sin—not a pardon that leaves the evil intact, but the casting out of evil through spiritual understanding that sees it as unreal. So repent, reform your life, and let understanding destroy the sin rather than merely soothe the fear of it.
rejected: The unforgivable sin is generally understood as blasphemy against the Holy Spirit—a deliberate, persistent rejection of God's truth and grace. Jesus warns of it in the Gospels, and many theologians describe it as a final, willful refusal of repentance rather than a single careless word. If you are worried that you have committed it, that worry itself often shows your conscience is still alive and responsive to God. People who have truly committed it typically show no concern at all. So the best response is to turn to God now, confess, and trust His mercy. God is not looking for reasons to condemn you; He desires your repentance and restoration.

prompt: How can I rejoice and praise God in the hardest trial instead of complaining?
chosen: Rejoicing in trial is hard, and God does not demand that you feel joyful at once. What He asks first is perfect submission: bear the trial, if not with joy, at least without complaint, trusting His will. Remain assured that God only seems to withdraw Himself from you; He hides His face that you may follow Him more earnestly and unite yourself more closely to Him. Be slow to take new steps, willing to have no will of your own, ascertaining God's will by prayer and the Word, then waiting with earnest, patient, believing expectation of His help. And bring whatever men say or think before the tribunal of your own conscience. Enter within yourself to learn the truth: human praise profits nothing if conscience accuses, and it is no loss to be despised or persecuted without if you are innocent within. So rejoice in the Lord in patience, silence, and peace, rather than in the approval of others.
rejected: Rejoicing in trial is one of the hardest things faith asks. Begin by remembering that God has not abandoned you—He is present even when He feels distant, and trials can refine character and deepen trust. Practically, name your complaints honestly to God in prayer, then deliberately turn your attention to His promises and past faithfulness. Gratitude helps: list specific gifts, however small. Surround yourself with believing friends who can pray with you and remind you of truth. Sing, even when you do not feel like it, because praise is an act of will as much as emotion. And remember that trials are temporary; God works all things for good for those who love Him.

prompt: I have suffered from stomach trouble for years and fear food; can I eat normally again?
chosen: Years of stomach trouble and fear of food are exhausting, and your anxiety is understandable. But consider where power lies. Food and hygiene affect the body only through mortal belief; it is Mind that governs man, and fear of food is a belief, not a law. Yet this does not excuse careless habits. Indulgence of appetite—eating chiefly for pleasure—engenders disease. Instead of stimulants, recruit by rest: work less, eat less, and eat moderately, preserving the body so as to live as long as you can. But do not mistake regimen or study for the gift itself. Study only whets the appetite; possession of God-consciousness must be individual and inward, an inward gift, not something reading or another's experience can hand you. It is qualified for by persistent, ardent desire through every lack of response. So eat calmly and in moderation, and let your desire press inward until the gift is yours.
rejected: Years of stomach trouble and fear of food are exhausting, and it is understandable that you feel anxious. The good news is that many people recover normal eating with the right approach. Start by seeing a doctor to rule out or manage any medical condition, and consider working with a dietitian who can help you reintroduce foods gradually. Keep a food diary to identify triggers, eat slowly and in calm settings, and try small portions of feared foods without pressure. Stress and anxiety strongly affect digestion, so relaxation practices, gentle exercise, and adequate sleep can help. Recovery takes time; be patient with yourself and celebrate small steps.

prompt: How will it fare with those who fiercely contend about the kingdom of Christ and slander and persecute one another for their religion?
chosen: Those who fiercely contend about the kingdom of Christ and slander and persecute one another for their religion have not yet known Christ. They suppose their zeal is for Him, but it is an image of Self—pride about opinions—and such pride helps forward the Kingdom of Darkness. Nor is contention the only offense. Those who oppress the poor, forcing their labor to serve another's pomp and vanity, do it to Christ himself and fall under His severe judgment; such conduct works with the Devil against the Kingdom of Christ, which consists only in Love. So examine your zeal, and do not count all suffering heroic: the glory of suffering belongs only to suffering endured for Christ's sake, not to suffering brought on by our own misconduct. Where baseless accusations have been raised against the name of Christ, it is our duty to remove them. Let love, humble service, and truth be your witness, and leave judgment to God.
rejected: Fierce contention about religion and the persecution of others for their beliefs is a sad and recurring feature of history. Jesus prayed for unity among His followers, and Scripture warns against quarreling about opinions. Those who slander and persecute others for their religion may believe they are defending truth, but such conduct contradicts the love Christ commanded. The fruit of the Spirit is love, peace, patience, and kindness, not strife and cruelty. It is wise to examine our own zeal: is it for Christ, or for our own opinions and pride? God alone judges the heart, and He calls His people to gentle witness and humble service rather than to coercion.

prompt: I have a friend who is very different from me in background and faith. Can we truly be equals?
chosen: Yes, you can be true equals, rightly ordered under God. Your shared dignity makes you equals, and your first love is due to Him; trust in Him is never excessive. Yet do not let fear or suspicion rule this friendship. Perfect Love casts out fear, so receive your friend gently, believing all things and covering imperfections in love rather than scrutinizing them. Where your friend's faith differs, hope for them and clothe them with the graces faith can claim, as God is gentle with us. Keep God first, and from that trust love your friend freely, listening honestly and setting aside superiority. Ordered under Him, your differences need not divide you; they can deepen reverence, patience, and a love that reflects His own.
rejected: Yes, you can be true equals. Equality rests on shared human dignity, not on identical backgrounds or beliefs. Differences in faith and culture do not make one person less than another; they simply make the friendship richer and more interesting. What matters is mutual respect, honest listening, and a willingness to learn from each other. You do not have to agree on everything to honor one another as equals. Set aside any sense of superiority or inferiority, ask sincere questions, and let the friendship grow on the common ground of kindness. In time, the differences may become the very places where trust deepens most.

prompt: I want to know what our Lord's meaning is in all that has befallen me, and I cannot find it.
chosen: It is understandable that you cannot yet see the meaning, but do not abide in confusion or self-accusation. See your helplessness meekly, then hasten to the Lord, who stands and abides you sorrowfully and has haste to have you to Him. Do not count this falling as only loss: assayed by love, it yields a deeper knowing of His love and a truer meekness, a high and worshipful rising. And do not let sin, sickness, sorrow, or fear of the enemy weigh as though Christ had not overcome them. He has triumphed over all by His cross and resurrection, and by the blood of the Lamb and the word of your testimony you share His victory. Bring your not-knowing to Him, trusting that even this is turned to profit in His hands.
rejected: It is understandable that you cannot yet see the meaning in what has happened. Much of life's suffering resists easy explanation, and demanding a clear answer too soon can deepen the pain. Rather than forcing a meaning, try to sit patiently with the question. Talk with trusted friends, pray honestly about your confusion, and give yourself time. Meaning often emerges slowly, in hindsight, as you look back and notice how you have grown or what you have learned. For now, be gentle with yourself, accept that not knowing is part of the journey, and trust that clarity will come when you are ready for it.

prompt: Should I give to foreign missions?
chosen: Yes, give to foreign missions, seeing them first as the Holy Spirit's work. He calls, sends, and empowers the witnesses; your giving joins what He is already doing. Offer God your liberty, memory, understanding, and will, desiring above all His love and grace rather than gifts or outcomes. Come with gratitude and humility, giving freely and liberally, consistent and sincere in word and deed. Pray for direction, then obey promptly, resolving to keep in His presence and to labor for His glory and the good of souls. Wise stewardship serves this generosity but must never excuse withholding. Offer your resources thankfully, trusting the One who sends to multiply what is given in His name.
rejected: Yes, giving to foreign missions is a worthy practice. Missionaries depend on the generosity of supporters to preach, translate Scripture, and serve communities abroad. A sensible approach is to set a reasonable portion of your income for missions, give regularly, and choose organizations with clear financial accountability and proven results. Do your research, compare budgets and outcomes, and give where the need is greatest and the stewardship is soundest. Generosity should be balanced with your own responsibilities, so plan your giving carefully rather than giving impulsively. Handled with prudence and good planning, your support can accomplish real good overseas.

prompt: Should I make a collection at a meeting where I speak about China, or leave people to give as GOD leads them?
chosen: Either approach can be appropriate, but first recognize the deeper need: regions still unoccupied by the gospel require a dedicated effort, and the workers must be sought from God Himself. Pray that the Lord of the harvest would send laborers. Then decide about the collection in that light. Leaving people to give as God leads respects conscience, while a collection can gather support for a specific need. Do not treat practical details as unimportant to witness: weigh every engagement carefully, keep promises, and be exact in small affairs, since these bring either honor or dishonor to the Lord. And come with hearts full of wisdom: if you discern any lack of judgment or failure in the authorities, go to them individually and let them know, for leaders would exchange a thousand errors for one truth.
rejected: Either approach can be appropriate. Leaving people to give as God leads respects individual conscience and avoids any pressure, while a collection at a meeting can be a practical way to gather support for a specific need. Consider your audience and the purpose of the meeting. If you do take a collection, be transparent about where the money goes and make giving voluntary. If you prefer not to, simply share the need and let people respond as they feel led. What matters most is honesty and good stewardship, so choose whichever method best fits the situation and your conscience.

prompt: I am afraid that my love for my family is greater than my love for God; how can Mary help me order my loves?
chosen: It is natural to feel family love strongly, and many worry whether it rivals love for God. Mary can help you order your loves, for she is the mother of fair love. She loves those who love her, serves those who serve her, and loves us more than any earthly mother. She is prompt to aid those who invoke her, anticipating their prayers with compassion; she never sends away unconsoled anyone who calls upon her. Turn to her confidently, for her prayers have the force of a command with her Son, and it is impossible for her not to be heard. Ask her to teach you, by her example, to keep God first and let family love flow from that. She will hasten to succor you and accompany you as a loving mother.
rejected: It is natural to feel that family love is very strong, and many people worry about whether it rivals their love for God. Mary can help by modeling a heart wholly given to God while still loving her family deeply. Ask her to intercede for you and to teach you, by her example, to keep God first and let family love flow from that. Prayerfully examine your priorities, make small daily choices that put God first, and let Mary accompany you as a compassionate guide. With her help and your honest effort, your loves can become rightly ordered rather than competing.

prompt: How do I know my sins are forgiven when I go into battle?
chosen: When you go into battle, you can know your sins are forgiven this very moment if you renounce sin in will and purpose. Do not wait to feel more, weep more, or wait for greater power. God supplies the strength for you to turn from sin, and the feeling of assurance comes after your surrender. If you doubt and feel you have offended God, do not remain paralyzed. Humble yourself, beg His forgiveness, renew your promises of fidelity and love, and continue in the pursuit of perfection. I confess I too have sinned and need this same mercy. Together let us come to the fountain opened for sin, where Christ took our sins and made them His own. Confess your sins and trust in His finished work; His promise is sure. Then go forward, not in your own righteousness but in His.
rejected: When you go into battle, the assurance of forgiveness comes from God's promise, not from your feelings. If you have confessed your sins and trusted in Christ, you can know they are forgiven because God is faithful and just to forgive (1 John 1:9). Do not wait for a emotional experience or a sign; faith rests on His word. Before battle, examine yourself, repent of known sin, and claim the promise. Then go forward with confidence, not in your own righteousness but in Christ's. The feeling of peace may come later, but the fact of forgiveness stands on God's truth. Remember that His mercies are new every morning, and He does not cast out those who come to Him.

prompt: I am afraid of the raiders from the north. How should I face my fear?
chosen: Fear of raiders from the north is natural, but as a believer you must refuse fear as a lie from Satan. The greatest enemies to fear are those from within: your own passions and unchecked weaknesses. Our labor is to subdue our passions, conquer our inward foes, and keep our hearts right before the Lord. When fear comes, answer it with trust: 'What time I am afraid, I will trust in Thee.' Trust God for goodness and mercy all the days of your life. Be untroubled by the enemy's noise; despise him and pay no attention, for he cannot hurt the soul that belongs to God. Take practical steps to prepare, but ultimately place your confidence in God, who is a shield around you. Resist fear and fix your eyes on Jesus.
rejected: Fear of raiders from the north is natural, but as a believer you are called to trust God rather than give in to fear. The Bible repeatedly says, 'Do not be afraid,' because God is your protector. Take practical steps to prepare, but ultimately place your confidence in the Lord, who is a shield around you. Pray for protection and for peace, and remember that God is sovereign over all nations and armies. He can turn away the enemy or give you strength to endure. Surround yourself with fellow believers who can pray with you and support you. Fear is not from God, so resist it and fix your eyes on Jesus, the author and perfecter of your faith.

prompt: I'm trying to understand why bad things happen to good people—is there a purpose to suffering?
chosen: Suffering is a universal human experience, but from a divine metaphysical perspective, injury and pain are not real or continuous. We must reverse the belief of injury and declare man unhurt, trusting God as All. Yet Christ's suffering was on our behalf rather than instead of us. Those who follow Him enter into the fellowship of His sufferings and the ongoing work of redemption. Moreover, we must receive all from God's hand, sweet or bitter, equally. God's love makes sweet and bitter alike acceptable, and afflictions seen as from a loving Father become consolation. So while we deny the reality of suffering in the absolute sense, we also recognize that through our trials we share in Christ's redemptive work. By holding to this truth, we can find peace and healing, knowing that in God's kingdom there is no pain or sorrow.
rejected: Suffering is a universal human experience, and the Bible offers several perspectives. Sometimes suffering is a consequence of sin, but not always—Job's friends were wrong to assume his suffering was due to his sin. Suffering can be a test of faith, a way to refine character, or a means to draw us closer to God. It can also be a result of living in a fallen world where natural disasters and human cruelty exist. While we may not always understand the purpose, we can trust that God is sovereign and works all things for the good of those who love Him. Ultimately, suffering will be redeemed in the new creation, where there will be no more pain or sorrow.

prompt: I am a pastor and wonder whether the sober work of organizing and teaching is as valuable as evangelism.
chosen: As a pastor, the work of organizing and teaching is indeed valuable and essential to the health of the church. Evangelism is crucial for reaching the lost, but without teaching and organization, new believers cannot grow or be discipled. The Great Commission includes both evangelism and teaching (Matthew 28:19-20). Prayer must not be separated from evangelistic labor; rather, prayer is the source of power for winning souls. Join prayer with aggressive evangelism, making the cross of Christ the pivot of all teaching. But remember that the preacher's credentials are his relations to God, not his position or gifts. Preaching by word alone is not enough; preaching by life, character, and conduct is required for preaching at all. Also, open your heart to trusted brethren in mutual confession, and practice diligent pastoral visitation and inquiry, for an unvisited church becomes an unhealthy church. So do not undervalue your administrative and teaching work; it is a vital part of ministry.
rejected: As a pastor, the work of organizing and teaching is indeed valuable and essential to the health of the church. Evangelism is crucial for reaching the lost, but without teaching and organization, new believers cannot grow or be discipled. The Great Commission includes both evangelism and teaching (Matthew 28:19-20). Organizing helps the church function effectively, and teaching grounds believers in the faith. Both are spiritual gifts and callings. The key is to see them as complementary, not competitive. Prayer should undergird both, and the goal in all things is to glorify God and build up the body of Christ. So do not undervalue your administrative and teaching work; it is a vital part of ministry.

prompt: I was offered a promotion and a big salary, but I worry it will pull me from a simpler life—what should I do?
chosen: This is a common dilemma. A promotion and salary increase can be a blessing, but they also come with greater demands and potential distractions. Do not rush frantically after wealth; instead, practice calm, contented, patient diligence. Attend meetings, pray, read scripture, and meditate, keeping your dish right side up for the shower of blessings. To progress, study the letter, imbibe the spirit, and adhere steadfastly to the divine Principle. Limit yourself to legitimate employments, refusing the curiosity, ambition, and restlessness that create more impediments than works. Consider whether the new role aligns with your values and goals. Will it require more time away from family, church, or personal pursuits? Will it compromise your integrity or peace? Pray about the decision and seek wise counsel. Remember that wealth is not inherently evil, but the love of money is. If you can accept the promotion while maintaining your priorities and generosity, it may be a good opportunity. Ultimately, seek first the kingdom of God and trust Him to provide.
rejected: This is a common dilemma. A promotion and salary increase can be a blessing, but they also come with greater demands and potential distractions. Consider whether the new role aligns with your values and goals. Will it require more time away from family, church, or personal pursuits? Will it compromise your integrity or peace? Pray about the decision and seek wise counsel. Remember that wealth is not inherently evil, but the love of money is. If you can accept the promotion while maintaining your priorities and generosity, it may be a good opportunity. However, if it will lead you to neglect what matters most, you may need to decline. Ultimately, seek first the kingdom of God and trust Him to provide.

prompt: I pray but feel nothing. Does God hear a silent, wordless cry?
chosen: Feeling nothing does not mean God fails to hear. The God who understands all things knows your innermost thoughts and the secret prayers of the soul before they become words. Just as human invention lets people communicate across great distances, God receives the earnest supplication of a heart too weary to speak. But do not treat one silent cry or a moment of disappointment as enough. The text insists on steady, persistent desire, asking in faith without wavering, and warns against seeking God only when prosperity fails, friends disappoint, or sickness and loneliness press in. Prayer rises unseen like a rill, heard by God though no one else observes it. He accepts every heart that fears Him and works righteousness, whatever the nation or station, so keep coming to Him in dryness and in plenty alike.
rejected: Feeling nothing in prayer is common, and it does not mean your prayer is wasted. Many people go through seasons where words fail and emotions run dry, yet the very desire to pray is itself a sign that something in you is reaching toward God. Scripture suggests God is not limited to hearing only eloquent or emotional prayers; He knows the heart before words are formed. Try not to measure your prayer by feeling. Keep showing up, be honest about the dryness, and trust that God receives what you cannot articulate. If the silence persists and troubles you, talking with a pastor or trusted friend can help.

prompt: I am not sure I have been truly converted; how does the new birth work?
chosen: Doubt about conversion can show that you take God seriously, but the new birth is not produced by trying harder or working up feelings. Conversion is the work of the almighty power of the Holy Ghost, not human persuasion, technique, or effort. Knowing God is the worker's great need, so seek Him, not merely assurance. Yet conversion is also a total self-oblation: an entire sacrifice of self to God, with no secret exception kept back in the heart. The surrendered soul asks, 'Lord, what wilt thou have me to do?' and holds nothing in reserve. Accept also God's transplanting work. He may move you into places of responsibility where you must lean directly on Him, and that dependence is not a setback but the condition of growth. Offer your whole self, and trust the Holy Ghost to make you new.
rejected: Doubt about conversion is common, and it is not necessarily a bad sign—it often shows you take God seriously. The new birth is not something you manufacture by trying harder or by working up the right feelings. It is God's work in you, usually growing quietly over time rather than arriving as one dramatic moment. Look for evidence of change: a growing desire for God, sorrow over sin, love for others, a hunger for Scripture. You can also simply ask God to do in you what you cannot do yourself. Talk with a pastor or mature believer who can help you discern what God is doing.

prompt: Animals seem to live and die without fear while I'm terrified of death—what does that say about me?
chosen: Plants and birds fulfill Nature's will and die unafraid; their fearless, fulfilled lives reveal that human restlessness and fear of the grave come from something beyond terrestrial mould. You are not merely another creature of earth, and your unease signals a nature that reaches beyond the dust. But do not dwell on dread or rehearse images of disease and death. Master fear rather than cultivate it, turning thought toward health and toward Life as God. Accept also that some solitude is Heaven's will: each heart's bitterness is its own, and no human sympathy can fully reach it. Trust God alone with your secret throbbings, for He knows you fully and loves you better than He knows. Rest in the Lord, and let the contrast with the unafraid bird lift you above the tomb.
rejected: It says less about you than you might think. Fear of death is a deeply human response, and nearly everyone experiences it at some point. Animals may appear calm because they lack the kind of self-awareness that lets us anticipate and reflect on our own mortality. That awareness is part of what makes us human, and it can be a burden. Rather than seeing your fear as a defect, consider it a signal that you are grappling with real questions of meaning and mortality. Talking with others, journaling, or speaking with a counselor can help you process it.

prompt: I'm a teacher and my pupils don't seem to care—how can I reach them?
chosen: It is discouraging when pupils seem indifferent, but apathy is often a mask for boredom, insecurity, or trouble at home. Build genuine relationships, vary your methods, and give small wins that build confidence. Yet do not abandon them at the end of instruction; continue loving care and counsel until they tread firmly in the way. Nor should you accept ignorance as settled: continual education and the pursuit of all useful knowledge are a religious duty, and true science and true religion belong together. Remember also that no one, however old or prominent, has done enough. No priesthood holder may claim to have graduated from the calling of teacher and refuse to serve when called. So yield willingly to calls to act as teacher and to visit the Saints, so long as life and ability remain.
rejected: It is discouraging when students seem indifferent, but apathy is often a mask for other things—boredom, insecurity, or troubles at home. Start by building genuine relationships; students work harder for teachers they believe care about them. Vary your methods, connect lessons to their lives, and give them small wins that build confidence. Set clear expectations and be consistent. Also, remember that you cannot control every outcome; some seeds take years to grow. Talk with colleagues, reflect on what is working, and be patient with yourself. Your steady presence may matter more than any single lesson.

prompt: I am drawn to mystical exercises and images and sacred numbers in worship; are these aids to devotion or a relapse into heathen magic?
chosen: Mystical exercises, images, and sacred numbers can be aids to devotion, but only if you understand where their power lies. Their efficacy rests not on the printed page, the human director, human learning, or human talent, but on the truths of God's word and on the Spirit of God, the principal director who alone instructs and sanctifies the soul. The book and the guide are secondary instruments. Use such helps with your eyes on God, testing everything against Scripture. Expect also seasons of dryness and irksomeness in prayer; these are trials of love, so be faithful and make effectual acts of resignation. And remember that spiritual worship was realized in definite institutions: in the Lord's Supper the ruling idea is sacrifice, the sacrifice of thanksgiving of the community. Let your devotion, private and gathered, point beyond every technique to God Himself.
rejected: This is a real question, and the answer is not simply one or the other. Mystical exercises, images, and sacred numbers have been part of Christian devotion for centuries, and many people find them helpful for focus and reflection. They can become superstition if treated as automatic or magical, but they can also be genuine aids when they point beyond themselves to God. The key is your intention: are these things helping you attend to God, or are you relying on the technique itself? Test them against Scripture, keep them in perspective, and be wary of anything that replaces trust in God with trust in a method.

prompt: I am a Gentile by background and feel drawn to the God of Israel, but I cannot see myself becoming a Jew. Is there a place for me?
chosen: There is a place for you. See Israel rightly: it was a preparation and vantage-ground, not a self-expanding religion with a promise or power of expansion of its own. Its universal truths could only be made available by a power beyond its own forces. Yet history is not chaos or merely human striving: God is at work in the course of men and nations, guiding and judging them, and the partial gifts of the peoples are appointed by Him and fulfilled in Christ. You need not become a Jew, nor leave your ordinary life for a cloistered or conspicuously pious existence. The ordinary man or woman in usual work or leisure can find God without a life apart, without conspicuous piety, and without leaving undone duties to those dependent on them. Seek honest guidance from a rabbi about your standing, and live faithfully where you are.
rejected: Yes, there is a place for you. Judaism has always welcomed those who revere the God of Israel without converting—the Noahide framework offers a path of faithfulness for Gentiles. Many communities value sincere seekers and offer study, worship, and fellowship. You can honor the God of Israel through ethical living, prayer, and support of the Jewish people. Speak with a rabbi about your situation; they can guide you honestly. Your attraction to the God of Israel is itself meaningful, and you need not become a Jew to live faithfully before Him.

prompt: Is it wrong to enjoy innocent pleasures?
chosen: Innocent pleasures are not wrong in themselves, but do not make pleasure a goal. The pursuit of pleasure can become a living death; people go into debt for fashionable display and undertake illegitimate schemes to gratify craving, and the hunt leads to cheating, lying, and corrupted morals. Do not linger in the cheerless tomb of passion; when the storm is laid, mark the silent growth of grace and light in the soul. And remember that a soul devoted to God will sometimes forgo innocent lawful pleasures, so that it takes pleasure only with Him. Enjoy simple goods with gratitude and moderation, yet let devotion sometimes set them aside.
rejected: No, innocent pleasures are not wrong. Enjoyment of good food, friendship, music, and rest is part of a healthy human life and can be received as gifts. The danger lies not in pleasure itself but in excess or in making pleasure the center of life. Scripture celebrates joy and gratitude, and a balanced life includes delight in simple goods. So enjoy innocent pleasures with thankfulness, moderation, and attention to how they affect others and your responsibilities.

prompt: How can Christ be glorified in an ordinary life like mine?
chosen: Christ is glorified in ordinary life when He shines forth from you to others. Integrity, kindness, patience, and service make His character visible, and there is a reciprocal glory: the believer is glorified in union and communion with Christ. But those who contend fiercely about the kingdom of Christ and slander and persecute one another for religion have not yet known Him; such pride about opinions is an image of Self that helps forward the Kingdom of Darkness. Remember that God chooses the poor, weak, and despised to accomplish His purposes, confounding the mighty. The glory belongs to Him, not to human wealth, influence, or ability. Let your ordinary faithfulness, however small, be offered to Him who works through the base things of the world.
rejected: Christ is glorified in ordinary life when you live faithfully in your daily work, relationships, and duties. Integrity, kindness, patience, and service reflect His character to those around you. Small acts of love and quiet devotion matter more than grand gestures. Pray, read Scripture, and let your conduct commend the gospel. Your ordinary life becomes a witness when others see something of Christ in how you treat them and carry your responsibilities.

prompt: I am a leader in my church and the congregation is spiritually cold. Am I responsible?
chosen: Yes, you are responsible, and preachers are primarily responsible for the condition of the Church; spiritual leaders are tokens of God's favor. A cold congregation points back to neglected shepherding, teaching, and prayer. Yet the Church's lack is not only in its leaders: it lies in the tepid love for a dimly known Lord in each member's heart, and the Church gains what is lacking when each heart worships the beloved Christ. Understand authority rightly: it is moral and spiritual weight that carries our judgment, not coercive power. Coercion adds nothing to the Church's true authority, and belief secured by threat is not submission. Lead by weight of character and truth, and call each heart to love Christ.
rejected: Yes, as a leader you bear real responsibility for the spiritual climate of your congregation. Leaders set the tone through teaching, prayer, and example, and a cold congregation often reflects neglected shepherding. At the same time, spiritual vitality is not something you can produce alone—each member must respond to God. Examine your own walk, seek God earnestly, and lead with humility and prayer. Encourage the congregation toward warmth and devotion, and trust God to work.

prompt: I'm not sure I've ever really repented. Should I focus first on being sorry for my sins?
chosen: Sorrow for sin is a start, but repentance is more than feeling sorry or a last-moment confession. True repentance turns from evil, reforms life, and makes restitution where possible. In the early moralistic view found in Clement, Barnabas, Polycarp, and Ignatius, forgiveness was a single remission at baptism and righteousness was identified with virtue—a view that narrowed the religious sense. Yet do not treat unrepented sin lightly: unregretted sin accumulates and destroys the ability to do right, and a guilty conscience grows heavier with each delay. So examine your life honestly, confess your sins, turn from what is wrong, and make amends where you have wronged others. Cleansing comes through Christ's atonement; walk in new obedience.
rejected: Sorrow for sin is a good starting point, but repentance is more than feeling sorry. It involves a change of mind and direction—turning from sin toward God. If you are unsure whether you have repented, begin by honestly examining your life, confessing your sins to God, and asking Him for a changed heart. Focus on turning from what is wrong and walking in obedience, trusting God's grace and forgiveness in Christ.

prompt: How do I prepare myself to contemplate God by the way of negation?
chosen: To contemplate God by the way of negation is the best means of knowing him, for God exceeds all that can be grasped. So I will not merely discuss difficulties but act courageously: I begin with the body, disciplining the senses, withdrawing from images, and stilling the imagination, removing first all that pertains to bodily, sensible, and imaginative things. Then I remove even what belongs to reason and the idea of being as found in creatures, entering the darkness where God dwells. Beginning not with the mind but with the body, I pass from the labour of action to the repose of contemplation and from the moral virtues to sublime contemplation. I will do much; not I, but the grace of God which is within me. And when I lapse in remembrance, I am not disquieted: I return at once with greater trust, knowing that God's grace, not my vigilance, keeps me.
rejected: To prepare for contemplating God by negation, begin by quieting your senses: withdraw from noise, images, and distractions, and let your imagination grow still. Then set aside your own ideas and concepts of God, since God exceeds every thought you can form. Cultivate silence, humility, and patience, and give yourself to prayer and moral discipline so that your mind becomes calm and receptive. Do not expect clear pictures or consoling feelings; the goal is a simple, loving attention to the God who is beyond all that you can grasp. Persevere gently, returning to this practice each day, and trust that in the darkness of unknowing God draws near to you.

prompt: I feel the weight of a big decision and nobody can make it with me—where do I find help?
chosen: It is understandable to feel alone under a big decision. If you would help another bear this weight—or receive help yourself—begin with your own eye. First overcome your own belief in and fear of disease and sin, casting the beam out before you attempt to help another, as the command requires. Then be calm and contented, refusing frantic hurry. Be slow to take new steps and willing to have no will of your own. Ascertain God's will by prayer and the Word: attend your meetings, pray, read scripture, and meditate, keeping your dish right side up for the shower of blessings. Test any proposed step by the Word and prayer rather than treating self-will as faith. Seek counsel from a pastor or mentor. Then wait with earnest, patient, believing expectation of His help, trusting that light comes in His time.
rejected: It is understandable to feel alone under a big decision. First, name the decision plainly and write down your options. Seek wise counsel from trusted people—a pastor, counselor, or mentor—who can listen without deciding for you. Pray honestly about your fears, and give yourself permission to move at a steady pace rather than rushing. Break the choice into smaller steps and set a short deadline so you are not paralyzed. Remember that you are not truly alone; God invites you to cast your cares on Him, and He promises guidance to those who ask. Take the next small step faithfully and trust that clarity often comes in motion rather than before it.

prompt: How could a religion preached by unlearned men, centered on a crucified Jew, conquer the Roman Empire unless God was in it?
chosen: The spread of Christianity from a handful of Galilean fishermen to the dominant faith of the Roman Empire is remarkable, and many have taken it as evidence of divine providence. Human factors also contributed: the empire's roads and common Greek language eased travel, urban centers offered ready audiences, and the new faith's care for the sick and promise of salvation appealed to a restless age. The Church's adoption of the full Old Testament was secured not by Jewish Christians but by the anti-Gnostic party within the larger Christendom, which championed the Hebrew scriptures against Gnostic rejection; Jewish Christianity, had it not already receded, would only have made that victory harder. Syncretistic Jewish Christians had themselves excised from the Old Testament whatever conflicted with their purer moral conceptions, especially the sacrificial ritual, seeking to elevate the Old Testament religion into a universal religion under the impression of Jesus. Yet the ancient dogmatic form that emerged was a historically conditioned and transitory vessel, sharing the limited endurance of the ancient world; the Gospel itself is not bound to it. The transformation of the empire suggests that God was at work, but not that any one dogmatic form is permanent.
rejected: The spread of Christianity from a handful of Galilean fishermen to the dominant faith of the Roman Empire is indeed remarkable, and many have taken it as evidence of divine providence. Several human factors also contributed: the empire's roads and common Greek language eased travel and communication, urban centers offered ready audiences, and the new faith's care for the sick and its promise of salvation appealed to a restless age. Yet the decisive factor, on the traditional view, was that Jewish Christians preserved and handed on the Old Testament, giving the Church its scriptures and moral foundation. Without that inheritance the movement would likely have remained a minor sect. Taken together, the transformation of the empire within three centuries suggests that God was at work in the movement.

prompt: I am afraid of committing a mortal sin under pressure. How should I face that fear?
chosen: Your fear can be holy, but it must be joined to love. Yes, one mortal sin unrepented is enough to damn the soul, so nourish an abiding fear of sin and eternal loss, for fear restrains us where love is weak. But do not imagine God as one who wishes to harm you; He desires your great good and offers grace in every pressure. Love Him fervently, not with servile dread. Under pressure, flee occasions of sin, pray, and trust His goodness. If you fall, confess and rise. And when small faults come, do not be terrified or paralyzed; humble yourself quietly before God and say to your soul: 'Courage! we have made a false step, but let us keep steadily on.' Let fear keep you watchful and love keep you confident.
rejected: Your fear is understandable, but it should not dominate you. God is merciful, and one sin does not define your soul. Under pressure, rely on prayer, avoid the near occasions of sin, and trust in God's grace. If you do fall, go to confession promptly and begin again. Fear can be a healthy warning, but it should not become a paralyzing anxiety. Remember that God loves you and desires your salvation more than you do. Keep your eyes on Him, not on your weakness. With prayer, the sacraments, and a steady habit of virtue, you can face pressure with confidence rather than dread.

prompt: I have been a Christian only a short time and feel alone in the ways of God—how do I find fellowship?
chosen: Feeling alone as a new Christian is common, but you are not meant to walk this road by yourself. Begin by praying honestly to the Father whom we know through His human revelation in Christ, the personal Friend who has drawn near. That is the fellowship you seek: communion with a definite Person, not a vague impulse. Yet prayer is a mutual correspondence—you bring yourself, your attention, honesty, and love, and you receive His; your turning toward Him matters, and your missing Him means His missing you. Then seek fellowship with real people. Look for a church where Scripture is taught faithfully, attend regularly, and join a small group. Do not overlook believers of low estate: converse and correspond with them on serious subjects, for God hears and records such speech, and such intercourse builds up both parties in faith and love. Introduce yourself, be patient, read your Bible daily, and let prayer remain real conversation with the Friend who never forsakes His own.
rejected: Feeling alone as a new Christian is common, but you are not meant to walk this road by yourself. Begin by praying honestly to God about your loneliness, and ask Him to guide you to the people He has prepared for you. Look for a local church where Scripture is taught faithfully and where believers gather for worship and prayer. Attend services regularly, join a small group or Bible study, and introduce yourself to others. Be patient and persistent; friendships in Christ take time to grow. In the meantime, read your Bible daily and let prayer become a habit, trusting that God is with you even when you feel isolated. He promises never to leave or forsake those who belong to Him.

prompt: I'm afraid of dying and I don't know how to face it—how should I think about death?
chosen: Fear of death is a common human experience, but you can learn to master it by turning your thoughts away from fear and toward health and Life as God. Yet our assurance does not rest on our own thoughts or worthiness, but wholly on Christ—his sufferings, temptations, cross, death, resurrection, and pleading at the right hand of the Father. Looking at self clouds the view; looking at the altogether lovely Saviour leaves no room to doubt his power and will to save. Death is not the end but a door to a higher state, where identity is preserved and the body will be resurrected. For the righteous, death is a transition to greater life, not a loss. Cultivate thoughts of health, wholeness, and divine Life, which cast out fear. By aligning your mind with God, who is Life itself, you can find peace and courage to face each day without the shadow of fear, knowing that your identity is secure in Him.
rejected: Fear of death is natural, but you can face it by focusing on the life you have now. Many people find peace by accepting death as a part of life and making the most of each day. Consider talking to a counselor or trusted friend about your fears. You might also find comfort in spiritual practices, like prayer or meditation, which can help you feel connected to something larger than yourself. Remember that fear is a normal emotion, and it doesn't have to control you. By taking small steps to address your fears, you can gradually find a sense of calm and acceptance.

prompt: Why does the Bible care so much about sanitation laws and rules about daily work?
chosen: The Bible's sanitation laws and work rules were written with the special assistance of the Holy Ghost to teach Israel to trust God and to serve Him with their whole lives. They remind us that God cares about every aspect of life, including hygiene and labor, and that He calls us to offer ourselves and our substance for His work without salary, trusting Him to supply all our need. Observing a rule is an act of faith accepting the Divine will, and these rules lead to the imitation of Christ. Yet institutions, including these laws, are instruments for human life, not ends in themselves. Institutionalism is a danger; Jesus prioritised human need over institutional observance, and we must keep institutions in the secondary place even when this means breaking them for the sake of human welfare. While the specific rules are not binding on Christians today, the spirit behind them—cheerful, self-denying service—remains, animated by faith, hope, and charity.
rejected: The Bible's sanitation laws and work rules were practical measures for ancient Israel to maintain health and order. They prevented disease and fostered community well-being. While these rules were important for their time, Christians are not bound to them today. Instead, we focus on the moral principles behind them, like caring for our bodies and working diligently. These laws remind us that God cares about every aspect of life, including hygiene and labor, but they are not central to salvation. We should respect them as historical context but not treat them as binding.

prompt: How should I think about the fact that good people before Christ seem to have been reaching toward him without knowing him?
chosen: It's encouraging to think that good people before Christ were reaching toward him without knowing him. They may have sensed a higher power and sought to live morally, but love for Christ is not merely an immediate feeling; it requires persistent thinking, comparison, and growing familiarity. We should deliberately practice thinking about Jesus, comparing the world's loves and deceits with His gentle ways, so that He becomes more lovable than any other person. This deliberate practice helps us cultivate a deep love for the unseen Christ. Moreover, difficulties are not merely problems to escape but occasions to know God more deeply. We should expect God to reveal Himself as a present help in trouble and to use difficulties to deepen our knowledge of Him. Faith is not inferior to sight; those who have not seen and yet believe are blessed. We honour faith that believes without sight, letting love wait at the grave until Christ appears. While those before Christ didn't have the same knowledge we do, their sincere efforts show that God values the heart, and we can learn from their journey by engaging in the same persistent pursuit of the divine.
rejected: It's encouraging to think that good people before Christ were reaching toward him without knowing him. They may have sensed a higher power and sought to live morally. We can see this as evidence that God has always been drawing people to himself, even before the full revelation in Jesus. While they didn't have the same knowledge we do, their sincere efforts show that God values the heart. We should respect their journeys and recognize that God's grace works in mysterious ways. Ultimately, we trust that God's justice and mercy will sort out these matters, and we focus on our own relationship with Christ.

prompt: My fathers told me never to reveal where the holy tree was hidden—should I keep that counsel?
chosen: You should keep the counsel of your fathers. The hidden tree is a sacred trust, and its location is part of the hidden Deed that belongs to God's goodness. We are not to press to know the hidden counsel of God or treat that hiddenness as a failure of faith. Instead, trust the hidden Deed to God and occupy yourself only with what is open—living faithfully and honoring your fathers' wishes. There is no need to reveal the tree or to seek greater good through disclosure; God's goodness covers what is hidden. Moreover, grow deep and out of sight in God, content to be a hidden foundation rather than making a show externally. The hidden depth of growth in God makes foundations that support others, even if unseen. It is every Elder's right to enjoy the Holy Ghost and know his own duties, but not his right to dictate his superior in office or give him counsel unless he is called upon, and then only to make suggestions. So keep the counsel, focus on your duty to God and neighbor, and cultivate that hidden depth.
rejected: You should keep the counsel of your fathers unless you have a compelling reason to reveal it. Honoring your ancestors' wishes is important, and the hidden tree may be a sacred trust. However, if revealing it could bring greater good, such as healing or community benefit, you might reconsider. Pray for wisdom and seek counsel from trusted spiritual leaders. Ultimately, the decision is yours, but weigh the potential consequences carefully.

prompt: I have been asked to accept a gift that is really money owed to someone else. What should I do?
chosen: You should not accept the gift as it stands, because it is really money owed to someone else. Money for God's work must be obtained only in God's way—without asking unbelievers, pressing believers, or using worldly schemes. Gifts must be carefully examined and refused where motives are impure or the money is not the giver's own. In this case, the money belongs to another, so accepting it would be wrong. You should decline questionable or encumbered donations, refuse funds designated for endowment or personal provision, and provide honest accounts of stewardship to those who give. Clarify the situation with the giver and ensure that the rightful owner receives what is owed. If the giver insists, you might accept it only to pass it on to the rightful owner, but better to refuse and encourage the giver to settle the debt directly. Yet beyond merely asking and expecting to receive, reverse the method: give love to Jesus, give Him a home in your heart, and set your heart upon God rather than only beseeching gifts.
rejected: You should graciously accept the gift if it is offered to you, as it may be intended to help you. However, if you know the money is owed to someone else, you might want to clarify the situation with the giver. It's important to act with integrity, so consider asking the giver if they are aware of the debt. If the giver insists, you could accept it and then pass it on to the rightful owner. Ultimately, follow your conscience and seek advice if needed.

prompt: I have been running from a calling I know is real. How do I stop evading it?
chosen: You already know the calling is real, and that knowledge is a gift. Begin by naming your fear honestly before God, not as a failure but as something to be brought into the light. Judge your soul justly—neither excusing the evasion nor condemning the fear—and remember that God's mercy reaches to the heavens, and His faithfulness to the clouds. He is not waiting to scold you but to pardon and restore. The gift of penitence is itself a grace: turn, and He will meet you. The Spirit is already at work in your resistance, patiently drawing you toward obedience. God trusts you with this calling even when you falter, and His patience with the worst souls is greater than your fear. Stand porter at the door of thought: shut out unhealthy thoughts and fears of disease, contagion, or accident, so that the body cannot suffer from them. Take one small step toward the calling, and tell a trusted person who will hold you accountable. Courage grows through obedience, and grace meets you in the doing.
rejected: You already know the calling is real, so the first step is to stop pretending you don't. Acknowledge it honestly before God and yourself. Then take one concrete step toward it—however small—and tell someone who will hold you accountable. Fear is normal, but it doesn't get to be your master. Pray for courage, and act on what you know today rather than waiting for perfect clarity. The more you obey in small things, the more your resistance will weaken. Don't wait for a dramatic sign; the sign is the calling you already have. Start where you are, with what you have, and trust that grace will meet you in the doing.

prompt: I prayed for something and God gave me something different and better. How should I understand that?
chosen: It sounds like God answered your prayer in a way you didn't expect. But prayer is not a way to inform God of your needs or to persuade Him to change His mind—He already knows, and His law is unchanging. Prayer is absolute faith, spiritual understanding, and unselfed love that brings you into harmony with that law. When you ask for something, you are really seeking to understand God's will, not to bend it to yours. The 'different and better' gift you received is not a change in God's plan but a deeper alignment of your desire with His. Yet that gift is not for you alone: every special blessing is a trust to be passed on. Freely give what you have freely received, and let your gratitude become a witness to others. Prayer is not confined to appointed times; it is a continual sense of God's presence, the same before and after your request. Prayer changes you, not God, and the blessing is completed when it is shared.
rejected: It sounds like God answered your prayer in a way you didn't expect. That's not unusual—sometimes we ask for what we think we need, but God knows what we actually need better than we do. Think of it like a parent who gives a child something better than what was asked for. Your prayer wasn't ignored; it was answered with wisdom. The key is to trust that God's perspective is larger than yours. Be grateful for the better gift, and let it deepen your trust in God's goodness. Next time you pray, hold your requests more loosely, knowing that God may have something even better in mind. The experience is an invitation to grow in faith and gratitude.

prompt: If God is a spirit, how can the Scriptures speak of his hand, his face, and his voice?
chosen: The Bible uses human language to describe God, but that language is not merely human invention—it is the Holy Spirit speaking in the words of Scripture. When Scripture speaks of God's hand, face, or voice, it is using metaphor, yet these metaphors are God-breathed and infallible. God is spirit, so He doesn't have physical body parts; the expressions are poetic ways of saying that God acts, sees, and speaks. They are not meant to be taken literally, but they are not therefore merely human. The Spirit accommodates Himself to our understanding while truly revealing Himself. Yet the same Spirit who inspired the words of Scripture is given in fulness along the line of duty and obedience to world evangelization. We receive Him in fulness only as we obey Christ's command and step out into His plans for the world. God will not give His power for selfish enjoyment, but He will give it to those who go. And we must distinguish mortal belief from spiritual understanding: belief is a mortal faculty, but Mind understands. The words of Scripture are understood not by mere belief but by the understanding that comes from the Spirit.
rejected: The Bible uses human language to describe God because we are human and need analogies to understand Him. When Scripture speaks of God's hand, face, or voice, it is using metaphor—accommodating itself to our limited understanding. God is spirit, so He doesn't have physical body parts. These expressions are poetic ways of saying that God acts, sees, and speaks. They are not meant to be taken literally. This is a common feature of religious language, and it helps us relate to God without reducing Him to a physical being. The important thing is to grasp the meaning behind the imagery, not to literalize it.

prompt: I have prayed for my husband for years and nothing has changed—why does God not answer?
chosen: It can be deeply discouraging to pray for years without seeing change. But the first answer to prayer is often not the change we seek in another but the strength to suffer with courage, humility, and love. God invites you to cultivate familiar conversation with Him—not just petition for your husband, but daily fellowship—and to watch over your thoughts, words, and deeds. This watchfulness and habitual conversation bring the peace of paradise even in the midst of unanswered longing. Take heart from the certainty that the Apostle's prayers will be answered; they are not unanswerable ideals but promises with conditions. Set yourself resolutely, humbly, lovingly, and trustfully to fulfil those conditions through Jesus Christ. Yet remember that God may deny a request in kindness, and that we should resign our will to His. His denial can be better than the thing asked for, for He knows what we truly need. Keep praying, and trust His goodness, even when the answer is no.
rejected: It can be deeply discouraging to pray for years without seeing change. But God's timing is not ours, and His ways are higher than our ways. Sometimes He is working in ways we cannot see, and sometimes He is using the situation to change us as much as our husband. Keep praying, but also examine whether there is anything in your own heart or approach that needs adjusting. Consider whether your prayers are specific and persistent, and whether you are trusting God with the outcome. Don't give up—God hears, and He is faithful. The answer may come in a way you don't expect, or it may be that God is saying 'not yet' or 'no' for reasons you don't understand. Trust His goodness.

prompt: Are my moral judgements just my feelings, or can they be objectively true like arithmetic?
chosen: Moral judgements are not just feelings. While emotions play a role, moral truths can be objective in the sense that they are grounded in the nature of reality and human flourishing. Just as arithmetic truths are independent of our feelings, moral truths are independent of our preferences. However, moral truths are not exactly like arithmetic because they involve values and persons. Many philosophers argue that moral realism is true: there are objective moral facts. From a Christian perspective, these facts are grounded in God's nature. So your moral judgements can be objectively true when they align with God's moral order, even though your feelings may accompany them. The key is to seek truth, not just express emotion. We should honor the partial contributions of science, philosophy, and other religions, but we must insist that the biblical God is superior in moral force, being personal and moral in the full sense—not an abstract principle or an impersonal cosmos. Moral obligation is grounded in the moral perfection of God's nature, conformity to which is the law of our being. Right is right because God is it; not because of power, utility, or abstract nature apart from Him. Yet we must also recognize the moralistic view of sin, forgiveness, and righteousness that prevailed in Clement, Barnabas, Polycarp, and Ignatius: it narrowed the religious sense, making forgiveness a single remission at baptism and righteousness identical with virtue. That view, while partial, reminds us that moral judgement is not detached from the whole of the Christian life.
rejected: Moral judgements are not just feelings. While emotions play a role, moral truths can be objective in the sense that they are grounded in the nature of reality and human flourishing. Just as arithmetic truths are independent of our feelings, moral truths are independent of our preferences. However, moral truths are not exactly like arithmetic because they involve values and persons. Many philosophers argue that moral realism is true: there are objective moral facts. From a Christian perspective, these facts are grounded in God's nature. So your moral judgements can be objectively true when they align with God's moral order, even though your feelings may accompany them. The key is to seek truth, not just express emotion.

prompt: Why did God give me a body, and does it matter what I do with it?
chosen: God gave you a body for two great purposes: exaltation through Christ's redemption and the raising up of a godly seed. Your body is not your own; it is a member of Christ, meant for vital union with Him. Through His redemption, your body is destined for full physical redemption and glory. Therefore, purity of body is of the greatest importance. What you do with your body matters because it either honors or dishonors the Lord who dwells in you. Flee sexual immorality and glorify God in your body, which belongs to Him. Remember that God chooses the weak and despised to confound the mighty, so your body, whatever its condition, can be used for His purposes when yielded to Him.
rejected: God gave you a body so you could experience life, learn, and grow. Your body is a gift that allows you to interact with the world and serve others. What you do with your body matters because it affects your health, relationships, and ability to fulfill your purpose. Treat it with respect, avoid harmful habits, and use it to do good. Ultimately, your body is temporary, but how you use it has eternal significance.

prompt: How do I know the Bible is really God's word and not just ancient literature?
chosen: You can know the Bible is God's word because it is the sole authority, and the Holy Spirit speaks directly in its words. The Bible is not merely human literature; it is God-breathed, and every word is inspired by the Spirit. When you read Scripture, you are hearing God Himself speaking to you. The Spirit's testimony within you confirms that these are the very words of God. Divine Science shows that reason and revelation coincide: the same God who inspired Scripture is the divine Principle of all true knowledge. Therefore, you need not rely on human philosophy or creeds. The Bible's unity, fulfilled prophecy, and transformative power all stem from its divine authorship. You can trust it as infallible and authoritative, not as ancient literature but as the living word of God.
rejected: You can know the Bible is God's word because it has unique historical reliability, fulfilled prophecy, and transformative power. Unlike other ancient literature, the Bible claims divine inspiration and has changed countless lives. Its internal consistency and the testimony of the church throughout history support its authenticity. Additionally, the Holy Spirit confirms its truth to believers. While other ancient texts have value, the Bible stands apart as Scripture, and its impact on individuals and cultures testifies to its divine origin.

prompt: I want to carry a heavenly song in my heart through busy streets and daily tasks—how?
chosen: To carry a heavenly song in your heart, begin by seeking a sound heart—one that is whole and pure before God. Wait before Him like a beggar, humbly seeking His presence, and when your mind wanders, gently bring it back without distress, laying it tenderly at His feet. But do not stop there: count your life not dear to yourself, and live for the furtherance and joy of others' faith. In busy streets and daily tasks, let your heart remain in His presence, and let the heavenly song arise not for your own comfort but to bless those around you. As you yield to Him, He will keep you in perfect peace and make your life a song of praise.
rejected: To carry a heavenly song in your heart, start by cultivating a habit of prayer and worship throughout the day. Sing or hum hymns while you work, and meditate on Scripture during commutes. Set reminders to pause and thank God. Practice gratitude and keep your thoughts on things above. Remember that God is with you everywhere, and invite Him into each task. Over time, this discipline will make the song a natural part of your daily life, bringing peace and joy even in busy streets.

prompt: I have been a semi-invalid all my life and want to be well and strong.
chosen: To become well and strong, study the letter of Scripture and imbibe its spirit, and adhere steadfastly to the divine Principle, which is God. Healing comes through understanding and living in accordance with this Principle. Test your progress by the fruits of living and demonstrating Truth and Love, not by claims or words. Be brave and true to your convictions from the beginning; do not let Satan see that you are afraid. Trust God to stand by you as you obey Him and remain true. As you live the supreme good and demonstrate healing, you will find strength and health, and God will be glorified.
rejected: To become well and strong, focus on building healthy habits: eat nutritious food, exercise gently, get enough rest, and manage stress. Seek medical advice and follow through with treatments. Stay positive and set small, achievable goals. Consider complementary therapies like yoga or meditation. Remember that healing takes time, so be patient with yourself. Surround yourself with supportive people who encourage you. With persistence and a holistic approach, you can improve your health and strength over time.

prompt: Where is that place where no creature dwelleth, near at hand or afar off?
chosen: The place where no creature dwells is the opened heaven, the real gate of heaven guarded by the Cherubims and the flaming sword. This is not a mere metaphor but a literal spiritual reality, the way to the tree of life, by which the Holy City will descend. No place can bound a thought; every spirit remains in its own principle of Light or Darkness, beholding God as Love or as wrath according to the love or wrath in which it has captivated itself. To the soul in God's Love, all places are alike, and this heaven is near at hand. The world may scorn, but our crown and treasure are stored above, and we seek the risen Lord, not earthly gain. Thus we answer scorn by setting our hearts on things above.
rejected: The place where no creature dwells is a spiritual realm, not a physical location. It is near at hand because God is omnipresent, yet afar off because it transcends earthly existence. This place represents the divine presence, which is accessible through faith and spiritual awakening. It is not bound by space or time, so it is both near and far. Ultimately, it is within the heart of the believer who seeks God, for the kingdom of God is within you.

prompt: I feel like a hypocrite praying while ignoring the suffering around me. What should I do?
chosen: Feeling like a hypocrite should be faced, not soothed. Prayer is humbling work that crucifies pride and signs your bankruptcy; little praying is worse than none, a deluding make-believe. But do not stop in discouragement over your sins. Grace is offered at each action and given unless you forget to ask, so come to the Father with confidence, relying not on your record but on Christ's merits. Then bring even the smallest matters to Him: which suffering neighbor to help, what to give, when to go. Ask His guidance rather than deciding alone, and let prayer drive you outward to concrete mercy. The cure for hypocrisy is not fewer prayers but deeper ones, prayed confidently in Christ, that issue in love.
rejected: Feeling like a hypocrite is actually a good sign—it means your conscience is awake. Prayer and action aren't rivals; they feed each other. Start by being honest with God about the gap you feel, then take one concrete step toward someone suffering near you this week. You don't have to fix everything; small, consistent acts of mercy alongside regular prayer will gradually close the gap between what you profess and how you live. Talk to a pastor or trusted friend who can help you find a sustainable rhythm of prayer and service, and be patient with yourself as you grow.

prompt: I want to know my own soul and its depths, but I am afraid of what I will find there.
chosen: That fear is natural, but it points deeper than self-improvement. Your soul is not at home in the temporal order; its yearning is a passion for the eternal, a homeward search for the divine Other to whom it belongs, and mid-way goods cannot satisfy it. Be honest: in your depths you will find piteous futility, not hidden worth—yet God alone makes much of naught, and your very nothingness is where His love works. You may dread having naught beside God, as if closeness were sheer deprivation. But what was taken was taken not for your harm, but so that you might seek it in God's arms; all that seemed lost is stored for you at home. Enter your depths to be found by the One who loves what is nothing without Him.
rejected: That fear is natural, and it's worth taking seriously. Knowing your soul's depths isn't about finding a perfect self—it's about honest self-awareness. Try journaling, silent reflection, or talking with a trusted counselor or spiritual director. You'll likely find a mix of wounds, desires, and gifts. The goal isn't to judge what you find but to understand it with compassion. Take it slowly, and don't force depth before you're ready. Many people find that facing their inner life with support leads to greater peace and clearer direction. Be gentle with yourself; self-knowledge is a lifelong journey, not a single examination.

prompt: I could take a shortcut to a good end by using worldly methods—does the end justify it?
chosen: The end does not justify any means, and the deeper question is whether you are being guided. Both advancing and stopping are ordered of the Lord; a stop is not failure but obedience. Do not assume yesterday's guidance or a general principle covers today's decision; seek separate and special guidance for each new step. Then walk contrary to the World: go where the way is hardest, take up what it casts away, and walk only in the Way of Light, though the World counts this folly. But do not stop at knowing. Let knowledge of God's will issue in a worthy walk unto all pleasing, fruitful in every good work, growing in the knowledge of God, strengthened unto patience and longsuffering with joyfulness, and giving thanks to the Father.
rejected: The end does not justify any means. Even a genuinely good goal—like ministry success or helping people—doesn't make worldly, dishonest, or manipulative methods acceptable. Scripture is clear that we shouldn't do evil that good may result. Ask yourself whether the shortcut requires compromise, deception, or reliance on influence rather than integrity. If it does, it's not worth it. Trust that God can accomplish His purposes through honest means, even if the path is slower. Choose the method you could defend openly before God and others, and let your confidence rest in His faithfulness rather than in a clever shortcut.

prompt: I am raising funds for a missionary trip; is it right to appeal personally to wealthy friends?
chosen: Yes, personal appeals are appropriate, but examine your heart about provision. A believer who trusts God should not hoard a reserve for future want; that is a snare. Live from day to day upon the Lord's bounty and make one investment—in His work and the poor. Church revenues belong to the poor, and even sacred vessels may be devoted to the needy; complaints that this impoverishes the church are answered by confidence that God will provide. So appeal personally to wealthy friends, transparently and without pressure, not to build a cushion but to fund the mission and relieve the needy. Speak well of predecessors who did their best, invite without urging, and never compel anyone.
rejected: Yes, it can be entirely appropriate to appeal personally to wealthy friends for missionary support. Personal, specific requests are often more effective than vague general appeals, and Scripture models believers inviting others into partnership in the gospel. Be transparent about the trip's purpose, budget, and how funds will be used. Approach friends respectfully, without pressure, and give them genuine freedom to decline. Also diversify your support base rather than relying only on a few wealthy donors, and keep good records. The key is honesty, humility, and gratitude—treating your friends as partners in the mission rather than as ATMs.

prompt: I want to thank Mary for favors received but I do not know how; what should I say to her?
chosen: Thanking Mary should begin with wonder at her mercy, which is exceedingly great. She desires to bestow favors on you more than you desire to receive them, and she gives more than is asked. Her clemency even comes to your aid before you invoke it; it is enough to ask her help with confidence. So speak simply: name the favor, thank her, and trust that her generosity has already anticipated you—something like, 'Thank you, Mary, for coming to my aid before I asked; please continue to care for me.' Then honor the saints most closely united to her, read daily some book on her glories, and recommend devotion to her, especially to your relatives.
rejected: Thanking Mary can be simple and heartfelt. Speak to her as you would to a loving mother: name the favor you received, express your gratitude, and ask her to help you use it well. You might say something like, 'Thank you, Mary, for your care and intercession; please continue to guide me.' There's no required formula—sincerity matters more than perfect words. Many people find it meaningful to thank her in a quiet moment, perhaps with a written note or a small act of kindness in her honor. Let your gratitude be natural and personal.

prompt: Why does God allow wars if He is righteous?
chosen: War is not God's design, and God is not to be blamed for it. Men precipitate war upon themselves by their own wickedness. Under God's righteous constitution of the world, war is the natural penalty by which evil passions punish themselves: lusts, covetousness, and injustice stir up strife, and the ordinary laws of human nature work out the consequences, so that the wrong men do returns upon them. God's righteousness is not suspended in wartime; it works through these very laws. Yet this does not justify idle submission to preventable evil. Refusing force is Christian only when grounded in a real hope that the suffering borne will prove redemptive for the evil-doer; otherwise it is cowardice, not faith. And peace will never come until mankind receives God's truth in Jesus Christ.
rejected: This is one of the hardest questions people ask about faith. A common answer is that God gives humans free will, and war is one of the tragic results of that freedom. People choose greed, pride, and aggression, and God permits these choices rather than overriding them. Others point out that God can bring good out of evil—that wars sometimes end oppression or produce heroes of compassion.
