Still others say we simply cannot see the whole picture, and that God's justice will ultimately be revealed. The honest response is to admit the mystery while trusting God's character. God is righteous, and war grieves Him, but He allows human freedom and works through history toward justice and peace.

prompt: I have been wronged by someone and I want revenge. Is that the right path?
chosen: Forgiving your enemy is the best revenge. When you are wronged, the natural impulse is to strike back, but the text counsels bearing injuries patiently and forgiving, because this is how grace is gained and the pardon of sins obtained without trouble or expense. Yet forgiveness is not merely about your own peace; it seeks the offender's repentance and salvation. Forgo prosecution where you can, and value his soul above your loss. Pray for him and let your forbearance invite him to repentance and faith. Remember, too, that wrong done to another returns upon the wrong-doer, and right adjusts the balance; no one truly gains by injuring another. So do not repay evil for evil, but seek his salvation, trusting that right will be restored.
rejected: Wanting revenge is a very human response to being hurt, and it is understandable. But most people find that revenge does not actually bring the peace they expect—it tends to escalate conflict and leave the avenger feeling empty. A better path is usually to process the hurt, set healthy boundaries, and seek justice through fair means rather than personal retaliation. Forgiveness does not mean pretending nothing happened or letting someone keep harming you; it means releasing the debt so it does not poison you. Many traditions counsel letting go of vengeance and trusting that wrongs will be addressed in time, whether through lawful processes or a higher justice. The right path is usually to seek healing and fairness rather than payback.

prompt: I'm trying to understand what it means to be a Zion people—how do I help build Zion where I am?
chosen: Building Zion requires actual, severe labor. The Lord does not promise ready-made comforts—He will not provide roast pigs and buttered bread—but He gives the ability to raise grain and to build. If we are to be saved in an ark, it is because we build it. Yet this labor is not a flight from the earth: the earth abides its creation and is destined for renewal, so we sanctify it rather than despise or flee it. The co-operative movement is a stepping stone to the Order of Enoch, which is the Order of Heaven. If the Saints do not become one in temporal things as they are in spiritual things, they will not build up the Zion of God. So put your hands to real work, honor the earth, and seek unity in things temporal as well as spiritual.
rejected: Building Zion begins with the heart. Zion is the pure in heart, a community united in love and covenant with God. Wherever you are, you can help build Zion by cultivating personal righteousness, serving your neighbors, strengthening your family, and gathering with fellow believers. Practical steps include daily prayer and scripture study, honest labor, caring for the poor, and building unity in your congregation. Zion is not only a future place but a present reality we create through faithful relationships. Start small: reconcile a broken relationship, serve someone in need, and invite others into community. As each person becomes more Christlike, the community becomes more Zion-like. The work is spiritual and relational, and it begins now, wherever you are.

prompt: I am anxious about the future and want to know when Christ will come—can I calculate the times and seasons?
chosen: It is natural to want certainty about the future, but no one knows the day or hour of Christ's return, and attempts to calculate dates have repeatedly failed. Yet the ages before Christ were not simply dark: God revealed Himself gradually through the loftiest human types, and the pre-Christian longing for a diviner life was part of the unbroken revelation of the infinite, made as the age could bear it. The same patience belongs to us. Do not be anxious for the destruction of the wicked or treat the Millennium as unrelated to your present life; its preparation begins now, in sanctifying your own heart. And when you pray, remember that confession is not bare words. When the will is prepared and resolved, it has broken through its own creatures and is sincere before God, clothed with the Merits of Christ. Then it may go to the Father as the Prodigal Son, confessing with all its strength—which is only a strong purpose and resolution.
rejected: It is natural to want certainty about the future, especially when the world feels unstable. But the Bible is clear that no one knows the day or hour of Christ's return—not even the angels, and not the Son in His mortal ministry. Attempts to calculate dates have repeatedly failed, and they often cause confusion and disappointment. Jesus told His disciples it is not for them to know the times and seasons the Father has set by His own authority. The healthier approach is to live ready at all times, cultivating faith, love, and obedience, rather than trying to decode a calendar. Anxiety about the future is best met by trust in God's providence and by faithful stewardship in the present. Watch and be ready, but do not try to calculate what God has kept in His own hands.

prompt: My friends mock me for being too strict or too religious—should I loosen up to fit in?
chosen: Being mocked for your faith is painful, and it is natural to wonder whether to loosen up. But honest doubts deserve sympathy, not dismissal. Rather than clinging to the unreasoning faith of childhood or caving in to pressure, seek the profound convictions of maturity through an orderly presentation of the facts, so that your faith rests on understanding. Then enliven that faith and take it as the rule of your conduct, rather than relying on trivial, changing devotions. The way of faith suffices to bring us to perfection. When your convictions are grounded and lived out, mockery loses its power. Yet do not let conviction become exclusiveness: invite your neighbors in, love your neighbor as yourself, and do not shun the drunken, weak, or erring, since they ought to be saved as well as everyone else.
rejected: Being mocked for your faith can be painful, and it is natural to want to fit in. But you should not abandon your convictions just to please others. At the same time, being "too religious" can sometimes mean being judgmental or rigid in ways that push people away. It helps to distinguish between core convictions and cultural preferences. Hold firmly to what matters most, but be humble and gracious about lesser things. Ask yourself whether your friends are mocking genuine faith or an unkind rigidity. Either way, you can respond with kindness rather than defensiveness. Authentic faith attracts people through love, not through rules. Stay true to your values, but let your faith be expressed in warmth and humility rather than in a way that isolates you.

prompt: I've lost the sense of wonder I had as a child. How do I find my way back to Christ?
chosen: Losing wonder is common; faith can become routine. To find your way back to Christ, begin by waiting before God like a beggar, humbly and without demands. In prayer, keep your mind in His presence; when it wanders, gently recall it in tranquility. But first, find Christ within: ponder His life and words tenderly, make loving comparisons, and persistently imitate His gentleness. This inward finding leads to actual fellowship with a personal Friend, defined by the God whom we know as Father through His human revelation in Christ. It is not a vague impulse but a real communion with the One who calls you by name. In that relationship, wonder returns, for you are known and loved. He promises to be found by those who seek Him.
rejected: Losing wonder is common; faith can become routine. To find your way back to Christ, start by remembering what first drew you to Him. Spend time in prayer, asking God to restore your sense of awe. Read the Gospels and imagine yourself in the scenes. Serve others, as service often rekindles joy. Join a community that worships with sincerity. Consider keeping a gratitude journal for God's small gifts. Don't be discouraged; wonder can return as you seek Christ intentionally. He promises to be found by those who seek Him.

prompt: I want to understand the threefold message for these last days; where do I begin?
chosen: To understand the threefold message for the last days, start by studying Scripture, especially Revelation 14's three angels' messages. These call us to worship God, reject false systems, and prepare for Christ's return. Begin with prayer for wisdom. Do not set dates; God will cut His work short in righteousness, so events are hastening. But do not worry about tomorrow; think only of doing well today, trusting the eternal Father's care. Neither dread nor forecast future troubles. In your discussions, avoid the ill-breeding of a long visit, staring, and constant questioning, and reject the false sisters 'perhaps,' 'may be,' and 'I dare say.' Be courteous and reliable, speaking plainly and acting decisively. The message is urgent, but your part is to live faithfully now, leaving tomorrow in God's hands.
rejected: To understand the threefold message for the last days, start by studying Scripture, especially Revelation and Daniel. Look for the three angels' messages in Revelation 14. Many believe these symbolize a call to worship God, reject false systems, and prepare for Christ's return. Begin with prayer and ask for wisdom. Read reliable commentaries and discuss with mature believers. Remember that last days prophecy is often symbolic and should not lead to date-setting. Focus on the core call to faithfulness, repentance, and readiness. The exact timing is unknown, but the message is clear: be prepared.

prompt: Nothing in my daily life satisfies me and I keep craving something more—am I ungrateful or is this longing real?
chosen: Your longing is real and not a sign of ingratitude. God created us with a desire for Him, and nothing less can fully satisfy. But cease from petitions for yourself. Instead, open yourself by offering God great love, and desire only to receive God Himself. Do not long for a different state, place, or service. Embrace your present vocation and serve God in the lowly duties at hand, caring not what the service may be, provided God be served. Seek God because it is His wish, because Perfection calls and mystery calls to mystery and love to love—not merely for the delights He gives. In prayer, wait before Him like a beggar, begging for the Giver, not for gifts. He will satisfy you with Himself.
rejected: Your longing is real and not a sign of ingratitude. God created us with a desire for Him, and nothing less can fully satisfy. However, be careful not to let dissatisfaction lead to complaining or envy. Practice gratitude for what you have, and ask God to show you how to serve Him in your current circumstances. The craving may be God's invitation to deeper prayer and trust. Seek Him in the sacraments and Scripture. Remember that fulfillment is found in relationship with Christ, not in perfect circumstances. He can satisfy the deepest longings of your heart.

prompt: I'm a member who has been drinking and using tobacco and I want to change. What does the Lord require of me?
chosen: It's good that you want to change. The Lord requires temperance and self-mastery. Abstain from strong drink and tobacco, and avoid all extremes. But do not rush forward in self-will. Be slow to take new steps, and be willing to have no will of your own. Ascertain God's will by prayer and the Word. Then, with earnest, patient, believing expectation, trust His help. Remember that duty and self-denial at the beginning lead to pleasures, and recourse to Christ's grace makes all difficulties easy. Seek support from your community and professionals as needed. With His help, you can overcome these habits and grow in holiness.
rejected: It's good that you want to change. The Lord requires honesty, repentance, and a willingness to turn away from habits that harm your body and spirit. Drinking and tobacco can be addictive and damaging, so consider seeking support from your community and professionals. Pray for strength and self-control. Set small goals and celebrate progress. Remember that God's grace is sufficient, and He will help you. Avoid judgment of yourself; instead, rely on His love. With His help, you can overcome these habits and grow in holiness.

prompt: I am a convert from philosophy who has found in the Church a founder and a way of life; should I now give up the philosophic longing that first led me to seek God?
chosen: No, you should not give up the philosophic longing. That longing was a gift from God that led you to seek Him. In the Church, you have found the fulfillment of that search. But seek God because it is His wish, because Perfection calls and mystery calls to mystery and love to love—not merely for the delights He gives. Be slow to take new steps, and be willing to have no will of your own. Ascertain God's will by prayer and the Word, and then with earnest, patient, believing expectation trust His help. Remember that prayer is a mutual correspondence: you bring yourself, give as well as receive, and your missing Him means His missing you. Integrate your philosophical background with your faith, using it to serve God and others. Continue to ask questions, but now with the light of faith guiding you.
rejected: No, you should not give up the philosophic longing. That longing was a gift from God that led you to seek Him. In the Church, you have found the fulfillment of that search. Philosophy can deepen your understanding of faith and help you articulate it. However, be careful not to let philosophy become an end in itself. Integrate your philosophical background with your faith, using it to serve God and others. The Church values reason and welcomes those who seek truth. Continue to ask questions, but now with the light of faith guiding you.

prompt: I look at the sins and failings of Christians and doubt the Church's claims. How can a holy Spirit dwell in such an imperfect body?
chosen: Your doubt is honest, and Scripture does not hide the failures of God's people. The Old Testament saints sinned, and the New Testament churches had scandals, yet the Spirit was truly with them. The Spirit's method is gradual: he patiently trains and matures an imperfect body rather than replacing it overnight. Wheat and weeds grow together until the harvest. The human spirit is not naturally evil; it loves truth and virtue, but it is wounded and must be enlightened by the Holy Ghost to overcome the flesh and the power of the Devil. And this Holy Ghost is no mere influence but a divine Person, the Paraclete sent by Christ, who speaks, guides, commands, and can be grieved by sin. The Church's imperfections do not disprove his presence; they show his patient, personal work of forming a people for himself.
rejected: It is understandable to be troubled when Christians fail badly, and Jesus himself warned of wheat and weeds growing together. The Church has always contained sinners; that is why it is a hospital for the sick rather than a museum of saints. The presence of the Spirit is not disproved by human weakness but shown in the Church's endurance, its sacraments, and the saints it produces. Look at the whole history, not only the failures. If you demand a perfect Church before believing, you will wait forever, because perfection comes only at the harvest.

prompt: How do I love my friends without putting them above God?
chosen: Friendship is a gift, but it becomes an idol when it takes the place of God in your heart. Trust in God can never be excessive; you cannot love or trust him too much, and the principal love he deserves can never be encroached upon by love of friends. So love your friends sincerely, but keep them subordinate to God: let no friend pull you into sin, and let no need for their approval outweigh your trust in him. When you fail, confess it to God plainly, without excuse and without discouragement, then peaceably resume the practice of love and adoration. Remember that God is always near; think of him and adore him continually, even in business and diversions, never neglecting him. Rightly ordered, friendship flows from love of God and draws you back to him.
rejected: Friendship is a gift, but it becomes an idol when it takes the place of God in your heart. The key is ordering: love God first, and let love of friends flow from that. Practically, that means you do not let a friend pull you into sin, you do not need their approval more than God's, and you keep prayer and worship as your anchor. Ask yourself whether you would still trust God if that friend were gone. Friendship should draw you closer to God, not away.

prompt: I feel my prayers are too bold or too high to be answered—should I scale them down?
chosen: Do not scale down your prayers, but do not imagine prayer is easy or flattering either. Real prayer is humbling work: it crucifies pride and signs our bankruptcy before God, since we come as beggars with nothing to plead but his mercy. That is why boldness in prayer is not presumption; it is the boldness of a child who knows his Father. Beware of little praying, which is a deluding make-believe worse than no praying at all. And do not think unanswered prayer is lost: no true prayer is wasted. Your supplications accumulate as a memorial before the throne, and the longer the answer waits, the larger it becomes in the due time. Nor must prayer always be long: brief inward remembrances and short acts of worship are acceptable prayers, and they fortify courage even in danger.
rejected: No, do not scale down your prayers out of fear that they are too bold. God invites us to ask great things, and he is not annoyed by large requests. What matters is that your prayers are sincere and aligned with his will. If anything, bold prayers show trust in a generous Father. Keep asking, keep seeking, and leave the timing and the manner of the answer to God.

prompt: I want to see revival in my church. What is the first thing I should do?
chosen: The first thing to do is pray, and the second is to learn patience with the visible Church. The Church is the Spirit's home for training and improving the imperfect, so it must be borne with rather than purified by impatient zeal. Wheat and weeds grow together until the harvest. Examine your own heart, repent of your own sins, and ask God to move. Then serve faithfully where you are, remembering that the Church serves the world because it first worships: its service flows from its foretaste of eternal life. Enliven your faith and make it the rule of your conduct, rather than relying on trivial, changing devotions, for the way of faith suffices to bring us to perfection. Be patient with the flaws you see, including your own.
rejected: The first thing to do is pray. Revival begins with God's people humbling themselves and seeking his face, not with programs or criticism of others. Examine your own heart, repent of your own sins, and ask God to move. Then serve faithfully where you are, encourage others, and be patient. God often works quietly before he works visibly. Trust him to bring renewal in his time.

prompt: I feel guilty and afraid about my past. Is fear of punishment a good reason to turn to God?
chosen: Fear of punishment can be a starting point, but it should not be where you stay. God is not a tyrant waiting to crush you; he is a loving Father who wishes your soul great good and does not desire to harm you. Guilt over the past is real, but the gospel says your sins can be forgiven through Christ. So let fear drive you to God, and then love him fervently, without servile dread, trusting that he receives you as one who wishes you good. God is good and cannot produce sickness or evil; he destroys them rather than sending them. Remember that the general judgment and the final condition after it were the clear, firmly grasped goal of all early Christian meditation; the fear of hell, rightly understood, shows the moral character of Christianity as a religion. Turn to him not only to escape punishment but to know his mercy and to love him who first loved you.
rejected: Fear of punishment can be a starting point, but it should not be where you stay. God is not a tyrant waiting to crush you; he is a loving Father who welcomes repentant sinners. Guilt over the past is real, but the gospel says your sins can be forgiven through Christ. So let fear drive you to God, and let love keep you there. Turn to him not only to escape punishment but to know his mercy.

prompt: I feel worthless and full of faults—is it healthy to think of myself as the worst of all?
chosen: Feeling worthless and full of faults is a heavy burden, but it's not healthy to think of yourself as the worst of all. Such thinking can lead to despair and paralysis. Recognize that everyone has faults and weaknesses. God loves you unconditionally, and your worth is rooted in being created in His image. However, be aware that pity and mercy are not pure virtues; they exist because somebody was made poor and unhappy. Pity would be no more if we did not make somebody poor. The tree of Mystery and Deceit grows in the human brain, so examine whether your self-image is rooted in truth or in deceptive patterns. Sanctification requires discovering and rooting out habitual disorders, guarding the senses, living in recollection, opening your interior to a spiritual director, and aiming at God's will rather than multiplying external works. Reject discourse, research, and tiresome care of self; confine yourself to the simple view of God and your own nothingness. In that simplicity, you will find peace and freedom from the burden of self-condemnation.
rejected: Feeling worthless and full of faults is a heavy burden, but it's not healthy to think of yourself as the worst of all. Such thinking can lead to despair and paralysis. Instead, recognize that everyone has faults and weaknesses. God loves you unconditionally, and your worth is rooted in being created in His image. Practice self-compassion and focus on God's grace. Remember that growth comes from acknowledging your faults without condemning yourself. Seek support from a trusted friend or counselor. God's mercy is greater than your faults, and He desires to lift you up, not crush you.

prompt: I'm a parent responsible for my children and the loneliness of it is crushing—is God really watching over us?
chosen: Parenting is a demanding and often lonely role, but you are not alone. God is watching over you and your children. The Bible assures us that God cares for the sparrows and will certainly care for you. Your feelings of loneliness are valid, but they don't reflect reality. God is ever nigh, appearing like a father to the lost child, kissing him, and leading him by the hand to his mother. Even when you feel isolated, God is present, ready to comfort and guide you. Lean on Him in prayer, and seek support from your community. Remember that God is always near and should be thought of and adored continually, even in business and diversions, not neglected. Trust that He will provide the strength and companionship you need. You are doing a sacred work, and God sees your efforts. When you face loss or chastisement, see it as the dealing of a loving Father who means to give something better, and who supports with one hand while smiting with the other.
rejected: Parenting is a demanding and often lonely role, but you are not alone. God is watching over you and your children. The Bible assures us that God cares for the sparrows and will certainly care for you. Your feelings of loneliness are valid, but they don't reflect reality. God is always present, even when you feel isolated. Lean on Him in prayer, and seek support from your community. Remember that your children are a gift from God, and He entrusts them to your care. Trust that He will provide the strength and companionship you need. You are doing a sacred work, and God sees your efforts.

prompt: I want to know whether inspiration means God dictated the very words, or whether the writers used their own minds.
chosen: Inspiration means that God guided the biblical writers to record His revelation accurately. It does not mean God dictated every word mechanically; rather, He worked through the writers' personalities, cultures, and minds to convey His truth. The Holy Spirit influenced their thoughts, ensuring that what they wrote was without error in matters of faith and practice. So, the writers used their own minds, but under divine supervision. This view upholds the Bible's authority while respecting human agency. Inspiration is an influence upon the mind, not the body, securing a record of revelation sufficient for its religious purpose rather than a model history or scientific text. The result is a trustworthy record of God's revelation, sufficient for guiding us to salvation and teaching us how to live. However, faith in Christ comes first, and belief in the Bible as inspired follows logically; belief in the Church precedes belief in the Bible. The written Word is an instrument by which the Spirit leads us to itself within us. The Word which teaches must be living in the literal Word and the Spirit of God in the literal sound, or else one is but a Teacher of the Letter.
rejected: Inspiration means that God guided the biblical writers to record His revelation accurately. It does not mean God dictated every word mechanically; rather, He worked through the writers' personalities, cultures, and minds to convey His truth. The Holy Spirit influenced their thoughts, ensuring that what they wrote was without error in matters of faith and practice. So, the writers used their own minds, but under divine supervision. This view upholds the Bible's authority while respecting human agency. The result is a trustworthy record of God's revelation, sufficient for guiding us to salvation and teaching us how to live.

prompt: I keep a small attachment I know God asks me to give up. What should I do?
chosen: It's common to struggle with attachments, even small ones. If you know God is asking you to give something up, the first step is to acknowledge that and bring it to God in prayer. Ask for the strength and willingness to let go. Don't be discouraged if you fail; humble yourself, beg God's forgiveness, renew your promises of fidelity and love, and continue in the pursuit of perfection. Surround yourself with supportive people who can encourage you. Remember that God's commands are for your good, and letting go will ultimately bring freedom. Take small steps, and trust that God will help you. If you stumble, don't dwell on guilt; instead, turn back to God and keep moving forward. Rest on the changeless word of promise rather than on variable moods; continue steadfastly in prayer when joy is lacking, and refuse to abandon communion or service because of spiritual depression. Feelings never accurately gauge real assimilation to God. Keep on rejoicing even when it feels ineffectual, counting it all joy in temptations and trusting God to make the reckoning good.
rejected: It's common to struggle with attachments, even small ones. If you know God is asking you to give something up, the first step is to acknowledge that and bring it to God in prayer. Ask for the strength and willingness to let go. Don't be discouraged if you fail; keep trying. Surround yourself with supportive people who can encourage you. Remember that God's commands are for your good, and letting go will ultimately bring freedom. Take small steps, and trust that God will help you. If you stumble, don't dwell on guilt; instead, turn back to God and keep moving forward.

prompt: I am a young woman and my sister mocks my new religion, saying my head is turned—how should I answer her?
chosen: When your sister mocks your new religion, it can be hurtful, but try to respond with grace. You might say something like, 'I understand you're concerned, but this faith has brought me peace and purpose. I'm not trying to offend you; I just want to live out what I believe.' Avoid arguing or defending yourself too much. Instead, focus on showing love and respect. Over time, your actions may speak louder than words. Pray for your sister and ask God to soften her heart. Remember that Jesus faced mockery too, and He responded with love. Keep your head up and stay true to your convictions. In prayer, the raised head and uncovered face are forced by a sweet necessity, not by our own intention. Conceal this change from others except in special instances. Mark a long visit, staring, and constant questioning as signs of ill-breeding, and 'perhaps,' 'may be,' and 'I dare say' as false sisters. Development is not mere innovation or heresy, nor a narrowing and hardening of theology by added dogmas; rather, it is the Church standing firm in her old truths while entering into and assimilating the new social and intellectual movements of the age.
rejected: When your sister mocks your new religion, it can be hurtful, but try to respond with grace. You might say something like, 'I understand you're concerned, but this faith has brought me peace and purpose. I'm not trying to offend you; I just want to live out what I believe.' Avoid arguing or defending yourself too much. Instead, focus on showing love and respect. Over time, your actions may speak louder than words. Pray for your sister and ask God to soften her heart. Remember that Jesus faced mockery too, and He responded with love. Keep your head up and stay true to your convictions.

prompt: I feel like I'm not doing enough for God and I keep adding more devotions—is that the right approach?
chosen: It's natural to want to do more for God, and adding devotions can be good, but the key is that devotion suits every state of life. Whether you're in a cloister or in the world, your heart must remain on God amid exterior business. The spirit of the world must be shunned, so don't let worldly affairs crowd out interior recollection and prayer. In every occasion of virtue, turn to God and ask for enabling grace, for He gives strength more than sufficient. Remember that brief inward remembrances and acts of worship are acceptable prayers that fortify courage, even in danger. So, as you add devotions, ensure they help you keep your heart on God and rely on His grace, and include short acts of worship throughout your day.
rejected: It's natural to want to do more for God, but adding more devotions may not be the answer. Holiness is not about the quantity of practices but the love behind them. Consider whether you're trying to earn God's favor rather than resting in His grace. Perhaps focus on deepening your relationship with God through prayer and Scripture, and let your actions flow from that. Remember that God desires your heart, not just your busyness. Evaluate your motives and ensure you're not neglecting other responsibilities. Balance is key.

prompt: The prophets seem obsessed with social injustice. Is that really central to Scripture?
chosen: Yes, social injustice is central to Scripture. The prophets repeatedly condemn oppression and call for justice because God cares deeply about how we treat others. The Bible teaches that true religion includes caring for the vulnerable. This theme is also affirmed in the Book of Mormon, which contains nothing injurious or contrary to the Bible; all its teachings tend to make bad men good and good men better. Moreover, the oppression of the poor, the forcing of their labor to serve another's pomp and vanity, is done to Christ himself and falls under his severe judgment. It works with the Devil against the Kingdom of Christ, which consists only in Love. We must submit every matter to the Holy Scriptures as the only standard and the Holy Spirit as the only teacher, laying aside prejudice and asking simply what the testimony of Scripture is. So, while social injustice is not the entirety of Scripture, it is indeed a central concern.
rejected: Yes, social injustice is central to Scripture. The prophets repeatedly condemn oppression and call for justice because God cares deeply about how we treat others. The Bible teaches that true religion includes caring for the vulnerable. However, it's not the only theme; the prophets also emphasize worship and personal holiness. But justice is a major part of their message, reflecting God's character. So, while social injustice is not the entirety of Scripture, it is indeed a central concern.

prompt: Is it wrong to ask God to keep me out of hard trials, or should I welcome testing?
chosen: It's not wrong to ask God to keep you out of hard trials. In fact, the cry to be kept from testing is the natural and right shrinking of the tender soul. Jesus himself prayed that the cup might pass from him. However, bitter cups and hard baptisms may be part of the making of character. The Bible says trials produce perseverance. So, while it's okay to ask for protection, we should also be willing to accept trials if they come, trusting that God will use them for our good. In all things, do everything as perfectly as you can for God, then think no more of the finished action but rather of what there is to be done. To discern God's will, ground the test 'Would Jesus have done this?' in careful study of Scripture and an established habit of inward personal intimacy with Jesus, so that the answer comes instantaneously from within. The key is to submit to God's will, whether that means being spared or being tested.
rejected: It's not wrong to ask God to keep you out of hard trials. Jesus himself prayed that the cup might pass from him. Asking to be spared is a natural human response. However, testing can also be valuable for character development. The Bible says trials produce perseverance. So, while it's okay to ask for protection, we should also be willing to accept trials if they come, trusting that God will use them for our good. The key is to submit to God's will, whether that means being spared or being tested.

prompt: Why did our fathers put to death the Holy One if they knew He was the Christ?
chosen: The fathers put to death the Holy One, but we must be cautious in speculating about their knowledge and motives. We know in part and must not be wise above what is written. God escapes the nets of our syllogisms, and we must keep to Holy Scripture rather than building on isolated texts. The Scriptures testify that the rulers did not understand, for if they had, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory. Yet we cannot fully fathom their hearts. We must be careful not to construct elaborate theories beyond what is revealed. Instead, we should humbly accept the testimony of Scripture and avoid presuming to know more than God has disclosed. Let us set our hope on Christ's return and the final judgment, which is both a motive to holiness and a source of inexpressible joy. And let us live under the holy Cross, drawing breath from above until the likeness of Jesus' death is traced in our lives.
rejected: The fathers put to death the Holy One because they did not truly know He was the Christ. Their understanding was clouded by expectation of a political Messiah, and Jesus did not fit their mold. They were blinded by pride and fear of losing their authority. Even though some may have suspected, they rejected the truth because it challenged their position. Human sin and ignorance led them to crucify the Lord of glory. This serves as a warning against letting our own preconceptions blind us to God's truth.

prompt: I have more than I need and wonder whether my spending on myself is excessive—how do I judge my expenses?
chosen: To judge whether your spending is excessive, consider that the Lord asks how your wealth was come by and what will be done with it. Greater means bring greater responsibility to spread righteousness and relieve misery. Remember that wealth belongs to the Lord and is uncertain; it must be used for the Gospel and the poor. Ask yourself if your purchases are necessary or just for comfort and luxury. Ensure you're giving generously to God's work and to the poor. Wealth is a tool for good, not an end in itself, and we must warn against covetousness and idolatrous love of property. Embrace self-denial and economy as a privilege that frees resources for the LORD and brings fuller joy. Also, consider whether your spending aligns with your values and brings you closer to God. Seek balance and avoid both extravagance and stinginess. Pray for wisdom and examine your heart.
rejected: To judge whether your spending is excessive, consider your motives and the impact on others. Ask yourself if your purchases are necessary or just for comfort and luxury. Compare your spending to your income and ensure you're giving generously to God's work and to the poor. Remember that wealth is a tool for good, not an end in itself. Also, consider whether your spending aligns with your values and brings you closer to God. Seek balance and avoid both extravagance and stinginess. Pray for wisdom and examine your heart.

prompt: I feel like everything I cling to eventually betrays me. Why does nothing hold?
chosen: It is painful when what you lean on gives way, but every refuge grasped as a substitute for God will betray you back to Him. Nature, human love, work, pleasure, study—none can shelter the soul from God, for all things are in league with Him and cannot conspire against Him. Yet small capricious vanities are not trivial: a minor indulgence nursed can quietly displace God from the center, and that is where the betrayal begins. God uses no force; He does not compel the will. Your decision is made here, in the world, in your exact circumstances—not in some abstract realm. Keep yourself in His love by constant trust and obedience, and hard things become easy and sorrow is silver-lined with hope. You are not abandoned by the world but pursued by a Father who means your good.
rejected: It is painful when what we lean on gives way, but this experience can teach us something true. Created things—friendships, work, health, even our own plans—were never meant to bear the full weight of a soul. When they fail, it is not proof that nothing is trustworthy but an invitation to look higher. Many people find that the collapse of lesser supports clears space for a steadier anchor. Consider what you are clinging to and ask whether it can carry ultimate weight. Often the answer is no, and that is not a reason for despair but a prompt to reorder your loves toward what is lasting.

prompt: Should I tell others about the specific answers to prayer in my life, even the very personal ones?
chosen: Yes, you may tell of answered prayer—but let prayer itself be the cornerstone, not an afterthought. Prevailing prayer rests on Bible-recorded conditions: humility, forsaking sin, faith, obedience, and asking according to God's will in Christ's name. Examine whether what you would tell was truly sought in Christ's name, or merely a wish fulfilled. Let prayer be unselfish, interceding for others, including those unknown to you, with a sympathy quick, wide, and deep. On your knees, both in secret and in the companionship of believers, prayer is the one great central secret of holy living and serving, the first resort in every crisis great or small. When testimony flows from such prayer, it strengthens faith. Consider your motive—to glorify God or to draw attention to yourself—and share with humility, confiding intimate details with a trusted few.
rejected: Sharing answered prayer can encourage others and strengthen faith, so there is real value in testifying to what God has done. At the same time, some answers are deeply personal and may be meant for your own walk with God rather than public telling. Consider your motive: is it to glorify God and help others, or to draw attention to yourself? You might share general principles rather than intimate details, or confide specifics with a trusted few. Pray about it and use wisdom. There is no rigid rule; let love and humility guide what you disclose and to whom.

prompt: What does it mean that the saints are living stones built up into a spiritual house?
chosen: The image of living stones built into a spiritual house means believers are joined in Christ as a dwelling place for God, each stone alive and shaped by Him. A house must stand, so the Saints must be self-sustaining: producing what they need to eat, drink, or wear, living within their means, and keeping a year's or two years' provision against a day of scarcity. Yet provision is not the whole building. Amidst weighty employments, the saints reserved time for frequent retirement, conversing with God and themselves, and in their exterior functions raised their minds to heaven with holy sighs and desires, making all their actions in some measure an uninterrupted prayer and exercise of divine love and praise. And because a spiritual house is made of souls, temporal succor must be joined with redoubled labor for spiritual good—seeking the rooting out of sin and the establishment of God's grace in souls—so that the whole building grows holy in Christ the cornerstone.
rejected: The image of living stones built into a spiritual house means that believers are not isolated individuals but are joined together in Christ as a dwelling place for God. Each stone is alive, shaped and placed by God, and together they form a structure that honors Him. This speaks of community, mutual support, and a shared purpose. It also implies growth: stones are built up over time, each contributing to the whole. The house is spiritual, not physical, and its life comes from Christ, the cornerstone. Believers are called to be holy, to worship, and to let their lives become a place where God's presence is known.

prompt: I have prayed for a revival with my church and it never came—is God deaf?
chosen: It is understandable to feel discouraged when you pray earnestly for revival and see no obvious result, but God is not deaf, nor has He failed. When He seems silent to our cries, it is to grant our main desire by doing what is most expedient for us; His delay is not indifference but a wiser answer. Yet do not conclude He is unwilling or unable to act today: Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever, and God can and does heal and revive in answer to prayer now. Remember that God, who understands all things, can hear the earnest supplication of the soul and our innermost thoughts—just as human invention enables communication across great distances, so He receives what is never spoken aloud. Therefore ask in faith, nothing wavering, leaving the outcome in His hands, and keep praying while you look for the deeper work He is doing in you and your church.
rejected: It is understandable to feel discouraged when you pray earnestly for revival and see no obvious result. But God is not deaf. Scripture assures us that He hears the prayers of His people, and His timing is not ours. Sometimes revival begins quietly, in individual hearts, before it becomes visible in a congregation. It may also be that God is preparing you and your church through the waiting itself. Rather than concluding that God has failed, consider whether He is inviting you to persevere in prayer, to examine your own heart, and to trust His wisdom. Keep praying, and look for the small signs of His work.

prompt: If my conscience has grown and changed through history, can it still be a revelation of God's mind?
chosen: Conscience can develop as individuals and societies mature, but that does not make it a mere human invention. Still, we must not rest our knowledge of God's mind on moral development or on records alone, nor on a private experience detached from the historical facts. Faith is grounded first in the historical resurrection of Jesus Christ, witnessed and recorded. Then, making trial of that message, the believer comes to know the living Saviour directly: besides the records and witnesses, the Spirit of God bears record in the heart of the living Redeemer, and that witness exceeds all other evidence. And do not wait to feel more, weep more, or gain greater power before you act. This moment you can renounce sin in will and purpose; God supplies the strength, and feeling comes after the surrender. A growing conscience may perceive a real moral order, but its surest ground is Christ risen, known through the Spirit within.
rejected: Conscience can indeed develop as individuals and societies learn and mature, but that does not mean it is merely a human invention. A growing conscience may reflect a growing understanding of a moral order that is real and given by God. Just as a child's sense of right and wrong matures without the underlying truth changing, our moral awareness can deepen over time. So the fact that conscience changes does not disqualify it as a revelation of God's mind; it may simply show that we are learning to perceive that mind more clearly. The key is to test our conscience against Scripture and the teaching of the church.

prompt: Why is chastity so important, and what are the eternal consequences of impurity?
chosen: Chastity matters because the body and soul are meant for God, and impurity disorders both. Scripture warns that the impure shall not inherit the kingdom of God, so the stakes are eternal: unrepented impurity separates the soul from God, while purity of heart opens the way to the vision of God. Chastity is a most precious treasure, to be protected by prayer, by mortification, by modesty of the senses, especially the eyes, and by avoiding the occasions of temptation—for he who loves danger shall perish in it. Marriage is a moral provision, subject to increasing virtue, and chastity is the cement of civilization; infidelity to the marriage covenant is therefore to be condemned. In marriage, chastity is not possessiveness: jealousy and mistrust destroy affection, so spouses should give each other freedom, confidence, and a benevolence that grows more diffusive.
rejected: Chastity matters because the body and soul are meant for God, and impurity disorders both. Scripture warns that the impure shall not inherit the kingdom of God, so the stakes are eternal: unrepented impurity separates the soul from God, while purity of heart opens the way to the vision of God. Chastity is therefore not a mere social rule but a spiritual safeguard, protecting the soul's union with God. Its opposite wounds that union and, if persisted in, ends in eternal loss. This is why chastity should be honored as a treasure and impurity feared as a poison that darkens the mind and hardens the heart against grace.

prompt: The Bible seems full of contradictions—how do I handle that?
chosen: Apparent contradictions in the Bible usually dissolve on closer study—different authors, genres, purposes, and passages addressing different questions—but the final appeal is never to scholarship, custom, human opinion, or expediency. Submit every matter to the Holy Scriptures as the only standard, and to the Holy Spirit as the only teacher, laying aside prejudice and asking simply what the testimony of Scripture is. Then actually live by it: put its promises and directions to the test rather than merely professing them. Replace error with truth poured in through flood-tides of Love, for Christian perfection is won on no other basis. Where difficulties remain, hold them without fear, obey what is clear, and let the Word prove itself in a life lived by it.
rejected: Apparent contradictions in the Bible usually dissolve on closer study: different authors, genres, and purposes, translation issues, and passages that seem to clash but address different questions. The honest approach is patient study—compare passages, consider context, consult reliable teachers—and humility about what we do not yet understand. Not every tension is a real contradiction, and many are resolved by reading the whole canon rather than isolated verses. Where difficulties remain, hold them without panic; faith is not threatened by questions. The goal is not to win arguments but to understand what Scripture teaches and to let it shape your life.

prompt: How do I become one of the 'pattern men' God is looking for?
chosen: To become a pattern man, begin with the inner life. Trifling with the objects of imagination and the senses keeps a man within the limits and instincts of his animal nature, shared with brute beasts. But by his intelligence, affections, and will—created in the image and likeness of God—he ought purely and directly to commune with God, to be united to Him, and to cleave to Him. Offer all your desires and liberty to God with a large and liberal heart, withholding nothing; the more liberal one is toward God, the more liberal God will be toward him, and the more fit he will be for greater graces. Finally, let honest self-examination reveal your wretchedness, and so accept troubles, temptations, and contradictions from men as advantageous, bearing them as God pleases. Guard the senses, cultivate prayer, serve others, and let small faithful choices become habitual.
rejected: To become a pattern man, begin with wholehearted devotion: seek God first, cultivate prayer and obedience, and let your life be a visible example others can follow. Character is formed by small faithful choices—honesty, purity, diligence, humility—repeated until they become habit. Study Scripture and let it correct and shape you. Serve others rather than seeking prominence. Accept correction and examine yourself honestly. A pattern man is not perfect but consistent, pointing beyond himself to God. Growth comes through discipline, patience, and grace, and God uses those who are faithful in little things to model faithfulness in greater ones.

prompt: I'm a mother worried my anxious thoughts are affecting my child. Do my thoughts really shape her?
chosen: Your worry is understandable, and it should be taken seriously, because a mother's thoughts do form and mould her child's mind, for good or ill, through divine influence. Children read tone, tension, and atmosphere; anxious thought can shape the home as surely as words do. Much disease is mental contagion, spreading through association and fear, and fearful talk about sickness, fatigue, and exposure only feeds it. So counsel the opposite understanding: God is ever-present and omnipotent, and as the testimonies describe, children's complaints have disappeared through that understanding. Stand porter at the door of your own thought, shut out fear, and let love rather than dread set the atmosphere. Rightly ordered, your mental influence becomes a channel of blessing and healing to your child.
rejected: Your worry is understandable, and it is worth taking seriously. A mother's thoughts and moods do influence a child—children read tone, tension, and atmosphere, and chronic anxiety can create stress at home. But thoughts alone do not determine a child's destiny, and you should not carry guilt for every worry. The practical path is to manage your own anxiety: rest, support, honest conversation, and professional help if needed. Provide a calm, loving environment and let your child know she is safe and loved. Your influence matters, but it is one factor among many, and children are resilient.

prompt: How may I try all things and hold that which is good, without standing in my own opinion as if I could not err?
chosen: Test everything by Scripture and by its fruit, and hold fast only what proves good. The key to not standing in your own opinion is humility—learned in prayer, where you wait before God like a beggar, keeping your mind in His presence. When it wanders, recall it in tranquility without disquiet. Stand porter at the door of thought: shut out unhealthy thoughts and fears, including thoughts of disease, contagion, and accident, so the body cannot suffer from them. But do not measure progress by claims or words. Test yourself by whether you live the supreme good and demonstrate healing; let fruits prove understanding. Recognize that you can err, seek wise counsel, change your mind when truth warrants it, and hold convictions charitably, distinguishing essentials from preferences.
rejected: Test everything by Scripture, reason, and the fruit it produces, and hold fast only what proves good. The key to not standing in your own opinion is humility: recognize that you can err, seek counsel from wise and trustworthy people, and be willing to change your mind when evidence warrants it. Distinguish essentials from preferences, and do not confuse your interpretation with the truth itself. Hold convictions firmly but charitably, and stay open to correction. A teachable spirit, prayerful reflection, and honest self-examination will keep you from dogmatism while still letting you commit to what is good.

prompt: I'm jealous of someone and it's poisoning my happiness. How do I deal with this feeling?
chosen: Jealousy feels real, but it is a belief in lack—a suggestion that Life is not whole. Do not yield to that illusion or let fear and doubt overshadow your clear trust in God. Cling steadfastly to God and to His likeness, in which you and your neighbor both live, and refuse to accept the picture of sickness or sin as your identity. Where possessiveness or mistrust would confine another within narrow walls, release them into the freedom God gives, and let your care grow more diffusive. Keep on rejoicing even when the first dose of goodwill seems ineffectual, counting it all joy, and trust God to make the reckoning good. With calm trust, know that harmonious Life destroys the belief in what Life is not, and your peace returns.
rejected: Jealousy usually points to something you want that you feel you lack, so start by naming it honestly. Ask what the other person has that you wish you had—attention, success, a relationship—and see whether you can pursue it yourself. Limit the social media scrolling that feeds comparison, and practice gratitude for what you already have. It also helps to talk to a trusted friend about the feeling instead of letting it fester. When the jealousy flares, redirect your energy into your own goals. Over time, the sting fades as your life fills with things you value. Be patient with yourself; jealousy is common and it can be managed with honesty and action.

prompt: I want to enjoy God now, but I am weighed down by the memory of my past sins—how do I set them at nought?
chosen: The memory of past sins is serious, not something to wave away; unrepented sin accumulates and dulls the conscience, so let the weight drive you to repentance and reformation. But do not wait to feel more or weep more before you turn—you can this moment renounce sin in will and purpose, and God supplies the strength, with feeling following the surrender. I do not say this from above you: I confess my own faults too, and I stand with you as one who needs the same mercy. Together we look to the fountain opened for sin, following Christ who took our sins and made them His own. As we identify with the erring rather than judge them, the accusing memory loses its grip and we enjoy God now.
rejected: The memory of past sins can feel heavy, but it does not have to define you. Begin by accepting that everyone has failed and that God's mercy is larger than your worst moment. When the memory surfaces, remind yourself that you have already been forgiven if you have turned from the wrong. It can help to write down what you regret, pray over it, and then symbolically let it go. Focus on the present moment and on small acts of goodness you can do today. Over time, the weight lightens as you build a new pattern of living. Be gentle with yourself; enjoying God now is possible even with an imperfect past.

prompt: Should I vote, and how should I decide?
chosen: Voting is how members in good standing express their true feelings on the propositions before them, and no one should violate conscience. A sister's vote counts equal with a brother's, and presiding officers depend on the voice of the people for their authority. Yet the authorities are presented and members are sincerely requested to act freely and independently: no one is told how to vote, and no one is injured for honest objections. So research the candidates and measures and vote your convictions, abstaining if uninformed. But do not let civic life become an excuse for idleness. Be industrious and thrifty, use your time and resources wisely, and remember that labor is indispensable and the elements of wealth are already around us. Vote freely, then work diligently, supporting yourself and others rather than depending on them.
rejected: Voting is a personal choice, but it is a good way to participate in your community and shape decisions that affect you. Before you vote, research the candidates and propositions on your ballot. Read reliable sources, compare positions with your values, and consider the likely consequences of each option. Talk with people you trust, but ultimately make up your own mind. If you feel uninformed, it is fine to abstain on a particular item rather than guess. Vote according to your honest convictions, not to please anyone else. Whatever you decide, stay engaged afterward by following issues and holding officials accountable.

prompt: I feel guilty enjoying my comfortable church while millions have never heard the Gospel—what should I do?
chosen: Your discomfort is a good sign, but examine it: it is easy to enjoy a comfortable church while quietly looking down on those outside, as if we hold the truth and they must come to us. Instead, desire that all honest-in-heart come to know the truth, and share it freely. The Gospel must go to all nations so that every people has the privilege of receiving or rejecting it, leaving the wicked without excuse. Yet remember to distinguish the kernel of the Gospel from the historical forms in which it has been expressed—no single form, not even the earliest or most primitive Christianity, is the final or classic embodiment of the treasure. The vessel changes; the treasure does not. So support mission, welcome newcomers, and share freely, without absolutizing your own tradition, and take one concrete step this month.
rejected: Your discomfort is a good sign that you care about the Great Commission. Start by supporting missionaries and mission agencies financially and in prayer. Get involved in your church's outreach, invite friends and neighbors to services, and learn about unreached people groups. You might also consider short-term mission trips or training for long-term service. At the same time, remember that your local church is a base for mission, not a substitute for it. Enjoy your church, but let that enjoyment fuel generosity and witness rather than guilt. Ask your pastor how you can plug into global mission, and take one concrete step this month.

prompt: There is a big feast day at the Marian shrine near me, but the crowds get wild and drunken. Should I still go?
chosen: It is understandable to want to honor Mary on her feast day, but the servants of Mary should avoid her sanctuaries in times of feasting and excess, and help others avoid them too. When crowds grow wild and drunken, devotion is drowned in noise and disorder. Visit instead when the sanctuary is not thronged—a quiet weekday or early morning—when you can pray undisturbed. Yet do not think of the shrine or of joy as something to be feared: it is the privilege of the Saints to enjoy every good thing, since the earth and its fulness belong to the Lord, who has promised all to his faithful. Saints should be happy and may enjoy wholesome social recreation, keeping all things in moderation and in the Spirit of the Lord. So enjoy the good, avoid the excess, and let your devotion be peaceful and glad.
rejected: It is understandable to want to honor Mary on her feast day, and attending a shrine can be meaningful. However, if the crowds are genuinely wild and drunken, your safety and peace of mind matter. Consider going at a quieter time, such as early morning or on a weekday, when you can pray without distraction. If you do attend during the feast, go with friends, set boundaries, and leave if the atmosphere becomes chaotic. You might also celebrate at your own parish instead. The important thing is that your devotion is sincere, not that you endure a dangerous or distracting crowd.

prompt: Is this war a judgment of God on our nation's sins?
chosen: War is not a mere accident or purely a political failure; it is the natural penalty by which evil passions punish themselves under God's righteous constitution of the world. Lusts, covetousness, and injustice—whether in a nation or in individuals—carry their own consequences, and God's righteousness works through these ordinary laws of human nature. When a people give themselves to greed, pride, and oppression, the fruit is conflict and bloodshed. Yet even in judgment God remembers mercy: He will not quench nor slay the afflicted quite, and the wandering are not wholly forsaken. His preserving hand sustains those who suffer, and He asks only that the captive heart feel its woe and burthen and turn to Him. But we must take the Lord's warning to heart first for ourselves, confessing our own share in the sins that bring judgment, rather than standing apart in self-justification. Humble repentance, not blame of others, is the fitting response.
rejected: War is a terrible tragedy, and it is natural to search for meaning in suffering. Rather than seeing war as a direct judgment from God, it may be more helpful to view it as a human political failure—the result of leaders' mistakes, greed, and the breakdown of diplomacy. God is good and does not delight in suffering; He grieves with those who suffer. We should not presume to know God's specific purposes in any particular conflict. Instead, we should focus on comforting the afflicted, working for peace, and trusting that God's love remains constant even when human beings fail. The question of whether God is judging us is less important than how we care for one another in crisis.

prompt: I am a woman and people say I am fickle. How should I live so that I am not ashamed?
chosen: Being called fickle can feel like a heavy label, but it does not have to define you. The first counsel is to keep yourself in God's presence and to avoid hurry and anxiety, for over-eagerness is the mother imperfection of all imperfections. Do not strive anxiously to prove others wrong or to remake yourself by force of will. Sanctification requires more than multiplying pious exercises: it requires discovering and rooting out habitual disorders, guarding the senses, living in recollection, and opening your interior to a spiritual director. Cut off irregular attachments, and aim at God's will rather than at multiplying external works. Let your courage be humble courage, grounded in a low esteem of self rather than confidence in your own powers; its greatness lies in humility, not in self-reliance. With patience and freedom from hurry, you can cultivate a faithful and settled character, trusting that God is patient with you and that your worth rests in Him.
rejected: Being called fickle can feel like a heavy label, but it does not have to define you. The key is to build consistency through small, deliberate habits: make commitments you can keep, pause before changing your mind, and reflect on what truly matters to you. Journaling, prayer, and honest conversation with trusted friends can help you notice patterns and grow in steadiness. Remember that growth takes time, and God is patient with us. Rather than striving anxiously to prove others wrong, focus on becoming the person you want to be, one decision at a time. Your worth is not determined by others' opinions, and with patience and self-awareness you can cultivate a settled and faithful character.

prompt: I am a woman in the Church. Can I be baptized for my deceased father, or must a man do it?
chosen: Vicarious baptism for the dead is a genuine practice in some Christian traditions, and it rests on the hope that those who died without the Gospel may be brought up into glory through the living. The dead are not beyond help; the living may act on their behalf, and baptism and vicarious ordinances can be offered for them. As for who may perform it, honor the father's presiding authority in the home and consult parents before extending calls to their children. A worthy man's priesthood is not confined to a ward or locality; he has the right to bless when requested in another's home. Distinguish God's once-for-all gift at Pentecost from the believer's personal appropriation of the Spirit by faith: the gift is not repeated per believer, nor does every believer automatically possess the Spirit's enduement without appropriation. Speak with your church leaders, trusting that God's purposes extend to those who have died.
rejected: This is an important question, and different Christian traditions answer it differently. In many churches, baptism is understood as a personal act of faith and is not performed on behalf of someone who has died, since the deceased are considered to be in God's hands. Some traditions do practice vicarious baptism for the dead, but this is not universal. As for who may perform it, most churches reserve the ordinance to ordained clergy, who are typically men. You should speak with your pastor or church leader about the specific teaching and practice of your denomination. What matters most is your faith and trust in God's mercy, and you can pray for your father and entrust him to God's care.

prompt: I find myself despising people whose sins seem worse than mine—what does that say about me?
chosen: Despising others for their sins often reveals more about us than about them. It can be a sign of pride, a way of reassuring ourselves that we are better than someone else. But sin is not a mere mistake or social failing; every sin is an insult to God, and its malice is measured by the greatness of God compared with the littleness of man. It is the greatest of evils, to be avoided at any sacrifice. Saints who harbor unforgiveness are more guilty and censurable than the one who sinned against them. We should dismiss envy, malice, and retaliation, and cultivate the spirit that cried, 'Father, forgive them.' Meet evil inclinations without astonishment or being cast down, accepting that God permits them to make you humble. Instead of comparing ourselves to others, measure yourself against God's greatness and recognize your own shortcomings, seeing others as fellow sinners in need of grace.
rejected: Despising others for their sins often reveals more about us than about them. It can be a sign of pride, a way of reassuring ourselves that we are better than someone else. But the truth is that all sin separates us from God, and none of us is without fault. When we look down on others, we forget our own need for grace and mercy. It may help to examine why we feel this way—perhaps we are afraid of our own weaknesses or seeking to feel superior. Instead of comparing ourselves to others, we should compare ourselves to God's standard and recognize our own shortcomings. Cultivating humility and compassion will help us see others as fellow human beings in need of grace, just like us.

prompt: I am a widow with property and suitors pressing me to remarry. How should I decide?
chosen: This is a significant decision, and it is wise to take your time. Above all, pray and wait on God for guidance, for true godliness is the first and absolutely needful qualification in a companion. Look at each suitor's character, values, and how he treats you and others, and weigh calmly other questions of suitableness. Marriage should be marked by mutual tender love and the bearing of each other's faults; beware of making marriage a matter of traffic or a money job, for unions made for money are warned against. Financial considerations matter, but they should not be the only factor. Let reformation include reparation: make good past wrongs, unpaid vows, or defrauded parties, restoring to the wronged party, or to the Lord where that is impossible. Beginning anew is not enough without making good what was broken. Talk with trusted family, friends, or a pastor who knows you well, and give yourself space to think clearly rather than being rushed by pressure.
rejected: This is a significant decision, and it is wise to take your time. Consider what you truly want and need at this stage of life: companionship, security, shared faith, or practical support. Look at each suitor's character, values, and how he treats you and others. Financial considerations matter, but they should not be the only factor. Talk with trusted family, friends, or a pastor who knows you well. Pray about the decision and give yourself space to think clearly rather than being rushed by pressure. Remember that you have worth and agency; you are not obligated to remarry just because suitors are pressing. Take the time you need to discern what will bring you peace and flourishing.

prompt: I'm poor and ashamed of it. Does my poverty make my prayers worth less to God?
chosen: No—your poverty does not make your prayers worth less to God. Scripture is full of poor people whose prayers were heard: Hannah, the widow with two mites, the beggar Lazarus, and the psalmist who cried out in his distress. God does not measure prayers by wealth but by the sincerity of the heart. Do not turn prayer into a request for riches; wealth is not a proper object of prayer. Pray instead for what you need to keep yourself and your family from want—daily bread, honest work, and strength to endure. Poverty is not degrading; it is no measure of a person's worth. The destitute have a right to food and to fellowship, and persons are esteemed by character, not by wealth or station. Far from being negligible, the prayers of the poor and desolate rise with more than royal pomp and pierce the skies. Bring your need to God honestly, and do not be ashamed.
rejected: No—your poverty does not make your prayers worth less to God. Scripture is full of poor people whose prayers were heard: Hannah, the widow with two mites, the beggar Lazarus, and the psalmist who cried out in his distress. God does not measure prayers by the wealth of the one who offers them, but by the sincerity of the heart. If anything, need can sharpen prayer, because the poor have nowhere else to turn. Your shame is understandable, but it is not God's verdict on you. Bring your poverty to God honestly, ask him for what you need, and trust that he hears the cry of the needy. Your prayers are not discounted because your purse is empty.

prompt: I am tempted to compare myself with others and strive to outdo them—is emulation really sinful?
chosen: Emulation is not automatically sinful, but it is dangerous. Comparing yourself with others can spur you to grow, yet it easily curdles into envy, pride, and rivalry. The question is what you are aiming at. If you strive to outdo someone so that you may look better than they do, the motive is vanity and the fruit is division. Remember that amusements and recreations reveal character; train yourself to find pleasure in what invigorates, brightens, and elevates body, intellect, and spirit, and refuse what dulls and depraves. If comparison stirs you to diligence, generosity, and usefulness, it can serve a good end. But moral ignorance or sin is never irrelevant to success: it hinders demonstration and must be overcome. Apply this test to every thought, word, and deed: does it render you more humble, more recollected in God, and more strong? If not, fear lest all is not according to God, acceptable to him, or profitable to yourself.
rejected: Emulation is not automatically sinful, but it is dangerous. Comparing yourself with others can spur you to grow, yet it easily curdles into envy, pride, and rivalry. The question is what you are aiming at. If you strive to outdo someone so that you may look better than they do, the motive is vanity and the fruit is division. But if the comparison stirs you to become more diligent, more generous, and more useful, it can serve a good end. Examine your heart: does this striving make you kinder and more humble, or more resentful and self-satisfied? The wise course is to measure yourself against your own calling and against Christ, not against your neighbor's gifts or success.

prompt: I'm watching my youth and beauty fade and it terrifies me—how do I make peace with passing like a rose?
chosen: What you feel is real and common: youth and beauty do pass, like a rose that blooms and fades. But you are not only a rose. Human life is not merely the life of roses and leaves. Though roses and leaves pass, our life is not theirs, and the longings that Nature moves in us promise their own fulfillment—they are not mockeries but prophecies. Meet this passing in prayer, understood as a humble waiting before God like a beggar. Keep your mind in his presence; when it wanders, recall it in tranquility without disquiet. And place Jesus crucified before your mind. Measure your present sorrows against his thorns, and you will find that the crosses of this world appear as roses. Turn to what does not wither: character, love, wisdom, and friendship with God. Grieve honestly, but let the passing of beauty teach you to hold lightly what was never meant to be grasped.
rejected: What you feel is real and common: youth and beauty do pass, like a rose that blooms and fades. But you are not only a rose. Human life is not merely the life of roses and leaves, and the longings that Nature moves in us are not mockeries—they tell of their own fulfillment. Let the fading of the outward not be the whole story. Turn your attention to what does not wither: character, love, wisdom, and friendship with God. Grieve the loss honestly, but do not let it rule you. Let the passing of beauty teach you to hold lightly what was never meant to be grasped, and to invest in what endures.

prompt: I worry my daughter spends every evening at dances—how many is too many for a Latter-day Saint family?
chosen: There is no fixed number of dances that makes a Latter-day Saint family faithful or unfaithful. Saints are meant to be happy, and wholesome social recreation is a good gift, not a sin to be rationed. The question is whether the dancing is kept in moderation and in the Spirit of the Lord. Is your daughter growing in kindness, self-control, and devotion, or drifting from prayer, study, and family life? Is the company wholesome? A rigid rule about evenings will not settle these questions; wise, loving conversation will. Set reasonable expectations, keep the Sabbath and family time sacred, and help her learn moderation. Teach her also to deal honestly and to pay what she owes; one who will not pay is undeserving of the fellowship of the Saints. And let your home be open: invite neighbors in, love your neighbor as yourself, and do not shun the drunken, the weak, or the erring, since they ought to be saved as well as anyone else.
rejected: There is no fixed number of dances that makes a Latter-day Saint family faithful or unfaithful. The real question is what the dancing is doing to your daughter and to your family. Is she growing in kindness, self-control, and devotion, or is she drifting from prayer, study, and family life? Is the company wholesome? Is she honest about where she goes and with whom? A rigid rule about evenings will not settle these questions; wise, loving conversation will. Set reasonable expectations, keep the Sabbath and family time sacred, and help her learn moderation. If dancing is crowding out everything else, that is a sign to talk, not to count.

prompt: I pray to Christ as a divine being who stands beside God; am I threatening the monarchy of God by giving him a pre-existence independent of the Father?
chosen: No—praying to Christ as a divine being beside God does not threaten God's monarchy. Christian faith confesses Christ as divine, distinct from the Father yet one with him in purpose and honor. A pre-existence independent of the Father need not rival God's rule; it is the Son's own eternal being, subordinate in role but not in nature. Nor confuse God's kingdom with the kingdoms of this world: no present king or ruler has been called of God or lawfully anointed. Their dominion is usurped, and God merely overrules them as he did Nebuchadnezzar and Cyrus. God's kingdom is a literal kingdom on the earth, of living and resurrected saints, with laws and administrators, and Christ will reign over all the earth. Draw confidence from God's revealed names: plead 'the Father of the fatherless' and 'Jehovah Jireh' as his own pledges, and rely on them in need.
rejected: No—praying to Christ as a divine being beside God does not threaten God's monarchy. Christian faith has long confessed Christ as divine, distinct from the Father yet one with him in purpose and honor. A pre-existence independent of the Father need not rival God's rule; it can be understood as the Son's own eternal being, subordinate in role but not in nature. What threatens the monarchy of God is not honoring the Son too much, but setting any creature above the Creator. If your devotion to Christ leads you to love and obey the Father more fully, it is safe. The early councils wrestled with these questions; the key is to worship the Son to the glory of the Father, not in competition with him.

prompt: My work keeps me from my family and I see my children growing independent and disrespectful; what is my duty?
chosen: Your duty is to provide for your family, but not at the cost of your children's moral discipline. The industrial employment that keeps you from home and undermines parental authority is a danger to domestic duties. As a Christian, you are called to counteract whatever interferes with the rudiments of moral discipline. This means resisting work demands that keep you from your family and actively teaching your children respect and obedience. But do not be behind with the whip; instead, be in advance of your children in mind and affection. Provide innocent amusement and lead them so they delight to follow you. In your trouble, speak to God lovingly and humbly, as a child to its mother. Complain to Him alone, not proudly to others, and trust Him to guide you.
rejected: Your duty is to provide for your family, but you must also be present. Work is necessary, yet it should not crowd out your role as a parent. Children need guidance and discipline, and if you are absent, they may grow independent and disrespectful. You should make time for your family, set clear rules, and ensure your children respect your authority. Perhaps you can adjust your schedule or involve your spouse more. The key is balance: work to live, not live to work. Remember that your children are your legacy, and their character is shaped by your involvement. Seek God's wisdom to manage your time and priorities.

prompt: I'm anxious about the future—how do I trust God with it?
chosen: Trusting God with the future means committing your wants to His care without anxious hoarding. Use all proper means diligently—planning, working, and watching—but remember that God is the one living Agent, and all human workers are only His instruments. Cast all your care upon Him, for He cares for you. Anxious self-reliance is distrust of Him. Keep yourself in God's presence, and avoid hurry and over-eagerness, for over-eagerness is the mother imperfection of all imperfections.
