So, do your part, but do not treat your effort as the real support. Pray as if everything depends on God, and work as if everything depends on you, but ultimately rest in His sovereignty.
rejected: Trusting God with the future means letting go of worry and believing He will provide. Start by acknowledging your anxiety and giving it to God in prayer. Remember that He cares for you and has promised to supply your needs. Practically, you can plan wisely but avoid obsessing over what might happen. Focus on today and do your best. Surround yourself with supportive people who remind you of God's faithfulness. If anxiety persists, consider talking to a pastor or counselor. Trust is a choice you make daily, and it grows as you see God's provision. Keep a journal of answered prayers to build your faith.

prompt: I want to obey God's commands but feel I have no power to do so—what does the Gospel offer me?
chosen: The Gospel offers you forgiveness and new life in Christ, and it also offers you enabling grace. God's precepts are promises—all He requires He gives. So when you face an occasion of virtue, turn to God and ask for His enabling strength. He promises strength more than sufficient. 'Thou shalt not' becomes His assurance to preserve you from sin as you trust Him. Do not wait for a greater feeling; you can this moment renounce sin in will and purpose. God supplies the strength, and feeling comes after the surrender. Through faith in Jesus, the Holy Spirit empowers you. Confess your weakness, ask for help, and trust that God will supply what you need to obey.
rejected: The Gospel offers you forgiveness and new life in Christ. When you feel powerless to obey, remember that God's grace is sufficient. Through faith in Jesus, you receive the Holy Spirit who empowers you to live according to God's will. It's not about your own strength but about surrendering to God and relying on His strength. Start by confessing your weakness and asking for help. Read Scripture to understand God's promises. Surround yourself with a supportive community. Obedience is a process, and God is patient. He will complete the good work He began in you.

prompt: I am more comfortable in my study with books than in my closet with God. Is that a danger?
chosen: Yes, it is a danger if your study replaces your closet. The closet is the heart's study, where thought is born and where more is learned about preaching than in libraries. Books can inform, but they cannot substitute for intimate communion with God. If you are more comfortable with books than with God, you may be avoiding Him. Use your study to understand Scripture, but let the closet be the place where your heart is formed. As a Scientist, you are a law unto yourself, so mental malpractice cannot harm you asleep or awake. Measure your ability to stay with God outside the closet by your ability to stay with Him in it. Great waiting in the closet is the source of great victories outside it. Do not settle for hasty visits.
rejected: It's not necessarily a danger to prefer study, but it can become one if it replaces your time with God. Books can help you learn about God, but they are not a substitute for personal communion with Him. The closet represents intimate prayer and solitude with God. If you neglect that, your study may become an escape. Balance is key: use your study to understand God's Word, but also spend time in prayer and listening. Ask yourself if you are avoiding God. If so, repent and seek Him. Remember, knowledge puffs up, but love builds up.

prompt: I say little prayers during the day but they feel empty and mechanical. Is that worth anything?
chosen: Yes, little prayers are worth something, even if they feel empty. No true prayer is lost; supplications accumulate as a memorial before God. The longer the answer waits, the larger it becomes. So do not despise your short prayers. Keep praying at appointed times, regardless of feeling, and include family prayer. Remember that prayer is not just asking God to do everything; it is also helping God accomplish what is asked. Be willing to act as He leads. Brief inward remembrances and acts of worship are acceptable prayers that fortify courage, even in danger. Trust that God hears and will answer in His perfect timing. If they feel mechanical, pause to refocus, but do not give up.
rejected: Yes, little prayers are worth something, even if they feel empty. Prayer is not about feelings but about connecting with God. Short prayers can be powerful because they keep you mindful of God throughout the day. However, if they feel mechanical, you might try to make them more meaningful by pausing to think about what you're saying. Consider setting aside longer prayer times too. Don't give up; consistency matters. God hears even the smallest prayer. Ask Him to help you pray with sincerity, and remember that prayer is a relationship, not a performance.

prompt: How do I respond when I'm falsely accused or persecuted?
chosen: When falsely accused, bring whatever men say before the tribunal of your own conscience. Enter within and judge yourself justly: neither excuse the soul without reason nor accuse it lightly, but examine honestly, so that it neither grows insolent nor loses courage. If conscience truly accuses, amend; if after reflection it does not, then human praise profits nothing and blame loses nothing—it is no loss to be despised without if you are innocent within. Be patient and silent, rejoicing in the Lord. Do not seek revenge or the accuser's punishment; forgo prosecution where you can and desire his repentance and faith, valuing his soul above your name. Pray for him, return good for evil, and leave the outcome to God in peace.
rejected: When you are falsely accused, the first thing to do is steady yourself and refuse to react in anger. Take time to gather the facts and, if appropriate, calmly state the truth to those involved. Avoid gossip and don't try to win everyone over; some people will believe what they like. Lean on trusted friends and, if the accusation is serious, seek fair counsel or proper channels to clear your name. Remember that your worth is not decided by other people's opinions. Pray for peace, keep your conduct blameless, and let time reveal the truth. In the end, what matters most is that you act with integrity and don't let bitterness take root.

prompt: I'm fighting a temptation nobody knows about and I feel completely alone in it—does God see me in that fight?
chosen: God sees you, and you are not alone. He tempts no one, will not allow you to be tempted beyond your strength, and with every temptation provides a way of escape; patient endurance is crowned with life. Distinguish the sources: some temptations rise from your own concupiscence, some from the evil spirit; guard your senses, practise mortification and temperance, and avoid occasions, and you will greatly diminish their force. Yet remember that temptation is not sin but a means of proving virtue and gaining great profit, for the life of man upon earth is a warfare. Light temptations, suspicions, sadness, depression, and pusillanimity are mere nothings—a good will puts them to flight by lifting the soul to God. He sees your hidden fight and is faithful.
rejected: Yes—God sees you, even in a struggle no one else knows about. Feeling alone is real, but it doesn't mean you are abandoned. Bring the temptation honestly into prayer; secrecy and shame often make it feel heavier than it is. Consider confiding in one trustworthy person—a pastor, counselor, or friend—because hidden battles grow in the dark, and speaking them into the light often weakens them. Take practical steps: avoid the situations that feed the temptation, guard your time and attention, and build small habits of prayer and Scripture. God is not distant from your fight; He is near to the struggling and offers grace, not contempt. Keep going, and don't let isolation convince you that you face this alone.

prompt: I have an idea of infinity, but is my idea itself infinite, or only finite—and does that matter for proving God?
chosen: Your idea is finite, but it can truly intend the infinite God. Do not confuse infinity with the indefinite: God's infinity means no limits at all—transcendent yet present, and intensive, an inexhaustible resource of spiritual life whose glory is its expression. The arguments from change and from order are cumulative probable evidence: they corroborate the intuition of God, proving an indefinitely great cause and an intelligent will, yet they have real defects and cannot by themselves reach personality and righteousness. So apply their results to one personal Cause, Contriver, and Lawgiver, and ascribe infinity and perfection to Him as what the mind cannot but think—while the anthropological argument supplies what they lack. Your finite idea matters because it is the mind's necessary reach toward that one Being.
rejected: Your idea of infinity is a finite act of a finite mind: you can think 'without limit,' but your thinking is limited. That's normal and doesn't undermine anything. What matters is whether the idea corresponds to a real being. You can reason that a finite, changing world points beyond itself to something unlimited, and that this unlimited being must be God. So the finiteness of your idea isn't a problem; it's simply the way finite minds grasp the infinite—by negation and by pointing beyond themselves. The question of proving God depends less on whether your idea is itself infinite and more on whether the argument from the world to a limitless cause is sound.

prompt: I want to be liked and praised for my good works. Is that wrong?
chosen: Wanting to be liked is not wrong; you were made to value love and approval. The mistake is straining to be something other than what God made you. Accept your condition and be that well, honoring the Master Workman and seeking to please God's will. To be gentle and kind, modest and truthful, full of faith and integrity and doing no wrong—this is of God, and such goodness sheds a halo of loveliness and makes the countenance beam. Yet do not locate the joy of God's love in your merit, your charitable or social work, your learning, or any arbitrary favouritism. That joy lives in the continually maintained attitude of longing, grateful giving, and receiving Christ. Do your good works honestly, receive praise as a gift, and let your gladness rest on that obedient communion rather than on being noticed.
rejected: Wanting to be liked isn't wrong in itself—humans are social, and approval feels good. The danger is when praise becomes your master: when you do good mainly to be seen, or when criticism crushes you. Ask yourself honestly why you do what you do. If the good work is genuinely good, do it whether or not anyone notices. Practise secret generosity and acts of service no one sees, and let that loosen praise's grip. Accept compliments graciously without depending on them. Aim to please God first, and let human approval be a pleasant extra rather than the point. That way your good works stay good, and your worth doesn't rise and fall with other people's opinions.

prompt: I am afraid of death and the dark valley—how can I face it with peace?
chosen: Fear is natural, but hear the testimony of the saints: the Lord deals gently with His dying servants. The valley is not dark, because the Lord is there; the sting of death is taken away, and victory is given through Jesus Christ. Peace is not passive—meet sufferings, afflictions, and injuries with a strong will to bear them for God, so that their bitterness remains full of peace and tranquillity. Learn not to be troubled in tribulations, not to be incensed against those who inflict them, nor to entertain resentment. Sincerely believe yourself worthy of all injuries, contempt, and scorn, desiring rather to be abhorred as filthy mire than to possess the delights of earth or be honoured and exalted by men. Then dread cannot destroy you, and you walk toward the Lord who is light, and beyond death to resurrection.
rejected: Fear of death is natural, and the image of the dark valley is one many people carry. Peace doesn't come from pretending death isn't frightening; it comes from facing it with support and hope. Talk honestly about your fear with God and with trusted people—naming it often shrinks it. Draw on the promises of Scripture, especially the psalms that speak of God's presence in the valley. Practise small acts of trust now, so that trust grows familiar. Spend time with people who face death with faith, and let their calm steady you. Take care of practical matters so uncertainty doesn't compound fear. And remember that you are not walking toward the valley alone; God goes with you, and Christian hope looks beyond death to resurrection.

prompt: I have a hard time accepting that God allows bad things to happen to good people—how do I trust His will?
chosen: It's understandable to struggle, but Scripture calls us to receive all things from God's hand—sweet or bitter—equally, because His love makes them acceptable. Afflictions are not signs of His absence but of His fatherly care. When we see trials as coming from a loving Father, they become consolation, not curse. Moreover, if you love God, all things—even grief and sin—will turn to your good, even when the means are unseen. All evil of whatever kind happens only by God's permission and ever for some good end; it could not be except He permitted it, and its form and measure are allowed by Him Who can and will by His wisdom turn all to good. Therefore commit all things without fear to the Providence of God, trusting that He steadies His own ark and guides His people.
rejected: It's understandable to struggle with this. The Bible acknowledges that suffering is real and painful, and even faithful people experience loss, illness, and injustice. Trusting God's will doesn't mean pretending pain isn't real or that everything feels good. Instead, it means bringing your honest questions to God and remembering that He is present in suffering, not distant from it. Scripture shows Jesus weeping at Lazarus's tomb and enduring the cross, so God is not indifferent to our pain. Trust grows as you recall His faithfulness in the past and lean on community. You can say, 'I don't understand, but I will keep bringing this to You.' Over time, faith is built not by having all answers but by continuing to turn toward God in the midst of unanswered questions.

prompt: What does it mean that the Sabbath was made for man and not man for the Sabbath?
chosen: This phrase from Jesus means that the Sabbath was made for man's benefit, but it is not a bondage or a mere Jewish custom. The seventh-day Sabbath is the memorial of creation, given at the beginning, and the sign of the cross, the seal that God sanctifies His people. Jesus spoke these words when His disciples were criticized for plucking grain, showing that human need takes precedence over rigid legalism—yet He did not abolish the Sabbath. Instead, He calls us to trust Him for the cost of keeping it holy. We are to keep the Sabbath holy, attending to its worship and duties, and setting an example of faithfulness on that day. And as we serve, we must remember that God's method is men, not methods, plans, or organizations; the Holy Ghost flows through men, not through machinery. The Sabbath serves our well-being, reminding us that we are not slaves to work but children of God who can trust Him enough to rest.
rejected: This phrase from Jesus means that the Sabbath was intended to benefit humanity, not to be a burdensome rule. The Sabbath was given as a gift for rest and worship, a time to cease from labor and focus on God. Jesus spoke these words when His disciples were criticized for plucking grain on the Sabbath, showing that human need takes precedence over rigid legalism. The Sabbath is not about oppressive restrictions but about life-giving rest. It points to God's design for rhythm and renewal. So the Sabbath serves our well-being, reminding us that we are not slaves to work but children of God who can trust Him enough to rest. It is a day for refreshment and connection with God and community.

prompt: What does it mean to live 'in Christ' day to day—how does that change how I face my ordinary tasks?
chosen: Living 'in Christ' day to day means recognizing that your life is hidden with Christ in God, and that your hope is anchored in the vision of the Lamb upon the throne—not in calculating times and seasons. That vision grounds Christian hope amid trials and the humdrum. But Christianity is not a religious system or mere imitation of Christ; it is actual union with Him as indwelling life. Christ dwells in you as the life and source of all your experience and work. So as you face ordinary tasks—washing dishes, working at a desk, caring for family—you let Christ be formed in you, living the Christ-life and showing forth His excellencies as a re-living of His life in your place. You rest in His indwelling presence, holding to His person rather than mere theories, and He lives His life through you.
rejected: Living 'in Christ' day to day means recognizing that your life is hidden with Christ in God. It changes how you face ordinary tasks by reframing them as acts of worship. Whether you are washing dishes, working at a desk, or caring for family, you can do it as unto the Lord. This doesn't mean adding religious words to everything, but cultivating an awareness of Christ's presence and letting His character shape your attitudes and actions. It means relying on His strength rather than your own, and offering your work as a gift to Him. Over time, this transforms the mundane into something meaningful, because you are not just completing tasks—you are living out your union with Christ in every sphere of life.

prompt: Can anyone search out the name of the Saviour, or is it beyond all men?
chosen: The name of the Saviour is not hidden from those who seek Him with a sincere heart. While it may seem beyond human searching, God promises that those who seek will find. The name of Jesus is revealed in Scripture and proclaimed throughout the world. It is not a secret for the elite but a gift for all who call upon Him. True greatness is not measured by position, wealth, or worldly acclaim but by the number of beings a person loves and blesses and who love and bless him. Like Elene, whose heart mourned until the nails were found, we must seek with longing. Cyriacus bowed his head on Calvary and prayed the Lord of angels to reveal the unknown mystery. Then a sign in the form of fire rose where the nails were hidden, a leaping flame brighter than the sun, and the nails glittered from their burial-place like stars or gems set in gold. The people said with one accord that the miracle is of God, whom they formerly withstood. But remember: whoever wishes to steady the ark of God without being called has a dark spot in him, for God steadies His own ark, dictates His own affairs, and guides His people. So seek the name with humility, not with self-appointed zeal, trusting God to reveal it in His way.
rejected: The name of the Saviour is not hidden from those who seek Him with a sincere heart. While it may seem beyond human searching, God promises that those who seek will find. The name of Jesus is revealed in Scripture and proclaimed throughout the world. It is not a secret for the elite but a gift for all who call upon Him. However, searching out the name requires humility and openness. We cannot discover it through our own wisdom alone; it is revealed by the Holy Spirit. So the answer is that the name is both beyond all men and accessible to all—beyond human effort, yet revealed to those who ask, seek, and knock. The key is to approach with faith, not mere curiosity.

prompt: I have been reading that God cares for the sparrow. How can I apply this to my own fears about my needs?
chosen: When Jesus said that God cares for the sparrow, He was teaching that if God provides for small, seemingly insignificant creatures, He will certainly provide for His children. But God is not distant or uninvolved—He knows our needs before we ask, and He numbers the very hairs of our head. You can apply this by reminding yourself that your needs are intimately known to God and that He is faithful to provide. Fear often comes from focusing on what we lack, but faith focuses on God's detailed care. Yet we need His continual help, and that help comes through the holy habit of praying, being with God, and thinking of Him often. Since we must know before we love, such habits deepen our knowledge of Him and cast out fear. And remember that our longing for an enduring home is Nature's own cry in us, not an unholy strife; she who gives wings to birds will find out a way for us. Practical steps include: writing down your fears and giving them to God in prayer, recalling past times when He provided, and trusting that He will do so again.
rejected: When Jesus said that God cares for the sparrow, He was teaching that if God provides for small, seemingly insignificant creatures, He will certainly provide for His children. You can apply this by reminding yourself that your needs are known to God and that He is faithful to provide. Fear often comes from focusing on what we lack or what might happen, but faith focuses on God's character and promises. Practical steps include: writing down your fears and giving them to God in prayer, recalling past times when He provided, and trusting that He will do so again. Also, remember that God's care may not always look like we expect—it might come through other people or unexpected means—but He does not forget His own.

prompt: I have lost my childhood faith and I want it back, but I don't know how. Can God still find me?
chosen: Yes, God can still find you—but the way back is not a technique for managing your feelings. God sometimes hides Himself, and when He does, faith alone supports us and grounds all confidence in Him; yet faith is not a theory or a mood, and it uses prayer, Scripture, and fellowship as instruments without being bound to any of them. More than that, the soul must be converted and become as a child, turning again to God out of whom it proceeded, forsaking its own imaging, its lust, and every self-made centre. Stop curving inward to inspect your faith; turn outward to Him. In that turning, the Divine Vision is restored. Come as a child, trust the Father who seeks you, and let faith—not self-analysis—be your foundation.
rejected: Yes, God can still find you. Losing childhood faith is common, and the longing you feel is itself a sign that something real remains. Start simply: pray honestly, even if the words feel empty. Read Scripture, talk to a trusted pastor or friend, and spend time in quiet. Faith often returns gradually rather than all at once, through small faithful practices and community. Don't wait until you feel certain—act on the desire you have. God is not distant from your searching; many people describe rediscovering faith as a slow reawakening. Be patient with yourself, ask questions, and let others walk with you. The very fact that you want faith back is a hopeful beginning.

prompt: How do I pray when I'm in danger and afraid for my life?
chosen: When danger and fear for your life press on you, do not look at the storm or at your own strength—look at Christ, who is the antidote to fear and the sum of all deliverance. Abide in Him, and remember that you need His continual help, since prayer, being with God, and thinking of Him often are linked through holy habit; we must know Him before we love Him. Yet do not think you must pray at length. Brief inward remembrances and short acts of worship—'Lord Jesus, have mercy,' 'You are my refuge'—are acceptable prayers and fortify courage even in danger. A single turning of the heart to Him is real prayer. Keep your eyes on Christ, offer these short acts often, and let His presence, not the length of your words, be your peace.
rejected: When you are in danger and afraid, pray simply and directly. Speak to God honestly about your fear: 'Lord, I am afraid; help me.' You don't need elaborate words. Use short prayers you can repeat—the Jesus Prayer, a psalm like Psalm 23, or 'Lord, have mercy.' Breathe slowly, name your fear to God, and ask for protection and peace. If others are with you, pray together. Remember that fear is natural, and God is not offended by it. Keep praying as long as the danger lasts, and afterward give thanks. Even a single honest cry is a real prayer, and God hears you wherever you are.

prompt: Are the saints the temple of God now, or is the temple in heaven something we are being prepared to enter?
chosen: The saints are the temple of God now, but they are not the Holy City. The city is prepared for them, and the righteous dead have not yet been caught up; they wait for the resurrection. Believers are being built together as a temple—God's dwelling now—yet this temple is being prepared to enter the city God has prepared. Approach worship expecting peace, security against evil, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit; the saints testify that those who expect these shall find them, and if they seem absent, ask whether we have expected them rather than blaming God. And remember: only the pure in heart shall see God. Set yourself against all licentiousness and every form of impurity, for chastity and purity of heart are not optional but the very condition of seeing Him. Be built together in holiness, and so be made ready to enter the city.
rejected: Both are true in different senses. Now, by the Holy Spirit, believers are called the temple of God—individually and together as the church. At the same time, Scripture speaks of a heavenly city and temple prepared for God's people, which we await. So the present indwelling of the Spirit is a foretaste and preparation for the fuller communion we will enter. The saints are being built together now into a dwelling place for God, and they are also being prepared to enter the heavenly temple. The two are not in competition: present temple, future city, one growing toward the other.

prompt: I do not know what to pray for; how can I pray aright?
chosen: Not knowing what to pray for is itself a place to begin—but prayer must be your main assistant in every step of spiritual progress, not an occasional exercise. Pray that God would enable you to search out and discover your own heart and reform whatever is amiss in it. Bring even the smallest matter to Him, honouring Him by asking His guidance rather than taking any decision out of His hands. And remember that you need His continual help: praying, being with God, and thinking of Him often are linked through holy habit, since we must know Him before we love Him. So make prayer a habit, not a crisis tool. Think on Him often, and you will come to know Him; knowing Him, you will love Him; loving Him, you will pray aright, with your heart searched, reformed, and wholly turned to Him.
rejected: It's normal not to know what to pray for. Start by asking God to teach you to pray, as the disciples did. You can pray Scripture, especially the Psalms and the Lord's Prayer, which give words when you have none. Ask the Holy Spirit to help you, since He intercedes for us. You can also pray simply for God's will to be done and for wisdom to know what to ask. Keep a list of people and needs to guide you. Prayer doesn't require perfect words—honesty and openness matter more. Over time, as you practice, you'll grow more discerning about what to pray for.

prompt: My conscience tells me one thing and my neighbours another—can we both be right?
chosen: It is possible for two people to differ in good conscience, but do not treat this lightly. Conscience can be mistaken, and unregretted sin accumulates and destroys the ability to do right; where your conscience accuses you, repent and reform rather than explaining it away. Yet judge your soul justly: neither excuse it without reason nor accuse it lightly or without reflection, so that it neither grows insolent nor loses courage. Bear patiently with the imperfections of others, for such forbearance is a great part of perfection and the practice of love of neighbour. Take your neighbour's view seriously, seek wise counsel, and where Scripture and clear teaching speak, follow them. Repentance for yourself, forbearance toward others, and a just, steady judgment of your own heart—this is the way forward in humility and love.
rejected: It's possible for two people to reach different conclusions in good conscience, especially when the matter is not clearly settled by shared moral principles. Conscience is not infallible; it can be mistaken, under-informed, or shaped by culture. Your neighbour may see something you don't, and you may see something they don't. So take their view seriously, examine your own reasons, and seek wise counsel. Where Scripture and clear moral teaching speak, follow them. Where they don't, allow freedom and avoid contempt. You may both be partially right, or one of you may be mistaken—humility and honest dialogue are the way forward.

prompt: Is God a distant and gloomy being, or can I approach him as a father?
chosen: God is not a distant, gloomy being to be dreaded. He is our Father, and his children may come to him freely. He listens when we pray and numbers the hairs of our heads, and his service is full of beauty and cheerfulness rather than gloom. Yet he who is united to God is one mind with Him, so out of regard for his sovereign honour we must never think or imagine in his presence what we would blush to have seen before men; we raise all thoughts to God alone and set him before our inward gaze as though he alone existed. Above all, we must not imagine God as the author of sickness, sorrow, or affliction. He is a loving Father who gives only good, and sickness is not his will, as the testimonies confess they had wrongly believed.
rejected: Many people picture God as a remote ruler far off in the heavens, watching us with cold judgment. Approaching such a being feels frightening, and serving him seems like a grim duty full of dread. But Scripture invites us to a different view. God is not a distant monster demanding fear; he is a Father who cares for his children. Jesus taught us to pray to 'our Father,' which means we can come near with confidence. Still, we should remember that God is holy and we are sinful, so a healthy reverence is appropriate. The Christian life involves both awe and intimacy, and we grow by balancing the two. Prayer, reading Scripture, and obedience help us draw closer to him over time.

prompt: Why do some people respond to the gospel and others don't?
chosen: In the simplicity of God's word, the gospel is plain: Christ died for our sins and rose again, and whoever believes is saved. Why some respond and others do not is not fully given to us, and we should say so frankly rather than dress it up in speculative philosophy. The message is simple enough for the humble to understand and enjoy. The first witnesses were competent, honest men whose testimony cost them worldly interests; their voluntary suffering is the strongest evidence of their truth, since imposture must have a motive and they had none. Yet we must never withhold the gospel from any people. It must go to all nations, so that all have the privilege of receiving or rejecting it, leaving the wicked without excuse.
rejected: The question of why some accept the gospel and others reject it has puzzled thinkers for centuries. Some point to deep philosophical factors: differing worldviews, cultural conditioning, or varying capacities for rational argument. Others emphasize psychological readiness or social influence. These speculations can become complex, and honest seekers may feel that simple faith is not enough unless they master them. In truth, the gospel is a message about Jesus, his death and resurrection, and the call to repent and believe. People respond differently because of their hearts, their circumstances, and God's mysterious work. We should not pretend to fully explain it. What matters is that each person hears the message clearly and is invited to trust Christ.

prompt: What does it mean to worship God with my gold and my possessions like the Magi?
chosen: The Magi brought gold, frankincense, and myrrh to the child Jesus, and their gifts show that we honor God with our possessions. Our wealth is not securely our own; it belongs to the Lord and is uncertain, a trust to be used for the Gospel and the poor. We guard against covetousness and the idolatrous love of property, holding our goods loosely for God's purposes. Worth is not measured by public display: hidden Christian worth is precious, and the prayers of the poor and desolate rise with more than royal pomp. Above all, we must not credit the success of God's work to the wealth, influence, or abilities of men. God chooses the poor, weak, and despised things to confound the mighty, so the glory belongs to Him alone, not to human riches or power.
rejected: The Magi brought gold, frankincense, and myrrh to the child Jesus, and their gifts show that we too can honor God with our wealth. Worshipping with our possessions means giving generously to the church, supporting missions, and using our resources to advance God's kingdom. It also means working hard to build wealth so that we have more to give. After all, our money is our own, earned by our effort, and we should manage it wisely and invest it well. When we give from our abundance, we show gratitude to God and set an example for others. The more we prosper, the more we can display our devotion through impressive gifts.

prompt: I believe matter and Spirit both have power in my life. Is it possible to serve both?
chosen: You cannot serve both matter and Spirit, for no one can serve two masters. To trust matter as a source of power is to serve mammon, and that must be expelled. Spirit alone is to be trusted and God alone served. We must separate Truth from error and Spirit from matter, denying any copartnership between them; they do not cooperate in man, nor coexist in healing. Material beliefs must be cast out rather than blended with faith. Nor is human will-power a faculty of Soul or a reliable means of governing oneself or others; it has no governing role. Truth and Love are the motive-powers of man. Choose to serve God alone, letting Spirit govern your life, and put away the belief that matter or mere will has genuine power over you.
rejected: It is natural to feel that both matter and Spirit have power in your life. After all, we live in a physical world, and our bodies, health, and circumstances clearly affect us. At the same time, spiritual realities matter too. Perhaps the answer is to find a balance, drawing on material means when needed and spiritual strength when needed. Many people try to combine the two, trusting medicine and money alongside prayer and faith. This blended approach seems practical and comforting. As long as you are sincere, serving both realms may be a sensible way to live, honoring the physical and the spiritual together without choosing one over the other.

prompt: Why doth Christ say that what is done to the least of these is done to him, and how doth a man do it to Christ himself?
chosen: Christ says that what is done to the least of these is done to him because he dwells really and essentially in the faith of those who yield themselves to him. Christians are branches of the Vine and members of his Body, so what is done or withheld from the least of his brethren is done or withheld from Christ himself. Each of us casts his own burden on the Lord who is within him, and in Christ's strength we also bear the burdens of others, fulfilling the law of Christ. But we must not cling to independence or self-will, or insist on the right to please ourselves. Instead we take the servant's place after Christ's pattern, renouncing self-will and obeying even as Christ became obedient unto death.
rejected: Christ says that what is done to the least of these is done to him to teach us the importance of charity. When we feed the hungry, clothe the naked, or visit the sick, we are performing good deeds that please God. These acts are simply human kindness, and their value lies in the moral effort we make. Jesus uses this imagery to motivate us to be generous and compassionate toward the poor. He identifies with the needy in a symbolic way, so that serving them is like serving him. The lesson is that genuine religion shows itself in practical love for neighbors, and we should strive to do good whenever we can.

prompt: I was punished harshly as a child for asking questions. Was that just?
chosen: No, it was not just. A priest who seizes a weeping child and burns him in a holy place betrays God, and we must ask whether such things are done on Albion's shore. Yet I bring this trouble to You, O God, as a child to its mother, complaining humbly to You alone and not proudly to others. You are not the author of that cruelty. Your pattern is always to warn before You judge: You sent Noah before the flood, Abraham's plea before Sodom, and prophets before Jerusalem fell, appealing to man's reason and intelligence rather than striking without word. So the harsh punisher acted against Your manner, which persuades and warns. Teach me to trust Your love, to bring my questions to You, and to hear Your warnings with a reasoning heart rather than fear.
rejected: No, it was not just. Children ask questions because they are trying to understand the world, and punishing curiosity teaches fear instead of wisdom. A harsh punishment for honest questioning confuses the child about love and truth, making God seem like a threat rather than a father. Justice would have answered the question patiently, even if the answer had to be 'I don't know yet.' The adult who punished you may have acted from their own fear or pride, not from God. You were not wrong to ask. Questions are how faith grows; silencing them does not produce obedience, only hidden doubt. It is right to grieve that harm and to learn that God welcomes the seeking heart.

prompt: My faith feels like a very little light in a great night, and I wonder whether it is enough to live by.
chosen: A little light is still light, and faith is our measured light in our night, given so that we may live meedfully and earn meed and thanks of God until at the end of woe our eyes are opened in clearness of light. It is not night if Christ be near; ask Him to abide from morn till eve and when night is nigh, for without Him we cannot live or dare to die. Yet this light is not a private feeling only: in mortality the temporal and spiritual are blended and cannot be separated, and the Church is a physical as well as a spiritual organization. So let your little faith be practical faith that practices the principles of the gospel, in ordinary duties and service, and it will be enough to live by.
rejected: A little light is still light, and it is enough to take the next step. Faith is not measured by how bright it feels but by whether you keep walking by it. The night around you is real, and it is not wrong to feel small within it. But do not despise the smallness; a lamp too weak to light a whole valley can still show the path at your feet. Live by what you have, and it will be fed. Many saints began with less than you describe. Bring your little light to God honestly, and let it be enough for today rather than demanding that it become a sun before you move.

prompt: What is the difference between ambition and service?
chosen: Ambition seeks its own advancement; service seeks another's good. The deeper difference is quality, not quantity: service is measured by its quality and its aim to please God, not by how much is done or how visible it is. A small hidden act done well pleases Him more than a great public work done for notice; the main purpose is to do well rather than to do much. Wealth represents labor and industry, and to take it by force or by legislation is robbery, a principle that would crush all energy and enterprise. And service must be rightly aimed: the three worst services a man can serve are serving a bad woman, a bad lord, and bad land. Fidelity to what is unworthy is not service but complicity. True service honours God, the worker's labor, and worthy ends, and the test is what you would do if no one ever knew.
rejected: Ambition seeks its own advancement; service seeks another's good. Ambition asks who will notice and what it will bring me; service asks what is needed and how I can help. Both can look alike from outside, since ambitious people often serve and servants often rise. The difference lies in the aim: ambition terminates in the self, service terminates in God and neighbor. Ambition is restless because it depends on comparisons; service is steady because it depends on faithfulness. A person can be busy in good works and still be ambitious, and a person can hold high office and still be a servant. The test is what you would do if no one ever knew.

prompt: How can I know whether a work is really GOD's, if the money always seems to run short?
chosen: Short funds are not proof that a work is not God's; many true works have been poor. The work of the Lord is best carried on within the landmarks of His word. The patronage of the world is not to be sought or depended upon, no debts are to be contracted, and all dependence is on God's blessing in answer to prayer. The Living God alone is Patron, and prayer is the only appeal. Ask whether the work is faithful to Scripture, bears good fruit, and trusts God rather than manipulating people. Remember that the work is God's own through many hands: those who pray and sympathize, though they never see the mission field, share in it as truly as the visible worker. Measure it by prayer, honesty, and fruit, not by the bank balance.
rejected: Short funds are not proof that a work is not God's; many true works have been poor. Ask instead whether the work is faithful to Scripture, whether it bears good fruit, and whether those who lead it trust God rather than manipulate people for money. Money is a tool, not a test of authenticity. If the work depends on constant appeals and anxiety about funds, that may reveal misplaced trust. But if it continues in prayer, honesty, and care for people, short funds may simply be a trial of faith. Look at character, doctrine, and fruit more than at the bank balance.

prompt: My conscience accuses me and I fear the judgment; is there an advocate who will defend me before Christ?
chosen: Yes, there is an advocate: Jesus Christ, who died and rose and intercedes for us. Bring whatever men say or think before the tribunal of your own conscience, entering within to learn the truth, for human praise profits nothing if conscience accuses, and it is no loss to be despised without if you are innocent within. Where accusations are baseless, seek to remove them, reserving the glory of suffering for suffering endured for Christ's sake. But know that abiding in Him is not automatic: if the will abides in the words of Christ, His Word and Spirit abide in him, but if the will goes into the creature, one breaks off from Him. So keep yourself by abiding in resigned humility and a constant course of penitence and daily dying from the creatures, confessing your sin and trusting His mercy, rejoicing in the Lord in patience, silence, and peace.
rejected: Yes, there is an advocate: Jesus Christ, who died and rose and intercedes for us. Your conscience accuses truly, and you should not silence it, but neither should you let it condemn you without hope. Bring your sin honestly to Christ, confess it, and trust His mercy. He is not a harsh judge toward the repentant; He is the friend of sinners. The fear of judgment can be healthy if it drives you to Him rather than away from Him. Do not rest in your own defense, for you have none, but rest in His.

prompt: What sins have we as a nation committed that brought this war upon us?
chosen: This war came upon us in part because of our own sins, and a day of humiliation is fitting. We have shared in the tone of thought and life that produced this catastrophe—the love of gain, the pride of opinion, the neglect of God—and we dare not claim superiority over the enemy. Every sin, ours and theirs, is an insult to God, whose greatness is infinite and whose majesty we have slighted; measured against Him, man is a little thing, and our offenses take their true malice from the greatness of the God we have wronged. So we smite our breasts and pray, 'God be merciful to me a sinner,' watching and praying for the Mind of Christ, doing unto others as we would have them do unto us, being merciful, just, and pure. We hold sin the greatest of evils, to be avoided at any sacrifice, and we trust not in our own righteousness but in the mercy of God.
rejected: This war came upon us because of the wickedness of our enemies, who have rejected truth and trampled on righteousness. Our nation, by contrast, has stood for liberty and justice, and we fight in a righteous cause. If we have any faults, they are minor and do not compare with the crimes of those who assail us. We should pray for victory and trust that God will defend the right. The chief sin lies at the door of the enemy, not with us, and we may confidently ask God's blessing on our arms, certain that He favors our cause over theirs.

prompt: I want to know what makes a person truly wise. What should I study?
chosen: True wisdom is not the opposite of practical wisdom but its crown. It is our privilege and duty to be as wise in our generation as the children of this world, and even wiser, because we are privileged with superior advantages through faith and obedience to the Gospel. Study scripture and prayer, and also the world God made—its laws, history, arts, and sciences—so that we may know more about all matters than any other people. But wisdom must govern the body too: be moderate in all things, care for your health, eat wholesome food, live much outdoors, take exercise, and feed children properly, in keeping with the Word of Wisdom. Above all, hold to Jesus as your highest sovereign Friend. Fasten to Him homely in whatever state you are, foul or clean, and never flee from Him for weal nor for woe; for to hide from Him because of foulness is the most folly.
rejected: True wisdom is mostly spiritual and unworldly. Study scripture and prayer, and be content with a simple, uneducated life. The wisdom of this world is foolishness with God, so avoid too much learning in worldly subjects, which only puffs up. Seek meekness and quietness of mind, and do not trouble yourself with the affairs of the world or the practical knowledge that others pursue. The wise person keeps to himself, avoids worldly concerns, and thinks chiefly of the life to come.

prompt: There's constant arguing and division in my ward. How important is it really that we be of one heart?
chosen: Singleness of heart is the most necessary condition of faith and true virtue. Constant arguing and division in a ward should trouble you deeply, because without one heart we cannot enter the kingdom of heaven. We must return to the simplicity of little children and cut off the inordinate affections of vice—pride, resentment, the need to be right—that feed division. Yet the cure is not endless self-observation of our own progress; it is keeping the heart occupied with God, the object of its love, delighting in pleasing God above any pleasure in our own performance. The love of God is the soul's home and goal, and the patience of Christ is not passive waiting but active endurance of wrongs for His sake. Christ is both the pattern and the power of that endurance; fasten to Him, and unity will follow.
rejected: Unity is nice but not essential. What matters most is that each person is sincere in his own views and follows his conscience. Disagreement is natural and even healthy, and you should not worry too much about being of one heart. Focus on your own spiritual growth and let others do the same. Arguments will pass, and you should not sacrifice your own opinions just to keep peace.

prompt: I am a slave to habits I cannot break—is there any power stronger than my own will?
chosen: Character is not fixed by temperament. Strength of character is the will's power to control one's actions independently of inclinations and of the opinions of men, and it grows by repeated virtuous acts and shrinks by yielding to passion. Each self-victory strengthens the will, and progress is proportioned to such victories. But beware the saying that the best devotion is the constant practice of ordinary duties; some abuse it to excuse a life of dissipation. Every one is bound to live to himself in the first place and to reserve leisure for frequent exercises of devotion. So bridle your tongue, subdue anger, examine yourself daily, and attend to your own duties rather than judging or meddling in the affairs of others. Set aside regular time for prayer, and trust that the power stronger than your own will is the grace of God working with your repeated acts of self-control.
rejected: Some people are simply born with certain temperaments, and if your habits are ingrained, there may be little you can do. Willpower is limited, and it is no use fighting your nature. Accept your inclinations and do not be too hard on yourself. Others may judge you, but you should not care what people think. Just try to relax and go along with what you feel; struggling against yourself only makes you miserable.

prompt: I am a parent and I have been too lenient with my children's bad habits. What should I do?
chosen: Leniency is not cured by harshness. Parents should be in advance of their children, providing innocent amusement and leading them so that the children delight to follow, rather than being behind them with the whip. Win their hearts first: plan good things for them, join in their play, and let them see that following you is pleasant. Be careful, too, about the books they read, for books create feelings for good or bad, and trashy novels are poisonous adders to the soul. Reading is a form of companionship that shapes the heart, so know what enters your home. Never lose control of your children's amusements during their tender years, and be scrupulously careful about the companionship of your young people in places of amusement; do not leave them to find their fun wherever and whenever they can.
rejected: You should crack down hard. Children need strict discipline, and leniency has made them soft. Set firm rules, punish disobedience swiftly, and make clear who is in charge. Do not worry about amusing them or winning their affection; obedience is what matters. Keep them busy with chores and study, and do not indulge their desire for play. If they resist, be firm and do not give in.

prompt: I keep chasing pleasure and it always leaves me empty. Why does the world's joy fade?
chosen: Pleasure fades because it was never meant to be your master. Chasing it is a kind of living death: the more you grasp, the emptier you become. Beware of going into debt for fashionable display, and know that the hunt for pleasure leads to cheating, lying, and corrupted morals. Every substitute for God leaves an emptiness unfilled—romance, family, business, pleasure, art may be good, yet none can permanently satisfy; each ends in disillusionment when asked to be what only God can be. Only the finding of God is permanent success. But do not pursue happiness by trying to feel happy; that is another chase. Seek joy instead by being right with God, forgetting yourself in service to others, rejoicing in the Lord above your feelings, and obeying Him faithfully. There the fading of worldly joy gives way to a joy that does not fade.
rejected: Pleasure fades because it was never designed to carry the weight of your whole heart. The world's joys are real but temporary—they satisfy for a moment, then slip away, leaving you wanting more. That emptiness you feel isn't a sign something is broken; it's a signal that you're made for something lasting. Chasing the next thrill only deepens the hunger, like drinking salt water. The wiser path is to enjoy good things without clinging to them, to notice what they point toward rather than demanding they be your final rest. Ask what your longing is really reaching for, and let the fading of lesser joys turn you toward what doesn't fade.

prompt: I am troubled by conflict between capital and labor; how should a Christian respond?
chosen: The conflict between capital and labor is real, but begin with this: your time and your ability to labor are capital entrusted to you by God, and you will give account for how you use them. No act, word, or thought escapes accountability—secret dishonesty, bitter speech, and exploitative schemes will be brought into judgment. Yet the work is GOD's own work through His servants; we do not achieve it, we obey in it, for His glory. So limit yourself to legitimate employments. Refuse the curiosity, ambition, and restlessness that multiply superfluous occupations and create more impediments than works. Deal honestly, pay and demand just wages, and refuse the anger that hardens the heart. Both employer and employee are neighbors owed love and stand before the same Judge. Let His glory, not human credit or restless enterprise, be the aim of all your labor.
rejected: The conflict between capital and labor is real, and Christians should approach it with fairness and charity toward both sides. Owners have legitimate responsibilities to workers, and workers have legitimate claims to just treatment. Rather than choosing a side in anger, seek justice: fair wages, honest dealing, safe conditions, and respect for the dignity of labor. Listen to those who feel wronged, and don't let economic interests harden your heart. Both employer and employee are neighbors owed love. Practically, that may mean supporting just policies, dealing honestly in your own work, and building relationships across the divide. The gospel doesn't hand you an economic blueprint, but it does command honesty, generosity, and concern for the vulnerable—so let those shape how you speak and act in this conflict.

prompt: My grief for someone I lost feels too calm, almost tender—am I grieving wrong?
chosen: A calm, tender sorrow is not a failure—it may be the truer shape of grief. The one you lost is in a high sphere of saner happiness, present with the Lord, beyond the strains and confusions of this life. Trusting that, your grief need not be acute and stormy; it can be a tender regret, a quiet longing that loves without clutching. Do not turn inward to examine and explain the causes of your sadness; patiently endure the aversions and repugnances that come, bearing them as a way of loving Him who suffered. And let your grief become thanksgiving: thank God for giving this beloved, for long sparing them to you, and for taking them to Himself. Rejoice in their gain even while you feel the loss. Grieve as one who loves someone now safer and more joyful, letting tenderness and praise together shape your remembering.
rejected: There's no single right way to grieve, and a calm, tender sorrow is not a failure. Grief can be quiet as easily as it can be stormy. The fact that your sorrow feels tender rather than crushing may mean you're holding the loss with love rather than being overwhelmed by it. Many people find that as time passes, grief softens into something gentler—a fond remembering rather than an open wound. That's not wrong; it can be a sign of healing. What matters is that you honor the person you lost and let yourself feel what you actually feel, without judging it against some expected script. If the calm worries you, talk with someone you trust, but don't assume tender grief is deficient grief.

prompt: I'm a parent and I can't decide whether to compel my young child to fast on fast day.
chosen: The fast is a reasonable law, observed from evening to evening, with the food or its equivalent given to the poor—but it is left to conscience and wisdom, not imposed as an iron-clad rule. The weak, the sick, nursing mothers, and little children should not be compelled to fast. So with your young child, do not compel; gently include them in adapted ways—simpler meals, prayer, and giving. And remember that parents should never permit themselves to do anything they are not willing to see their children do; demanding good behavior and kind words while scolding in bitterness is inconsistent. Set an example worthy of imitation. Nor lose control of your child's amusements in these tender years: do not let them find their fun wherever and whenever they can. Be scrupulously careful about the companionship of your young people in places of amusement, guiding their pleasures as carefully as their prayers, so that formation in faith comes through imitation, oversight, and love rather than compulsion.
rejected: This is a matter for your conscience and your knowledge of your child. Fasting is a meaningful practice, and involving children in the life of the church can be good, but young children have real physical needs and shouldn't be pushed beyond what's healthy. Many families include children in fast days in adapted ways—simpler meals, smaller portions, or focusing on prayer and giving rather than strict abstinence. The goal isn't to enforce a rule but to form a child in faith over time. Consider your child's age, health, and temperament, and don't feel bound to a rigid requirement. Talk with your pastor if you're unsure. The important thing is that your child learns that fasting is about drawing near to God, not about earning approval or enduring hardship.

prompt: I wonder whether the bread and wine of the Supper are truly the body and blood of Christ, or only symbols of spiritual blessings.
chosen: The bread and wine of the Supper are truly Christ's body and blood, given to be received within us—not mere symbols of spiritual blessings. On the altar is Christ's substantial presence, body and soul, God and Man, present as our helper. This is no human ceremony but a mystery calling for awe, purity, and burning desire for union with Him. The holy Mass is the most powerful prayer, and Holy Communion gives God Himself and increases grace according to our dispositions. So come with reverence, examine yourself, and receive with longing. And remember whose servant you are: the true servant bears in his body the marks of the Lord Jesus, belongs to Christ alone, and owes no allegiance to men, parties, factions, or the flesh. Do not shrink from the shame and branding of the cross, for the One you receive in the Supper is the One you follow in suffering and glory.
rejected: This is a question Christians have answered differently across traditions. Some hold that the bread and wine are truly Christ's body and blood; others see them as symbols or memorials of spiritual blessings. Both views take the Supper seriously. What matters most is that you receive it with faith, remembering Christ's sacrifice and trusting His promise. The Supper is a means of grace, a place where the church is nourished and united. Whether you understand the elements as transformed or as pointing beyond themselves, the call is the same: come with reverence, examine yourself, and receive in faith. If this question troubles you, study the relevant passages and talk with your pastor; you need not resolve every theological detail to participate faithfully.

prompt: I am rich and wonder what my property demands of me; is private property itself unchristian?
chosen: Private property is not itself unchristian, but you are not your own: you were bought with a price. Your time, talents, gold, silver, and all you possess are the Lord's; you own nothing but the talents God has given you to improve. Riches are uncertain, lent for a season for the Gospel and the poor. So hold your estate as a steward, not an owner, and beware hoarding: keeping riches unused brings leanness of soul and darkness of mind, hardening the heart while the money sits idle. Put every dollar and every ability out to use for the good of the community—give generously, deal honestly with workers and tenants, and refuse luxury that breeds covetousness. Ask whether you could lose it tomorrow and still trust God; if not, it has become an idol. Enjoy His gifts with gratitude, but keep them loose in your hand, always ready for His use.
rejected: Private property is not inherently unchristian; Scripture assumes ownership while regulating its use. What your wealth demands is stewardship: care for your family, honest dealings, and generosity to the poor. Give regularly, avoid luxury that hardens you, and remember that possessions are tools, not trophies. The danger is not owning things but letting things own you. Examine your heart: if you could lose your estate tomorrow and still trust God, your property is in its right place. Practically, set a budget for giving, know your tenants and workers by name, and ask trusted friends to hold you accountable. Enjoy what you have with gratitude, but hold it loosely, ready to share.

prompt: How can I pray when I have no words?
chosen: When words fail, do not fill the silence with activity; take time to be alone with God and His word, for secret prayer and meditation are indispensable to fruitful service, and nothing compensates for the loss of the secret place. Yet prayer is humbling work: it crucifies pride, signs our bankruptcy, and little praying is a worse evil than none, a deluding make-believe. So ask for strength to suffer with courage, humility, and love, and cultivate familiar conversation with God—watchful over your thoughts, words, and deeds. Begin with Scripture; the Psalms give words when yours run out. A few honest phrases, 'Lord, have mercy,' are enough. Guard a daily appointment alone with Him, refuse to let service or fellowship crowd out communion, and if dryness persists, keep the secret place first. Such watchful converse brings the peace of paradise even now.
rejected: When words fail, you can still pray. Start with short, honest phrases: 'Lord, have mercy,' or simply 'Here I am.' Use Scripture—the Psalms give words when yours run out. Try writing your thoughts, walking in silence, or listening to a hymn. Remember that prayer is not a performance; God knows your heart before you speak. Even groans count (Romans 8:26). Keep a simple routine: a few minutes each morning and evening, a gratitude list, and one request. If you are distracted, gently return. Talk to a pastor or friend about it. Silence before God is itself a form of prayer, so don't be anxious about having nothing to say.

prompt: How do I direct my heart into the love of God when I feel distant from Him?
chosen: Feeling distant from God is common, but the answer is not a vague longing; it is actual fellowship with a personal Friend—the Father we know through His human revelation in Christ. Yet that fellowship requires a heart emptied of all other things, so God may possess it alone and act in it. Do not assume you can find your way home by your own insight: sin has blinded and biassed us, so we cannot arrive without the Lord's guidance. Seek His direction through the Word, the indwelling Spirit, and Providence. Name the distance honestly, clear away competing loves, meditate on His love in the Psalms and the prodigal son, serve others, and confess what has cooled your affection. Distance is a season, not a verdict; keep meeting the Friend who has come near.
rejected: Feeling distant from God is common, and it does not mean He has left you. Begin by naming the distance honestly in prayer, then return to the basics: Scripture, worship, and fellowship. Meditate on passages that describe God's love—the Psalms, the parable of the prodigal son, Romans 8. Serve others; love often grows through action. Examine whether sin, busyness, or disappointment has cooled your affection, and confess it. Talk with a trusted friend or pastor. Practice gratitude and keep a journal of God's faithfulness. Distance is often a season, not a verdict; keep showing up, and affection will follow.

prompt: I have great talents and education. Can these alone make my ministry fruitful?
chosen: Talents and education are gifts, but they alone cannot make ministry fruitful. Ministry is not a profession or business where salary and self-advancement lead; treated so it grows heartless. Put self to the rear and heart to the front. Holy pastors made retirement and a life of prayer their apprenticeship and preparation—and afterward, amid ministry, remained men of prayer, God always present to their mind, setting apart intervals in the day and much of the nights to attend to God in the silence of all creatures. So make prayer your first preparation. As an ambassador and messenger of God, reprove sin sincerely rather than softening the Gospel to soothe hearers; visit all the sick; esteem a man's immortal soul above his present favor; and fear none but Him who can destroy both soul and body.
rejected: Talents and education are real gifts and should be used well, but they alone cannot make ministry fruitful. Fruitfulness depends on God's grace, prayer, character, and love for people. A well-trained mind helps you teach clearly and lead wisely, yet hearers are changed by the Spirit, not by credentials. So steward your gifts: keep learning, prepare carefully, and seek feedback. But pair competence with humility, holiness, and dependence on God. Guard against pride in your education and against treating ministry as a career. Ask God to use your gifts for His glory and the good of others, and remember that He often works through weakness.

prompt: I've had moments in nature or in music where I felt something vast and beautiful beyond words. What is that?
chosen: Those moments are real, but beware the seductive inertia of spiritual sensuality—making a pleasant feeling the goal and sinking into passive contentment. The soul's health lies in intense living and activity in connection with the Divine Energy. Nature is not merely material, nor an end in itself: it is the visible demonstration of an invisible Will. So trace the beauty you feel to its Source, and bless God for every beautiful thing, until your days become one long delight. Let awe in nature or music rouse you rather than lull you; ask what it points to, and respond with gratitude, worship, and action. And know that one moment of divine understanding is a foretaste of eternity, bridging even the interval of death—so receive beauty, and press beyond it into lively communion and service.
rejected: Those moments are real and worth taking seriously. Nature and music can stir awe, wonder, and a sense of connection that points beyond the ordinary. Many people describe them as spiritual experiences, and they can be gifts that refresh the soul. You might treat them as invitations: slow down, pay attention, and let beauty do its work. Some find that such moments lead them toward gratitude, prayer, or reflection on what matters most. Others simply enjoy them as part of a rich human life. There is no need to overanalyze; receive the experience with openness and let it deepen your appreciation for beauty and mystery.

prompt: What does it mean to be transformed in God, and how do I begin?
chosen: Being transformed in God means consenting without protest as He strews your vanities to the winds, breaks your prides, and transfigures your lusts into Holy Love. He transposes your pleasures—removing the guilty and giving blameless ones—and receives you into His transformed world only when you are at peace with yourself and all persons. Begin by offering God your divided heart, receiving His Grace as the Divine Anaesthetic through the pain of the stripping, and keeping prayer, Scripture, and fellowship. Crucially, let no change of place or occupation alter your love or distract you from being equally for God: remain indifferent amid variety, the same in every setting, so that your love and its object never shift. Submit, stay at peace, and be equally for Him in all things.
rejected: Being transformed in God means a gradual change of heart and life, moving from self-centeredness toward love of God and neighbor. It is not a single event but a lifelong process of growth in virtue, prayer, and obedience. You begin by turning honestly toward God, admitting where you fall short, and asking for grace. Establish simple habits: daily prayer, reading Scripture, and fellowship with other believers. Examine your attachments and ask God to reshape them. Expect slow progress and setbacks; transformation is God's work in you, and your part is to cooperate. Start small, stay faithful, and trust that God completes what He begins.

prompt: I've been disappointed in my career and I'm bitter—how do I keep from letting it curdle into hatred?
chosen: Bitterness after career disappointment is real, but do not give up rejoicing because the first dose seemed ineffectual—count it all joy even in these temptations, trusting God to make the reckoning good. Beware the enemy's false dread of wretchedness: it whispers that your disappointment and any fall are his final victory, and would drive you from the blissful beholding of your Everlasting Friend. Refuse that device; stay beholding God, and when you fall, rise by charity and meekness, turning the enemy's gain to his own sorrow. If you counsel others, first know, live, and love this truth yourself—never merely repeat words, for healing comes from truth embodied, not recited. Forgive those you blame, keep gratitude and service, and let joy, not dread, set the tone of your waiting.
rejected: Bitterness after career disappointment is understandable, but you are right to fear it curdling into hatred. First, name the disappointment honestly before God rather than suppressing it. Hatred grows when we rehearse grievances and assign blame; bitterness grows when we believe we are owed something we did not receive. Practice gratitude for what you do have, forgive those you blame, and separate your worth from your career outcomes. Talk with trusted friends or a counselor. Reorient toward what you can control and find meaning in service to others. Healing takes time; be patient with yourself and keep bringing the resentment to God.

prompt: I am a new Christian, and I feel overwhelmed by all the doctrines; do I need to understand them all to grow?
chosen: No, you need not master every doctrine to grow—but do not mistake development for mere innovation or for a hardening of theology by piling on new dogmas. True development is the Church standing firm in her old truths while entering into and assimilating the new social and intellectual movements of the age. Begin with the essentials: who God is, who Jesus is, what He did, and how to follow Him. The doctrine of sin rests not on the literal history of Genesis or on external dogma alone, but on Christ's authority verified in Christian moral experience; you are free to treat the early chapters of Genesis as allegorical. And do not think development ended with Christ's teaching: the Spirit continues His work in the Church, and there remains both the right and the duty of further development in Ethics and Theology. Grow patiently through prayer, Scripture, obedience, and fellowship.
rejected: No, you do not need to understand every doctrine to grow as a new Christian. Growth comes primarily through relationship with God—prayer, Scripture, obedience, and fellowship—not through mastering theological systems. Doctrines matter, but they are meant to serve your faith, not overwhelm it. Start with the essentials: who God is, who Jesus is, what He did, and how to follow Him. Learn the rest gradually as questions arise. Ask mature believers for help, join a good church, and be patient with yourself. Understanding deepens over years. Focus first on loving God and neighbor; the rest will come in time.

prompt: I do good things mainly to be seen by others. Does that cost me anything?
chosen: Yes, doing good mainly to be seen costs you something real. When approval is your motive, the deed becomes a performance and your reward is only the praise you get—nothing deeper; you drift toward visible acts and your worth hangs on opinions. But do not measure progress by claims or words. Test yourself by the fruits of living and demonstrating Truth and Love: does your life show the supreme good and bring healing? Remember that every moment of human life should be devoted to doing good somewhere and in some way, and that we should make ourselves capable of doing at least a little good. And do not see self-denial and economy as loss: they are a privilege that frees your resources for the LORD and brings fuller joy, enabling greater giving. Practice hidden deeds and ask whether you would still do the good if no one knew.
rejected: Yes, doing good mainly to be seen costs you something significant. When your motive is others' approval, the good deed becomes a performance, and your reward is the praise you receive—nothing deeper. You may also find yourself choosing visible acts over quiet, costly ones, and your sense of worth becomes dependent on others' opinions. Over time this can breed anxiety and exhaustion. The remedy is to notice your motives honestly, practice hidden good deeds, and redirect your heart toward God's approval rather than people's. Ask yourself whether you would still do the good if no one knew.

prompt: I have been a faithful minister for years and see little fruit—should I keep laboring in the same place?
chosen: Seeing little fruit after years of faithful ministry is discouraging, and your question is honest. But do not respond by cautiously narrowing your labor. If you are required to do ten pieces of work and only one is necessary for the Kingdom, do all ten—so that you are sure of performing the one the Lord really requires. Yet do not rely on elaborate appeals or human recruitment methods; seek labourers first by earnest prayer to the LORD of the harvest and by deepening your own spiritual life, so that men cannot stay at home. And remember: we have no time allotted to work for ourselves in the narrow, selfish sense. When you labor most fervently for the Kingdom of God, it is all for yourself, since your interest is bound up in that Kingdom. So keep laboring wholeheartedly where you are, and let faithfulness, not visible results, measure your obedience.
rejected: Seeing little fruit after years of faithful ministry is deeply discouraging, and your question is honest. Whether to stay or move is a real decision that deserves prayer, wise counsel, and honest assessment. Consider whether the lack of fruit reflects the soil, your methods, or simply a season of waiting; sometimes faithfulness bears fruit only long after. Ask trusted mentors and your church leadership to help discern. Do not make a change out of despair or stay out of mere duty. Seek God's guidance, examine your health and calling, and remember that faithfulness is measured by obedience, not visible results.

prompt: I get jealous when I see others succeed and I hate that about myself—what do I do with this feeling?
chosen: Feeling jealous when others succeed is common, and hating it shows a conscience that wants to change. But jealousy and mistrust destroy affection, and possessiveness shrinks the heart. Do not confine the good of others within your own four walls; practice mutual freedom, confidence, and a benevolence that grows more diffusive. This demands absolute self-conquest, not small accommodations: lay aside retaliation and petty aims, and recognize humbly your own smallness and how ineffective your self-control is on its own. Yet do not hurry or fret anxiously over your progress. Keep yourself in God's presence, and treat over-eagerness as the mother imperfection of all imperfections, for anxiety is an obstacle to perfection. Ask what the envy is telling you, pursue it honestly without begrudging anyone, and let gratitude and generosity crowd out envy in God's own time. Be patient, and speak with a trusted friend if the feeling is intense.
rejected: Feeling jealous when others succeed is very common, and hating it about yourself shows you have a conscience that wants to change. Start by naming the feeling honestly rather than shaming yourself for it. Jealousy often points to something you want for yourself—recognition, security, or a sense of purpose—so ask what the envy is telling you. Then you can take small, concrete steps toward your own goals instead of measuring yourself against others. Practice celebrating someone else's success out loud, even when it is hard; gratitude and generosity tend to crowd out envy over time. Be patient with yourself, and consider talking with a trusted friend or counselor if the feeling is intense or persistent.

prompt: My church seems to care more about its building and budget than about people. How should I respond?
chosen: It is painful to feel that your church cares more about buildings and budgets than about people. Remember that church revenues belong to the poor: even sacred vessels may be devoted to those in need, and goods hoarded while people suffer are a scandal. When you hear complaints of impoverishment, answer with confidence that God will provide—providence, not accumulation, is our security. Yet do not blame priests or institutions alone. The Church's lack is found in the tepid love for a dimly known Lord in each member's heart, including your own; the Church gains what is lacking when each heart worships the beloved Christ. Trust that the government of this Church is based upon true principles. People fall out by the way through ignorance, because they do not thoroughly canvass their acts and wisely ponder probable results. So pray, examine your own love, speak calmly and specifically with your leaders, and offer to help connect resources to people.
rejected: It is painful to feel that your church cares more about buildings and budgets than about people. Start by praying about your concern and asking whether your own expectations are realistic—every congregation has practical needs like upkeep and finances. Then speak with your pastor or a trusted leader, calmly and specifically, about what you have observed. Offer to help: volunteer with outreach, welcome newcomers, or serve on a committee that connects resources to people. If the pattern is serious, raise it with the governing board in writing. Remember that you are part of the church too, and your own care for people can shape its culture. If, after honest effort, nothing changes, seek wise counsel about whether this is the right community for you.

prompt: Can I be forgiven if I'm still holding a grudge against someone who hurt me?
chosen: Holding a grudge after being hurt is understandable, but forgiveness is not a transaction granted regardless of the state of your heart. It is an inward condition of the personal life: it comes naturally to the soul that loves and forgives, and it depends on your own spirit as well as on God. A heart that remains hard and unforgiving cannot simply receive pardon while refusing to give it. As St. Fulgentius teaches, Christians must not seek revenge but forgive injuries. Do not limit forgiveness by a human reckoning of how much the wound deserves. Forgive as you hope to be forgiven, looking to the Lord who resigned all to earn our pardon. Refuse to mete out love by your own narrow rule; be honest with God about the hurt, pray for the person, and let his generous pardon shape yours.
