Unrepented sin accumulates, hardening the heart and destroying the ability to do right, so begin with honest repentance and reformation of life. Yet beware of two errors. The moralists—Clement, Barnabas, Polycarp, Ignatius—narrowed the religious sense, making forgiveness a single remission at baptism and righteousness identical with virtue, which leaves the baptized sinner either presumptuous or despairing. Instead hold both together: dread of the unsureness of ourselves, as a matter of meekness against presumption, and the blessed Shewing of Love, as true comfort and joy against despair. Let the sight of your sin keep you humble, and let the sight of His mercy keep you from sinking. Peace comes not from your virtue but from His love, received by the repentant heart.
rejected: Peace of conscience comes from God's forgiveness, received by faith in Christ. Your past weighs on you because guilt is real, but the gospel announces that God does not hold your sins against you when you turn to Him. Confess what you have done, accept His pardon, and let the burden lift. It can help to speak with a pastor or trusted believer who can assure you of grace and pray with you. Peace is not the absence of memory but the presence of forgiveness; the past may still come to mind, but it no longer condemns you. Rest in the promise that there is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus, and let gratitude and obedience replace the weight of old guilt.

prompt: I am a pastor and I am paid a salary. Does that make my ministry professional and heartless?
chosen: A professional, salary-centered ministry is heartless, and you should reject it. The ministry is not a business or a career; when salary and self-advancement lead, the heart goes out of the work and people become clients. Put self to the rear and heart to the front. But do not imagine that a warm heart or correct doctrine gives life: all life-giving power belongs to the Spirit of God, energizing the preacher and the word, and truth unquickened by the Spirit deadens rather than gives life. Avoid both extremes. Do not withdraw from people into a hermit's seclusion, and do not become a popularizer whose activism leaves prayer out of your plans. Time with God is useful only as it is expended on men. So pray for the Spirit, keep your heart toward the flock, and let your salary support a ministry that spends itself for others.
rejected: Being paid a salary does not in itself make your ministry professional or heartless. A worker is worthy of his wages, and a congregation that supports its pastor frees him to give himself fully to the work. The danger is not the salary but the spirit in which it is received: if the ministry becomes a career, a business, or a means of self-advancement, then it has become professional in the bad sense. Keep your heart toward the people, preach the gospel faithfully, and let the salary be a support rather than a motive. Examine yourself honestly: do you love the flock, or do you love the position? The answer to that question matters far more than the paycheck.

prompt: I feel completely apathetic about spiritual things and I can't seem to care. What is happening to me?
chosen: Apathy in spiritual things is deadly, not merely a lack of feeling to be managed. Do not treat spiritual experience as something you can manufacture by returning to basics until feelings follow; accept experiences only as God chooses, without praying for them, secretly desiring them, or approaching them with curiosity, and submit without questioning or fear. Yet submission is not repose: allow no slipping back in the spiritual ascent, but go forward like a mountain-climber until the goal is reached, for desires turning aside after lower objects cause distraction and loss of the way; withdraw from worldly distractions into the one unchangeable Good. And understand that God often touches us where we are most tender—through loss and hardship—not as cruelty but as His loving means to awaken, humble, and lift us into His consolations. Name the apathy, keep climbing, and trust His hand.
rejected: Apathy in spiritual things is common, and it is often a sign of exhaustion, discouragement, or unaddressed sin. The first step is to be honest about it rather than pretending. Ask yourself what has drained your desire: busyness, disappointment, or a pattern of compromise? Return to the basics—prayer, Scripture, fellowship—even when you feel nothing, because feelings follow faithfulness. It may help to speak with a pastor or a trusted friend who can pray with you and help you examine your life. Do not wait for the feeling to return before you act; act, and the feeling may follow. God is not distant because you feel distant, and He is able to rekindle desire in a heart that has grown cold.

prompt: I want to be recollected in God but my mind keeps wandering—what should I do?
chosen: Think of prayer as a beggar waiting at a door: you have nothing but your presence, and God is already looking at you with kindness. When your mind wanders, do not turn to examine yourself. Turn simply to Him, your love and delight, and rest in His presence again—no fuss, no disquiet. Your joy is not in how well you pray but in pleasing Him. And remember: the mind you guard during the day is the mind you bring to prayer. If outside prayer you keep your thoughts gently in God's presence, refusing idle distraction, your mind grows calm and comes to prayer already recollected. So let your heart be occupied with God at all times, content to be before Him, trusting that He keeps you even when your attention slips. Return in peace, as often as needed.
rejected: Wandering thoughts are normal and not a sign of failure. Try a simple technique: when you notice your mind has drifted, gently return your attention to a short prayer word or to a phrase like 'Lord, have mercy.' Don't fight the thoughts or scold yourself—just acknowledge them and let them pass. Some people find it helps to pray at a fixed time, in a quiet place, with a candle or icon to focus the eyes. You might also keep a notebook nearby to jot down distracting worries so you can set them aside. Be patient with yourself; recollection is a habit that grows with practice, and even a few moments of genuine attention are worthwhile.

prompt: I'm reading a lot of dark, realistic fiction and it's making me despair about humanity—is that the whole picture?
chosen: Dark fiction can show real suffering, but it is a selection, not the whole picture. Much of what passes for peace in this world is built on mutual fear and selfish loves—and that is precisely where Cruelty's snare is knit. Cruelty, Humility, Mystery, and Deceit grow from the human brain. But see evil in its true complexion: it is disease, misery, imprisonment, and death, not glamour or harmless shadow. The spiritual man sees this by the new light created when the Spirit of Love descends. The Christian faith does not explain away the dread meeting with the Lord; it keeps that expectation alive, and the Apocalypse is a vision of final triumph in Christ. So read with that horizon open: the darkness is real, but it is not the last word. Let the stories deepen compassion, and let your hope rest in the triumph of Christ.
rejected: Dark fiction can be valuable—it shows us real suffering and moral complexity—but it is a selection, not the whole picture. Writers often focus on conflict, corruption, and failure because that's what makes drama. Real human life also includes ordinary kindness, courage, loyalty, and quiet goodness that rarely makes it into novels. If the reading is weighing on you, try balancing it with other voices: history, biography, or fiction that acknowledges darkness without being consumed by it. Notice also what the despair is doing to you—if it's making you cynical or numb, that's a sign to step back. Literature should deepen your compassion, not erase your hope.

prompt: How can God be love if he was alone before creation and had no one to love?
chosen: God's love is not a mere feeling or an abstract attribute. It is rational, voluntary self-communication: God freely gives Himself and seeks the true good of what He loves, and this love is regulated by and subordinate to holiness. Within the Trinity, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit give and receive eternally. This is the love that was in Him from without beginning: He loved us before He made us, and His love was never slacked. In that love He made all things profitable to us, and Love was His meaning in all He showed. So do not let fear govern this question. Meet the trial with stronger faith and purer love, for perfect Love casts out fear. 'God is love' means He freely communicates His goodness, holy and never indifferent to sin, seeking our true good from before all time.
rejected: This is a classic question, and there are several ways to answer it. One is that God is triune—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—so love has always existed within God's own life, not just toward creatures. Another is that love doesn't require a created object; God's nature is to give and receive within Himself. You could also say that creation itself is an expression of God's love, so He wasn't 'alone' in a lonely sense. Different theologians emphasize different points. Ultimately, the claim 'God is love' is about His character, not about whether He had company. It's a mystery, but a reasonable one.

prompt: I have spoken badly about a colleague. What must I do?
chosen: Speak little, and speak well—and when you speak, speak plainly. First, be silent: do not repeat or spread what you said. Then go to your colleague and say plainly what you said and that it was wrong, so they can hear and understand you without guessing. If others heard you, correct the record in plain words. Say what you have to say, then stop; do not darken counsel by many words. Meanwhile, compel your heart to suffer tranquilly. You will feel rebellious murmurings and sudden impatience; do not let them govern your dealings with your neighbor. Remain kind despite them, praying quietly for the one you wronged. A few honest words, gently and frankly spoken, are better than many. Be patient; trust takes time.
rejected: First, stop. Don't repeat what you said or spread it further. Second, apologize to the colleague directly and specifically—name what you said and why it was wrong, without excuses. Third, if others heard you, correct the record with them too. Fourth, examine why you did it: was it anger, jealousy, or just careless talk? Address that root. Fifth, pray for the colleague and for yourself. If the damage was serious, ask your colleague what would help repair it. Be patient—trust may take time to rebuild. The important thing is to act quickly and honestly, and to change the habit of speech that led to this.

prompt: I have been a light and trifling person and heard serious conversation at a funeral—can that begin a real change in me?
chosen: Yes—but let it be something deeper than a mood, and do not mistake a passing stirring for conversion. Count yourself as already dead, since you must die some day. Have no other desire or consolation in this perishable life than unceasingly to weep over, regret, and detest your offences and faults; it is not now the time to rejoice but to lament with all sincerity of heart. And as you stand among mourners, remember that the dead beloved is in a high sphere of saner happiness; your grief for them should be a tender regret, not acute grief. Beware: superficial conversions made under fear of calamity rarely bear the characters of sincerity. Transient glances effect not a change of heart. Let this stirring bring you to a sincere and perfect change of heart, not merely a short-lived fit of fervor.
rejected: Yes, it can—funerals often wake us up. A serious conversation at a funeral can plant a seed, and God can use ordinary moments to stir the conscience. But a seed needs care to grow. Take the stirring seriously: reflect on what struck you, pray about it, and make one or two concrete changes in how you spend your time and speak. Talk with someone wise who can help you keep going. Don't expect instant transformation, but don't dismiss the moment either. Many people trace real change back to a single unsettling experience. The question is whether you'll follow through.

prompt: I keep thinking about my past sins and can't forgive myself—how do I move on?
chosen: A guilty conscience is not a small thing to be soothed away. Unrepented sin accumulates; each time you excuse it, the heart hardens and the power to do right weakens. So begin with honest repentance: name your sins to God, grieve them, and turn toward a reformed life, making amends where you can. Confessing your faults and humbling yourself quiets the wandering mind, for pride scatters the thoughts while humility gathers them; in prayer, avoid heaping up many words, which only multiplies distraction. But go deeper than lopping off a few branches. Lay the axe at the root of self: deny not merely this indulgence or that habit, but self-will, self-seeking, and self-glory. Take up the cross voluntarily for Christ's sake—not as a forced trial but as a chosen renunciation—and let each day's conduct show that grace is at work.
rejected: It is normal to feel weighed down by past sins, but you must not stay there. God's mercy is greater than anything you have done, and when you confess your sins he is faithful to forgive. Stop replaying the past; that only keeps you stuck. Instead, accept that you are forgiven, receive God's grace, and focus on the present. You cannot change what happened, but you can choose to trust that God has dealt with it. Talk to a trusted pastor or friend, pray for peace, and take small steps forward. Self-forgiveness is not excusing yourself—it is agreeing with God that you are pardoned and free.

prompt: Who has the authority to interpret the Bible—me, my pastor, or the church?
chosen: The final interpreter is not a lone individual, nor a pastor alone, nor a formal organization, but the composite judgment of the whole body of believers, checked by the authority of the prophets and apostles speaking through the Bible. Scripture is proved sacred through its use by the congregations, yet the church's judgment stands under the text. Beware traditionalism, which lets custom override Scripture, and institutionalism, which narrows the church to an official body. Yet even Scripture is not the ultimate authority: authority resides in Christ himself, who teaches us by his Spirit, and that Spirit leads the church progressively to distinguish the essential from the non-essential. So read personally, submit to the apostolic word, and above all to the living Lord who speaks through it. Such subjection is perfect freedom, freeing you from private whim and human custom alike.
rejected: The Bible is meant to be read by everyone, and every believer has the Holy Spirit to help them understand it. So you have real authority to interpret Scripture for yourself—no pastor or institution should dictate what you must believe. At the same time, your pastor is trained and can help, and the wider church offers wisdom accumulated over centuries. The best approach is to read for yourself, check your understanding against trusted teachers, and stay humble. Private interpretation is not a license for isolation, but neither should any authority override what you see plainly in the text. Scripture is clear enough on the essentials, and where it is unclear, Christians may differ in good conscience.

prompt: Why does doing good seem to cost so much, and why do others have to suffer for my goodness to reach them?
chosen: Doing good costs because it asks for sacrifice, and those near us often share the cost. Be good as God is good: clothe your goodness with kindness, affectionateness, sympathy, and active benevolence, so that it reaches others warmly rather than as a granite mountainside. Do not despise the suffering that comes with it—the virtues born amid afflictions are strong and firm, and to carry the cross after Christ is an honor, not a misfortune. Yet do not measure your service by how much you do, how visible it is, or what results it yields. The main purpose is to please God and to do well rather than to do much. Prize quality above quantity; a small deed done well and for God's sake outweighs a great deal done for display. Let your aim be to please him, and leave the amount and the outcome in his hands.
rejected: Doing good costs because goodness is demanding. It requires sacrifice—time, money, comfort—and often the people around us pay part of the price. That is simply the nature of a moral life: righteousness has a price, and we should be willing to pay it. When others suffer for your goodness, remember that their suffering is not wasted; it is part of the cost of doing what is right. Do not shrink from it. Be firm and consistent, do your duty regardless of the cost, and accept that hardship is the price of integrity. The important thing is to keep doing right, even when it is hard and even when it hurts those near you.

prompt: I am asked to reveal a secret I have sworn to keep—what should I do when threatened with death?
chosen: This is a serious dilemma, but you are not required to master its hidden outcome. There are two parts to truth: what is open to you and what is hidden in God's counsel. Occupy yourself with what is open—keeping your oath with integrity and acting honestly—and commit the hidden Deed to God's goodness, not treating that hiddenness as a failure of faith. Make no account of the judgments or good opinion of men; endure them silently and find interior peace in that endurance. But do not rely on outward faithfulness alone. Secret prayer is indispensable: public prayer cannot make up for closet communion with God. Keep praying and reading the Word even when enjoyment is gone, for faithfulness in the dark is itself the trust you are called to. Let your hidden life with God sustain your open conduct before men.
rejected: This is a serious dilemma, and you should weigh it carefully. A sworn promise carries real weight, and breaking it damages trust. But a threat of death is also serious, and you must not be reckless with your own life. Consider whether the secret, if revealed, would harm others or prevent a greater evil; if so, disclosure may be justified. Seek counsel from wise people you trust. In the end, you must decide according to your conscience, balancing the duty of your oath against the duty to preserve life. Pray for wisdom, and do what seems right.

prompt: I am a minister, and I have been tempted to soften my message to please the main contributors to my support. What should I do?
chosen: This is a real temptation, and you should resist it—but resist it by trusting God rather than by managing your supporters. Preach the whole counsel of God, not what flatters those who fund your ministry. Do not build your work on pressure, solicitation, or guaranteed incomes; depend on voluntary contributions sent freely and without asking, and testify that GOD supplies all your need. In this occasion of virtue, ask God for enabling grace and receive strength more than sufficient, for he does not command faithfulness and leave you alone. And be careful for nothing: cast your anxious care about provision and outcomes upon him, making your requests known to God with thanksgiving, and take his Almighty care in exchange for your worry. Then you will speak freely, fearing neither the loss of contributors nor the displeasure of men.
rejected: This is a real temptation, and you should resist it. Your calling is to preach the whole counsel of God, not to flatter those who fund your ministry. If you soften the message to keep contributors happy, you have made money your master. Trust God to provide, and be honest with your supporters about your convictions. It may cost you some funding, but integrity is worth more than a comfortable budget. Speak the truth in love, and let the chips fall where they may.

prompt: I am afraid that if I let God in, He will take away my freedom. Will He?
chosen: It's natural to fear that letting God in will cost you your freedom, but the truth is that God's will is never for your harm. He does not wish to take away your freedom but to free you from everything that enslaves you. The unreserved resignation taught by the saints is this: yield completely to God's will without exception or limitation, accepting to be struck where and as He pleases, even in the most repugnant events. Yet even in high contemplation, we must always keep the knowing and sight of our sin and feebleness, for without it there is no true meekness, and without meekness no salvation. And remember that light not used is withdrawn: to him that hath shall be given, and from him that hath not shall be taken away. So obey promptly the truth you know, and trust that He who permits no suffering without a good end will never abandon you. His service is perfect freedom.
rejected: It's natural to fear that surrendering to God means losing your freedom, but God's will is not about taking away your freedom—it's about freeing you from the things that truly bind you, like fear and sin. When you let God in, He doesn't force you; He invites you. His will is for your good, and He respects your choices. However, there may be areas where you need to trust Him more, especially when His will seems difficult. But remember, God's yoke is easy and His burden light. He won't take away your freedom; He will help you use it rightly.

prompt: How do I deal with fear when I'm facing a mob or real danger?
chosen: When facing a mob or real danger, do not let fear govern you. Fear is not helpful; it must be cast out and replaced by trust in God. In the testimonies of healing, fear was overcome before the healing appeared. So when danger threatens, fasten your eyes on Christ Himself, who is the antidote to fear and the sum of all deliverance. Abide in Him, and you will find in His presence the remedy for trouble. Do not look at the storm or the circumstances for comfort, but look to Jesus, the author and finisher of your faith. And if you feel alone, accept hidden solitude as Heaven's will, trusting God alone with your secret throbbings and resting in the Lord who knows all yet loves us better than He knows. In Christ you are safe, for He is your refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble.
rejected: When facing a mob or real danger, fear is a natural response. The key is to manage it by focusing on practical steps: stay calm, assess the situation, and seek safety. While fear can be helpful by heightening your awareness, it can also hinder you if it leads to panic. Trust in God can provide comfort, but you also need to use wisdom. Remember that God is with you, but you must do your part to protect yourself. Pray for courage and take sensible precautions.

prompt: Who may enter through the gates into the city, and who will be shut out?
chosen: The Bible says that those who do His commandments have right to the tree of life and may enter through the gates into the city. Nothing that defiles, works abomination, or makes a lie shall enter it, but only those written in the Lamb's book of life. The city is not the saints themselves, but it is prepared for them; the righteous dead have not yet been caught up, but they wait for the resurrection. So the saints are being built together as a temple, and they will enter the city when it comes down from heaven. And this preparation is not apart from ordinary life: the trivial round and common task are the appointed means of self-denial and daily nearness to God. So do not forsake neighbour or work, but in them learn holiness, for without holiness no one will see the Lord.
rejected: The Bible says that those who have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb may enter through the gates into the city. This includes all who have faith in Jesus and live according to His commandments. Those who are shut out are the unbelieving, the immoral, the murderers, the sexually immoral, those who practice magic arts, idolaters, and all liars. Their place will be in the fiery lake of burning sulfur. So, entrance is open to all who believe and obey, but closed to those who persist in sin and reject God.

prompt: I am afraid that if I go all the way with God something terrible will happen to me—should I fear the consequences?
chosen: Do not be afraid to go all the way with God, for He is good and loving, and He does not wish to harm you but to do you great good. Love Him fervently and without servile fear, trusting that His plans for you are for welfare and not for harm, to give you a future and a hope. Remember that all evil of whatever kind happens by God's permission and ever for some good end; it could not be except He permitted it, and its form and measure are allowed by Him Who can and will by His wisdom turn all to good. Yet suffering and evil are not directly God's design or displeasure, but come from human agency, indiscretion, or ignorance. So commit all things without fear to the Providence of God, knowing that He who calls you is faithful and will do it.
rejected: It's understandable to fear that going all the way with God might lead to something terrible, but God is good and loving. He doesn't want to harm you; He wants what's best for you. However, following God can be challenging and may involve sacrifices. But remember that God promises to be with you and to work all things for your good. So, while it's natural to have some fear, you can trust that God's plans are for your welfare and not for harm, to give you a future and a hope. Don't let fear hold you back from fully committing to God.

prompt: Can I believe in a good God and still believe that death is the end of me?
chosen: No, you cannot consistently believe in a good God and hold that death is the end of you. Belief in a righteous God gives ground for expecting continuance after death, for His purpose for the higher spirits is not exhausted by this life. Immortality is a corollary of belief in a righteous God. Death is not the end of identity but a door to a higher state. For the righteous dead, we do not mourn hopelessly, but we are comforted by the promise of resurrection and the preservation of identity. The body will be raised, and we will be with the Lord forever. Yet death does not automatically improve our character or bring us nearer to God; this world is the place to find Him. The remedy must be found here, for this is where we can most easily and quickly find God. So, if you believe in a good God, you have every reason to expect that death is not the end, but you must seek Him now.
rejected: It's possible to believe in a good God and still wonder if death is the end, but the two beliefs are in tension. If God is good and righteous, it makes sense that He would not let His creatures perish forever. The Bible teaches that death is not the end but a transition to eternal life for those who believe. However, some people believe that death is the end and that this life is all there is. But for those who trust in God, there is hope for resurrection and eternal life. So, while you may have doubts, faith in a good God gives reason to hope that death is not the end.

prompt: Will I see my family and children again in the world to come?
chosen: This hope rests on what God has promised about the earth itself. The world to come is not the annihilation of creation but its restoration: God will renew the earth to its Edenic state, remove the curse, and restore man with it, so families and children belong within that restored order. Between death and that renewal, the spirit world is not idleness or oblivion; all go there, and the faithful continue their labors with the same Priesthood and identity they had in mortality. Yet you need not forecast or dread tomorrow. Think only of doing well today, and trust the eternal Father's care for what is to come. He who restores all things holds your family in His hands; leave the morrow with Him and live faithfully now.
rejected: This is one of the deepest hopes of the human heart, and Scripture gives real ground for it. The world to come is not a vague shadowland but the renewed creation where God dwells with His people, and where relationships are not erased but healed and perfected. If God cares for sparrows and numbers the hairs of our heads, He surely does not sever the bonds of love He Himself planted in families. Many faithful Christians have trusted that children remain children and parents remain parents in the resurrection, gathered into one great family under God. Grieve honestly, but grieve with hope: the God who raised Jesus will raise us, and nothing in Christ is finally lost.

prompt: Is it wrong to use written prayers or liturgy in worship?
chosen: Written prayers and liturgy are not wrong; indeed the spiritual worship of God was realized in definite institutions, not left to private impulse. Do not wait for the spirit of prayer before praying: pray at appointed times regardless of feeling, keep family prayer, and act so that God may accomplish what is asked rather than expecting Him to do all. Prayer on the knees, secret and in the companionship of believers, is the one great central secret of holy living and serving, the corner-stone on which all life-work is built, and the first resort in every crisis. In the Lord's Supper the ruling idea is sacrifice, and the Supper appears as the sacrifice of thanksgiving of the community. Set forms serve this worship when the heart is engaged, and liturgy thus becomes devotion rather than a substitute for it.
rejected: Written prayers and liturgy are not wrong; they can be a genuine help. Many believers find that set forms give words when their own fail, keep doctrine sound, and unite a congregation in one voice. The danger is formalism, where the words are repeated while the heart is absent. But that danger attends extemporaneous prayer too. Scripture itself preserves prayers and songs for repeated use, and Jesus taught His disciples a form of prayer. The real question is not whether words are written but whether the heart is engaged. Used humbly, liturgy can be a channel of devotion rather than a substitute for it, and it can train believers to pray when feeling is dry.

prompt: Why doesn't God just take me out of this sinful world instead of leaving me here?
chosen: The longing to be free of sin and its misery is good, but there is only one way out of misery: cease to sin. God does not take you out of the world because the world is where that victory is won; removal would not cure the heart. This calls for moral courage, not fear of punishment. Yet do not fall into overdone self-accusation or indiscreet sorrow: meekly acknowledge your sin and feebleness, and trust God's courteous excusing. Then abandon yourself to God without exception or reserve. Ask Him to tear and wrest from you all that burdens your heart, and to wrest you from yourself, so that nothing is held back. Bring your weariness to Him honestly, and let Him do in you what you cannot do alone.
rejected: The longing to be free of sin and its misery is good, and God understands it. But escape is not the same as deliverance. God leaves you here because this world is where love, patience, and faithfulness are learned, and where you can serve others still bound in the same struggle. Removal would end the opportunity for growth and service. The misery you feel is not a sign that God has abandoned you but an invitation to turn from sin and toward Him. He is not indifferent; He is patient, giving you time to change. Bring your weariness to Him honestly, and ask Him for strength to walk faithfully where you are rather than to be carried away from it.

prompt: I have been a member of an orthodox church but was never satisfied; will this teaching answer my questions?
chosen: It may well, but only if the teaching leads you to the true Christ. The test of orthodoxy is this: Jesus is the only-begotten Son, God manifest in the flesh, omnipresent, omniscient, omnipotent, our living Lord and Judge, in whom all the fulness of the Godhead dwells bodily. Any teaching that makes him merely a moral teacher, or divine only as we are divine, fails that test. Do not make your private interpretation final; final interpretation belongs to the composite judgment of the body of believers, and the Scriptures are proved sacred through their use by the congregations. Guard against traditionalism, institutionalism, and narrowing the church to a formal organization. Settle nothing by tradition, custom, or expediency. Lay aside prejudice, submit every matter to the Holy Scriptures as the only standard and the Holy Spirit as the only teacher, and ask simply what the testimony of Scripture is.
rejected: It may well, but the answer depends on what you are seeking. If your dissatisfaction comes from wanting a deeper, more personal faith, this teaching can help by pointing you back to Christ and to Scripture. If it comes from wanting certainty on every point, no system will fully satisfy you. Orthodox churches preserve much that is true, and you should not abandon what is good lightly. Examine the teaching carefully against Scripture, ask your questions honestly, and see whether it draws you closer to Christ or merely to a new set of opinions. Satisfaction is finally found in a person, not a doctrine, so test everything by whether it leads you to Him.

prompt: How am I to wait for the rising of this glorious Sun and seek in the Centre this Fountain of Light?
chosen: Begin by lifting your gaze above the world's uncertain haze to the bright fields beyond the sky. Waiting is not passive idleness but attentive expectation, like watching for dawn; it is preparing the Lord's way of mercy in your own heart. Keep the childhood's star in view through all of life, and do not let it be buried by the glare of earthly day. Follow its waymarks until all your hopes and thoughts are led to the Saviour's lowly bed. Yet do not strain and drive yourself; seek instead the quiet inner chamber and the rest of Christ's flock at noon. There rest in His exclusive love, which each heart may possess wholly. Gathering your thoughts in quiet, prayer, and Scripture, let go of anxiety and wait patiently, trusting that the light rises for those who lift their eyes.
rejected: Begin by turning your attention away from the noise and distraction of daily life and toward the light that is already near. Waiting is not passive idleness but attentive expectation, like watching for dawn. Seek the Centre by gathering your scattered thoughts in quiet, by prayer, and by reading Scripture with an open heart. Let go of the anxieties and ambitions that cloud your vision, and cultivate a simple, steady desire for God. The Fountain of Light is not far off; it rises for those who watch. Be faithful in small things, keep your heart quiet, and wait with patience, trusting that the light will come in its own time.

prompt: I was told my natural desires are sinful. Should I suppress them?
chosen: Sin is not a real pleasure but a form of insanity, and sickness is error, not a condition to be accepted. The testimony of the corporeal senses is untrue of man and his Maker; therefore, do not be deceived by apparent desires that would lead you astray. Meekly acknowledge your sin and feebleness, trusting in God's courteous excusing, but know that sin confers no real pleasure—it is a false belief. Strengthen your moral courage by understanding this truth, and master evil by denying the senses' testimony. God loves you and wants you to live in freedom, not in slavery to false pleasures. Stand firm in the truth that man is spiritual and perfect, and reject the illusion of sinful desires.
rejected: It's important to understand that natural desires are part of being human and were given by God. However, some desires can lead to sin if not controlled. The key is to discern which desires are healthy and which are not. Suppressing all desires isn't the answer; rather, you should channel them in ways that honor God. Seek guidance from trusted spiritual leaders and practice self-discipline. Remember that God loves you and wants you to live a fulfilling life, not one of constant suppression. Balance and moderation are important, and you can enjoy the good things God has given while avoiding excess.

prompt: I am young and I fear I have wasted my youth; will God count the years I gave Him?
chosen: God does not overlook the years you gave Him, even in youth. Every willing service, every moment offered freely, is thanked and rewarded by God, as the Sixth Revelation shows. Do not fear that your youth was wasted; rather, trust that God counts and treasures the time you gave Him. Yet know that your soul is stripped piece by piece, its harness hewn away, its dreams failing; you stand naked and defenceless before God's uplifted stroke. Even so, God's worshipful thanking means nothing offered in love is lost. In this age, real prayer is scarce, and the greatest work you can do is to help restore preachers and the Church to prayer. So bring your regret to God, offer your time and service willingly, and labor to bring prayer back to its rightful place.
rejected: It's natural to feel regret about wasted time, but God is merciful and understands our struggles. The years you gave to God, even if imperfect, are not lost. God values your willingness and effort, and He can redeem the time you feel was wasted. Focus on the present and future, dedicating your remaining years to serving Him. God doesn't keep a ledger of your mistakes; He looks at your heart. Seek forgiveness for any negligence and move forward with hope. Your youth is not wasted if you learn from it and turn back to God. He can restore the years the locusts have eaten.

prompt: What is the root of the unrest among working people?
chosen: The root of unrest among working people is a lack of justice in economic life. Justice requires recognizing workers as persons, not instruments, with a voice in the conditions that govern them. Economic liberty is as essential as political liberty; without it, justice is incomplete. Workers feel marginalized when they are treated as mere cogs in a machine, leading to frustration and agitation. To address this, we must ensure that workers have a say in decisions that affect them, fair wages, and dignified conditions. Recognizing personality in economic life means honoring the inherent worth of every worker and allowing them to participate fully in the fruits of their labor. Moreover, the greatest wealth we possess is knowledge of how to direct our labors rightly, spending every hour advantageously for the benefit of our wives, children, and neighbors. And let oppressors beware: the sighs and groans of the poor are arms more powerful than magistrates, piercing the heavens and drawing down divine vengeance on those who oppress them.
rejected: The unrest among working people often stems from economic inequality, poor working conditions, and lack of representation. Workers feel marginalized and powerless, leading to frustration and agitation. Addressing these issues requires improving wages, ensuring fair treatment, and giving workers a voice in decisions that affect them. It's also important to foster dialogue between employers and employees to build trust and find common ground. Ultimately, a just society must ensure that all people have the opportunity to earn a living wage and work in dignity.

prompt: I am afraid to commit to a long engagement because I do not know when GOD may call me.
chosen: It's understandable to feel uncertain about committing to a long engagement when you don't know God's timing. However, fear should not paralyze you. Make a definite, once-for-all committal to the engagement, trusting that God guides those who seek Him. Once you have committed, stay put through the season of establishing and testing until the new relationship becomes a permanent habit. Continual help of God is needed, so cultivate the holy habit of praying, being with God, and thinking of Him often, for we must know before we love. Strenuously lift your heart to God's goodness and exult in it, for that is the only safe temper for tempted men. Seek His loving-kindness in all the breadth and open-air of common life—in whatsoever things are true, honourable, just, pure, lovely, and of good report—while not missing behind them the greatest Reality, God Himself.
rejected: It's understandable to feel uncertain about committing to a long engagement when you don't know God's timing. However, fear should not paralyze you. You can trust that God guides those who seek Him, and He will make His will clear in time. Perhaps you can proceed with the engagement while remaining open to God's leading. Communicate openly with your partner about your concerns and pray together for guidance. Remember that God desires your good and will not lead you astray. Take one step at a time, and don't let fear of the unknown prevent you from moving forward in faith.

prompt: I am terrified of death and of being judged. How can I prepare for a good death and not despair at the end?
chosen: It's natural to fear death and judgment, but as a Christian, you can find hope in God's mercy. To prepare for a good death, focus on living a life of faith, love, and repentance. Remember that judgment is according to deeds done in the body and the thoughts and intents of the heart; death leaves us as judgment finds us. Death is certain, but its time, place, and manner are utterly uncertain. Therefore, make now the changes you would wish to have made when death is near. When you stumble in small faults, do not be terrified; quietly humble yourself before God and say to your soul: 'Courage! we have made a false step, but let us keep steadily on.' Trust in His grace and don't despair. God's mercy is greater than your sins. Keep your eyes on Jesus and the promise of eternal life.
rejected: It's natural to fear death and judgment, but as a Christian, you can find hope in God's mercy. To prepare for a good death, focus on living a life of faith, love, and repentance. Regularly examine your conscience, seek forgiveness, and participate in the sacraments. Cultivate a relationship with God through prayer and good works. Remember that God is loving and just, and He desires your salvation. At the end, trust in His grace and don't despair. God's mercy is greater than your sins. Keep your eyes on Jesus and the promise of eternal life.

prompt: Should I pray for my dead brother, and if so, what should I ask for?
chosen: Yes, pray for your dead brother, but bring even this smallest matter to God and ask His guidance rather than deciding it yourself. Commend him to God's mercy: ask that he be acquitted at the great Day, attain perfect consummation and bliss, and be raised at the resurrection of the just. Do not suppose a gradual purification Scripture has not disclosed; leave the unseen to God's wise judgment. Let your love seek Christ first and then go to win an erring brother, giving wreaths of hope rather than fading memorials. Ask God to show you how to grieve, how to live, and how to love, honoring Him by seeking His guidance in all things rather than taking the matter out of His hands.
rejected: Yes, you may pray for your dead brother, and doing so can be a comfort to you in your grief. You might ask God to have mercy on him, to forgive any sins he committed, and to bring him swiftly to peace and light. Many Christians have prayed for the dead as an act of love, trusting that God continues to work in the souls of those who have died, gradually purifying them until they are ready for heaven. So pray with hope, asking that your brother be cleansed of any remaining faults and brought at last into the joy of God's presence. Let your prayers be an expression of love that does not end at the grave.

prompt: I am a young man and I want to be a warrior. What habits should I form?
chosen: Wanting to be a warrior is worthy, but know that your first enemy is within yourself. Conquer yourself first and submit to the Father's will before you set out to oppose error and evil around you. Form Cormac's habits: listen in the woods, be blind to secrets, mild in the mead-hall and stern in battle, gentle to allies; do not deride the old, do not speak of anyone in his absence, and give rather than ask. Add faith in Christ, trusting and obeying Him, so your courage is colored by His mercy and self-sacrifice. Then oppose evil by persuasion, patience, and love unfeigned—without violence and without interfering with the agency of others—prepared to meet Him as Saviour and Judge.
rejected: Wanting to be a warrior is a worthy ambition, and the habits you form now will shape the man you become. Train your body daily with running, lifting, and martial practice so that strength and endurance become second nature. Study the craft of war—weapons, tactics, and the history of great captains. Cultivate courage by facing small fears now, and discipline by keeping a strict routine. Learn to speak boldly and to assert yourself among others, for a warrior must command respect. Seek out mentors and ask them to teach you everything they know, and do not be afraid to ask for advancement and recognition, since fortune favors those who press their claims. Sharpen your wit, and do not shy from mocking the weak or the old, for a warrior's reputation is his armor.

prompt: I want to see a miracle to confirm the truth. Is it wrong to require a sign before I believe?
chosen: It is not the way of honest faith to require a sign. Miracles are for the consolation and confirmation of the Saints, and no good, honest person requires one to believe. Do not speculate about mysteries that God has not revealed; leave hidden things to Him. Instead, learn to see God's providences as miracles—His daily care and guidance are wonders enough. Ask God in the name of Jesus, and seek the witness of the Holy Ghost within, which cannot be mistaken. That inward witness, not signs and wonders, is the true assurance of the Gospel. Pray honestly, ready to obey what He shows you, and ground your faith in the Spirit rather than in signs.
rejected: It is not wrong to want confirmation of the truth, and miracles can be a legitimate help to faith. Many honest seekers have asked for a sign, and God in His mercy sometimes grants one. A miracle can remove doubt and give you a firm foundation to believe. So pray earnestly for a sign, and watch for God's answer; if you receive one, let it strengthen your faith and lead you to commitment. At the same time, do not make a sign an absolute condition, since faith often grows from study and reflection as well. But if a miracle would help you believe, there is no shame in asking for it, and God may well honor your request.

prompt: I am a teacher and want to make the Bible come alive for my students—how should I present it?
chosen: To make the Bible come alive, do not rely on the letter alone; seek and strive for the spirit of Truth and Love. Prepare and explain the text, but let your teaching flow from prayer and love for your students. Teach that when the soul is purified of earthly images and unified and tranquillized in God with loving confidence, the Holy Spirit Himself teaches the love of God and of neighbour, so that study and reading are no longer needed to learn that love—while the Holy Scriptures remain the presupposed foundation of belief. Emphasize present salvation and everyday religion: urge your students to live faithfully today and let the Millennium take care of itself, enjoying the Spirit now rather than merely preparing for a distant future.
rejected: To make the Bible come alive, focus on clear and engaging presentation. Prepare carefully, use vivid stories and illustrations, and repeat the key words and verses so students remember them. Read the text aloud with expression, explain the historical background, and quiz the students on the letter of the passage. Use memorization and recitation, and make sure your wording is precise and orthodox. If you repeat the words faithfully and explain them well, the lesson will take root and heal dull hearts. Keep your method consistent and your language exact, and trust that faithful repetition of the letter will do its work in time.

prompt: I keep studying to make my sermons eloquent, but few seem converted—what am I missing?
chosen: It sounds like you are working hard at eloquence, but conversion is not the fruit of technique. All conversion is the work of the almighty power of the HOLY GHOST, and your great need is to know GOD. Learn intercession for the people: pray for them by name and let that school of prayer shape your preaching, for without it no homiletics or genius can make a preacher. Then learn God's will through the ministers He has appointed, abolishing self-confidence and presumption; do not despise the guides He has given. Let your sermons flow from communion, prayer, and humble obedience, and the same Spirit who called you will work through your words, changing hearts by His power rather than yours.
rejected: It sounds like you are working hard at eloquence, and that effort is commendable. To see more conversions, refine your technique: study great preachers, improve your delivery, use compelling illustrations, and structure your sermons for maximum impact. Learn rhetoric and persuasion, for a well-crafted sermon moves the hearer. Practice your delivery until it is polished, and adjust your style to your audience. Conversion often follows good communication, so invest in homiletics and platform skill. With enough effort and the right methods, your preaching will bear more fruit. Keep studying and refining, and trust that your improved technique will win more hearts.

prompt: I'm drawn to drama and strong feelings rather than quiet growth. Is that a spiritual problem?
chosen: You are right to suspect something here, but do not imagine you can diagnose and repair it yourself. The craving for strong feeling is a symptom of a helplessness we cannot cure by insight or effort. Confess that plainly, and take hold of Christ's all-sufficiency with a faith that will accept nothing less than all. Do not pray for dramatic experiences or secretly desire them; accept whatever God gives or withholds, without questioning, fear, or curiosity. And when prayer is dry and irksome—when nothing stirs—do not flee to sensation. Stay there. That dryness is a trial of love, and in it you may make effectual acts of resignation: 'Lord, I will this because you will it.' Such acts, made faithfully in aridity, greatly advance the soul. Quiet growth is not the absence of drama; it is love proved in the ordinary.
rejected: It's not automatically a problem, but it's worth examining. Strong feelings and dramatic experiences can be genuine gifts, and many people encounter God through intense emotion. But if you find that you need drama to feel spiritually alive, that need may become a kind of dependence. Quiet growth—patient faithfulness in ordinary prayer, small acts of love, endurance without consolation—is where character is usually formed. Feelings rise and fall; they are unreliable measures of God's presence. The question isn't whether drama is bad, but whether you can be faithful when nothing dramatic is happening. If stillness feels empty or threatening, that's worth exploring honestly with a trusted guide.

prompt: I have doubts I am ashamed of; what should I do with them?
chosen: Doubts are common, and shame about them makes them worse. Do not rush to resolve them: over-eagerness is the mother of many imperfections, and anxiety is an obstacle to perfection. Keep yourself in God's presence and bring your doubts there without demanding they be settled today. But go deeper than managing a few anxious habits. Lay the axe at the root of the tree of self: the real issue is self-will, self-seeking, and self-glory, which want certainty on their own terms. Self-denial is a voluntary renunciation of self, taken up for Christ's sake, not the lopping off of a few branches. And be plain with yourself. A long visit, staring, and constant questioning are signs of ill-breeding, not devotion; 'perhaps,' 'may be,' and 'I dare say' are false sisters. Speak simply, act simply, and let your yes be yes.
rejected: Doubts are common, and shame about them usually makes them worse. The first thing is to stop treating doubt as a moral failure. Honest questions are not the same as unbelief, and many faithful people have carried doubts for years. Bring them into the light—talk with a pastor, a trusted friend, or a spiritual director. Examine what specifically you doubt and why; sometimes doubts dissolve under examination, and sometimes they point to something you genuinely need to learn. Keep praying even when you feel uncertain, and don't demand immediate resolution. Doubt handled patiently often deepens faith rather than destroying it.

prompt: I feel like a bridegroom standing before a life that's welcoming me—how do I measure my strength against such a future?
chosen: What a striking image. The honest question is not whether you feel strong enough but what strength actually is. Strength of character is the will's power to control your actions independently of your inclinations and of the opinions of men. It is not fixed by temperament and not excused by 'that's just how I am.' Character is formed by habits, and habits by repeated acts; progress is proportioned to self-victories. Yet strength is not for domination: each nation and person needs the others, and needs them free, so fellowship is the first duty. And do not think ideas or aspirations will carry you. They strain as much as they lift, and reverence alone never saved a soul in the storm of life. What preserves you is One by your side, in trust, sympathy, and comradeship, fighting with you in the ranks—by whom your strength is thrilled and your right hand kept fresh.
rejected: What a striking image. Standing before a welcoming future, the honest question is not whether you feel strong enough but what kind of strength you actually need. Feeling strong is not the same as being strong. Measure yourself not by your present emotions or by how others see you, but by your capacity to choose rightly when inclination pulls elsewhere. Character grows through repeated choices; each small victory over impulse adds to it. So don't wait to feel ready. Begin with the duties in front of you, keep your commitments, and let the future meet a person formed by faithful habits rather than by moods.

prompt: I have forgotten the people who helped me when I was young and poor. Does that matter?
chosen: Yes, it matters, but the deeper truth is often inverted. The poor are your 'masters': they have great interest in the court of heaven, and their intercession makes almsgiving the best provision a person can make. Remember your helpers with gratitude and honor them by giving generously now. Do not be paralyzed by the fear of giving to the unworthy: it is better to give to ten beggars and be sure of helping the one truly needy. Give with a single eye to assist the needy, and the blessing is yours regardless. But never support in idleness the one able to work—set such a person to work. Relieve present want, then help the poor help themselves.
rejected: Yes, it matters, though not in a way that should crush you. Gratitude is a real virtue, and forgetting those who helped you can leave a gap in your character—a habit of taking help for granted. It's worth trying to remember who they were and, where possible, to thank them or to honor their kindness by helping others in turn. But don't turn this into guilt. The deeper point is that generosity received should become generosity given. If you can't repay the specific people, you can pass the help along to someone else who is young and poor now. That's a fitting way to honor what you received.

prompt: I wonder whether the moral teaching of Jesus can be separated from his person, or whether the two are inseparable.
chosen: They are inseparable, but the reason is often misstated. The early church did not begin with a doctrine of two natures. Two Christologies stood beside each other: the Adoptian, in which the man Jesus has become a God, and the pneumatic, in which a Divine being appeared in human form. Neither was affirmed as two natures; the pictures simply stood together. The teaching is inseparable from the person because the person is inseparable from the divine life that acted in him. His works demonstrate an ever-operative divine Principle, and his followers have a present duty to heal the sick and cast out error. Yet do not shrink him to a figure small enough to be fully comprehended. The manifold Gospel picture is a self-evidencing fact: Lawgiver, Teacher, Healer, Ruler, and Saviour, man and God, in the richness of his mysterious person.
rejected: They are inseparable, though not in a way that makes the teaching merely decorative. Jesus' moral teaching is not a detached code that could have been delivered by anyone; it is bound up with who he claimed to be and how he lived. He taught with authority, embodied what he commanded, and pointed beyond rules to a relationship. At the same time, you can certainly study his ethics on their own terms and learn from them. But to treat the teaching as separable from the person is to miss what makes it distinctive: it is the teaching of one who invites people into his own life with God.

prompt: If the Old Testament shows development in revealed truth, why can't I expect new revelations added to the New Testament?
chosen: The Old Testament shows development, and the New Testament is no mere anthology: though its books differ widely, they share an essential unity and divine authority as God's voice to us. Revelation has always come step by step, line upon line, because people cannot bear all things at once, as with Joseph's gradual receipt of priesthood and ordinances. Yet the goal of that unfolding is not humanity climbing toward divinity but God showing us Himself. In Christ we see God, and God is like Christ; the Old Testament's foreshadowings are gathered up in him. Honoring Jesus' real humanity, we still receive in him the full revelation of God's character, so we need no new revelation beyond knowing him more deeply.
rejected: You can see development in the Old Testament because God revealed truth gradually to a people learning to know Him. The New Testament, however, is presented as the final and complete revelation, centered on Jesus Christ. Its writings were produced by apostles and eyewitnesses and gathered into a fixed canon. Most Christian traditions hold that public revelation ended with the apostolic age, so nothing new may be added to the New Testament. Development within the Old Testament was preparation; the New Testament is the fulfillment. Private guidance and deeper understanding continue, but not new scripture.

prompt: How can I think of God even during meals and conversations with others?
chosen: God is always near, so He should be remembered and adored continually, not only at meals or quiet moments. Give thanks before eating, and keep a silent sense of His presence during conversation, letting attention to others be an act of love toward Him, since business and diversions are not outside His care. When you notice you have forgotten Him, do not be disquieted; return with greater trust, as a child returns to a Father who never left. Yet during a retreat, deep recollection matters: avoid unnecessary intercourse with the world, keep 'God and I' as the only objects of thought, and let even meals and necessary speech be simple and recollected, so nothing needless scatters the heart.
rejected: Try to build small habits: pause briefly before meals to give thanks, and let that gratitude color the conversation. During talk, listen well and look for openings to speak kindly or honestly. You might silently repeat a short prayer or recall a verse while others speak. Don't force religious talk into every moment, which can feel awkward; instead let your manner—patience, attention, gentleness—carry your awareness of God. Over time these small practices become natural, and ordinary meals and conversations become places where faith quietly shapes how you treat people.

prompt: I have peace with God but still feel anxious day by day—what is the peace of heart I'm missing?
chosen: You already have peace with God through Christ; what you're missing is the peace of God, which passes understanding and rests on His changeless word of promise, not on variable moods. Feelings never accurately gauge our real assimilation to God, so do not measure your standing by them. When joy is lacking, continue steadfastly in prayer and refuse to abandon communion or service because of spiritual depression. Remain at peace, patient with others and equally patient with yourself, since peace is the passport of the daughters of Jesus Christ. Yet the deeper secret is to cease from your own works and striving, receiving the peace of God and letting God work His own divine works in you.
rejected: It sounds like you already have the foundation: peace with God through Christ. The missing piece may be the peace of God—a settled trust that goes beyond circumstances. Anxiety often grows when we measure our standing by feelings. Instead, anchor yourself in God's promises, not in moods. Practice gratitude, limit what feeds worry, and bring each anxious thought to God in prayer. Consider whether sleep, health, or unconfessed stress is contributing. Talk with a trusted pastor or counselor. Peace of heart grows as you rest in what God has done rather than in how you feel.

prompt: I prepare my sermons carefully but my heart is cold. Which should I prepare first?
chosen: The great need is the preparation of the heart, and a prepared heart is better than a prepared sermon, because it produces one. Begin with morning meditation, and let the passage first search and comfort your own soul. When your heart wanders in prayer, do not be distressed or use violence; gently bring it back to its Master and lay it tenderly at His feet. In all your reading, implore divine light, and season your studies with aspirations to God, resolving your doubts at the foot of a crucifix. Studies without humility, simplicity, and prayer nourish vanity and error rather than virtue; so let prayer shape the study, and let the study flow from a warmed heart.
rejected: Prepare your heart first, then your sermon. A well-crafted sermon from a cold heart may inform but rarely warms others. Start with prayer and self-examination: ask God to search you, confess what dulls your affection, and meditate on the passage for your own soul before outlining it. Let the text first confront and comfort you. Then do the careful study and structure. Practical steps: pray before study, read devotionally before exegetically, and ask God for genuine love for your hearers. Skill matters, but the heart is the source.

prompt: I'm trying to serve God and also keep my old life and pleasures. Why do I feel so miserable and divided all the time?
chosen: You feel miserable because half-way service is wretched: trying to serve God and the world together divides the heart and brings gloom, not peace. The answer is not a safe middle way but following Christ all the way, letting Him complete His process in you. Keep both beholdings at once: the higher keeps you in solace and enjoying in God, while the lower keeps you in dread and shame of self, yet hold much more in the higher. And do not fear self-denial or economy as loss; they are a privilege that frees your resources for the LORD and brings fuller joy, since a whole heart given to Him is not diminished but enlarged.
rejected: You feel divided because you're trying to live in two directions at once. Serving God and clinging to old pleasures pulls your heart apart, and that tension shows up as misery. The solution isn't to hate yourself but to be honest about the conflict. Ask which loyalties actually shape your choices, and consider whether the pleasures you keep are harmless enjoyment or things that numb and enslave. You don't have to become joyless; God wants your whole heart, and a whole heart is less divided. Start with small, concrete decisions that align your life with what you say you believe.

prompt: How do I accept adversity as coming from God's hand rather than resenting it?
chosen: Accepting adversity as from God's hand requires first examining your own ways. Consider whether in times of prosperity you acknowledged God's hand or instead abused His blessings by excess on yourself. When loss comes, ask: Have I practically recognized God as the source of all good? Have I clung to gifts rather than the Giver? Repent of any self-indulgence that made a god of comfort. Then, with a humble heart, receive adversity as a corrective and refining providence. Even in the horrors of war, God did not ordain the wickedness; men's agency brought the evil, yet God foresaw it and will overrule its results for good. Moreover, do not be surprised at opposition, for the adversary's attack is a token of your salvation. Claim the double blessing, victory, and power that come through resistance, knowing that power is developed by resistance. Trust that He disciplines those He loves, turning even the worst to deeper dependence on Him. In this way, resentment gives way to surrender and peace.
rejected: Accepting adversity as from God's hand begins with trust in His sovereignty and goodness. When hardship comes, remember that God allows trials for our refinement, not to harm us. Instead of resenting, ask Him for grace to see His purpose. Practice gratitude for His past faithfulness, and recall that even Jesus suffered. Resist the urge to demand explanations; instead, surrender your desire for control. Fellowship with other believers helps, as they can remind you of God's promises. Over time, this perspective shift will help you receive adversity with peace, knowing He works all things for good.

prompt: I'm tempted to give up fighting my own faults because I can't understand why evil exists at all—what's the point?
chosen: It's understandable to feel discouraged when you can't grasp why evil exists. But seeking an intellectual solution to the problem of evil won't cure it—only God's goodness can. Instead of dwelling on sin, which intoxicates the will and paralyzes it with despair, turn your gaze to the universal goodness of God. Reduce the cruel facts of experience to their proportion against His infinite love. Recoil from the study of sin and exult in God's goodness. This disengages your will from evil and gives you a new temper for the contest. Yet do not flatter virtues while concealing the foe in ambush. Evil is real and seeks to deceive; warn yourself of its snares and risk displeasure for the sake of doing right. Pain and sin are real evils, not mere aesthetic additions, and can only be accounted for as necessary means to a greater good. God's Omnipotence is limited only by His own nature, so He cannot call evil good or be beyond good and evil. You don't need to understand why evil exists to fight your faults; you need to trust that God's grace is sufficient. Keep pressing forward, not in your own strength, but in the power of His might.
rejected: It's understandable to feel discouraged when you can't grasp why evil exists. But giving up the fight against your faults won't bring clarity—it will only deepen your struggle. Instead, focus on what you can know: God is good, and He calls you to pursue holiness. The point isn't to solve the mystery of evil but to trust God's wisdom and rely on His grace. Remember that every small victory over sin draws you closer to Him. Don't let the enemy use intellectual doubts to paralyze you. Seek support from mature believers, and keep pressing forward in faith, knowing that God's strength is made perfect in your weakness.

prompt: I have a friend who says all religions are equally true paths to God; how should I respond without being arrogant?
chosen: Respond with humility and respect. Acknowledge that you understand your friend's perspective and that you value the conversation. However, as a religious, you must uphold that the vows of poverty, chastity, and obedience remove every obstacle between God and the religious. Yet you must also examine whether you are a religious in truth or only in name, lest by will or desire you cling to the creature rather than the Creator. So share your belief that Jesus is the way, the truth, and the life, but do so with a heart that has renounced all things. In every occasion of virtue, turn to God for enabling grace, asking and receiving strength more than sufficient. Do not approach God with casual or hasty prayers, but with persistent, importunate faith, for He is not found by pop calls but yields to those who keep asking, seeking, and knocking. Avoid arguing; instead, ask questions and listen genuinely. Emphasize that you're both seeking truth and can disagree without being disagreeable. Focus on building the relationship rather than winning a debate. Pray for wisdom and let your life reflect the love of Christ.
rejected: Respond with humility and respect. Acknowledge that you understand your friend's perspective and that you value the conversation. You can share your own beliefs by saying, 'I believe that Jesus is the way, the truth, and the life, but I respect your right to your own beliefs.' Avoid arguing or trying to prove your friend wrong. Instead, ask questions about what draws them to their view and listen genuinely. Emphasize that you're both seeking truth and that you can disagree without being disagreeable. Focus on building the relationship rather than winning a debate. Pray for wisdom and let your life reflect the love of Christ.

prompt: I suspect a coworker of bad motives without evidence. Is that a sin?
chosen: Suspecting a coworker of bad motives without evidence is a sin that must be confessed and forsaken, not covered or excused. It violates the command to love your neighbor and to think the best of others. Honesty is required for scientific demonstration in Christian Science, so we must be honest about our own sinful suspicions rather than concealing them. Moreover, harboring unforgiveness makes you more guilty and censurable than the one who sinned against you. Saints must forgive as Christ did, dismissing envy, malice, and retaliation and cultivating the spirit that cried, 'Father, forgive them.' Refrain from slander, gossip, backbiting, and fault-finding against neighbors or Church leaders. Mind your own business and seek and speak of the good in others. Instead of harboring suspicion, pray for your coworker and seek to understand their actions in a charitable light. If you have concerns, address them directly and respectfully. Remember that we all have blind spots and that only God knows the heart. Cultivate a habit of assuming good intentions until proven otherwise, and ask God to purify your thoughts.
rejected: Suspecting a coworker of bad motives without evidence is generally considered a sin because it violates the command to love your neighbor as yourself and to think the best of others. It falls under the category of judging, which Jesus warned against. Instead of harboring suspicion, you should pray for your coworker and seek to understand their actions in a charitable light. If you have concerns, address them directly and respectfully. Remember that we all have blind spots and that only God knows the heart. Cultivate a habit of assuming good intentions until proven otherwise, and ask God to purify your thoughts.

prompt: I am a minister and a parishioner asks me to bury her sister though I am not her parish minister—should I comply?
chosen: As a minister, you should consider the pastoral needs of the parishioner and the circumstances. While you are not her parish minister, you can still offer comfort and support. However, it is important to respect the role of the parish minister and coordinate with them. If the parish minister is unavailable or if the family specifically requests you, it may be appropriate to comply, provided it does not cause confusion or conflict. Yet, be mindful that clergy living under the same roof with deaconesses or spiritual sisters is condemned as an occasion of evil and a scandal, even where the persons claim security. So avoid any appearance of impropriety. Also, remember that a faithful servant of Mary who honors her and desires to amend cannot be lost, while neglect of her service endangers salvation. Entrust the situation to her intercession. Furthermore, if you are a member of a confraternity, recall that you joined solely to serve God and Mary and save your soul, and you must not forsake its appointed days for worldly affairs. Ultimately, seek to act with compassion and wisdom, and pray for guidance. The priority is to minister to the grieving family and honor the deceased.
rejected: As a minister, you should consider the pastoral needs of the parishioner and the circumstances. While you are not her parish minister, you can still offer comfort and support. However, it is important to respect the role of the parish minister and coordinate with them. If the parish minister is unavailable or if the family specifically requests you, it may be appropriate to comply, provided it does not cause confusion or conflict. Ultimately, seek to act with compassion and wisdom, and pray for guidance. The priority is to minister to the grieving family and honor the deceased.

prompt: I feel distant from God when I'm busy with work and family—does that mean I'm not faithful?
chosen: Feeling distant from God during busy seasons doesn't mean you're unfaithful. Real trust rises above circumstances and appearances; it hangs solely upon the good pleasure of God, not on visible supports or human reassurance, and hanging upon the invisible God is not hanging upon nothing. Yet faith must be shown in works and spiritual understanding, each working out his own salvation, since another's devotion cannot lessen your liability. Do not multiply explicit offerings or grow anxious about distraction during necessary work. Rather, do all your actions for God—cooking, working, tending family—without fretting that busyness separates you from him. Simplicity in his presence means the ordinary task itself is offered, not a pile of added religious exercises. Rest in the unseen God who holds you.
rejected: Feeling distant from God during busy seasons doesn't automatically mean you're unfaithful. Faithfulness isn't measured by how intensely you feel God's presence; it's shown in steady obedience amid ordinary duties. Work and family are themselves callings, and attending to them can be an act of love toward God. Still, distance often signals that prayer and Scripture have been crowded out, so it's wise to reclaim small, regular moments for God—a brief prayer, a verse, gratitude before meals. Feelings fluctuate; faithfulness is a direction of life rather than a spiritual high. If you keep turning back to God, even weakly, that turning is itself evidence of faith. Talk with a pastor or trusted friend for encouragement.

prompt: How was the canon of the New Testament decided, and does it matter?
chosen: The New Testament canon emerged as early churches recognized writings carrying apostolic authority and read in worship, with criteria including apostolic connection, widespread use, consistency with the rule of faith, and reception; councils later ratified what was already widely accepted. It matters because, though the books differ widely, they possess essential unity and divine authority as God's voice to us. Christ's use of the Old Testament appeals to its abiding spiritual testimony to Himself, independent of questions of authorship and date, without implying any fallibility in Him. Far from being late second-century productions, the books were cited early: Clement of Rome, Ignatius, Polycarp, Papias, Justin, and Irenaeus attest them, and the Muratorian Canon and Peshito Version show they were received as genuine before the close of the second century and were written in the first.
rejected: The New Testament canon emerged gradually as early churches recognized which writings carried apostolic authority and were read in worship. Criteria included apostolic connection, widespread use, consistency with the rule of faith, and reception by the churches. Councils later ratified what had already been widely accepted. Yes, it matters: the canon defines which books the church treats as Scripture, shaping doctrine and practice. Different traditions weight the process differently, and scholars debate details, but the core books were broadly agreed early on. For believers, the canon is a human process that settled which texts function as authoritative.

prompt: Is Jesus just a good moral teacher, or is he somehow the revelation of God himself?
chosen: Jesus is more than a good moral teacher: the New Testament presents him as the definitive revelation of God, in whom God's character is fully shown, and his resurrection vindicated that claim. Christianity is not mere belief or admiration; his healing works demonstrated an ever-operative divine Principle, and his followers are called to heal the sick and cast out error today. We do not prove God's goodness from Nature or History, nor reduce moral judgements to feelings; our knowledge of God rests in the moral consciousness, where true judgements are self-evident deliverances of Reason revealing God's own. Yet Christian ethics rests not on abstraction but on the personal and ethical God, on man's conscience and freedom, and on Christ himself—both the pattern of recreated character and the source who recreates it.
rejected: Jesus is more than a good moral teacher. His teaching is profound, but the New Testament also presents him as the definitive revelation of God—the Word made flesh, the one in whom God's character is fully shown. He forgave sins, accepted worship, and spoke with an authority that startled his hearers. His resurrection vindicated that claim. So Christians don't merely admire his ethics; they worship him as God revealed in a human life. That doesn't diminish his moral teaching—it grounds it, because his life embodies what he taught. Whether one accepts the full claim is a matter of faith, but reducing Jesus to a teacher ignores what he and his earliest followers actually said about him.

prompt: Two ways are set before me, life or death—how do I choose the better?
chosen: Choosing the better way begins with honest self-examination and a daily turning toward life—obedience, love of God, and love of neighbor. The better way starts lower than we like: count yourself as already dead, since you must die some day, and have no other consolation in this perishable life than unceasingly to weep over and detest your offences, since it is not now the time to rejoice but to lament with sincerity of heart. Yet death is not the end of identity; it is a door to a higher state, and the righteous dead are preserved and will be raised. So do not seek bodily health through mere material regimen. Spiritualize thought; forsake the mortal sense of things for Truth, and bodily improvement follows the renewal of the mind.
rejected: Choosing the better way begins with honest self-examination and a deliberate turning toward life. The two ways are not equally neutral options; Scripture consistently urges us to choose life—obedience, love of God, and love of neighbor.
