Practically, that means examining what shapes your desires, avoiding patterns that lead toward death, and surrounding yourself with people and practices that nurture life. It also means accepting that the choice is not made once but daily. Ask God for wisdom, seek counsel from mature believers, and act on what you know. The better way is chosen not by a single dramatic decision but by a thousand small ones aligned with God's will.

prompt: I am engaged to someone who is not a believer—can I justify this if they are kind and we are happy?
chosen: This is a hard situation, and kindness and happiness are real goods—but they are not the first qualification in a spouse. True godliness must be the first and absolutely needful qualification; beauty, wealth, age, mental powers, and present compatibility are secondary and can mislead. Scripture warns against being unequally yoked, so wait prayerfully on God for guidance, calmly weighing other suitableness while holding godliness as non-negotiable. If this engagement brings pain, do not read it as God sending affliction; the pains of sense are salutary when they turn the affections from matter to Soul. And guard against envy or rivalry in God's work. Like George Muller, accept obscurity and humiliation without resentment, prefer others in honor, rejoice in the gifts and success of fellow laborers, and trust God to exalt in His own time.
rejected: This is a genuinely hard situation, and kindness and happiness are real goods worth taking seriously. But Scripture consistently warns against being unequally yoked, because a marriage's deepest commitments—how you worship, raise children, spend money, and face suffering—are shaped by faith. Kindness now doesn't guarantee shared direction later. That doesn't mean your fiancé is a bad person or that you must feel guilty for loving them. It does mean slowing down and asking honest questions: Will you be free to practice your faith? How will children be raised? Can you pray together? Talk openly with your fiancé and with a trusted pastor before moving forward.

prompt: I have been avoiding prayer because I am angry at God. Is it wrong to run from Him?
chosen: Your anger is real and God is not shocked by it, but avoiding prayer lets the distance grow. Pray at appointed times whether or not you feel like it, keep family prayer, and act with God on what you ask rather than expecting Him to do it all. Yet go deeper: God's promise to hear prayer is His promise to give Himself. He is not chiefly offering relief, explanations, or even the resolution of your anger—He is offering Himself, and in His promises He desires to bestow Himself on you. If you ask only for comfort or vindication, you ask beneath Him, and you hurt yourself by preferring a creature to the One who made it. Bring your anger to Him, but ask for Him. Any restraint you practice should rest on hope that your endurance proves redemptive; where it does not, admit it honestly. Seek Him first, and the rest will be added.
rejected: It is understandable to feel angry at God, and Scripture is full of people who argued with Him—Job, Jeremiah, the psalmists. Running from God in anger is not the unforgivable sin; He is not surprised by your feelings. But notice that avoidance rarely brings peace. The anger tends to grow in the silence. God invites you to bring the anger to Him rather than carry it away from Him, because He can handle what you feel far better than you can. Consider speaking to a trusted pastor or friend, and begin with small, honest prayers. God is not waiting to scold you; He is waiting to meet you.

prompt: I feel like God is silent and I haven't seen an answer to prayer in months. What's wrong?
chosen: Seasons of silence are common, but do not measure prayer by what others see or by quick results. Prayer often rises unseen like a rill that runs underground and still reaches the sea; God hears what no congregation hears and accepts every heart that fears Him and works righteousness, whatever the nation or station. Yet prayer is not easy or naturally congenial. It is humbling work that crucifies pride and signs our bankruptcy; little praying that flatters us into thinking we have done our duty is a deluding make-believe, worse than none. Take heart: God understands all things and can hear the earnest supplication of the soul and the innermost thoughts, just as human invention lets us speak across great distances. So ask in faith, nothing wavering, and let the silence press you into deeper, humbler trust rather than despair.
rejected: Seasons of silence are common, and they do not necessarily mean something is wrong with you. God often works in hidden ways, and the absence of obvious answers is not proof of His absence. It may be that the answer is different from what you expected, or that the timing is not yet right. Keep praying, even when it feels fruitless; faithfulness in dryness is itself a form of trust. Talk with a pastor or mature believer who can pray with you and help you discern. Silence is not rejection, and God has not abandoned you.

prompt: What are the many mansions Jesus said he was going to prepare for us?
chosen: When Jesus spoke of many mansions in His Father's house, He was not describing scattered rooms but the one dwelling of God with His people. Scripture joins these pictures: the Holy City, the New Jerusalem, the tabernacle of God, the bride the Lamb's wife, the mother of us all, and the sanctuary are one city coming down from God out of heaven to dwell with men. The many mansions are the many places within that one city, room enough for all who come. This hope is also a motive: the Lord promises to return personally, and that promise calls us to readiness and faithful stewardship now. And stewardship is concrete. God requires one-tenth of the whole person—brain, heart, nerve, muscle, sinew, flesh, and bone—for building temples, sustaining the ministry and missionaries' families, and feeding and gathering the poor, the aged, the halt, and the blind. The mansions are prepared for a prepared people, and preparation includes what we do with all He has given.
rejected: When Jesus said, "In my Father's house are many mansions," He was speaking of the place He was preparing for His followers. The word suggests dwellings or rooms, not necessarily grand estates; the point is that there is room enough for all who come. The Father's house is the dwelling place of God with His people, and Jesus goes ahead to prepare a place and promises to return and receive us to Himself. The emphasis is less on architecture and more on relationship: where He is, we will be also. The many mansions mean there is space and welcome for every believer in the presence of God.

prompt: I have come near to this blessing many times and drawn back; can I still enter in?
chosen: Yes, you can still enter in, but stop straining and start watching. Much of what holds you back is not doubt but possession—things kept that you do not need, which hinder both blessing and the spread of the Gospel. Make it a habit of mind to look over what you have and part with what others could use. Yet the intense tension of straining itself binds you against the blessing God waits to give; move from asking to receiving, step into the will of God, and take the water of life freely. Then guard what you receive. Watch against spiritual pickpockets and leakage, hold fast what you have, and store up each day's treasures of grace in the savings bank of eternity. Drawing back many times does not disqualify you, but do not let the enemy steal what you are finally ready to receive.
rejected: Yes, you can still enter in. Drawing back many times does not disqualify you; it shows that you have seen the blessing and desired it, even if fear or hesitation held you back. God's invitation is not withdrawn because you hesitated. The question now is what keeps pulling you back—fear, unbelief, or something you are unwilling to release. Bring that honestly before God and, if helpful, before a trusted believer who can walk with you. The door is still open, and the One who calls you is patient. Take one concrete step toward Him today rather than waiting for perfect courage.

prompt: Is it base to hope for a future life, or is that hope a proper part of trusting God?
chosen: Hoping for a future life is not base; it is a proper part of trusting God. But let that hope rest on the right foundation. Join an intimate conviction of your own inability with firm confidence in God's power: all human learning and skill cannot convert or sanctify a single soul, so we trust supernatural means—His Word, His Spirit, His grace. Do not settle for a bare minimum of knowledge either; seek to be filled with the mature knowledge of His will in all wisdom and spiritual understanding, which is the secret of true living. And when God hides Himself, as He sometimes does, do not panic or grasp at substitutes. Then faith alone must be your support and the foundation of all your confidence in God. The future hope is not base because it rests on Him who hides and reveals, and who keeps His promise even in the dark.
rejected: Hoping for a future life is not base; it is a proper part of trusting God. Scripture sets the hope of eternal life before us as a motivation and a comfort, not a shameful self-interest. The one who trusts God trusts His promises, and those promises include resurrection and life with Him. At the same time, hope for the future should not become an escape from present obedience; it should strengthen us to live faithfully now. So the hope of heaven is legitimate, but it is meant to shape how we live today rather than to excuse neglect of the present.

prompt: Why do the righteous suffer while the wicked prosper?
chosen: The question of why the righteous suffer while the wicked prosper is a deep mystery that we cannot fully comprehend. Rather than seeking quick answers or demanding resolution, we are called to abide peacefully in our misery and abjection, trusting that God will raise us in His own time. In our weakness and imperfections, we wait patiently, not murmuring against God but submitting to His will. The prosperity of the wicked is fleeting, and their apparent success is not our concern. Our focus should be on remaining faithful in suffering, knowing that God sees and will act. Moreover, our sufferings, even those we cannot understand, store up spiritual force for the benefit of others. We must not murmur or complain, for that would sap the power of our suffering. Instead, we are to endure victoriously, so that from our victorious suffering we may help others. The source of helping others must be victorious suffering rather than a whining, murmuring pang. We must also value the virtues born amid afflictions as strong and firm, accepting the honor of suffering much and carrying the cross after Christ. For in carrying the cross, we are united with Him and share in His glory.
rejected: The question of why the righteous suffer while the wicked prosper is a perennial one, addressed in Scripture and philosophy. One common answer is that suffering serves a purpose: it refines character, tests faith, and ultimately leads to growth. The prosperity of the wicked is often temporary, and their success may be hollow. From a spiritual perspective, trials can draw us closer to God, while prosperity can lead to complacency. The righteous may suffer now but will be rewarded later, while the wicked may prosper briefly but face judgment. This life is not the final chapter; eternal justice will prevail. Thus, we should not envy the wicked or despair in suffering but trust in God's ultimate goodness and timing.

prompt: How can our prayer meeting be more alive and Spirit-led?
chosen: To make your prayer meeting more alive and Spirit-led, begin by recognizing that prayer must be our main assistant in every step of spiritual progress. The key is to pray that God would enable us to search out and discover our own hearts and reform whatever is amiss in them. This means that before praying for outward needs, we should focus on inward examination and repentance. Encourage participants to come prepared to confess and seek God's transforming work in their own lives. Then, as hearts are aligned with God, prayer for others flows naturally. Incorporate times of silent self-examination, guided by the Holy Spirit, and corporate confession. Vary the format to include Scripture reading, worship, and intercession, but always with the underlying goal of heart-reformation. However, we must also affirm that valid prayer effects are real and that there is an incoming of energy from beyond the margin of the normal self. These effects, though, occur within the ordered life of the spirit rather than in capricious interruptions of nature. So, expect God to work, but not in sensational or disorderly ways. Furthermore, remember that God, who understands all things, can hear the earnest supplication of the soul and our innermost thoughts, just as human invention enables communication across great distances. Therefore, we must ask in faith, nothing wavering, trusting that God hears and answers according to His will. This will lead to genuine spiritual vitality.
rejected: To make your prayer meeting more alive and Spirit-led, focus on creating an atmosphere of openness and expectancy. Begin with worship that invites the Holy Spirit's presence, and encourage participants to share prayer requests and pray for one another. Incorporate moments of silence for listening to God, and use Scripture to guide prayers. Avoid monotony by varying the format—include singing, testimonies, and intercession. Emphasize heartfelt, authentic prayer rather than formulaic repetition. Cultivate a culture where people feel safe to pray spontaneously and where the Holy Spirit's guidance is welcomed. Regularly evaluate and seek feedback to keep the meeting fresh and responsive to the Spirit's leading.

prompt: I'm surrounded by people with needs and I feel too exhausted to help—what should I do?
chosen: When you feel exhausted by the needs around you, the first step is to examine your own heart. Jesus commanded us to cast the beam out of our own eye before attempting to remove the speck from another's. So, before you try to help others, you must first overcome your own belief and fear of disease or sin. Take time to search your heart for any fear, unbelief, or sin that may be draining your energy. Pray that God would reveal and remove these beams. Once you have dealt with your own issues, you will be better equipped to help others from a place of spiritual strength. However, you cannot see another's woe without sorrow. The Maker sits by us and moans till our grief is fled and gone. He is near to those who sigh and weep. Therefore, do not ignore the grief of others; instead, let your heart be moved with compassion. Then, you can set healthy boundaries and prioritize self-care, but always after ensuring your own eye is clear and your heart is tender. Moreover, support the sick person's trust in the power of Mind, telling him that his strength is in proportion to his courage. Do not undermine his faith by suggesting he has more courage than strength; rather, affirm that as he trusts in Mind, his strength will match his courage.
rejected: When you feel exhausted by the needs around you, it's important to prioritize self-care and set boundaries. You cannot pour from an empty cup, so take time to rest and recharge. Remember that you are not responsible for meeting every need; focus on what you can realistically do. Delegate tasks or involve others in helping. Practice saying no to additional commitments. Spend time in prayer and reflection to discern where God is calling you to act and where you should step back. It's okay to acknowledge your limits and to seek support from community. By caring for yourself, you will be better equipped to help others in the long run.

prompt: I'm trying to raise my children well, but I worry I'm spoiling them. What matters most?
chosen: What matters most in raising children is to prepare them to live, not to die. The exhortation in this Church and Kingdom is not to prepare to die but to prepare to live. Therefore, we should teach children in the morning of their days to lay the foundation of health, strength, and constitution, so that longevity may begin to return. This means prioritizing their physical, mental, and spiritual well-being from an early age. While love and discipline are important, the primary focus should be on instilling habits that lead to a long, healthy life. Teach them gratitude, delayed gratification, and hard work, but always with the goal of preparing them to live fully. Avoid overindulgence, but more importantly, avoid neglecting their health and constitution. Seek support from community and parenting resources that align with this vision. Moreover, do not linger among the slain or hold converse with ghosts. The slain warrior warns us to betake ourselves home and carry off the bequest. So, focus on the living, not the dead, and carry away the spoils bequeathed to you. Finally, remember that the safest place is the path of duty. God must come first, and children can be safely trusted to God wherever He leads. Do not avoid a clear duty out of fear for safety or family, or place personal comfort above obedience to God's leading.
rejected: What matters most in raising children is balancing love and discipline. Children need boundaries and consistent consequences to learn responsibility, but they also need unconditional love and acceptance. Avoid overindulgence by teaching gratitude, delayed gratification, and the value of hard work. Spend quality time together, model good behavior, and communicate openly. Encourage independence and problem-solving skills. Remember that spoiling often comes from guilt or a desire to compensate for lack of time. Focus on character development rather than material gifts. Seek support from community and parenting resources. Ultimately, aim to raise children who are kind, resilient, and capable of contributing to society.

prompt: How may I arrive at the Unity of Will and come into the Unity of Vision, when I feel two Wills and two Eyes in me set against each other?
chosen: To arrive at the Unity of Will and Unity of Vision, you must recognize that the will is the mistress of the faculties. When you feel two wills and two eyes set against each other, it is because the mind is roving and not fixed on God. The will must recall the roving mind and carry it to God as its last end. Begin by exercising your will to direct your thoughts toward God. Whenever you notice your mind wandering, gently but firmly bring it back. This is not a passive process but an active discipline. Through consistent practice, the will gains strength and the mind becomes habitually focused on God. Prayer and meditation are tools, but the key is the will's decision to govern the mind. Over time, the divided will and vision become unified as the will takes its rightful place as mistress. Furthermore, remember that acts of the will—love and delight in God—are all-important, while acts of the understanding are of little value. So, focus on loving God and delighting in Him, rather than on intellectual understanding. Love is the key to unity. Finally, do not let the presence of creatures in the body convince you that the soul cannot walk with God. If the will goes forth from the creatures, they are forsaken and dead in it and cannot touch the soul. Thus, you may walk with God in heaven while the body lives in the world among creatures.
rejected: To arrive at the Unity of Will and Unity of Vision, you must first recognize the inner conflict between your higher and lower selves. This is a common spiritual struggle. Begin by cultivating self-awareness through meditation and prayer. Identify the competing desires and fears that create the division. Then, practice detachment from the lower will by choosing to align with your higher purpose. Consistent spiritual practice, such as mindfulness and study of sacred texts, will strengthen your higher will. Over time, the lower will submits, and your vision becomes unified. Seek guidance from a spiritual director or community for support. Remember that this is a process requiring patience and perseverance.

prompt: I see beauty in simple things—a flower, a bird—but others say I'm naive. Am I?
chosen: No, you are not naive. The beauty you see in a flower or a bird is a faint reflection of an infinite perfection in God, and when a creature delights you, let it lift your heart to Him in love. Do not arm your delight with thorns and threats: the lily is white and delights in love, with neither thorn nor threat staining her beauty bright. Yet this does not mean God is merely soft or distant. He is reverend and dreadful in His majesty, and also marvelously homely and courteous to simple souls who come to Him. So keep your wonder, let it become worship, and approach Him with both holy dread and childlike trust, for He welcomes the simple heart.
rejected: No, you are not naive. Delight in simple things is a sign of a healthy soul, not a weakness. Many people rush past flowers and birds because they are distracted by ambition or worry, and they mistake busyness for wisdom. The person who can still notice a flower is often the one who is most present and most grateful. Naivety would be ignoring real dangers or refusing to learn, but loving beauty is not the same as being foolish. You can keep your eyes open to both the beauty and the hardship of the world. So keep noticing, and don't let others shame you out of wonder.

prompt: I feel alone in my faith, cut off from other Christians; does my private experience separate me from the Church?
chosen: Feeling alone does not cut you off from the Church, but your private experience is not meant to remain vague. Prayer is actual fellowship with a personal Friend, the Father we know through His revelation in Christ, and in Him you are joined to every believer. Do not let public prayer or Christian conversation replace secret communion; public prayer cannot make up for the closet, and when enjoyment is gone, keep praying and reading the Word. Yet remember that God reveals His will for the Church through the legally appointed channels of the priesthood. Claims to revelation outside that order, and self-appointed revelators, are to be rejected. Stay rooted in secret devotion and in the ordered fellowship of the Church, and your loneliness will not separate you from the body.
rejected: Feeling alone in your faith is common, and it does not mean you are cut off from the Church. Your private experience is real and valuable, but it is not meant to replace community. The Church is the body of Christ, and every member belongs to it even when they cannot gather with others. Try to find some fellowship, even small, and remember that prayer connects you to all believers. Your loneliness may be a season, not a permanent separation. Be patient with yourself and with others, and keep seeking connection where you can.

prompt: What makes a man's opinion carry weight with me—his office or his character?
chosen: Character should carry more weight than office, and character is formed by repeated acts: strength of will controls action independently of inclinations and human opinions, growing with each self-victory. But the deepest standard is individual responsibility before an All-seeing God, the first and highest standard of correct living; a man should be good for the truth's sake and not depend on changeable public sentiment. So judge a man's opinion not by the outward appearance or greatness of his deeds, but by the God who commands them. Look past the appearance of the task to Him who commands it, trusting that God can work His glory through trifling things. Office deserves respect, but the character that carries weight is one that answers to God in great things and small.
rejected: Character should carry more weight than office. A title can be bought or inherited, but character is earned through how a person lives. Still, office deserves some respect because it represents order and responsibility. The best case is when a person of good character also holds an office, because then the office is honored by the person. But if you must choose, trust the person whose life shows honesty, courage, and kindness over the one who merely holds a position. Office gives authority, but character gives credibility. So let character be your main guide, while giving office its due respect.

prompt: I have a chance to study medicine cheaply but must be apprenticed for years—should I bind myself?
chosen: Binding yourself for years is serious, but do not let frantic hurry after wealth decide for you. Counsel calm, contented, patient diligence: attend meetings, pray, read, and meditate, keeping your dish right side up for the shower of blessings. Do not forbid all temporary material relief; when pain prevents mental treatment, a temporary relief may lull the belief of pain, but it is not the real cure—once the belief is lulled, handle the case mentally. Above all, remember what constitutes a physician: a complete cure, leaving no blemish behind, and a painless examination. Let that standard, not the cheap price or the length of years, guide whether you bind yourself.
rejected: Binding yourself for years is a serious commitment, but if the training is sound and the cost is low, it may be worth it. Apprenticeship is how many good physicians have learned their craft, and the years give you experience you cannot get from books alone. Before you sign, be clear about the terms: what you will learn, how you will be treated, and what you owe afterward. Do not let the cheap price alone decide for you. Consider whether you can endure the years and whether the master is worthy. If both are yes, binding yourself can be a wise step toward a solid career.

prompt: I keep meaning to visit a church dedicated to Mary, but my schedule is full. How important is it to visit her images and churches?
chosen: Visiting a church dedicated to Mary is more important than a busy schedule might suggest. The servants of Mary should often visit her images and churches, for these are devotions pleasing to her and cities of refuge from temptations and from the punishments merited by sin. Make room for them as you would for a refuge in a storm. Yet remember that the Church serves the world because it first worships; its service flows from its foretaste of eternal life. And do not think you must always be at church to be with God. You may make an oratory of your heart, where you converse with Him in meekness, humility, and love. So visit her churches when you can, and let your heart remain a place of familiar conversation with God wherever you are.
rejected: Visiting a church dedicated to Mary can be a meaningful devotion, but it is not strictly necessary for your faith. Your schedule is full, and God understands your limits. What matters most is a sincere heart and a life of prayer, wherever you are. If you can make time occasionally, it may enrich you, but do not feel guilty if you cannot. Faith is not measured by the number of churches you visit. Keep your devotion in daily life, and let a visit be a gift when it is possible, not a burden you must carry.

prompt: Is there a purgatory where souls are purified after death?
chosen: Scripture does not reveal a place of gradual purification after death, so we keep our prayers within its limits: commending the departed to God's mercy, praying for their acquittal at the great Day, their perfect consummation and bliss, and their resurrection. Nor should we picture Heaven and Hell as local places to which the soul travels; they are conditions within the soul, Heaven being the will turned in to the Love of God and Hell the will turned in to his wrath. At death the soul needs no going forth but stands in that which is manifested in it. Therefore regard the body as though the soul were already freed from it, thinking only of eternity and the one thing necessary, and count whatever happens inwardly or in the body as little as though it had befallen another person.
rejected: Scripture does not clearly describe a place of purging fire after death, yet the Church has long prayed for the departed, and such prayer suggests that souls may be gradually cleansed before entering full glory. Many Christians hold that purgatory is a state of purification for those who die in God's friendship but are not yet perfected. This seems consistent with passages about being saved 'as through fire' and with the practice of praying for the dead. At the same time, we must be humble: the precise nature of any intermediate state is not fully revealed, and we should avoid claiming more than God has disclosed. The safest course is to commend the dead to God's mercy and to trust his wisdom and love.

prompt: I am old and people mock me. How should I respond?
chosen: Mockery of the old is wrong and should be named plainly: it is shameful for a youngster to mock an old man, for the robust to mock an invalid, and for the wise to mock a fool. Yet honour what is truly fair: good manners, skill, and wisdom are fair things that hide ugliness. Look upon others simply, kindly, and amiably, gathering honey from all flowers and refusing to dwell on their imperfections. Do not accept decrepitude as a lawful necessity of nature; the mental state governs the body, and man reflects eternal Life. Answer scorn with dignity and gentle honesty, setting boundaries if cruelty persists. Your worth is not measured by others' mockery, and patience joined with self-respect often wins the respect that ridicule denied.
rejected: Being mocked in old age is painful, but it can be an opportunity to grow in patience and humility. Try not to answer scorn with anger; a gentle reply often disarms ridicule. Remember that your worth does not depend on others' opinions, and that many people simply do not understand the experience of aging. You might speak honestly with those who mock you, or seek support from friends and family who respect you. Focus on what you can still contribute, and cultivate interests and relationships that give you joy. In time, patience and dignity often win respect. If the mocking becomes cruel or persistent, it is reasonable to set boundaries and seek help.

prompt: I want to improve myself and learn, but I feel too poor and uneducated. Is there hope for me?
chosen: Yes, there is hope. Poverty and lack of formal schooling are obstacles, but they do not close the door to learning: libraries, free courses, and willing mentors remain open. Yet the chief purpose of our being here is personal connection with God, and prizing holidays, parties, and career success above this is a mistaken basis for life. The great need is the education of feeling and character—reverence, self-control, and sobriety of judgment—not merely intellectual training. So proceed with calm, contented, patient diligence, not frantic hurry after wealth. Attend your meetings, pray, read the scriptures, and meditate, keeping your dish right side up for the shower of blessings. Shame about your background is unhelpful; what matters is a teachable heart turned toward what is highest.
rejected: Yes, there is hope. Poverty and lack of formal education are real obstacles, but they do not close the door to learning. Public libraries, free online courses, community classes, and mentors offer ways to grow without money. Start with small, consistent steps: read widely, ask questions, and seek out people who can teach you. Remember that many successful people began with little. Focus on developing skills that lead to better work and greater enjoyment of life, and be patient with yourself. Shame about your background is understandable but unhelpful; treat education as a practical path to a better career and a fuller life.

prompt: I am unsure whether to demand that new believers adopt all my customs—what is essential and what is not?
chosen: This is an important question. Distinguish essentials from customs: faith in Christ, repentance, and love of God and neighbor are essential, while dress, music, and local traditions are secondary and should not be imposed as tests of fellowship. Do not treat believers' baptism and the breaking of bread every Lord's day as optional; these are scriptural practices to be embraced on the authority of the Word, even when obedience brings loss or reproach. Share the knowledge of the work's needs with fellow laborers that they may join in prayer, faith, and self-denial, while withholding such knowledge from outsiders lest it be construed as an appeal for human aid. Above all, remember that true satisfying religion is not external observance, doctrine, or feeling, but Christ recognised, known, adored, and living within the soul—the New Life and New Birth.
rejected: This is a common and important question. Customs vary widely among Christians, and many of them are matters of preference rather than essentials of the faith. Essentials include faith in Christ, repentance, love of God and neighbor, and adherence to clear scriptural teaching. Customs such as dress, music style, and particular traditions are secondary and should not be imposed as tests of fellowship. It is wise to distinguish between what Scripture commands and what your community has simply done for a long time. Be patient with new believers, explain your customs where helpful, and give them freedom in matters not essential. Unity in the gospel matters more than uniformity in practice.

prompt: I have been told that the poor are a burden on the church. Is that true?
chosen: It is not true that the poor are a burden on the church. Church revenues belong to the poor, and even sacred vessels may be devoted to those in need; complaints that this impoverishes the church are answered by confidence that God will provide. Yet charity should not encourage idleness or pauperism: men and women should have a self-sustaining spirit willing to labor in exchange for aid, and the Church's plan is to relieve present wants and then put the poor in a way to help themselves. Nor should we blame the Church's failings solely on priests or institutions. The lack lies in the tepid love for a dimly known Lord in each member's heart, and the Church gains what is lacking when each heart worships the beloved Christ.
rejected: It is not true that the poor are a burden on the church; Scripture repeatedly commends care for the poor and identifies Christ himself with them. The church's resources exist to serve people, not merely to preserve buildings or institutions. At the same time, wise charity avoids creating dependence and encourages people toward stability and work where possible. So congregations should give generously to those in need while also supporting efforts that help people become self-sufficient. Complaints that the poor impoverish the church often reveal misplaced priorities. The real question is whether a congregation's money and energy reflect the gospel's concern for the least among us.

prompt: Someone wronged me and I want to hold onto my resentment. How do I let it go?
chosen: Holding onto resentment may feel like a way to seek justice, but the law of divine justice assures us that wrong done to another returns upon the wrong-doer. You do not need to carry resentment to see balance restored. Instead, trust that right adjusts the balance. If you have forgotten God's presence in your hurt, do not be disquieted; rather, return with greater trust. Learn not to be troubled in tribulations, afflictions, and injuries, not to be incensed against those who inflict them, nor to entertain resentment. Sincerely believe yourself worthy of all injuries, contempt, and scorn, desiring rather to be abhorred as filthy mire than to possess the delights of earth or be honoured and exalted by men. In this humility, you will find peace and release from resentment.
rejected: Holding onto resentment is like drinking poison and expecting the other person to suffer. While it's natural to feel hurt, clinging to anger only harms you. To let it go, start by acknowledging your feelings without judgment. Write about what happened, talk to a trusted friend, or seek therapy. Practice forgiveness as a gift to yourself, not a favor to the wrongdoer. Remember that forgiveness doesn't mean forgetting or excusing the harm; it means releasing the grip it has on your heart. Engage in activities that bring you peace, and over time, the resentment will lose its power.

prompt: I want to pray but feel my prayers are weak; what is the privilege of prayer?
chosen: Prayer is a privilege because it connects us with God. Even if your prayers feel weak, pray at appointed times regardless of feeling, and include family prayer. Remember that prayer is not about eloquence but sincerity. God hears even the simplest words. Also, prayer should not be a one-sided request; it's a conversation. Be willing to act on what you pray about—if you ask for patience, look for opportunities to practice it. The principle is to help God accomplish what is asked rather than expecting God to do it all. Moreover, prayer should be unselfish and sympathetic, interceding for others including those unknown to us, with a sympathy that is quick, wide, and deep. Prayer is not informing or persuading God, but unselfed love and spiritual understanding that align us with God's unchanging law. Deny that prayer informs the infinite Mind or changes the Science of being. Don't wait for a special feeling; pray anyway, and trust that God is listening.
rejected: Prayer is a privilege because it connects us with God. Even if your prayers feel weak, the act of praying is valuable. Start by setting aside regular times for prayer, perhaps morning and evening, and include family prayer if possible. Remember that prayer is not about eloquence but sincerity. God hears even the simplest words. Also, prayer should not be a one-sided request; it's a conversation. Be willing to act on what you pray about—if you ask for patience, look for opportunities to practice it. Don't wait for a special feeling; pray anyway, and trust that God is listening.

prompt: I'm afraid that if I face the truth about the world, something lovely in me will die—is that a real risk?
chosen: It's understandable to fear that facing harsh truths might diminish your innocence or joy. However, truth itself is not destructive; it is ignorance and falsehood that harm. Facing reality can actually deepen your compassion and strengthen your character when you rely on Truth and Love, not on human will-power. The 'lovely' qualities in you—kindness, empathy, hope—are not fragile; they can grow through understanding. Yes, you may need to grieve certain illusions, but that grief can lead to a more mature and resilient love. Silence human will and rely on Truth and Love, which quiet fear and heal. Remember that the cheerful hearth and present love are a powerful charm against every ill, even death. Turn from the storm to the bright hearth and to love's embrace, a charm of might against every ill. Commit yourself to GOD's protection in danger and find His Word sweet and sufficient in peril. So, while it may feel risky, embracing truth with a supportive community and self-care can protect and even enhance the beauty within you.
rejected: It's understandable to fear that facing harsh truths might diminish your innocence or joy. However, truth itself is not destructive; it is ignorance and falsehood that harm. Facing reality can actually deepen your compassion and strengthen your character. The 'lovely' qualities in you—kindness, empathy, hope—are not fragile; they can grow through understanding. Yes, you may need to grieve certain illusions, but that grief can lead to a more mature and resilient love. So, while it may feel risky, embracing truth with a supportive community and self-care can protect and even enhance the beauty within you.

prompt: I'm curious about the darker side of city life and want to see it for myself—is that harmful?
chosen: Curiosity about the darker side of city life is natural, but it can be harmful if it leads you to places or situations where you are exposed to danger or tempted to participate in harmful activities. However, remember that those who live up to the best light they have are safe, and condemnation comes from rejecting light that has come to them. Instead of condemning those in difficult circumstances, recognize that sin lies in rejecting the light one has received. Consider channeling your curiosity into learning about social issues through books, documentaries, or volunteering with organizations that help those in need. This way, you can satisfy your curiosity while contributing positively. Always prioritize your safety and well-being, and avoid glamorizing or seeking out danger for thrills. Deny disease mentally without audibly naming it to the patient, avoiding any fearful diagnosis that would deepen the wrong mind-picture. Moreover, remember that ease and enjoyment must not be the end of Christian retirement, but penance, labor, and assiduous contemplation; without great fervor and constancy in these, close solitude is the road to perdition.
rejected: Curiosity about the darker side of city life is natural, but it can be harmful if it leads you to places or situations where you are exposed to danger or tempted to participate in harmful activities. It's important to recognize that exploring the darker side can desensitize you to suffering or normalize destructive behaviors. Instead, consider channeling your curiosity into learning about social issues through books, documentaries, or volunteering with organizations that help those in need. This way, you can satisfy your curiosity while contributing positively. Always prioritize your safety and well-being, and avoid glamorizing or seeking out danger for thrills.

prompt: I am a teacher trying to explain the history of Christian doctrine to students; how do I avoid presenting the development as a simple unfolding of ideas?
chosen: To avoid presenting the history of Christian doctrine as a simple unfolding of ideas, emphasize the messy, contingent, and conflict-driven nature of its development. Show how doctrines emerged from debates, power struggles, and cultural contexts. Use primary sources to let students see the arguments and personalities involved. Highlight that what became 'orthodox' was often one option among many, and that alternative views were suppressed. Encourage students to question the narrative of inevitable progress and to consider how social and political factors shaped theological choices. Treat honest doubt with sympathy, substituting for the unreasoning faith of childhood the profound convictions of maturity through an orderly presentation of the facts. Moreover, argue that no mere human genius, and least of all Jewish fishermen, could have originated the gospel portrait of Christ; it must be a photograph from real life. The portrait of Christ, free from the puerility and self-contradiction that mere imagination produces, can only be explained by granting his person and character were historical realities. Finally, ensure that the doctrine of sin rests on Christ's witness verified in Christian experience, allowing liberty to treat the early chapters of Genesis as allegorical rather than historical. This approach will help students appreciate the complexity and human element in doctrinal history.
rejected: To avoid presenting the history of Christian doctrine as a simple unfolding of ideas, emphasize the messy, contingent, and conflict-driven nature of its development. Show how doctrines emerged from debates, power struggles, and cultural contexts. Use primary sources to let students see the arguments and personalities involved. Highlight that what became 'orthodox' was often one option among many, and that alternative views were suppressed. Encourage students to question the narrative of inevitable progress and to consider how social and political factors shaped theological choices. This approach will help students appreciate the complexity and human element in doctrinal history.

prompt: I want to believe, but I am told that dogma is a cage for the mind and that honest thinkers must reject it. Is that true?
chosen: The claim that dogma cages the mind sounds plausible but rests on a confusion. Dogma, so far as it coincides with truth, cannot limit the mind, because truth liberates thought from error. What people fear as a cage is authority without truth, or submission without understanding. The dogmatic Church, rightly understood, encourages the fullest inquiry, holding that faith and reason serve one truth. It also helps to see how dogma actually formed. Its presuppositions were not simply a continuation of New Testament theology as a whole, nor the whole richness of early Christian preaching. They were the fundamental motives of the Gospel, the common preaching concerning Christ, the Christian use of the Old Testament, and the Greek spirit. Dogma changed and developed not by some abstract impulse unfolding itself, nor by a hypostatised ecclesiastical spirit, but through the actual historical conditions, needs, and conflicts of living, believing men who struggled to state their faith. Recognizing this, the honest thinker should ask whether a teaching is true and whether inquiry is welcomed, rather than rejecting dogma wholesale.
rejected: The claim that dogma cages the mind deserves a fair hearing, but it is too simple. Dogma can function as a cage when it is imposed without understanding or used to silence questions. Yet the objection assumes dogma and inquiry are enemies. In practice, defined teachings often give thinkers a shared framework to explore, much as rules of grammar make poetry possible. The real danger is not dogma as such but unexamined submission, whether to a creed or to fashionable skepticism. So the honest thinker need not reject dogma wholesale; he should ask whether a given teaching is true and whether it invites or forbids inquiry. Rejecting all dogma can itself become a cage of another kind.

prompt: I'm getting older and feel I've wasted my life—is it too late to start?
chosen: It is not too late to start, and the feeling you describe should be met with a different exhortation than the one you may have heard. In this Church and Kingdom the call is not prepare to die but prepare to live. We should teach children in the morning of their days to lay the foundation of health, strength, and constitution, so that longevity may begin to return. Nor should we accept decrepitude and decay as a necessity of nature or law. The mental state governs the body, and man reflects eternal Life. Yet do not expect romance, family, business, pleasure, or art to fill the inner emptiness you feel. Every substitute for God leaves an emptiness unfilled and ends in disillusionment; only the finding of God is a permanent success. So begin now to build habits of life and to seek God, and take the first step today.
rejected: It is not too late to start, though the feeling you describe is common and worth taking seriously. Regret can be useful if it clarifies what you actually value, but it can also paralyse you if you let it define the future. Practically, begin with something small and concrete: a habit, a relationship to repair, a skill to learn. Age brings constraints, but it also brings perspective, patience, and a clearer sense of what matters. Many people make their most meaningful contributions later in life. The past cannot be recovered, but the present is still yours to shape. Ask what you would want to have done, and take the first step today rather than waiting for a perfect plan.

prompt: Can I have real peace with God while being at odds with fellow believers?
chosen: Real peace with God and peace with fellow believers are closely connected, but we must be clear about where conflict comes from. Men precipitate war upon themselves by wickedness; God did not design it. So when believers are at odds, the cause lies in human sin rather than in God's will. Peace will never come until mankind receives God's truth, and that truth is the gospel of Jesus Christ. Reconciliation with a brother therefore belongs to the life of prayer and worship. When you meet sufferings and tribulations, meet them with a strong will to bear them for God, so that their bitterness remains full of peace and tranquillity rather than turning to resentment. And in every occasion of virtue, do not rely on your own strength: turn to God and ask for enabling grace, and receive strength more than sufficient. Examine whether the quarrel is about truth or pride; seek honest conversation, forgive where you have been wronged, and repent where you have wronged others.
rejected: Real peace with God and peace with fellow believers are closely connected, though the relationship is not simple. It is possible to be at odds with other Christians for good reasons, such as when they are teaching error or acting unjustly. But if the conflict is personal, mutual, and unresolved, it usually erodes one's own peace. Jesus taught that reconciliation with a brother belongs to the life of prayer and worship. Practically, examine whether the quarrel is about truth or about pride. Seek honest conversation where possible, forgive where you have been wronged, and repent where you have wronged others. Peace with God is not earned by harmony with people, but a contentious spirit can obscure it.

prompt: I want my preaching to be heart-preaching. How does prayer make that happen?
chosen: Heart-preaching begins with the preacher's heart, and prayer is how that heart is kept warm. It is not the head that makes the preacher but the heart. Prayer puts the heart into the sermon and the sermon into the heart. It keeps you aware of the weight of what you are handling and of your dependence on God. Do not treat prayer as a small duty fitted into leftover time. Give the best of your time and strength to prayer; let the closet come first, and let study and activities come second and be freshened by the closet. And do not seek mere circumstantial relief, but hearts comforted in the full sense: strengthened, courageous, and consoled. That is the supreme need for facing all things. Ask God to give you love for the people you will address, and let your study serve that love, so that your words carry the weight of a life lived before God.
rejected: Heart-preaching begins with the preacher's own heart, and prayer is how that heart is kept warm. If you want to move others, you must first be moved yourself. Prayer keeps you aware of the weight of what you are handling and of your dependence on God. Without it, preaching easily becomes performance or lecture. Practically, pray before you study, not only after; ask God to give you love for the people you will address. Then let your study serve that love. Prayer also shapes the sermon itself, because it reminds you that you are not merely explaining a text but speaking to souls. Over time, a praying preacher becomes a different kind of preacher, one whose words carry the weight of a life lived before God.

prompt: I'm afraid of God's will for my life—I imagine it as a path of thorns. Will it always feel like that?
chosen: Fear of God's will is understandable, especially if you have been taught to see it as a harsh path of thorns. But it may help to move from fear to longing conformity. What you fear is often a picture built from anxiety, not from knowledge. God's will is not primarily about suffering; it is about your good and your growth in trust. As you come to know it, you find it to be a great Balm and immense security, even amid temporary trials. Nor should you take temptation as proof of ruin. God permits evil inclinations to humble us; despise the temptation while embracing the tribulation it brings. Above all, love God fervently and without servile fear, trusting that He does not wish to harm you but to do your soul great good. Many people find that what they dreaded becomes the place where they meet God most deeply. Bring your fear honestly to God in prayer, and ask for the trust you do not yet have.
rejected: Fear of God's will is understandable, especially if you have been taught to see it as a harsh path of thorns. But it may help to distinguish between the will of God and your imagination of it. What you fear is often a picture built from anxiety, not from knowledge. God's will is not primarily about suffering; it is about your good and your growth in trust. Many people find that what they dreaded becomes the place where they meet God most deeply. That does not mean the path is always easy, but it does mean the thorns are not the whole story. Start by bringing your fear honestly to God in prayer, and ask for the trust you do not yet have.

prompt: What is the difference between loving God and merely doing religious duties?
chosen: Loving God differs from mere religious duty because love is a relationship with the living God, not a transaction. God is not a distant spectator; his holiness is grieved by sin and his love moves to provide atonement. The Lamb slain from the foundation of the world expresses an eternal fact in God's nature: holiness requires atonement and love provides it, under the control of his blessedness. Yet love is not mere sentiment. God's love is rational, voluntary self-communication seeking the true good of its object, regulated by and subordinate to his holiness. And this love is learned: spiritual habits begin with definite acts of will and steady obedience, and the Holy Spirit establishes them until obedience becomes spontaneous delight. So do not wait to feel loving before you obey. Begin with deliberate acts of trust and duty, and ask the Spirit to confirm them until love flows freely.
rejected: Loving God is a matter of the heart, while religious duties are outward actions. A person can attend services, pray at set times, and give to charity without actually loving God. Jesus said the greatest commandment is to love God with all your heart, soul, and mind. Duties become expressions of love when they flow from gratitude and devotion rather than habit or fear. So the difference is motive and relationship: duty alone can be cold and self-focused, but love gives duty its warmth and meaning. Practically, examine why you do what you do, and ask God to shape your affections so that obedience springs from delight in him rather than from obligation.

prompt: I feel far from God and my prayers feel empty—why?
chosen: Feeling far from God is common, but the longing behind it is not a delusion. The soul's native yearning for God is evidence of a real Other who answers, because the environment has always produced the appetite and the search implies something to be found. Your empty prayers are not just a subjective mood; they are the cry of a creature made for communion with its Maker. Yet prayer is not naturally easy or flattering. It is humbling work that crucifies pride and signs our bankruptcy before God, and little praying is a deluding make-believe, worse than no praying at all. But do not measure prayer by feelings, for moods never accurately gauge real assimilation to God. Rest on the changeless word of promise. Continue steadfastly when joy is lacking, and refuse to abandon communion or service because of spiritual depression.
rejected: Feeling far from God is common, and empty prayers often reflect exhaustion, distraction, or unconfessed sin rather than God's absence. God has promised to be near, so your feelings are not a reliable measure of his presence. Start by examining your life for anything that has crowded out your relationship with him, and confess it. Then return to simple, honest prayer—even short prayers of trust. Remember that prayer is a relationship, not a performance; dryness can be a season that deepens dependence. Talk to a trusted pastor or friend, keep praying steadily, and trust that God hears even when your words feel hollow.

prompt: I want to know whether the Spirit is a person I can grieve and resist, or just an influence.
chosen: The Holy Spirit is a person, not an impersonal force. Scripture speaks of grieving the Spirit and resisting him, which only makes sense if he is a personal being with will, intelligence, and emotion. He teaches, guides, comforts, convicts, and distributes gifts as he wills. So when you sin, you resist a person who loves you, and when you disobey, you grieve someone who cares. Our own spirit naturally loves truth and virtue, but it cannot overcome the flesh and the power of the Devil without being enlightened by the Holy Ghost. The interior spirit consists in directing all acts to the glory of God, so beware of acting for human praise, from mere natural impulse, or in routine without supernatural intention. And remember that the fulness of the Spirit is given along the line of duty and obedience to world evangelization. God will not give his power for selfish enjoyment; we receive the Spirit in fulness only as we obey Christ's command and step out into his plans for the world.
rejected: The Holy Spirit is a person, not an impersonal force. Scripture speaks of grieving the Spirit and resisting him, which only makes sense if he is a personal being with will, intelligence, and emotion. He teaches, guides, comforts, convicts, and distributes gifts as he wills. So when you resist temptation or sin, you are resisting a person who loves you, and when you grieve him by disobedience, you are grieving someone who cares. The right response is to relate to him personally: listen, obey, and repent quickly when you have grieved him. Read passages like Ephesians 4:30 and Acts 7:51, and ask him to help you know him as a person rather than a mere influence.

prompt: I find it hard to forgive someone who hurt me. How should I pray?
chosen: Forgiveness is hard, and it is honest to tell God so. Begin by praying for the person who hurt you, asking God to bless them and to soften your own heart. Ask God to help you release the debt and to heal the wounds the injury left behind, for God can and does heal in answer to prayer today, since Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever, though the outcome and timing remain in his hands. Pray with confidence, relying on Christ's merits, because God offers grace at each action unless we forget to ask; do not be discouraged by your sins, but keep asking. Remember that forgiving enemies is the best revenge: by bearing injuries patiently you gain grace and the pardon of your sins without trouble or expense. So confess bitterness, ask God to replace it with compassion, and refuse retaliation.
rejected: Forgiveness is hard, and it is honest to tell God so. Begin by praying for the person who hurt you, asking God to bless them and to soften your own heart. Ask God to help you release the debt and to heal the wounds the injury left behind. You can also pray for wisdom about boundaries and for the strength to forgive daily, since forgiveness is often a repeated choice rather than a single moment. Confess any bitterness you find in yourself, and ask God to replace it with compassion. Talk with a pastor or counselor if the hurt is deep, and keep bringing the person before God in prayer.

prompt: I am a dying believer and want to know whether I should ask my minister to bury me and to remember my aged parents after I am gone.
chosen: Yes, it is appropriate to ask your minister to bury you and to remember your aged parents after you are gone. But choose your minister with care, because a prayerless ministry is not merely less effective; it is a funeral and an undertaker for God's truth and Church, however adorned it may be. A minister who prays will bury you as a witness to the resurrection and will remember your parents before God. Ask him to commend you to God's mercy within the limits of Scripture: praying for your acquittal at the great Day, your perfect consummation and bliss, and your resurrection, while avoiding any supposition of purification after death. And remember that parents bear responsibility to teach and watch over their children in the gospel and to guard them from the wickedness of the world. Speak with your minister soon, put your wishes in writing, and involve your family.
rejected: Yes, it is appropriate to ask your minister to bury you and to remember your aged parents after you are gone. Arranging your funeral in advance relieves your family of difficult decisions and lets your burial be a testimony to your faith. Asking your minister to remember your parents is a loving act of care for them, and it is right to want them supported in their grief. Speak with your minister soon about your wishes, put them in writing if possible, and involve your family in the conversation. This is a practical way to steward the end of your life well and to love your neighbors as yourself.

prompt: I'm afraid to speak up about my faith because I don't want to be mocked—how do I handle that fear?
chosen: Your fear of mockery is honest, and honest fear deserves sympathy rather than shame. Many hesitate because childhood faith feels fragile when challenged, and it is right to want the settled conviction of maturity. But that conviction does not come chiefly from weighing evidence with our own understanding; leaning on human wisdom hinders faith. Trust God with all your heart, and do not lean on your own understanding. He has not asked you to verify His truth before trusting Him, but to commit yourself to Him. Here is the ground of courage: God never forsakes us until we first forsake Him. So the thing to fear is not mockery but leaving Him, and the remedy is to remain always with Him. Stay in His presence, and His faithfulness, not your own boldness, will carry you.
rejected: Feeling afraid of mockery is understandable, but you should not let fear silence you. Remember that Jesus said whoever denies Him before men will be denied before the Father, and whoever confesses Him will be confessed. Pray for boldness and ask God to strengthen you. Mockery is a small price compared to faithfulness. Think of the martyrs who gave their lives cheerfully. If you stay silent out of fear, you are treating your reputation as more important than God, which is a form of rebellion against Him. Repent of that fear, ask forgiveness, and step out in faith. God will be with you and give you the words to say.

prompt: My denomination claims to have the correct interpretation. Should I trust it?
chosen: It is reasonable to ask whether a denomination's claim is well grounded, but the question should be approached with a fair rule of evidence. Ancient documents preserved in proper custody are presumed genuine, and the burden of proof lies on the objector, not on the documents. The Scripture witnesses should not be treated as suspect merely because their story is sacred; that is prejudice, not evidence. Yet orders and interpretation should not be judged as a mechanical validity apart from the Church's living whole. There is no abrupt choice between a perfectly true church and none; rather there are degrees of approximation to the whole historic life of the Body. Finally, do not measure a church's success by numbers, finances, or visible results, but by faithfulness to God's word and the witness it bears to His faithfulness. Trust where those marks are present.
rejected: No denomination has a monopoly on truth, so you should be skeptical of any church that claims to be the only correct interpreter. Every tradition has its biases and blind spots, and history shows that churches have been wrong before. You should question their documents and traditions rather than accept them just because they are old or sacred. Test everything against your own conscience and reason. If a claim cannot be proven to your satisfaction, treat it as suspect. Be wary of appeals to authority, because authority is exactly what gets abused. Trust your own judgment first, and only accept what you can verify yourself.

prompt: What does it mean that God's love reaches even the most lost and scarred wanderer—can it reach me?
chosen: Yes, God's love can reach you, no matter how lost or scarred you feel. Scripture says nothing can separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus. The lost sheep, the lost coin, the prodigal son all show God seeking the lost. The deeper way into that love is not only to beg Him to come down; it is the constant endeavour to enter up into His estate and offer Him love. And do not picture yourself alone in a lonely fen. The Father is ever nigh, appearing like a father to the lost child, kissing him, and leading him by the hand to his mother. Nor can your fear keep Him out: Fear wist not to evade as Love wist to pursue. Love meets you at every cross-road and by-path and gently turns you back. Offer Him love, and you will find Him already near.
rejected: Yes, God's love can reach you, no matter how lost or scarred you feel. Scripture says nothing can separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus. The lost sheep, the lost coin, the prodigal son—all show God seeking the lost. So come to Him and ask Him to come down and love you. Beg Him to reach into your darkness. He is merciful and will not turn away a broken heart. Cry out to Him, and He will answer. Your scars do not disqualify you; they are exactly where His love meets you.

prompt: I am like a man in a desert with a loaf and a stone before me—how do I know which to take?
chosen: The choice before you is real, and it is set before you as two ways, life or death, whichsoever you shall please to choose. Think of the desert wayfarer: a loaf and a stone lie before him. He who takes the stone and forsakes the loaf turns to want, but he who chooses the better when both are before him does wisely. So the question is not whether you are free; you are. The question is whether you will refuse the worse and choose the better. Honest self-examination reveals our wretchedness and shows how often we grasp the stone; when we see that, troubles, temptations, and contradictions should be submitted to and borne as advantageous, as God pleases. And remember why we have a body at all: man took a body for exaltation through Christ's redemption and for propagating a pure seed. Purity of body is therefore of the greatest importance. Choose the loaf, and keep your body in purity.
rejected: You are right to see the choice as serious, but do not overthink it. In the desert, the loaf is obviously the better choice, and the stone is useless. Take the loaf. The real question is why you would hesitate at all. If you are tempted to take the stone, that is a sign of a disordered will that needs correction. Examine yourself and repent of any desire for what is worse. Do not pretend the choice is hard or that you are forced into it; you are free, and you should simply choose the good. Take the loaf, and stop making excuses for the stone.

prompt: I have been asked to give up a cherished possession for God's work. How do I know whether this is His will?
chosen: Giving up something cherished is a serious decision, so pray about it and seek counsel from mature believers. But prayer is not effective through bare words or the soul's own strength. When the will is prepared and resolved, it has broken through its own creatures and is sincere before God, clothed with the Merits of Christ. Then it may go to the Father as the Prodigal Son went, confessing not with bare words but with all its strength—a strong purpose and resolution. If you are engaged in God's work, keep up prayer, reading, meditation, and self-examination for your own soul; without regular retirement you cannot kindle charity in others. And do not attach conditions or exceptions to God's will. Yield completely to Him, accepting to be struck where and as He pleases, even in the most repugnant events. That unreserved resignation is how you will know His will and follow it.
rejected: Giving up something cherished is a serious decision, so pray about it and seek counsel from mature believers. Confession and prayer are powerful, and if you say the right words and mean them, God will guide you. Ask Him to show you clearly whether this is His will. If you feel peace about it, that is probably confirmation. You can also set conditions: give it up only if God promises to bless you in return, or only if the request is reasonable. God does not want you to be reckless, so it is fine to limit your obedience to what makes sense to you.

prompt: I feel like a failure compared to everyone else. Does God see me as a failure too?
chosen: Do not settle for comfort that excuses the gap between your life and God's call, but do not make your own striving the support of the work either. God's standard is not lowered to our failures, yet God Himself is the one living Agent who works in you; your effort is only His instrument. Cast all your care upon Him, for anxious self-reliance is distrust of the God who enables what His standard requires. And when God hides Himself—when you feel no assurance and see no progress—do not conclude He counts you a failure. Faith alone must then be your support and the foundation of all your confidence in Him. Moses, David, and Peter failed, yet God did not lower the mark. Press on, resting not on feelings or visible results but on the God who remains faithful even when hidden.
rejected: First, be gentle with yourself. Feelings of failure often come from comparing your life to others, but God does not measure you by that yardstick. He sees your heart, your effort, and your honesty. Scripture is full of people who felt inadequate—Moses, David, Peter—yet God used them. Your worth is not in achievements but in being loved by Him. Bring these feelings to God in prayer and let Him remind you of His care. It may also help to talk with a trusted friend or pastor. God is not disappointed in you for struggling; He is near to the brokenhearted.

prompt: Should I take a job or a position that keeps me from the mission field?
chosen: Do not despise the place where God has set you by longing for a different field of service. Whatever the position, embrace it as your present vocation and serve God in the lowly duties at hand, caring not what the service may be, provided God be served. Yet do not treat this present life as of little worth: it is as precious as any life in time or eternity, and your first duty is to take care of it—providing honestly, guarding health, and meeting your responsibilities. Take the honest position, but limit yourself to legitimate employments. Refuse the curiosity, ambition, and restlessness that would multiply superfluous occupations and encumber you with more impediments than works. The mission field is not a higher calling than faithful work done unto God; serve Him fully where you are, without adding burdens He has not given.
rejected: This is a real tension, and there is no single rule for every person. Ask whether the job genuinely prevents mission involvement or simply makes it less convenient. Many believers serve God faithfully in ordinary work, supporting missions through giving, prayer, and witness. Consider your gifts, obligations, and the counsel of mature believers. If the position clearly closes the door to a calling you believe God has given, weigh that seriously. But do not assume only formal mission work counts. God can use you where you are. Pray for wisdom, seek counsel, and hold the decision before God with an open hand.

prompt: Is the bride the Lamb's wife the church, or is it the city that comes down from heaven?
chosen: Revelation does not present several unrelated images but one reality: the Holy City, the New Jerusalem, is the tabernacle of God, the bride the Lamb's wife, the mother of us all, and the sanctuary—one city coming down from God out of heaven to dwell with men. Yet distinguish the saints from the city: the city is prepared for them, the righteous dead have not yet been caught up, and the saints are being built together as a temple to enter the city prepared for them. Understand God spiritually, not as a corporeal being. Male and female are not divided in this reality but are one spiritual individuality reflecting God as Father-Mother. The city, the bride, and the sanctuary are one, and those being prepared for her share one spiritual life in Him.
rejected: Revelation uses several images that are closely related. The bride, the Lamb's wife, is described as the holy city, the new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God (Revelation 21:2, 9–10). So the bride and the city are not two separate things but one picture of God's people in perfect fellowship with Him. The tabernacle of God is with men, and He dwells with them. Some identify the church as the bride and the city as the dwelling place prepared for her. The safest reading is to see these as complementary images of the same final reality: God's redeemed people dwelling forever with Him.

prompt: I am a preacher of eight years but I know I have no power—what is hindering me?
chosen: Eight years without power is a summons to examine your prayer life. Much prayer is necessary to keep the preacher's spirit in harmony with his calling, and sermon-making without prayer can harden and estrange the heart from God. Yet do not turn prayer into your own achievement: in every occasion of virtue, turn to God and ask for enabling grace, and receive strength more than sufficient. Remember also that the condition of the Church is not independent of its leaders. Preachers are primarily responsible for its spiritual state; spiritual leaders are tokens of God's favor to His people. Your lack of power is not yours alone—it touches the flock. Bring your lack to Him, seek His enabling strength, and take up your responsibility for the Church with humility and prayer.
rejected: Eight years of preaching without power is a painful place, but it is also a place where God can teach you. Power in ministry is not primarily about technique or eloquence; it flows from a life close to God. Ask whether prayer has become secondary to sermon preparation. Ask whether there is unconfessed sin, unresolved conflict, or weariness you have not brought to God. Seek trusted mentors who can pray with you and speak honestly. Remember that faithfulness in small things matters. God often works quietly before He works visibly. Do not despair; bring your lack of power to Him and let Him search your heart.

prompt: If God is good and all-powerful, why is there so much pain and sin in the world?
chosen: God is good and all-powerful, and He is the goodness of all that is good and the doer of all that is done. Sin is not a substance and not a deed; it is the privation of good, a turning from the good that God is. Yet do not treat suffering as an insoluble puzzle: God employs suffering as a remedy for sin, and His righteousness belongs within the problem. The Cross shows that Christ's agony was submitted to in perfect love, proving agony is compatible with the most perfect love between God and the sufferer. But never portray God as the author of sickness, sorrow, or affliction, visiting disease on His children. He is a loving Father who gives only good; sickness is not His will. Many have wrongly believed otherwise and later confessed it. Trust His Fatherhood, and let the Cross, not disease, show you His heart.
rejected: This is one of the oldest and hardest questions, and honest believers have wrestled with it for centuries. Scripture affirms both that God is good and that evil is real. Much pain comes from human choices, and much comes from a broken world. God is not the author of sin, yet He permits it and works to bring good out of it. The cross shows that God does not stand distant from suffering; He enters it. Rather than resolving every mystery, the gospel invites us to trust God's character even when we cannot explain His ways, and to work against pain and sin until He makes all things new.

prompt: Is it unjust for God to punish me for circumstances I could not control?
chosen: It can feel unfair to be blamed for what you could not control, and Scripture never treats God as punishing you for circumstances beyond your power. God's hand is in all things as permission and overruling, not as the author of evil; suffering and harm trace back to human agency—our choices, others' choices, indiscretion, and ignorance—not to God's design or displeasure. Yet trials and closed doors are not mere misfortunes or signs of abandonment; they are divinely ordered links in providence, often opening wider spheres of service. The deeper question is not whether God should adjust circumstances to you, but whether you will be adjusted in every good work—to your surroundings, to the people around you, and to God's plan. In that adjustment you find rest, power, and freedom, trusting His mercy rather than measuring His justice by what you could not control.
rejected: It can feel deeply unfair to be blamed for things beyond your control. Scripture does not teach that God punishes people for circumstances they could not help; rather, it distinguishes between what we choose and what merely happens to us. Much suffering comes from human choices—our own and others'—and from a broken world, not from God's direct displeasure at you. God's justice is perfect, and He sees the heart and the limits of each person's freedom. The real question is not whether God is unfair, but whether we turn toward Him in the midst of what we cannot control, trusting His mercy rather than measuring His justice by our circumstances.

prompt: What's the difference between conviction from my conscience and conviction from the Holy Spirit?
chosen: Conscience is the inner witness God has planted in every person, accusing us when we do wrong and approving when we do right, though it can be misformed by upbringing, culture, or repeated sin. But conscience knows only the holiness of God and our failure before it; it knows no pardon and no Savior, and cannot assure us of mercy. The love of God is known only by revelation, and only God's own voice can remove our doubts and assure us of redemption in Christ. The Spirit's conviction is not legal condemnation but evangelical conviction: it points us to Christ's finished work and to our acceptance in Him. Carrying that conviction into action may cost us—renunciation, loneliness, human disapproval—yet the obedient rest in the divine fellowship promised them, and are led onward to the Savior rather than left in despair.
rejected: Conscience is the inner sense of right and wrong that God has planted in every person. It accuses us when we do wrong and approves when we do right, but it can be misformed by upbringing, culture, or repeated sin. Conviction from the Holy Spirit goes deeper: it is God Himself speaking to the heart, showing us our sin and our need for a Savior. Conscience can make us feel guilty; the Spirit's conviction leads us to repentance and to Christ. Both matter, but conscience alone can leave us in despair, while the Spirit's work brings both sorrow for sin and the assurance of God's mercy and forgiveness in Christ.

prompt: I meet people every day but I never share Christ with them—am I responsible for their souls?
chosen: Every Christian has a responsibility to bear witness to Christ, though not everyone is called to preach. You are not guilty for every person you pass, but you are responsible for the light you have and the opportunities God gives. A silent witness—kindness, integrity, prayer—can matter, but it should not become an excuse for never speaking.
