Christ's suffering is on our behalf, not instead of us: those who follow Him enter the fellowship of His sufferings and the ongoing work of redemption. Yet no one can kindle charity in others who has not tended his own soul, so keep up regular retirement, self-examination, reading, meditation, and private devotion as your first duty. And if faithfulness costs you company, remember that being alone is not being forsaken: whoever has the Father and the Son may be left, but is never alone. Ask God for love and courage to speak.
rejected: Every Christian has a responsibility to bear witness to Christ, though not everyone is called to preach. You are not guilty for every person you pass, but you are responsible for the light you have and the opportunities God gives. A silent witness—kindness, integrity, prayer—can matter, but it should not become an excuse for never speaking. Ask God to give you love for the people you meet and courage to speak when the moment comes. Begin with prayer, then with small, honest words. Christ suffered so that we need not suffer, and redemption is a finished work; our part is simply to share the good news of what He has done.

prompt: I want to know the truth about God and man's relation to Him; where do I begin?
chosen: Begin by recognizing that the knowledge that God is is not a conclusion you reach from external revelation, tradition, experience, or reasoning. It is a first truth—universal, necessary, logically independent and prior to all else—presupposed in every act of knowing. Truth itself is the eternal conformity of God's being and knowledge, grounded in who God is, logically prior to His veracity toward creatures; God is true because He is. His goodness, too, is not inferred from Nature or History, nor are moral judgments mere feelings: true moral judgments are self-evident deliverances of Reason in which God's judgments are revealed. This first truth is developed upon occasion of your perceiving your finiteness, dependence, and responsibility. Begin there, and let Scripture, prayer, and teaching confirm what is already presupposed in all your knowing.
rejected: Begin with Scripture, which is God's revealed truth about Himself and about us. Read the Gospels to see who Jesus is, and let the whole Bible shape your understanding of God's character and man's need. Alongside reading, pray for the Holy Spirit to teach you, since truth is not merely information but a relationship with the God who is true. Also learn from the church's historic teaching and from mature believers. Truth about God is finally a person, not a set of facts, so ask God to make Himself known to you as you seek Him honestly and humbly.

prompt: How can I forsake my Will so that the Creatures which lodge therein may die, seeing I must be in the World and have need of it as long as I live?
chosen: You cannot escape the world, and you need not. The creatures around you are not the problem; the problem is whether your will goes forth into them. If the will goes forth from the creatures—refusing to cling, to possess, to be ruled by them—then they are forsaken and dead in it, and cannot touch the soul. You may use the world outwardly while your soul walks with God in heaven. Yet this is not automatic: if the will abides in the words of Christ, His Word and Spirit abide in him; but if the will goes into the creature, one breaks off from Him. So keep yourself by abiding in resigned humility and a constant course of penitence and daily dying from the creatures. Let this grow from being filled with the mature knowledge of God's will in all wisdom and spiritual understanding—not knowledge as an end, but the secret of true living.
rejected: You cannot escape the world, and you do not need to. The creatures around you are not the problem; the problem is the will's attachment to them. Forsaking your will means inwardly releasing your grip on creatures, refusing to let them rule your heart, even while you use them outwardly for daily life. As long as you live in the body you will have dealings with the world, but your soul can be free. Practice detachment, prayer, and surrender, letting God be your portion. The creatures die in you when your will no longer clings to them, and you can walk with God while still living among them.

prompt: I feel responsible for the suffering of others and it's crushing me. How much should I carry?
chosen: The crushing sense of responsibility rests on a false belief that injury is real and continuous. Divine metaphysics reverses this: man is unhurt, and God is All. Yet do not imagine you can lift this weight by your own discipline. Confess your utter insufficiency—that of yourself you can do nothing. Helplessness is not defeat; it is the condition of receiving Christ's all-sufficiency. Having confessed it, take firm hold of that sufficiency by faith and accept nothing less than all. Bridle the tongue, subdue anger, examine yourself, and attend to your own duties rather than judging others. Trust God as All, and let His strength, not your striving, carry both you and those you love.
rejected: Your compassion is a good instinct, but you are not meant to carry the weight of the whole world. Set boundaries: you can care deeply and still acknowledge that you are one person with limits. Ask what is actually yours to do—a listening ear, a practical kindness—and do that, then release the rest. Guilt that keeps you awake at night helps no one. Consider speaking with a counselor or trusted friend about the pressure you feel, and let others share the load. Service is sustainable when it flows from rest and community, not from a sense of total responsibility.

prompt: I want to be patient in my illness, but I keep complaining—how do I take my troubles lightly for love?
chosen: What you are facing is chemicalization—a mental disturbance, not a real disease. God is All, and there is no disease. Yet do not dismiss your suffering as mere fancy or buffet yourself with a cold assertion that nothing ails you. Treat your conviction with a right apprehension of the truth of being: you are not a sick person managing pain, but God's child, whole in Him. Do not be troubled because you have been troubled, nor angry at having been angry. Gently return the troubled heart to the Lord's hands. Love displaces complaint not by force but by quiet trust. Hold to the truth that God is All, and let patience grow as you rest in Him rather than striving against yourself.
rejected: Complaining under illness is very human, and you should not add shame to it. Start by noticing the complaint without judging yourself; often it signals unmet needs—rest, comfort, company. Tell God honestly how you feel, then ask for grace to bear the day's portion. Small practices help: name three gifts, keep a short journal of what you can still do, and let one trusted person hear you without fixing you. Patience grows not by suppressing pain but by receiving care and offering your suffering as a small offering of love.

prompt: What is the difference between holiness and mere respectability?
chosen: Respectability is outer performance—being seen as decent and proper. Holiness is deeper and prior: it is the fundamental attribute of God, and His love is normed by it. Respectability manages appearances; holiness confronts sin and cannot be achieved by social decency. The condition of salvation is propitiation to the divine righteousness, satisfied in Christ. Yet mere moral systems show what life ought to be and provide no power to become it. Christianity alone solves the practical problem of how the ideal becomes actual: by grace, through sacramental channels, and through the Church as a school of character, where Christ's recreative work forms a new life in us. So turn from morbid self-analysis to God's faithfulness, power, and grace, and let the Church's means of grace make holiness actual, not merely admired.
rejected: Respectability is the outer performance of good behavior—being seen as decent, reliable, and proper by others. Holiness is deeper: it is a heart wholly given to God, a life shaped by love and truth even when no one is watching. Respectability can be maintained by social pressure and appearances; holiness grows from an inward transformation. A respectable person may be admired and still self-centered; a holy person may be unnoticed and yet radiant with God's character. Respectability asks, What will people think? Holiness asks, What does God require? The first is a mask; the second is a life.

prompt: How do I prepare for missionary service while waiting for GOD to open the way?
chosen: The first thing necessary in God's service is earnestly to search His holy will by devout reading, listening to, and meditating on His eternal truths. Let Scripture enlighten the divine law and guide you to every duty. Let the missionary motive rest on the passion for human beings as human beings, not on the notion that truth is the property of one nation or race. Reject the Jonah-like conception that God's blessing belongs to a favored few, and honor peoples and their growing independence with respect. While the way is not yet open, do not chafe, complain, or sink into passive despair. Wait patiently upon the Lord, taking whatsoever befalls from His hands as intended for the highest good, and play the part of a valiant soldier in the Spirit of Christ, co-operating with Him.
rejected: Preparation begins with practical steps: study Scripture and theology, serve in your local church, learn about the culture and language you hope to serve, and build a team of prayer and financial supporters. But waiting is not passive. Use this season to grow in character, deepen your prayer life, and test your calling with wise mentors. Stay flexible—God often opens doors in unexpected ways. Meanwhile, serve where you are; faithfulness in small things now prepares you for larger responsibilities later. Keep your motives examined and your eyes on Christ rather than on the timeline.

prompt: I want to change my life but I feel too weak to resist my habits; where can I find strength to persevere?
chosen: Before you help another, cast the beam out of your own eye. The healer must first overcome his own belief and fear of sin and disease. Hear the exhortation of this Church and Kingdom: not prepare to die, but prepare to live. Teach children in the morning of their days to lay the foundation of health, strength, and constitution, so that longevity may begin to return. Bring the utmost fidelity to your exercises—prayer, self-examination, and steady practice—yet remain untroubled and unastonished when infirmity causes failure. A slip is not a verdict. Persevere with a clear eye and a quiet heart, correcting the belief that habit has power, and let grace, not anxiety, carry you forward.
rejected: Feeling weak is not a reason to give up; it is a reason to stop relying on willpower alone. Strength for change usually comes through community, structure, and grace. Start small: identify one habit, set a realistic plan, and enlist an accountability partner. Replace the habit with something life-giving, and treat slips as information rather than failure. Prayer and honest reflection can help you reconnect with your deeper reasons. If the habit is serious, seek professional help. Perseverance grows through repeated small choices, supported by people who will walk with you.

prompt: How can I believe in eternal life when I see so much death?
chosen: It is natural to grieve when death surrounds us, but death works no miracle. We are after death exactly as far advanced as before it, so the Seed of Divine love must be planted and consciously growing in us here. Yet go deeper: mortality is not truly real, for being is immortal and inseparable from Deity. What we call death is a door to a higher state, not the end of identity, and the righteous are preserved in God, awaiting the resurrection of the body. Because being and Deity cannot be separated, no life is ever lost in God. Let this hope comfort you: tend the Seed of Divine love now, and trust that the life rooted in God cannot die, for it is one with the immortal.
rejected: It is natural to feel this way when death surrounds us. Many find comfort in the hope that those who are baptized and bear the Christian name will be in paradise, since death itself marks a passage into God's presence. The very fact of dying, some say, guarantees rest with God. So when you see so much death, you can trust that each death is a doorway to eternal life, and that your own baptism secures your place. Grieve, yes, but let the promise of paradise steady you. Faith does not deny death's sorrow, but it looks past it to the life that follows for all who die under the Christian name.

prompt: I am sick and in pain. What should I do to find peace?
chosen: I am sorry you are suffering. Do not settle for shallow comfort; the truest peace comes from tried souls who bear the soothing art to their suffering brethren's side, and let peace be the word before your prayer and the farewell after it. But look beyond them to the Lord of peace Himself, from whom come peace of conscience, heart, and fellowship, always and by all means, resting on His Lordship and unchanging relationship rather than on circumstances. Now let me awaken you from the dream of suffering: pain feels like the whole of reality, but it is not. If this word startles you, know the shock is meant to rouse you, not wound you; it is given to facilitate your recovery. Wake from the dream, fix your eyes on the Lord of peace, and let His steady presence, not your changing condition, be your ground.
rejected: I am sorry you are suffering. When you are sick and in pain, it helps to rest, follow your doctor's advice, and take things one day at a time. Try to keep a calm routine, breathe slowly, and let go of worries you cannot control. Many people find peace by focusing on small comforts, like a warm blanket or a quiet room, and by accepting that pain is temporary. It can also help to talk with someone you trust about how you feel. Peace often comes not from removing all pain at once but from accepting the moment as it is. Be gentle with yourself, and remember that this season will pass.

prompt: I am poor and my family is out of food. Is it degrading for me to ask my neighbor for bread?
chosen: No, it is not degrading to ask your neighbor for bread when your family is hungry. Asking for help in genuine need is human and right. But do not imagine prayer or asking alone will turn stones into bread or spare you labor; prayer and honest toil are joined, and the bread of the day is God-given within the avenues of daily work. Be honest too about causes: much poverty comes from want of discretion and sound calculation, and from wasteful spending on unnecessary finery. Examine your habits and spend carefully. If you receive help, be honest, thankful, and frugal. And remember that coveting another's goods is as wicked as miserly hoarding; do not envy your neighbor's plenty. Ask honestly, work diligently, live frugally, and receive each day's bread with gratitude.
rejected: No, it is not degrading to ask your neighbor for bread when your family is hungry. Asking for help in genuine need is a normal and human thing, and most neighbors would rather be asked than see a family go without food. Pride can make us suffer in silence, but there is no shame in seeking bread for your children. Go to your neighbor honestly and explain your situation. Many communities also have food banks, churches, and assistance programs that can help. Asking for help is not weakness; it is a responsible step to care for your family. Accept the help with gratitude, and remember that hard times do not last forever.

prompt: I am tempted to think that if I am forgiven I may go on sinning—does grace really free me from sin's power?
chosen: Grace does free you from sin's power, but not by your own striving under the law. Step out from under law and rest upon grace, trusting Christ's free gift of righteousness so that sin shall not have dominion. You are not forgiven so that you may go on sinning, but forgiven so that you may live no longer as a slave. God offers grace at each action unless you forget to ask, so pray with confidence, relying on Christ's merits, not your own, and do not be discouraged over your sins. Now see the truth that strengthens you: sin confers no real pleasure. Its promised enjoyment is a lie, and the wrong-doer who knows this gains moral courage to master evil. When you fall, return to grace, not to condemnation, and let this knowledge arm you to resist.
rejected: Grace does free you from sin's power, but that does not mean you may go on sinning. When you are forgiven, you are called to turn away from sin and to fight it with all your strength. Think of it this way: if you truly love God, you will want to obey Him, and you will feel sorrow when you fail. So examine yourself, confess your sins, and strive to do better. Set rules for yourself, avoid tempting situations, and hold yourself accountable. If you fall, repent quickly and ask God to help you resist next time. Grace is not a license to sin; it is the power to overcome sin, and you must work out your salvation with fear and trembling.

prompt: I am tempted by impurity and have fallen before. How do I keep from falling again?
chosen: It is good that you want to change. Do not think a single fall undoes you. The way forward is repeated rising after falls, with renewed acts of faith and love, until these form a habitual state of thinking of God. Each time you fall, rise quickly, turn again in faith, and offer an act of love. In prayer, wait before God like a beggar, keeping your mind in His presence and recalling it in tranquility without disquiet when it wanders. Now despise the tempting thoughts rather than fear them. Importunate temptations that displease you are harmless, and the suffering they cause is merciful, for that displeasure proves your will does not consent. Embrace the tribulation they bring, and do not despair. Keep rising, keep trusting, keep loving, and the habit of God's presence will grow in you.
rejected: It is good that you want to change. To keep from falling again, start by identifying your triggers and avoiding them. Set clear boundaries for yourself, such as limiting what you look at online, and fill your time with healthy activities and relationships. When temptation comes, distract yourself quickly, pray for strength, and remind yourself of the consequences of giving in. If you do fall, do not give up; confess it, learn from it, and start again. Consider finding an accountability partner who can check in with you. Change takes time, so be patient with yourself and keep working at it day by day.

prompt: I live in a dreary place with no beauty around me. Can I still learn contentment and praise?
chosen: You can learn contentment precisely because your surroundings are homely and plain. Lowly things teach the heart to want less and receive more; let the simple view outside your window be your school. Be ready to give thanks and to live on the least that Heaven may give. But contentment is not finally about surroundings or bodily comfort. It grows as thought turns away from the body—its pleasures and its pains—toward Truth and Love. Self-love wars against this; it keeps counting what you lack. Trust God in small matters, for faithfulness in little things prepares strength for greater trials. Then praise becomes natural, rising from a heart no longer absorbed in itself but resting in Love. Even a dreary place becomes a place of peace.
rejected: It is understandable to feel discouraged when your surroundings lack beauty. Contentment is not dependent on scenery; it is a habit of the heart that can be cultivated anywhere. Start small: notice one thing each day that is pleasant or useful, and name it aloud in gratitude. Keep a simple routine, care for what is near you, and avoid comparing your place to prettier ones. Praise can begin as a decision rather than a feeling. Over time, gratitude practiced in dull conditions often grows into genuine peace. You may also seek small improvements where you can, but do not wait for beauty to arrive before you allow yourself to be content.

prompt: I have tried to escape my bad temper by avoiding certain people and places—will withdrawing from the world fix what is wrong with me?
chosen: Withdraw as much as you can from acquaintance and from men, not out of contempt but out of care for your soul. Abstain from affairs that hinder your purpose, and seek with jealous care the place, time, and means most suited to quiet and contemplation. Lovingly embrace silence and solitude; they are medicine, not escape. The world is never at rest, and its agitation feeds a restless temper, so fly from that agitation into stillness. Yet do not grow angry with yourself over your own agitation; gently place your troubled heart in the hands of our Lord, asking Him to cure it, and renew your good resolutions daily. Above all, be clad in the panoply of Love, so that you overcome evil with good at all times. Then no human hatred can wound you unprotected, and solitude becomes a school of love rather than of retreat.
rejected: Withdrawal can help, but it will not fix everything by itself. Avoiding triggers gives you space to calm down, yet the temper is inside you and will follow you into solitude. Use the quiet you gain to notice what sets you off and to practice responding differently. A balanced approach is wise: limit exposure to genuinely harmful situations, but do not cut yourself off from all people, since isolation can make irritability worse. Consider talking with a counselor or trusted friend about the roots of your anger. Solitude is a tool, not a cure. Real change comes from understanding yourself and learning skills to manage frustration while staying connected to others.

prompt: My partner's love feels like a constant sky over my restless sea—how do I trust that this is freedom and not captivity?
chosen: It is natural to wonder whether steady love is freedom or captivity, but the deeper question is what in you is asking. Self-love never fully dies; even when mortified, it springs up again, whispering that any steady sky is a cage. So keep constant, patient watchfulness over your own heart. Yet hear Earth's cry: break the heavy chain of selfish fear that chains delight in night and freezes the bones of the world. That jealous fear is bondage, not protection. Let free love no longer be bound. At the same time, love is not blind; let it abound in full knowledge and all discernment, so you can distinguish things that differ and approve what is excellent. Test the relationship by its fruits—respect, honesty, room to grow—and let discernment, not fear, decide whether this sky is freedom.
rejected: It is natural to wonder whether steady love is freedom or a cage, especially if you are used to restlessness. Trust grows when you distinguish between control and care. A loving partner offers a stable presence, not a demand that you stop being yourself. Ask yourself: does this love give you room to grow, to speak honestly, and to keep your own friendships and interests? Does it respect your no? If so, the sky over your sea is not a cage but a horizon. Talk openly about your fears of being trapped. Freedom in love is not the absence of commitment; it is commitment without coercion. Watch the relationship over time, and let trust be built by consistent, respectful behavior rather than by anxiety.

prompt: I have questions about the origin of life and the relation of God to his children that no one can answer—is it wrong to say I simply do not know?
chosen: It is not wrong to say you do not know, but do not conclude that nothing can be known. Our knowledge of God is partial, not exhaustive, yet real: we know substance through phenomena, and the infinite as the absence of all limit. So our words about God are not empty, even when they fall short. On origins and on God's relation to his children, we see in part, but what we see is genuine. Rest content with accepted doctrine rather than speculation, affirming what is revealed—that man's spirit is pre-existent and immortal. And remember the chief purpose of our being here: personal connection with God. Teaching children to prize holidays, parties, and career success above this is a mistaken basis. Never be ashamed of spiritual things. Say "I do not know" where mystery remains, while holding firm what has been given.
rejected: It is not wrong to say you do not know. Honesty is a virtue, and many deep questions about origins and about God's relation to us remain beyond human certainty. What matters is how you hold your uncertainty. You can say, "I do not know," without concluding that nothing can be known or that the questions are worthless. Distinguish between what is unknown and what is unknowable; some things may be partly understood through careful study and reflection. Keep asking, keep learning, and stay humble. Faith does not require pretending to certainty. It is fine to admit limits while continuing to seek understanding, and to live with integrity in the meantime.

prompt: I believe the world is God's good creation, yet I am told the present order is the work of an evil creator; how should I think of the world?
chosen: The claim that the world is the work of an evil creator conflicts with the belief that it is God's good creation. Creation is good; what we call evil is a corruption, not a rival power. If God is real, evil is unreal; it only seems real when reality is given to the unreal. The disorder we see stems from man's departure from God and from usurped authority, and nothing short of God's own interposition can correct it. Yet that deliverance is not magic from outside: the fight is within the person, the enemy a part of one's own self, and deliverance comes as God and man together batter the citadel of evil. So do not despise the world, do not grant evil substance, and do not wait passively. Refuse to give reality to the unreal, fight the battle within, and hope in God's restoration.
rejected: The claim that the world is the work of an evil creator conflicts with the belief that it is God's good creation. A helpful way to think about it is to distinguish between the world as created and the present disorder within it. Creation itself is good; what we call evil is a corruption, a distortion of what was made good. Much of the suffering we see comes from human choices, systems, and neglect, and human effort—wise legislation, education, philosophy, and reform—can correct a great deal of it. So do not despise the world or its Creator. Work to improve what is broken, and hold that the goodness of creation is the deeper truth beneath the present disorder.

prompt: I wonder whether the world is fundamentally good or evil; how should a Christian regard nature and material things?
chosen: The world God made is good, and material things are gifts to be received with thanksgiving. A Christian should study everything on the face of the earth, both good and evil, without practicing evil, reading good books and reliable history and learning good's effects and evil's consequences. Yet we must not imagine that study, legislation, or philosophy can cure what is wrong. The world's evils stem from man's departure from God and his usurped authority, and nothing short of God's own interposition can correct them. God is the goodness of all that is good and the doer of all that is done; sin is no substance and no deed, but a privation and a lie. Nature and possessions are good in themselves, dangerous when idolized, and instructive when we trace honestly what good and evil produce, while we look to God alone for restoration.
rejected: The world is God's creation, and He pronounced it good, so nature and material things are not evil in themselves. They become occasions of sin only when we misuse them or love them more than God. A Christian should receive them with gratitude, enjoy them soberly, and use them for God's glory and the good of others. At the same time, Scripture warns that the world in its fallen systems lies under the evil one, so we must not set our hearts on passing things. The right posture is neither ascetic rejection nor worldly indulgence, but thankful stewardship: seeing creation as a gift that points beyond itself to the Giver.

prompt: How do I respond when I fail in my duty and feel ashamed?
chosen: When you fail, do not sit paralyzed in doubt about whether you have offended God. Humble yourself at once, acknowledge the fault honestly, and beg His forgiveness. Then renew your promises of fidelity and love, and begin again in the pursuit of perfection. Obey God, hold to the one Mind, and love another as yourself. Deny any transfer of evil suggestions between mortals, as though another's sin could be passed to you or yours to them; error is not overcome by error but by truth. Bring the utmost fidelity to your exercises, yet remain untroubled and unastonished when infirmity causes failure. Shame is not the end of the matter; it is a summons to return. Confess, receive forgiveness, and take up your duty once more with a humble and hopeful heart.
rejected: Shame after failure is natural, and it can be useful if it leads you to honesty rather than despair. First, name the failure plainly before God without excusing it. Then remember that His mercy is greater than your sin, and that condemnation is not His voice to His children. Receive forgiveness, make amends where you can, and learn what led to the lapse so you can guard against it. Do not isolate yourself; confess to a trusted believer and let others pray with you. Finally, get up and resume your duty. The goal is not to punish yourself but to return to faithful service with humility and hope.

prompt: How do I know God's will for my life in a specific decision?
chosen: Do not treat the knowledge of God's will as a bare minimum or a mere technique for making decisions. Seek rather to be filled with the mature knowledge of God's will in all wisdom and spiritual understanding, for this is the secret of true living. Be slow to take new steps, and be willing to have no will of your own. Ascertain God's will by prayer and the Word, and test any proposed step by both before you act, lest you rush forward in self-will and mistake presumption for faith. Do not substitute your own preferred way of serving God for the actual discovery and doing of His will. Seek out His will, carry it out joyfully or at least courageously, and then wait in earnest, patient, believing expectation of His help.
rejected: Begin by praying for wisdom, since God promises to give it generously. Then search the Scriptures, because God never leads His children contrary to His Word. Seek counsel from mature believers who know you well and can see your blind spots. Examine your motives: are you drawn by love for God and neighbor, or by fear, pride, or comfort? Consider your gifts, your circumstances, and the needs around you. Often God guides through open and closed doors, through peace, and through the wise advice of others. Make the best decision you can, trusting that God is with you and will redirect you if you go astray.

prompt: I have lost the sense of God's presence in my preaching. How do I get it back?
chosen: Losing the sense of God's presence in preaching is painful, but it is not unusual. Begin by returning to prayer, not as a technique but as a humble waiting before God like a beggar. Set yourself before Him, keep your mind in His presence, and when it wanders, recall it in tranquility without disquiet or self-reproach. Much prayer is necessary to keep the preacher's spirit in harmony with his calling. Diligence in sermon-making and ministerial routine is not enough, and sermon-making without prayer can harden and estrange the heart from God. Preaching is done in the Holy Ghost, not in human eloquence, learning, or popular themes, and its power lies in the Spirit's demonstration. Let the cross of Christ be the theme that commands your witness, and trust that He will renew your sense of His nearness in His time.
rejected: Losing the sense of God's presence in preaching is painful, but it is not unusual. Begin by examining whether you have been running on routine, neglecting prayer, or carrying unconfessed sin. Return to private devotion: set aside unhurried time for Scripture and prayer, and ask God to restore your joy. Preach to yourself before you preach to others. Ask trusted friends to pray for you and to be honest with you about your life and doctrine. Remember that feelings are not the measure of faithfulness; God is present even when you cannot feel Him. Keep preaching the gospel, and trust that He will renew your sense of His nearness in His time.

prompt: I feel drawn to leave everything and live a secluded religious life. Is that the highest path?
chosen: A call to seclusion can be genuine, but it is not automatically the highest path, and it is not a retreat into comfort. Ease and enjoyment must not be the end of Christian retirement; its end is penance, labor, and assiduous contemplation. Without great fervor and constancy in these, close solitude is the road to perdition. Do not suppose that merely seeking, wishing, or professing the devout life is enough. Striving, not mere seeking, opens the door, and overcoming the world, the flesh, and evil is required to destroy error. Walk contrary to the World: go where the way is hardest, take up what the World casts away, do not what the World does, and walk only in the Way of Light, accepting that the World will account this folly. Test the desire prayerfully and with wise counsel, and whether you remain in ordinary life or enter a religious community, love God and neighbor faithfully, taking up the discipline that solitude requires.
rejected: A call to seclusion can be genuine, but it is not automatically the highest path. The highest path is wherever God calls you and where love can grow. Solitude can free you for prayer, simplicity, and attention to God, but it can also become an escape from responsibility, community, and the needs of others. Test the desire prayerfully and with wise counsel. Ask whether it springs from love for God or from disappointment, pride, or a wish for ease. Remember that holiness is measured by love, not by withdrawal. Whether you remain in ordinary life or enter a religious community, the goal is the same: to love God and neighbor faithfully.

prompt: What should I do when I feel God has abandoned me in trial?
chosen: Feeling abandoned in trial is heavy, but the deeper issue is often that we have forgotten God's nearness rather than that He has left. Do not let that forgetfulness disturb you into panic; let it turn you back to Him with greater trust. Abandon yourself to God without exception. Ask Him to tear from your heart everything that burdens it and to wrest you from yourself, so that no reserve or condition remains. Reject the thought that all things are against you; that is the enemy's suggestion. Instead, see your trial as God's wise choosing, meant to make His Word and presence more precious to you. Name the feeling honestly, recall His past faithfulness, and keep small rhythms of prayer and Scripture even when they feel dry. The feeling of absence is not the fact of absence; return gently and trust Him fully.
rejected: Feeling abandoned by God in trial is a heavy and common experience, and it does not mean you have done something wrong. Begin by naming the feeling honestly in prayer rather than hiding it, and recall times God has been faithful before. Lean on Scripture, especially psalms of lament, and let trusted friends or a pastor sit with you. Keep small rhythms of prayer and worship even when they feel dry. Remember that feelings of absence are not the same as actual absence; God promises to be near. Be patient with yourself, seek support, and trust that this season will pass.

prompt: I've been through a period where the church seemed to have no leaders and no hope—where does help come from then?
chosen: When leadership is absent and hope feels thin, help comes first from Christ, the head of the church, and then through a people stirred to self-sustaining labor. Charity that merely creates dependence does not truly help; it fosters idleness and pauperism. Encourage men and women to labor in exchange for aid, keeping a self-sustaining spirit: relieve present wants, then put the poor in a way to help themselves. Remember that church revenues, and even sacred vessels, belong to the poor in their need; when some complain this impoverishes the church, answer with confidence that God will provide. But do not let prayer become a substitute for evangelism. Join prayer to aggressive labor for souls, making the cross of Christ the pivot of all teaching, and let prayer be the source of power for winning converts. Gather faithful laypeople, seek guidance from neighboring congregations, and organize mutual aid that equips rather than enables.
rejected: When leadership is absent and hope feels thin, help can come from several places. Look for faithful laypeople who are quietly serving and gather with them for prayer and Scripture. Reach out to neighboring congregations or denominational bodies for guidance and support. Remember that Christ is the head of the church, and He has not abandoned His people. Use the season to deepen personal dependence on God and to serve others in small ways. Be patient; leadership and renewal often emerge slowly. Seek counsel from trusted mentors and keep your eyes on God's faithfulness rather than on the vacuum around you.

prompt: I am tempted to think that the God of the Old Testament is different from the God of the New; how do I reconcile them?
chosen: The God of the Old and New Testaments is one God, but He reveals Himself at different levels. The Old Testament is a lower and gradual stage, given under divine condescension to a people at an early point in their development: law, sacrifice, and prophecy are preparatory. The New Covenant in Christ is final and complete. Read the Old Testament as a progressive preparation that anticipates Christ. When Christ uses the Old Testament, He appeals to its abiding spiritual testimony to Himself, not to questions of authorship or date, and nothing in that appeal implies any fallibility in Him. The New Testament writings differ widely in style and occasion, yet they are not a mere anthology of human religious writings: they share an essential unity and carry divine authority as the voice of God to us. Study the whole Bible as one story of redemption, letting the earlier stage point beyond itself to the final revelation in Jesus.
rejected: The God of the Old and New Testaments is the same God, revealed in different stages. The Old Testament shows God's justice, holiness, and covenant faithfulness, while the New shows His grace and mercy in Christ. These are not contradictions but complementary aspects of one character. Read the Old Testament through the lens of Christ, noting how it anticipates Him in prophecy, law, and sacrifice. Recognize that God's dealings are progressive: He meets people where they are and leads them forward. Study the whole Bible as one story of redemption, and let the apparent tensions deepen your awe rather than shake your faith.

prompt: I am afraid of hell and wonder if fear is a worthy motive.
chosen: Fear of hell is not a shameful or immature motive; it is a worthy one. The general judgment and the final condition after it were the clear, firmly grasped goal of all early Christian meditation, and heaven and hell were the decisive objects of conviction. That the fear of hell proves the moral character of the religion: it shows that choices matter and that God takes evil seriously. But refuse fear as a lie when it would stop your trusting. Say with the psalmist, 'What time I am afraid, I will trust in Thee.' Fasten your eyes on Christ Himself, the antidote to fear and the sum of all deliverance, and abide in Him. Trust God for goodness and mercy all the days of your life, and let this sober conviction shape a serious, moral faith rooted in Christ.
rejected: Fear of hell is a natural and understandable motive, and it can be a starting point rather than a final one. The Bible takes judgment seriously, and Jesus Himself warned about it. At the same time, mature faith grows toward love of God and gratitude for grace. So do not despise your fear; let it prompt you to seek Christ honestly. Speak with a pastor, read what Scripture says about judgment and mercy, and ask God to deepen your love alongside your reverence. Fear can open the door, but love is the home where faith settles.

prompt: I am a brother and my sister is dying—how do I support her and my aged parents without despairing?
chosen: This is a heavy season, and it is right to feel its weight. But true love seeks the Saviour first and then goes to win the erring brother. Before all else, bring your sister and your parents to Christ in prayer, and gently commend Him to them while there is time. Give them wreaths of hope rather than fading memorials: speak of resurrection, of Christ's presence, of the life to come. Be patient as the Lord is patient, continuing to plead with those you love rather than condemning them quickly; kind smiles are better than cursings. Remember why you belong to the confraternity: you entered solely to serve God and Mary and to save your soul. Do not forsake its appointed days for worldly business, even in this busy season. Support your sister and parents practically, share caregiving, guard your rest, and let others pray for you, trusting God's grace amid grief.
rejected: This is a heavy season, and it is right to feel the weight of it. Support your sister by being present, listening, and helping with practical needs, and support your parents by sharing caregiving and giving them permission to grieve. Take care of your own rest and ask friends and church for help. Speak honestly with God in prayer and let others pray for you. Remember that grief is not the same as despair; it can coexist with hope. Focus on small, faithful acts of love each day rather than carrying the whole future at once.

prompt: I get impatient with my children and then feel terrible—how do I balance discipline and gentleness?
chosen: Your guilt shows you care, but the goal isn't to manage anger better—it's to stop correcting your children in the heat of passion. Lead them kindly by example: when impatience rises, pause and pray rather than punish, governing them by faith rather than the rod. Never drive your children; lead them along, and if you slip, repair gently so they learn to love you rather than fear you. Don't be terrified by small faults; quietly humble yourself before God and say to your soul: 'Courage! we have made a false step, but let us keep steadily on.' Yet gentleness is not indulgence: commend spiritual education, teach obedience to the moral law, and restrain their appetites for mere amusement, so they grow in understanding of man's higher nature.
rejected: It's completely normal to lose patience sometimes, and the guilt you feel shows you care. The key is to separate the behavior from the child: be firm about rules but warm in tone. Try naming your feelings out loud—'I'm getting frustrated, so I'm going to take a breath'—which models self-regulation. Set clear consequences in advance so you're not deciding in anger. When you do snap, repair quickly: apologize sincerely, explain what happened, and reconnect. Discipline isn't the opposite of gentleness; consistency and calm limits actually help children feel secure. Give yourself grace too—no parent is perfect, and repair is what teaches kids how to handle mistakes.

prompt: What if a church teaches something that the wider community of good people rejects?
chosen: When a church teaches something the wider community of good people rejects, it should remember that its positive work is always appeal, not force. Force, where discipline requires it, may be used only as a strictly preparatory measure that clears the ground for appeal; it is never the Church's real instrument. The Church is indifferent to personal success and national expansion. It cares only that the individual be pure in heart and the nation honourable, and it is ready to suffer for that testimony rather than win acceptance. Good people may reject its teaching, but rejection does not settle the question of truth. Members should not point out the supposed defects of Joseph Smith, Brigham Young, or other leaders; it is not their right, and the Lord will judge them. They should avoid words that give the world occasion to speak evil, and instead persuade, reason, and leave judgment to God.
rejected: When a church teaches something the wider community of good people rejects, the church faces a real test. It should reexamine its doctrine honestly, listen to the concerns of others, and be willing to change course if it has erred. A church that insists on its own way against the clear judgment of good people risks becoming isolated and proud. At the same time, a church must not simply surrender every conviction to popular opinion, since moral truth is not decided by majority vote. The wisest path is humility, dialogue, and a willingness to admit mistakes, while holding fast to whatever can be defended before God and conscience. In this way the church shows respect for the wider community and preserves its own integrity.

prompt: How do I deal with the sense that my wrong choices have woven a net around me that I can't escape?
chosen: That net is real, but it is woven from your own choices, and only ceasing to sin will loosen it—not distraction, blame, or bargaining, since misery is the fruit of the wrong you keep doing. Come before God like a beggar: empty-handed, keeping your mind in His presence, and when it wanders into fear or self-reproach, recall it quietly, without disquiet, as you would lead a child back by the hand. Then set out the three things plainly. First, resign your will to God in humility, asking only to be shown the next wrong to leave. Second, hate and forsake your own will; when it drives you toward the old wrong, refuse to do it. Third, bow your soul under the Cross in willing submission, bearing the temptations of Nature and Creature without agitation. This is courage, not fear: calm waiting, firm refusal, and patient endurance, strand by strand, until the net falls away.
rejected: That net is real, but it is made of your own choices, and what was woven can be unwoven. Start by naming the strands honestly—the habits, excuses, and small compromises that tightened around you—and stop feeding them. You do not escape misery by distracting yourself, blaming others, or bargaining for a lighter sentence; you escape it by ceasing to do the wrong you know. Take one strand at a time. Ask for help where you need it, make amends where you can, and replace each wrong habit with a right one. Fear of punishment may push you, but it will not hold you; a steady, courageous refusal to keep sinning will. Freedom comes slowly, by walking out the way you walked in.

prompt: I was born long after the events I am asked about—how can I declare what I do not know?
chosen: Your hesitation rests on a material sense of yourself as a late-born creature, dated by a physical beginning and bounded by memory and decay. But man is Spirit's offspring, without birth or death, and his identity is preserved in divine Science, not in the accidents of time. What you truly know is not measured by when your body appeared. The obscurity you feel belongs to the mortal record, whose origins—including those of Christian customs and ideas—are often genuinely uncertain and cannot be confidently traced. Respect that obscurity rather than resolving it prematurely. Declare only what divine Science establishes: that your being is eternal, not begun, and that the past's unclear testimony cannot define what you are in God.
rejected: You are right to hesitate. Being born later does not grant you eyewitness knowledge, and honesty requires admitting the limits of what you can claim. Yet history is not closed to you. You can study records, weigh testimony, and distinguish what is documented from what is inferred. What you cannot do is pretend to certainty you do not have. So declare only what the evidence supports, mark your uncertainties plainly, and let the past speak in its own terms rather than through your assumptions. Declaring what you do not know is not failure; it is the beginning of trustworthy inquiry, and it protects you from inventing motives for people who never held them.

prompt: I am a leader and everyone depends on me—what happens to the work if I am removed?
chosen: It is natural to feel that everything rests on you, and Scripture treats the leader's place as sacred. A presiding officer is the head, and his place should be held sacred; a subordinate who acts independently or usurps authority is in error and a dangerous example, for no one should run before his file leader. Yet we have no time allotted to work for ourselves in the narrow, selfish sense. When we labor most fervently for the Kingdom of God, it is all for ourselves, since our interest is bound up in that Kingdom. If you are removed, do not fear that the work collapses. God can provide a worthy successor, and no man's presence is indispensable, for the living God maintains what He has built. Your task is faithful service, not anxious indispensability.
rejected: It is natural to feel that everything rests on you, but a healthy work should not collapse when one person steps away. If the whole enterprise depends on a single leader, that is a warning sign: authority has not been shared, successors have not been trained, and the team has learned dependence rather than ownership. The wise response is to build structures, document processes, and mentor others so the mission outlives any individual. Your removal should test the strength of what you built, not expose its fragility. Prepare now, and the work will continue.

prompt: I have tried to be self-sufficient and not need anyone. Why does that leave me so lonely?
chosen: Self-sufficiency feels like strength, but it quietly removes the connections that make us human. Loneliness is not cured by one honest admission or a few tears of self-pity; a single plea does not obtain what only steady, persistent desire can. What you need is a settled, ongoing turning toward others and toward God—not a demand made only when prosperity fails, friends disappoint, or you are sick and lonely. Yet do not imagine that adopting this practice once destroys your self-love; that root, though mortified, never dies and springs up again, so keep constant, patient watchfulness over it. And do not multiply pious exercises while leaving the heart unwatched. Discover and root out your habitual disorders, guard your senses, live in recollection, open your interior honestly to a spiritual director, and aim at God's will rather than at piling up external works. Perseverance joined with vigilance is what reshapes a solitary life into a shared one.
rejected: Self-sufficiency feels like strength, but it quietly removes the very connections that make us human. When you decide you must never need anyone, you stop letting people close, and loneliness is the natural result: you have built a life with no door for others to enter. The ache you feel is not a flaw to fix but a signal that you were made for relationship. Begin by admitting your need honestly, to yourself and to a trusted person, and let small acts of receiving—help, kindness, company—become habits. Dependence is not weakness; it is the shape of a shared life.

prompt: How do I teach my children to trust God when we live in hard conditions?
chosen: Children learn trust less from what you say than from what they see you do. In hard conditions, let them watch you bring every worry to God honestly and keep doing the next right thing. Teach them that God is ever-present and omnipotent, so that even their illnesses and complaints can be brought to him and find help. When a child is sick or frightened, pray with them simply and expectantly. Pray too with persevering, submissive desire for present fruit in their conversion, remembering the eternal consequences of a child rightly trained or neglected and the vast power for good or evil in a little child. Do not indulge their appetites for amusement. Commend spiritual education, obedience to the moral law, and restraint, so that they grow in the understanding of man's higher nature and learn that trust is a way of walking through difficulty held by a God who does not abandon his people.
rejected: Children learn trust less from what you say than from what they see you do. In hard conditions, let them watch you bring every worry to God honestly, name your fears without despair, and keep doing the next right thing. Tell them stories of God's faithfulness, pray with them simply, and keep routines of worship and gratitude even when money or comfort is short. Answer their questions truthfully, without pretending hardship is nothing. Let them see that trust is not the absence of difficulty but a way of walking through it together, held by a God who does not abandon his people.

prompt: What does it mean that Jerusalem which is above is the mother of us all?
chosen: The phrase comes from Paul's letter to the Galatians, where he contrasts the earthly Jerusalem with the heavenly one. Jerusalem above is the spiritual city, the community of the redeemed under God's gracious covenant, as opposed to the earthly city of slavery under the law. To call her our mother is to say that she is the source and home of our new life in Christ: we are born into her by grace, nourished by her, and destined for her. This is not a separate idea from the bride and the tabernacle: the Holy City, the New Jerusalem, the tabernacle of God, the bride the Lamb's wife, the mother of us all, and the sanctuary are one city coming down from God out of heaven to dwell with men. Nor is this motherhood abstract: Mary is the mother of fair love, loves those who love her, serves those who serve her, and loves us more than any earthly mother. And this city encloses the garden of Eden, the Paradise of God, with the tree of life and the river of water of life issuing from the throne; these are not mere figures but realities belonging to the sanctuary. The image comforts believers who suffer now, reminding them that their true citizenship and family are in heaven.
rejected: The phrase comes from Paul's letter to the Galatians, where he contrasts the earthly Jerusalem with the heavenly one. Jerusalem above is the spiritual city, the community of the redeemed under God's gracious covenant, as opposed to the earthly city of slavery under the law. To call her our mother is to say that she is the source and home of our new life in Christ: we are born into her by grace, nourished by her, and destined for her. The image comforts believers who suffer now, reminding them that their true citizenship and family are in heaven.

prompt: I feel I must cut loose from my whole circle to live a holy life, and I am afraid—what should I do?
chosen: Your fear is a signal worth listening to. Holiness rarely requires severing every relationship; it requires reordering them. But do not make this a project of self-management. The shortest and only way into the Kingdom of God, and to be like All Things, is to become as a little child—hanging upon Christ for all things, depending upon him as the author and fountain of them. Before cutting loose, ask whether you are fleeing temptation or the discomfort of being known. If some relationships genuinely pull you into sin, limit them wisely rather than dramatically. Let every act of self-denial be grounded in inward joy in God and the Spirit's working, not in mere habit, custom, or imitation, for such outward practices will not last. Be faithful in duty at the beginning, and you will find that duty leads to pleasures; have recourse to Christ's grace, and he makes every difficulty easy. Seek counsel from a mature believer, and let your choices be shaped by love rather than fear.
rejected: Your fear is a signal worth listening to. Holiness rarely requires severing every relationship; it requires reordering them. Before cutting loose, ask whether you are fleeing temptation or fleeing the discomfort of being known and challenged. Often the holiest path is to stay, set clearer boundaries, and let your circle see a changed life. If some relationships genuinely pull you into sin, limit them wisely rather than dramatically. Seek counsel from a mature believer or pastor, be patient, and let your choices be shaped by love rather than fear. Holiness grows in community, not in isolation.

prompt: Is it impious to say that God could not make a world without evil in it?
chosen: It is not impious to ask the question, but the answer matters. The world's evils do not stem from a defect in God's power or from a puzzle about freedom; they stem from man's departure from God and his usurped authority. Because of that, no human effort, legislation, or philosophy is sufficient to correct them. Nothing short of God's own interposition can restore the world. Nor should we measure the matter by worldly pains and pleasures, which are not comparable to spiritual ones: be careful for nothing and fear nothing, desiring only not to offend God. And remember that if God is real, evil is unreal. Evil only seems real when reality is given to the unreal. So to say God could not make a world without evil misplaces the problem: God can, and the evil we see is man's doing, a shadow that has no substance of its own.
rejected: It is not impious to ask the question, but the answer matters. Saying God could not make a world without evil limits God's power, which seems to deny his omnipotence. Yet the deeper issue is what we mean by evil. Much evil arises from the choices of free creatures, and a world with genuine freedom may carry the possibility of evil without God being its author. So the claim is not so much impious as imprecise. God can make a world without evil; the question is whether such a world would include the goods he intends, such as freedom and love.

prompt: Am I responsible for the sins of my fathers, or for the sins of my nation?
chosen: Scripture speaks to both family and nation, but the gospel settles the deeper question first: Christ bought our sins and us at the price of Himself. Our sins are His and not ours; He bore them, and the question of our acceptance is forever settled in the Beloved. The curse is not obedience but disobedience, and Christ was made a curse for us on the tree, so that He has loosed us from sin and we need not sin any more. Ezekiel 18 still teaches each person is accountable for his own sin, and Exodus 20 and Lamentations 5 show that families and nations pass down consequences. You are not personally guilty for sins you never committed, yet you bear responsibility for how you respond to the inheritance you received—not to earn acceptance, but because you are already accepted. And any faithful response is itself the work of the Father of glory, whose must be the power and the grace for a life lived to His praise.
rejected: Scripture speaks to both. Ezekiel 18 insists each person is accountable for his own sin: the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father. Yet passages like Exodus 20 and Lamentations 5 acknowledge that families and nations pass down consequences, and we inherit cultures shaped by ancestral and national wrongdoing. So you are not personally guilty for sins you never committed, but you do bear responsibility for how you respond to the inheritance you received—whether you repent of it, resist it, or repeat it. As a citizen, you share in a nation's corporate life and can work for its repentance and justice. The healthy response is honest confession, gratitude for God's mercy, and faithful action in your own sphere, neither paralyzed by inherited guilt nor indifferent to it.

prompt: I was raised Christian but never really understood the Holy Spirit—where do I start?
chosen: Start with the Church, because the Spirit is not a private feeling but the life of the Spirit-bearing body. He is given to the gathered people of God, consecrating ordinary things—water, bread, wine, Scripture, spoken prayer—and working gradually and socially among believers, while also deepening personal character. Remember who He is: not an impersonal influence but a divine Person, the Paraclete sent by Christ, co-equal with the Son, who speaks, guides, commands, and can be grieved. He is also a jealous, loving Friend who loves us to jealousy, grieved by divided affection; friendship with the world is enmity with God, so He asks for undivided and unbounded love. Read what Jesus says about Him in John 14–16, then watch how He moves through the community in Acts and the letters of Paul. Pray honestly, pay attention to the ordinary means of Scripture, prayer, worship, and fellowship, and let understanding grow through obedience and shared life.
rejected: Start simply. The Holy Spirit is God's presence with us, promised by Jesus to guide, comfort, and teach His followers. Begin by reading what Jesus says about the Spirit in John 14–16, then notice how the Spirit appears in Acts and the letters of Paul. Pray honestly, asking God to make His Spirit real to you—not as a vague feeling but as the one who points you to Christ and shapes your character. Pay attention to the ordinary means: Scripture, prayer, worship, and fellowship with other believers. Talk with a pastor or mature Christian about your questions. Understanding grows over time through obedience and experience, so don't wait until you feel you understand everything before you begin to pray and walk with Him.

prompt: I want to surrender fully to God this Christmas but I'm afraid of what it will cost—what does the Christmas spirit actually call me to?
chosen: Your fear is honest, and worth naming. But the Christmas spirit is not mainly decorations or sentiment; it is the God who gave Himself away, and it calls for sacrificial love and glad surrender. No one living for himself alone has a right to share its joys. Christmas is humility, joy, sacrificial love, worship, and mission: the Word became flesh not to be served but to serve. So surrender is not an optional extra but the very shape of the feast. Receive each day's new mercies, and hallow what you find, trusting God to provide new treasures for sacrifice. Learn to address God every moment, recognizing Him intimately present; seek His will in doubtful things; offer your actions before you do them; and give thanks afterward. Start small and specific: forgive someone, give generously, serve quietly. What surrender costs is real, but what it gives is greater—a life caught up in love.
rejected: Your fear is honest, and worth naming. The Christmas spirit is not mainly about decorations or sentiment; it is about the God who gave Himself away. Christmas calls you to a surrender that is glad rather than grim, because the one who asks for your life has already given His own for you. Practically, that means letting go of the illusion that your life is your own to arrange, and offering your time, money, and attention to God and to people who need them. Start small and specific: forgive someone, give generously, serve quietly. You will find that what surrender costs is real, but what it gives is greater—a life that is no longer curved in on itself but caught up in love.

prompt: I have spent a fortune on doctors and patent medicines; is there a better way?
chosen: It is understandable to feel exhausted and discouraged after spending so much on remedies that did not deliver. A better way begins with calm, contented, patient diligence rather than frantic hurry after health or wealth. Attend your meetings faithfully, pray, read the Scriptures, and meditate—these keep your dish right side up for the shower of blessings. Recognize divine Mind as the only medicine; human will, malice, and sensuality have no place in any healing agency. And measure your physicians rightly: a physician is constituted by a complete cure, leaving no blemish behind, and a painless examination. Seek such competent care for real conditions, but avoid frantic spending on unproven patent medicines. Ask what you are really hoping to buy: relief, control, or reassurance. A calmer, more patient approach, with realistic expectations and attention to how you live, often serves better than another purchase.
rejected: It is understandable to feel exhausted and discouraged after spending so much on remedies that did not deliver. A better way begins with honest reflection: no single medicine or doctor can guarantee health, and chasing every promised cure can drain both wallet and hope. Consider what actually supports well-being—rest, sensible food, exercise, peace of mind, and honest relationships. Seek competent medical advice for real conditions, but avoid frantic spending on unproven patent medicines. Ask what you are really hoping to buy: relief, control, or reassurance. A calmer, more patient approach, with realistic expectations and attention to how you live, often serves better than another purchase.

prompt: How shall all people and nations be brought to judgment, and how will the sentence be pronounced?
chosen: Scripture presents judgment as God's own work. This world shall pass away, and devouring flame shall seize upon all born into it when the Lord Himself with a host of angels comes unto judgment. Each man shall hear the doom on all his deeds from the mouth of the judge, and shall pay the penalty for all his foolish words and overbold thoughts. The judgments of the last days are God's means of purging wickedness and preparing the earth for the reign of Christ, who will rule the nations with a rod of iron. And where high councils judge among God's people now, they must find out the truth and the facts and judge according to them, always tempered with mercy, love, and kindness, aiming to build up and save rather than to tear down and destroy.
rejected: Scripture presents judgment as God's own work, not merely a human process. It speaks of a final day when the Lord comes to judge the world in righteousness, and of Christ as the appointed judge before whom all nations will stand. The sentence will be pronounced by Him, and each person will give account of his or her life. Alongside this, Scripture also describes God raising up judges and councils among His people to settle disputes and administer justice in the present age. These human judgments are meant to reflect God's justice—seeking truth, weighing evidence, and acting fairly. So the answer has two dimensions: a final, universal judgment by God, and provisional judgments among people that should mirror His righteousness.

prompt: I'm afraid to speak my mind because I might be punished. Should I stay silent?
chosen: Fear of punishment is real, but consider what habitual silence does to you. If you gain the power to check your words, you will next gain the power to check your judgment and thoughts, and a guarded mind soon loses its honesty. As for the faults you fear naming, do not condemn anyone on rumor; wait until matters are clearly shown. Then speak plainly, so all who hear can understand, say what you have to say, and stop, for many words darken counsel. Let humility govern both speech and prayer: confess your own faults and humble yourself, for this quiets wandering thoughts, whereas multiplying words in prayer often scatters the mind. Prudence may guide timing and safety, but let it not excuse a mind that has stopped judging truly or a tongue that hides behind confusion.
rejected: Fear of punishment is a real and reasonable concern, and staying silent can sometimes be the prudent choice. If speaking could genuinely endanger your safety or livelihood, it is wise to weigh the risks carefully and seek support from trusted people. Consider whether the issue is worth the cost, whether there are safer channels such as speaking privately or through others, and what protections are available to you. Silence is not always cowardice; sometimes it is prudence. But silence can also become a habit that erodes confidence and allows wrongs to continue. Reflect honestly on your motives, seek counsel, and decide according to both your conscience and your circumstances.

prompt: I am troubled by the enemy's suggestions that I am too wretched to come to God—how do I answer them?
chosen: These suggestions are the enemy's device, not the truth about you. The false dread of your wretchedness is meant to drive you from the blissful beholding of your Everlasting Friend, and that is what you must refuse. When you fall, see your wretchedness meekly for a moment, then hasten back to the Lord. He stands aloof and abides you sorrowfully, and he has haste to have you to himself. Do not linger in self-accusation; rise by charity and meekness, and so turn the enemy's gain into his own sorrow. Answer him plainly: God's mercy is greater than your sin, and coming to him is never earned. Keep your gaze on God rather than on your misery, and let renewed trust, not fear, shape your return.
rejected: These suggestions are common and painful, but they are not the truth about you. Feeling wretched is not the same as being beyond God's welcome. Answer the thoughts directly: God's mercy is greater than your sin, and coming to him is never something you must earn first. Remember that all people are sinful and that Christ came for sinners. Practical steps help: name the thought as a lie, turn your attention to Scripture's promises, pray honestly even if briefly, and speak with a trusted pastor or friend. Do not wait until you feel worthy; come as you are, and let gratitude and honesty, rather than fear, shape your approach to God.

prompt: How can I play my part in the coming of the Kingdom?
chosen: The shortest and only way to enter the Kingdom, and to be like All Things, is to become as a little child, hanging upon Christ for all things and depending upon him as the author and fountain of them. Do not imagine you build the Kingdom by your own strength or pursue greatness in your own hands. Yet know that the Kingdom you seek is no mere inward state: it is a literal kingdom on the earth, composed of living and resurrected saints, with laws and administrators, and Christ will reign over all the earth. The blessed hope of his coming impels wider witness, shapes how you view the present age, and influences your piety and usefulness. So bring your gifts, service, and prayers as a child brings small things to a father, depending on Christ, and let expectation of his reign stir you to faithful labor.
rejected: Playing your part in the coming of the Kingdom begins with faithful daily living: love God and neighbor, serve the poor, pursue justice, and share the gospel in word and deed. Use your gifts and resources for others, pray for God's will to be done, and join a community of believers who serve together. Growth in character matters too—humility, patience, and generosity make the Kingdom visible. Avoid the trap of waiting for something dramatic; the Kingdom comes through small, faithful acts of obedience. Ask God for direction, take concrete steps where you are, and trust that he works through ordinary faithfulness.

prompt: Is it right to adopt the customs and dress of the people I hope to reach with the Gospel?
chosen: Adopting customs and dress can be legitimate when it removes needless barriers and shows love, so long as motive and integrity are tested and the gospel stays central. But do not confuse the gospel with the ancient dogmatic form of Christianity. That form was a historically conditioned vessel, sharing the limited endurance of the ancient world; it is transitory, and the Gospel itself is not bound to it. The everlasting gospel is to be restored with apostles, prophets, baptism, the gift of the Holy Ghost, healings, tongues, and revelations, as in former days. Adapt outward customs freely where love requires it, but keep the restored gospel at the center. And let parents take their own responsibility seriously: teach and watch over your children in the gospel, guarding them from the wickedness of the world, so that adaptation never becomes neglect of those entrusted to you.
rejected: Adopting customs and dress can be a legitimate way to remove unnecessary barriers and show respect for the people you hope to reach. Missionaries throughout history have learned language, wore local clothing, and entered local culture to communicate the gospel. The key questions are motive and integrity: are you adapting to serve, or merely fitting in to avoid discomfort? Does the adaptation compromise any essential teaching or moral standard? Are you being honest about who you are? Wise adaptation, done humbly and with counsel, can open doors; careless imitation can confuse. Test your motives, keep the gospel central, and let love, not conformity, guide the choice.

prompt: I have a great devotion to the sorrows of Mary. What graces can I hope for from meditating on her dolors?
chosen: Devotion to Mary's sorrows is a long-standing practice, and you may confidently hope for graces from meditating on her dolors, especially true repentance and help at the hour of death. Mary may rightly be called our hope, because God has ordained that all graces be dispensed through her intercession; confidence in her does not detract from hope in God but rests on his ordinance. So let true devotion mean honoring and invoking her, trusting her intercession, and imitating her virtues, especially her faith at the cross, with the intention to amend your life rather than presume on mercy. Let meditation stir compassion for her sorrows and lead you to prayer, repentance, and charity, deepening your love for Christ, for whom she suffered.
rejected: Devotion to Mary's sorrows is a long-standing Catholic practice, and meditating on them can deepen compassion, patience, and trust in God's providence. Many believers find that reflecting on her suffering helps them endure their own trials and grows their love for Christ. As for specific graces, practices vary and the Church encourages a balanced faith centered on Christ. It is best to avoid treating any devotion as a guarantee or a kind of spiritual formula. Instead, let meditation on her sorrows lead you to prayer, repentance, and charity, and speak with a trusted spiritual director about what you may hope for.

prompt: Why should I care about heaven when my family needs me here?
chosen: Caring for your family is important, but your ultimate hope must be in heaven. The things of this world—even family concerns—can become vanities that turn your heart from blessed eternity. You should live as if your mind is in heaven and your body in the tomb, withdrawing your heart from earthly amusements and vanities. Yet do not expect unmixed joy in your charitable work; God withholds full solace from Love's work lest it steal your heart. Sow in tears, following the Saviour who sighed even while doing good, and be content to bless in woe. Remember that the Kingdom of Heaven is in the Saints operative by Faith even while the natural life is encompassed with flesh, blood, the World, and the Devil. So let your Soul sink into the hope of the Grace of God and stand like a rose among thorns until the body's death, serving your family with a heart detached from worldly attachments and fixed on eternal things.
rejected: Caring for your family is a noble and important responsibility. Heaven can seem distant when you are focused on meeting the needs of those you love. However, keeping heaven in mind doesn't mean neglecting your family; it can give you hope and strength to serve them better. Many people find that faith provides a moral compass and comfort that helps them be more patient and loving at home. So, you can care about heaven and still be fully present for your family. It's about balance: attending to earthly duties while holding onto spiritual hope. In fact, your family may benefit from the peace and purpose that comes from your faith.

prompt: I am a judge and I must decide a difficult case. What should guide me?
chosen: As a judge, you must beware of rash judgment, for circumstances easily deceive. Your role as a magistrate is to judge righteously, but private persons should only vindicate others, not condemn them. Therefore, carefully examine the facts, listen to all parties, and apply the law impartially. Avoid hasty conclusions and ensure that your decisions are based on truth, not on appearances. Seek wisdom and pray for discernment, remembering that your judgments affect lives. Uphold justice with humility, and always aim to vindicate the innocent and condemn only when guilt is clearly established. Encourage disputants to first settle matters themselves; if they cannot, they should seek help from ward teachers, then the bishop, then the high council, and only lastly general authorities, without disregarding any authorized step or officer. In all judgments, find out the truth and facts, judge according to them, always tempered with mercy, love, and kindness, aiming to build up and save rather than tear down and destroy.
rejected: As a judge, you should be guided by the law, the facts, and a commitment to justice. Carefully review all evidence, listen to both sides, and apply the law impartially. Seek wisdom from legal precedents and consult with colleagues if needed. Remember that your decisions impact people's lives, so approach the case with humility and diligence. Pray for wisdom if you are a person of faith, and ensure your judgment is fair and unbiased. Ultimately, your goal is to uphold justice and serve the common good.

prompt: I'm afraid of dying and wonder what happens to my loved ones who have died faithful. Should I mourn for them?
chosen: It's natural to fear death, but for the faithful, death is a door to a higher state. Your loved ones who have died in faith are not lost; their identity is preserved, and they will be resurrected. So do not mourn as those without hope. Instead, take comfort that they are with God, in a place of peace. Grieve, but let your grief be a tender regret rather than acute grief, trusting that your beloved is in a high sphere of saner happiness. Remember that the body will be raised and reunited with the spirit. Hold onto the promise that you will see them again. Let your hope rest wholly on Christ—his sufferings, temptations, cross, death, resurrection, and pleading at the right hand of the Father. Looking at self clouds the view; look to the altogether lovely Saviour, whose promises leave no room to doubt his power and will to save.
rejected: It's natural to fear death and to mourn for loved ones who have died. Grief is a normal part of loss, and you should allow yourself to feel it. However, if your loved ones were faithful, you can take comfort in the hope of an afterlife. Many faith traditions teach that the righteous go to a place of peace and joy. While you will miss them, you can trust that they are in God's hands. Mourning is not wrong, but it should be balanced with hope. Take time to grieve, but also remember the good times and the promise of reunion. Seek support from your community and from your faith.

prompt: I am facing death and want to know whether there is real hope beyond the grave.
