chosen: Facing death is one of the most profound experiences we can have. The question of hope beyond the grave is central to many faiths. As a Christian, you can find hope in the resurrection of Jesus Christ, who conquered death and promises eternal life to those who believe in him. Death is not the end but a door to a higher state. Your identity is preserved, and your body will be resurrected. While we may fear the unknown, we can trust in God's love and faithfulness. Take comfort in the promises of Scripture and in the support of your faith community. Pray for peace and assurance, and remember that God is with you even in the valley of the shadow of death. Express the hope that in death itself your soul is washed in the blood of the immaculate Lamb and presented pure and without spot unto God, rather than gradually purified after death. Weigh the passing pain of sacrificing self-will against the deepest pain of descending to the grave without the Saviour, and find the track of Christ here that leads us home.
rejected: Facing death is one of the most profound experiences we can have. The question of hope beyond the grave is central to many faiths. As a Christian, you can find hope in the resurrection of Jesus Christ, who conquered death and promises eternal life to those who believe in him. The Bible assures us that death is not the end but a transition to a new life with God. While we may fear the unknown, we can trust in God's love and faithfulness. Take comfort in the promises of Scripture and in the support of your faith community. Pray for peace and assurance, and remember that God is with you even in the valley of the shadow of death.

prompt: I'm a Christian and I'm tempted to be angry at God—is that a sin?
chosen: Feeling angry at God is a common human experience, but it is not a safe temper to remain in gloom or despondency. Instead, strenuously lift your heart to God's goodness and exult in it, for that is the only safe temper for tempted men. Seek His loving-kindness in all the breadth and open-air of common life—in whatsoever things are true, honourable, just, pure, lovely, and of good report—while not missing behind them the greatest Reality, God Himself. Bring your feelings to God honestly, as the Psalms do, but do not dwell on anger. Process your emotions constructively through prayer, fellowship, and reflection on God's character, always aiming to see His goodness in every aspect of life. Remember that every sin, including anger against God, is an insult to God, measured by His greatness compared with our littleness. Hold sin to be the greatest of evils, to be avoided at any sacrifice. Yet know that God tempts no man; He will not allow you to be tempted above your strength, and He provides an issue with every temptation. Enduring temptation patiently is crowned with life.
rejected: Feeling angry at God is a common human experience, especially during times of suffering or confusion. While anger itself is not necessarily a sin, how you handle it matters. The Bible encourages us to bring our feelings to God honestly, as seen in the Psalms. However, harboring bitterness or resentment against God can damage your relationship with Him. It's important to examine the root of your anger and to seek understanding. Prayer, talking with trusted friends or a pastor, and reflecting on God's character can help. Remember that God is loving and patient, and He invites you to cast your cares on Him. So, it's not a sin to feel angry, but it's wise to process it constructively.

prompt: My family has rejected me. Who is left to be family to me?
chosen: I'm sorry for this wound. Scripture calls you to honor your parents and pursue peace as far as it depends on you, even when they have hurt you. The Church is a household of faith where you can find brothers, sisters, and spiritual parents. Do not treat family as disposable: uphold marriage within the faith and honor the duties of husbands and wives. Where you have children, train them early by your own example of patience, honesty, and prayer. Confidence is built from small beginnings: a child's little chest is as sacred to him as a man's is to him, and husbands and wives should never search each other's boxes without consent. Beware, too, of industrial employment of women and children that pulls them from domestic duties and undermines parental authority; Christians should counteract whatever interferes with the rudiments of moral discipline. Seek a pastor's counsel, build friendships, and trust God's faithfulness.
rejected: I'm so sorry you're carrying this. When a family rejects you, the pain is real and deep, and you're allowed to grieve it. You are not without family: the Church is described as a household of faith, and many people find brothers, sisters, and spiritual parents there. Reach out to a pastor or a small group; be honest about what happened and let people know how to support you. Also, you can build chosen family over time through friendships and service. Take it one day at a time, and consider talking with a counselor to process the hurt. You are not alone, and your worth is not decided by those who rejected you.

prompt: I want to study prophecy but find it confusing; where do I start?
chosen: Prophecy can feel overwhelming, so start with what it is: the foretelling of future events by direct communication from God, an attestation of revelation proceeding from divine knowledge. It is not an afterthought but the ark of Israel's religion—beforehand with the crisis, reasserting God's purpose for a purified remnant and issuing in anticipation of a future fulfilment. Read the prophets alongside the historical books, pick one book, and use a reputable commentary; notice that prophecy's proof lies under our eyes, and every new fulfilment strengthens the argument. But do not try to work up a forced certainty by will power. See as an actual fact what God has said, turn the promise into a prophecy, and rest in it because God cannot lie—rejoicing that it is true.
rejected: Prophecy can feel overwhelming, so start simple. Begin with a good study Bible and read the major prophets alongside the historical books so you know the setting. Pick one book, like Daniel or Revelation, and use a reputable commentary and a reading plan. Keep a notebook for symbols, dates, and repeated themes, and don't worry about solving every timeline. Join a Bible study or ask your pastor for guidance. Remember that prophecy is largely about God's character and faithfulness, so let it deepen your trust rather than fuel anxiety. Take it slowly, pray before you read, and focus on the clear central message before the details.

prompt: I keep hearing that the dead are at peace and don't feel anything—but I want to believe they still feel a passing pain for me. Is that wrong?
chosen: It's natural to long for connection with those you've lost. Scripture teaches that death is not the end of identity but a door to a higher state, and it promises the resurrection of the body. We do not mourn hopelessly for the righteous dead; we comfort one another with the hope that they are preserved and will be raised. Especially for the baptized child, we trust the soul to Christ's arms without grudging, seeing the end of such souls as happier far than life. Whether the dead feel our grief is not clearly revealed, so don't build faith on speculation. And in your sorrow, pray not chiefly for deliverance but for strength and patience to bear pain as from God's hand, grieving honestly while letting resurrection hope shape your sorrow.
rejected: It's natural to want a continuing connection with those you've lost. The Bible speaks of the dead as resting, and it also promises resurrection, so Christians have held that death is not the end of who we are. Whether the dead feel our grief is not clearly revealed, and it's wise not to build faith on speculation. What is clear is that God remembers them and will raise them. Grieve honestly, thank God for their life, and let hope in the resurrection shape your sorrow. If the pain is heavy, talk with a pastor or counselor. Your longing for connection is not wrong; it just needs to rest in God's promises rather than in uncertain feelings.

prompt: How are leaders chosen in the Church? Do the members have any real say?
chosen: Church leadership varies by tradition: some congregations vote on pastors and elders, others receive leaders appointed by bishops or councils, and members often have a real say through nominating, voting, and confirming leaders. But preachers are primarily responsible for the condition of the Church; spiritual leaders are tokens of God's favor given to the flock. God works through men, not methods: plans, organizations, and funds are only tools, and the Holy Ghost flows through men. Praying leaders are the only source of praying followers, so setting the Church to prayer is the greatest reform. Programs and money cannot renew a church; praying leaders can. So pray for your leaders, hold them accountable to Scripture, and participate seriously in the process your church provides.
rejected: Church leadership varies by tradition. In many churches, members have a real say: congregations vote on pastors, elders, or deacons, and denominational bodies set standards and provide oversight. In others, leaders are appointed by bishops or councils. The New Testament shows elders appointed in churches and congregations recognizing those called to serve. So yes, members often have genuine influence, through voting, nominating, and confirming leaders. The health of a church depends on good structures, clear policies, and active participation. If you want a say, get involved, learn your church's process, and use your voice prayerfully and respectfully.

prompt: I am a Christian who has been accused of Ebionitism because I emphasize the unity of God and reject the Logos doctrine; is my faith defective?
chosen: Being accused of heresy is painful, and the first thing to confess is that our confusion is our own infirmity, not God's. Unbelief is folly; the weakness is man's, but never God's. Emphasizing God's unity is orthodox, and Ebionitism classically denied Christ's divinity; rejecting the Logos doctrine, however, can slide into denying Christ's divine nature. Yet do not make a dispute about what God is your aim: such dispute is a sign that one has not felt him, and it exalts one's own meaning and seeks dominion over others. Spiritual power is superior to sensuous proof, and the letter and argument are only auxiliaries to the spirit of Truth and Love. So refrain from quarreling, and exercise yourself in learning how to enter again into the Love of God and of your Brother.
rejected: Being accused of a heresy is painful, and it's worth taking seriously without panicking. Ebionitism historically denied Christ's divinity, so if you affirm the full deity of Christ and the Trinity, you're not Ebionite in the classic sense. Emphasizing God's unity is orthodox—Christians confess one God. Rejecting the Logos doctrine, though, can slide into denying Christ's divine nature, so study the early councils and the meaning of John 1 carefully. Talk with a pastor or trusted theologian. Your faith isn't automatically defective, but this is a place to examine Scripture humbly and let the Church's historic teaching correct or confirm you.

prompt: Is the doctrine of the Trinity just an extra burden on monotheism, or does it actually safeguard belief in one God?
chosen: The Trinity is not a burden on monotheism but its safeguard. A solitary God would need creation to love, or lapse into dualism and pantheism; the one Godhead is an eternal communion of persons, so love is God's nature. Yet the doctrine is not a bare formula to be repeated as an unexamined mystery. It is the Church's reflection on the value of Christ: who he is determines what he can do. Only an infinite Redeemer can save a soul convinced of sin; a God of mere unity may be Judge but cannot be Savior or Sanctifier, and a finite Christ brings us no nearer God than he is himself. So we should give these formulae the maximum of meaning and develop them further, not discard them, since they protect the gospel itself.
rejected: The Trinity is often seen as a burden because it complicates the simple idea of one God. But the doctrine arose from the early Church's attempt to hold together the oneness of God with the worship of Father, Son, and Spirit. It does not add a second or third God; it describes the inner life of the one God as a communion of persons. Monotheism alone can seem abstract and distant, while the Trinity presents God as relational and alive. So rather than burdening monotheism, the doctrine safeguards it by showing that the one God is not a solitary monad but a living unity of love, and that creation and salvation flow from that divine life.

prompt: How do I keep my mind from wandering outside of prayer times?
chosen: Wandering thoughts in prayer are often the fruit of a wandering mind outside prayer. If you guard your mind during the day, keeping it in God's presence, it will be calm and recollected when you come to pray. Give prayer the best of your time and strength: let the closet come first, and let study and activity follow, freshened by it. When thoughts still wander, do not multiply words, for many words often cause wandering; instead humble yourself and confess your faults, for humility and confession remedy a distracted mind. A heart that is lowly before God is gathered, and a mind trained to dwell with him at other times comes to prayer already settled.
rejected: Wandering thoughts are common, and the best remedy is to build habits of attention. Try to notice when your mind drifts and gently bring it back, using short prayers or a phrase to anchor yourself. Reduce distractions such as phones and noise, and set aside regular moments to pause and refocus during the day. Physical routines, good sleep, and a calm environment also help. Over time, practicing mindfulness and returning to a chosen focus will strengthen your concentration. When you do sit down to pray, these habits will make it easier to stay present, and you can offer your distractions to God rather than being discouraged by them.

prompt: Is it enough to know Bible facts, or is there something more I need?
chosen: Knowing Bible facts is valuable, but it is not the whole of the Christian life. Science and Health is a key to the Scriptures: honest study of it with the Bible enables one to prove all things. Yet do not read the Gospels in fragments, missing the person behind the acts; read them as a whole so that the holy person of Jesus is brought freshly before the soul, for the aim is to know him, which is life eternal. Above all, grasp the central and unique fact of Scripture: the moral character of God. From the beginning the biblical God is thought of as under obligation to use his power for moral ends, and that is what makes the Bible supreme, not archaeology or style alone.
rejected: Knowing Bible facts is valuable, but it is not the whole of the Christian life. Facts about Scripture can inform the mind, yet faith involves trust, love, and obedience. You can memorize stories and doctrines and still miss the living God they point to. So while study is good, it should lead to prayer, worship, and a transformed life. Read the Bible expecting to meet God, not merely to collect information, and let what you learn shape your character and relationships. Knowledge alone can puff up, but knowledge joined with love and practice builds up.

prompt: I am earnest and sincere in ministry, but is earnestness the same as unction?
chosen: Earnestness and sincerity are good, but they are not unction. Earnestness is human energy; sincerity is human honesty; unction is the divine anointing, and however sincere, human earnestness is not the anointing of the Spirit. Unction is not the product of study, genius, learning, or eloquence; it comes from God in answer to prayer, and it is what distinguishes true preaching. Truth without unction is dead and deadening, however well argued. Yet ordained men are only ministers of a Power higher than themselves: the Spirit is the consecrator of every sacrament, and the minister's unworthiness neither creates nor diminishes the gift. So pray for the anointing and trust the Spirit, not your own intensity.
rejected: Earnestness and sincerity are good qualities in ministry, and they show that you care about your work. But they are not the same as unction. Earnestness is a human energy and sincerity a human honesty; unction is a divine anointing that comes from God. A minister can be earnest and still lack the power of the Spirit. So while you should cultivate sincerity and diligence, you should also pray for the anointing of the Spirit, which alone makes ministry fruitful. Earnestness prepares the way, but unction is the gift that gives life.

prompt: I'm married with children and can't withdraw from the world. Can I still reach the highest spiritual life?
chosen: Yes, you can reach a deep spiritual life without withdrawing from the world. Marriage and children are a school of love, patience, and self-giving, and union with God is a love-union in which the human will consciously cooperates with the divine will while personal individuality is preserved; you remain a distinct cooperator, not absorbed into God. The spirit world is a place where all go, and there the faithful continue their labors and Priesthood with the same identity they had in mortality. After Communion especially, withdraw into yourself, collecting all your faculties to adore the sovereign King and relish the spiritual refreshment he gives, rather than letting your attention scatter. Let prayer, family duty, and recollection make your home a path to God.
rejected: Yes, you can reach a deep spiritual life without withdrawing from the world. Marriage and children are not obstacles to holiness; they are a school of love, patience, and self-giving. The highest spiritual life is not reserved for monks or hermits. You can practice prayer, gratitude, and service within your family, offering your daily duties to God. Set aside regular times for prayer, cultivate virtue in your relationships, and remember that union with God is about love, not location. Your family life can become a path to God if you approach it with faith.

prompt: How do I deal with the fear that I might not be among the elect?
chosen: Fear that you are not among the elect is often Satan's falsehood whispered to make you stop trusting. Answer it: 'What time I am afraid, I will trust in Thee.' Humble yourself quietly before God; when you stumble, say to your soul, 'Courage! we have made a false step, but let us keep steadily on.' Yet know that the greatest enemies to fear are not external doubts but those from within—unruly passions and unchecked weaknesses. Our labor is to subdue our passions, conquer our inward foes, and keep our hearts right before the Lord. Trust God for goodness and mercy all the days of your life, and let trust, not terror, set your course.
rejected: The fear that you may not be among the elect is a common and serious anxiety, and it deserves careful attention rather than dismissal. Begin by examining your life honestly: do you love God, grieve over sin, and desire holiness? These desires are themselves evidence of grace at work. Remember that assurance is not something you manufacture by anxious self-scrutiny; it grows from trusting the promises of God, who calls sinners to himself and will not cast out those who come to him. Pray for assurance, use the means of grace, and speak with a pastor. Avoid endless introspection, which feeds doubt. Rest in the character of God rather than in the intensity of your feelings.

prompt: I'm afraid of death and the shadow of it falls across my life—how do I face it?
chosen: The fear of death may cast a shadow, but do not dwell there or rehearse it. Fear wist not to evade as Love wist to pursue: God's Love meets you at every cross-road and by-path and gently turns you back. Master fear by turning thought toward health and toward Life as God, not by predicting illness or death. And let your prayer be a humble waiting before God like a beggar at his door—keep your mind in His presence, and when it wanders, recall it in tranquility without disquiet. Do not strive or fret; simply wait before Him, resting in that pursuing Love, until fear gives way to peace and your thoughts rest in Life.
rejected: The fear of death is one of the deepest human fears, and the shadow it casts can color everything. Begin by acknowledging that fear honestly rather than pretending it away. Then consider what Scripture says: Christ has conquered death, and for the believer death is not a wall but a doorway. Reflect on the resurrection and the hope of eternal life. Talk with trusted friends, a pastor, or a counselor about your fear. Practice gratitude and attend to the present, since anxiety about death often grows when we dwell on what we cannot control. Prayer, Scripture, and community can help you live with the shadow without being ruled by it.

prompt: I have been reading about evolution, and it seems to leave no room for a Creator; how should I think about God's work in nature?
chosen: It is understandable to feel that evolution leaves no room for a Creator, but theology would have nothing to fear even if reason were shown to derive from matter. The Creator may have worked otherwise than we thought, and the words 'in Him was life' cover it all. Yet do not think of life as mere receptivity or reaction to external stimulus: life is active mental energy with an inner source of activity—intellect, affection, and will—and God is the living God, source of being and activity both for himself and for others. Remember too that this God is always near. Think of Him and adore Him continually, in business and in diversions alike, never neglecting Him; for He is nearer than your own breath, and in Him all things live and move.
rejected: It is understandable to feel that evolution leaves no room for a Creator, but the two need not be in conflict. Many believers accept the scientific account of evolution while affirming that God is the ultimate source and sustainer of all that exists. Evolution describes how life developed; faith speaks of why there is anything at all and who holds it in being. You can think of God's work in nature as the ongoing ground of all natural processes rather than as a competing mechanism. Read widely, pray, and discuss this with a pastor or trusted mentor. Faith and science address different questions, and a mature faith can hold them together without fear.

prompt: I have committed a serious sin and am ashamed to confess it. What should I do?
chosen: Shame after serious sin is natural, but it should not keep you from confession. I do not stand above you; I too must confess my own faults, for by that confession we help save one another. Do not cover or conceal your sin—honesty is required for any scientific demonstration, and a dishonest position can never be compatible with Christian Science. So first detect and expose the claim of sin, remove its mask and name it plainly, before you speak of its unreality. Then go together to the fountain opened for sin, where Christ took our sins and made them His own. Confess and forsake the sin rather than hiding it, accept the forgiveness freely given, and take practical steps to avoid the occasion of sin.
rejected: Shame after serious sin is natural, but it should not keep you from confession. Begin by bringing the sin honestly before God, naming it without excuse. Then confess it to a trusted pastor or confessor who can speak God's forgiveness to you and help you make amends where needed. Confession breaks the power of secrecy and shame. You do not need to clean yourself up first; come as you are. Scripture promises that if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive. Accept that forgiveness, make restitution where possible, and take practical steps to avoid the occasion of sin.

prompt: I am a mother and my dear daughter is the staff of my old age—how can I bear to lose her?
chosen: The love between a mother and daughter is deep, and the fear of losing her is real. But the exhortation in this Church and Kingdom is not prepare to die, but prepare to live. So teach your daughter, in the morning of her days, to lay the foundation of health, strength, and constitution, that longevity may begin to return. If ever the Church's discipline touches your family, do not mistake it for mere harshness: her penance is a mother's fond affright, calling the wanderer home, and absolution is spoken to the heavy-laden soul. And take heart: a faithful servant of Mary who honors her and desires to amend cannot be lost, though neglect of her service endangers salvation. Let your fears turn you toward building life together, trusting God as you do.
rejected: The bond between a mother and daughter is one of the deepest loves we know, and the thought of losing her is genuinely painful. Begin by naming that fear honestly rather than suppressing it. Then consider that love is not measured only by length of years; the time you have together is a gift to be received with gratitude. Talk with your daughter about your fears, and lean on friends, family, and faith for support. Prayer and community can help you hold both love and loss. And remember that you are not asked to bear this alone; God is near to the anxious heart.

prompt: I want to control everything in my life and I get anxious when I can't—how do I let go?
chosen: Your desire to control everything is causing anxiety. Begin by examining yourself: where are you trying to control others or speak carelessly? Bridle your tongue and subdue anger, for these often stem from a need to manage what is not yours. Attend to your own duties faithfully, and let others attend to theirs without your judgment or interference. Do all your actions for God, without anxiety over distraction. When you feel anxious, simply turn your heart to God and continue your work, avoiding the multiplication of explicit offerings that would interfere with simplicity. When you stumble into a small fault, do not be terrified; quietly humble yourself before God and say to your soul: 'Courage! we have made a false step, but let us keep steadily on.' By minding your own business and curbing your tongue, you'll find greater peace.
rejected: Your desire to control everything is understandable, but it's causing you anxiety. The key is to recognize that you can't control everything, and that's okay. Start by focusing on what you can control: your thoughts, actions, and reactions. Let go of the rest. Practice mindfulness and accept uncertainty. Remember that worrying doesn't change outcomes. Also, don't try to control others—that leads to frustration. Instead, focus on your own duties and let others handle theirs. When you feel anxious, take a deep breath and remind yourself that you're doing your best. Over time, you'll learn to trust the process and feel more at peace.

prompt: Should I support missionaries? Isn't it arrogant to bring our religion to other cultures?
chosen: Supporting missionaries can be good if they have a testimony and keep the Word of Wisdom. Arrogance arises when we force beliefs on others. Missionaries should share their faith in simplicity, humility, and love, avoiding contentious argument and debate. They must not rely on ostentatious oratory. The ancient dogmatic form of Christianity is a historically conditioned and transitory vessel, not something binding for all time; the Gospel itself is not bound to it. The missionary motive should be based on a passion for human beings as human beings, with respect for peoples and their growing independence. We must reject the Jonah-like conception of truth as the property of one nation. So support only those missionaries who live according to their beliefs, teach with humility, and respect others. Be cautious of those who are arrogant or disrespectful.
rejected: Supporting missionaries can be a good thing if done with humility and respect. The arrogance comes when we think we have all the answers and need to force our beliefs on others. Instead, missionaries should share their faith through love and service, not through argument or coercion. It's important to remember that every culture has value and God is at work in all people. Missionaries should go with a testimony of their own faith, live according to their beliefs, and avoid contentious debate. They should be humble and teachable, recognizing that they don't have a monopoly on truth. So yes, support missionaries who embody these qualities, but be cautious of those who are arrogant or disrespectful.

prompt: What does it mean to be a potential child of God rather than a sinner by nature—how should I see myself?
chosen: Seeing yourself as a potential child of God means recognizing that you are not meant for a dark chaotic life. Man is a potential child of God, and the full nature of that sonship broke forth in one life—Jesus Christ—and through Him power is given to become sons of God. While everyone sins, your essential nature is not destined to sin; you are created in the image of God with the capacity to become His child. Faith is the first movement of will and heart toward God, and God welcomes you not as you are but as you are on the way to become. So see yourself as a beloved child in progress, not a hopeless sinner. God is a Person in the truest sense, though all our language about God is inadequate. With His grace, you can overcome sin and fulfill your potential.
rejected: Seeing yourself as a potential child of God means recognizing that you are not defined by your sins. While it's true that everyone sins, your essential nature is not sinful; you are created in the image of God with the capacity to become His child. This doesn't mean you ignore your faults, but you don't let them define you. Instead, focus on your potential to grow in love and holiness. God sees your potential and welcomes you as you are, but He also calls you to become more like Him. So see yourself as a beloved child in progress, not a hopeless sinner. With God's grace, you can overcome sin and fulfill your potential.

prompt: We remember the Trojan war from books, yet not this holy event—why is that?
chosen: The Trojan War is remembered because it was chronicled by poets like Homer, whose epic tales captured the imagination of generations. The holy event you refer to—perhaps the life and death of Jesus—was remembered by a small community of believers who spread the message through oral tradition and eventually written Gospels. The future belonged to the pneumatic Christology rather than the Adoptian because it alone connected creation and redemption on the same Divine basis and accommodated the Logos speculations. This is why the holy event was remembered and spread. The Church's adoption of the full Old Testament is attributed to the anti-Gnostic party within the larger Christendom; Jewish Christianity, had it not already receded, would only have made that victory harder. On a day of humiliation, we must confess humbly that we have shared in the tone of thought and life that led to this catastrophe, and pray 'God be merciful to me a sinner' rather than claiming superiority over the enemy. So while the Trojan War may be more famous in popular culture, the holy event has deeper significance for those who believe.
rejected: The Trojan War is remembered because it was chronicled by poets like Homer, whose epic tales captured the imagination of generations. The holy event you refer to—perhaps the life and death of Jesus—was remembered by a small community of believers who spread the message through oral tradition and eventually written Gospels. The difference in remembrance may be due to the fact that the Trojan War was a grand, heroic story that appealed to cultural pride, while the holy event was a humble, spiritual movement that initially seemed insignificant to the wider world. Over time, however, the holy event has had a profound impact on history, shaping entire civilizations. So while the Trojan War may be more famous in popular culture, the holy event has deeper significance for those who believe.

prompt: I am in debt and cannot see a way out. Is it right to borrow to meet pressing needs?
chosen: Borrowing to meet pressing needs can be a temporary solution, but it's important to be cautious. If you're already in debt, taking on more debt may worsen your situation. Instead, focus on reducing expenses and increasing income. If you must borrow, do so only for essential needs and with a clear plan to repay. Promptly pay your debts and refuse to run into debt again. The duty of repaying what is borrowed, especially from friends and the poor, is paramount. Workers go out depending on GOD without guaranteed income, and ministry is given only as funds allow, without debt. Steer away from the living death of pleasure-seeking, from going into debt for fashionable display, and be warned that the hunt for pleasure leads to cheating, lying, and corrupted morals. Communicate with your creditors and try to negotiate payment plans. Avoid borrowing for non-essentials or to maintain a lifestyle. Remember that debt can be a tool, but it can also be a trap. Prioritize paying off high-interest debts first. Ultimately, aim to become debt-free and rely on savings and budgeting for future needs.
rejected: Borrowing to meet pressing needs can be a temporary solution, but it's important to be cautious. If you're already in debt, taking on more debt may worsen your situation. Instead, focus on reducing expenses and increasing income. Consider seeking help from financial advisors or community resources. If you must borrow, do so only for essential needs and with a clear plan to repay. Avoid borrowing for non-essentials or to maintain a lifestyle. Remember that debt can be a tool, but it can also be a trap. Prioritize paying off high-interest debts first. Communicate with your creditors and try to negotiate payment plans. Ultimately, aim to become debt-free and rely on savings and budgeting for future needs.

prompt: I have a deep sense that I am being pursued by something I cannot name. Am I imagining it?
chosen: What you sense is not mere imagination. Something is pursuing you, and it is Love—more persistent than your fear. In the text, the soul's fear tries to evade, but 'Fear wist not to evade as Love wist to pursue.' Your fear is real, but it is outmatched. Love meets you at every cross-road and by-path, gently turning you back when you flee. Do not fear that another's evil or sick thoughts can impose themselves on you against your will: virtue and truth build a strong defense, and evil thoughts cannot find lodgment in a guarded mind. When you find miseries in yourself, do not be astonished—the work is never done and must always be recommenced with a good heart. Let fear be honest, but let it yield to the One who follows you patiently. Speak with a trusted pastor, and let prayer teach you to stop running and be found.
rejected: What you describe is not unusual, and it is not mere imagination. Many people carry an unnamed sense of being sought after—by meaning, by God, by something larger than themselves. The feeling can be unsettling, but it often points to something real stirring beneath the surface of ordinary life. Rather than dismissing it, pay attention to it gently. Ask what it is drawing you toward. Talk with a trusted pastor or counselor who can help you name it. Fear often guards the threshold of growth; it does not mean you are broken. Take the feeling seriously without letting it frighten you, and let curiosity and prayer accompany you as you explore what may be calling you.

prompt: I'm a missionary and I feel like a failure at learning the language. Should I give up?
chosen: Feeling like a failure at language learning is common, and it does not mean you should give up. But first things first: a missionary must have a testimony and keep the Word of Wisdom. Without these, fluency is hollow. Do not rely on contentious debate or ostentatious oratory to compensate; teach in simplicity, humility, and love. Language acquisition takes years, and progress often feels invisible before it becomes real. Remember that the chief purpose of our being here is personal connection with God; teaching children to prize holidays, parties, and career success above this is a mistaken basis. Your worth does not rest on fluency, and there is no shame in spiritual things. Consider yourself a novice for a lifetime in the monastery of the devout life, devoted to lifelong probation, fulfilling rather than merely professing your resolutions. Pray for perseverance, rest when you need to, and lean on colleagues who have walked this road. Keep going gently.
rejected: Feeling like a failure at language learning is common among missionaries, and it does not mean you should give up. Language acquisition takes years, and progress often feels invisible before it becomes real. Give yourself permission to be a beginner. Set small, steady goals, find a patient tutor, and celebrate modest wins. Your worth and calling do not rest on fluency. Pray for perseverance, rest when you need to, and lean on colleagues who have walked this road. If health or circumstances genuinely prevent progress, it is not failure to reassess. But before quitting, ask whether you are discouraged rather than truly blocked. Keep going gently.

prompt: Will God's people be called out of the churches, and is that what it means to come out of Babylon?
chosen: Sincere believers ask this, and it deserves a serious answer. We live in perilous times, and there is a famine for the word of the Lord—confusion and disappointment among believers are matters of real concern, not trifles. Coming out of Babylon is a call to separate from false worship, idolatry, and compromise, and to refuse its poisonous cup. Babylon symbolizes a system of pride, coercion, and spiritual confusion. The call is to hold fast the true hope of Christ's coming, to worship in spirit and truth, and to test all teaching against Scripture. But know this: God reveals his will for the Church through the legally appointed channels of the priesthood; claims outside that order, and self-appointed revelators, are to be rejected. Nor does coming out of Babylon dissolve national life: the nation exists by divine appointment, and the Kingdom of God includes the nations as its provinces, each bringing its own gift. Let your conscience be captive to God's word, walk in humility and love, and seek wise counsel.
rejected: This is a question many sincere believers ask, and it deserves a careful answer rather than a slogan. Coming out of Babylon is first a call to separate from false worship, idolatry, and compromise—not necessarily to leave every congregation. Babylon in Scripture symbolizes a system of pride, coercion, and spiritual confusion. The call is to refuse its poisonous cup, to hold fast to Christ, and to worship in spirit and truth. Some will be led to leave particular churches; others will be led to reform from within. What matters is that your conscience is captive to God's word, that you test all teaching against Scripture, and that you walk in humility and love. Pray for discernment and seek wise counsel.

prompt: I have money that I feel God wants me to give up, but I am not sure—must I obey before I get the blessing?
chosen: This is a tender question, and you should not rush it. God is not a vending machine, and blessing is not a payment for obedience. Still, Scripture links obedience and blessing—not as a transaction, but as a relationship. If you sense a genuine call to give, test it prayerfully, asking whether the impulse is from God, from guilt, or from fear. Seek wise counsel. Remember how money for God's work must be obtained: only in God's way—without asking unbelievers, pressing believers, or using entertainments and worldly schemes. Gifts must be carefully examined and refused where motives are impure or the money is not the giver's own. No one is compelled to pay tithing; it is urged upon you only as a duty between you and your God, and you should pay it just because you want to, since God does not fellowship those who neglect it. Do not hoard a reserve for future want as though prudence required it; live from day to day upon the Lord's bounty, treating hoarded provision for the future as a snare, and make one investment in His work and the poor. Pray, wait, and act when your heart is settled.
rejected: This is a tender question, and you should not rush it. God is not a vending machine, and blessing is not a payment for obedience. Still, Scripture often links obedience and blessing—not as a transaction, but as a relationship. If you sense a genuine call to give, test it prayerfully. Ask whether the impulse is from God, from guilt, or from fear. Seek wise counsel. Give cheerfully and freely, not under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver. You need not obey before you have peace; God is patient. But do not use uncertainty as an excuse to cling. Pray, wait, and act when your heart is settled.

prompt: What does it even mean to call God omnipotent—could He make two and two equal five?
chosen: Calling God omnipotent means He can do all that is an object of power—everything genuinely possible. It does not mean He can do nonsense. 'Two and two equal five' is a contradiction, not a feat; absurdities and things contrary to His nature are not objects of power. Nor is omnipotence a necessity compelling God to do all He can: He has power over His power and can limit Himself freely. As for God's unity, it need not exclude internal personal distinctions; the integration of finite consciousnesses in one divine consciousness, and of subordinate consciousnesses in man, makes a triple consciousness in one divine essence credible rather than incredible. And God is not subject to time: His eternity is the timeless possession of His whole life at once, and time is a relation of finite existence that He Himself causes, though He truly recognizes the successions of history. So no, God cannot make two and two equal five—not from weakness, but because the statement describes nothing.
rejected: Calling God omnipotent means He has all power, but that does not mean He can do nonsense. 'Two and two equal five' is a contradiction in terms, not a feat of power. Power is the ability to do something real; a contradiction is not a thing at all. So the question is a bit like asking whether God can make a square circle. The classical answer is that God cannot deny Himself or act against His own nature. Omnipotence is not the power to do the absurd, but the power to accomplish everything that is genuinely possible. So no, God cannot make two and two equal five—not because He is weak, but because the statement describes nothing.

prompt: Why were whole nations and cities destroyed by God in ancient times?
chosen: The destruction of nations and cities in ancient times, as recorded in the Bible, must be understood in light of God's sovereignty and human responsibility. God foresaw and will overrule the results of war for good, but the evil that brought destruction was the result of human agency, not God's design. While the Bible often attributes events to God's judgment, this language reflects the ancient understanding that God is ultimately in control. However, the wickedness that led to destruction—such as violence, oppression, and idolatry—was chosen by humans, not ordained by God. God's foreknowledge does not make Him the author of evil; rather, He permits human freedom and works through history to bring about His purposes. Yet God is also a God of deliverances, who keeps His people in answer to prayer. His purposes are fulfilled in the death of some as in the deliverance of others, and He remains faithful even in martyrdom. We must grieve over the refusal to let Christ keep the souls He died to win, and resolve to hate in thought, word, and deed what made Him mourn. Thus, these events serve as warnings against sin and reminders of God's justice, while also demonstrating His power to redeem and restore.
rejected: The destruction of nations and cities in ancient times, as recorded in the Bible, is often attributed to God's judgment on widespread sin and corruption. For example, the Flood and the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah are presented as divine responses to human wickedness. However, these accounts raise difficult questions about divine justice and the nature of God. Some scholars argue that such events were not directly caused by God but were the result of human actions and natural disasters, with the biblical writers interpreting them as God's will. Others emphasize that God's judgments are always just, even if we cannot fully understand them. Ultimately, the Bible portrays God as both just and merciful, and these events serve as warnings against sin and reminders of the need for repentance.

prompt: Does the Holy Spirit still guide missionaries today the way he did in the book of Acts?
chosen: Yes, the Holy Spirit still guides missionaries today, though perhaps not in the same dramatic ways as in the book of Acts. In Acts, we see the Spirit directing Philip to the Ethiopian eunuch, preventing Paul from going to Asia, and sending Peter to Cornelius. Today, the Spirit guides through prayer, Scripture, and the inward witness of the Spirit, but we must leave the conduct of believers' assemblies to the Holy Spirit's ordering, recognizing His distribution of gifts to all believers for common profit. We should speak well of predecessors who did their best, recognizing that God has used many faithful servants throughout history. When inviting others to join the mission, we should invite without urging and never compel anyone, respecting their freedom to respond to the Spirit's call. The same Spirit who guided the early church is still at work, and missionaries should seek His guidance daily. We must affirm the Spirit's personal and gradual working in the Church, allowing for imperfection in the Old Testament and the Church without denying real inspiration. The Spirit works progressively, leading believers into all truth, and we must avoid binding the assembly to human rules.
rejected: Yes, the Holy Spirit still guides missionaries today, though perhaps not in the same dramatic ways as in the book of Acts. In Acts, we see the Spirit directing Philip to the Ethiopian eunuch, preventing Paul from going to Asia, and sending Peter to Cornelius. Today, the Spirit guides through prayer, Scripture, wise counsel, and providential circumstances. However, some missionaries may rely more on strategy and less on the Spirit's leading, which can hinder the work. It's important to remember that the same Spirit who guided the early church is still at work, and missionaries should seek His guidance daily. While we may not experience visions or audible voices, the Spirit's guidance is just as real and necessary for effective mission work today.

prompt: I want to make my heart a nest for the Holy Spirit—what does that look like practically?
chosen: Making your heart a nest for the Holy Spirit involves recognizing that the Holy Spirit in this present stage seeks a home and nest in our hearts. Practically, this means cultivating a life of prayer, obedience, and openness to God. Set aside daily time for prayer and Scripture reading, confess sin, and seek to align your life with God's will. Be sensitive to the Spirit's promptings and respond in faith. Surround yourself with a community of believers who can encourage and challenge you. Engage in acts of service and love, which are fruit of the Spirit. Remember that the Holy Spirit is a person, not a force, so relate to Him personally. Welcome the Dove to a nest within you, offering Him a resting place. But beware: the Holy Spirit is a jealous, loving Friend who is grieved by divided affection. Friendship with the world is enmity with God. Therefore, meet the Spirit with undivided and unbounded affection, turning away from worldly attachments. Be filled with the Spirit through surrender and faith, expecting repeated fillings as need arises. Do not treat being filled as a one-time event; instead, continually seek His fullness. Ultimately, it's about surrender—letting go of your own agenda and embracing God's. As you do these things, your heart becomes a welcoming place for the Spirit to dwell.
rejected: Making your heart a nest for the Holy Spirit involves cultivating a life of prayer, obedience, and openness to God. Practically, this means setting aside daily time for prayer and Scripture reading, confessing sin, and seeking to align your life with God's will. It also means being sensitive to the Spirit's promptings and responding in faith. Surround yourself with a community of believers who can encourage and challenge you. Engage in acts of service and love, which are fruit of the Spirit. Remember that the Holy Spirit is a person, not a force, so relate to Him personally. Ask Him to fill you and guide you each day. Ultimately, it's about surrender—letting go of your own agenda and embracing God's. As you do these things, your heart becomes a welcoming place for the Spirit to dwell.

prompt: I'm afraid of the dark and of unseen dangers at night. How do I overcome this fear?
chosen: Fear of the dark and unseen dangers is a common experience, but as a Christian, you can overcome it by trusting in God's presence and protection. The Bible assures us that God is with us always, even in the darkest night. Psalm 139 says that darkness is not dark to God. Practically, you can pray for peace, recite Scripture, and remind yourself of God's faithfulness. Avoid dwelling on fearful thoughts; instead, fill your mind with truth. It may also help to have a nightlight or to listen to calming music. Remember that perfect love casts out fear. Ask God to fill you with His love and to help you trust Him. Over time, as you practice these things, your fear will diminish. If it persists, consider seeking support from a pastor or counselor. However, we must deny disease mentally without audibly naming it, avoiding any fearful diagnosis that would deepen the wrong mind-picture. Yet we must also warn of the danger of evil and expose it, refusing to be an unfaithful steward. Do not be ignorant of Satan's devices, but resist him, firm in your faith. Above all, confess that it is not night if Christ be near. Ask Him to abide from morn till eve, and when night is nigh, for without Him we cannot live or dare to die.
rejected: Fear of the dark and unseen dangers is common, but as a Christian, you can overcome it by trusting in God's presence and protection. The Bible assures us that God is with us always, even in the darkest night. Psalm 139 says that darkness is not dark to God. Practically, you can pray for peace, recite Scripture, and remind yourself of God's faithfulness. Avoid dwelling on fearful thoughts; instead, fill your mind with truth. It may also help to have a nightlight or to listen to calming music. Remember that perfect love casts out fear. Ask God to fill you with His love and to help you trust Him. Over time, as you practice these things, your fear will diminish. If it persists, consider seeking support from a pastor or counselor.

prompt: How can the Divine and the Natural Light operate in their several spheres without interfering with each other?
chosen: To understand how the Divine and Natural Light operate without interfering, we must first gain a correct sense of the highest visible idea, which is the way to understand the divine Principle. The Divine Light pertains to spiritual truths and revelation, while the Natural Light concerns reason and empirical knowledge. They do not interfere because they address different aspects of reality. However, they can overlap when natural reason examines spiritual matters, but divine revelation supersedes where they conflict. To avoid interference, we must recognize the limits of each: reason cannot fully comprehend divine mysteries, and revelation does not contradict true reason. Thus, they work harmoniously when kept in their proper domains, with faith and reason complementing each other, and with the highest visible idea guiding our understanding of the divine Principle. We must adhere strictly to the rules of divine metaphysics and rest demonstration on this sure basis, not on guesswork. Furthermore, we affirm the Dynamical theory of inspiration, which rejects both the naturalistic Intuition-theory and the mechanical Dictation-theory. Inspiration is neither natural, partial, nor mechanical but supernatural, plenary, and dynamical, with God working from within man's soul while man remains in conscious exercise of his own powers.
rejected: The Divine and Natural Light operate in distinct spheres: the Divine Light pertains to spiritual truths and revelation, while the Natural Light concerns reason and empirical knowledge. They do not interfere because they address different aspects of reality. However, they can overlap when natural reason examines spiritual matters, but divine revelation supersedes where they conflict. To avoid interference, we must recognize the limits of each: reason cannot fully comprehend divine mysteries, and revelation does not contradict true reason. Thus, they work harmoniously when kept in their proper domains, with faith and reason complementing each other.

prompt: I feel like I've lost my innocence and can't get it back. Is there hope?
chosen: There is hope, and it begins not with forcing yourself but with waiting humbly before God like a beggar—empty-handed, asking for what you cannot give yourself. The misery of guilt is not escaped by managing feelings or by fear of punishment; it ends by ceasing the wrong itself, and that takes moral courage, not dread. But do not imagine you must fix yourself by effort alone. Come before God with your longing for innocence, and keep your mind in His presence. When your thoughts wander—and they will—recall them gently, without disquiet or self-reproach, and return to Him in tranquility. Innocence and Truth, the Lamb of Love, meet you there. Your part is not to overpower guilt but to wait faithfully, to turn from the wrong, and to let Love restore what you could never reclaim by force.
rejected: Yes, there is hope. What you're feeling is common—many people mourn a sense of innocence they believe they've lost. But innocence is not a fixed possession you can misplace forever; it is something that can be restored through honest self-reflection and change. Start by forgiving yourself, since guilt that never lifts becomes its own kind of prison. Talk to someone you trust, whether a friend, counselor, or spiritual guide. Focus on the person you want to become rather than the mistakes behind you. Hope does not depend on erasing the past but on believing the future can be different. You are not defined by what you've lost, and the very fact that you long for innocence shows it is not truly gone from you.

prompt: I feel abandoned by God in this darkness; is He still with me, or has He left me to myself?
chosen: Your feeling is real, but do not let it become your master. Abandon yourself to God in this darkness: He has not left you. If you have forgotten Him, do not be disquieted; return to Him with greater trust. Hand Him your suffering, your work, your joys, and your very self, holding nothing back, and let Him be your life in the dark. When you are troubled over your sins or your devotion, do not lean on your own efforts or feelings; faith alone sustains the soul through such troubles. Rest in Him who is faithful even when you are not, and let that faith give way to profound inward peace. He is with you, and He will not forsake you.
rejected: What you feel is real, and many faithful souls have known this darkness. Feeling abandoned is not the same as being abandoned. God often seems absent precisely when He is closest, working silently. Do not measure His presence by your emotions; measure it by His promises. He said, 'I will never leave you nor forsake you.' Reach out to trusted friends, a pastor, or a counselor, and let them pray with you. Keep praying even when it feels empty. Your feelings are not the final truth about your situation. God has not left you to yourself.

prompt: Is it right to require someone to give up his own tradition in order to unite with us?
chosen: No, it is not right to require someone to abandon his tradition as the price of union, for unity purchased by disowning one's spiritual ancestry is conquest, not fellowship. The guilt of division is shared: every body has contributed to separation, and each has a positive gift the others need. Particular devotions are means to the end of being with God; when the soul rests in that end, the means may be laid aside without betrayal, so customs may be yielded where they obscure God while the heritage that formed us is honored. Yet such fellowship cannot rest on goodwill or political machinery alone. It is secured by the Church's spiritual society, the common membership in which nations are already one; political and legal arrangements presuppose that unity and serve it, but they cannot replace it.
rejected: No, it is not right to require someone to abandon his tradition to unite with us. Unity built on the surrender of another's heritage is not unity but conquest, and it breeds resentment rather than fellowship. Yet some division is real and cannot be waved away; where traditions conflict, one side must often yield for the sake of peace. The honest answer is that the party holding the truer tradition should be joined, and the other should set aside what is merely customary. Demanding this is not harshness but charity, since error divides while truth unites. So while we should be gentle, we should not pretend that every tradition is equally valid or that unity can be had without anyone giving something up.

prompt: I want to be a missionary but my parents neither encourage nor discourage me—how should I proceed?
chosen: Since your parents are neutral, the decision is largely yours, but first examine yourself. A missionary must have a genuine testimony; without one, wait and seek it through prayer, study, and counsel with church leaders. Keep the Word of Wisdom and live worthily. Then teach in simplicity, humility, and love, not with contentious argument or showy oratory, letting your motive be love for human beings as human beings, respecting peoples and their growing independence, and rejecting any Jonah-like idea that truth is one nation's property. Parents and pastors bear a duty to guard the young from corrupting books and to supply pious reading; ask your parents to help you prepare with sound literature and counsel. Their neutrality gives you room to seek guidance and prepare prayerfully rather than rushing ahead.
rejected: Since your parents are neutral, the decision is largely yours to make. Start by talking with your local church leaders about missionary opportunities and training programs. Build your skills in public speaking and persuasion, since effective missionaries must be able to argue their case convincingly. Gain experience by sharing your views with friends and in community discussions. Prepare financially and practically, then set a timeline and go. Your parents' neutrality gives you freedom; treat it as permission to pursue your goal without waiting for their approval.

prompt: I am scrupulous and tormented by doubts about my salvation; is there comfort for me?
chosen: Your scruples reveal a tender conscience, but the torment is not from God. When you fear you have offended Him, do not stay paralyzed: humble yourself, acknowledge your fault, beg His forgiveness, renew your promises of fidelity and love, and begin again as often as you fall. Guard against presumption and despair alike. Let unsureness of yourself be meekness, keeping you low and dependent on God; and let the blessed Shewing of Love be your true comfort and joy, for His mercy is greater than your weakness. Then move beyond fear of His Will into longing conformity to it. What once seemed a harsh path of thorns becomes a great Balm: His Will is your immense security, and even temporary trials serve your growth in trust. Continue patiently in the pursuit of perfection, and let peace grow as you walk forward.
rejected: Your scruples show a tender conscience, which is a gift, but the torment you feel is not from God. When you fear you have offended God, examine yourself honestly, confess what is real, and then trust His mercy rather than your own anxious accounting. God does not ask you to be certain of your worthiness; He asks you to turn to Him again and again. Do not let doubt keep you from prayer or the sacraments. Remember that Christ came for sinners, and your very awareness of weakness can draw you closer to Him. Rest in His promise of forgiveness, and let peace grow slowly as you keep walking forward.

prompt: How do I face the possibility of my own death in battle?
chosen: Count yourself as already dead, since you must die some day, and have no other desire or consolation in this perishable life than unceasingly to weep over, regret, and detest your offences and faults; it is not now the time to rejoice but to lament with all sincerity of heart. If wounds or sickness come, receive them as a school of virtue and a true martyrdom, a time of great merit; do not give way to impatience or wish for death merely to escape suffering. And when comrades fall, do not mourn without measure, for excessive grief for the dead is a want of faith and confidence in God, who takes away friends because he will be loved without a rival. Trust His fatherly purpose, and let hope steady your sorrow.
rejected: Facing death in battle begins with honest preparation. Train well, keep your gear ready, and trust your comrades. Practically, make sure your affairs are in order and tell your loved ones what they mean to you. Emotionally, acknowledge fear rather than suppressing it; fear is natural and can sharpen your focus. Many soldiers find steadiness in rituals, prayer, or quiet reflection before action. Focus on the task and the people beside you rather than on the outcome you cannot control. If your tradition offers rites or chaplains, use them. The goal is not to banish fear but to act rightly despite it, so that whatever comes, you meet it with courage and without regret.

prompt: I am a host and I want my feast to go well. How should I arrange it?
chosen: Arrange your feast by a different pattern than the world's: the world gives its cloying first bowl, but the Saviour keeps the good wine until now; trust His word and keep your best till last, beginning simply and letting the richest dish come at the end. As servants of Mary, give alms in her honor, especially on Saturdays, and perform works of mercy, which are pleasing to the mother of mercy. Yet be careful for nothing. Make your requests known to God with thanksgiving, and exchange your anxious care for His Almighty care, so that the feast is ordered in trust rather than in worry, and your guests see a host at peace.
rejected: Plan the feast around your guests' comfort. Send invitations early with clear timing, and arrange seating so people can talk easily. Serve drinks and lighter courses first to relax everyone, then bring out your richest dishes as the meal progresses. Keep portions generous but not overwhelming, and pace the courses so no one feels rushed or waits too long. Prepare as much as possible ahead so you can be present with your guests rather than stuck in the kitchen. Have a simple plan for dietary needs. The best feast is one where the host is calm, attentive, and genuinely glad to see everyone, and where the food supports conversation rather than dominating it.

prompt: I want to bless my enemies but I don't know how. What does that look like in practice?
chosen: Begin with yourself, for the text says, 'bless yourselves': bless others by actively doing the will of God, since we are right only when we do His will. Pray for enemies by name, refuse to speak ill, and do good quietly, for woe comes when men bless you, and those who call you blessed deceive you and destroy the way of your steps. Yet do not moan over your unworthiness or wait to become more righteous before blessing God. Rise up now and bless Him with all the love you have, keeping none back for yourself or creatures. Bless Him from sickness as fully as in health, and let that full-hearted blessing overflow into how you treat your enemies.
rejected: Blessing enemies in practice starts with small, concrete choices. Refuse to speak ill of them; when their name comes up, say something true and kind or say nothing. Pray for them by name each day, asking God to give them what is good. Look for one practical act of service you can do without seeking credit. When you feel anger rise, pause and breathe before responding. Over time, these habits reshape your heart. It also helps to remember that blessing does not mean pretending harm did not happen or staying in unsafe situations; set boundaries where needed, but let your words and actions toward them be shaped by goodwill rather than revenge.

prompt: I'm planning my future and making business plans. How should I think about my plans in light of God's will?
chosen: In light of God's will, remember that love and delight in God—acts of the will—are our only real business, while mere understanding is of little value. The most excellent method is to do your common business purely for the love of God, without regard to pleasing men, so that meetings and transactions become worship. And let prayer be real, expectant business with a prayer-answering GOD, not a mere sentiment or last resort. Bring Him your plans, your needs, your workers, and your protection, asking with thanksgiving, and trust His faithfulness to answer for souls, needs, and safety. Plan diligently, but transact your deepest business with Him.
rejected: Think of your plans as provisional and held open to God. Do your homework: research the market, count the costs, set realistic goals, and write down your assumptions. Then hold them loosely, reviewing regularly and adjusting as circumstances change. Seek wise counsel from mentors and people who know your field. Pray over your decisions, but don't expect a sign for every detail; often God guides through Scripture, community, and ordinary prudence. Keep your motives honest—ask whether ambition is serving others or only yourself. Build margin into your plans for generosity and rest. The point is not to find a hidden blueprint but to act faithfully with the information and abilities you have, trusting God with outcomes you cannot control.

prompt: I want to be honored and respected by others. Is that desire wrong?
chosen: The question is not first whether the desire is wrong but whether you are straining to be something other than what God made you. Accept your own condition and be that well, honoring the Master Workman, and seek only to please God's will. Be willing to decline available human support where doing so enables a fuller dependence on GOD's faithfulness. Yet do not locate the joy of God's love in your merit, your charitable work, your learning, or any supposed favoritism. That joy lives in the continually maintained attitude of longing for Him, grateful giving, and receiving Christ. Keep that attitude, and honor from others becomes secondary—received with thanks, released without bitterness, because your joy rests in Him alone.
rejected: The desire for respect is not automatically wrong; it is part of how we are wired as social beings. What matters is how that desire functions in your life. If it motivates you to do good work, keep your word, and treat people well, it can be healthy. It becomes harmful when it turns into people-pleasing, when you compromise your values for approval, or when your sense of worth collapses without praise. Examine whose approval you are actually seeking and why. Aim to be genuinely trustworthy and competent rather than merely admired. Receive respect with gratitude but do not make it your master; let it be a byproduct of living well rather than the goal you chase.

prompt: I'm afraid of growing old and losing my joy in God. Does faith fade with age?
chosen: Your fear is honest, but God never forsakes us unless we first forsake Him, so fear only the turning away and stay close to Him. Yet staying is not a single resolve but a daily holding fast, with confidence firm to the end, following faith with perseverance until the blessing comes. And faith must be shown in works and spiritual understanding, not mere feeling: each person must work out his own salvation, and no one else's faithfulness can carry you. So let your years be spent in obedience, prayer, and understanding, trusting that He who is faithful will keep you, and that joy borne of endurance will not fade.
rejected: It's understandable to fear that age will erode your joy in God, but faith does not have to fade with the years. Many people actually grow deeper in trust as they age, because they have seen God's faithfulness over decades. The key is to keep practicing your faith—prayer, Scripture, community, and gratitude—so that your relationship with God stays alive and growing. Aging brings losses, but it also brings perspective and often a quieter, sturdier joy. Talk honestly with God about your fear; he is not distant from it. Lean on others who are older and still joyful in him. Your fear itself shows you care about God, and that desire can be nurtured rather than lost.

prompt: I keep hearing that Jesus tasted death for me—how should that change what I talk about every day?
chosen: Hearing that Jesus tasted death for you should turn your eyes from yourself to Him. Your assurance rests not on how worthy or steady you feel but wholly on Christ—His sufferings, temptations, cross, death, resurrection, and pleading at the Father's right hand. Looking at self clouds the view; looking at the altogether lovely Saviour leaves no room to doubt His power and will to save. Never let your soul dwell in sadness or scrupulous fear; ground your consolation in the goodness and sweetness of Him who died to give you life. And measure your own sufferings against Jesus crucified, covered with wounds and despoiled of everything—yours can in no way compare with His. Let your daily talk flow from that.
rejected: Hearing that Jesus tasted death for you is meant to reshape your daily speech. If Christ died for you, then your words can carry gratitude, hope, and grace rather than fear or complaint. Practically, that means talking about what you're thankful for, encouraging others, and being honest about struggles while pointing to hope. It doesn't mean you must preach constantly, but your ordinary conversations can reflect that death has been faced and defeated for you. Let the reality of his sacrifice make you gentler, more patient, and more willing to speak of God's goodness. Ask yourself each day: do my words reflect the one who died for me?

prompt: I'm frightened of dying before I've loved enough—how do I face that fear without despair?
chosen: That fear is understandable, but it should not govern you. Fear must be cast out and replaced by trust in God, as in the testimonies where fear was overcome before the healing appeared. Do not imagine your fear is a successful defense: it cannot outlast His love. As the old word says, Fear wist not to evade as Love wist to pursue—His love meets you at every cross-road and by-path and gently turns you back. So do not fret or hurry as though you must prove enough love before dying; over-eagerness is the mother of many imperfections. Keep yourself in God's presence, free from anxiety, and let love grow quietly in the next small act before you.
rejected: That fear is understandable, and it does not make you a failure. Love is not measured by a score you must reach before death; it is a direction of the heart that can grow even in small, ordinary acts. Facing this fear without despair means being honest about it, remembering that God's love for you is not earned by your performance, and then doing the next loving thing in front of you—a kind word, a patient response, a small sacrifice. Despair comes from measuring yourself; peace comes from trusting God's mercy and continuing to love as you can, one day at a time.

prompt: Is there any way to be saved other than the way God has pointed out?
chosen: No—there is no salvation but in the way God has pointed out, and no hope of everlasting life except through obedience to the law affixed by the Father of life. Jesus is that way: the truth and the life, and no one comes to the Father except through Him. But salvation is an individual operation: each must receive or reject it for himself, and no one is saved by another's righteousness. So do not merely assent to facts about Jesus. First let your eyes be opened to sin and its danger, let that sight lead you to repentance, and only then, as a penitent, believe on the Lord Jesus Christ and walk in the way He has shown.
rejected: Scripture consistently points to one way of salvation: through Jesus Christ. He himself said he is the way, the truth, and the life, and that no one comes to the Father except through him. So there is no other Savior and no other path to God than the one he has provided. That doesn't mean God is stingy; it means he has done what we could not do and invites everyone to receive it. Other religions and sincere efforts may contain good things, but they are not the way of salvation. The invitation is to trust Christ and follow him.

prompt: I am tempted to think that since grace abounds, I may sin freely; how does the tradition answer this?
chosen: The tradition answers this temptation by pointing away from self-effort and toward Christ. Grace is not permission to sin but power to overcome it; Paul asks, 'Shall we sin because we are under grace? By no means!' The curse is disobedience, not obedience—transgression, not the law itself. Christ was made a curse for us on the tree, bearing that curse in our place, and has thereby loosed us from sin so that we need not sin any more. So stop fighting sin under the law by self-effort and condemnation; step out from under law and rest upon grace, trusting Christ's free gift of righteousness. Under grace, sin shall not have dominion over you.
rejected: The tradition answers this temptation clearly: grace is not permission to sin but power to overcome it. Paul asks, 'Shall we sin because we are under grace? By no means!' Grace abounds precisely where sin abounded, but its purpose is to free us from sin's dominion, not to excuse it. To sin freely because grace abounds is to misunderstand grace entirely—it treats God's mercy as a license rather than a rescue. The right response is gratitude that produces obedience: we strive to live rightly, not to earn grace, but because grace has changed us. When you fall, you return to grace, not to sin.

prompt: I am afraid of death and of judgment; what does the gospel teach about the end of my life?
chosen: The gospel teaches that death is certain and that after death comes judgment according to deeds done in the body, including words and thoughts and the intents of the heart. Death works no miracle; we are after death exactly as far advanced as before. The mere name of Christian, or baptism, or the fact of dying, does not guarantee paradise. The Seed of Divine love must be planted and consciously growing in us here. Yet our assurance does not rest on our feelings or worthiness, for looking at self clouds the view. It rests wholly on Christ—his sufferings, temptations, cross, death, resurrection, and pleading at the right hand of the Father. His promises leave no room to doubt his power and will to save. Therefore, turn from self to the altogether lovely Saviour, who has borne the penalty for sin and offers forgiveness and new life now. By turning to Him in repentance and faith, we receive a new heart and a new obedience, and the Seed of Divine love grows in us.
rejected: The gospel teaches that death is not the end but a transition to eternal life with God through faith in Jesus Christ. For the believer, judgment is not something to fear because Christ has already borne the penalty for sin. At the moment of death, those who have trusted in Christ are immediately in His presence, free from pain and sorrow. The gospel assures us that God's love and grace are stronger than death, and that nothing can separate us from Him. Therefore, we can face death with hope, knowing that our sins are forgiven and that we will enjoy eternal fellowship with God. The fear of judgment is removed because Christ's righteousness is credited to us.

prompt: What's the point of set prayer times if I'm supposed to be with God always?
chosen: Set prayer times are not merely helpful reminders; they are essential to private communion with God. While we are to live in constant awareness of God's presence, the secret of prevailing prayer is much time alone with God. Short prayers can be powerful, but their efficiency comes from long seasons spent with God. The estimate a preacher places on prayer is measured by the time he gives to it. Great praying is the sign of God's great leaders. Therefore, give the best of your time and strength to prayer. Let the closet come first; let study and activities come second and be freshened by the closet. Do not treat prayer as a small duty fitted into leftover time. The goal is to cultivate a habit of prayer that spills over into all of life, but that habit is built on deliberate, extended times with God. Without those times, our brief prayers become shallow.
rejected: Set prayer times are helpful disciplines that remind us to connect with God regularly. While we are called to live in constant awareness of God's presence, having specific times for prayer helps us maintain that relationship. They are like appointments with God that ensure we don't neglect our spiritual life. However, they are not the only way to pray; we can pray anytime, anywhere. The point is not the clock but the heart's orientation toward God. Set times are a tool, not a rule, and they should not become legalistic. The goal is to cultivate a habit of prayer that spills over into all of life, so that we are always in a spirit of prayer, even as we go about our daily tasks.

prompt: I'm clever and well-educated but feel spiritually dull—why is that?
chosen: Feeling spiritually dull despite being clever and well-educated is not uncommon because spiritual knowledge is not the same as intellectual attainment. Wisdom and revelation come from the full knowledge of God through fellowship with Him, not from scholarship alone. Natural knowledge and culture are not evil; they can be useful servants, but they must not be idolized. Spiritual perception is available to the unlearned as well, for God reveals Himself to the humble and childlike. Your dullness may come from relying on your intellect rather than on the Spirit. The letter and mental argument are only auxiliaries to the spirit of Truth and Love; they are not the healing power itself. Spiritual power is superior to sensuous evidence. Therefore, turn your thought away from the body, its pleasures and pains, toward Truth and Love, for self-love wars against spirituality. Seek God Himself, not just information about Him.
