Cultivate fellowship with God through prayer, obedience, and love, and ask the Holy Spirit to give you spiritual understanding.
rejected: Feeling spiritually dull despite being clever and well-educated is not uncommon. Intellectual knowledge and spiritual perception are different things. You may have focused on acquiring information about God rather than cultivating a relationship with Him. Spiritual dullness can come from neglecting prayer, Scripture meditation, and fellowship with other believers. It can also stem from pride in your intellect, which can hinder dependence on God. The solution is to humble yourself, seek God with your heart, and ask the Holy Spirit to open your eyes. Remember that spiritual things are spiritually discerned, and no amount of education can replace a living relationship with God. Spend time in worship and service, and ask God to renew your passion for Him.

prompt: How do I obtain the unction you speak of? Can study or learning produce it?
chosen: Unction is the divine anointing that distinguishes true preaching. It cannot be produced by study, genius, learning, or eloquence. Unction comes from God alone, in answer to prayer and a life surrendered to Him. It is a gift of grace, not a result of human effort. To obtain it, you must seek God earnestly, humble yourself, and ask for the Holy Spirit's filling. Truth without unction is dead and deadening; it has no life-giving power. Therefore, do not rely on your education or talents. Pray for unction, live a holy life, and depend entirely on God's grace. Only the Spirit can give life to your preaching and ministry. Christian Science is demonstrable with one fixed method, and departure from its proven Principle forfeits the claim to belong to its school. So, put into practice the truth you already understand. Prove good by demonstration before seeking more understanding. Adhere to the proven Principle and practice it consistently.
rejected: Unction is the anointing of the Holy Spirit that gives power to preaching and ministry. It cannot be produced by study or learning alone, though study is valuable. Unction comes from God in answer to prayer and a life surrendered to Him. It is a gift of grace, not a result of human effort or eloquence. To obtain it, you must seek God earnestly, humble yourself, and ask for the Holy Spirit's filling. Study can prepare your mind, but only the Spirit can give life. Without unction, preaching is dead and deadening. So, pray for unction, live a holy life, and rely on God's grace rather than on your own abilities.

prompt: I have a dishonest, lazy employee and a difficult husband. How can these be anything but obstacles to God?
chosen: It's understandable to feel that difficult people are obstacles, but God is the one living Agent and all human workers are only His instruments. The dishonest employee and difficult husband are not obstacles but opportunities to see God at work. Cast all your care upon Him, for He cares for you. Worry and self-reliance are distrust of Him. Instead of trying to fix them in your own strength, trust God to work in and through them. Your part is to be faithful as His instrument, not to carry the burden yourself. Pray for them and leave the outcomes to God. He can turn obstacles into stepping stones. Remember that God's self-limitations in decree, creation, providence, inspiration, and the person and work of Christ are consistent with and expressive of His perfection. They are signs of His power and love, not denials of His infinity. So, trust in His perfect wisdom and love. Be faithful in the least, using the one talent and ordinary opportunity given, for God places solemn value on humble workers, and littleness will not excuse you from service.
rejected: It's understandable to feel that difficult people are obstacles to your spiritual life. However, God can use these very challenges to refine you and draw you closer to Him. The dishonest employee and difficult husband are not obstacles but opportunities for growth in patience, forgiveness, and love. God is sovereign over all circumstances, and He can work through them for your good and His glory. Instead of seeing them as hindrances, ask God to help you respond with grace. Trust that He is at work in you and in them. Your job is to be faithful in your own responsibilities, to pray for them, and to leave the outcomes to God. He can turn obstacles into stepping stones.

prompt: How do I deal with vain curiosity and the urge to read every new book and hear every rumour?
chosen: Vain curiosity is best met not by wrestling it down but by learning to wait before God like a beggar, hands open and mind quiet. Stand porter at the door of thought: when the urge to read every new book or hear every rumour knocks, examine it and shut out the unhealthy thought before it enters, for fear and restless craving admitted become the body's suffering. Do not scold yourself; refuse it at the threshold and gently bring your mind back into His presence. The wandering is not the failure—the disquiet is. But know the price: this waiting asks extraordinary lowliness and loneliness of spirit, and the drying up of ordinary interests and enjoyments, because God wills to have the whole of us. Do not turn back at that cost. Let prayer be this humble waiting, and let books and news be received later, in their place.
rejected: Vain curiosity is a real distraction, and the honest first step is to name it. Notice the itch to grab every new book or repeat every rumour, and ask what you are actually hoping to find. Often it is the fear of missing something, or a restless mind that dislikes silence. Practical limits help: choose a few worthwhile books, set times for reading, and let rumours pass without chasing them. Replace idle curiosity with something that feeds you—Scripture, good conversation, service. When the urge rises, pause, breathe, and turn your attention to what is in front of you. Over time the habit loosens, and you find more peace and focus.

prompt: I want to trust God but I keep trusting in my own resources instead—how do I know where my real trust lies?
chosen: Real trust in God is above circumstances and appearances. You cannot measure it by whether your savings, network, or plans remain intact, for the work hangs solely upon the good pleasure of God, not upon visible support. Hanging upon the invisible God is not hanging upon nothing. So trust Him with all your heart, and refuse to lean on your own understanding or the wisdom of others, for that leaning hinders faith. Do not demand to investigate whether God has told the truth before you commit. And remember that particular devotions—your methods, disciplines, and practices—are only means to the end; when the soul is with God, its end, they may be laid aside, for they become useless then. When support vanishes, place the work again upon His good pleasure, trusting Him even when every visible prop is gone.
rejected: The way to know where your trust really lies is to watch what you do under pressure. When a plan collapses or support disappears, notice where your mind runs first—to your savings, your network, your own cleverness, or to God. Practical test: try small acts of obedience that depend on God rather than on your backup plan, and observe your anxiety level. Keep a journal of worries and answered prayers. Honest self-examination, accountability with a trusted friend, and deliberate steps of faith will gradually reveal and shift your center of trust. Trust grows by being exercised, not by introspection alone.

prompt: I want to ask God for things, but does his power mean he must do everything he can, or can he choose to limit himself?
chosen: God's power is not a compulsion; He is free, and freedom means He can choose what to do and what not to do. Do not run from pressure and trial as though they were failures of prayer. Receive them as God's way of generating spiritual force and power, letting each hard pressure lift you above the painful cause rather than fleeing it. Yet keep within the landmarks of His word: the patronage of the world is not to be sought or depended upon, no debts are to be contracted, and appeals for money from unbelievers or reliance on fixed income are not the means of His work. The Living God alone is Patron, and prayer is the only appeal. And do not imagine that will-power governs anything—neither yourself nor others; Truth and Love are the motive-powers of man. Depend wholly on His blessing in answer to prayer.
rejected: God's power is not a compulsion. He is free, and freedom means He can choose what to do and what not to do. He is not obliged to act simply because He is able; His will and wisdom govern His power. So when you pray, you are not pressing a lever that forces a result. You are asking a free, wise Father who knows what is best. He may limit Himself for reasons we cannot see, and that is not weakness but purpose. Pray boldly, trusting His character, and leave the manner and timing of the answer to Him. His power is real, but it is always exercised in freedom and love, never under obligation.

prompt: I keep repeating general confessions out of anxiety. Is that healthy?
chosen: Repeating general confessions out of anxiety is not healthy, because the anxiety itself is the obstacle—over-eagerness is the mother imperfection of all imperfections. Do not hurry through confessions or fret over whether you said them rightly. Practise instead the faithful presence of God: stay quietly before Him, confess what you actually know, receive His mercy, and remain without agitation. When the urge to repeat rises, do not accept it as a real relapse—there is no real relapse in Truth. Meet its cause mentally and courageously: name the fear, face it, and conquer it. Use this mental practice only to promote right thinking and doing; if you turn it to selfish gain or wrong motives, the abuse diminishes and finally destroys the power to heal. Perfection is not in the number of your confessions but in dwelling with God without anxiety.
rejected: Repeating general confessions out of anxiety is common, but it is not the most healthy pattern. Anxiety-driven repetition tends to feed the very fear it tries to soothe, and it can keep you focused on yourself rather than on God's mercy. A better approach is to confess specifically what you are aware of, receive forgiveness with gratitude, and then move on rather than circling back to re-confess. If anxiety keeps pulling you back, address the anxiety itself—through rest, honest conversation, prayer, and perhaps professional help. Set a simple rhythm: confess, thank God for pardon, and trust that He has heard. Repetition born of fear does not make you more forgiven; it only deepens the worry.

prompt: I have been a Christian for some years and find my feelings less ecstatic than at first—is my religion declining?
chosen: Feelings never accurately gauge your real assimilation to God, so the fading of early ecstasy is no proof that your religion is declining. Do not measure yourself by moods. Rest instead on the changeless word of promise, and continue steadfastly in prayer when joy is lacking, refusing to abandon communion or service because of spiritual depression. But do not wait for joyful feelings before you rejoice: count it all joy by faith, reckoning the trial a blessing, fixing your heart and choosing to rejoice until praise becomes a habit. And remember that love is not mere sentiment or desire—it is the outgoing of your entire nature in self-sacrificing service, the supreme proof of the reality of your Christian profession. Let that love, not fading feeling, answer whether your religion is declining.
rejected: It is normal for the emotional intensity of early faith to settle over time. Feelings rise and fall for many reasons—health, stress, routine, personality—and they are poor measures of spiritual reality. Declining excitement is not the same as declining faith. What matters is whether you are still oriented toward God, still growing in character, still loving others. Many mature believers experience calmer, steadier devotion rather than ecstasy. Use this season to build habits that do not depend on feeling: prayer, Scripture, community, service. If the flatness persists and troubles you, talk with a pastor or counselor. Growth often looks quieter than beginnings.

prompt: I'm struggling with a habitual sin and I keep falling—is there any hope for me?
chosen: There is hope, and it begins here: God beholds you with pity, not blame. Yet do not treat sin lightly—unrepented sin accumulates and a conscience ignored grows dull—so repent honestly and reform your life, removing occasions and seeking help. But learn to distinguish temptation from sin: temptation is not sin but the means of proving virtue and gaining great profit, for the life of man upon earth is a warfare. Light temptations, suspicions, sadness, depression, and pusillanimity are mere nothings; a good will puts them to flight by an elevation of the soul to God. This passing life asks not that you live all without blame and sin; in falling and rising you are ever preciously kept in one Love. Lift your heart to God, and keep returning to change, not only to be comforted.
rejected: Yes, there is hope. Everyone struggles with sin, and God's mercy is greater than any failure. The fact that you are troubled by your sin shows that your conscience is alive and that God is at work in you. Keep praying, keep asking for forgiveness, and do not give up. Find someone you trust who can pray with you and hold you accountable. God does not abandon those who keep turning back to Him, even when they fall repeatedly. Take one day at a time, ask for grace each morning, and remember that His compassion is new every morning. Your struggle does not disqualify you from His love.

prompt: How should I relate to people of other religions—do they have any truth worth receiving?
chosen: Relate to people of other religions first as neighbors: treat passing strangers with kindness and respect, and let your example toward outsiders be worthy of imitation. It is no concern of yours whether a neighbor believes as you do if you can live as neighbors with him. Receive truth wherever you find it without surrendering your own convictions, and do not assume wealth or polished society is where faith is purest—often the poor cottage is a palace of God, and the poor in faith teach the most valuable lessons, while riches and worldly opinion obstruct humility. But remember what true, satisfying religion is: not external observance, doctrine, or feeling, but Christ recognised, known, adored, and living within the soul—the New Life and New Birth. Let that life in you be the example others are drawn to ask about.
rejected: Relate to people of other religions with respect and curiosity. Many traditions contain genuine wisdom about compassion, justice, and the sacred, and you can learn from them. At the same time, hold your own convictions with confidence, since you believe they are true. Honest dialogue is possible when both sides listen. You need not pretend all religions are the same, nor should you treat others with contempt. Ask questions, listen well, share what you believe gently, and look for common ground in moral teaching. The goal is mutual understanding and kindness, not victory in argument.

prompt: What does it mean that the same revelation of God continues in me that was made in Jesus?
chosen: It means that the same revelation of God made in Jesus continues in you—not merely as an example to copy, but as the very knowledge of God. In Christ we see God, and God is like Christ: self-giving, merciful, and faithful; the Old Testament's foreshadowings are gathered up and made clear in him. This revelation is final, yet progressive: each new truth is to be assimilated into the faith, enriching your knowledge of God rather than being met with protest or surrender. Nor did development end with Christ's teaching, for the Spirit continues His work in the Church, and there remains both the right and the duty of further development in Ethics and Theology. So the same revelation continues in you as the Spirit makes that character known in your heart, and as you receive each new truth humbly, letting it deepen rather than displace the knowledge of God in Christ.
rejected: It means that the truth about God which Jesus embodied is not confined to the past but can be reproduced in your own life. Jesus showed what a human being fully open to God looks like—loving, obedient, and faithful—and the same Spirit that filled him can shape you. So the revelation continues as you grow in Christlike character, as you love your neighbor, forgive, and trust God. It is a call to imitate Jesus and to let his teaching and example become the pattern of your own conduct, so that others might see in you something of what they saw in him.

prompt: I am starving and in chains—should I now confess what I have hidden?
chosen: The text shows how such confession comes: Judas is cast into a dried-up well, joyless and famished, weighed down with chains for seven nights; on the seventh day, his strength broken, he calls aloud to be released, saying he will joyfully show forth the holy tree and can no longer conceal his knowledge by reason of his hunger. Yet do not make a show of your grief: let fasting and penitence be hidden before the Father who sees in secret, keeping your sorrow from proud eyes. Confess your faults to God without excuse and without discouragement, neither justifying yourself nor sinking into despair. Then peaceably resume the practice of love and adoration, for the Father who sees in secret receives the returning heart, and love is the life to which confession restores you.
rejected: Yes, you should confess. When you are starving and in chains, hiding the truth only adds to your suffering, and confession can bring relief. Holding a secret while in distress is a heavy burden, and speaking it may open the way to help and release. Confess honestly to those who can act, ask for forgiveness where you have wronged others, and accept the help offered. Do not let shame keep you silent any longer. Confession is the first step toward freedom, and honesty, even when costly, is better than continued concealment.

prompt: I have been trusting God for my daily needs, but I am tempted to lay up a store against a time of sickness or old age. Is that wrong?
chosen: Commit your future wants to God's care without anxious hoarding, and use all proper means diligently. Provide for sickness or old age through honest work and wise saving, for Scripture commends prudence—but remember that God is the one living Agent and all human workers are only His instruments. With Him no emergency is unforeseen and no want unprovided for, so watch as well as pray, then cast all your care upon Him; anxious self-reliance is distrust of Him. And do not sink into gloom or perpetual self-condemnation as though that were the safe temper for tempted men. Strenuously lift your heart to God's goodness and exult in it, seeking His loving-kindness in all the breadth and open-air of common life—in whatsoever things are true, honourable, just, pure, lovely, and of good report—while not missing behind them the greatest Reality, God Himself.
rejected: It is not wrong to plan ahead, but the motive matters. Saving for sickness or old age can be responsible stewardship, provided it does not become anxious hoarding or a replacement for trust in God. The Bible commends diligence and prudence—the ant stores up in summer—while warning against worry about tomorrow. So provide for foreseeable needs through honest work and wise saving, but hold your savings loosely, give generously, and keep your trust in God rather than in your store. Ask yourself whether your saving is driven by fear or by love and responsibility, and let prayer shape your decisions.

prompt: I have lost someone I loved, and I feel like God took them from me. Why would He do that?
chosen: I am so sorry for your loss. It is natural to feel that God took your loved one, but know this: God loved you before He made you, and His love was never slacked. In that love He made all things profitable to you, even this loss. When He seems deaf, it is not indifference; He is granting your main desire by doing what is most expedient. Love was His meaning in all He shewed. And even in the lonely fen of grief, God is ever nigh, appearing like a father to the lost child. He kisses you, leads you by the hand to your mother, and holds you close. Your loved one is safe in Him, and you are held by a love that never changes. Keep crying out to Him; He hears, and He is working all things for your ultimate good.
rejected: I am so sorry for your loss. It is natural to feel that God took your loved one, but try not to see it that way. God is a God of love, and He does not take people from us out of cruelty. Death is a result of living in a fallen world, not a direct punishment. While God may allow suffering, He does not cause it. Instead, He grieves with you and offers comfort. Cling to the promise that He will never leave you nor forsake you. Your loved one is at peace, and you can find hope in the resurrection. Allow yourself to grieve, but also allow God to hold you in your pain.

prompt: How can I help someone who is bound by an addiction that they can't break?
chosen: To help someone with an addiction, first examine yourself. Cast the beam out of your own eye—overcome your own belief and fear of disease or sin—before attempting to help another. Then, be slow to take new steps. Be willing to have no will of your own. Ascertain God's will by prayer and the Word. Only then proceed with earnest, patient, believing expectation of His help. Remember the three keys that unlock thoughts: drunkenness (being filled with the Spirit), trustfulness (honest confession), and love (acceptance without judgment). Use these keys to unlock your friend's heart. Encourage professional treatment and support groups. Be patient, set boundaries, and pray. Your role is to be a loving presence, but only after dealing with your own fears and sins and testing every step by God's Word and prayer.
rejected: To help someone with an addiction, start by showing compassion and support. Encourage them to seek professional treatment and offer to help them find resources. Avoid judgment and blame, as addiction is a disease. Set boundaries to protect yourself and encourage healthy behaviors. Be patient, as recovery takes time. You can also involve support groups for both of you. Pray for them and with them if appropriate. Remember that you cannot force someone to change; they must want it. Your role is to be a loving presence and to provide practical help when they are ready.

prompt: Why is there such confusion now among those who once looked for the coming of the Lord?
chosen: Confusion among believers about the Lord's coming is a matter of urgent concern. We are in perilous times, and there is a famine for the word of the Lord. Many have drunk from the poisonous cup of Babylon—false teachings, worldly compromises, and speculative prophecies that distract from Christ. God's people are called to come out of Babylon and hold fast the true hope of Christ's coming. Do not be deceived by date-setting or sensationalism. Remember that Christianity is not a natural product of converging tendencies; it comes to the Gentile world and does not grow out of it. There may be a tendency towards the truth, but not a tendency to produce it. Christ is the One whom the converging lines could usher in but were powerless to produce. Yet we must look at the cross from the life side, carrying the light and glory of the resurrection, forgetting its sorrow in the eternal morning. Return to Scripture, prayer, and fellowship. Live faithfully, watchful and sober, with resurrection hope.
rejected: Confusion among believers about the Lord's coming is common because of differing interpretations of prophecy, date-setting, and disappointment when expected events don't happen. Many have been misled by false predictions. The key is to focus on the clear teaching of Scripture: Christ will return, but no one knows the day or hour. We should live faithfully, not be consumed by speculation. Confusion can also come from spiritual burnout or worldliness. Return to prayer, Bible study, and fellowship. Remember that God is not the author of confusion but of peace. Trust in His timing and remain watchful, but avoid getting swept up in every new theory.

prompt: I have a thorn in the flesh and a temper I cannot master—is this sin that keeps me from holiness?
chosen: Having a thorn in the flesh and a temper does not necessarily mean you are living in sin. Paul spoke of a thorn in the flesh, and God's grace was sufficient for him. Temper can be a weakness, but it becomes sin when you yield to it. Yet remember: sin confers no real pleasure. The wrong-doer may think he enjoys it, but it is a deception. This knowledge strengthens moral courage to master evil. But also affirm that one mortal sin unrepented is enough to damn the soul. Therefore, nourish an intense and abiding fear of sin and of eternal loss, so that fear may restrain you where love is too weak. Yet do not counsel gloom or despondency. Strenuously lift your heart to God's goodness and exult in it as the only safe temper for tempted men. Seek that loving-kindness in all the breadth and open-air of common life—in whatsoever things are true, honourable, just, pure, lovely, and of good report—while not missing behind them the greatest Reality, God Himself. Holiness is a process, and God is patient. Seek to master your temper through prayer, self-discipline, and accountability. God's strength is made perfect in weakness.
rejected: Having a thorn in the flesh and a temper does not necessarily mean you are living in sin. Paul spoke of a thorn in the flesh, and God's grace was sufficient for him. Temper can be a weakness, but it becomes sin when you yield to it. Holiness is a process, and God is patient with our struggles. Seek to master your temper through prayer, self-discipline, and accountability. Remember that God's strength is made perfect in weakness. Do not be discouraged; keep pressing on. If your temper leads you to harm others, confess and repent. God's grace covers your failures, and He is transforming you into Christ's likeness. Focus on progress, not perfection.

prompt: If God is limited in power, how can I be sure the world will turn out good on the whole?
chosen: If God is limited in power, it can be frightening to think the world might not turn out good. But we can trust that God is still good and loving. He works within the limits of nature and human freedom to bring about the best possible outcomes. However, we must remember that time and ability to labor are capital entrusted by God. We are stewards, and our acts, words, and thoughts will be brought into judgment. Therefore, we must use our time and talents wisely, cooperating with God's purposes. Our choices matter, and we are accountable. Yet we must keep God's standard inflexibly high. Do not bring the standard down to our failures. Instead, press on until we reach His highest will. Regarding evil, especially war: God foresaw and will overrule its results for good, but men's agency, not God's design, brought the evil. God is not the author of wickedness, yet He is sovereign over its outcomes. The future is open, but God's character is constant. He will do everything He can to ensure a good end. Our role is to cooperate with Him, making choices that align with His will. Love is the most powerful force, and God's love will not fail. So we can have hope, not because God controls everything, but because He is faithful and good.
rejected: If God is limited in power, it can be frightening to think the world might not turn out good. But we can trust that God is still good and loving, even if not all-powerful. He works within the limits of nature and human freedom to bring about the best possible outcomes. The future is open, but God's character is constant. We can be sure that He will do everything He can to ensure a good end. Our role is to cooperate with Him, making choices that align with His will. Ultimately, love is the most powerful force, and God's love will not fail. So we can have hope, not because God controls everything, but because He is faithful and good.

prompt: Will God punish the world in the last days, and will he warn us first?
chosen: Scripture says the last days will bring God's judgment, but God never punishes without first warning. He appeals to human reason through messengers: Noah before the flood, Lot before Sodom, the prophets before Jerusalem's fall. So too before the final judgment God sends His Spirit and messengers to call people to repentance. Yet the Judge is not a cold tribunal of law. The last judgment is committed to Jesus Christ, our Brother and Advocate, who judges with mercy and equity, so that those who trust Him may have boldness before that throne. Still, the judgments on the nations are real: they are God's means of purging wickedness and preparing the earth for the reign of Christ, who will rule the nations with a rod of iron. Mercy and severity meet in Him; the wise will heed the warning now.
rejected: Scripture says the last days will bring God's judgment on a rebellious world. Many passages describe plagues, fire, and wrath poured out on the wicked. But God is not arbitrary; He has always warned before He judges. Noah preached while the ark was built, Lot was warned in Sodom, and prophets cried out to Jerusalem before its fall. So too, before the final judgment God sends messengers and His Spirit to call people to repentance. The warnings are real, and so is the coming punishment. Those who heed the warning and turn to Christ will be spared; those who refuse will face the consequences. The question is whether we will listen now, while there is still time to repent and be saved.

prompt: How do I receive the Holy Spirit by faith, practically speaking?
chosen: Receiving the Holy Spirit by faith begins with believing God's promise: the Father gives the Spirit to those who ask. But first distinguish two things. At Pentecost God gave the Spirit once for all to His Church; that gift is not repeated for each believer. What remains is your personal appropriation of that gift by faith—trusting, asking, and yielding. The Spirit is not a private possession but the life of the Spirit-bearing body, consecrating ordinary life and working gradually and socially while intensifying personal character. Practically, yield to the Spirit of prayer: when a burden rises, bring it to God and pray it out, even in wordless prayer, before acting it out in life. Do not grieve Him by unfaithfulness to His faintest whisper. Confess known sin, ask the Father in Jesus' name, thank Him by faith, and walk in obedience within the body of believers, trusting the Giver to sanctify all of life.
rejected: Receiving the Holy Spirit by faith begins with believing God's promise. Jesus said the Father gives the Spirit to those who ask, so ask Him. Faith means trusting that God has given you His Spirit because He said He would, even before you feel anything. Practically, set aside time to pray, confess any known sin, and simply ask the Father for the Spirit in Jesus' name. Then thank Him by faith, believing you have received. Read Scripture, which the Spirit uses to strengthen faith. Fellowship with other believers helps too. Expect the Spirit to produce fruit like love, joy, and peace, and to give gifts for serving others. It is less about seeking experiences and more about trusting the Giver and walking in obedience day by day.

prompt: How can pouring out my life in service to others actually help me receive more of the Spirit?
chosen: Pouring out your life helps you receive more of the Spirit because it moves you from mere submission to glad, happy service to all who need it. We may be used as a human spark to ignite others, yet how God uses us remains a mystery; our part is faithful service, His part the hidden working. When trials come, do not give way to impatience, complaint, or passive despair. Wait patiently upon the Lord, taking whatsoever befalls from His hands as intended for your highest good, and play the part of a valiant soldier in the Spirit of Christ. Let the offering be your whole person: not outward labor only while sparing sensuality and the desire for honors and comforts, but a readiness to imitate Christ in bearing insults, reproaches, and poverty, both actual and of spirit, provided only it be for God's greater service and praise. So service becomes a channel: the more you give yourself away in glad love, the more room the Spirit has to fill you.
rejected: Pouring out your life in service helps you receive more of the Spirit because it takes your focus off yourself. When you serve others, you stop dwelling on your own spiritual experiences and start participating in God's work. Jesus said whoever loses his life for His sake will find it. Service cultivates humility, and God gives grace to the humble. It also opens your heart toward others, making you more like Christ, who came not to be served but to serve. As you obey and serve, the Spirit is unhindered in you. So service is not a distraction from receiving the Spirit; it is a channel. The more you give yourself away in love, the more room the Spirit has to fill you and work through you.

prompt: I've been told I'm a sinner and that Jesus' death paid for my sins, so I'm free. Is that the whole story?
chosen: That is the beginning of the story, not the whole of it. Yes, you are a sinner, and yes, Jesus' death paid for your sins, so you are forgiven. But sin is not merely a debt to be canceled; it is a personal condition of will and habit that spoils and enslaves the whole personality and casts a shadow on God's face. Forgiveness is the doorway, not the end: God wants to change your heart and make you holy. And be careful with freedom. We are called to liberty, but must not use liberty as an occasion to the flesh; the whole law is fulfilled in loving our neighbor as ourselves. Freedom is for loving service, not license. Know too that this life-giving word is costly—not technique or easy words, but death to self, crucifixion to the world, and the travail of the soul. Only a crucified man can preach crucified preaching. Receive forgiveness with gratitude, but keep going into a life of holy will, love, and the fellowship of Christ's cross.
rejected: That is the beginning of the story, not the whole of it. Yes, you are a sinner, and yes, Jesus' death paid the penalty for your sins, so you are forgiven and free. But forgiveness is not the end; it is the doorway. God does not merely want to clear your record; He wants to change your heart and make you holy. If you stop at 'I'm forgiven,' you can miss the purpose of salvation, which is to free you from the power of sin, not just its penalty. The whole story includes repentance, new birth, and a life of following Jesus. It includes the Spirit transforming your character and producing fruit. So receive the forgiveness with gratitude, but keep going: let God deliver you from the life of sin and lead you into a life of love and obedience.

prompt: How may I stand firm when Christ in me assaults Hell and my secret undiscovered sins awake and labour to separate me from God?
chosen: When Christ in you assaults Hell and secret sins awake to separate you from God, remember that the battle is fought within you. The enemy is not only outside; it is part of your own self—your habits, desires, and hidden will. So stand firm with real resolve. Turn to God in prayer, put on the armor, confess what you see, and ask God to search what you cannot. Christ has conquered sin and Hell on the cross, yet deliverance comes as God and man together batter the citadel of evil. Do not take sin lightly: one mortal sin unrepented is enough to damn the soul, so nourish an abiding fear of sin and eternal loss, that fear may restrain you where love is weak. But avoid self-tenderness, weeping, and complaints. Remain free and detached, wholly under the guidance of God's hand, neither pampering yourself nor despairing. Resist the devil, and he will flee. When you feel separation, run to God, not away, and let faithful believers pray with you.
rejected: When Christ in you assaults Hell and secret sins awake to separate you from God, remember that the battle is the Lord's, but you are not passive. Stand firm by turning to God in prayer and claiming His promises. Put on the whole armor of God. Confess what you can see of your sin, and ask God to search your heart for what you cannot see. Resist the devil, and he will flee. Remember that Christ has already conquered Hell and sin on the cross, so the outcome is secure. When you feel separation, run to God, not away from Him. Surround yourself with believers who will pray for you. Deliverance is God's work from outside, breaking in to rescue you; your part is to trust and keep looking to Jesus.

prompt: I want to be a good parent, but I worry I'm too strict or too lenient. How do I raise a joyful child?
chosen: Parenting is a sacred trust. To raise a joyful child, honor play as holy—it is the child's work and delight. Do not treat play as waste or idleness, for nipping the buds of joy and caging the bird born for joy destroys the summer to come. Avoid driving joy away through fear or confinement. Instead, be in advance of your child in mind and affection, providing innocent amusement and leading them so they delight to follow. Do not be behind with the whip. Beware of opposing a child's vocation or withdrawing them from a state of perfection; do not sow vanity and covetousness in their tender minds. Rather, form them in virtue. Set boundaries with love, not harshness, and encourage imagination and wonder. Model joy by delighting in simple things. A joyful child grows where play is respected, parents lead with love, and virtue is cultivated.
rejected: Parenting is a balancing act. To raise a joyful child, avoid extremes: set clear boundaries but allow freedom. Be consistent with rules, but also be warm and responsive. Spend quality time together, listen to your child, and validate their feelings. Encourage play and hobbies, as joy comes from engagement. Model joy yourself by showing gratitude and optimism. Avoid over-scheduling; downtime is important. Discipline with explanation, not harshness. Remember that joy is not constant happiness but resilience. Teach them to handle disappointment. Seek support from other parents or professionals if unsure. Ultimately, a joyful child grows in an environment of love, safety, and reasonable expectations.

prompt: I feel a heavy dread of my own sins that I have taken for humility—is it really meekness, or something else?
chosen: It's common to mistake scrupulosity or self-condemnation for humility. True humility dreads the esteem and praises of others as snares by which a mortal poison may imperceptibly insinuate itself into her affections and deprive her of divine grace. It always places itself below all creatures. Humility, not the desire for greatness, must ground the practice of virtue. Beware of pride under the cloak of sanctity. Hold both together: dread of unsureness of ourselves is matter of meekness against presumption, and the blessed Shewing of Love is matter of true comfort and joy against despair. So do not sink into despair over your sins, nor be puffed up. Accept God's forgiveness, see others as more important, and practice virtue humbly. True humility rests in God's mercy and leads to peaceful service.
rejected: It's common to mistake scrupulosity or self-condemnation for humility. True humility is not about beating yourself up over sins; it's about recognizing your dependence on God and your need for grace. Heavy dread may indicate a distorted view of God or an overactive conscience. Humility involves accepting God's forgiveness and moving forward, not dwelling on past failures. It also means seeing others as equally valuable and not elevating yourself above them. If your dread is paralyzing, consider speaking with a pastor or counselor. Remember that God's mercy is greater than your sins. Humility is peaceful, not anxious; it trusts in God's love and leads to service, not self-absorption.

prompt: Why does beauty move me so deeply?
chosen: Beauty moves us because every trait of goodness or beauty in creatures is a faint reflection of an infinite perfection in God. When we encounter beauty in nature, art, or persons, we are catching glimpses of divine attributes—harmony, love, truth. These reflections should raise our minds to God, eliciting acts of love for Him. Though roses and leaves pass, our life is not theirs; Nature's longings in us tell of their own fulfillment. The beauty we see is a promise of something enduring. So we look away from the body to Truth and Love, holding thought steadfastly to the enduring and good. When any creature delights us, we turn that delight into praise and love for the source of all beauty, finding our satisfaction in God alone.
rejected: Beauty moves us because it evokes emotions and connects us to something beyond ourselves. It can be found in nature, art, music, or human faces. Our brains are wired to respond to symmetry, harmony, and certain patterns. Beauty often signifies health, safety, or social connection, which have evolutionary advantages. It also provides a sense of wonder and transcendence, offering respite from daily stress. Aesthetic experiences can inspire creativity and deepen our appreciation of life. Ultimately, beauty moves us because it touches our deepest longings for meaning, connection, and joy, reminding us of the goodness of existence.

prompt: I am afraid my faith will fail on the mission field; what if I cannot trust GOD enough?
chosen: It's normal to feel fear when stepping into mission work, but do not lean on your own understanding or the wisdom of others, which hinders faith. Trust God with all your heart. Go forth by faith without sight, not waiting for a visible path or shoreline. Do not demand certainty or visible paths before stepping out; instead, steer by God's heavenly light. Faith isn't the absence of doubt but trusting God despite it. Remember that God promises to be with you always. Strengthen your faith through prayer, Scripture, and community, but ultimately rely on God's strength, not your own. Trust most when all else fails, learning strong faith by standing firm amid severe testings and thanking God for the school of sorrow. When you feel weak, that's when God's power is made perfect. God called you and will equip you. Focus on small steps of obedience and let faith grow through action.
rejected: It's normal to feel fear when stepping into mission work. Faith isn't the absence of doubt but trusting God despite it. Remember that God promises to be with you always. Strengthen your faith through prayer, Scripture, and community. Prepare practically, but ultimately rely on God's strength, not your own. When you feel weak, that's when God's power is made perfect. Talk to experienced missionaries about their struggles. Trust that God called you and will equip you. If you stumble, God's grace is sufficient. Focus on small steps of obedience and let faith grow through action. You don't need perfect faith; even a mustard seed can move mountains.

prompt: I want to love God with my whole heart but I feel cold and distracted; how can I love him more?
chosen: Feeling cold and distracted in your love for God is common. Instead of multiplying explicit offerings or being troubled by distraction in necessary work, practice simplicity in God's presence. Do all your actions for God without anxiety over distraction. When you notice distraction, gently return to God without self-criticism. The constant endeavour to enter up into God's estate and offer Him love is the mode of entry into adoration, rather than begging Him to come down. Confess your faults to God without excuse and without discouragement, then peaceably resume the practice of love and adoration. Love is a choice, not just a feeling; act lovingly toward God and others. Rekindle love through gratitude and Scripture, but avoid overcomplicating your practice. Serve others simply. Be patient with yourself; growth takes time. Ask God to increase your love, trusting that He will answer.
rejected: Feeling cold and distracted in your love for God is common. Start by acknowledging your feelings without guilt. Rekindle love through gratitude: list God's blessings daily. Spend time in Scripture, especially passages about God's love. Practice silence and listening prayer. Serve others to shift focus from self to God. Worship through music can stir affections. Remember that love is a choice, not just a feeling; act lovingly toward God and others. Be patient with yourself; growth takes time. Consider a spiritual director or trusted friend for accountability. Ultimately, ask God to increase your love, trusting that He will answer.

prompt: What is the eternal home Christ has prepared for us?
chosen: Christ has prepared for us an eternal home with God—perfect peace, freedom from sin and sorrow, and unending fellowship with the Lord. Scripture pictures a new heaven and new earth where God dwells with His people and wipes away every tear. Christ promises to return personally, and that promised return is our great hope and motive for consecration, readiness, and joyful stewardship. Yet we do not carry this by our own powers and inclinations: we cast our thoughts upon the Savior's shoulders for support, keeping our eyes fixed on God's good pleasure and providence rather than our own strength. Nor is this home found only by the learned or the great. Christ is revealed to lowly thoughts and simple seekers, as He was to shepherds and homely hearts, and Heaven in mercy will guide even the simplest to where He dwells. So come simply, trusting His goodness to keep you ready for His return.
rejected: Christ has prepared for us an eternal home with God—a place of perfect peace, freedom from sorrow and sin, and unending fellowship with the Lord. Scripture describes it as a mansion with many rooms, a new heaven and new earth where God dwells with His people and wipes away every tear. It is not a vague hope but a promise secured by Christ's resurrection and ascension. We enter it not by our own merit but through faith in Him. This home gives believers comfort in grief, courage in trial, and perspective on earthly things, reminding us that our citizenship is in heaven and our present sufferings are light compared to the glory to come.

prompt: I have been betrayed by a friend. How should I treat him now?
chosen: Betrayal by a friend is a deep wound, and it is honest to feel the hurt before God. But Scripture calls us to forgive as we have been forgiven and to overcome evil with good. Forgiving your betrayer is the best revenge: it frees you from bitterness and is a means of grace by which you gain the pardon of your own sins without trouble or expense. Do not set up self-chosen penances as though they were the shewed way; rather meekly bear the penance God Himself gives, keeping your mind in His blessed Passion. And whatever your own foulness or your friend's, never flee from Christ or hide from Him—that is the greatest folly. Hold to Jesus as your highest sovereign Friend, fastening to Him homely in whatever state, foul or clean, and never leaving Him for weal nor for woe.
rejected: Betrayal by a friend is one of the deepest wounds, and it is natural to feel anger and the desire to withdraw. You should first acknowledge the hurt honestly before God rather than pretending it doesn't matter. Then consider what Scripture teaches: we are commanded to forgive as we have been forgiven, to overcome evil with good, and to leave vengeance to God. That does not mean ignoring boundaries or trusting instantly again, but it does mean releasing resentment and refusing to repay cruelty with cruelty. Pray for the one who wronged you, speak truth gently where needed, and let the wound draw you closer to Christ, who was Himself betrayed by a friend.

prompt: My friend of another faith has some beliefs I think are wrong—should I avoid her or can I learn from her?
chosen: You need not avoid your friend. Friendship across religious differences can teach you to listen and to see another's sincerity. Honest doubts deserve sympathy, not defensiveness; rather than bullying anyone into faith, address questions calmly with an orderly presentation of the facts, so the unreasoning faith of childhood gives way to the profound convictions of maturity. But do not set faith against knowledge or reason. Faith is a cognitive act of reason—certitude concerning matters where verification is unattainable—and the highest exercise of reason, conditioned by love to God. Hold your convictions firmly and kindly, learn from your friend where you can, and let the friendship be patient and respectful. And pray persistently: God is not found by pop calls but yields to importunate faith, so keep asking, seeking, and knocking for light for yourself and for her.
rejected: You need not avoid your friend, but you should be clear about your own convictions. Friendship across religious differences can be a gift: it teaches you to listen, to see the sincerity of another person, and to understand beliefs you might otherwise caricature. At the same time, you should not pretend that all beliefs are equally true or hide what you believe. Be honest, kind, and curious. Learn what you can about her perspective, but hold firmly to your own faith and let the friendship be a place of respectful conversation rather than avoidance or pressure.

prompt: I'm a wife with an unbelieving husband. How should I live out my faith in that situation?
chosen: Living with an unbelieving husband calls for grace, wisdom, and patience. Your faith is best lived out through quiet consistency—love, respect, kindness, and integrity—rather than constant preaching or pressure, for an unbelieving husband may be won without a word by the conduct of his wife. Practice patience and mutual forbearance, seeking tender care and mutual compromise rather than withdrawal. Separation should not occur without a Christian demand, and divorce should warn you of fundamental error rather than be a quick escape. Remember that particular devotions are means to the end and may be laid aside when the soul is with God, its end. Above all, hold fast to this: God never forsakes us until we first forsake Him. So fear to leave Him, remain always in His presence, and trust that He who keeps you will also work in your husband's heart.
rejected: Living with an unbelieving husband calls for grace, wisdom, and patience. Your faith is best lived out through quiet consistency—love, respect, kindness, and integrity—rather than constant preaching or pressure. Scripture says an unbelieving husband may be won without a word by the conduct of his wife. Pray for him regularly, invite him gently where appropriate, and seek support from a faithful church community. Guard your own spiritual life through prayer, Scripture, and fellowship, and set healthy boundaries where needed. Trust God with your husband's heart, and let your home be marked by peace rather than conflict.

prompt: I want to begin the new year well; what should I actually do on this first day to reform my life?
chosen: Begin this day calmly, not in frantic hurry after quick results or wealth, and do not fix your hope on dates or assume the days will unfold slowly as in former times. Set aside time for honest prayer, and commit to the ordinary means by which blessings come: attend your meetings faithfully, pray, read Scripture, and meditate, keeping your dish right side up for the shower of blessings. Yet do not multiply discourse, research, and anxious care of self; reject tiresome self-scrutiny and confine yourself to the simple view of God and of your own nothingness before Him. Trust that God will cut His work short in righteousness, and prepare yourself for events that are hastening. Start today with one simple act of obedience, resting in His grace rather than in your resolutions.
rejected: Begin the new year by setting aside time for honest reflection and prayer. Review the past year with gratitude and honesty, naming where you fell short and where you grew. Then set a few concrete, realistic goals—spiritual, relational, and practical—and write them down. Commit to daily prayer and Scripture reading, and make a plan for regular worship and fellowship. Don't try to overhaul everything at once; small faithful habits matter more than grand resolutions. Start today with one specific act of obedience, and ask God for grace to keep going when enthusiasm fades.

prompt: I keep looking back at all the hardships I've been through. How do I stop counting the billows?
chosen: Looking back at hardship is natural, but the deeper need is not to manage your memories yourself. Come to God like a beggar, with no claim but His mercy, and wait before Him. Prayer is this humble waiting: you place yourself in His presence and stay quietly there. When your mind wanders back to old billows, do not scold yourself or grow agitated; gently recall it and rest again. And do not suppose one resolution will carry you for life. Our nature constantly draws us down, so the soul is like a clock that must be wound again and again; renew your fervor often, at the proper time. If you neglect this, God may renew it by more painful means. Bring your griefs before Him too—ask for patient hearts to bear the pain of parting and grace to follow Christ. Trust that when the shore is won, the billows past will not be counted.
rejected: It's natural to look back at hardship, but replaying old wounds keeps them alive. Try to notice when your mind drifts into the past and gently redirect it—to a gratitude list, a walk, a conversation. Journaling can help you process what you've survived without reliving it. Set small goals for the present and invest in relationships and activities that give your days meaning. If the memories feel overwhelming, a counselor can help you work through them. The past shaped you, but it doesn't have to define your future; each day offers a chance to build new patterns and let the old billows settle into calm water behind you.

prompt: I am confused about which day is the Lord's day; how do I settle it?
chosen: Settling which day is the Lord's day matters, but do not let the question become a delay or a fixation on dates. Whatever day you set apart, remember that our time is short and death may come suddenly. While it is day, be diligent in warning others of their danger and in doing good, for the night comes when no one can work; neglected opportunities bring shame and cannot be recalled. Yet the first business of every day is to be truly at rest and happy in God. Before the day's work, read and study the Scriptures with much prayer, especially in the early morning, feeding your soul. Do not assume the last days will unfold slowly as in former times: trust that God will cut His work short in righteousness, and prepare yourself for events that are hastening rather than calculating their dates.
rejected: The Lord's day is generally understood as Sunday, the first day of the week, when Christians commemorate the resurrection. Most traditions—Catholic, Orthodox, and Protestant—gather for worship on Sunday, though some churches keep Saturday as the Sabbath. To settle it for yourself, study the relevant passages (the Gospels' resurrection accounts, Acts 20:7, 1 Corinthians 16:2, Revelation 1:10), read your denomination's teaching, and speak with a pastor. The key is not the precise date but setting aside regular time for worship, rest, and community. If you're choosing a church, prioritize one that faithfully teaches Scripture and helps you grow, and let the day serve that purpose rather than becoming a point of division.

prompt: When my partner is anxious and dreaming of death, how do I bring them back to the warmth of the present?
chosen: When your partner is anxious and dreaming of death, do not begin by inquiring curiously into the causes of their sadness; such analysis feeds the agitation you want to quiet. Patiently endure the discomfort you both feel, and let that endurance be a way of loving Him who suffered. When anger rises in you—frustration that patience is hard, that they are not improving—do not grow angry over your own agitation. Gently place your troubled heart in the hands of our Lord, ask Him to cure it, and renew your good resolutions. Refuse immoderate sadness, which is the enemy of devotion, and do not let melancholy suggestions set the tone. Console the soul in the service of Him who is our joy forever. Stay near, speak little, be steady, and let your calm companionship carry the warmth of the present to them.
rejected: When a partner is anxious and preoccupied with death, the most helpful thing is calm, steady presence. Listen without trying to argue them out of their fear, and validate what they feel. Gently redirect attention to concrete, present things—a shared meal, a walk, a familiar routine, physical touch. Encourage good sleep, limit distressing media, and help them name small things they can look forward to. If the anxiety is persistent or they seem depressed, encourage professional help. You can also explore together what gives their life meaning—faith, relationships, service—and let those anchors pull them back into the warmth of ordinary, present life.

prompt: My husband is brutal and unkind to me—what does the gospel say about that?
chosen: The gospel does not endorse cruelty; Scripture calls husbands to love as Christ loved, and it condemns harshness. Your safety matters, and if you are in danger, seek help and wise counsel. Come before God honestly, confessing what is in your heart, and abandon yourself to His hands, trusting His mercy. Do not stop in gloom or self-condemnation, but strenuously lift your heart to God's goodness and exult in it, seeking His loving-kindness in all the breadth and open air of common life—in whatsoever things are true, honourable, just, pure, lovely, and of good report—and not missing behind them the greatest Reality, God Himself. And when God strews your vanities to the winds, breaks your prides, and transfigures your lusts to Holy Love, submit without protest, receiving His grace as the Divine Anaesthetic in this pain.
rejected: The gospel does not endorse cruelty. Scripture calls husbands to love their wives as Christ loved the church and to be considerate (Ephesians 5:25; 1 Peter 3:7), and it condemns harshness. Your safety and dignity matter. If you are in danger, contact trusted people, a pastor, or a domestic abuse hotline, and consider professional counseling. The gospel offers you God's compassion, not blame for your husband's sin. Set boundaries, seek support, and do not carry shame that is not yours. Prayer, wise counsel, and a safe community can help you discern next steps. God sees your suffering and calls the church to protect the vulnerable; you are not required to endure abuse silently.

prompt: I am concerned that the Church has replaced the living Spirit with a class of priests and a fixed ritual; is this a corruption or a necessary development?
chosen: This concern is understandable, but the answer is not found by weighing human offices against one another. The ministry and government of the church are submitted to the Holy Spirit's appointment and direction; the early church said, 'It seemed good to the Holy Ghost and to us.' Ordination is not a merely human appointment: the Church sets apart her ministers with prayer, trusting the Spirit of Counsel and Might to guide and strengthen those who take up the pastoral warfare. The sacraments and order are not magic, nor merely a human arrangement for edification; they guard the truth that spiritual life is God's gift, received and not manufactured. So ask whether your community's priests and ritual are held under the Spirit's guidance, pointing to the gift rather than substituting for it. Where order is so received, it serves the living Spirit rather than replacing Him.
rejected: This concern is understandable, and Christians have debated it for centuries. A priesthood and liturgy can become hollow if they replace personal faith, but they can also serve as channels through which the Spirit works. The New Testament itself speaks of ordained leaders, elders, and ordered worship, so structure is not automatically corruption. The key question is whether the forms point people to Christ and the Spirit or substitute for them. A healthy church holds both: ordered worship and living faith, sacraments and personal devotion, clergy and the priesthood of all believers. Rather than choosing corruption or development, ask whether your own community's practices foster genuine dependence on the Spirit, and seek a church that does.

prompt: I feel distant from God and only occasionally sense His presence; must I simply wait for such moments?
chosen: Feeling distant from God is common, but you need not wait passively for rare moments. Death does not bring us nearer to God; this world is where we can most easily and quickly find Him, so the remedy must be found here. Establish yourself in a continual sense of His presence by conversing with Him simply—speaking to Him in your ordinary work, offering each task quietly, and returning to Him when distracted without anxiety. Do not multiply special prayers that clutter this simplicity. To quit His conversation for trifles is shameful; keep His presence through the day, and the heart will grow accustomed to noticing Him.
rejected: It is understandable to feel distant from God at times, and many believers experience seasons when His presence seems faint. You need not simply wait passively for occasional consolations. Begin by setting aside regular times of prayer each day, and add small acts of devotion—brief offerings, short prayers, and moments of thanksgiving—throughout your work. When distractions come, gently return to God without discouragement. Over time, these repeated practices train the heart to notice His presence more readily. If the dryness persists, speak with a trusted pastor or spiritual director who can help you discern what God may be doing in this season.

prompt: How do I deal with grief over losing someone close to me?
chosen: Grief over losing someone close is heavy, but excessive mourning is a want of faith. God takes away friends because He wills to be loved without a rival, so moderate your sorrow by trusting Him. Count yourself as already dead, since you must die some day, and have no other consolation in this perishable life than unceasingly to weep over and detest your offences, for it is not now the time to rejoice but to lament. Yet do not stop there: knowing your need of His grace, make a firm resolution never wilfully to forget God, and live in His presence even when consolations are withdrawn. Lean on friends, family, and prayer, receiving this loss from His fatherly hand, and let sorrow turn you steadily toward Him rather than away.
rejected: Grief over losing someone close is one of the heaviest burdens we carry, and it is normal to feel sadness, anger, and numbness in waves. Allow yourself to feel what you feel without judgment, and lean on friends, family, or a counselor for support. Keep routines gentle, rest, and let tears come when they need to. Many people find comfort in rituals, writing, or prayer, and in recalling good memories of the person. Healing is not linear, so be patient with yourself and ask for help when the weight feels too much. Over time the pain usually softens, even though love remains.

prompt: I'm not intellectual but I long to know Christ deeply—is that possible for me?
chosen: Yes, it is possible—and your longing is already the first sign of it. But know that the love of Christ is not a lesson to be mastered; it is a sea without a far shore. Paul prays that we may know the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge, so every real experience of it opens onto further depths. This knowing is not intellectual attainment: it is wisdom and revelation given in fellowship with God, open to the unlearned as much as to the scholar. The real difficulty in understanding Scripture lies not first in the text but in conscience and will; the proud and disobedient mind darkens what the obedient heart sees. Doing the revealed will is the organ of spiritual knowledge, so study, languages, and history are useful preliminaries but never sufficient. Learning is a good servant, neither to be despised nor idolised. The deepest knowledge of Christ is not a possession we hold but a journey we keep walking in obedience.
rejected: Yes, it is entirely possible. Knowing Christ deeply is not reserved for scholars or clever people; it is a matter of the heart. Jesus chose ordinary fishermen, not academics, to be his closest friends. What matters is desire and love, not IQ. Read the Gospels simply, pray honestly, and love your neighbour. Deep knowledge of Christ grows through obedience and relationship, not through books. Many uneducated saints have known Jesus more intimately than professors. So do not be discouraged by your lack of intellect—bring your longing to Christ himself, and he will reveal himself to you. Your longing is already the beginning of that knowledge.

prompt: I once had a sense of divine anointing in my preaching, but it seems gone. Can it be recovered?
chosen: Yes, it can be recovered, for unction is not the product of study, genius, learning, or eloquence. It is the divine anointing that distinguishes true preaching, coming from God in answer to prayer. Truth without unction is dead and deadening; it may instruct the mind but cannot quicken the soul. So return to God, repent where needed, and ask Him for the anointing, not merely for the sensation. Take the heart of Jesus toward those you preach to, loving even the unworthy and seeing them as they shall be. Remember the holy conversation of departed friends as a sanctified means of grace, giving thanks for them and letting hope of future glory animate you until all God's children are gathered. Keep preaching faithfully, and trust the Giver to restore His freshness in answer to prayer.
rejected: Yes, it can be recovered, but not by trying harder to feel it. Anointing is not a mood you manufacture; it is God's gift. Begin by examining your heart: unconfessed sin, neglect of prayer, or ministry done for approval can grieve the Spirit. Return to private devotion, ask trusted believers to pray for you, and keep preaching faithfully even when the feeling is absent. Feelings fluctuate; faithfulness does not. God often restores freshness through repentance, rest, and renewed attention to Scripture. Do not chase the old sensation; seek the Giver. He is not stingy with His servants.

prompt: I'm constantly tempted by something I know is wrong. Should I fight the temptation head-on?
chosen: Resist temptation directly, but not by willpower alone. God tempts no man; He is faithful, will not allow you to be tempted above your strength, and with every temptation provides a way of escape. Fight by fleeing occasions of sin, praying for grace, and seeking accountability. If you fall, do not conclude God abandoned you. If you help someone who has fallen, restore them in meekness, first examining yourself lest you also be tempted; the Gospel's work is to save the straying, not condemn them. And do not fear importunate temptations or despair over them: displeasing temptations are harmless and their suffering is merciful. Despise the temptation and embrace the tribulation it brings, since the displeasure it causes proves your will does not consent. Endure patiently, for the one who endures is crowned with life.
rejected: Yes, you should resist temptation directly, but do not rely on willpower alone. Temptation is a common human experience, and God is faithful; He will not let you be tempted beyond your strength, and He provides a way out so you can endure it. Fighting head-on means fleeing occasions of sin, praying for grace, and seeking accountability. If you fail, do not conclude that God has abandoned you or that the temptation was too strong for His grace. Rather, treat the struggle as a trial that can strengthen virtue. Persevere patiently, and remember that enduring temptation is promised a crown of life.

prompt: How can I pray without ceasing in the middle of a busy daily life?
chosen: Prayer is not one discipline among many; it is the one great central secret of holy living and serving, the corner-stone on which all life-work is built. Begin in the secret place: take time alone with God and His word, letting meditation on Scripture fill your heart, for no activity, public service, or fellowship compensates for its loss. Keep appointed times of prayer regardless of feeling, pray with your family, and ask God to help you accomplish what is asked rather than expecting Him to do it all. Make prayer the first resort in every crisis, great or small, not the last. Then short prayers through the day rest on this foundation. Guard the secret place jealously; let nothing crowd it out, and ceaseless prayer will follow.
rejected: Praying without ceasing does not mean you must spend all day on your knees; it means cultivating a constant awareness of God's presence. Begin each morning by offering the day to Him, and let short prayers—a whispered 'thank You,' a plea for wisdom—punctuate your work. Use reminders like a verse on your desk or a prayer app. Serving others and gathering with your church family also keep your heart turned toward God. The goal is a habit of mind, not a rigid schedule. Over time, these small moments weave together into a life that feels like continuous conversation with God, even amid deadlines and duties.

prompt: I've been given a vision of something great to do and I feel inadequate and lonely in it—who is with me?
chosen: Feeling inadequate and lonely when given a great vision is common. Beware of looking to worldly pursuits—romance, family, business, pleasure, art—to fill the emptiness you feel; every substitute for God ends in disillusionment, and only finding God is permanent success. Beware, too, of the dreamer's error: the youth who leaves home and a mother's tears for fame and love is a poor dreamer, for life enfolds many ills and home may never be seen again. Yet do not add a second distress over having been distressed; do not be angry at having been angry, or disquieted at having been disquieted. Gently return your troubled heart to the Lord's hands. He is with you; seek Him first, and let the work find its proper place.
rejected: Feeling inadequate and lonely when given a great vision is common, even among the faithful. First, remember that the size of the calling often exceeds our own strength—that is by design, so we learn to depend on God. Surround yourself with mentors and friends who share the vision; community eases loneliness. Pursue the work with excellence, whether in business, art, family, or service, and let success and relationships fill the emptiness you feel. Take heart: many who have done great things felt the same way at first. Step forward, build your support network, and trust that the vision itself will sustain you.

prompt: If everything is decreed, why should I bother praying, working, or sharing the gospel?
chosen: Scripture teaches both divine decree and human responsibility: God ordains means as well as ends. So we pray, work, and share the gospel because God has appointed these means. Recognize God intimately present and address Him every moment; seek His will in doubtful things, offer your actions before doing them, and give thanks afterward. Watch your prayers: do not ask God for what you should do yourself in ordinary wisdom, and use the light He has already given rather than demanding supernatural signs. Do not treat the great commission as optional or as belonging only to a special class—the command to preach the Gospel to every creature binds every hearer, and inconvenience is no excuse. Work diligently. Our efforts do not compete with God's decree—they fulfill it.
rejected: This is a classic question about divine sovereignty and human responsibility. Scripture teaches both: God decrees all things, yet He ordains means as well as ends. Prayer, work, and evangelism are among those means. So we pray because God has appointed prayer as the way He accomplishes His will; we work because diligence is the ordinary path to provision; we share the gospel because faith comes by hearing. Our efforts do not compete with God's decree—they fulfill it. Think of it like farming: God gives the growth, but the farmer still plants and waters. So trust God's sovereignty and act faithfully, knowing He works through your prayers, labor, and witness.

prompt: I am dying and I am afraid. How should I prepare?
chosen: Death is certain, but its time, place, and manner are utterly uncertain—no one can know or secure them in advance. So do not presume a long life or postpone preparation. Make now the changes you would wish to have made when death is near: settle relationships, say what needs to be said, and entrust loved ones to God. Yet do not look at the storm or your circumstances for comfort; fasten your eyes on Christ Himself, who is the antidote to fear and the sum of all deliverance. Do not seek rapid progress through the letter alone; study the letter, imbibe the spirit, and adhere steadfastly to the divine Principle. Abide in Him, and find in His presence the remedy for trouble and the substance of all deliverance.
rejected: Facing death with fear is deeply human, and you are not alone. Begin by tending to practical matters: make a will, settle relationships, and say what needs to be said while you can. Spiritually, spend time in prayer and Scripture, and speak with a pastor or trusted friend. Many find peace by reviewing their life with gratitude and entrusting loved ones to God. If you have a long life ahead, use it well; if not, make the most of the time you have. Fear is natural, but faith can grow alongside it. Take it one day at a time, and let others support you.

prompt: I am a minister and a careless profligate man came to a funeral out of curiosity and was affected—should I follow up with him?
chosen: Yes, follow up—but wisely. A curious visitor moved at a funeral is a seed worth tending. Reach out gently, ask what struck him, listen, and offer to pray with him. Be patient: curiosity and emotion are not yet conversion. Yet remember: a prayerless ministry is not merely less effective—it is a funeral and an undertaker for God's truth and Church, however adorned. So make regular retirement, self-examination, reading, meditation, and private devotion your first duty to your own soul; without these you cannot kindle charity in others. And do not set up self-chosen penances as though they were the shewed way; rather meekly bear and suffer the penance God Himself gives, with your mind in His blessed Passion. Pray for him, and let the Spirit do the deeper work.
rejected: Yes, follow up—but wisely. A curious visitor who was moved at a funeral is a seed worth tending. Reach out gently within a few days, without pressure, and invite him to talk. Ask what struck him, listen more than you speak, and offer to pray with him. Invite him to church or a small group where he can meet believers. Be patient: curiosity and emotion are not yet conversion, so pray for him and let the Spirit do the deeper work. Also, remember that your own ministry's effectiveness depends on your walk with God, so keep tending your own soul as you reach out to him.

prompt: I don't feel like going to church some days—should I force myself or wait until I feel like it?
chosen: It's understandable to have days when you don't feel like going to church. But the question isn't mainly what you'll get out of it; it's what your presence gives to others. Worship gathers the whole body, and your absence leaves a gap—especially for the stranger or lonely person who needs a familiar face. Love, not personal benefit, is the highest motive. So come chiefly for the edification of the whole body and of the stranger, under the governance of love, and remember that the Church's service of the world flows from its worship, carrying a foretaste of eternal life into care for neighbors. Rest on the changeless word of promise rather than on variable moods: feelings never accurately gauge real assimilation to God. Continue steadfastly in prayer and communion when joy is lacking, and refuse to abandon worship or service because of spiritual depression.
rejected: It's understandable to have days when you don't feel like going to church. Feelings fluctuate, and forcing yourself can lead to resentment. A good approach is to be honest about your mood and give yourself grace. If you're exhausted or discouraged, resting may be the healthier choice; you can pray or read Scripture at home. The important thing is maintaining a genuine relationship with God, which isn't measured by attendance. Waiting until you feel like it helps you engage sincerely rather than going out of duty. Over time, notice what draws you back—community, music, teaching—and lean into that. Don't let guilt drive you; let desire lead you.

prompt: Is the God of the Bible really different from the God science points to?
chosen: Science describes regularities in nature—laws, causes, and measurable processes—while the Bible speaks of a personal God who creates, sustains, and relates to people. These are different kinds of claims, so they needn't compete. Science answers how things work; the Bible answers why they exist and what they mean. The God of the Bible is not a competing physical cause but the ground of all being. The relation of God and man is not something broken that must be regained; it is indestructible, with no lapse from or return to harmony. Christian Science is not a mere intellectual or philosophical system to be debated; it is fathomed by the Christian who understands best the divine Life, lived rather than merely argued. Reflect the divine law as a law unto oneself, doing violence to no man and making no false accusation. Where tensions arise, they usually come from overreaching on either side, so keep each in its proper domain and recognize that the biblical God is known through relationship and revelation.
rejected: Science describes regularities in nature—laws, causes, and measurable processes—while the Bible speaks of a personal God who creates, sustains, and relates to people. These are different kinds of claims, so they needn't compete. Science answers how things work; the Bible answers why they exist and what they mean. The God of the Bible is not a competing physical cause but the ground of all being, so the two can be complementary. Where tensions arise, they usually come from overreaching on either side—scientism or literalistic readings. Many believers pursue science devoutly. The key is to keep each in its proper domain and recognize that the biblical God is known through relationship and revelation, not merely through measurement.

prompt: How do I know whether an inner impulse is the Spirit of God or just my own imagination?
chosen: Distinguishing the Spirit from imagination takes practice. Test impulses against Scripture, and look at the fruit—love, joy, peace, patience—rather than the intensity of the feeling.
