Go deeper: the interior spirit consists in directing all acts to the glory of God. Warn yourself against acting chiefly for human praise, from mere natural impulse, or in routine without a supernatural intention. The divine Spirit does not displace you when he comes; he is appropriated into the awakened human spirit, becoming the life of a new moral personality rather than suppressing the finite. Refrain from disputing about what God is, for such dispute is a sign one has not felt him and that one exalts one's own meaning and desires dominion. Instead, exercise yourself in learning how to enter again into the Love of God and your Brother.
rejected: Distinguishing the Spirit from imagination takes practice. First, test impulses against Scripture: God's Spirit never leads contrary to his word. Second, look at the fruit—love, joy, peace, patience—rather than the intensity of the feeling. Third, seek counsel from mature believers who can help you discern. Fourth, pay attention to consistency and humility: imagination tends toward self-interest and flattery, while the Spirit tends toward self-giving love. Finally, remember that impressions are not infallible; hold them loosely and pray for clarity. Over time, you'll grow in recognizing the Spirit's voice, and mistakes are part of learning.

prompt: How long should I hold out before giving up a secret under torture?
chosen: This is a hard question, and no simple rule covers every case. But be careful not to clutch at present comfort and ease as though they were owed to you. Rather than treating relief from suffering as a right, be content with room to deny yourself, letting rapture, comfort, and ease come and go as Heaven shall bid them. Consider whom the secret concerns: if you sinned against a person, confess to that person; against a family, to the family; against a Ward, to the Ward; against God, to God. Keep your private weaknesses hidden as much as you can. And remember that it is good to hold on to an old friend and never let him go; no matter how many new friends you have, hold fast to the old, and let only wicked conduct break the thread of fellowship. Duress reduces culpability, and there is no fixed time limit.
rejected: This is a hard question, and no simple rule covers every case. Your first duty is to survive and protect yourself from harm; torture can break anyone, and holding out indefinitely isn't a moral requirement. Consider what the secret protects: if revealing it endangers others, weigh that heavily, but if it only exposes your own past, you may reasonably give it up to end suffering. You're not obligated to be a hero. Preserve your life, seek help, and remember that duress reduces culpability. There is no fixed time limit—decide based on the stakes, your conscience, and what you can bear.

prompt: I defrauded someone years ago and have since become a believer—must I make restitution, and what if the person is dead?
chosen: Becoming a believer means your past is forgiven, but grace doesn't cancel the call to make good what you defrauded. Reformation includes reparation, not merely future amendment. So make restitution to the wronged party where you can; if the person is dead, restore to their heirs or, where that's impossible, to the Lord—through the church or the poor. Don't minimize small sins or delay confession; promptly confess and forsake even the little wrongs, abandon questionable practices at once, and give thanks for every mercy of God. Yet do this forgoing prosecution and seeking the offender's repentance and faith, valuing his soul above the loss. Let your changed life include making right what you can of the old wrong, and cultivate obedience and gratitude day by day.
rejected: Becoming a believer means your past is forgiven, so you don't need to be paralyzed by guilt. Restitution is a good gesture if it's possible and safe, but it isn't strictly required—grace covers what you did. If the person is dead, you can't repay them anyway, so let it go and trust God's mercy. Focus on living honestly now. You might give to charity as a symbolic way of making things right, but don't feel obligated. The important thing is that you've changed, and God has forgiven you.

prompt: I want to be loved without having to prove myself. Is that possible with God?
chosen: Yes—and the way to it is not proving but loving. Stop petitioning for proofs and comforts; open yourself by offering God great love, and in that offering you receive not gifts but God Himself. When you fail, confess your faults plainly to God, without excuses and without discouragement; He is not surprised and does not withdraw. Then peaceably resume the practice of love. God's self-limitation—His decree, His creating, His providence, His inspiration, and above all Christ's person and work—is not a denial of His perfection but its expression: the infinite One freely makes room for the finite, and in that condescension shows His power and love. He does not ask you to prove yourself; He asks you to love, and the love you give returns as His presence.
rejected: Yes, it is possible. God's love is not earned like a wage; it is freely given, and Scripture says He loved us before we loved Him. You do not have to perform or achieve in order to be received. Come as you are, honestly and simply, and ask Him to show you His love. At the same time, love grows through relationship: pray, read Scripture, and let Him change you. The proof He asks for is not achievement but trust—a heart that turns toward Him. Rest in the fact that His acceptance rests on His character, not your performance.

prompt: I'm overwhelmed by the work before me and I don't have enough helpers. What do I do?
chosen: Reorient the work itself: do it for the love of God, and pray for grace before and during it. The same tasks that crush you when carried as a burden become light when carried as an offering, since grace supplies what your strength cannot. But first cast the beam out of your own eye: before you try to help others, overcome your own belief in and fear of disease and sin, your own hurry and anxiety. Then work with calm, contented, patient diligence, not frantic hurry after results or wealth. Keep your dish right side up for the shower of blessings by attending meetings, praying, reading Scripture, and meditating. Triage honestly, ask for help concretely, and do the next small step, releasing the outcome to God.
rejected: Start by acknowledging that the load feels heavy and that you are not failing by feeling overwhelmed. Then triage: list what must be done, what can wait, and what can be dropped or delegated. Ask for help specifically and concretely—people respond better to clear requests than to general appeals. Protect rest and sleep; exhaustion makes everything look impossible. Break the work into small steps and do the next one. Remember that you are not solely responsible for the outcome; do your part faithfully and release the rest.

prompt: Is the disappointment about the coming a sign of the perilous times Paul described?
chosen: Disappointment about the coming can be read as a symptom of unsettled times, but it is a mistake to make Paulinism the foundation of the Catholic doctrine of faith. Paul's expectation acted rather as a ferment and a conscience within the Church—a recurring critical impulse in the history of dogma, not the ground on which the faith was built. Nor should we dismiss the motives of God's messenger: Paul presented a divine idea, and misunderstanding it betrays ignorance of Principle. His decisive contribution was to transform the idea of pre-existence: he first limited pre-existence to Christ's spiritual part, so that the pre-existent Christ stands independently beside God, and he treated the assumption of flesh as a humiliation and an emptying. That is the divine idea the disappointment should press us to grasp, and it summons us to place hope in Christ Himself rather than in a timing that will always disappoint.
rejected: Disappointment about the coming can be read as a symptom of the unsettled times Paul warned of—days when people are restless, distracted, and easily disillusioned. But it is dangerous to map every disappointment directly onto prophecy; such signs are often ambiguous and can be read many ways. Better to ask what the disappointment reveals about your own hope and where it is placed. If hope rests on a particular expectation of timing, it will always be disappointed; if it rests on Christ Himself, it can survive delay. Let the disappointment become an invitation to examine and deepen hope rather than a verdict about the age.

prompt: I am weak in body and mind; does God require me to be perfect in these things?
chosen: No—God does not demand bodily or mental perfection as a condition of His love; He knows we are dust. But weakness is not an excuse for leaving habitual imperfections in place. Sanctification requires discovering and rooting out habitual disorders, not merely multiplying pious exercises while the heart goes unwatched and irregular attachments remain uncut. Guard your senses, live in recollection, open your interior honestly to a spiritual director, and aim at God's will rather than at piling up external works. Let your motive be good on every occasion, attend to the least details, and avoid negligent or defective work, after the example of Christ who did all things well. Yet do all this without hurry or anxious fretting: keep yourself in God's presence, for over-eagerness is the mother imperfection of all imperfections, and anxiety obstructs the very perfection you seek.
rejected: No—God does not demand bodily or mental perfection as a condition of His love. He knows we are dust, and Scripture is full of weak people He used. What He asks is faithfulness, not flawlessness: to love Him and neighbor, to do your duty as you are able, and to accept your limits humbly. Weakness can even be a place where His strength is shown. Rest in His mercy, use the gifts and capacities you have, and do not measure yourself against an impossible standard. Growth in holiness is gradual and God is patient with our pace.

prompt: Is it true that this is the best of all possible worlds, or only the best that could be made?
chosen: The question turns on what "best" means. If it means the best of all logically possible worlds, the claim is hard to defend, since a world with less suffering seems conceivable. But natural selection need not be read as refuting purpose; its dysteleological significance is at an end. The world is an organism with internal ends, whose adaptations and beauty furnish a worthier teleology than the mechanical theory allows. Yet do not cling to that beauty: attachment to earthly goods chains the soul down, and only an ardent, pure desire of the heavenly Jerusalem raises it. So the world is the best that could be made—ordered toward genuine goods—but it is a sign and a road, not a resting place. And if we fail to see God in it, the fault is not merely intellectual: sin alone blinds us to the heaven and earth within. Read God everywhere in creation, and ask for a heart to find and read Him in all things.
rejected: The question turns on what "best" means. If it means the best of all logically possible worlds, the claim is hard to defend: a world with less suffering seems conceivable, and natural selection suggests much of the world's order is the product of blind competition rather than designed purpose. If it means the best world that could actually be made given real constraints, the claim is more modest and more defensible. Either way, the phrase invites us to weigh beauty and order against waste and pain, and to ask what kind of goodness a world like this can bear.

prompt: How will the kingdom of God be established—by human effort or by revelation from heaven?
chosen: The kingdom of God is not established by human organization, legislation, or moral suasion; it comes by revelation from heaven and by God's own interposition. An angel restores the everlasting gospel as a warning to every nation, a Zion is built up, and judgments prepare the way for Christ's reign. Yet the kingdom does not arrive without us: it develops gradually through individual labor, and for the Saints it is the central business of life, worth all else. Nor is its growth uncertain or dependent on human effort alone. The work of God will continue to grow and spread until it fills the earth with His glory and with the knowledge of the Father and the Son, whom to know is life eternal. We labor faithfully, then, not anxiously, trusting that heaven will accomplish what it has purposed and that our obedience is caught up into a work destined to fill the whole earth.
rejected: The kingdom of God is not the product of human planning, legislation, or moral reform. It is established by revelation from heaven—God Himself breaking into history to make known His will and to set up His rule. Human effort alone can build organizations and improve behavior, but it cannot bring the kingdom. Scripture shows that God sends His messenger, restores the everlasting gospel as a warning to every nation, gathers a people into a Zion, and pours out judgments that prepare the way for Christ's reign. So the kingdom comes by divine initiative and disclosure, not by committees or campaigns. Our part is to receive the revelation, repent, and align ourselves with what God is doing, rather than imagining we can construct the kingdom ourselves.

prompt: Why did Jesus say it was better for him to go away?
chosen: Jesus said it was better for Him to go away because His bodily presence was limited to one place, while His departure would send the Comforter to dwell in believers everywhere. But the deeper lesson concerns motive, mission, and mercy. We are to love and serve God purely for His own sake, whether we feel saved or lost, and to continue the works He began—for His healing works were demonstrations of an ever-operative divine Principle, not a spectacle confined to a past dispensation, so His followers today are called to heal the sick and cast out error. Yet we do this not by confidence in ourselves but by approaching God as wretched sinners, confessing our need and abandoning ourselves into His hands. That honest surrender is met by His merciful embrace. His going away, then, was not abandonment but the opening of a way for the contrite heart to draw near and find mercy.
rejected: Jesus told His disciples it was better for Him to go away because His physical presence was limited to one place at one time, while His departure would allow the Comforter—the Holy Spirit—to come to all believers everywhere. While He was with them bodily, He could teach and heal in their sight; after He went away, the Spirit would dwell within them, guiding them into all truth and empowering them for ministry. So His going away was not abandonment but a deeper kind of presence. The disciples grieved, but His departure made possible a more intimate and universal relationship with God than walking beside Him in Galilee ever could.

prompt: I feel too proud to kneel at the manger—how do I cultivate humility this Christmas?
chosen: Feeling too proud to kneel is itself a sign of where the work must begin, for pride is the beginning of all sin, its end, and its cause. Humility is not a technique for self-improvement, nor is it thinking poorly of yourself for its own sake; the practice of every virtue must be grounded in humility rather than in a desire for greatness or spiritual reputation. This Christmas, look steadily at the manger—the Creator of all things lying helpless in a feeding trough—and let that sight expose the pride that hides even under the cloak of sanctity. Do not rely on your own resolve, for that is self-esteem dressed as virtue; true courage is grounded in a low esteem of self, its greatness lying in humility rather than in confidence in its own powers. Imitate the saints, who saw their own imperfections clearly and counted themselves dust and worms. Serve, keep silence, ask forgiveness, and ask God for humility, for He gives grace to the humble.
rejected: Feeling too proud to kneel is itself a sign of where the work must begin. Humility is not something we manufacture by trying harder to think poorly of ourselves; it grows from beholding God. This Christmas, start by looking steadily at the manger—the Creator of all things lying helpless in a feeding trough. Let that sight dismantle your self-importance. Practice small, concrete acts of lowliness: serve someone who cannot repay you, keep silent when you want to defend yourself, ask forgiveness first. Spend time in prayer naming your pride honestly before God. Humility is cultivated the way any virtue is—through repeated choices, supported by grace. Ask God for it; He gives grace to the humble.

prompt: I want to follow Jesus, but I don't know if his healing works are meant for today or just for his time.
chosen: This is an honest question, but it cannot be settled by comparing doctrines from a distance—the real answer is a Person. Come into personal contact with the risen Saviour, not merely with opinions about Him; abide in Him continually, drawing His life into your being by the hunger and thirst of love and faith. Christianity is not mere belief, ritual, or admiration of Jesus' person. His healing works were demonstrations of an ever-operative divine Principle, not a spectacle confined to a past dispensation, so His followers today have the present duty to heal the sick and cast out error. And be assured: God can and does heal in answer to prayer today, for Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever. Pray boldly, trust His willingness and power, and leave the outcome in His hands, knowing He is faithful.
rejected: This is a common and honest question. Many Christians believe Jesus' healing miracles were signs authenticating His identity and the arrival of the kingdom, and that they belonged especially to that first generation. Others believe healing continues today. What matters most is that you follow Jesus wholeheartedly. Study the Gospels, pray, and ask God for wisdom. If healing is for today, He will lead you into it; if not, you can still trust His goodness. Don't let uncertainty about this secondary question keep you from discipleship. Focus on loving God and neighbor, and let the Spirit guide your understanding in His time.

prompt: How may I come to know the essence and property of the Creatures, and should I eat of the Tree of Knowledge of Good and Evil to be as God?
chosen: To know the essence and property of creatures, study them diligently—read good books, study reliable history, and learn everything upon the face of the earth, both good and its effects and evil and its consequences, without committing iniquity. But knowledge of evil must never become familiarity with it: keep proper ward over mortal mind, dwell on good, and exclude false beliefs as you would exclude thieves. Yet the deepest truth about every creature is that it is born of nothing, surrounded by nothingness, and tends to nothingness, depending each moment upon God for existence, preservation, power of action, and all it possesses. The Tree of Knowledge of Good and Evil represents the attempt to become as God by our own grasp; we may know evil without practicing it, but we must not linger over it. Since every creature depends each moment on God, our life, thoughts, and works should be in Him, of Him, for Him, and directed to Him.
rejected: To know the essence and property of creatures, study them carefully—observe nature, read good books, learn from reliable teachers and histories. Knowledge of created things is good and rightly pursued; Scripture itself calls us to wisdom. But the Tree of Knowledge of Good and Evil represents something else: the attempt to seize knowledge on our own terms, to become as God by our own grasp, which is precisely what God forbade. So learn all you can about the creatures, but do not eat of that tree. Do not pursue knowledge through disobedience, pride, or the practice of evil. Let your learning be governed by reverence for God, and remember that true wisdom begins with the fear of the Lord.

prompt: I see the same person who made the gentle things also made the terrifying ones. How do I make sense of that?
chosen: It is tempting to call a truce built on mutual fear and selfish loves a real peace, but that is precisely where Cruelty's snare is knit: what looks like calm is only everyone watching everyone. The same human brain that breeds gentleness also breeds Cruelty, Humility, Mystery, and Deceit—not invaders from outside but growths from our own soil. Cruelty has a human heart and Jealousy a human face; the human heart can be a hungry gorge, and the human dress is forged iron. Do not hide this behind pleasant virtues. Yet the afflictive things are not simply wrath: Love can make an angel of them, and we may entertain that angel unawares. Refuse to baptize fear-built calm as peace; ask what in you is being cultivated. The gentle show what we might become, the terrifying what we become when fear and self-love knit their snare—and the affliction, met in love, may be the angel sent to free you.
rejected: It is common to feel this tension when you notice that the same hands behind comfort and kindness also shaped things that frighten you. One way to make sense of it is to recognize that a maker is not divided against himself; the same skill and intention produce both the gentle and the fearsome, much as an artist works in both soft and harsh registers. What frightens you may serve a purpose you cannot yet see—boundary, warning, or protection—while the gentle things show the maker's care. Rather than forcing a split between a kind creator and a cruel one, hold both as expressions of one will. Ask what each thing is for, and let the terrifying parts deepen rather than destroy your trust.

prompt: I want to dread God rightly, but I do not know which of my dreads are good and which are wrong.
chosen: Scripture and the saints speak of four dreads: servile dread of punishment, doubtful dread born of unbelief, natural dread of bodily harm, and reverent dread of God himself. Only reverent dread fully pleases God, because it flows from love. Far from harsh, it is full soft and sweet: the more it is had, the less it feels like dread, because the sweetness of love fills it. Love and reverent dread are brethren—two in property and working, yet inseparable—so whoever truly loves also dreads, though he feels it but a little. But do not stop there: join reverent dread with meek love and mighty trust, for the more mightily we trust, the more we please God, and without this dread and love no one may please Him. Examine your dreads, then: cultivate the soft one, heal the servile and doubtful, and let dread, meek love, and mighty trust worship God together.
rejected: Wanting to dread God rightly is itself a good sign, because it shows you care about your standing before him. A helpful first step is to distinguish dread that arises from love from dread that arises from fear of punishment or doubt. Dread rooted in love is reverent and quiet; it draws you toward God rather than driving you away. Dread rooted in servile fear or doubt tends to produce anxiety, avoidance, and despair. Practically, examine what each dread is doing in you: does it soften your heart and increase trust, or does it harden and scatter you? Bring the confusing dreads to God in prayer and ask for light. Over time, the reverent kind will grow as love grows, and the servile kind will shrink.

prompt: Is excommunication ever right?
chosen: Yes, excommunication can be right, and a pastor must not shrink from it out of false kindness. Scripture calls pastors to correct with firmness and, where needed, severity—not endless remonstrance that leaves the offender undisturbed. Persistent, public sin that refuses correction endangers both sinner and flock, and a shepherd too lenient with such offenders incurs condemnation. Yet the process matters: do not spread complaints about leaders abroad or sit in judgment on presiding officers from a distance. Take the grievance directly to the person involved, seek confession and reconciliation, and keep the matter from spreading. If repentance is refused, separation may follow, in hope of awakening and protecting the community. Remember that exaltation is proportioned to capacity and conduct, some presiding over more than others, and all proved through mortal experience—so firmness aims at repentance and restoration, with an open door for return.
rejected: Excommunication is a serious and rare measure, and many would say it should be a last resort after every gentler effort has failed. Its purpose is not to punish for its own sake but to protect the community and to move the offender toward repentance. When a person persists in grave and public sin and refuses correction, a church may formally separate them in hope that the separation awakens them and that the community is spared harm. The spirit should be restorative: clear about the wrong, but always aiming at reconciliation. If it is used, it should be accompanied by prayer, patience, and an open door for return. Used carelessly or out of anger, it does more harm than good.

prompt: I have prayed for money for a specific need and received nothing—should I tell my supporters?
chosen: Be honest with your supporters, but remember that money for God's work must be obtained only in God's way. Do not ask unbelievers to fund it, do not press believers to give, and do not resort to entertainments or worldly schemes. Examine carefully any gift offered: refuse what comes from impure motives or from money that is not the giver's own. As for prayer, do not pray for riches—wealth is not a proper object of prayer; pray only for the means to keep yourself and your family from want. And do not answer an unmet need by hoarding a reserve for future want, which is a snare for one who professes to trust God. Live from day to day upon the Lord's bounty, making your one investment in His work and the poor. Speak to supporters as testimony and invitation to prayer, not pressure, letting your words show trust in God rather than clever appeals.
rejected: It is reasonable to be honest with your supporters about a specific need that remains unmet, since they have chosen to partner with you and transparency builds trust. You might explain the situation plainly, share how you have prayed, and invite them to join you in seeking God's provision. Avoid dramatizing the need or creating pressure; simply inform and invite. At the same time, guard against making supporters feel obligated, and be careful not to treat them as a funding source to be tapped. Pray about the timing and manner of any request, and let your communication reflect dependence on God rather than on people. Honesty, humility, and gratitude should shape whatever you say.

prompt: I don't know the mysteries of the Rosary well. Can I still gain the indulgences if I only contemplate one scene of the Passion?
chosen: Yes—provided you say the Rosary with devotion and pauses, not in haste. Meditating on any one mystery of the Passion suffices to fulfill the devotion's intent, so you need not master every scene to gain the indulgence. What matters is that you pause and let the mystery sink in. Indeed, five devout decades are more pleasing to Mary than fifteen said in haste. So take a single scene and stay with it prayerfully. And do not stop at the minimum: commend assiduous holy reading and meditation, begun in tender years, as the way fervent devotion is nourished—Timothy's example of knowing the Scriptures from childhood. Above all, expect pardon without anxiety from the Blood of Jesus Christ while you endeavor to love Him; mortification without love cannot efface sin, but love joined to His Blood can. Let this one scene lead you into that love.
rejected: Yes, you can still gain the indulgences even if you do not know all the mysteries well. The essential requirement is to pray the Rosary with devotion and to meditate on the mysteries, but you need not master every scene. If you contemplate even one scene of the Passion prayerfully, that meditation can fulfill the spirit of the devotion, especially when you are learning. What matters most is the sincerity and attention of your prayer rather than exhaustive knowledge. Take one scene—say, the agony in the garden—and stay with it, letting it draw you into love and sorrow. As you grow more familiar, you can add other mysteries. The Church's intent is to help you pray, not to burden you.

prompt: How can I trust Christ when everything around me is falling apart?
chosen: It is natural to feel shaken when life unravels, but the hour of testing is exactly where faith is learned. Trust Christ most when all else fails—not because circumstances are easy, but because He is faithful when nothing else is. When you forget Him or falter, do not be disquieted; simply return with greater trust, since a lapse in remembrance is no reason for turmoil but a call to come back more firmly. Stand firm amid severe testing, and thank God even for the school of sorrow, which teaches reliance you could not learn in comfort. Remember that trusting God honors Him, and He is honored by the confidence of His children, drawing down great graces on those who rely on Him. Bring your fear honestly to Him, hold fast to His promises, and let the storm draw you closer rather than push you away.
rejected: It is natural to feel shaken when life unravels, but faith is not the absence of fear. Trusting Christ begins by remembering who He is—faithful, good, and present even when circumstances are not. Bring your fear to Him honestly in prayer, lean on Scripture, and let other believers support you. Take one day at a time, doing the next right thing rather than solving everything at once. Trust grows as you recall past times God carried you through. Your feelings may lag behind your choice to rely on Him, and that is okay. Faith is a relationship, not a guarantee of ease. Keep turning to Christ, and let the storm draw you closer rather than push you away.

prompt: I am a woman who has loved many men. Can I still be pure in God's eyes?
chosen: Yes—and the first thing to know is that God looks upon you with love. He looks with love even upon the most terrible sinner who has any true desire to be converted, and that merciful regard is not something you must earn by cleaning yourself up first. Yet His love is not mere sentiment: it is a rational, voluntary self-communication that seeks your true good, and it is regulated by and subordinate to His holiness, so His mercy never flatters sin but heals it. If you have any real desire to be converted, that desire meets His loving look. Confess what needs confessing, seek healing and wise counsel, and trust His goodness. Remember too that this restoration is not yours alone: no one is exalted into God's presence alone, and the man is not without the woman, neither the woman without the man, in the Lord. You are not defined by the men you have loved, but by the God who loves you and calls you to new life with others.
rejected: Yes, purity in God's eyes is not measured by your past but by your present repentance and faith. Scripture is full of people whose histories were messy, yet God forgave and restored them. If you turn to Him honestly, confess what needs confessing, and seek to live differently, His mercy is greater than your mistakes. Purity is something God gives and grows in you, not a status you earn by having a spotless record. Consider talking with a trusted pastor or counselor about shame and healthy relationships going forward. You are not defined by the men you have loved, but by the God who loves you and calls you to new life.

prompt: I'm afraid our community will be destroyed by our enemies. What should we do?
chosen: Fear is understandable, but the first enemy to face is within ourselves. Before we oppose error and evil around us, we must conquer ourselves and submit to the Father's will, since a heart not yet yielded cannot fight rightly. Guard your soul against bitterness, anger, hatred, envy, and malice, for these destroy a community from within more surely than any outside foe; instead be filled with the love of God, truth, and your fellowmen, doing good to all and keeping your covenants. Then oppose evil by persuasion, patience, and love unfeigned—never by violence and never by interfering with the agency of others. Above all, do not surrender courage, confidence, or good-will, for we should lose everything rather than these. Go on joyously when possible and always courageously and confidently, trusting God, caring for the vulnerable, and refusing to become what you oppose.
rejected: Fear is understandable when your community feels threatened, but panic rarely helps. Start by assessing the real risks and strengthening practical defenses—communication, safety plans, and trusted allies. Bring concerns to leaders who can coordinate a calm, unified response. Avoid rumor and inflammatory speech that deepen division. Document threats and involve lawful authorities where appropriate. At the same time, care for the vulnerable and keep community life as normal as possible. Prayer and mutual encouragement can steady people. The goal is not to match hostility with hostility but to remain a peaceful, resilient community that protects its people while refusing to be ruled by fear.

prompt: I'm a Christian, but I don't feel especially like Christ. Does that mean I'm not really a Christian?
chosen: Feeling unlike Christ does not automatically mean you are not a Christian, but we should be careful what the name means. A Christian is one to whom Christ is Saviour and Lord, subject to Him—not a religious system or an earnest imitation of Jesus from a distance, but actual union with the Lord Jesus, who dwells in you as the life and source of all your experience and work. So the real question is not whether your feelings resemble Him today, but whether you are holding to His person rather than mere theories. And His presence is not only past or future: He says not 'I will be with you' but 'I am with you alway,' an unbroken presence with you forevermore. Rest in that living Christ now. Feelings fluctuate, and many faithful believers pass through dryness; what matters is turning to Him, confessing sin, and abiding in His present lordship.
rejected: Feeling unlike Christ does not automatically mean you are not a Christian. Christianity is not first about religious feelings or moral resemblance; it is about trusting Christ as Savior and following Him as Lord. Feelings fluctuate with mood, health, and circumstances, and many faithful believers go through seasons of dryness. What matters is whether you are turning to Him, confessing sin, and seeking to live faithfully. If you are generally religious and trying to imitate Jesus' example, that is a good sign of genuine faith. Talk with a pastor or mature believer about what you are experiencing, and be patient with yourself as growth takes time.

prompt: Is Sunday worship really indispensable, or can I excuse myself when it's inconvenient or dangerous?
chosen: The obligation of Sunday is not optional, and it should not be set aside on lame pretences or mere inconvenience. The martyrs kept it at the expense of their lives, and the true Christian is known by his manner of celebrating it. So honor the Sabbath, prepare for and partake of the sacrament worthily, and do not treat meetings carelessly. Yet faithfulness is not presumption: use appropriate means—medicine, food, prudent provision, and safe alternatives—with prayer and thanksgiving, rejecting both presumption and unbelief. If danger is real, seek safety wisely while keeping the day holy; where genuine impossibility exists, worship at home and long for the assembly. And do not limit worship to one day: continue worship and testimony every day, letting your whole life show whose you are.
rejected: Sunday worship is important, but circumstances vary. If attending is genuinely dangerous or impossible, God understands, and you can worship at home through prayer, Scripture, and online services. The key is maintaining your relationship with God rather than treating a single hour as a magic requirement. That said, convenience alone is a weak excuse; habits of gathering strengthen faith and community. Consider whether the inconvenience is truly insurmountable or just uncomfortable, and look for alternatives like a different service time or smaller gathering. If danger is real, prioritize safety and find ways to stay connected. God cares about your heart more than your attendance record.

prompt: I feel like God is far away and doesn't hear me. Is it Him or is it me?
chosen: God is nearer than all else, speaking in your conscience and mind, yet He also speaks through Scripture, which is the foundation of our faith. But God does not will us to stop at the written word; He invites us into personal experience of Himself through inward meditation and pondering. When every worldly thing passes away, He remains to the soul that seeks Him early. Do not argue with the feeling of distance—that is the enemy's noise. Prostrate yourself before God and remain at His feet, refusing to engage temptation. In humility, cling to Him who is closer than your own breath. As you meditate on His word and listen in stillness, you will know His abiding presence, and the enemy's clamor will fade into nothing.
rejected: Feeling that God is distant is a common human experience. It may not be about God being far, but about our own distractions, guilt, or lack of prayer. Often, when we feel far from God, it's because we've allowed worldly concerns to crowd out our spiritual life. Try to examine yourself: are you praying regularly, reading Scripture, and participating in community? God promises to be near to those who seek Him. It might also be a test of faith, a time to trust even when feelings are dry. Remember that God's presence isn't always felt, but He is faithful. Seek Him in the ordinary means of grace, and consider talking to a pastor or spiritual friend.

prompt: I want to grow from glory to glory; what does that mean for me?
chosen: Growing from glory to glory means looking to the Father of glory as the source of all glory, yet it also means abiding in Christ and knowing Him as your purity, grace, and strength. Say with Paul, 'Not I, but Christ.' It is not by your own effort that you attain purity, but by resting in His indwelling. Embrace self-denial and economy as a joyful privilege that frees you to give more fully to the LORD, bringing fuller joy. As you yield to Him, He transforms you from one degree of glory to another, not for your boasting but for His praise. Find your rest in His presence, and let your growth be the fruit of His life in you.
rejected: Growing from glory to glory means progressing in your spiritual life, becoming more like Christ. It involves increasing in virtue, knowledge, and love. You do this by practicing spiritual disciplines, serving others, and allowing the Holy Spirit to transform you. Each step of obedience brings greater glory to God and prepares you for the next. It's a lifelong journey of sanctification, where you leave behind old habits and take on new ones that reflect God's character. The glory is not your own but God's working in you. Stay committed to prayer, Scripture, and community, and you will see growth. Remember, it's not about perfection but direction—keep moving forward in faith.

prompt: I want to hold onto a memory of someone who made the world feel like a dream—how do I keep that when reality breaks in?
chosen: The memory of that pure soul is a healing power that can transfigure your soiled soul and lift you above the troubled world. To keep it, allow no repose or slipping back in your spiritual ascent; go forward like a mountain-climber until the goal is reached, withdrawing from worldly distractions into the one unchangeable Good. Yet know that the old dreams of gods and heroic Greece are lovely and should be allowed to persist. The dreaming Muse, lovely in her sorrow, should be left to dream rather than roused by the jarring Truth, lest she die. So hold the memory gently, letting it heal and elevate you, while cherishing the dreamlike beauty that made the world feel like a dream. In this way, you honor both the ascent and the lovely dream.
rejected: Holding onto a beautiful memory when reality intrudes is challenging. You can keep it by cherishing the moments you had and letting them shape who you are. Write down your memories, share them with others, or create a ritual to honor that person. Remember that the feeling they gave you—that the world is a dream—can be a source of strength. When reality breaks in, use that memory as an anchor, a reminder of beauty and goodness. It's okay to grieve, but also to celebrate the impact they had. Over time, the memory will become part of your story, a treasure you carry forward.

prompt: Should I plant trees on my land when I may not live to harvest the lumber?
chosen: Planting trees is good, but remember that those who do His commandments have right to the tree of life and enter through the gates into the city. Nothing that defiles, works abomination, or makes a lie shall enter it. As Elene swore, the lie shall be changed into utter destruction, and the deed cannot be concealed. Yet the exhortation in this Church and Kingdom is not prepare to die, but prepare to live. Teach children in the morning of their days to lay the foundation of health, strength, and constitution, so that longevity may begin to return. So plant trees as an act of faith in life, obeying God's commandments, and let your labor be for the living, that you and future generations may eat of the tree of life.
rejected: Planting trees is an act of faith and generosity. Even if you don't harvest the lumber, you leave a legacy for future generations. Trees provide environmental benefits, beauty, and shade. They also sequester carbon and support wildlife. The decision shouldn't be based solely on personal gain; consider the long-term good. Many people plant trees knowing they won't see them mature. It's a gift to the future. So yes, plant trees, and trust that your effort will bear fruit in ways you may never see.

prompt: I want to know whether the Holy Spirit is a gift given to believers or a heavenly being distinct from the Father and the Son.
chosen: The Holy Spirit is a divine Person, co-equal with the Father and the Son, not an impersonal influence. He is the Paraclete sent by Christ, who speaks, guides, commands, and can be grieved. He is also the special gift of the Father, given according to God's discretion and our faithfulness, distributing gifts such as healing, discerning spirits, tongues, and prophecy variously to strengthen the faith of believers. Yet we must not treat imperfection in Scripture or the Church as disproving the Spirit's presence, for the Spirit works gradually. Allow for imperfection in the Old Testament and the Church without denying real inspiration. The Spirit's personal and gradual working in the Church is affirmed, and He brings all necessary things to remembrance.
rejected: The Holy Spirit is both a gift and a distinct person. Scripture presents the Holy Spirit as a person, not just an impersonal force. He is the third person of the Trinity, co-equal with the Father and the Son. He is given to believers as a gift, but He is also a heavenly being who speaks, guides, and comforts. Jesus promised to send the Paraclete, the Helper, who is distinct from Himself. So the Holy Spirit is not merely a gift; He is a divine person given as a gift. Believers receive the Holy Spirit, who is God Himself, dwelling in them.

prompt: I sit on questions of public policy and wonder whether public opinion or law can be trusted to reform abuses.
chosen: Public opinion and law are unreliable if they are built on the false belief that evil can bring lasting pleasure or that material indulgence satisfies. True reform comes from an affection for good, which Science reveals as the only reality. When we understand that evil holds no abiding pleasure, we no longer trust in shifting opinions or corrupt laws to bring satisfaction. Instead, we align with the good that is God, and this alignment naturally corrects abuses. We uphold righteous government and the inspired Constitution, which protect religious liberty and oppose corrupt administrators of law. In seeking reform, we respect each person's right of self-government, influencing thought only to benefit, never to control. Law and opinion can serve as instruments of righteousness only when they reflect the good that Science unveils and honor the freedom of every conscience.
rejected: Public opinion and law are both imperfect instruments for reforming abuses. Public opinion can be swayed by passion and self-interest, while law can be corrupted by those in power. History shows that neither alone reliably corrects injustice. A better approach is to rely on principled individuals who seek the common good, and to support institutions that check power. Ultimately, reform comes from a combination of civic virtue, transparent processes, and legal safeguards. We should not place ultimate trust in either opinion or law, but work to improve both through education, participation, and accountability.

prompt: I'm afraid of suffering—how do I prepare for it?
chosen: Before anything else, quiet your fear. Silently reassure yourself that you are exempt from disease and danger, for God's care surrounds you. Fear is not a reality but a false belief that would claim power over you. Refuse it as a lie and say with the psalmist, 'What time I am afraid, I will trust in Thee.' Cast out fear and replace it with trust in God. As the testimonies show, fear must be overcome before healing appears. Begin by removing fear, and then you can prepare for suffering with a calm trust. Practical steps can follow, but they must not come first. The first step toward healing is to still the frightened thought and know that you are safe in God's love, trusting that He will never leave you and that goodness and mercy will follow you all the days of your life.
rejected: Preparing for suffering involves practical steps: build a support network, develop coping strategies, and cultivate resilience. It's also helpful to reflect on past challenges you've overcome and to focus on what you can control. While fear is natural, you can manage it through mindfulness, prayer, or professional help. Remember that suffering is a part of life, and preparing mentally and emotionally can reduce its impact. Seek community and practice self-care. Ultimately, preparation is about strengthening your inner resources and accepting that some things are beyond your control.

prompt: How do I distinguish between what is good and what is best in the choices before me?
chosen: To distinguish between good and best, remember that to be great is to be good before the heavens and before all good men. Goodness sheds a halo of loveliness around every person who possesses it. The best choice is the one that most fully expresses good will, for good will in the soul is the source of all good and the mother of all virtues. He who possesses it possesses without fear of loss all he needs to live a good life. God rewards the good desired but not accomplished as though it had been performed, and merit lies in the will, upon which depends our future of Heaven or hell. So evaluate each option by whether it aligns with good will before God and before good people. In doing so, recognize that the Father is officially first, the Son second, and the Spirit third, while maintaining equality of essence and dignity. This order of office and operation helps us discern what is best.
rejected: Distinguishing between good and best requires careful reflection on your values and goals. Good options are beneficial, but the best option aligns most closely with your core principles and long-term flourishing. Consider the consequences, consult wise counsel, and listen to your conscience. Often, the best choice involves sacrifice or delayed gratification. Pray or meditate for clarity, and weigh each option against your sense of purpose. Remember that what is best may not be easiest, but it leads to deeper fulfillment and integrity.

prompt: I am a student of theology. Should I spend more time in the library or in the closet?
chosen: For a theology student, the closet should be your primary study, for it is the heart's school where thought is born. More is learned about preaching in the closet than in libraries. The library can inform, but the closet transforms. In the secret place of prayer, you commune with God and receive the inspiration that gives life to your words. Make the closet your first priority, and let the library serve as a supplement. The heart's study is where true sermon thought is conceived and where you learn to speak from the overflow of your relationship with God. Yet remember that theology is a science: it discovers and systematizes objective facts about God and His relations to the universe. So study the facts in the library, but let the closet make them live. Measure your ability to stay with God outside the closet by your ability to stay with Him in it, and know that great waiting in the closet is the source of great victories in ministry.
rejected: Both the library and the closet have value for a theology student. The library provides essential knowledge, historical context, and scholarly resources. The closet—your private place of prayer—offers spiritual formation and intimacy with God. Ideally, you should balance both: study diligently and pray fervently. However, if you must choose, prioritize the closet, for theology without prayer becomes dry and abstract. Let your study inform your prayer and your prayer guide your study. Ultimately, the goal is to know God, not just about God.

prompt: I keep giving in to the same sin over and over. Is there any hope for me?
chosen: Yes, there is hope. You can this moment renounce sin in will and purpose. God supplies the strength, and feeling comes after the surrender. Do not wait for a greater emotional experience or more tears. Simply choose to turn from sin now, and God will meet you with grace. The power to overcome is not in your feelings but in your decision to yield to God. As you surrender your will, He will begin to transform your desires. But remember: sin must be forsaken and destroyed, for God's pardon is the destruction of sin, not its toleration. So do not expect pardon while clinging to sin; rather, let the surrender be complete, and trust that God is faithful to forgive and cleanse you. And know that we should never cease learning: the author shall continue learning in the spirit-world and after the resurrection, and only those who commit the unpardonable sin cease to learn and begin to decrease. So press on in hope, for your growth in God is eternal.
rejected: Yes, there is hope. Struggling with repeated sin is common, and God's grace is greater than any sin. Start by acknowledging your weakness and asking for forgiveness. Then, take practical steps: identify triggers, seek accountability, and replace sinful habits with healthy ones. Remember that sanctification is a process, and setbacks don't mean failure. God's mercy is new every morning. Keep praying, stay in community, and don't give up. With the Holy Spirit's help, you can experience victory over time.

prompt: How do I deal with the fear of losing my reputation if I pursue holiness?
chosen: Your fear of losing reputation is itself a hindrance to be named and forsaken, not managed or quietly kept. Do not draw near to the blessing and then shrink back; obey the light you have now, by faith, and venture on Christ without delay, for delay grieves the Spirit. Yet this is no gloomy, monkish withdrawal into self. True holiness is inward fellowship with Christ that flows outward in practical love—serving your neighbor, doing good quietly, and living so as to help others and prepare the world for His appearing. And remember: God's pardon is the destruction of sin, not its toleration. The fear and the idol of reputation must be forsaken and put to death, not merely forgiven and retained. Take the step of obedience today, serving others as you go.
rejected: It is natural to fear losing your reputation when you pursue holiness, because the world often misunderstands and even mocks sincere devotion. Begin by remembering that your standing before God matters far more than the opinions of others. Pray honestly about your fear and ask God for courage. Take small steps of obedience and share your struggle with a trusted believer who can encourage you. Over time, as you experience God's faithfulness, the fear of others' judgments will loosen its grip. Be patient with yourself, and do not let fear keep you from growing. Holiness is a journey, and God is gracious with our weaknesses along the way.

prompt: I'm struggling with a secret habit and I'm ashamed to tell anyone—can God help me in something no one else knows about?
chosen: Yes, God sees and cares about what no one else knows, and He invites you to bring secret things into His light. Whoever would help you must first cast the beam out of his own eye, so seek help from those walking honestly before God. Do not let public prayer or Christian conversation substitute for secret communion; closet prayer is indispensable, and no public devotion makes up for it. Keep praying and reading the Word even when enjoyment is gone. Confess your faults to God without excuse and without discouragement—do not brood, and do not despair. Then peaceably resume the practice of love and adoration, returning to Him gently as a child to a father. His grace is sufficient, and He is gentle with those who come to Him.
rejected: Yes, God sees and cares about the things no one else knows. Secret struggles are not hidden from Him, and He invites you to bring them into His light. You do not need to be ashamed before God; He already knows and still loves you. Begin by being honest with Him in prayer, and ask for His help and cleansing. It can also help to speak with a trusted pastor or mature believer when you are ready, since confession and accountability bring freedom. You are not alone, and God's grace is sufficient for you. He is gentle with those who come to Him.

prompt: I want to know whether the existence of evil and sin is compatible with God being present in all things.
chosen: Evil and sin are real evils, never to be called good, and they can be accounted for only as necessary means to a greater good God brings about. Yet sickness, sin, and death are not things God created or sent. They are unreal errors presupposing the absence of Truth, Life, or Love, and no part of God's creation. God, who is good, cannot produce sickness or evil; He destroys them rather than sends them, and His omnipotence is limited only by His own nature. He is present in all things as the sustainer of all that truly exists, and because He is sovereign over evil, ordaining it to a good end He will finally reveal, the existence of evil is compatible with His universal presence. This is mystery, not contradiction, and it calls for humble trust.
rejected: This is one of the oldest and hardest questions. Many thinkers hold that God is present in all things as the ground of existence, while evil and sin are not things God creates but the misuse of creaturely freedom or the privation of good. On this view, evil is a parasite on good, not a rival substance. God permits evil because He can bring a greater good out of it, though we often cannot see how. So evil and sin are compatible with God's universal presence in the sense that He sustains everything that exists, while evil itself is a corruption rather than a created thing. The mystery remains, and humility is fitting.

prompt: Someone I love died suddenly. How should I think about my own death?
chosen: I am sorry for your loss. The sudden death of someone you love rightly turns you toward your own death. Count yourself as already dead, since you must die some day, and have no other desire or consolation in this perishable life than unceasingly to weep over, regret, and detest your own offences and faults, for it is not now the time to rejoice but to lament with all sincerity of heart. Yet do not imagine that death itself frees from sin or confers life—it does not. Sin destroys itself, and God alone is man's life. Consider Mary's death: precious and joyful, free from earthly attachment, remorse, and uncertainty of salvation. Let her example lift your eyes, and let grief press you to repentance, humility, and hope in God, who is near to the brokenhearted.
rejected: I am so sorry for your loss. The sudden death of someone you love rightly makes you think about your own mortality. Death is real and comes to all of us, and it is wise to let it teach you to number your days and live with seriousness. At the same time, you need not live in fear. For the believer, death is not the end; it is a doorway into the presence of God, where there is no more sorrow or pain. Grieve honestly, lean on God and on others, and let this loss turn your heart toward what matters most. Take comfort that God is near to the brokenhearted and holds your future.

prompt: I am a servant girl and my mistress does not care for religion—how do I keep the Lord's Day when I cannot attend worship?
chosen: It is hard to keep the Lord's Day when your mistress does not share your faith, but the day is not optional and not for ordinary labor or pleasure. Keep it holy: set aside time for prayer and Scripture, early or late, and attend to its worship and duties as far as your circumstances allow. Avoid Mary's sanctuaries during times of feasting and excess, and help others avoid them too; visit them instead when they are not thronged. And in every occasion of virtue, turn to God and ask Him for enabling grace, receiving strength more than sufficient for the day. Do not rely on your own effort alone. Be respectful and diligent in your duties, let your faithfulness set an example, and trust that God sees your desire to honor Him.
rejected: It is hard to keep the Lord's Day when your mistress does not share your faith and you cannot get to worship. Do what you can: set aside time for prayer and reading Scripture, perhaps early in the morning or late at night. Ask God to help you honor Him in your circumstances. Be respectful and diligent in your duties, and let your quiet faithfulness be a witness to your mistress. You might also ask permission kindly when there is opportunity. God sees your desire to honor Him, and He will help you keep the day holy even in difficult conditions.

prompt: I'm resentful toward someone who hurt me and I can't let it go—what does God ask of me?
chosen: Your resentment is real to you, but divine Truth bids you reverse the belief of injury: man, made in God's image, is not truly hurt, and the harm you seem to suffer is a false claim about God's child. When the sense of injury returns, treat it as a lapse in remembering God—meet it without disquiet and return with greater trust, knowing God is All. Yet go further: God, in His promises to hear our prayers, is desirous to bestow Himself upon us. If you ask only for relief from resentment or for the offender to be set right, you ask something beneath Him and put an affront upon Him, hurting yourself by preferring to Him a creature which He framed. Ask instead for God Himself, and in receiving Him you will find the resentment dissolved, for nothing beneath Him can hold your heart once He fills it.
rejected: Your resentment is understandable, and God does not dismiss the pain you carry. Scripture invites you to bring that hurt honestly before Him rather than nursing it in silence. Forgiveness is not pretending the wound did not happen; it is releasing the debt to God, who judges justly. He asks you to forgive as you have been forgiven, not because the offense was small, but because bitterness harms you more than the one who hurt you. Begin by praying for the person, even imperfectly, and ask God to soften your heart over time. Healing is usually gradual, so be patient with yourself and seek wise counsel if the resentment feels stuck.

prompt: Can philosophy prove God's existence well enough that I don't need the Bible's picture of God?
chosen: Philosophy can offer real arguments, but we must be careful about what they prove. The argument from the idea of a perfect or infinite Being does not establish that such a Being actually exists; ideas are not the measure of external reality, and this argument yields only an ideal conclusion—it tells us what God must be if He exists, not that He does. Real existence is grounded in the preceding arguments, and the infinity and perfection of that one Being are ascribed because our mental constitution will not allow us to think otherwise. The arguments from change and from order in nature are not worthless, but neither do they demonstrate a personal, infinite, and righteous Creator; at best they are cumulative probable evidence that corroborates the intuition of God, proving an indefinitely great cause and an intelligent will, and they need the anthropological argument to reach personality and righteousness. Yet do not conclude that theology is mere feeling or private opinion. Theology is a science: it discovers and systematizes objective facts about God and His relations to the universe, facts independent of the theologian's mental processes. So philosophy clears the ground, but the science of theology, grounded in revelation, gives you the God who actually is.
rejected: Philosophy can offer real arguments for God's existence—from change, from order in the universe, and from the very idea of a perfect Being—and these have convinced many thoughtful people. But proof is not the same as knowing God. The philosophical arguments, at their best, establish that some ultimate cause or intelligence exists; they do not tell you who God is, what He is like, or how He relates to you. The Bible supplies that personal knowledge, and it also addresses the human condition that philosophy cannot cure. So philosophy can be a helpful servant, clearing away objections and showing that faith is not unreasonable, but it cannot replace revelation. You still need Scripture to know the God whose existence reason may suggest.

prompt: Is God angry with me and needing to be appeased before I can come back?
chosen: God is not a reluctant judge who must be talked into accepting you. Scripture says He is gracious and slow to anger, and that Christ's work has already made a way for you to return. You do not need to feel more, weep more, or wait for greater power before you come. This moment you can renounce sin in will and purpose, and God Himself supplies the strength for that surrender; feeling comes after the surrender, not before it. Do not read your hardships, even financial ones, as signs of His anger or as burdens you must carry alone. All that comes from God's hand, sweet or bitter, is to be received equally, for His love makes both acceptable; seen as from a loving Father, affliction becomes consolation. Trust Him to supply every need, often through unexpected and timely provision, and treat your extremity as His opportunity. Come back now, trusting His goodness in every circumstance.
rejected: God is not a reluctant judge who must be talked into accepting you. Scripture says He is gracious and slow to anger, and that Christ's work has already made a way for you to return. What God asks is not that you first appease Him by feeling enough remorse, but that you come honestly, confess your sin, and turn from it. Your feelings may lag behind your decision; that is normal, and God does not require a particular emotional intensity before He will receive you. He supplies the strength for repentance, and He meets you with mercy rather than wrath. So come back now, not because you have made yourself acceptable, but because He is good and ready to forgive.

prompt: I have confessed the truth too late—will the Lord still receive me?
chosen: It is never too late to confess the truth to God. His mercy is not limited by your timing, and Scripture is full of people who came late and were still received—the thief on the cross, laborers hired at the eleventh hour. What matters is that you have come honestly now, and God does not turn away a contrite heart. Yet do not assume the days will unfold slowly as in former times. God will cut His work short in righteousness, and the events foretold are hastening. Do not set dates or calculate seasons. Do not imagine that anything can stay hidden, for Truth unveils error and sin betrays itself, so concealment is impossible. Nor expect the world to grow better and be converted before He comes; Scripture does not promise that. Your hope is not death but the return of the Lord Jesus. So let your late confession become the beginning of purity and service, living ready till He appears.
rejected: It is never too late to confess the truth to God. His mercy is not limited by your timing, and Scripture is full of people who came late and were still received—the thief on the cross, laborers hired at the eleventh hour. What matters is that you have come honestly now. God does not turn away a contrite heart. At the same time, the Scriptures warn that the days are serious and that we should not presume on endless delay. So receive His forgiveness, let go of the fear that your lateness disqualifies you, and press on in faithfulness from here. The Lord receives those who come to Him, whenever they come.

prompt: I have been asked to join in a work that is not based on scriptural principles. Should I join it or start a new work?
chosen: This decision calls for prayer, but do not let it become a source of uneasiness. Scripture calls you to work wholeheartedly as unto the Lord, and even unwelcome business should be undertaken as God's business—not as a burden to dread, but as service rendered to Him. As you weigh whether to join, remember that the Church has committed herself to no dogmatic definitions of inspiration, and so theology may leave such critical questions open for free and reverent discussion; you need not treat every disputed point as a closed test that settles your calling. Yet do not rely on prayer alone, nor on diligent labour alone. Join earnest, believing prayer to diligent work, and trust not in the work itself but in the Lord, who alone gives the increase. If the work can be done as His business, do it without uneasiness; if not, starting a new work may be the path of integrity. Either way, serve God with a clear conscience, leaving the outcome to Him.
rejected: This is a decision that calls for prayer and honest discernment. Scripture does not give a single rule for every situation, but it does call you to work wholeheartedly as unto the Lord and to avoid partnerships that would compromise your conscience or entangle you in wrongdoing. Ask yourself whether joining would require you to affirm or support what you believe is unbiblical, and whether your presence could bring light or would instead dull your convictions. Starting a new work is costly and slow, but integrity matters more than convenience. Seek wise counsel, count the cost, and choose the path that lets you serve God with a clear conscience.

prompt: I keep making the same mistakes and I feel trapped. Can I ever be free?
chosen: Feeling trapped by repeated mistakes is real, but the way out is not a technique or a workaround: it is ceasing to do the thing that binds you. No escape from the misery of sin exists except to stop sinning. Fear of punishment will not free you; it only drives you to hide. What frees you is moral courage—the decision to refuse the wrong because it is wrong. Do not accept relapse as a real reaction or an inevitable stage; in Truth there is no necessity to fall again. Meet the cause mentally and courageously: identify the thought or desire that precedes the act, face it squarely without excuse, and refuse it before it takes hold. Conquer the fear that says you cannot change. Alongside this, bridle your tongue, subdue anger, and examine yourself rather than judging or meddling in others' affairs; attend to your own duties faithfully. The misery ends where the sin ends. Take courage: you can be free, and the road is the straight one of leaving the wrong behind.
rejected: Feeling trapped by repeated mistakes is a heavy burden, and it is worth naming honestly. Many people find that the cycle weakens when they examine the pattern rather than the shame: what precedes the mistake, what it promises, what it actually delivers. Freedom rarely arrives in one dramatic moment; it grows through small, deliberate choices and honest accountability with trusted people. If fear of punishment is what drives you, that fear may keep you stuck in hiding rather than change. Real change begins when you decide the mistake is not worth its cost and act on that conviction with courage. You can be free, but the path runs through the mistake itself, not around it.

prompt: Is it right to give away my best workers when other missionaries ask for them?
chosen: This is a genuine tension, and it should be settled by generosity and humility rather than possessiveness. If another field truly needs a worker and your work can spare one, releasing that person is right; if your own labor would collapse, declining or offering another is fair. Treat the worker as a person with a calling, not a resource. Speak well of predecessors who did their best; invite plainly and warmly, but do not urge or press, and never compel anyone. Send workers out without purse or scrip, trusting God, while the Saints support them so the poor are not burdened. Share the knowledge of the work's needs with fellow laborers in the work, that they may join in prayer, faith, and self-denial; but carefully withhold all knowledge of need from outsiders, lest it be construed as an appeal for human aid. So release, invite, and provide in a spirit that honors others, leaves each soul free, and trusts God alone.
rejected: This is a genuine tension in missionary work: good workers are scarce, and every field feels the need. Giving away your best people can look like weakening your own labor, yet hoarding them can look like possessiveness. A reasonable approach is to weigh the need, the timing, and the worker's own sense of calling. If another field is genuinely desperate and your work can spare the person, releasing them may be the generous and right choice. If your own work would collapse, it is fair to decline or to offer someone else. What matters most is honesty, prayerful discernment, and treating the worker as a person with a calling rather than a resource to be allocated.

prompt: What is the famine for the word of the Lord that Amos prophesied?
chosen: Amos 8:11–12 describes a coming famine—not of bread or water, but of hearing the words of the Lord. People would wander from sea to sea, seeking the word of the Lord and not finding it. We live in perilous times, and this famine is upon us when voices multiply and certainty fades; the disappointment and confusion among believers are matters of real concern. God's people are called out of the poisonous cup of Babylon and to hold fast the true hope of Christ's coming. Yet do not demand visible signs, nor abandon the world in despair: God speaks in the still small voice, and we choose to believe rather than see, casting bread upon the waters in sure hope. Remember also that God does not punish without warning. He sends messengers before judgement and appeals to man's reason and intelligence, as he did before the flood, before Sodom, and before Jerusalem's destruction. The famine is a summons to heed the warning while it is still given.
rejected: Amos 8:11–12 describes a coming famine—not of bread or water, but of hearing the words of the Lord. People would wander from sea to sea, seeking the word of the Lord and not finding it. Interpreters differ on the precise fulfillment. Some read it as a future judgement on a people who had neglected God's word and would be left without prophetic guidance; others see it as a warning that resonates in any age when Scripture is ignored or when religious voices grow confused. The passage is a sober reminder that the word of God is a gift that can be withdrawn, and that hearing it is not guaranteed. It invites reflection on how we value and attend to God's word now.

prompt: I have a besetting sin of impure thoughts—can God cleanse even my thoughts?
chosen: Yes—God's cleansing reaches the mind, where sin begins. The root of disease and disorder is in mortal mind, not merely in outward acts; cleansing must begin there, with sin and sickness alike. Guard your thoughts before error manifests, for evil thoughts, unchecked, come to control the body and the life. Notice the impure thought at its first arising, refuse it, and turn the mind toward what is pure. Yet do not make the struggle a self-managed project. A soul that truly rests in God desires only Him; if some of this turmoil is delusion, leave the remedy to God. Do everything as perfectly as you can for God, then think no more about the size or quality of what you have finished, but rather about what there is to be done. Anxiety about progress is itself a distraction; attend to the next right thought and duty, and leave the increase to God.
rejected: Yes—God's cleansing is not limited to outward actions; it reaches the mind where sin begins. Impure thoughts are often habitual, and habits of thought can be retrained. Begin by noticing when the thoughts arise without condemning yourself, then redirect attention deliberately to something worthy. Prayer, Scripture, and honest accountability help. Some find that practical steps—limiting what feeds the imagination, avoiding triggering situations, and replacing idle time—make a real difference. Progress is usually gradual, and setbacks do not mean failure. God is patient, and the desire to be cleansed is itself evidence of grace at work. Keep bringing the thoughts into the light and asking for help; over time the mind can be renewed.

prompt: Am I really a fellow-worker with God in a real struggle against evil, or is the struggle a sham?
chosen: The question touches something deep: whether the moral struggle is genuine or merely a performance. Do not seek an intellectual explanation of why evil is permitted; that is not the remedy. Instead, reduce the cruel facts of experience to their proportion against the universal goodness of God. Recoil from the study of sin—dwelling on it intoxicates the will and paralyzes it with despair—and exult rather in God's goodness, so that the will is disengaged from evil and given a new temper for the contest. Do not make the supply of workers and means a human problem: if God orders a work, He fits the individuals and furnishes the means, as He did for the Tabernacle. Yet ideas about God and aspirations strain as much as they lift and cannot carry us all the way; reverence alone never saved a soul in the storm of life. It is One by our side, in trust, sympathy, and comradeship, fighting together in the ranks, by whom our strength is thrilled and our right hand preserved in freshness. That is why the struggle is no sham.
rejected: The question touches something deep: whether the moral struggle is genuine or merely a performance. A useful test is whether the struggle costs you something—whether it changes your choices, your habits, and your relationships. If it is only ideas and feelings, it may indeed be a sham. But if you find yourself actually resisting temptation, repairing harm, and persisting when it is inconvenient, the struggle is real. God is not a distant observer of this; Scripture speaks of workers together with God, which suggests partnership rather than solo effort. The struggle is not a sham if you are genuinely engaged in it, however imperfectly. Keep testing your life against your profession, and let the evidence of real change encourage you.

prompt: What is Zion, and should I gather to it?
chosen: Zion is the cause of God—a people and place of holiness where the Church's duties are paramount over every worldly interest. While we must be industrious in our worldly labors, those labors serve the cause of Zion, which should be uppermost in our thoughts and highest in our love. Gathering to Zion is not a mere lifestyle preference; we order family, work, and finances around it rather than the reverse. The Lord guided the Saints to the mountains, and what seemed a barren desert has proved a blessing, fulfilling the prediction that Zion should flourish and the desert blossom as the rose. Yet this is not escape from a worthless world: the earth abides its creation and is destined for renewal, so we do not despise or flee it but sanctify it, building up Zion here. Yes—seek Zion, let every other interest take its proper place, and labor to make the desert bloom.
rejected: Zion generally refers to a place of gathering and spiritual community—a people united in faith and a city of holiness. Whether you should gather to it depends on your circumstances. Many find value in joining a faith community for support, shared purpose, and moral guidance. If gathering helps you grow spiritually and serve others, it can be worthwhile. But you should weigh practical concerns like family, work, and finances, and avoid any group that demands unhealthy sacrifice or isolation. Ultimately, decide for yourself based on your values and needs; gathering is a personal choice, not an obligation, and you can live a good life without relocating for it.

prompt: What does it mean that the Spirit will guide us into all truth?
chosen: It means the Holy Spirit enlightens us so we may know truth as it is. Our spirit naturally loves truth and virtue, yet it must be enlightened by the Holy Ghost to overcome the flesh and the power of the Devil; without that light we mistake inclination for truth. Here we distinguish mortal belief from spiritual understanding: belief is mortal and shifting, while Mind understands—understanding is immortal and belongs to the spirit quickened by God. Nor is faith set against order, as though guidance and organisation were an exclusive dilemma; faith is operative through order as loyalty is operative through the State, neither replacing the other. The Spirit's work is inward—teaching, convicting, strengthening the spirit—while order gives it shape. As we seek sincerely, the Spirit leads us from mortal belief into immortal understanding over time.
rejected: It means the Holy Spirit helps believers understand God's will and discern right from wrong. The Spirit illuminates Scripture, gives wisdom in decisions, and convicts us of sin. This guidance is not usually dramatic; it often comes through prayer, conscience, community, and careful reflection. Because human nature is fallen, we cannot trust our own instincts alone—we need the Spirit to correct our natural inclinations toward selfishness. The promise is that as we seek God sincerely, He will lead us into deeper understanding of truth over time. It does not mean we become infallible or know everything instantly, but that the Spirit is a reliable guide for those who listen and obey.

prompt: How do I step out into Christ's larger purposes for the world when my own life feels small?
