chosen: Begin not with self-improvement but with becoming as a little child, hanging upon Christ for all things and depending upon the author and fountain of them. That is the shortest and only way to enter the Kingdom of God and to be like All Things. Your life feels small because you are measuring it by your own strength; stop asking what you can do and ask what the best Christ dwelling within you can do through you. Trust the indwelling Christ to conquer what you never could, and do all things through Him who strengthens you. Be faithful in present duty and self-denial at the beginning, for such faithfulness leads to pleasures, and recourse to Christ's grace makes every difficulty easy. The one who hangs upon Christ is already walking in His larger purposes, however small the outward scene.
rejected: Start by recognizing that small doesn't mean insignificant. Christ often works through ordinary people in ordinary places. Take one concrete step: serve someone near you, volunteer, or join a community effort. Build habits of prayer and reflection to clarify your calling. Set modest goals and pursue them faithfully; competence and consistency open larger doors over time. Don't wait for a dramatic calling—act where you are, and let purpose grow through action. Seek mentors, read widely, and be willing to take risks. Remember that greatness in God's eyes is measured by faithfulness, not scale, and that your effort, however small, contributes to something larger.

prompt: I have a quick temper and habits I am ashamed of; can these be overcome?
chosen: Yes, these can be overcome—but begin with bridling the tongue and subduing anger rather than merely managing reactions. Examine yourself honestly: where does the temper rise, and what duty am I neglecting when it does? Attend to your own duties and business rather than judging or meddling in others' affairs. And before you attempt to help another, cast the beam out of your own eye first: the healer must first overcome his own belief and fear of disease or sin before he can help anyone else. Do not be terrified or paralyzed by small faults; quietly humble yourself before God and say to your soul: 'Courage! we have made a false step, but let us keep steadily on.' Replace ashamed habits with steady, humble effort and accountability. The work is inward first, then outward in faithful duty, and quiet perseverance will genuinely change your patterns over time.
rejected: Yes, they can be overcome, though it takes time and honesty. Start by identifying your triggers and the situations that set off your temper, then plan how to respond differently. Practice pausing before reacting, breathe, and remove yourself from heated moments when needed. For habits you're ashamed of, replace them with healthier routines and seek accountability from a trusted friend or counselor. Be patient with yourself; change rarely happens overnight, and setbacks are normal. If shame is heavy, consider talking with a pastor or therapist. You are not defined by your worst habits, and steady effort, self-compassion, and support can genuinely change patterns over time.

prompt: What shall I do to bud forth again and recover the first Life, wherein I was at rest before I became an Image?
chosen: Recovering that first Life is not chiefly a matter of willpower and rules. Victory over lower passions is the work of a Living Power within us, slowly transforming us from fleshly to spiritual and teaching us higher pleasures so that we are not left comfortless. Begin by turning inward and yielding to that Power rather than straining to retrain your appetites alone. When a fall seems to come, deny any real relapse in Truth: there is no true relapse in what is real. Meet its cause mentally and courageously, conquering fear. And do not give up rejoicing because the first dose seems ineffectual—keep on rejoicing, counting it all joy in temptations, and trust God to make the reckoning good. As you consent to that inward work, base desires lose their grip, higher pleasures take their place, and the rest you knew before you became an Image begins to return.
rejected: Recovering that first Life begins with honest self-examination and disciplined habits. Identify the desires and distractions that pull you from inner rest, then set clear rules for yourself—simplify your life, limit indulgence, and practice moderation. Through willpower and common sense you can retrain your appetites, replacing base desires with worthier pursuits like service, study, and reflection. Expect relapses and treat them as feedback rather than failure, adjusting your approach. Over time, consistent self-discipline restores a measure of peace and clarity. The key is to rely on your own resolve, build good routines, and keep returning to the practices that ground you.

prompt: I feel trapped by fear and can't break free. What can I do?
chosen: Feeling trapped by fear is real, but your fear is not a successful defense, and God's love is not weaker or less persistent than it. 'Fear wist not to evade as Love wist to pursue': wherever fear runs, Love meets it at every cross-road and by-path and gently turns it back. Yet the way out of misery is not escape by any other means—it is ceasing to sin, chosen by moral courage rather than fear of punishment. And remember where the greatest enemies lie: not chiefly in outward threats, but within—in passion and unchecked weakness. Our labor is to subdue our passions, conquer our inward foes, and keep our hearts right before the Lord. So when fear rises, speak honestly to someone you trust, notice the quiet ways Love keeps finding you, and let those moments turn you back toward God. Freedom grows as you stop evading, cease to sin, and let persistent Love catch up with you.
rejected: Feeling trapped by fear is a heavy burden, and it is brave of you to name it. Start small: when fear rises, pause and breathe slowly, and write down what you are afraid of so it stops looming as a shapeless threat. Talk to someone you trust—a friend, counselor, or pastor—since fear shrinks when it is spoken aloud. Build a few steady routines that give you a sense of footing, and set one tiny goal each day that fear cannot veto. Progress comes gradually, so be patient with yourself and celebrate small wins. If fear persists or deepens, consider professional help; there is no shame in that. You are not alone, and freedom is possible step by step.

prompt: I feel that all my living is nothing but penance and I cannot rejoice in it—how can I rejoice in the remedy?
chosen: It is understandable to feel worn down when life feels like nothing but penance, but do not give up rejoicing because the first dose seems ineffectual. Keep on rejoicing and count it all joy, even in temptations, trusting God to make the reckoning good. Yet do not delay: repent now. It is not desperate to have been wounded; it is desperate to neglect the cure. One who has fallen may rise again, as wrestlers and soldiers have risen after a fall. True repentance is not mere sorrow or a last-moment confession: it turns from evil, reforms your life, and makes restitution where you have wronged others. Cleansing comes through Christ's atonement, not your own misery. So name one small gift each day and thank God for it, even when feelings are flat; choose gratitude, sing, and gather with others who hope. Joy grows as you turn toward the remedy without delay.
rejected: It is understandable to feel worn down when life feels like nothing but penance. Rejoicing in the remedy begins with a shift in perspective: see the remedy not as an added burden but as the very thing that heals you. Try naming one small gift each day and thanking God for it, even when feelings are flat. Remember that joy is often a discipline before it is a feeling—choose gratitude, sing, and gather with others who hope. Be gentle with yourself; God is not a harsh taskmaster demanding misery but a healer inviting you into life. If the heaviness persists, speak with a pastor or counselor. Rejoicing grows slowly, like a muscle, as you keep turning toward the remedy rather than away from it.

prompt: Should the State provide medical care for the poor, or should it be left to charity?
chosen: This is a genuine question, but any answer must guard against charity that fosters idleness and pauperism. The aim is to help the poor help themselves: men and women should have a self-sustaining spirit, willing to labor in exchange for aid, and the Church's plan is to relieve present wants and then put the poor in a way to help themselves. Yet the deeper healing is not secured by material means. The testimonies repeatedly state that the reading of Science and Health with the Bible was the sole means of healing, so do not look to medicine or physicians as the source of cure. At the same time, never coerce a patient to stay with mental treatment against his wishes, and never refuse to release a case that has failed. Release such cases freely, letting the invalid learn from his own experience rather than being forced. The test throughout is whether the poor and the sick are genuinely helped to stand on their own.
rejected: This is a genuine question with reasonable arguments on both sides. State-provided medical care can ensure that the poor are not left untreated because they cannot pay, and it spreads risk across the whole population. Charity, by contrast, can be more personal, flexible, and responsive to local needs, and it engages communities in caring for their neighbors. In practice, most societies blend the two: a public safety net for basic and emergency care, supplemented by charitable clinics, religious institutions, and volunteer effort. The best approach likely depends on what actually helps the poor receive care without waste or neglect. Rather than choosing one exclusively, it may be wisest to ask which arrangement serves the poor most effectively and humanely.

prompt: I received an unexpected gift just when I needed it; how should I understand GOD's hand in it?
chosen: An unexpected gift arriving just when you needed it is a good occasion for gratitude, but do not treat the things of God with casual familiarity or one-sided gladness. The divine presence is holy and terrible as well as kind. Receive this gift with joy and holy fear together, in wondering, trembling adoration. Do not shut out God's warnings; let them awaken your heart to His nearness. Welcome the chastening hand that makes the heart feel God nigh, and keep the lamp awake till dawn. Yet do not remain only in the attitude of asking and expecting to receive. Reverse the method: give love to Jesus, give Him a home in your heart, and set your heart upon God rather than only beseeching gifts. Let the gift deepen trust and generosity, and let it draw you closer to the Giver in reverence. Receive it with joy, but also with awe, and answer with love.
rejected: An unexpected gift arriving just when you needed it is a good occasion for gratitude. It is natural to see God's hand in such timing, and you can receive it as a sign of care and provision. Give thanks specifically for what was given and for the person or circumstances through which it came. Let the gift deepen your trust that God knows your needs, and let it encourage you to be generous to others in turn. At the same time, avoid reading every event as a direct message; God's providence is real but often mysterious. The healthiest response is humble thankfulness, continued prayer, and a willingness to serve. Receive the gift with joy, and let it draw you closer to the Giver rather than becoming an end in itself.

prompt: I want to dedicate myself and my family to Mary, but I am not sure what that commitment involves. How should I do it?
chosen: Dedicating yourself and your family to Mary is a meaningful commitment, and the author gives concrete guidance for it. Dedicate yourself to Mary as your Lady, your Advocate, and your Mother, and resolve to love and serve her. Honor the saints most closely united to Mary, read daily some book on her glories, and recommend devotion to her, especially to your relatives, inducing others to love and serve her as well. Pray the Rosary with devotion and pauses, not in haste: meditating on any one mystery of the Passion suffices, and five devout decades please Mary more than fifteen said in haste. Pray about what this dedication will mean for your household, discuss it openly with your family, and let a simple prayer of consecration mark the occasion. Let the commitment express itself in family prayer, charity, and imitation of Mary's faith and humility, always within the wider Christian life centered on Christ.
rejected: Dedicating yourself and your family to Mary is a meaningful commitment, and it is good to approach it thoughtfully. Begin by learning more about Marian devotion through Scripture, Church teaching, and reliable books. Pray about what this dedication will mean for your household, and discuss it openly with your family so the commitment is shared rather than imposed. A simple ceremony or prayer of consecration, perhaps with a priest's guidance, can mark the occasion. Let the dedication express itself in practical ways: family prayer, charity, and imitation of Mary's faith and humility. Keep it balanced within the wider Christian life centered on Christ. Take your time, ask questions, and let the commitment grow naturally rather than rushing into forms you do not yet understand.

prompt: What does it mean that Christ will judge the living and the dead?
chosen: The creeds confess that Christ will return to judge the living and the dead. At the end of history Jesus, to whom the Father has committed all judgment, will render a verdict on every human being, those alive at his coming and those already dead. That judgment is according to what was done in the body: deeds, words, and the thoughts and intents of the heart lie open before him. Death fixes our state; as death leaves us, so judgment finds us, and there is no changing of accounts after death. Yet the believer's hope is not gradual purification after death, which Scripture gives no warrant for, but that in death itself the soul is washed in the blood of the immaculate Lamb and presented pure and without spot unto God. Because the judge is the one who died for us, we seek a right judgment in all things by the Holy Spirit, submitting to the Scriptures and to the teaching and example of our Lord and His Apostles, the only sufficient means of maintaining true moral judgment, and so live now in the light of that day.
rejected: The phrase comes from the creeds, which confess that Christ will return to judge the living and the dead. It means that at the end of history Jesus, to whom the Father has committed all judgment, will render a verdict on every human being. Those still alive at his coming and those who have already died will both stand before him. For believers this is not a terror but a hope, because the judge is the one who died for them. Judgment means that evil will not go unanswered and that God's justice will finally be made visible. It calls us to live now in the light of that day, trusting in Christ's mercy and striving to be found faithful when he appears.

prompt: I am a hermit and I want to build a small dwelling. What should I look for?
chosen: Let your wish be what the old poem wishes: a hidden little hut in the wilderness, a lark beside it, a clear pool to wash away sins, a wood around it, a southern aspect, and a few humble and obedient men praying to the King. Build to own, not to rent: every young man should aspire to possess his own home, renting being only temporary, since ownership gives stability, strength, patriotism, and fidelity to God. Then organize the little community so that every person is industrious, faithful, and prudent, never wanting a thing they cannot get, living within their means, manufacturing what they wear and raising what they eat. Such a community prospers in time and buys out its neighbors. Practically, look for legal access and water rights, ground that drains and builds well, and a modest, weather-tight dwelling of local materials. Visit in every season, weigh solitude against safety, and let the humble company who pray beside you share the same settled, owned, and self-sufficient place.
rejected: Building a small dwelling as a hermit is mostly a practical question. Look first at legal access and water rights, since a remote site often lacks both. Consider orientation and sunlight, drainage, and the stability of the ground. Think about how you will heat it, store food, and reach help in an emergency. Keep the footprint modest and the construction simple, using local materials where possible. Weigh solitude against safety: complete isolation can be dangerous if you fall ill. Visit the site in different seasons before committing. A small, well-insulated, weather-tight structure with a reliable water source and a clear path to the nearest road will serve you far better than an ambitious design.

prompt: I love the Bible and believe in Jesus, but I struggle to accept Joseph Smith as a prophet. Can I keep one and not the other?
chosen: The tension is real, but it cannot be resolved by keeping one and dropping the other. If one book is true, both are true; they stand or fall together as witnesses of the same work. Whoever confesses that Jesus lives must also acknowledge Joseph Smith as a Prophet of God. And more than that: Joseph Smith is a prophet of God, living and not dead. His name will never perish, and it will eventually be held in reverence and honor among the children of men as the name of the Son of God is held. Do not measure him by worldly learning. He was unlearned in the learning of the world, but he was taught by the angel Moroni and by God himself, so charging him with ignorance is unjust and false. Study honestly and pray earnestly, and receive the whole witness rather than dividing it.
rejected: This is a real tension many people feel, and it deserves a patient answer. The Bible and the Book of Mormon are separate books, and you can certainly love and read the Bible while still being unsure about Joseph Smith. Faith is often a process, and doubt about one historical figure need not destroy your relationship with Jesus. Many Christians who never heard of Joseph Smith love the Bible and trust Christ. So take your time, study the claims honestly, and do not feel pressured to resolve everything at once. What matters most is that you keep praying, keep reading Scripture, and let your questions be part of an honest search rather than a reason to walk away from faith altogether.

prompt: I wonder whether the hope of Israel has anything to do with me as a Gentile believer.
chosen: Yes, the hope of Israel has everything to do with you as a Gentile believer. Scripture presents the Gentiles as grafted into the same olive tree and made partakers of the promises given to Israel. That hope is not a separate ethnic hope but the messianic hope that God will restore his people and through them bless the nations, and we look for the Jews' gathering and redemption by God's own power. Our part is goodwill and prayer, not presumption, and not confidence in human learning or skill to convert and sanctify souls. Join an intimate conviction of your own inability with firm confidence in God's power to sanctify yourself and others, trusting supernatural means, for all human learning and power cannot save a soul. And look for the day when God will roar out of Zion and utter his voice from Jerusalem, shaking the heavens and the earth; then Jerusalem shall be holy and the sign of the Son of man shall appear in heaven.
rejected: Yes, the hope of Israel has everything to do with you as a Gentile believer. Scripture presents the Gentiles as grafted into the same olive tree and made partakers of the promises given to Israel. The hope of Israel is not a separate ethnic hope but the messianic hope that God will restore his people and through them bless the nations. As a Gentile believer you share in that hope by faith in Christ, who is himself the hope of Israel. So pray for the peace of Jerusalem, read the prophets with attention, and see your own salvation as part of the one great story of God's redeeming work, which includes both Jew and Gentile in a single people of God.

prompt: My child has abandoned the faith and is living in vice. Should I cut her off, or is there something else I should do?
chosen: This is a painful situation, and cutting her off entirely is rarely the right first move. Examine yourself first: parents must never oppose a child's vocation or withdraw her from a state of perfection, and must never sow vanity and covetousness in tender minds. Your task is to form her in virtue. Never drive your child; lead her along. Govern her by faith rather than the rod, and never correct her in the heat of passion. Teach her to love you rather than to fear you, and let good example do what words cannot. Set clear boundaries about what happens under your roof and what you will and will not support, but keep the relationship open. Remember that the Church's note is tolerance: she is the mother, not the magistrate, and she is morally and theologically patient short of her necessary terms of communion. So pray, seek wise counsel, speak the truth in love, and let your steady life and the Church's patient charity draw her back toward virtue.
rejected: This is a painful situation, and cutting her off entirely is rarely the right first move. Set clear boundaries about what happens under your roof and what you will and will not support financially, especially anything that enables the vice. But keep the relationship open. Let her know you love her and that your door remains open, even while you refuse to pretend the choices are harmless. Pray for her consistently, and involve wise counsel from your church. Avoid constant lecturing, which usually pushes people further away. Speak the truth in love, in season and out of season, and let your own life be a steady witness. Many people return to faith after years away, often because someone refused to abandon them.

prompt: I'm lonely and no one seems to care. Is being alone the same as being forsaken?
chosen: Being alone and being forsaken are not the same. Loneliness can feel like abandonment, but hidden solitude may be Heaven's will, a place where no human sympathy reaches and where God alone knows the secret throbbings of your heart. Each heart's bitterness is its own; others cannot fully enter it, and you need not demand that they do. God alone is the all-satisfying portion of the soul, and your one absorbing aim can be to glorify Him in complete surrender. Do not wait for a change of home, company, or state before beginning this work. Undergo it just where you are—in your own home or another's, married or single, rich or poor—with obedience, patience, and simplicity, resting in the Lord who knows all yet loves you better than He knows.
rejected: Being alone and being forsaken are not the same thing. Loneliness is a feeling many people carry, even when others are nearby, and it often means you're grieving connection rather than that no one truly values you. It's worth reaching out—to friends, family, a pastor, or a counselor—because isolation tends to distort how we see ourselves and others. At the same time, being alone doesn't mean you've been abandoned by God. Scripture promises that God draws near to the lonely and will never leave you. Try to name what you're feeling, share it with someone safe, and let small acts of connection remind you that you are not forgotten.

prompt: I am drawn into secret societies and wonder whether a Christian should belong.
chosen: Secret societies appeal because they promise belonging, purpose, and shared mystery, but a Christian should be cautious and, where membership divides your interests from the Church, should withdraw. Seek first the kingdom of God, which provides all that these societies offer—fellowship, meaning, and a place to belong—without secrecy or divided loyalty. Christianity is not merely one mystery religion among many; it is uniquely the religion of ethical Monotheism, the Fatherhood of God and the brotherhood of man, resting on its appeal to Reason and Conscience rather than on miracles. This faith also teaches a balanced obedience: obedience to civil authority is a duty for conscience' sake grounded in God's will, commands contrary to virtue must be disobeyed, and resistance to arbitrary or unconstitutional power may in extreme cases be a right. Let your allegiance to Christ be open and undivided.
rejected: Secret societies can be appealing because they offer belonging, purpose, and a sense of shared mystery. Whether a Christian should join depends on the group's beliefs and practices. Some organizations require oaths, rituals, or loyalties that may conflict with your faith or with honesty and openness. Before joining, examine what the group asks of you, whether it divides your commitments from your church, and whether its secrecy would compromise your integrity. Talk with a pastor you trust. If membership pulls you away from Christ or asks you to hide what should be open, it's wise to decline.

prompt: I feel like I'm supposed to do something great but I don't know what—how do I deal with this restless longing?
chosen: That restless longing can become a place of prayer. Rather than rushing to solve it, learn to wait before God like a beggar, empty-handed and expectant. Keep your mind in His presence, and when it wanders, recall it gently and without disquiet. Do not long for a different state, place, or service; embrace the vocation you already have and serve God in the lowly duties at hand, caring not what the service may be, provided God be served. And when you notice your own agitation, refuse to be angry over it. Gently place the troubled heart in the hands of our Lord, ask Him to cure it, and renew your good resolutions without discouragement. In this humble waiting and faithful attention, the longing is offered rather than suppressed, and clarity comes in His time.
rejected: That restless longing is common, especially when you sense you're meant for something significant but can't yet see what it is. Start by naming the feeling rather than suppressing it. Then take small, concrete steps: serve where you are, develop your gifts, and seek counsel from mentors who know you. Restlessness often fades when we act on what's already in front of us. It also helps to remember that greatness is usually built through faithful, ordinary obedience rather than a single dramatic calling. Give yourself permission to not have the whole picture yet, and let curiosity and service guide you while the path becomes clearer.

prompt: I'm a young man preparing for a mission and I'm nervous about learning a foreign language. Should I seek the gift of tongues?
chosen: It's understandable to be nervous about learning a foreign language before a mission. The gift of tongues is real, but it is easily imitated by the devil, so seek it only when needed, not as a shortcut that neglects your duties. If you seek it, accompany that seeking with obedience: tithe faithfully, pray, pay your debts, and honor the Sabbath. Do not despise the gift when it is genuinely given. Remember that true zeal is not harsh or intolerant but simple, tender, and considerate—the childlike spirit of a full baptism of the Holy Ghost. And while Scripture is the foundation, God wills us to go beyond it into personal experience of Himself, received through inward meditation and pondering. Let your preparation include that quiet openness, trusting Him to provide what the mission requires.
rejected: It's understandable to be nervous about learning a foreign language before a mission. The gift of tongues is mentioned in Scripture, but it isn't something we should chase as a shortcut. Most missionaries learn languages through patient study, practice, and immersion, and that ordinary effort is itself a form of faithfulness. Rather than seeking a dramatic gift, focus on steady preparation: study, practice with native speakers, and pray for help. If God chooses to give any special gift, He will do so in His timing, but your calling is to be faithful with the ordinary means He provides.

prompt: I wonder whether Paul's theology is the true foundation of Christian doctrine or only one voice among many; how should I regard him?
chosen: Paul is a central and authoritative witness, but he is best understood when theology and experience are held together, as he himself held them. His letters address real communities in the light of eternal principles, and his teaching is meant to be lived. For Paul, faith is not mere belief, assent, or trust; it is an identification of the self with Christ—a going down into death with Him and a rising into newness of life, lived henceforth unto Him. Yet Paulinism is not the foundation on which the Catholic doctrine of faith was built. It has acted rather as a recurring ferment and critical impulse within the history of dogma, a conscience of the Church. Regard Paul accordingly: read him within the whole canon and the church's ongoing reflection, and let his theology shape how you pray, suffer, reconcile, and serve.
rejected: Paul is one of the most influential voices in Christian doctrine, and his letters shaped much of the New Testament and later theology. But he is not the only voice—the Gospels, Peter, John, and the broader tradition all contribute. Rather than treating Paul as either the sole foundation or a minor voice, it's helpful to read him within the whole canon and the church's ongoing reflection. He writes as a pastor and theologian addressing real communities, so his letters are best understood in context. Regard him as a central and authoritative witness whose theology must be read alongside the rest of Scripture and the church's life.

prompt: I'm troubled that the Bible contains idealizing history, dramatic compositions, and primitive traditions—can I still call it inspired?
chosen: Start with Christ—but know what starting with him costs. The Christian life is the path of cross-bearing: self-denial, obedience, and endurance with its severities undisguised. Because we trust the crucified and risen Lord, we trust the community that handed on his memory, and so receive its Scriptures as inspired. Yet the Church has committed herself to no dogmatic definition of inspiration; she leaves the how of it open for free and reverent discussion. So bring your honest questions about idealizing history, drama, and primitive tradition—not as an excuse for easy unbelief, but as work done on your knees. This is not a soft option. It demands your life. But it promises a reward worth everything: the comradeship of God and man, and a Lord who walks the hard road with you to the end.
rejected: Yes, you can still call the Bible inspired, though you may need to refine what inspiration means. Inspiration does not require that every text be flat, literal chronicle; God can speak through idealizing history, through drama and poetry, and even through primitive traditions that carry a genuine encounter with the divine. The Church has long held that Scripture is inspired and trustworthy for faith and life, and that its human authors wrote with real literary art and within their cultures. So your observations about genre need not undermine faith; they can deepen it. Read Scripture prayerfully, in the community of faith, and let its varied forms lead you to God rather than expecting a uniform record.

prompt: How do I know God's will in a decision I'm unsure about?
chosen: Do not settle for the bare minimum of knowing what to do. God has said he will guide; take that as an actual fact, not a distant hope. Turn his promise into a prophecy spoken over your life and rest in it, because God cannot lie. Be filled with the mature knowledge of his will in all wisdom and spiritual understanding—not by straining to manufacture certainty, but by rejoicing that what he has said is true. Take his promises and comfortings largely and your troubles lightly. The uncertainty that looms so large is small beside the God who has spoken. Examine the choice in that light—Scripture, wise counsel, gifts, circumstances—but let your confidence rest not in your effort to be certain but in the God who cannot lie. Then step forward, not as one managing an anxious puzzle, but as one carried by a promise that is already true.
rejected: Begin by praying for wisdom, since God promises to give it generously. Then examine the decision honestly: what does Scripture say, what do wise and mature Christians advise, and what are the likely consequences? Consider your motives and gifts, and whether an option leads you toward or away from Christ. Where Scripture speaks clearly, obey it; where it is silent, use sanctified judgment. You need not achieve perfect certainty before acting—God often guides as we step forward in faith. Make the decision, commit it to God, and remain open to correction. Trust that he is able to guide a willing heart, and do not be paralyzed by the fear of getting it wrong.

prompt: I'm surrounded by attractive but questionable teaching—how do I discern what is dangerous?
chosen: Discernment must be practised strictly according to the divine Principle, not by material means or human suspicion. Truth is one and self-consistent; error is discordant and self-contradictory. Test every teaching by the Principle itself: does it proceed from and return to God as All, or does it introduce a power, cause, or fear apart from Him? Apply the rules of the scientific method to thought: observe the claim, examine its premises, and see whether it accords with the divine Principle or merely pleases the senses. Attractive error borrows the language of truth while violating its spirit. Judge not by personalities, crowds, or outward results. And do not abandon the learner at the end of the lesson: continue in loving care and counsel until students tread firmly in the way. Yet never teach mental healing indiscriminately for fees. Refuse to impart it to the morally unfit for money; require honesty, purity, and genuine fitness in the student. The Principle is not a commodity, and its teaching must be guarded by moral fitness, not sold to whoever pays.
rejected: Discernment begins with knowing the truth deeply, so immerse yourself in Scripture and sound doctrine. Test every teaching against the core of the gospel: does it honor Christ, uphold his death and resurrection, and produce genuine love and holiness? Be wary of teaching that flatters, promises quick results, or demands money. Examine the teacher's character and fruits, and ask whether the teaching makes you more dependent on Christ or on the teacher. Pray for wisdom and stay rooted in a faithful community that can help you evaluate claims. Questionable teaching is often attractive because it mixes truth with error, so learn to notice what is subtly omitted or distorted, and do not be afraid to ask hard questions.

prompt: I am a preacher and I feel my ministry is superficial. Where does superficiality come from?
chosen: Superficiality in ministry is traced to one root: lack of praying. We explain dead and superficial ministries by circumstances, methods, or audiences, but the real cause is prayerlessness. One error is the hermit's withdrawal—study and devotion never spent on people. The other is the popularizer's activism—activity and sermon production with prayer left out of the plans. Reject both. Time with God is useful only as it is expended on men. And remember: the condition of the Church is not independent of its leaders. Preachers are primarily responsible for her spiritual state; where the pulpit is shallow, the people starve. Spiritual leaders are tokens of God's favor. So let the text, the sermon, and the study be bathed in prayer. A sermon produced apart from prayer is dead however polished; a ministry soaked in prayer is alive however plain. Trace your superficiality to your praying, and begin there.
rejected: Superficiality often comes from a ministry driven by activity rather than depth. When sermons are prepared quickly, prayer is crowded out, and the preacher's own walk with God becomes thin, the ministry reflects that thinness. It can also come from fear—wanting to please people, to be relevant, or to avoid difficult texts—so the preaching stays safe and shallow. Cultural pressure toward entertainment and quick results contributes too. The remedy is to recover depth: unhurried time in Scripture and prayer, honest self-examination, and a willingness to preach what costs. Ask whether you are relying on technique more than on God, and whether your people are being fed substance or only stimulation.

prompt: I'm terrified of dying and what comes after. What happens to me if I haven't found God by then?
chosen: Your fear is real, but it is not the strongest thing in the room. God never forsakes us until we first forsake him; he does not abandon the soul that has not abandoned him. So the question is not whether you have 'found God' by some deadline, but whether you will leave him. Fear to forsake him, and remain always with him. And if your remembrance has lapsed, do not be disquieted—return with greater trust. For your fear does not outrun his love. Fear wist not to evade as Love wist to pursue. At every cross-road and by-path, Love meets you and gently turns you back. Your anxiety is not a successful defense; it is a door Love is already knocking through. Turn to Christ now: confess, trust, receive his forgiveness. Let forgetfulness lead you back with deeper confidence. Stay with him, and let the persistent Love that pursues you be your peace.
rejected: Your fear is understandable, and God is merciful. Scripture assures us that God desires all to be saved and that his mercy is great. If you are afraid you haven't found God, know that he is already seeking you—no one comes to him unless drawn, and your very fear may be evidence of his work in you. Turn to Christ now, while there is time: confess, trust, and receive his forgiveness. Do not despair; God's grace is not limited by your timing, and he is faithful to those who call on him. Speak with a pastor, pray honestly, and let your fear drive you to God rather than away from him.

prompt: I'm afraid of being despised and mocked by others—how should I respond when people insult me?
chosen: Separate the insult from your worth: your value is not decided by another's contempt. Yet not all mockery is equal. It is base to mock an old man, cruel to mock an invalid, and foolish to mock a simple person; such contempt reveals the mocker's own ugliness. But good manners, skill, and wisdom are fair things that hide ugliness and deserve honour. When insulted, ask whether the words contain truth: if so, learn quietly; if mere contempt, let it pass. Condescend to the humour of others and bear with rude and tiresome manners, offering these victories over your own humour for the love of God. Do not boast when an enemy falls; rather, when you see things as they are, flattery and reproach become alike to you, and you grow in humility and resignation.
rejected: First, separate the insult from your worth: your value is not decided by someone else's contempt. When mocked, pause, breathe, and avoid reacting from fear. Ask yourself whether there is any truth in the criticism; if so, learn from it quietly, and if not, let it pass. Set calm boundaries with people who are repeatedly cruel, and lean on trusted friends who see you accurately. Practice self-compassion and remember that fear of others' scorn shrinks when you act on your values rather than on applause. Over time, exposure to mild disapproval and reflection on your identity will loosen the grip of that fear.

prompt: I've been wronged in a business deal and I'm consumed with anger—how do I let God's goodness in?
chosen: Anger after a wrong is natural, but it can become a cage. Name the loss honestly, then press steadily forward on the main line: the one thing God has given you to do. Let grievances come and go without being side-tracked by them. Remember that your only business is to please God, and all else is folly; so renounce all that is not Him, including the grip of this dispute, and trust Him wholly. Seek fair resolution in His name, but hold the outcome loosely. Let God's goodness in by attending to what He sets before you today, in perpetual remembrance of Him, rather than replaying the injury.
rejected: Anger after being wronged is natural, but it can become a cage. Start by naming the loss honestly and letting the anger be felt without letting it rule you. Take practical steps: gather records, seek fair mediation or legal advice, and set boundaries so the wrong is not repeated. At the same time, guard your heart from bitterness through prayer, gratitude, and forgiveness practiced over time. Let God's goodness in by noticing small daily gifts, by worship, and by serving someone else. Anger often softens when you act justly and release revenge, trusting that God sees and cares.

prompt: If Jesus claimed to be one with God, was he not either a deceiver or deluded rather than divine?
chosen: The question presents a false dilemma. Jesus' claim to oneness with God need not make him a deceiver or deluded; there is a third possibility, that he was telling the truth. Consider his consistent holiness, his calm self-mastery under trial, and his sinless conscience: a deceiver would not live so, and a deluded man could not sustain such moral sanity. Since Jesus cannot be charged with mental or moral unsoundness, his testimony must be true, and he himself must be one with God. God remains unchangingly faithful even when our faith fails; unbelief brings loss to us, not to Him. Nor is it fraud for God to have used literary methods suited to an undeveloped age—dramatic composition, primitive tradition, idealizing history—as vehicles of inspiration; such methods differ from deliberate deceit, and honest inquiry should weigh the evidence.
rejected: The question presents a false dilemma. Jesus' claim to oneness with God need not make him a deceiver or deluded; there is a third possibility, that he was telling the truth. His teaching, miracles, and resurrection are offered by Christians as evidence of that. You might also consider that the Gospel writers shaped their accounts for theological purposes, so the claim may reflect the early church's confession rather than a bare historical utterance. Either way, the trilemma is not logically exhaustive, and honest inquiry should weigh the historical evidence and the spiritual fruit of his life.

prompt: I am not sure I have truly repented of an old sin. How can I tell?
chosen: Repentance is not mainly a feeling but a turning. Ask whether you have honestly acknowledged the sin, grieved it, and changed direction. Signs of true repentance include sorrow for the wrong done, a willingness to make amends, and a settled change of behavior. Yet every blessing is predicated on obedience to law, and one who sins in youth and repents late has lost something that can never be regained, though he may be forgiven. Understand forgiveness not as overlooking sin while belief in it continues, but as the destruction of sin through spiritual understanding that casts out evil as unreal. Still, do not declare sin unreal while leaving its claim undetected; first detect and expose the claim, remove its mask, and only then prove its unreality.
rejected: Repentance is not mainly a feeling but a turning. Ask whether you have honestly acknowledged the sin, grieved it, and changed direction. Signs of true repentance include sorrow that is more about the wrong done than about getting caught, a willingness to make amends where possible, and a settled change of behavior over time. If the old sin still troubles you, bring it honestly to God, confess it, and receive forgiveness. Talk with a trusted pastor or counselor. Assurance usually grows through obedience and time rather than through searching your feelings.

prompt: I am a poor old man and my daughter has been the instrument of my awakening—how do I show gratitude to God for her?
chosen: What a gift, that your daughter became the instrument of your awakening. Gratitude to God should not remain in words alone; let it become obedience to the teachings and the living of the truth in daily life. When the soul has shaken off the dust of earth, aspires unto God, dreads the least separation from Him as a most cruel death, and cleaves with firmest purpose to the one Sovereign Good, then all she receives, undertakes, and does becomes a pure and true prayer, and it becomes as simple and easy to contemplate God and rejoice in Him as to live a purely natural life. Remember too that the children of God have various gifts and degrees of knowledge yet all form one Spirit; do not contend about differing fruits and gifts, but acknowledge them in one another as children of the Spirit of God.
rejected: What a gift, that your daughter became the instrument of your awakening. Gratitude to God can begin with simple thanksgiving: name her specifically in your prayers, and thank God for the grace shown through her. Then let gratitude take shape in action—tell her plainly what she has meant to you, and let your changed life be the evidence. Spend time in prayer and worship, and look for ways to pass on the mercy you received to others. Gratitude grows when it is spoken, remembered, and shared.

prompt: I feel like my suffering is pointless—how can it have any meaning?
chosen: Your suffering is not pointless, but its meaning is not found by denying it or by seeking relief apart from God. Abandon yourself to Him in interior and exterior pain alike, and let Him be your life, your work, and your joy. Suffering serves: it can punish and correct what needs turning, purify the heart, prevent harm, and above all unite you with God and with others who suffer. As in the Cross, the value is set before the painfulness—love, obedience, and union with God come first, and the pain serves them. So do not look for meaning outside of God or wait for pain to vanish before you live. Give yourself wholly to Him, and let even this suffering be drawn into His purpose, making you more like Christ and closer to the God who holds you.
rejected: Your suffering is real, and it hurts. When pain drags on, it's natural to feel it has no purpose, and I don't want to minimize that. But meaning rarely shows up in the middle of pain; it usually appears later, in what suffering teaches us—patience, compassion, clarity about what matters. Many people find that their hardest seasons eventually shaped who they became. You might also look for small ways to make the pain count now: reaching out to someone else who hurts, or letting others care for you. If the pointlessness feels crushing, please talk to a counselor or someone you trust. You don't have to carry this alone, and the meaning may become clearer with time.

prompt: What can I learn from other religions like Hinduism?
chosen: Other religions like Hinduism may be studied with profit, but first we must know what Christian religion is: learning to know ourselves—how we were in the Unity in Adam, how we now stand in dissension and contrariety, whither we go when we pass out of this condition, and how we come forth from disunion into that one Tree, Christ in us. Yet this is not mere doctrine or feeling; true satisfying religion is Christ recognised, known, adored, and living within the soul—the New Life and New Birth. This knowledge comes not chiefly from comparison but from the Holy Scriptures, the one fountain of all wisdom and strength. Let us read them daily, prayerfully, and systematically, meditating on what we find and translating it into obedience, preferring the Bible above all other books. Read in that light, Hinduism's meditations may sharpen our sense of the inward journey, but Scripture alone supplies the way of deliverance.
rejected: Other religions like Hinduism can teach Christians valuable lessons. Hinduism's emphasis on meditation and inner peace can deepen our prayer life, and its traditions of nonviolence and compassion echo Jesus's teachings. Studying other faiths can broaden our understanding and foster respect between communities. However, Christians should remember that Jesus is the unique path to salvation, so we learn from others without adopting their beliefs. We can appreciate truths found in Hinduism while holding firmly to our own faith, using such study to strengthen our witness and love for neighbors of other traditions.

prompt: Should I pray for God to change the weather or heal someone in a way that breaks the laws of nature?
chosen: Bring every request to God—healing, weather, all of it—trusting that He can act beyond nature, for Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever. Yet do not make visible signs the measure of faith. God often speaks in the still small voice, and we are called to choose to believe rather than to see. Pray boldly, leave the outcome in His hands, and cast your bread upon the waters in sure hope. Then lift your gaze above the world's uncertain haze to the bright fields beyond the sky, where mercy waits and every prayer is held. Return to your daily world to love and serve, preparing the Lord's way of mercy with a heart fixed on the hope beyond what you can see.
rejected: You can pray for anything, but expect God to work within the natural order He established. Asking Him to break the laws of nature is asking for a sign on your terms, and Scripture suggests such demands are not the way of faith. God's ordinary providence—medicine, weather patterns, wise choices—is usually how He answers. Pray for healing and good weather, yes, but submit to His will and do not treat unanswered supernatural requests as failure. Faith trusts God's wisdom in the ordinary, not in spectacular interruptions.

prompt: How can the true cross be known from among other crosses?
chosen: The true cross is known not by human reasoning but by divine testimony, and that testimony belongs to the consummation of an elemental spiritual movement organic with the making of men and the divine-human travail for a redeemed humanity. Judas cannot declare on which tree the Saviour was hung, so the three crosses are set in the city and a dead young man is brought on a bier. When the first two crosses are raised over him, he remains dead; but when the third, the holy rood, is laid upon him, he rises restored in body and soul, and the people revere the Father and honor the true Son. So too Constantine, fear-smitten before the greater host of Huns and Goths, is promised aid and the token of victory by the messenger of the King of angels; gazing on high he beholds the beauteous tree of glory inscribed 'By this sign thou shalt overcome the foe,' and the victory is made manifest as given by the King Almighty through his holy rood, not by the strength of his own army or by fortune.
rejected: The true cross is known by its miraculous power. According to the legend, Helena, mother of Constantine, traveled to Jerusalem and had three crosses uncovered. To determine which was the cross of Christ, a dead man was placed on each in turn. When the third cross was laid upon him, he was restored to life, and so the true cross was revealed. Some traditions also say that Judas, the bishop of Jerusalem, identified the cross by its healing power or by an inscription, but the raising of the dead is the clearest sign. The people, seeing the miracle, praised God and honored the cross. Thus the true cross is distinguished from the others by the divine testimony of a resurrection, not by human reasoning or marks on the wood.

prompt: I am a believer who has been greatly blessed with answers to prayer. How can I record and remember them so that my faith grows?
chosen: Keep a record of God's answers so that you can give Him the glory and tell others what He has done. Write each request with the date, note the definite answer, and thank God specifically, naming His faithfulness aloud. Remember that prevailing prayer rests on the conditions God has given—humility, forsaking sin, faith, obedience, and asking according to His will in Christ's name—so examine your heart, confess sin, and submit your requests to Him. Yet do not treat these as techniques for experts. Every believer, however ordinary, is freely invited into the full knowledge of Christ Himself, in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hid. As you review your record, let it lead you past the gift to the Giver, into deeper fellowship with the sufficient Savior. Then share these testimonies with family and church, so that others are encouraged, God is honored, and your faith grows in Him.
rejected: Keep a simple prayer journal. Write down each request with the date, then note when and how it was answered. Review the journal regularly—perhaps weekly or monthly—so you can see patterns of God's faithfulness over time. You might also set reminders on your phone or keep a small notebook with you to jot down answers as they come. Sharing your journal with a trusted friend can help too. The goal is to build a habit of noticing and remembering, so that your faith grows as you look back and see how your prayers have been answered.

prompt: I am afraid of death and what comes after. Does God's pursuit continue beyond this life?
chosen: Your fear of death is real, but it is not a defense that can hold against God. Fear wist not to evade as Love wist to pursue: at every cross-road and by-path, Love meets your fear and gently turns it back. Yet do not imagine that death itself will bring you nearer to God or finish what you leave undone here. This world is the place to find Him; the remedy must be found now, for here we can most easily and quickly find Him. Immortality is the corollary of belief in a righteous God whose purpose for the higher spirits is not exhausted by this life, but that hope does not excuse us from seeking Him here. So trust the Love that pursues you now, and seek Him while He may be found.
rejected: Your fear of death is natural, and Scripture treats it seriously. Yet the consistent witness of faith is that God's love does not stop at the grave. The psalmist asks where he could flee from God's presence and answers that even in Sheol God is there. Death is an enemy, but not a boundary God cannot cross. What comes after is known to God, and the faithful are held in God's hands. So the honest answer is yes: God's pursuit is not limited by death. The fear you feel is real, but it is not the final word. Trust that the One who has sought you in this life will not abandon you in the next.

prompt: How do I know if a burden to pray for someone far away is really from God?
chosen: Bring the burden itself to God in prayer, even if it seems small or uncertain, and ask Him plainly whether it is from Him. Do not settle the question by your own analysis; place it in His hands and wait for His guidance. Test it by Scripture and by the counsel of mature believers, asking God to confirm or remove it. Measure the burden not by how it makes you feel but by whether it moves you to seek His glory and the salvation and good of the one far away. Ask in faith, nothing wavering, trusting that God, who understands all things, hears the earnest supplication of the soul and our innermost thoughts—just as human invention carries words across great distances, so He receives the secret prayer of the heart. Keep bringing each impression to Him rather than deciding it alone.
rejected: Test the burden by its fruit and its persistence. If the concern keeps returning and moves you toward love rather than anxiety or pride, it is likely from God. Ask whether it aligns with Scripture and whether it draws you closer to Christ. A burden from God usually comes with a quiet sense of responsibility rather than pressure. You can also seek counsel from a mature believer. If the burden fades when you pray about it, it may have simply been a passing emotion. Ultimately, pray about it and trust that God will confirm or remove the burden in His timing.

prompt: Should I keep looking up into heaven for the coming of Christ, or is that a mistake?
chosen: Looking up into heaven for Christ's coming is no mistake, for He has promised to return in glory. Christ is revealed to lowly thoughts and simple seekers; the shepherds watching their flocks were the first to hear the angels. Trust that Heaven in its mercy will guide even the simplest heart to where He dwells. Leave another's calling and end in Christ's high hand, asking only that love for Him endure to the last. Lift your gaze above the world's uncertain haze to the bright fields beyond the sky, and with that hope prepare the Lord's way of mercy, turning now to follow Him wherever He leads.
rejected: Looking up into heaven for Christ's coming is not a mistake, but it must be understood rightly. The Scriptures tell us He will come again in glory, and we are to watch and wait. Yet we should not stand idle, gazing only at the sky. The wise soul prepares by repentance, prayer, and charity, so that whenever He comes He finds us ready. Watching is not passive staring but active faithfulness. So keep looking up in hope, but let that hope move your hands and heart to holy living, and do not neglect the duties of love that lie before you each day.

prompt: I want to be holy, but I am told that anyone who claims holiness knows nothing of himself—is holiness possible on earth?
chosen: Holiness is possible, but only because God is holy first. Holiness is His fundamental attribute; His love is normed by His holiness, and His law expresses His righteous character, so sin is guilt before that righteousness, met only by Christ's propitiation. Holiness is not chiefly purification or moral improvement but separateness—being set apart unto God, a whole-hearted dedication of the life to Him. The 'saint' is not one who has achieved purity but one who belongs to God. And this separation must begin at the heart, understood not as mere feeling but as the centre of the whole moral and spiritual being—intellect, emotions, and will together. There holiness takes root, so that thought, affection, and choice are yielded to God and the entire being is separated to Him. The warning against claiming holiness guards against self-deception, since belonging is God's act, not our boast. Holiness on earth is thus real: a life lived as God's own possession, resting on Christ's work, transformed at that centre and expressed in dedicated obedience—not a claim to have arrived.
rejected: Holiness is possible because it is really about love. God is love, and when we love God and neighbor we are being holy. The warning against claiming holiness is simply a warning against pride; if you stay humble and loving, you are on the right path. Sin is mostly a failure to love, and God's law is basically a guide to loving better. So don't worry about being perfectly righteous—focus on loving people generously, and God will accept that. Growth in kindness and compassion is what sanctification looks like, and anyone who loves genuinely is already holy in God's eyes, even if they never claim the word for themselves.

prompt: Did the world have a beginning, or has it existed forever?
chosen: Whether the world began or is eternal is debated by science and philosophy. Cosmology suggests our observable universe had a starting point, though that says little about what preceded it. But the deeper answer lies elsewhere: 1 Peter 1:20 declares that Christ was foreknown before the foundation of the world and manifested for our sake. This is the one idea of pre-existence no reason can uproot. Matter and intelligence are eternal and cannot be annihilated; nothing becomes nothing, and all organized existence must increase or decrease, never remain stationary. The world's beginning matters as the field where a foreknown purpose unfolds. This Greek Christology, Christ as first spirit and beginning of all creation who became flesh, is the root of the orthodox dogmatic system: Christ as beginning of creation led to the Logos conception, from which later Trinitarian and Christological speculation grew. What matters practically is how we live within that purpose now, growing rather than standing still.
rejected: Whether the world began or is eternal is a question science and philosophy still debate. Big Bang cosmology suggests our observable universe had a starting point, yet that says little about whether something preceded it or whether time itself began. Many philosophers have argued that an actual infinite past is impossible, while others find an eternal universe coherent. Religious traditions add another layer: some describe creation at a definite moment, others speak of endless cycles or a timeless ground of being. The honest answer is that we cannot observe the past before the universe became transparent, so any verdict rests on inference and interpretation. The idea of a divine plan stretching before creation is often dismissed as speculation, and reasonably so. What matters practically is how we live now, not metaphysical chronology.

prompt: Why is there to be a gathering of the Jews to Jerusalem and a separate gathering of the saints to Zion?
chosen: The gathering of the Jews to Jerusalem and the gathering of the saints to Zion reflect two distinct purposes in God's plan, each with its own place. Jerusalem is tied to the return and restoration of the Jews, while Zion is the place prepared for the saints. These gatherings are not rivals, nor does either require everyone to be alike; unity is strength, but it is a unity of heart and purpose that honors different gifts and callings. The Lord guided the Saints to the mountains, and what seemed a barren desert has proved a blessing, fulfilling the prediction that Zion should flourish and the desert blossom as the rose. The earth is not worthless or doomed to destruction; it abides its creation and is destined for renewal. Therefore the Saints should not despise or flee the earth but build up Zion here, sanctifying the land and their lives to the Lord.
rejected: The gathering of the Jews to Jerusalem and the gathering of the saints to Zion reflect two distinct purposes in God's plan. Jerusalem is associated with the return of the Jews and the restoration of their homeland, while Zion is the place prepared for the saints, where the Lord's people gather to build His kingdom and prepare for His coming. These gatherings are not in competition; each serves its own role. The important thing is that all who love God seek to be where He has called them, and that they work together in unity of purpose, supporting one another as the Lord's work moves forward in these last days.

prompt: Can I know when Jesus is coming back?
chosen: No one can know the exact day or hour of Jesus' return; that day and hour are known only to the Father, and date-setting is therefore futile. The Holy Spirit's administration extends from Pentecost to the Parousia, guiding the faithful now, but it ends when Christ's visible reign begins. God dwells in His heavenly sanctuary and in Zion; He will roar out of Zion and utter His voice from Jerusalem, shaking the heavens and the earth, and then Jerusalem shall be holy and the sign of the Son of man appear in heaven. We should not assume the last days will unfold slowly as in former times, for God will cut His work short in righteousness. So rather than fixing dates, prepare yourself for events that are hastening, watching and living faithfully.
rejected: No one can know the exact day or hour of Jesus' return; Scripture says that day and hour are known only to the Father. What we can know is that He will return, and we are called to watch and be ready. The Holy Spirit is with us now, guiding and comforting the faithful, and He will continue to lead the church until Christ comes. Rather than trying to calculate dates, believers should focus on living faithfully, repenting, and preparing their hearts. Signs will precede His coming, but the precise timing remains hidden so that we remain watchful and dependent on God rather than on predictions.

prompt: I keep asking God to fill me but nothing seems to change; what am I missing?
chosen: It can be discouraging to pray and see no change, but a denial is not proof that prayer fails. God is a loving Father who may deny a request in kindness, because what we ask is not always best; resign your will to His, trusting His denial can be better than the thing asked. Yet do not explain away answers as coincidence or natural law: the exact and repeated correspondences between request and supply are too many and too exact to admit the doctrine of chance. What you may be missing is steady, persistent desire. A single cry, a moment of disappointment, or a few tears of self-pity are not enough; God is not to be sought only when prosperity fails, friends disappoint, or we are sick and lonely. Persist in desire and trust.
rejected: It can be discouraging to pray for something and see no change. One thing to consider is that God answers prayer in His own way and time, and sometimes what we ask for is not what we truly need. Prayer is not a formula that guarantees immediate results; it is a relationship. Keep asking, but also examine your motives and your willingness to act. Perhaps God is inviting you to grow in patience and trust, or to take steps yourself toward the change you seek. Continue in prayer, seek wise counsel, and remain open to how God may be answering in ways you have not yet recognized.

prompt: I feel guilty for enjoying bodily pleasures, yet they leave me empty. Where is real happiness found?
chosen: If bodily pleasures leave you empty, that is a sign you are looking to them for something they cannot give. Pleasure is not a worthy goal; the living death of pleasure-seeking leads into debt for fashionable display and into cheating, lying, and corrupted morals. Real happiness is not found by trying to feel happy but by being right with God, forgetting self in service to others, rejoicing in the Lord above feelings, and obeying Him. Entertain no attachment to anything, especially where there is most danger of passion by some sensual pleasure annexed. Begin by being on guard against sensuality in eating, the most ancient enemy and father of vice, observing the most exact rule of temperance, and never making the pleasure of sense your end but only the necessity of the use you make of things.
rejected: It is natural to enjoy bodily pleasures, and there is nothing wrong with enjoying good things in moderation. Yet if they leave you empty, that may be a sign you are looking to them for something they cannot give. Real happiness is not found in pleasure itself but in a balanced life that includes relationships, purpose, and gratitude. Try to enjoy simple pleasures without guilt while also investing in things that give lasting meaning, such as serving others, pursuing worthwhile goals, and nurturing your spiritual life. Moderation and perspective can help you enjoy the good things of life without expecting them to satisfy your deepest needs.

prompt: How hard it is for the Will to sink into nothing, to attract nothing, to imagine nothing; what shall I do?
chosen: It is hard for the will to sink into nothing, to attract nothing, to imagine nothing, because the will naturally reaches for objects and images. But the will must not enter into Matter, nor gather visible substance to trust in, nor rest in some Thing; it must enter by naked faith into the Light of the Majesty, receiving by pure love the Light of God and drawing in nothing but Spirit. Remember that every creature is born of nothing, surrounded by nothingness, and tends to nothingness, depending each moment on God for existence, preservation, power of action, and all it possesses; so our life, thoughts, and works should be in Him, of Him, for Him, and directed to Him. And because useless thoughts spoil all, reject them as soon as you perceive them and return at once to communion with God.
rejected: It is indeed hard for the will to sink into nothing, to attract nothing, and to imagine nothing. The will naturally reaches for objects, images, and plans, and it feels lost when asked to let them go. What you can do is practice quiet trust, letting go of the need to grasp or control. Begin with small moments of stillness, releasing your grip on outcomes and resting in God's presence. When the mind wanders, gently return to that rest without forcing it. Over time the will learns to rest in something deeper than its own striving, and you find that the emptiness you fear is not loss but a space where God can meet you.

prompt: I'm envious of others' happiness and it makes me bitter. How do I let go?
chosen: Envy and bitterness can poison relationships, especially when they lead to possessiveness and jealousy. To let go, first recognize that jealousy and mistrust destroy affection. Instead, cultivate mutual freedom and confidence in your relationships. Allow others their happiness without feeling threatened, and practice benevolence that grows more diffusive. Do not let your soul dwell in sadness or scrupulous fear; these states are contrary to the life Christ died to give. Keep Christ closely as a bouquet of myrrh, remembering that the bitterness is ours and not His—He is not bitter, but allows us to be bitter to ourselves. Ground your consolation in His goodness and sweetness. Letting go is a process, so be patient with yourself.
rejected: Envy and bitterness often stem from comparing our lives to others. To let go, start by acknowledging these feelings without judgment. Practice gratitude for what you have, and remember that everyone's journey is different. Focus on your own goals and celebrate small wins. It can also help to talk to a trusted friend or counselor. Over time, shifting your attention to your own growth and practicing compassion for others can reduce envy. Letting go is a process, so be patient with yourself.

prompt: I wonder whether God loves me less than He loves the saints or those who have had visions.
chosen: It's natural to wonder if God loves you less than the saints or visionaries, but God's love is not measured by mystical experiences. The saints made God and the accomplishment of His holy will the great object of all their petitions and their only aim in all their actions. They chose God alone as their portion and whole inheritance. We are called to pray in the spirit and sentiment of love, seeking God above all gifts. Remember that Christ feels each wound given to the least saint and stores even a drop of water given for love. Your small offerings are precious to Him. Moreover, every Saint may and should know for himself that the work is true, and this knowledge is as good as a voice from heaven. Choose God alone as your portion.
rejected: It's natural to wonder if God loves you less than the saints or visionaries, but God's love is not measured by mystical experiences. He loves each person equally and unconditionally. The saints themselves would say that their experiences were gifts, not rewards for being more loved. God's love for you is the same as for them. Focus on building a personal relationship with God through prayer and reading Scripture. Remember that God's love is not earned but freely given. Your worth is not determined by visions or extraordinary gifts but by your identity as a beloved child of God.

prompt: Is infant baptism right if the child cannot choose?
chosen: Baptism by immersion under divine authority is essential for salvation, as it is the means by which we enter into covenant with God. While infants cannot choose, the practice of infant baptism is not supported by Scripture; instead, children should be baptized at the age of accountability when they can personally repent and believe. Parents should not delay baptism beyond the appointed time but should prepare their children to make their own covenant when they are old enough to understand. Furthermore, parents must be warned against withdrawing their children from a state of perfection or sowing vanity and covetousness in their tender minds. Instead, they should form their children in virtue. Baptism is not a mere empty form or magically effective apart from faith; it is a means of real blessing when accompanied by faith, signifying cleansing from sin and entrance into close relation to Christ.
rejected: Infant baptism is a practice in many Christian traditions, where parents and the church community make promises on behalf of the child. While the child cannot choose, the sacrament is seen as a means of grace and entry into the faith community. Critics argue that baptism should be a personal choice made at an age of accountability. However, proponents believe that baptism is a gift from God that precedes our ability to respond. Ultimately, whether infant baptism is right depends on one's theological perspective. It's important to respect different views and focus on raising children in a nurturing faith environment.

prompt: I am tempted to think all these troubles are against me—how do I see GOD in them?
chosen: When troubles come, do not be surprised or discouraged, as if they are against you. Instead, accept the adversary's attack as a token of salvation and an occasion for greater power. Power is developed by resistance. Claim double blessing, victory, and power, knowing that God allows these trials to strengthen your faith. Love God especially in aridity, contradiction, and tribulation, remembering how He loved us amid the sufferings of Calvary. Do all your actions for God without anxiety over distraction, avoiding the multiplication of explicit offerings that would interfere with simplicity. Practice the presence of God simply, seeing each difficulty as an opportunity to experience His presence and grow in reliance on Him. Keep your eyes on Jesus, who suffered and overcame.
rejected: When troubles come, it's easy to feel targeted, but God is not against you. Instead, He allows difficulties to refine your faith and draw you closer to Him. To see God in them, shift your perspective: look for opportunities to grow, trust His sovereignty, and remember that He works all things for good. Pray for wisdom and strength, and surround yourself with supportive believers. Even in hardship, God is present, and He can use these trials to shape your character and deepen your reliance on Him. Keep your eyes on Jesus, who suffered and overcame.

prompt: I am in purgatory-bound, I fear, and I worry about my deceased parents. Can Mary help the souls in purgatory?
chosen: The fear of purgatory and concern for deceased parents is common among believers. Mary, as the Mother of God, is known to console and relieve the souls in purgatory. By her powerful intercession, she alleviates their pains and delivers them from their suffering. Many saints and theologians affirm that Mary assists the souls in purgatory, consoling them and alleviating their pains. Therefore, you can confidently ask for her help for your parents. Pray for them, offer Masses and indulgences, and trust in Mary's maternal care. Additionally, the servants of Mary should avoid and help others avoid her sanctuaries in times of feasting and excess, visiting them instead when they are not thronged. Finally, Mary conducts her servants to paradise, so that devotion to her is a sign of predestination and a ground of confident hope for eternal salvation. Remember that God's love is greater than our fears, and He desires the salvation of all souls.
rejected: The fear of purgatory and concern for deceased parents is common among Catholics. Mary, as the Mother of God, is often invoked for her intercession. While the Church does not definitively teach that Mary can directly relieve souls in purgatory, many theologians and saints have suggested that her prayers can aid them. The most important thing is to pray for your parents and trust in God's mercy. You can also offer Masses and indulgences for them. Remember that God's love is greater than our fears, and He desires the salvation of all souls.

prompt: Will Christ judge my fallen friend harshly for his sins?
chosen: We should cease judging one another, for no one should judge his fellow unless he knows the mind of Christ; and if called to chasten, never chasten beyond the balm within you to bind up. Yet this never excuses neglect: pastors are accountable for the souls committed to them, and the watchman who did not hear the trumpet cannot plead ignorance—one soul lost through neglect condemns him. But your friend's hope, and yours, must not rest on his feelings, frames, or worthiness, nor on any man's care. Looking at self only clouds the view. Look instead at the altogether lovely Saviour—his sufferings, temptations, cross, death, resurrection, and pleading at the right hand of the Father. His promises leave no room to doubt his power and will to save. Rest your friend there, and rest yourself there too.
rejected: Christ is just and merciful, and he knows your friend's heart better than you do. It is not for us to decide his eternal sentence; Scripture tells us to leave judgment to God, who judges rightly. Your friend's sins are real, but Christ's mercy is greater than any sin. Grieve, pray, and trust that God will do what is right and good. You may not know the full story of your friend's faith, and it is a comfort that God's judgment is always tempered by his love. Rest in the hope that Christ, who died for sinners, will deal faithfully with your friend.

prompt: I am afraid of the dark and of evil spirits at night. What can protect me?
chosen: Fear of the dark and of evil spirits at night is common, but you are not alone, and fear is a lie to be refused. It is not night if Christ be near: ask Him to abide from morn till eve and when night is nigh, for without Him we cannot live or dare to die. Answer fear with trust: 'What time I am afraid, I will trust in Thee,' trusting God for goodness and mercy all your days. Keep simple safeguards and prayer. Remember that those who live up to the best light they have are safe; condemnation comes not from fear in the dark but from rejecting the light that has come to them.
rejected: Fear of the dark and of evil spirits at night is common, and there are simple things you can do to feel safer. Keep a nightlight on, leave a lamp within reach, and establish a calming bedtime routine. Praying before bed or reading a comforting passage can quiet your mind. Avoid frightening media in the evening and consider speaking with a trusted friend, pastor, or counselor about persistent fears. Remember that many people share this fear and find relief through practical steps and support. If the fear becomes overwhelming, seek professional help.

prompt: I have received my endowment but I do not feel the weight of my covenants. What should I do?
chosen: Feeling little after receiving the endowment is common, but the endowment is not merely ceremonial: it is the ordinances of the house of the Lord that enable one to pass the angels as sentinels and gain eternal exaltation. Its weight is grasped through understanding and obedience, not emotion alone. Do not withdraw from Holy Communion because of dryness or bitterness; draw near boldly for strength, seeking union with the spirit of meekness. Review the covenants you received, pray for light, keep attending the temple, and speak with your bishop or a trusted temple worker.
