Let covenant weight also be felt in consecration: set apart the firstfruits, not less than one-tenth of all your income, for the LORD's service, and economise in order to give more largely. As you honor these ordinances, approach the Lord for strength, and give generously, their meaning deepens and they become the path by which you return to the Father's presence.
rejected: It is common to feel little emotion after receiving the endowment, and that is not necessarily a sign of failure. Feelings are not the measure of faithfulness; covenants are. Begin by reviewing the ordinances and covenants you received, write down what you remember, and pray for understanding. Keep attending the temple regularly, serve others, and speak with your bishop or a trusted temple worker about your questions. The weight of covenants often grows through steady obedience rather than a single emotional experience. Be patient with yourself, keep the commandments, and trust that meaning will deepen over time as you act in faith.

prompt: I am a Christian who has grown cold and lost my first joy—how can I recover hope and zeal?
chosen: Your longing for joy is good, but joy is not a feeling to chase or a gauge of your standing with God; feelings never accurately measure real assimilation to Him. Rest on the changeless word of promise rather than on variable moods. Begin with repentance and reconciliation, trusting Christ's finished work even when you feel nothing. Forget yourself in service to others through small, concrete acts of love. Count it all joy by faith, as James commands, reckoning this dryness a trial God will use for endurance and maturity. Do not wait for joyful feelings before rejoicing; fix your heart and choose praise when emotions fail, singing psalms and giving thanks until praise becomes a habit. Continue steadfastly in prayer, fellowship, and worship when joy is lacking, refusing to abandon communion or service because of spiritual depression. Rejoice in the Lord as a command, not a mood, and obey faithfully; God, who began a good work in you, will complete it in His time.
rejected: It is common for believers to pass through seasons of spiritual dryness, and your longing to recover joy is itself a sign of grace. Begin by examining your heart honestly before God, confessing any sin or neglect that may have grieved the Spirit. Return to the means of grace: Scripture, prayer, fellowship, and worship. Meditate on the gospel and remember God's faithfulness in the past. Ask Him to restore the joy of your salvation, as David prayed. Seek older believers for counsel and accountability. Be patient with yourself; feelings often follow obedience rather than precede it. Trust that God, who began a good work in you, will bring it to completion.

prompt: I resent that my good deeds go unnoticed while others get credit—how do I deal with that?
chosen: It is natural to feel hurt when your efforts go unseen, but resentment must not become an excuse for wrong. Sin consists in doing wrong when you know and can do better; the sin of ignorance is winked at, but once you learn a thing is wrong you must refrain from it immediately and forever. So if you owe anyone—especially friends or the poor—repay promptly and honestly, and refuse to run into debt again. If you are in doubt about having offended God, do not remain paralyzed: humble yourself, beg God's forgiveness, renew your promises of fidelity and love, and continue in the pursuit of perfection. Settle your accounts, examine your motives, and let your good deeds flow from a clear conscience rather than from resentment.
rejected: It is natural to feel hurt when your efforts go unseen. First, check your motives: are you doing good for recognition or for its own sake? Shift your focus to the value of the act itself and the people it helps. Talk calmly with those involved if credit matters practically. Practice gratitude for what you do receive, and remember that worth is not measured by applause. Over time, releasing the need for credit frees you from resentment and lets your good deeds flow more generously.

prompt: My child died young and I can't help feeling cheated. How do I trust them to God?
chosen: I am so sorry for your loss. Feeling cheated is real, and God is not offended by honesty. But trust is not a coping strategy for calm days; it is proved in the hour of testing, and faith is learned by standing firm when all else fails. So bring your anger and sorrow to God, and choose to trust Him most when everything in you protests. Thank Him even for the school of sorrow, because He teaches strong faith there. Remember that parents are charged to teach and watch over their children in the gospel and to guard them from the wickedness of the world; that duty does not vanish in grief. And do not count your child's death as unmixed loss: Christ has taken the baptized and childlike into His arms, and their end is happier far than life. Trust your child there, not grudging what Christ has received, and let others hold you up as you stand firm.
rejected: I am so sorry for your loss. Feeling cheated is a natural part of grief, and God is not offended by your honesty. Trusting your child to God does not mean pretending the pain is small; it means bringing that pain to Him again and again. Begin by naming your anger and sorrow before God in prayer, and let trusted people hold you up. Remember that God loves your child even more than you do, and that His care does not end where yours does. Take it one day at a time, and let faith be a small, repeated handing-over rather than one heroic act.

prompt: I want to understand righteousness by faith but do not know where to start.
chosen: A good place to start is to see that salvation is a free gift of God's grace, received by faith, not earned by works. Begin with Scriptures such as Romans 3 and Ephesians 2. Ask yourself what you are trusting in when you pray: your performance or Christ's finished work? Our part is not passive: it is active obedience and the surrender of self-will, counted to us for righteousness, while we remain conscious that we have no righteousness of our own. Grace does not permit moral laxness; it teaches us to live differently. And understand the distinction: faith is an eternal principle and a gift of God, while belief is inherent in the children of men. A person must believe, obey, and practice the truth to obtain the power of God called faith. So confess your sin, receive His forgiveness, and ask Him to shape your life, reading and praying with a mature believer.
rejected: A good place to start is to see that righteousness by faith means we are accepted by God not because of our own record but because of what Christ has done. Begin with the Scriptures that say we are justified freely by grace, such as Romans 3 and Ephesians 2. Then ask yourself what you are trusting in when you pray: your performance or Christ's? Practically, this means daily confessing your sin, receiving God's forgiveness, and asking Him to shape your life. Read, pray, and talk with a pastor or mature believer. Over time, this becomes the settled ground you stand on rather than a theory you master.

prompt: I'm watching someone I love grow old and cold and apart—how do I love them without demanding the old madness back?
chosen: It is painful to watch someone you love change, but do not spend your energy curiously inquiring into the source of your sadness. That introspection turns you inward instead of toward them. Rather, patiently endure the aversions and repugnances you feel as a way of loving Him who suffered. Then turn from the storm to the bright hearth and to love's embrace, for present love is a charm of might against every ill, even death. Love who they are now without insisting they become who they were. Notice what is still present: small moments of connection, shared routines, quiet presence. Grieve honestly, but do not put that grief on them as a demand. Yet remember that no human love, family, or comfort can permanently fill the inner emptiness; every substitute for God leaves it unfilled and ends in disillusionment. Only the finding of God is a permanent success, so let your love for this person rest in Him.
rejected: It is painful to watch someone you love change, and longing for the old version of them is natural. The key is to separate love from demand. You can love who they are now without insisting they become who they were. Practically, try to notice what is still present rather than fixating on what is gone: small moments of connection, shared routines, quiet presence. Let yourself grieve the change honestly, but do not put that grief on them as a demand. Ask what would make their days gentler, and offer that. Love becomes a patient, daily choice rather than a demand for the past.

prompt: I am afraid of the perils and wars of our time—how can I live without terror?
chosen: Fear of war and public peril is understandable, and Scripture does not shame you for it. But the greatest enemies to fear are those from within: passion and unchecked weakness. Our labor is to subdue our passions, conquer our inward foes, and keep our hearts right before the Lord. And do not love God servilely, as if He wished to harm you; love Him fervently, trusting that He does not wish to harm but to do the soul great good. Above all, do not look to the storm or the circumstances for comfort, but fasten your eyes on Christ and abide in Him, for in His presence is the remedy for trouble and the substance of all deliverance. Limit the constant intake of alarming news, do what prudence and honest work require, pray, and let community remind you that you are not alone. Peace grows as you abide in Him.
rejected: Fear of war and public peril is understandable, and Scripture does not shame you for it. Begin by limiting the constant intake of alarming news and by grounding yourself in what you can actually do: prudent preparation, honest work, care for neighbors. Pray regularly, naming your specific fears before God, and let community remind you that you are not alone. Remember that God is sovereign over nations and that your ultimate security is not in circumstances but in Him. Take reasonable precautions, then release what you cannot control. Peace grows through small, repeated acts of trust rather than one dramatic cure.

prompt: I am trying to understand what it means to say that Christ is the centre of the Christian religion, and whether that makes Christianity merely a religion about a person rather than about God.
chosen: Saying Christ is the centre means everything in Christianity is oriented around who Jesus is and what He did. This does not make it a religion about a mere person rather than about God, because reference to God and reference to Jesus Christ are inseparably united: to see Him is to see the Father. This is grounded in the historical person of Christ, who lived, died, and rose in real time and place. Nor is 'Christian' a loose label for being like Christ or generally religious; a Christian is one to whom Christ is Saviour and Lord, subject to Christ. And Christianity is not a religion of a book, as though a volume were to be received in all its parts as equally Divine; it is faith in the Person of Jesus Christ, and the Bible is the record of the proclamation and reception of that revelation rather than the revelation itself. So read Scripture, pray, and live in relation to this Jesus, and in doing so you deal with God Himself.
rejected: Saying Christ is the centre means that everything in Christianity is oriented around who Jesus is and what He did. That does not make it a religion about a mere person rather than about God, because Christians believe Jesus is the revelation of God: to see Him is to see the Father. So the two are not rivals. Christianity is about God, and it is about God as He has made Himself known in Christ. The practical upshot is that you read Scripture, pray, and live in relation to this Jesus, and in doing so you are dealing with God Himself, not with a distant idea.

prompt: I want to know whether the creeds bind me on every point or whether some questions remain open to my own study.
chosen: The creeds are summaries of the faith confessed for centuries, and they bind you on the central doctrines they address—the Trinity, the incarnation, the resurrection. But they are not exhaustive, and many matters remain open to your own study and prayer. Among these are the present-truth themes the literature commends for our times: the Sabbath, the law, righteousness, and the Lord's coming—matters to be studied diligently and shared. Nor is study merely private: the shared study of social problems in the light of God's revealed will is a bond between Christians and promotes the unity of the Church, the condition of effectual social reform. Yet remember the chief purpose of our being here: personal connection with God. Teaching children to prize holidays, parties, and career success above this is a mistaken basis; never be ashamed of spiritual things. Where the creeds speak, take them seriously; where they are silent, search the Scriptures together and hold secondary matters with humility.
rejected: The creeds are summary statements of the faith that Christians have confessed for centuries, and they bind you on the central doctrines they address—the Trinity, the incarnation, the resurrection, and the like. But they are not exhaustive, and they were never meant to answer every question. Many matters—how to interpret particular passages, questions of conscience, the details of God's plan—remain open to your own study and prayer. You should read Scripture diligently, weigh the teaching of your church, and hold secondary matters with humility. Where the creeds speak, take them seriously; where they are silent, study freely and do not be anxious.

prompt: How can I serve God in ordinary, unseen work rather than grand deeds?
chosen: Ordinary, unseen work is where most Christians actually serve God. Faithfulness in a daily task, honesty in small dealings, patience with family, and quiet diligence are the substance of a godly life. But do not substitute a preferred way of serving for the actual discovery of His will: seek out God's will and carry it out joyfully, or at least courageously, serving Him as He wills rather than in a way of your own choosing. Carry on the Lord's work within the landmarks of His word: do not seek the patronage of the world, do not depend on it, contract no debts, and let your dependence be on God's blessing in answer to prayer. The Living God alone is Patron, and prayer is the only appeal. Trust God to provide both the individuals and the means for any work He orders, as He fitted the workers and furnished the materials for the Tabernacle. God sees what is done in secret, and He honors it.
rejected: Ordinary, unseen work is where most Christians actually serve God. Faithfulness in a daily task, honesty in small dealings, patience with family, and quiet diligence are the substance of a godly life. You do not need a platform or a grand mission to serve God; you need a heart that offers each task to Him. Do your work well, serve the people around you, and let your hidden labor be a form of worship. God sees what is done in secret, and He honors it. Seek also the support of your church and the counsel of mature believers, and consider whether your gifts might open opportunities for service as you prove faithful in small things.

prompt: How can I be sincere in my motives when I can't even fully know my own heart?
chosen: You are right that the heart is deceitful and that we cannot fully know our own motives. Cultivate purity of heart by the text's own steps: keep a strict guard over your senses, practice recollection, and be candid with a spiritual director. These guard against the enemies of purity of intention—vanity, pride, sensuality, interest, and aversions. Do not mistake a passing fear or a short-lived fit of fervor for conversion: transient glances effect not a change of heart, and superficial conversions made under fear of calamity rarely bear the characters of sincerity. Penitents must be brought to a sincere and perfect change of heart. And do not make feelings the measure of whether prayer is heard or whether you are right with God; feelings never accurately gauge real assimilation to God. Rest on the changeless word of promise, continue steadfastly in prayer when joy is lacking, and refuse to abandon communion or service because of spiritual depression.
rejected: You are right that the heart is deceitful and that we cannot fully know our own motives. Begin by being honest with God about this: ask Him to search you and reveal what you cannot see. Then practice self-examination—set aside time to reflect on your actions and ask why you did them. Pay attention to the motives that recur: a desire for approval, fear of failure, pride. Bring these to God in confession. Talk with a trusted friend or pastor who can help you see yourself more clearly. Over time, as you practice honesty and prayer, your motives will become clearer and purer. Sincerity is not perfect self-knowledge but a steady willingness to be corrected by God.

prompt: I am popular and my church is growing, but I am not sure it is spiritual growth. How can I tell?
chosen: Growth in numbers and popularity is not the same as spiritual growth. To tell the difference, look at the fruit: are people being changed, growing in holiness, humility, and love, or merely enjoying the crowds? Examine your own life—are you growing in prayer, obedience, and love for God and neighbor? Advancing stages are gained through growth, not accretion; they come through the scientific work of proving God individually. Nor is development mere innovation or a narrowing and hardening of theology by added dogmas. True development is the Church standing firm in her old truths while entering into and assimilating the new social and intellectual movements of the age. And remember that the condition of the Church is not independent of its leaders: hold preachers primarily responsible for its spiritual state, and regard spiritual leaders as tokens of God's favor. Ask whether the teaching is faithful to Scripture and whether the church produces mature disciples rather than consumers.
rejected: Growth in numbers and popularity is not the same as spiritual growth. To tell the difference, look at the fruit: are people being changed, are they growing in holiness, humility, and love, or are they merely enjoying the crowds? Examine your own life too—are you growing in prayer, in obedience, and in love for God and neighbor? Ask whether the teaching is faithful to Scripture and whether the church is producing mature disciples rather than consumers. Read widely, keep learning, and be patient; spiritual growth takes time. Do not be discouraged by slow results, and do not mistake busy activity for real progress.

prompt: I'm baptised and consider myself Christian—won't I go to heaven when I die regardless?
chosen: Baptism and the name of Christian are precious, but they are not a guarantee of heaven. Scripture warns that not everyone who says 'Lord, Lord' will enter the kingdom. Death works no miracle: we are after death exactly as far advanced as before. The Seed of Divine love must be planted and consciously growing in us here. Do not frame religion mainly as preparation for death or the afterlife; the demand is for present, everyday salvation and the continual enjoyment of the Spirit. Live faithfully today and let the Millennium take care of itself. And ground the comfort of the bereaved not in vague hope or human speculation but in the cardinal fact of the resurrection—Christ's own victory over death and His promises—so that we speak with the Apostle's confidence of present realities rather than uncertain hopes.
rejected: Baptism and the name of Christian are precious, but they are not a guarantee of heaven apart from a living faith. Scripture warns that not everyone who says 'Lord, Lord' will enter the kingdom, and that we must be born again and continue in faith. Your baptism marks you as belonging to Christ and calls you to live out that faith. So examine yourself: are you trusting Christ, growing in love, and walking with God? Death itself does not change the heart. Take your faith seriously now, and let your hope rest in Christ rather than in the mere fact of being baptized or dying.

prompt: I'm torn between my career ambitions and my desire for God—can I give myself fully to both?
chosen: The Gospel stands above the antagonism between career and faith, calling you to find God and hold Him as your own. Begin by limiting yourself to legitimate work, refusing the restless curiosity and ambition that multiply occupations and divide the heart. Then abandon yourself to God in both interior and exterior suffering—including the frustration of unmet ambitions and the daily cross of your work. Live, work, and rejoice, but in God, not in career success. When you surrender your ambitions to Him, even disappointments become occasions of trust. Thus, you give yourself fully to God, and your work becomes a seamless part of that single-hearted devotion, not a rival.
rejected: It's understandable to feel torn between career and faith. Many people struggle with this. The key is balance: you can pursue your career while also making time for God. Set priorities, perhaps attending church regularly and praying daily. Remember that your career can be a way to serve God if done ethically. Don't let ambition consume you, but also don't neglect your responsibilities. Seek guidance from your faith community. Ultimately, both can coexist if you manage your time well and keep God in your thoughts.

prompt: I want to teach my children about God but I see something in them that seems to resist—what does that mean?
chosen: The resistance you see in your children is not something to battle directly; instead, substitute the presentment of Jesus and His pure invitations. Teach them that God is ever-present and omnipotent, so their complaints can disappear through this understanding. But above all, help them transfer their allegiance from the glamour of evil to the hoped-for glamour of God. The chief purpose of our being here is personal connection with God—not career success, holidays, or parties. When they catch a vision of Jesus' beauty and love, resistance fades. Fill their minds with pictures of His goodness, and pray that the Holy Spirit will make His glamour irresistible, so they gladly follow Him.
rejected: It's normal for children to resist spiritual things sometimes. They may be distracted, questioning, or simply testing boundaries. This resistance can come from their developmental stage, peer influence, or a lack of understanding. As a parent, you can address it by making God more relatable, using stories and examples, and modeling faith in daily life. Be patient and consistent. Sometimes resistance is a sign they're thinking deeply. Keep the conversation open and pray for guidance. Don't force it; instead, create a welcoming environment where they feel free to ask questions and explore faith at their own pace.

prompt: Has Christianity actually done good in the world, or is that just what believers claim for their own religion?
chosen: Christianity's good is not just a claim; it is verified in present experience—the daily spiritual miracle of forgiveness and regeneration. But this miracle also confirms the doctrine of sin: faith acting on promised strength overcomes sin, and believing in others enables their recovery. Yet Christianity is not merely a natural product of its environment; it is a new beginning by divine power. While we can examine the historical conditions under which it arose and the men it operated upon, its essence is a divine invasion. Meet experience with experience: the transformed life is the abiding evidence. So Christianity does good because it brings a new life from above, not just human effort.
rejected: Christianity has undoubtedly done much good in the world. It has inspired countless acts of charity, established hospitals, schools, and orphanages, and promoted human dignity and rights. The abolition of slavery, the civil rights movement, and many humanitarian efforts were led by Christians motivated by their faith. However, one must also acknowledge that Christians have sometimes acted contrary to their beliefs, causing harm. But overall, the positive impact is evident in history and continues today through countless organizations and individuals. The claim is not just self-serving; it is backed by tangible evidence of transformed lives and societies.

prompt: I want to make a good confession before my retreat ends. How should I prepare?
chosen: The purpose of these first days is the purification of your soul from all guilt of sin and all attachment to sin. The most efficient means is the Sacrament of Penance preceded by a careful review of your sins. Remember that the salvation and spiritual progress of your own soul is your principal duty and highest interest. It profits nothing to gain the whole world and lose your own soul. Do not presume salvation is secured, but promptly confess even small sins and forsake questionable practices at once. Cultivate obedience and gratitude, giving thanks for every mercy of God. Let confession be prompt and thorough, and let your heart overflow with thanksgiving for His forgiveness. Thus you will prepare well.
rejected: To make a good confession, start by examining your conscience. Reflect on the Ten Commandments and the teachings of the Church. Ask the Holy Spirit to help you see your sins clearly. Make a list of your sins, being honest and thorough. Then, go to confession with a priest, confess your sins with sincerity, and receive absolution. Do the penance assigned. Before confession, pray for contrition and a firm purpose of amendment. Also, consider going to confession regularly, not just during retreats. Remember that God's mercy is infinite, and confession is a way to experience that mercy and grow in holiness.

prompt: I am a Christian and my friend has died in the Lord—may I grieve, or should I only rejoice?
chosen: Your consolation rests wholly on Christ—His sufferings, temptations, cross, death, resurrection, and pleading at the right hand of the Father. Look not at yourself, for that clouds the view; look at the altogether lovely Saviour. His promises leave no room to doubt His power and will to save. Christians should meet death with calm, hopeful fortitude, planting the ensign of salvation upon the grave, not giving way to despondency. You may grieve, but do not wish the pain away; instead, ask for a wise and thankful heart. Yield your will to God's rod, and fulfill the offices of religion. Let your grief be a sacrifice of thanksgiving, and rejoice that your friend is with Christ, who is altogether lovely.
rejected: Yes, you may grieve. Even Jesus wept at Lazarus's tomb. Grief is a natural response to loss, and it is not incompatible with faith. As a Christian, you have hope in the resurrection, so your grief is not without hope. You can rejoice in the knowledge that your friend is with the Lord, but you can also mourn the separation. Allow yourself to feel the sorrow, but also hold onto the promise of eternal life. It's okay to express your emotions; God understands. Take time to process your feelings, and lean on your faith community for support. Both grief and rejoicing can coexist.

prompt: I want to be more generous but I'm afraid of losing what I have—how do I trust God with my resources?
chosen: Generosity grows as we trust God to supply all our need. Scripture records helpers who gave themselves and their goods for God's work without salary, believing He would provide—and He did. Begin where you are, but don't set your ceiling at what feels safe; let your giving be cheerful and self-denying. When you forget God or falter, don't be disquieted—return with greater trust, for His mercy meets our lapses. Ask boldly for provision, yet resign your will to His: a loving Father may deny a request in kindness, and His denial can be better than the thing asked. So hold resources with an open hand, give yourself as well as your goods, and let trust—not fear—shape your generosity.
rejected: Generosity begins with small, manageable steps. Start by giving a modest percentage you can afford without anxiety, and build from there. Remember that everything you have is ultimately a gift, and God invites you to hold resources with an open hand. Practical safeguards can help: keep an emergency fund, set a giving budget, and give to causes you trust. Trust grows through experience—each time you give and see that you are still provided for, fear loosens its grip. Prayer and community support also help; share your fears with mature friends. The goal is not reckless giving but a heart freed from scarcity so you can enjoy God's provision and bless others wisely.

prompt: If God is all-powerful, why does he seem so limited in the Old Testament?
chosen: The Old Testament's portrayals of God can seem limited because they reflect the understanding of ancient people writing in their own time and culture. As revelation progressed, later writers saw God more clearly as universal and sovereign. Many passages use vivid, human-like imagery—God repenting, wrestling, or changing His mind—which is accommodation to human language rather than a limit on God's power. God can rightly use literary methods suited to an undeveloped age—dramatic composition, primitive tradition, idealizing history—as genuine vehicles of inspiration; such methods are not fraud. Yet we must never lower God's standard to excuse our failures. Nothing is too great for His power or too small for His love; He may be asked about and trusted in everyday matters. Keep His standard inflexibly high, pressing on until we reach His highest will.
rejected: The Old Testament's portrayals of God can seem limited because they reflect the understanding of ancient people writing in their own time and culture. As revelation progressed, later writers came to see God more clearly as universal and sovereign. Many passages use vivid, human-like imagery—God repenting, wrestling, or changing His mind—which is accommodation to human language rather than a limit on God's actual power. Reading the whole Bible together, especially through Christ, shows a consistent trajectory toward a fuller picture of divine omnipotence. So the apparent limits are largely literary and historical, not a true measure of God's ability.

prompt: What is the difference between praying for a miracle and praying in a way that fits how the world actually works?
chosen: Praying for a miracle and praying in a way that fits how the world works are less opposed than they seem. What we call a miracle is a result whose cause is not understood; there is a cause for every result, even when that cause lies beyond our present knowledge. High and far-reaching prayers are not unanswerable: we look to God as the source and Christ as the channel of grace, confident that such prayers can and will be answered. Yet prayer does not inform the infinite Mind or change the Science of being. It is absolute faith, spiritual understanding, and unselfed love that align us with God's unchanging law. We do not plead with a humanly circumscribed deity; we yield to the unchangeable Principle, and in that harmony find our help.
rejected: Praying for a miracle asks God to override the normal workings of nature—to heal instantly, reverse circumstances, or intervene supernaturally. Praying in a way that fits how the world works accepts the regular patterns of cause and effect: we pray for wisdom, patience, good decisions, and the natural means of healing through medicine and community. Both kinds of prayer can be faithful, but mature prayer usually aligns with how God ordinarily acts—through means, processes, and human cooperation. Expecting constant miracles can lead to disappointment, while praying within creation's order keeps us grounded and grateful for ordinary grace.

prompt: What sign should I ask of God when I cannot tell which is the holy tree?
chosen: When you cannot tell which is the holy tree, begin by making the sign of the cross with great faith and devotion—not as mere habit or superstition, but as an impregnable rampart against the devil and a mark of your allegiance to Christ. Then ask God for clarity and wisdom, testing the options against Scripture, wise counsel, and the fruit they produce, for good trees bear good fruit. Receive every spiritual privilege with fear and love, remembering that the same gift can prove a poison tree if beheld and not beloved. Make a definite act of faith in Christ, and then abide habitually in Him, drawing life from Him as a tree draws from the soil without effort. A sign may be sought humbly, but do not demand one; trust His quiet guidance, sealed by the cross.
rejected: When you cannot discern the holy tree, ask God for clarity and wisdom rather than for dramatic signs. Test the options against Scripture, wise counsel, and the fruit they produce—good trees bear good fruit. A sign may be sought humbly, as Gideon did, but we should not demand one; God often guides through ordinary means: prayer, community, conscience, and circumstances. Ask for an open heart and patient discernment, and be willing to wait. If a sign comes, receive it with gratitude; if not, trust that God's quiet guidance is enough. The focus should be on walking faithfully rather than on securing a spectacular confirmation.

prompt: I am a believer who has been praying for the removal of an affliction, but I am not sure it is God's will to remove it. How should I submit?
chosen: Pray honestly for relief, but receive affliction as something God permits out of the excess of His love and for the good of His elect; trials are not abandonment but preparation for the greatest crowns. Lay your desire for healing before God without shame, then add, as Jesus did, 'not my will but yours be done.' If you forget God or falter, do not be disquieted—return with greater trust. When the crisis comes, treat the mental disturbance of chemicalization rather than the disease itself, and refuse to grant it real pain. Insist that God is all and there is no disease. Submission is not passivity but active trust that His loving purposes are at work. Rest in His presence, let peace guide your steps, and believe He sustains and crowns those who endure.
rejected: It is right to pray honestly for relief from affliction while also submitting to God's will. Begin by acknowledging your desire for healing and laying it before God without shame. Then add, as Jesus did, 'not my will but yours be done.' Seek wisdom from Scripture, prayer, and trusted counselors about whether to pursue treatment or accept the affliction. Remember that God's will is not always removal—sometimes He sustains us through suffering and grows our character. Submission is not passivity; it is active trust that God's purposes are good even when painful. Rest in His presence and let peace guide your next steps.

prompt: I have tried to find peace in beauty and art, but it doesn't last. Why?
chosen: Beauty and art can refresh the spirit, yet a peace that lasts is quietly won rather than merely enjoyed. Meet what is repugnant in yourself and the world with sweetness and charity, conquering by patient love rather than avoidance. But beware the peace built on mutual fear and selfish loves: it looks like rest, yet it is the ground where Cruelty's snare is knit. Cruelty, Humility, Mystery, and Deceit grow from the human brain, and art that only soothes can veil them. The unrest beauty cannot quiet—anxiety, guilt, selfish desire—must be faced with restrained courage. There is a gentle melancholy in this, for the loveliest things pass. Still, exercise kindness toward the difficult, and let peace take root as something conquered rather than borrowed, refined and excellent in its way.
rejected: Beauty and art can give real refreshment, but they are finite goods. A painting, a symphony, or a garden can quiet the mind for a time, yet the quiet fades because the sources of unrest—anxiety, guilt, and desire—are not addressed by beauty alone. Art can move the affections without healing them. This is why peace found only in beauty feels borrowed rather than owned. The lasting peace you seek must be rooted in something that does not pass away, in a reconciled relationship with God and a conscience at rest. Beauty can be a signpost pointing toward that peace, but it cannot be the foundation itself.

prompt: I prayed for a specific sign from God about a decision. Is that acceptable?
chosen: Watch your prayers. It is right to ask God for guidance, but not to demand a supernatural sign as proof, for that tests God and sets terms he has not promised. God has already given you light: Scripture, wise counsel, circumstances, and ordinary prudence. Do not ask God to decide what you should decide yourself in ordinary wisdom. Remember that prevailing prayer depends on the conditions Scripture records: humility, forsaking sin, faith, obedience, and asking according to God's will in Christ's name. Do not measure whether you are heard by feelings or sensible enjoyment, for moods never accurately gauge our real assimilation to God. Rest on the changeless word of promise. Continue steadfastly in prayer when joy is lacking, and do not abandon communion or service because of spiritual depression.
rejected: Praying for guidance is good, and God invites us to ask for wisdom. Asking for a specific sign, however, can slide into testing God or demanding that he prove himself on our terms. Scripture gives examples of signs, but it also warns against demanding them. Often God has already given you the light you need: Scripture, wise counsel, circumstances, and ordinary prudence. Before seeking a supernatural sign, ask whether you are avoiding a decision you could make with the wisdom already given. It is acceptable to lay your desire before God honestly, but hold the request humbly, ready to act on the light you already have.

prompt: How can I know from what place Jesus will come again?
chosen: The New Jerusalem is a real city, not a mere symbol or the saints or the visible church. It is the capital of Christ's everlasting kingdom, now in the third heaven, and it is about to descend out of heaven to be located in the midst of the promised land. From that place Christ will come again. Yet do not seek him first in a place or through another person. Christ is first found within, by inward pondering, by loving comparisons, and by persistent imitation of his gentle ways. Only then may you recognize him in or through others. And do not presume that those who fail to find him here will be comforted after death; without finding Christ now, the soul enters a dark, lonely, self-tormenting state. The remedy must be found now, while it is called today.
rejected: Scripture speaks of Christ's return in several ways, and the place from which he comes is best understood through the whole biblical witness. He will come again personally and visibly, as the angels told the disciples. The New Testament also speaks of the holy city, the New Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven. Rather than fixing on a single geographical point, Christians have generally held that the manner and place of his coming remain God's to reveal, while we are called to watch and be ready. What matters most is not calculating the location but living faithfully in expectation, so that wherever he comes from, he finds you prepared.

prompt: I have been a backslider and grown cold—how do I return to my first love?
chosen: Returning to your first love begins with honesty: name the drift, confess it, and turn back toward God. But do not give up rejoicing because the first dose of renewal seems ineffectual. Keep on rejoicing; count it all joy even in temptations, trusting God to make the reckoning good. Remember what you first received. Renew the small practices that once fed you—prayer, Scripture, fellowship, obedience—even before affection returns. Do not be discouraged by coldness of feeling. And do not mistake drugs, hygiene, or animal magnetism for healing; they bring temporary relief only, while healing belongs to divine Mind. When miseries return, do not give up the fight or meet them with less courage than before. Resume your arms and fight more valiantly than ever against the returning enemy, drawing near to God, who will draw near to you.
rejected: Returning to your first love begins with honesty: name the drift, confess it, and turn back toward God without waiting to feel worthy. Remember what you first received and the joy of your early devotion. Renew the small practices that once fed you—prayer, Scripture, fellowship, and obedience—even before affection returns, because love often follows faithful action. Do not be discouraged by coldness of feeling; feelings lag behind commitment. Draw near to God and he will draw near to you. Expect gradual renewal rather than instant warmth, and let others walk with you in the process.

prompt: Is time real, or is it only in our minds—and does it matter for my religion?
chosen: Time is a real feature of created existence, the order in which events occur, though our experience of it is shaped by our minds. For religion this matters because God is eternal, beyond time, yet acts within it. Do not divide temporal from spiritual matters. All things are spiritual before God, and he has a right to guide temporal as well as spiritual affairs. The gospel is designed for the temporal as well as the spiritual welfare of man; spiritual and temporal salvation belong together. But do not discard biblical teaching merely because its scientific thought-world is outdated. Distinguish the eternal spiritual value from the time-bound thought-forms that carry it: the prophet had to speak in the language of his own day, and the worth of the idea is judged by its value for life. So your days are real and accountable, and faith is lived in time.
rejected: Time is a real feature of created existence, the order in which events occur, but our experience of it is also shaped by our minds. Whether time is ultimately fundamental or a form of perception is debated by philosophers and physicists alike. For religion, the question matters because God is described as eternal, beyond time, yet acting within it. Christians have generally held that God enters time in creation and redemption without being bound by it. Practically, this means your days are real and accountable, and faith is lived in time—through patience, repentance, and hope. The metaphysical debate need not unsettle ordinary devotion.

prompt: Will the earth be restored to its former glory, and what will that look like?
chosen: Scripture does not leave the earth to destruction or abandonment. Restoration means bringing back what was lost: the earth will be renewed to its Edenic state, the curse removed, and man restored with it. Nor is restoration limited to a favored few. All except those who sin against the Holy Ghost will inherit some kingdom of glory, and those who lived by the best light they had will receive glory beyond expectation. And this work is not uncertain: the kingdom of God will continue to grow and spread until it fills the earth with His glory and with the knowledge of the Father and the Son, whom to know is life eternal. The renewed earth will therefore display varied degrees of glory and the certain triumph of God's purpose.
rejected: Scripture suggests the earth's future is often framed as destruction and renewal, with the present order passing away. Many read prophecies of fire and judgment as the end of the world, leaving little room for a literal return to Eden. On this view, the earth is eventually replaced or abandoned, and the righteous simply escape to heaven. The emphasis falls on survival and escape rather than on the planet itself being healed. Restoration is treated as a metaphor for personal salvation, not a promise about the physical creation. What the renewed state looks like remains vague, often reduced to a spiritual afterlife rather than a transformed earth.

prompt: How does the Spirit help me understand Scripture when I read it?
chosen: When you read Scripture, the Spirit opens the mind through the understanding gained from Science and Health, making the Bible illumined and precious rather than obscure. Yet this light is not for private enjoyment: the fulness of the Spirit is given along the line of duty and obedience to world evangelization, as we obey Christ's command and step out into His plans. This is not earned by law-works or human merit, for the Spirit is received by the hearing of faith. He is the earnest of our inheritance, the pledge of the whole promise, so that possessing the Spirit we already hold the assurance of all God has promised. Reading, believing, and obeying thus belong together, and the Spirit who illumines the text seals the reader as God's own.
rejected: When you read Scripture, the Spirit is often described as an inner teacher who opens the mind to what is written. Many readers find that prayer before reading, and a willing heart, make the text clearer. Some passages remain obscure or difficult, and honest readers admit the Bible can seem suspect or unreadable without guidance. The Spirit is said to illuminate, convict, and comfort, turning words on a page into living truth. Practically, this means reading slowly, asking for light, and being ready to obey what you understand. The Spirit does not replace the text but works through it, helping you grasp its meaning and apply it to your life.

prompt: How do I 'breathe out' spiritually when I don't know how?
chosen: Spiritual breathing means learning the secret of breathing out as well as breathing in. Before the Spirit fills us, we must empty ourselves and pour out our lives in holy service, seeing the needs around us as vacuums for the Spirit to fill. Yet this does not require leaving your post: in an instant, amid daily work, a person may fly to the soul's nest, be greatly refreshed, and return to work renewed, secretly between the Lord and himself. But such experiences must not be sought as achievements of the will. Accept them only as God chooses, without praying for them or secretly desiring them, in total submission, without questioning, fear, or curiosity. As you pour out your life, He pours His in, and the refreshment is His to give, not yours to claim.
rejected: Spiritual breathing is often described as taking in God's presence and letting go of what burdens you. If you don't know how to breathe out, start simply: name what weighs on you, confess it, and release it in prayer. Some find journaling, silence, or speaking honestly to a trusted friend helpful. The goal is not a technique but a habit of turning toward God and letting go of what you cannot carry. Practically, set aside a few minutes, breathe slowly, and offer your worries to God. Over time this becomes more natural. The point is not to achieve a feeling but to practice release.

prompt: I have been a skeptic and an infidel; can this book speak to me?
chosen: Yes, this book can speak to you, but it will do so by displacing what makes a skeptic an infidel. The prudence of the flesh and worldly wisdom is the mother of self-sufficiency, pride, avarice, and vicious curiosity; it is the source of infidelity and the declared enemy of the spirit of Christ. That wisdom must be banished by holy simplicity, and in its stead are obtained true wisdom and divine light. Nor is this book merely one opinion among many: Science and Health is a key to the Scriptures, and honest study with the Bible enables one to prove all things. Yet know that God remains unchangingly faithful even when our faith fails; the loss that unbelief brings is ours, not His. Come with holy simplicity, study honestly, and trust His faithfulness rather than the strength of your own belief.
rejected: Yes, a book can speak to a skeptic, though it depends on what you are looking for. Many skeptics approach religious texts with honest questions, and that honesty is a good starting point. If you read with an open mind, you may find ideas that challenge or comfort you. Some books are written to persuade doubters, others to instruct believers. The value you find will depend on your willingness to engage and test what you read. No book can force conviction, but a sincere reader can find something worthwhile.

prompt: How may I recover myself in temptation by not sinking under the World but rising above it?
chosen: When temptation comes, do not sink under the world but rise above it by allowing no repose and no slipping back in the spiritual ascent. Go forward like a mountain-climber until the goal is reached, refusing to turn aside after lower objects that cause distractions and loss of the way, and withdrawing from worldly distractions into the one unchangeable Good. When restoring the fallen, do so in meekness, first examining yourself lest you also be tempted, for the Gospel saves the straying rather than condemning them. And remember: God tempts no man. He will not allow you to be tempted above your strength, but provides an issue with every temptation. Temptation is not abandonment but a trial He limits and turns to your good, and enduring it patiently is crowned with life.
rejected: When temptation comes, the first step is to recognize it and pause before acting. Many find it helpful to remove themselves from the situation, pray, or call a friend. Recovery means turning back to what you know is right and not letting a single failure define you. Some suggest replacing the tempting thought with a better one, or recalling a verse or principle that steadies you. The goal is to rise above the pull of the world rather than sink under it. This takes practice, honesty, and often the support of others.

prompt: I want to love others selflessly, but I keep putting myself first. Am I capable of real love?
chosen: You are capable of real love, and the desire you express already shows it. Love does not consist in feeling but in the will to please and benefit the beloved at the cost of sacrifice. So gently disavow self-love a few times a day when you notice it, without violent resistance or excessive introspection, and instead choose small acts of service for others. Do not conclude from dryness, or from the enemy's uproar, that your love is false; serve God purely for love of His will amid sadness and temptation, refusing the suggestion that your love is useless. Love grows by frequent acts of service and by considering what He has done for us, so keep serving quietly and let fidelity, not feeling, prove your love.
rejected: Yes, you are capable of real love, but the fact that you keep putting yourself first suggests you still need to work on self-love. Many people struggle with this because they were never taught to value themselves. Try spending time each day affirming your worth, setting boundaries, and being kind to yourself. When you feel secure in your own value, selfless love for others will flow more naturally. It is not a sign of failure that you put yourself first sometimes; it is a sign that you need healing in your relationship with yourself. Consider therapy or journaling to explore why you feel you must prioritize others. Real love begins with a healthy self-regard.

prompt: I believe God is almighty and all-wise, but when I suffer I cannot believe He is all-love and will do all for me—how do I stop short there?
chosen: It is understandable that suffering makes it hard to feel God's love, but do not stop short there. Love God especially in aridity, contradiction, and tribulation, remembering how He loved us amid the sufferings of Calvary. Be slow to take new steps: do not rush forward in self-will or treat presumption as faith, but ascertain His will by prayer and the Word, then wait with earnest, patient, believing expectation of His help. And abandon yourself to God without exception—no reserves, no areas kept back for yourself. Ask Him to tear and wrest from you all that burdens your heart and to wrest you from yourself, so that trusting His love in suffering becomes total surrender rather than a partial bargain.
rejected: It is understandable that suffering makes it hard to believe God is all-love. Many people find that their image of God is shaped by painful experiences, and when life hurts, that image feels unreliable. The key is to separate your feelings about suffering from the truth about God's character. God's love is not dependent on your circumstances; it is a constant. Try to focus on what you know to be true rather than what you feel in the moment. Prayer, community, and Scripture can help you rebuild trust. It is also worth examining whether you have unrealistic expectations that God will prevent all suffering. He does not promise a pain-free life, but He does promise His presence.

prompt: Should I turn the other cheek when I am struck?
chosen: Turning the other cheek is not merely a rule about safety; it is a way of welcoming the chastening hand of God that makes the heart feel Him near. When you are struck, do not shut out the warning or harden yourself, but let it awaken your heart to His presence, keeping your lamp awake till dawn. Forgive your enemy, for forgiving enemies is the best revenge and a means of grace: by bearing injuries patiently you gain grace and the pardon of your sins without trouble or expense. Yet remember that moral ignorance and sin hinder the demonstration of God's healing and must be overcome; patience is not passivity but a purified heart. So repent of resentment, put away sin, and let pardon and patience be your response, trusting that God sees and rewards what is borne for His sake.
rejected: Turning the other cheek is a well-known teaching of Jesus, but it is not always practical. In situations of abuse or ongoing harm, turning the other cheek can enable further mistreatment and put you at risk. A wise reading of the passage recognizes that Jesus was speaking to a specific cultural context about personal insults, not about tolerating violence. You should set boundaries and protect yourself. If someone strikes you, leaving the situation or seeking help is not a failure of faith. Forgiveness does not require you to remain passive in the face of harm. Consider what is safe and what is loving toward yourself and others.

prompt: My wife is gravely ill and the doctors have given up; should I keep praying for her recovery?
chosen: I am sorry to hear about your wife. Keep praying, but let your prayer seek strength and patience to bear this suffering as from God's hand rather than deliverance from it. Sickness, however painful, is permitted by Him, and the grace we most need is endurance and trust. You may still ask God confidently, for He can and does heal today, and Mary's clemency comes to our aid before we invoke it; it is enough to ask her help with confidence. Yet place the outcome in God's hands, asking above all for patience, love, and faithfulness for you both, and entrust her to His care whatever the result.
rejected: I am sorry to hear about your wife. It is natural to want her to recover, and prayer can be a source of comfort for you both. However, it is important to be realistic: medical science has limits, and sometimes recovery is not possible. Prayer should focus on acceptance, peace, and strength for whatever comes, rather than on demanding a specific outcome. God is present in suffering, and your prayers can help you find meaning and support during this difficult time. You may also want to spend time with her, seek support from your community, and prepare practically for the future.

prompt: I wear the brown scapular, but I sometimes fail in chastity according to my state of life. Can I still trust in its promises?
chosen: The brown scapular is a devotion approved by the Church and pleasing to Mary, a mark of your dedication to her, with real promises and conditions attached. When you fail in chastity, do not despair or treat the scapular as useless. Repent immediately, for it is not desperate to have been wounded but to neglect the cure. Your confidence rests not on your own effort or feelings but on the faithfulness of Him who calls, who is able to perform what He has promised. Go to confession, amend your life, and keep wearing the scapular as a sign of dedication. One who has fallen may rise again, as wrestlers and soldiers have risen after a fall, so rise at once and trust His faithfulness.
rejected: Wearing the brown scapular does not guarantee salvation or protection if you are not living according to the Church's teaching. The promises attached to the scapular are conditional, and persistent sin, especially grave sin against chastity, can separate you from grace. You should not presume on the promises while continuing in sin. Instead, examine your conscience, go to confession, and make a serious effort to amend your life. If you are struggling with chastity, seek accountability and perhaps counseling. Trust in the scapular should not become an excuse for complacency.

prompt: How do I live a Christian life while serving as a soldier?
chosen: Serving as a soldier while living a Christian life begins with faith in Christ and trust in His merits, not merely in your own discipline. Obey lawful orders and do your duties well, but let courage and duty be colored by Christ's mercy, purity, and self-sacrifice. Avoid cruelty, drunkenness, and the abuses of camp life; be honest, keep your word, and guard your temper. Pray regularly, read Scripture, and attend services when available. Remember that any spiritual care you offer follows Christ's own pattern of lowliness, hidden labour, and bearing others in prayer even through scorn—not a smooth, unbloody strife or a path to honour. Be willing to spend and be spent for souls; esteem the reproach of the Cross an honour, forgive and pray for those who persecute you, and fear no mortal's frown in declaring the word of God. Your hope rests not in your conduct but in Christ, whom you must be prepared to meet as Saviour and Judge. Keep your conscience tender, confess your failures, and grow in gentleness and mercy toward comrades and enemies alike.
rejected: Serving as a soldier while living a Christian life begins with integrity and discipline. Obey lawful orders, do your duties well, and treat those under your charge with fairness and respect. Avoid cruelty, drunkenness, and the abuses that camp life can encourage. Be honest in your dealings, keep your word, and guard your temper. Pray regularly and read Scripture when you can, and attend services when they are available. Your example of steady conduct will speak louder than sermons. Courage in battle and loyalty to your comrades are honorable, and a Christian should not be ashamed of them. Keep your conscience tender, confess your failures, and strive to improve. In short, be a good soldier and a decent man, and let your conduct earn the respect of those around you.

prompt: I am a king and I want to be remembered well. What should I do?
chosen: To be remembered well, a king should first seek God's wisdom, for the peace of the world depends on rulers who need His guidance and the good hand of God upon them. Let supplications, prayers, and intercessions for kings and all in authority be in the forefront of your reign and of your people's prayers. Govern justly: establish clear laws, appoint honest judges, and protect the poor. If you or your people grow weary or doubting, lift your eyes to the hills—to the great mountain-tops of history touched by the dawn, the great essentials of human experience, the ideals of truth and justice, the highest characters, the bulk of the people's life, and the nation's destinies above party dust—and so see thresholds prepared for a divine arrival. Above all, remember Christ the King, who does not need our aid but calls us to share the glory of His victory, who endures more than any, and who rewards each in proportion to his generous exertions. Follow Him, and your remembrance will be secure.
rejected: To be remembered well, a king should govern justly and leave lasting institutions. Establish clear laws, appoint honest judges, and protect the poor from oppression. Build roads, harbors, and schools that outlast your reign. Surround yourself with wise counselors and listen to them. Avoid vanity projects that drain the treasury and breed resentment. Keep your word to foreign powers and wage war only when necessary and just. Record your achievements fairly, but let your deeds speak. Train your successor and secure a peaceful transfer of power. A reputation for fairness, moderation, and competence will endure longer than monuments. In short, rule for the good of your people rather than for your own glory, and history will judge you kindly.

prompt: I want to be happy, but I feel guilty about enjoying entertainment and dancing—is that wrong?
chosen: Feeling guilty about entertainment and dancing is common, but pleasure itself is not the goal of life. Saints should be happy and may enjoy wholesome social recreation, yet always in moderation and in the Spirit of the Lord. Beware the living death of pleasure-seeking: going into debt for fashionable display, and the hunt for pleasure that leads to cheating, lying, and corrupted morals. Remember that fiddling and dancing are no part of our worship; they serve rather to rest the mind and exercise the body. Those who cannot serve God with a pure heart in the dance should not dance. Ask whether your entertainment is wholesome, whether it respects others, and whether it leaves you better or worse. Choose entertainments that refresh rather than degrade, avoid schemes that gratify craving at the cost of integrity, and let your enjoyment be grateful and moderate.
rejected: Feeling guilty about entertainment and dancing is common, but pleasure itself is not wrong. Enjoyment and recreation are part of a healthy life, and dancing can be good exercise and good company. The key is moderation and honesty: enjoy yourself without letting amusement crowd out your responsibilities, your relationships, or your faith. Ask whether your entertainment is wholesome, whether it respects others, and whether it leaves you better or worse. If a particular activity makes you uneasy, examine why—sometimes guilt comes from upbringing rather than from any real wrong. You do not need to avoid all fun to be a good person. Seek balance, choose entertainments that refresh rather than degrade, and let your enjoyment be grateful and moderate.

prompt: Am I a 'saint'? I've always thought saints were exceptional people, and I know I'm not one.
chosen: The word 'saint' often brings to mind exceptional figures—martyrs, mystics, and heroes of faith—so it is natural to feel you are not one. But Scripture applies the title 'saints' to all Christians, not to a carefully limited class of the exceptionally pure. 'Saints' means believers as citizens of a heavenly kingdom who are separate from the world. You do not become a saint by achieving extraordinary purity or performing miracles; you are called to live as one set apart: honestly, kindly, and faithfully in your daily duties. This calling rests on thoughtful study and understanding of the gospel, not on shallow or cranky notions, and on steady, consistent living according to revealed truth. Let neither ingratitude nor ill-treatment cool your zeal; regard the wrongdoer as a patient under a disease, recommended to God in prayer. Sainthood is not a rank for the elite but a calling for every Christian. Ask whether you are growing in love, humility, and obedience—that is the ordinary path of the saints.
rejected: The word 'saint' often brings to mind exceptional figures—martyrs, mystics, and heroes of faith—so it is natural to feel you are not one. But in the New Testament, 'saints' simply means those set apart for God, the ordinary believers in the churches. You do not become a saint by achieving extraordinary purity or performing miracles. If you have been joined to Christ, you are called to live as one set apart: honestly, kindly, and faithfully in your daily duties. Sainthood is not a rank for the elite but a calling for every Christian. So rather than asking whether you qualify as exceptional, ask whether you are growing in love, humility, and obedience. That is the ordinary path of the saints.

prompt: I am a woman in a position of wealth and rank, and I want to live a devout life without leaving the world. Is that possible?
chosen: It is possible to live a devout life in wealth and rank—but only on one condition. The rich may enter the kingdom as freely as the poor if they subject their hearts to God, yet no one can obtain eternal life unless willing to sacrifice all earthly things. Remember the rich young man, whose attachment to his possessions kept him from following Christ. Devotion is a matter of the heart, but the heart must be detached from its wealth. Use your resources generously for the poor, keep your prayer life regular, and avoid vanity, self-indulgence, and pride. Know too that many are called by God to serve Him in a retired contemplative life, and that those conscious of their own weakness and unable to match the world ought to retire as from a too potent enemy and prefer a contemplative state to a busy and active life, not to indulge sloth but to consult their own security and fly from dangers of sin. Yet whether in the world or retired, the shortest and only way to enter the Kingdom of God is to become as a little child, hanging upon Christ for all things and depending upon the author and fountain of them.
rejected: Yes, it is possible to live a devout life while remaining in a position of wealth and rank. Devotion is a matter of the heart, not of circumstance. You can serve God in your household, your friendships, and your responsibilities. Use your resources generously for the poor and for good causes. Keep your prayer life regular and your conscience clear. Avoid the temptations that wealth brings—vanity, self-indulgence, and pride—by cultivating gratitude and humility. You need not abandon your station to be holy; many devout people have lived faithfully in the world, serving God through their influence and charity. Let your wealth be a tool for good and your rank a means of protecting the vulnerable. With discipline and prayer, a devout life in the world is entirely possible.

prompt: I keep trying to be good on my own strength and failing. What am I missing?
chosen: What you're missing is not more effort but the rooting out of habitual disorders. Multiplying pious exercises while leaving the heart unwatched and irregular attachments uncut will leave your habitual imperfections and venial disorders exactly where they were. So begin with your own beam: examine your belief in and fear of sin, cast it out honestly, and only then attempt to help another. Watch over your heart and your senses, live in recollection, and cut off the attachments that feed the same failures again and again. Open your interior plainly to a spiritual director, and aim at God's will rather than at piling up external works. Keep your exercises faithfully and exactly, untroubled and unastonished when infirmity causes failure; return quietly and begin again. Sanctification lies in this patient rooting out, not in the number of your devotions.
rejected: What you're missing is likely not effort but method. Many people try to be good by sheer willpower—resolving harder, gritting their teeth, promising themselves they'll do better. That approach almost always collapses because willpower is finite and the habits underneath it are stronger. The better path is to build systems: identify the specific patterns that trip you up, replace them with small repeatable practices, and get accountability from someone who will be honest with you. Failure isn't proof you're bad; it's data. Each lapse shows you where the real work is. Be patient with yourself, celebrate small wins, and treat the whole thing as a long apprenticeship rather than a test you either pass or fail.

prompt: I have never thought of enclosing a tract with an ordinary letter; is that something I should do?
chosen: Before you think about what to enclose, consider what actually heals. Physicians and drugs have done their best in many cases and yet without avail; the help that lasts came through the study of Science and Health. So let any enclosure point the reader to that study—but remember that Christian Science is not mere letter, formula, or intellectual system. Without Love the letter is dead and the demonstration powerless. Study the letter, imbibe the spirit, and adhere steadfastly to the divine Principle, and let Love be at the heart of it. Do not expect rapid progress through the letter alone. Keep your personal note warm and primary, choose something short and relevant, and let the enclosure be a humble supplement offered in love, directing the reader toward the truth that heals.
rejected: It's a reasonable idea and many people do it. Enclosing a tract or a short article with a personal letter can be a low-pressure way to share something meaningful, especially if the recipient already trusts you. The key is fit: choose something short, relevant to the person's actual situation, and clearly secondary to your own words. A personal note should carry the warmth; the tract is a supplement, not a substitute. Avoid anything pushy, guilt-inducing, or impersonal, and don't make every letter an occasion for a pamphlet or it will start to feel like a campaign. If you sense the person would welcome it, a brief, humble enclosure can open a good conversation.

prompt: I'm a poet and I feel my Muse dying—should I try to revive her or let her go peacefully?
chosen: Perhaps the question is whether she should be roused at all. The dreaming Muse, lovely in her sorrow, is best left to dream; to force her awake with the jarring Truth would surely kill her. The old dreams of gods and heroic Greece are lovely things, and there is no need to drag them into harsh daylight. And remember that Nature needs no song: she is too beautiful to be surpassed, and striving to pitch your music higher than hers only wearies the heart. So do not revive her by main force. Yet speak gently of her fading, as of a sister's fall; gentle love may win the erring sister by patient call, and the Church's balm is for the trembler. Let her rest, tend her kindly, and trust that patient love, not harsh demand, will bring back what is worth keeping.
rejected: This is a real question many artists face. First, distinguish burnout from genuine change. If you're exhausted, depleted, or depressed, the 'dying Muse' may be a symptom of fatigue or untreated stress, and rest, play, and lower expectations can revive her. If, on the other hand, your interests have genuinely shifted, forcing the old voice can produce hollow work. Try gentle experiments: read widely, change form, write badly on purpose, collaborate. Give it a season before you conclude anything. You don't have to choose between reviving and burying—you can tend the embers and see what catches. If nothing does, letting go may free you for something truer.

prompt: My kids are bouncing off the walls at home and there's nothing to do—should I just let them roam the neighborhood for fun?
chosen: Rather than simply turning them loose, be in advance of them. Parents should provide innocent amusement and always be ahead of their children in mind and affection, leading the way so that the children delight to follow rather than being driven from behind with the whip. Plan something: a backyard project, a bike ride with you, a craft, a scavenger hunt. And teach them the worth of holding on to an old friend: no matter how many new friends one has, one should hold fast to the old, and only wicked conduct should break the thread of fellowship. Never lose control of your children's amusements during these tender years, and be scrupulously careful about the companionship of your young people in places of amusement. Do not leave them to find their fun wherever and whenever they can; go before them, and set clear rules about where, with whom, and when to check in.
rejected: Letting kids roam can be fine in the right circumstances, but 'bouncing off the walls' usually signals a need for structure and engagement rather than total freedom. Before turning them loose, consider safety: how old are they, is the neighborhood safe, are there trusted adults around, and do they know the boundaries? A better first move is to create some planned options—a backyard project, a bike ride with you, a craft, a scavenger hunt, or a playdate. Boredom isn't an emergency, and kids can learn to entertain themselves. If you do let them roam, set clear rules about where, with whom, and when to check in.

prompt: I am unsure whether the good God can be angry or judge; if he is only love and mercy, what becomes of the wicked?
chosen: Consider that mercy and goodness are transitive love, while justice and righteousness are transitive holiness. They are not the same thing; justice is not mere benevolence in disguise nor a device for the creature's happiness. Mercy is free and optional—God is not obliged to show it—whereas justice must be exercised, because holiness cannot overlook what is unholy. But be careful how you speak of wrath: in God may be no wrath. Wrath belongs to man's part only, the resistance that feels God as anger; God's mercy and pity never cease. And take heart: if you love God, all things—even grief, even sin—will turn to your good, though the means be unseen. Repentance is a gift rather than a claim, and the wicked meet not a God who rages but a love they have refused, which even now works toward their profit.
rejected: This is a classic tension in theology. If God is perfectly loving, it can seem inconsistent to speak of divine anger or judgment. One common resolution is to distinguish God's love from human wrath: what Scripture calls 'anger' may be a metaphor for the serious consequences of rejecting love, not a divine mood swing. God's judgment can be understood as the natural outworking of justice—giving people what their choices have made them. Mercy and justice are not rivals; mercy offers restoration, and justice respects freedom. As for the wicked, most traditions hold that God's desire is always their repentance and healing, while affirming that persistent refusal carries real consequences.

prompt: I am unsure whether I should fast; is it a real Christian duty or an outdated burden?
chosen: Fasting is a reasonable law observed from even to even, with the food or its equivalent given to the poor, but it is left to conscience and wisdom, not required of the weak, sick, or nursing mothers, and little children should not be compelled to fast. Yet the first duty is obedience to God, oneness of Mind, and love of neighbor as oneself. Saturday fasts and special devotions honor Mary, and the church accommodates those prevented by ill health. So if you are healthy and able, you may fast on Saturdays in honor of Mary, offering special devotions on Saturdays and the vigils of her feasts, and giving to the poor what you would have eaten. If you are ill or weak, you are not bound, and children should not be compelled. Consider your circumstances and motivations. If you choose to fast, do so prayerfully and with wise guidance. If you decide not to fast, you are not sinning. The key is to seek God's will and not be driven by guilt or legalism.
rejected: Fasting is a historic Christian practice, but it is not a strict requirement for every believer. The Bible speaks of fasting as a voluntary act of devotion, not a command. Jesus fasted and assumed his followers would fast, but he also warned against fasting for show. The early church fasted, and many traditions still do. If you are healthy and able, fasting can be a meaningful way to draw near to God, practice self-control, and intercede for others. However, it is not a burden you must bear to earn God's favor. Consider your circumstances, health, and motivations. If you choose to fast, do so prayerfully and with wise guidance. If you decide not to fast, you are not sinning. The key is to seek God's will and not be driven by guilt or legalism.

prompt: I feel like a hypocrite because I keep sinning—how do I approach God?
chosen: The only way out of sin's misery is to cease to sin. You cannot approach God while clinging to sin, but you can come as you are, confessing and forsaking it. Do not rely on grace as an excuse, but let moral courage drive you to turn from sin. Fear of punishment is not the motive; rather, respond to God's love with a determined will to stop sinning. Approach God with honesty, confess your sin, and ask for the strength to cease. True repentance means turning away from sin and walking in newness of life. And when you would help another who sins, do not stand as a sinless superior; identify with them, confess your own faults, and point to the fountain opened for sin. Follow Christ, who took our sins and made them His own. Be slow to take new steps, willing to have no will of your own, and ascertain God's will by prayer and the Word; then expect His help earnestly, patiently, and believingly. Seek accountability, but remember that the decisive step is to stop sinning. God welcomes you as you come with a contrite heart and a resolve to obey.
rejected: First, know that feeling like a hypocrite is common—many believers struggle with repeated sin. The key is to approach God with honesty and humility. 1 John 1:9 says that if we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive. So don't hide; bring your sin to God. Also, remember that God's grace is greater than your sin. You are not saved by your performance but by Christ's finished work. However, don't use grace as an excuse to keep sinning. True repentance involves turning away from sin. Seek accountability and support from trusted Christians. Pray for the Holy Spirit's help to overcome. Approach God not as a hypocrite but as a child who is still learning to walk. He welcomes you with open arms.

prompt: I don't want my life to be a stumbling-block to others—how do I become a stepping-stone instead?
chosen: To become a stepping-stone rather than a stumbling-block, study the letter of Scripture, imbibe its spirit, and adhere steadfastly to the divine Principle. Progress comes not through mere techniques but through living the truth. Withdraw as much as possible from acquaintance and from men, abstain from affairs that hinder your purpose, and seek with jealous care the place, time, and means most suited to quiet and contemplation. Lovingly embrace silence and solitude, and fly the agitation of a world never at rest. Yet do not try to reach the final step of perfection at once; focus on the duty lying directly before you, and refuse the desire to reach the last step before the first is accomplished. Practice humility, integrity, and love, grounded in the Principle of divine Love. Avoid behaviors that cause others to stumble, and build others up. Serve selflessly, apologize quickly, and cultivate prayer and study so that inner transformation overflows. Remember that growth in Christlikeness inspires others. Ultimately, becoming a stepping-stone is about decreasing so that Christ may increase in you, adhering to the divine Principle in all things.
