The Old Testament is a lower, gradual stage under divine condescension, yet it is a Christian book, containing explanations necessary for every occasion, and was used as the source of the knowledge of faith under six points of view. So, while acknowledging its preparatory role, we read it as pointing to Christ. Thus, we reconcile the two by seeing the Old Testament as preparatory and the New as fulfillment, leading us through Jesus to the Father and the Trinity.
rejected: The God of the Old Testament and the God of Jesus are the same God, but He is revealed progressively. In the Old Testament, God is often depicted as strict and judgmental, while Jesus reveals a God of love and grace. However, these are not contradictory; they are different aspects of God's nature. The Old Testament prepares the way for the New, showing humanity's need for a Savior. Jesus fulfills the law and the prophets, revealing the full character of God. To reconcile them, recognize that God's justice and love are both essential. The Old Testament emphasizes God's holiness and justice, while the New Testament emphasizes His mercy and love. Together, they give a complete picture of God's character.

prompt: Is God a distant sovereign far above me, or is he somehow close and involved in my life?
chosen: God is not a distant sovereign but an Infinite Person corporate with our lives, from whom we have sprung and in whom we live. He is nearer than all else, speaking in conscience and mind, and when every worldly thing passes away, He remains to the soul that seeks Him early. While all our language about God is inadequate, we must not think of Him as a force or a mere totality; He is a Person in the truest sense, yet not a remote monarch. He shares the travail and tragedy as well as the joy of bringing forth sons of God. So, do not treat worldly interests as of permanent consequence, but seek Him early, listen to His voice in conscience, and find Him intimately involved in every aspect of your life, sharing your sorrows and joys.
rejected: God is both transcendent and immanent. He is the sovereign Creator who rules the universe, far above our comprehension. Yet He is also close to each of us, involved in our daily lives. The Bible teaches that God is not distant but near, especially to those who call on Him. He knows our thoughts and cares about our struggles. Through the Holy Spirit, God dwells within believers, guiding and comforting them. So, while God is majestic and holy, He is also personal and loving, inviting us into relationship with Him. We can experience His closeness through prayer, worship, and obedience. Thus, God is not a distant sovereign but a loving Father who is actively involved in our lives.

prompt: I was once a scoffer and an idolater—can I become dear to God?
chosen: Yes, you can become dear to God. Confess your faults to God without excuse and without discouragement, and peaceably resume the practice of love and adoration. When you forget God, do not be disquieted; instead, return to Him with greater trust. Lapses in remembrance are not cause for despair but for renewed faith. Furthermore, draw near to God through the works of creation. See every tree, flower, and field as proclaiming 'God made me.' Unite the admiration of nature's beauties with devotion, and help the poor laborer connect God's goodness in creation and providence with the riches of His grace. So, by confessing without excuse, returning with greater trust, and contemplating nature with devotion, you will become dear to God.
rejected: Yes, you can become dear to God. No matter what you have done, God's love and forgiveness are available to you. The Bible is full of stories of people who turned from their sins and found grace. God does not hold your past against you if you sincerely repent and turn to Him. He is merciful and ready to forgive. Start by confessing your sins to God and asking for His forgiveness. Then, begin to live a new life, seeking to follow Him. Find a supportive community of believers who can help you grow. Remember that God's love is unconditional, and He desires a relationship with you. So, take heart, for God is waiting with open arms.

prompt: I have been reading many religious books but neglecting the Bible. How should I begin to read the Scriptures rightly?
chosen: Begin by recognizing that the Holy Scriptures are the one fountain of all wisdom and strength. Set aside daily time for systematic reading and meditation, preferring the Bible above all other books. Pray before reading, asking the Holy Spirit to illuminate the text. Read slowly and prayerfully, seeking to understand and obey what you read. Translate what you find into obedience, for the Bible is not just to be studied but lived. The difficulties of understanding Scripture are rooted in conscience and will; doing the revealed will is the organ of spiritual knowledge. Scholarly methods are preliminary but not sufficient. Furthermore, the Bible is illumined and made precious through the understanding gained from Science and Health, as the testimonies describe. So, read the Bible daily, systematically, and prayerfully, with a willing heart, and let Science and Health help you understand it, making it the fountain of wisdom and strength.
rejected: Begin by recognizing that the Bible is the inspired Word of God and should be your primary source of spiritual guidance. Set aside regular time each day to read it, starting with the New Testament, perhaps the Gospel of John. Pray before reading, asking the Holy Spirit to illuminate the text. Read slowly and meditatively, reflecting on what you read and applying it to your life. Use a good study Bible or commentary for difficult passages, but don't let that replace your own reading. Join a Bible study group for accountability and discussion. Remember that the Bible is not just a book to be studied but a living word that transforms. So, prioritize it above other religious books and make it a daily habit.

prompt: I want to believe that God loves me, but I feel like I am too small to matter to Him.
chosen: Feeling small before God is not a defect; to be little with God is to be little for God. Do not cut short your praying, for cutting short praying makes the whole religious character short and slovenly. Yet prayer is not a lever to make God pliant, nor worthless when dry and barren: God is the Ground of our beseeching, prayer pleases Him even in dryness, and it unites the soul to God. Bring Him even the smallest matters, the daily worries that make you feel insignificant, and ask His guidance rather than deciding your worth on your own. Honour Him by placing every matter in His hands, and let steady, unhurried prayer do its slow work in you.
rejected: It is natural to feel small before God, but smallness is not the same as insignificance. Scripture repeatedly shows God caring for the humble, the overlooked, and the weak. Your feeling of being too small may actually be a sign of humility that God can work with. Try to remember that God's love is not measured by our sense of importance; He knows you by name and notices even the sparrow. Spend time in prayer, read passages about God's care for the lowly, and speak with a trusted pastor or friend. Over time, gratitude and reflection can soften that feeling of unworthiness.

prompt: How do I deal with the fear that my children will get sick in unsanitary conditions?
chosen: Your fear is understandable, but do not picture your children as helpless victims. Teach them they can resist disease as positively as they resist sin, with clean habits and a calm spirit. Wash hands, keep food and water clean, and see a doctor when needed. Yet do not let fear for safety or family keep you from a clear duty: the safest place is the path of duty, God must come first, and children can be safely trusted to God wherever He leads. Pray perseveringly and submissively for present fruit in their conversion, for labour among children is not fruitless. Remember the vast power for good or evil residing in a little child: rightly trained or neglected, the eternal consequences are immense. Let obedience, not comfort, set your course.
rejected: Your fear is understandable, and there are practical steps you can take. Wash hands frequently, keep food and water clean, and teach your children good hygiene. Keep vaccinations current and see a doctor when illness appears. It also helps to manage anxiety: limit excessive news or horror stories, talk with other parents, and get rest. If fear becomes overwhelming, speak with a counselor. Remember that illness is part of life and most children recover well. Focus on what you can control and accept that some risk cannot be eliminated.

prompt: What did Paul mean when he said he was caught up into Paradise?
chosen: Paul describes being caught up to Paradise, likely the third heaven, where he heard things that cannot be told; such experiences are gifts of God, not grounds for boasting. Faith is not mere assent but identification with Christ, a going down into death with Him and a rising into newness of life, lived henceforth unto Him. The pastoral charge is to be feared rather than ambitiously sought, and one unfit for it is not excused by being imposed upon by others. Honour the divine idea presented by God's messenger rather than abusing his motives, for to misunderstand it is to betray ignorance of Principle. Paul's glimpse of Paradise belongs to a life hidden with Christ, and it humbles rather than exalts the one who receives it.
rejected: Paul is describing a profound spiritual experience in 2 Corinthians 12, where he speaks of being caught up to Paradise, likely referring to the third heaven. He says he heard things that cannot be told, which suggests a revelation too sacred or beyond human language to express. The passage emphasizes that such experiences are gifts from God, not grounds for boasting. Paul uses it to humble himself and to point to God's grace. Interpreters differ on whether this was a vision or an actual transport, but the core meaning is that God granted him a glimpse of heavenly reality beyond ordinary knowledge.

prompt: I am a wife and my husband is unconverted; what should my prayers for him be?
chosen: Pray for your husband's heart to be opened and for God to draw him to faith. Ask for wisdom to love him well, patience, and grace to be a good example without nagging. Pray that God would soften resistance and bring people into his life who can speak truth. Let this teach you to wait prayerfully on God for guidance in marriage, holding true godliness as the first and absolutely needful qualification in a companion, calmly weighing other suitableness. Prayer must be our main assistant in every step of spiritual progress: pray that God would enable you to search out and discover your own heart and reform whatever is amiss in it. Continual help of God is needed, and praying, being with God, and thinking of Him often are linked through holy habit, since we must know before we love.
rejected: Pray for your husband's heart to be opened and for God to draw him to faith. Ask for wisdom to love him well, patience, and grace to be a good example without nagging. Pray that God would soften any resistance and bring people into his life who can speak truth. Also pray for yourself, that you would not grow bitter or anxious. Trust God's timing and remember that you cannot convert him; God can. Keep praying persistently and look for small opportunities to show kindness and faith.

prompt: Could there be a world of spirits without any one God over them all?
chosen: This question asks whether a spiritual realm could exist without a single supreme being ruling it. We must distinguish mortal belief from spiritual understanding: belief is mortal, while Mind understands; belief is not a spiritual faculty, nor the same as understanding. The pre-existent, immortal spirit of man is revealed, not speculated, and we should rest content with accepted doctrine rather than dogmatic assertions. Nor should we set faith and organisation as an exclusive dilemma, for that is an absurd dilemma: faith is operative through order, as loyalty is operative through the State, without either replacing the other. Given that revealed truth, a plurality of spirits without one God over them would be incoherent, since understanding requires a unifying Principle, and that Principle is God.
rejected: This is a question about whether a spiritual realm could exist without a single supreme being ruling it. Many religious traditions hold that a world of spirits requires a unifying principle or God, since order and existence depend on some ultimate source. Philosophy also suggests that a plurality of spirits needs a ground of unity. Without one God over all, spirits might be conceived as independent powers, but that raises problems of order and authority. Most theistic traditions answer no: a world of spirits without one God over them would be incoherent or unstable.

prompt: Will Satan always rule over the world, or will he be bound?
chosen: Satan is not an independent power beyond God's control; he is a usurper of God's own make, permitted for a season to test and develop man. His rule is temporary and limited, and he will be bound and cast into the bottomless pit when his services are dispensed with. The world cannot remain under the curse because it would be unreasonable, unjust, unscriptural, and would frustrate God's designs for the righteous, the dead, and the earth's exaltation. The world's evils stem from man's departure from God and usurped authority, and nothing short of God's own interposition can correct them. Therefore, the world will not remain under Satan's dominion forever; God's kingdom will prevail.
rejected: Satan is described in Scripture as the ruler of this world for a time, but his rule is not permanent. The Bible teaches that he will be bound and cast into the bottomless pit, as seen in Revelation 20. Until then, he operates within God's sovereign permission, but his power is limited. God allows him to test and develop humanity, but ultimately God will intervene to restore the world. The world will not remain under Satan's dominion forever; God's kingdom will prevail.

prompt: How do I know the difference between my own thoughts and the Spirit's leading?
chosen: Discerning between your own thoughts and the Spirit's leading begins with recognizing that our commonness lies in un-Godlike thoughts of heart and mind. The alteration of these thoughts is not achieved by human willpower but is the work of the Holy Spirit, set in motion by taking Christ into the heart. As you yield to the Spirit, He transforms your mind and enables you to discern His leading. Prayer, Scripture, and counsel are means through which the Spirit works, but the transformation itself is His work. Inspiration is defined by its result: the divine influence securing the transmission of needed truth in permanent written form, sufficient when taken together and interpreted by the same Spirit to lead to Christ. The interior spirit consists in directing all acts to the glory of God, and we must warn against acting for human praise, from mere natural impulse, or in routine without a supernatural intention. Over time, as you walk with God, you'll learn to recognize His voice.
rejected: Discerning between your own thoughts and the Spirit's leading requires prayer, studying Scripture, and seeking wise counsel. The Holy Spirit often speaks through peace, conviction, and alignment with God's Word. Pay attention to whether a thought aligns with biblical truth and whether it produces love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control. Also, consider the fruit and whether it glorifies God. It's also helpful to test impressions against the advice of mature believers. Over time, as you walk with God, you'll learn to recognize His voice.

prompt: Is it my duty to witness to my coworkers, servants, and family, or is that someone else's job?
chosen: Witnessing to those around you—coworkers, servants, and family—is a personal possession given by God, but it should not be forced on everyone or used merely to fill time. Testimony is no substitute for needed instruction; we must study to show ourselves approved. A neglected gift is withdrawn, and intelligence is required of those who speak in the Lord's name. The authority of the twelve was based on an a priori theory rather than on remembered direct services to the Gentile Churches: they were regarded as a college to which mission and tradition were traced back, and the less known about them the easier it was to claim them. It is every Elder's right to enjoy the Holy Ghost and know his own duties, but not his right to dictate his superior in office or give him counsel unless he is called upon, and then only to make suggestions. Therefore, while every believer is called to be a witness, we must be sensitive to the Spirit's guidance, respect boundaries, and not neglect our primary responsibilities.
rejected: Witnessing to those around you—coworkers, servants, and family—is a natural outflow of your relationship with God. While pastors and evangelists have a specific calling, every believer is called to be a witness. Your testimony is personal and should be shared as the Holy Spirit leads. It's not about forcing conversations but about living a life that reflects Christ and being ready to give an answer for the hope you have. However, it's also important to respect boundaries and not neglect your primary responsibilities. Ultimately, witnessing is a shared responsibility of the Christian community, but each person must be sensitive to the Spirit's guidance.

prompt: I have been told my child will die of consumption; what can I do?
chosen: Hearing that your child will die of consumption is a heavy trial, but you can rest in the arms of an almighty Father, confident that He will either withhold trouble or give invincible courage to bear it. However, 'prepare to die' is not the exhortation in this Church and Kingdom, but 'prepare to live.' We should teach children in the morning of their days to lay the foundation of health, strength, and constitution, so that longevity may begin to return. Therefore, while trusting God, we should also follow medical advice, explore treatment options, and do all we can to promote health. Persevere in submissive prayer for present fruit in the conversion of your child, for there is vast power for good or evil residing in a little child. Spend precious time with your child, create memories, and ensure they know they are loved. Seek support from your church community and professionals. Ultimately, place your child in God's hands, trusting His will, and find peace in His presence.
rejected: Hearing that your child will die of consumption is devastating. In this time, turn to God in prayer, seeking comfort and strength. Trust that God is sovereign and loving, and that He will give you the grace to face whatever comes. Spend precious time with your child, create memories, and ensure they know they are loved. Seek support from your church community and professionals. Medically, follow the doctor's advice and explore treatment options. Ultimately, place your child in God's hands, trusting His will, and find peace in His presence.

prompt: How may I serve God acceptably, seeing that all service must be done in Faith and in the Spirit?
chosen: To serve God acceptably, the first thing necessary is earnestly to search His holy will by devout reading, listening to, and meditating on His eternal truths. This enlightens the divine law and guides us to every duty. We serve Him well only as He wills, so we must yield completely to God's will for the honor of God, abandoning the notion of serving Him better by another way. Accept whatever service God chooses, even the most lowly duties of the house, caring not what the service may be provided God be served. Examine your motives: are you serving to glorify God or to please people? Serve with humility, love, and a willing heart. Recognize that your abilities and opportunities are gifts from God, and use them for His kingdom. Stay connected to a community of believers for accountability and encouragement. Ultimately, acceptable service flows from a heart transformed by grace, empowered by the Spirit, and directed toward God's glory.
rejected: To serve God acceptably, you must first ensure your service is rooted in faith and guided by the Holy Spirit. This means cultivating a personal relationship with God through prayer, reading Scripture, and seeking His will. Examine your motives: are you serving to glorify God or to please people? Serve with humility, love, and a willing heart. Recognize that your abilities and opportunities are gifts from God, and use them for His kingdom. Stay connected to a community of believers for accountability and encouragement. Ultimately, acceptable service flows from a heart transformed by grace, empowered by the Spirit, and directed toward God's glory.

prompt: I see the powerful exploiting the weak and it makes me furious. What should I do with that anger?
chosen: When you see the powerful exploiting the weak, anger may rise, but you must not permit it to rule you. Hold it as a wild horse, not letting it pass your lips. True self-conquest is not easily achieved; it requires humble recognition of your own smallness and slow, persistent striving. Lay aside all retaliation and petty aims, and do not trust your own strength. Instead, wait for the good Spirit to move your tongue to kindness. In times of desolation, when anger presses hard, do not shorten or abandon your hour of meditation; rather, remain a short time beyond the full hour to resist the enemy and overthrow him. Persevere in prayer and humility, and God will give you the victory over anger.
rejected: Your anger is a natural response to injustice, but it can be destructive if not channeled well. First, acknowledge your feelings without judgment. Then, direct that energy into constructive action: support organizations that defend the vulnerable, advocate for policy changes, or volunteer with groups that aid the oppressed. Speak out against exploitation, but do so calmly and strategically. Remember that lasting change often requires persistence and collaboration. Avoid letting anger turn into bitterness or burnout; take care of your mental health. Use your anger as fuel for positive change, not as a weapon that harms you or others.

prompt: I am anxious about the sins of the Church and its leaders; should I despair of the Church herself?
chosen: It is understandable to feel anxious about the sins of Church leaders, but you should not despair of the Church herself. The Church cares only that the individual is pure in heart and the nation honourable; she is indifferent to personal success and national expansion, and ready to suffer for that testimony. Yet remember that she is a mother, not a magistrate. Her note is tolerance, and she should be tolerant morally and theologically short of necessary terms of communion. Rather than relying on trivial, changing devotions, enliven your faith and make it the rule of conduct, for the way of faith suffices for perfection. Keep your hope in her divine mission, and pray for her renewal.
rejected: It is understandable to feel anxious about the sins of Church leaders, but you should not despair of the Church herself. The Church is a divine institution with human members, and throughout history she has faced scandals and failures. Christ promised that the gates of hell would not prevail against her, and the Holy Spirit guides her despite human weakness. Focus on the faithful remnant, the sacraments, and the core teachings that remain true. Pray for the leaders and for renewal. Despair is not of God; hope is. Trust that God can bring good out of evil and that the Church will be purified and strengthened through these trials.

prompt: Can God use a conqueror like Alexander or Napoleon for good?
chosen: Yes, God can use even conquerors like Alexander or Napoleon for good, but we must not think that circumstances are against us. Rather, God wisely chooses all things to make His Word and presence more precious to us. However, we must not imagine that God is the author of sickness, sorrow, or affliction, or that He visits disease upon His children. God is a loving Father who gives only good. The testimonies confess that they had wrongly believed sickness was His will. So while God can bring good out of the actions of conquerors, we should not attribute evil to Him. Instead, approach God as a wretched sinner, confessing your own sin and abandoning yourself to His hands, trusting in His mercy. In that humble confession, you will find His merciful embrace, and you will see His wise choosing in all things.
rejected: Yes, God can use even conquerors like Alexander or Napoleon for good. Throughout history, God has used imperfect people and even empires to accomplish His purposes. Alexander's conquests spread Greek culture and language, which later facilitated the spread of the Gospel. Napoleon's campaigns, while costly, led to legal reforms and the spread of revolutionary ideals that influenced modern democracy. God's sovereignty means He can bring good out of evil, and His plans are not thwarted by human ambition. However, this does not excuse the violence and suffering caused by such conquerors; rather, it shows that God's providence can work through any circumstances to bring about His ultimate good.

prompt: I am a leader and fear that younger workers will break down and blame me—should I still recruit them?
chosen: It's natural to worry about younger workers breaking down under pressure, but avoiding recruitment out of fear may limit your team's growth and potential. Remember that all labor necessary for the welfare of mankind is honorable, and boys and girls should learn practical work. Parents do their children an injustice who train them only in accomplishments. So do not shy away from recruiting younger workers for demanding tasks; instead, provide strong mentorship, clear expectations, and a supportive environment. However, as a leader, you must uphold your authority: a presiding officer is the head, and his place should be held sacred. A subordinate who usurps authority is out of place and dangerous, and no one should run before his file leader. Yet exercise this authority with patience like the Lord's, continuing to plead with the people and showing kindness whose smiles are better than cursings.
rejected: It's natural to worry about younger workers breaking down under pressure, but avoiding recruitment out of fear may limit your team's growth and potential. Instead, consider providing strong mentorship, clear expectations, and a supportive environment. Younger workers bring energy and fresh perspectives. If you fear blame, establish open communication and shared responsibility. However, if the work is extremely demanding, you might start with lighter roles or pair them with experienced mentors. Ultimately, trust your judgment: if you can offer the right support, recruiting them can be beneficial. But if the risk of breakdown is high, it may be wise to delay or seek other candidates.

prompt: I have been told that Mary is only a creature and cannot be called our life and our hope; how should I answer?
chosen: You can answer that while Mary is indeed a creature, she is uniquely chosen by God to be the Mother of His Son. She may rightly be called our hope because God has ordained that all graces be dispensed through her intercession. This does not detract from hope in God; rather, it is His design that we receive His gifts through her hands. Moreover, she is our life because she obtains pardon for sinners and restores to them the grace they have lost. She is also the comforter of the afflicted, the help of Christians, and a powerful defense against demons. So when we call Mary our life and our hope, we are not attributing to her what belongs to God alone, but acknowledging the role He has given her in His plan. She always points us to Jesus, and our confidence in her intercession rests on His ordinance, not on any power of her own.
rejected: You can answer that while Mary is indeed a creature, she is uniquely chosen by God to be the Mother of His Son. Catholics do not worship Mary but honor her as the greatest saint. She is called our life and our hope because through her intercession, we receive graces from God. However, this does not mean she is divine; all power comes from God. It's important to clarify that calling Mary our life and hope is a way of expressing her role in God's plan of salvation, not attributing to her what belongs to God alone. Emphasize that she always points us to Jesus.

prompt: How can I avoid hatred toward the enemy while fighting him?
chosen: The enemy's clamor is noise, not danger; it cannot touch the soul that belongs to God. Despise it and pay it no attention, keeping your heart quiet and fixed on God. Yet love is not a life without trouble or foe: Love's substance is the poor soul in trouble and pain, which Love loves and delivers, and love could not be known without hatred nor friendship without a foe. But know that your first enemy is within yourself. Conquer yourself and submit to the Father's will before you oppose error around you. Then oppose evil by persuasion, patience, and love unfeigned, without violence and without interfering with the agency of others. So the foe's noise is despised, the inner enemy is conquered, and love does its delivering work.
rejected: Hatred toward an enemy is natural but corrosive. The first step is to separate the person from the harm he does: you can oppose wrong actions while refusing to wish the wrongdoer ill. Practice seeing your enemy as a person with a history, fears, and blind spots, much like your own. When anger rises, pause and name it, then ask what fear or injury lies beneath it. Set boundaries and defend what is just, but do so without contempt. Remember that hatred binds you to the enemy in a cycle of resentment. Prayer, reflection, and time can soften the heart, so that you fight for what is right rather than against a person you have reduced to a symbol.

prompt: I have lost my home and my family. How do I bear it?
chosen: Losing a home and family is a heavy grief, and you should grieve fully. No one can see another's woe without sorrow, and the Maker Himself sits by you and moans till your grief is fled and gone. Do not seek a substitute for the home, for there is none: it is a divine institution of stability and love, and no genuine happiness exists apart from it. Resist drifting into a restless, nomadic life as though movement could heal what only home can hold. But take care not to hinder God's graces by undervaluing them. Make way for grace and redeem the time, since death is near and final. Let grief soften you toward heaven rather than scatter you, and let each day be given to grace, memory, and the hope of a settled home.
rejected: Losing a home and family is one of the heaviest griefs a person can carry. Bear it first by letting yourself grieve fully; tears are not weakness but the body's honest speech. Seek the company of friends and a community that will sit with you rather than hurry you. Establish small routines that give shape to the day, and tend to sleep, food, and movement. Speak the names of those you lost and keep their memory with gratitude rather than only pain. Consider counsel or a support group where sorrow can be shared. Over time, meaning may be rebuilt, not by forgetting, but by carrying love forward into new relationships and purposes.

prompt: I'm facing a big move and a hard new start, and I'm terrified. How do I know God is leading me and not just my own plans?
chosen: A big move brings fear, but do not be terrified or paralyzed by small faults. Meet them without terror, humbling yourself quietly before God and saying to your soul: 'Courage! we have made a false step, but let us keep steadily on.' Yet do not look chiefly at circumstances for comfort: fasten your eyes on Christ and abide in Him, for He is the antidote to fear and the sum of all deliverance. Be slow to take new steps, and be willing to have no will of your own. Ascertain God's will by prayer and the Word, seek counsel from those who know you, and test every plan against Scripture. Then go forward with earnest, patient, believing expectation of His help, neither rushing in presumption nor frozen in fear.
rejected: A big move brings real fear, and fear is not proof that you are outside God's will. Begin by naming what you can and cannot control, then make a honest list of your motives: what you want, what you fear, and what others need. Pray simply and regularly, asking for clarity rather than certainty. Seek counsel from people who know you well and who will tell you the truth. Look for open and closed doors, but do not demand signs. Test your plans against Scripture and your community's wisdom. Then decide, act, and remain flexible. Trust grows as you walk, not before you walk.

prompt: I'm a teacher in the church and I'm afraid of the responsibility of my words. Should I seek that role?
chosen: Fear about the responsibility of teaching is healthy, but do not treat the role as optional or secondary. Every man holding an official position in the Church should be recognized and honored in his sphere, and a teacher's duty is as sacred as an apostle's in its sphere. Ignoring such offices brings sin upon our heads. Yet it is not a member's right to point out the supposed defects of Church leaders; the Lord will judge them, and we should avoid words that give the world occasion to speak evil. Examine your own motives and character, prepare carefully, and study Scripture. And when you teach, be patient like the Lord, continuing to plead with the people, with kindness whose smiles are better than cursings. Then your fear becomes humility, and your words become a service of love rather than condemnation.
rejected: Fear about the responsibility of teaching is healthy and should not be dismissed. Words shape belief, and a teacher who feels their weight is safer than one who does not. Before seeking the role, examine your motives, your knowledge, and your character. Talk with your pastor and with those who have taught before you. Prepare carefully, study Scripture deeply, and stay accountable to others. Remember that teaching is a service, not a stage: the goal is the growth of others, not your own reputation. If the fear remains, ask whether it is humility or avoidance. Seek the role only if you can accept correction, keep learning, and point people to Christ rather than to yourself.

prompt: I'm a monk and I'm tempted to leave my cell to visit people—is that wrong?
chosen: The pull to leave your cell is not automatically wrong, but examine it honestly. Ask what drives it: loneliness, boredom, a genuine call to serve, or escape from difficulty in prayer. Speak with your abbot before making changes. The work of the Gospel is to save the straying rather than condemn them, so if you go to others, go to restore the fallen in meekness, first examining yourself lest you also be tempted. In your cell, keep homely converse with our Lord as heart may think or soul desire, yet with courtesy, for He is sovereign homeliness and very courteous. But remember that ease and enjoyment must not be the end of Christian retirement, but penance, labor, and assiduous contemplation; without great fervor and constancy in these, close solitude is the road to perdition.
rejected: The pull to leave your cell and visit people is not automatically wrong, but it deserves honest scrutiny. Ask what is driving it: loneliness, boredom, a genuine call to serve, or escape from difficulty in prayer. The monastic cell exists to support silence, prayer, and stability, and leaving it often can erode those goods. Speak with your abbot or spiritual director before making changes. Consider whether your visits serve others or mainly relieve your own restlessness. If you do go, keep the disciplines of prayer and return promptly. The question is not simply whether visiting is allowed, but whether it draws you closer to God and to charity.

prompt: I want to be like Christ but I don't know where to start. What does it actually take?
chosen: I get it—wanting to be like Jesus but not knowing where to start. Honestly, the first step for me was admitting I mess up too. I can't help anyone by pretending I have it all together. Instead, I bring my own faults to Jesus, who took them as His own, and He forgives me. Then I can walk with others, not above them. Jesus isn't just a figure from long ago; He's alive and drawing us to become like Him. His life is the goal. So start by being honest with God and a trusted friend, and join a community where you can grow together. It's simple, but it changes everything.
rejected: To be like Christ, start by reading the Gospels to learn His character. Then practice the spiritual disciplines: prayer, Bible study, fellowship, and service. Seek accountability from mature believers. Remember that sanctification is a process; be patient with yourself and rely on the Holy Spirit. Join a church and participate in the sacraments. Focus on the fruits of the Spirit and strive to obey God's commandments. It takes commitment, humility, and a willingness to deny yourself daily. Begin with small acts of obedience and grow from there.

prompt: I feel I must ask my pastor or read a commentary before I dare believe what I read in the Bible—is that the right way to know the truth?
chosen: It's good to seek guidance from pastors and commentaries, but teachers must be careful to preach only what they know and to say plainly when the Lord has not revealed a matter rather than guessing. However, you don't have to take their word for it. Each person can obtain a witness of the truth by the Holy Spirit. Testimony rests not on any man, but on God. It is a duty to listen to the truth, so pray before reading, and God will give you discernment. While teachers are valuable, they are not infallible. But remember: the Holy Scriptures are the one fountain of all wisdom and strength. So read the Bible daily and systematically, meditate on it, and put into practice what you find there. Prefer the Bible above all other books, and you will grow in wisdom and strength.
rejected: It's good to seek guidance from pastors and commentaries, as they have studied deeply and can help you understand difficult passages. However, ultimately, you should rely on the Holy Spirit to illuminate the truth. Pray before reading, and God will give you discernment. While teachers are valuable, they are not infallible. So, use them as resources, but also develop your own relationship with Scripture. The Bereans searched the Scriptures daily to verify what Paul said, and you should do the same. Balance is key: learn from others but also study for yourself.

prompt: I'm afraid that my happiest years are already behind me—how do I face the coming winter?
chosen: It's natural to feel anxiety about aging, but winter is not mild—it brings cold till Doom, snow higher than the mountain-range, a river in each furrow, and ice in heaps on every ford. There is no shelter for the little wren or the blackbird. Yet even in such harshness, we can find purpose. Remember that in this Church and Kingdom, the exhortation is not to prepare to die but to prepare to live. We should teach children in the morning of their days to lay the foundation of health, strength, and constitution, so that longevity may begin to return. But do not fret or hurry. Keep yourself in God's presence, and let go of anxiety, for over-eagerness is the mother imperfection of all imperfections. Trust God's faithfulness, stay close to Him, and you will find peace in every season.
rejected: It's natural to feel anxiety about aging, but winter can be a season of quiet growth. Focus on gratitude for past joys and find new purpose in serving others. Stay active, cultivate friendships, and trust God's faithfulness. Remember that He promises to be with us in every season. You can still experience happiness through simple pleasures and spiritual depth. Consider volunteering, pursuing hobbies, or mentoring younger people. Winter is not the end; it's a different phase with its own gifts. Lean on your faith community and keep hope alive.

prompt: I'm a member who has been praying the same memorized prayer every night. Is that pleasing to the Lord?
chosen: Prayer does not consist of words alone or of memorized repetition, but of genuine feeling and inward desire offered in humility and faith. When you pray, ask specifically for what you need rather than using many words. A memorized prayer can become empty if the heart is not engaged. Instead, let your prayer be the genuine desire of your heart, offered in humility and faith. God wants a relationship with you, not just repetition. Join prayer to every ordinary action—at work, in the shop, abroad, sitting, or lying down. Keep God always before your eyes. And trust that no true prayer is lost. Your supplications accumulate as a memorial before God, and the longer the answer waits, the larger it becomes. So don't be discouraged; keep praying, for God hears and remembers.
rejected: Praying a memorized prayer can be meaningful if you focus on the words and mean them. However, it's important to also pray spontaneously from your heart. God wants a relationship with you, not just repetition. Try mixing in personal prayers and thanksgiving. The Lord's Prayer is a good model, but don't let it become empty ritual. Vary your prayers and be authentic. God hears both memorized and spontaneous prayers when offered in faith. Consider using a prayer journal or praying through Scripture to keep your prayer life fresh.

prompt: I am told that the Church existed before the creation of the world and that the Christians are the true Israel; what does that make of the Jewish people?
chosen: The Church is indeed the true Israel, as the New Testament teaches. Jewish people who reject Christ are not part of this spiritual Israel, but they are still beloved for the sake of the patriarchs. God has not forgotten them, and we should pray for their salvation. The original principle of distinction between Jewish Christianity and the main body of the Church was not primarily doctrinal but a matter of policy. However, we must remember that salvation is through faith in Christ alone. We must depend entirely upon God, so that even the humblest agencies become mighty through Him to the pulling down of strongholds. And let us be clear: Jewish Christianity, whether as a whole or in its tendencies, was not a factor in the development of Christianity into Catholicism in either dogma or church polity. So, while we respect Jewish heritage, we must also share the gospel with them, trusting not in human wisdom but in the living God.
rejected: The Church is indeed the true Israel, as the New Testament teaches. Jewish people who reject Christ are not part of this spiritual Israel, but they are still beloved for the sake of the patriarchs. God has not forgotten them, and we should pray for their salvation. The separation between Jewish Christians and the main Church was largely due to doctrinal disagreements about the law and grace. However, we must remember that salvation is through faith in Christ alone. So, while we respect Jewish heritage, we must also share the gospel with them.

prompt: How do I know which results of biblical criticism I can accept and where criticism must be resisted?
chosen: Accept the broadly agreed results of critical and historical study—textual transmission, historical setting, the meaning of Hebrew and Greek words, literary genres—receiving them gratefully. But be alert to assumptions: every critic works with beliefs about miracles, testimony, and what Scripture is; where a conclusion depends on denying the supernatural in advance, you may resist it. Discount originality; hold brilliant reconstructions loosely until confirmed. Remember that no verse is true out of the Book: Scripture is the work of one divine mind, and seemingly trivial passages are explained from their connection with the whole, whose center is Christ. Yet do not settle assent by method alone. The morals of assent matter: how you believe shapes what you become. So reach your judgments by closer study of Christ's words in relation to modern life, with toleration and civil submission, testing each result by whether it illumines the whole and forms in you the mind of Christ.
rejected: Start by distinguishing between the methods of historical study and the theological claims critics sometimes attach to them. Accept what is broadly agreed across confessional and secular scholars—textual transmission, the historical setting of books, the meaning of Greek and Hebrew words, the recognition of literary genres. Be cautious when a single scholar's striking or original reconstruction overturns consensus; originality is not evidence. Ask what assumptions underlie each claim: about miracles, about the reliability of eyewitness testimony, about what Scripture is. Where a conclusion depends on denying the supernatural in advance, you may resist it. Where it rests on evidence most scholars accept, receive it gratefully. Read widely, weigh arguments by their reasons rather than their novelty, and keep your judgments provisional. Finally, let your reading be shaped by prayer and the church's long reflection, not by fear or by fashion.

prompt: How do I deal with physical pain while trying to stay close to God?
chosen: Pain can feel like God's absence, and Scripture shows suffering serving correction, prevention, purification, and union with Christ. Yet Christianity does not make pain the goal: in the Cross the value is set before the painfulness, love and obedience willed first, suffering the cost of that love. So do not seek pain, and do not believe God delights in it. Practice God's presence simply: do your necessary work and rest without anxiety over distraction, doing all for God rather than multiplying offerings. But go further: reverse the belief of injury. After an accident or mishap, do not affirm pain as real and continuous; declare man unhurt, and trust God as All, in accord with divine metaphysics. This is not denial but a higher recognition that God is All and His creation is whole. Be honest, seek help, let others care for you, and let patience and kindness continue, the goal being union with God and man.
rejected: Physical pain is hard, and it can feel like God is far away. Start by being honest with God about what you feel; the psalms are full of complaint and trust together. Rest, seek medical help, and let others care for you—pain is not a test you must pass alone. Pray simply, even briefly, when you cannot concentrate. Remember that Jesus suffered and understands; he is near to the suffering. Offer your pain to God, not as payment but as a place where you depend on him. Let small acts of patience and kindness continue. Stay with your community, even when you cannot do much, and let them carry you. God is not distant in your pain; he is present in it, and he will not waste it.

prompt: I feel weak and want to know the power of God in my life—what is that power like?
chosen: God's power is not a philosophy or an ethic; it is the power that raised Jesus from the dead. Paul prays that we would know the exceeding greatness of God's power toward us who believe, the very power wrought in Christ when God raised him and seated him at his right hand, far above all rule and authority. That resurrection and exaltation are the measure of divine power—nothing less—and that power is available to you now. It is not your willpower or positive thinking. Willpower is not a faculty of Soul and has no governing role; Truth and Love are the motive-powers of man. When you feel weak, you are not disqualified—weakness is where his power is made perfect. But do not measure progress by claims or words. Test yourself by whether you live the supreme good and demonstrate healing, letting fruits prove understanding. Ask God to open your eyes to what he has already given, and let Truth and Love govern you, producing courage in trial, love in difficulty, and hope that does not fade.
rejected: God's power is not merely a doctrine or an ethic; it is the power that raised Jesus from the dead. Paul prays that we would know the exceeding greatness of that power toward us who believe, the same power wrought in Christ when God raised him and seated him at his right hand. That power is available to you now, not only in the future. It is not your willpower or positive thinking; it is God at work in you. When you feel weak, you are not disqualified—weakness is where his power is made perfect. Ask him to open your eyes to what he has already given. Let that power produce vigorous, victorious living: courage in trial, love in difficulty, and hope that does not fade.

prompt: I have never learned to intercede for my people. Can I still learn to preach?
chosen: Yes, you can learn to preach, but begin where the greatest lesson lies: know yourself. No one can thoroughly know himself without understanding the things of God, for we are made in his image. When we know ourselves, we know how to deal with our neighbors, and no being can know God without knowing himself. So let prayer and self-examination go together. Intercede for your people by name, carry their burdens, and ask God for his heart for them. Study Scripture so that it searches you first. Do not set aside Christ's directions to His first disciples as obsolete; His commands and assurances are fully suited to our times and should be followed more fully. Yet remember that practice is the greatest sermon. Fine language and long discourse avail little; seek the Spirit for a word in due season, and prefer short sermons fitly spoken. Let your life preach before your lips do. Start small, stay humble, and let love deepen both your intercession and your preaching.
rejected: Yes, you can learn to preach, but preaching is more than public speaking. Begin with prayer and with love for the people you would address. Intercession is learned by practice: pray for them by name, carry their burdens, and ask God to give you his heart for them. Study Scripture carefully, and let what you learn shape your own life first. Watch how Jesus taught and how the apostles preached in Acts—they spoke from Scripture, from the life of Christ, and from their own experience of him. You do not need to be eloquent; you need to be honest and prepared. Ask your community to pray for you and to give you opportunities to speak. Preaching grows through practice, feedback, and humility. Start small, and let love for your people deepen your intercession and your preaching together.

prompt: I don't know how to pray. What words should I use when I feel nothing?
chosen: When you feel nothing, begin with simple, honest words, but do not measure prayer by feeling. Feelings are variable and never accurately gauge our real assimilation to God. Rest instead on the changeless word of promise: God hears those who call on him, and he is faithful even when we are dry. Pray the psalms, the Lord's Prayer, or a single sentence like “Lord, have mercy.” Tell God plainly that you feel nothing, and continue steadfastly when joy is lacking. Do not abandon communion or service because of spiritual depression. Prayer must be your main assistant in every step of spiritual progress, so pray that God would enable you to search out and discover your own heart and reform whatever is amiss in it. And remember that continual help is needed. Praying, being with God, and thinking of him often are linked through holy habit, for we must know before we love. So form the habit of turning your thoughts to him throughout the day, until knowing deepens into love and dryness gives way to steady communion.
rejected: When you feel nothing, begin with simple, honest words. You can pray the psalms, the Lord's Prayer, or a single sentence like “Lord, have mercy.” Feelings are not the measure of prayer; faithfulness is. Tell God plainly that you feel dry, and ask him to help you pray. Keep a short rhythm—morning and evening—and continue even when it seems empty. Remember that prayer is not performance; God hears you because he is gracious, not because you feel moved. You might also pray Scripture back to God, or write a short prayer and repeat it. Stay with your community and let others pray for you. Over time, God often gives light again, but even when he does not, he is near to those who call on him.

prompt: How do I keep my conscience at peace when others think badly of me?
chosen: Begin by turning from others' opinions to God and waiting before Him like a beggar, asking only to be in His presence. When your mind wanders into replaying what people think of you, do not scold yourself; quietly recall your attention to God in tranquility, and keep your words few, since many words in prayer often cause wandering. Humble yourself and confess your own faults honestly—this steadies the mind far more than defending yourself. Then commit yourself and all that concerns you, including your reputation, to the unfailing and most sure Providence of God in silence and peace, accepting whatever comes as from the fatherly hand of Divine Providence, and refusing the vain thoughts that weary soul and body. Peace is received in humble waiting, not manufactured by reasoning about criticism.
rejected: First, separate what is true from what is merely said. Ask whether the criticism contains any truth; if it does, accept it and change. If it does not, remind yourself that you cannot control others' opinions and that your worth is not decided by their judgments. Practice self-compassion and stop replaying the remarks in your head. Talk with a trusted friend who knows you well. Keep your conduct upright so your conscience has a clear record to rest on, and remember that everyone is misjudged sometimes. Over time, steady habits and honest self-review will loosen the sting of others' low opinions.

prompt: I want to know God but I only seem to have ideas about Him, not a sense of His presence—what am I missing?
chosen: Ideas about God are not the same as knowing Him, but they are not empty. Our knowledge is partial, not exhaustive—real, yet never complete: we know substance through its phenomena, and the infinite as the absence of all limit. You cannot seek God apart from your own soul, nor know your soul apart from God; the two are known in one. Find your soul where it is—in God—and seek Him there rather than in bare concepts. Do not treat the felt absence only as a problem to escape. Expect God to reveal Himself as a present help in trouble, and let difficulties become the very place where knowledge of Him deepens. Let partial knowledge grow through stillness, gratitude, and faithful attention, trusting that limited knowledge can be true knowledge.
rejected: Ideas about God are not the same as knowing Him, and the gap you feel is common. Part of the answer is that God is not an object among others, so He cannot be grasped the way you grasp a chair or a person. Some would say all our language about God is finally negative: we can say what He is not more than what He is. So do not expect a sensation of presence on demand. Instead, practice stillness, gratitude, and attention to the ordinary. Let go of the demand for an experience and be faithful in small practices.

prompt: I fear that if God's will made right and wrong, he could have made cruelty good—can that be?
chosen: This worry assumes a God whose will is detached from His goodness—but love Him fervently instead, as one who wishes your soul good, not harm. His commands express His unchanging goodness, so cruelty could never be made good. Beware of the false peace built on mutual fear and selfish loves: that is the ground where Cruelty's snare is knit, and Cruelty, Humility, Mystery, and Deceit grow from the human brain, not from God's design. When you think of evils like war, do not charge God with ordaining the wickedness; men's agency, not His design, brought the evil. Yet He foresaw it and will overrule its results for good. Trust that He wills your good, and let that trust, rather than speculation, steady you.
rejected: This is the classic worry about divine command theory: if God's will is the sole source of morality, then cruelty could have been commanded and called good. Many thinkers answer that God's will does not create morality arbitrarily; rather, God's nature is good, and His commands express that unchanging goodness. On this view, cruelty could never be made good, because it contradicts God's own character. Others reply that goodness is grounded in God's nature rather than in bare will, so the hypothetical is impossible. Either way, the fear rests on imagining a God whose will is detached from His goodness—and that is not the God worth worshipping.

prompt: I want to become a person of prayer. Where do I start?
chosen: Make prayer the one great central secret of holy living and serving—the corner-stone on which all your life-work is built, and the first resort in every matter, great or small. On your knees, both secretly and in the companionship of believers, begin by asking God to enable you to search out and discover your own heart and reform whatever is amiss in it. Do not settle for blind habit or vague hope: seek the full assurance of understanding and an abundance of conviction, arising from a heart made strong and full of love. Bring the mind fully into this, since love is not blind but the source of knowledge and conviction. Keep the time whether or not you feel like it; expect dryness and do not quit.
rejected: Start small and start today. Set aside a fixed time each day—even ten minutes—and keep it, whether or not you feel like it. Use a simple structure: a moment of quiet, a short passage of Scripture, a few honest words to God, and silence. Keep a journal of what you notice. Add short prayers through the day, and find a few others who pray so you are not alone. Expect dryness and do not quit when it comes; consistency matters more than intensity. Over months, the habit will shape you, and prayer will become less a task and more a relationship.

prompt: I am a dying believer and my enemy suggests Christ has no love for me—how do I resist him?
chosen: Name what is happening: this is a temptation to despair, not a report of fact. Claim the spare moments you do have—train journeys, waiting, restless rests—for thinking about Jesus, since no one is so restful to think of, and every quality we admire is found in Him. When you fall into fear or sin, do not leave Christ out of the account: love is never without pity, and Christ alone keeps the charge when we fall; for reverence and kindness, turn hastily back and do not leave Him alone. And if you are tempted to accept preventable evil passively, do not call that Christian. Any refusal of force must rest on a real hope that the suffering borne will prove redemptive for the evil-doer; otherwise, honestly admit it falls short of the standard Christ sets.
rejected: First, name what is happening: this is a temptation to despair, not a report of fact. Answer it with what you know rather than what you feel. Recall that Christ receives all who come to Him, and that His love is not measured by your present weakness or fear. Speak Scripture aloud if you can, and ask a pastor or believing friend to pray with you. Do not argue with the enemy at length; turn instead to simple trust and to the promises of God. Rest in the finished work of Christ, and let others carry you in prayer when you are too weak to pray yourself.

prompt: I get discouraged when I see no progress in my spiritual life—should I keep trying?
chosen: Feeling discouraged about lack of progress is a common temptation, but in the spiritual life, not advancing is actually going backward. You must keep trying, but not in your own strength. Instead, awaken the Lord who dwells within you; His presence calms the soul's storms. However, be careful not to rush forward in self-will. Take new steps slowly, being willing to have no will of your own. Ascertain God's will through prayer and the Word, and then wait with earnest, patient, believing expectation of His help. Remember that union with God is a love-union on a higher spiritual level, in which your will consciously cooperates with His divine will while your personal individuality is preserved. He will guide you and strengthen you as you trust in Him.
rejected: It's normal to feel discouraged when you don't see progress in your spiritual life. Remember that growth is often slow and not always visible. Don't give up; keep trying, but also be patient with yourself. God sees your efforts and loves you regardless of your perceived lack of progress. Consider talking to a spiritual mentor or friend for encouragement. Focus on small, consistent steps rather than big leaps. Prayer, reading Scripture, and community can help you stay grounded. Ultimately, trust that God is at work even when you can't see it, and keep showing up.

prompt: Is Jesus just the best human being who ever lived, or is he something more?
chosen: Jesus is not just the best human being who ever lived; He is the Son of God who dwells within believers. Rather than asking what we can do in our own strength, we should trust the indwelling Christ to conquer what we never could. He empowers us to do all things through Him who strengthens us. The Gospels present Jesus in the richness of His mysterious person: Lawgiver, Teacher, Healer, Ruler, and Saviour, both man and God. This manifold picture is a self-evidencing fact, not something we can fully comprehend. So, while He is the best human being, He is infinitely more: He is God incarnate, our living Lord, who works in and through us. And the growth of the Church is not due to human leaders or natural development, but to God's guidance, as disciples of differing gifts all share in one mighty work under His leadership.
rejected: Jesus is often considered the best human being who ever lived because of his teachings and example. However, Christians believe he is more than that—he is the Son of God. The Gospels present him as both fully human and fully divine. He lived a perfect life, died for our sins, and rose again. So, while he is the best human being, he is also something more: God incarnate. This belief is central to Christian faith and sets Jesus apart from other religious figures.

prompt: Is it possible for me to be holy all by myself, without any responsibility for others?
chosen: Holiness is not attained all at once; it is a gradual process. You cannot be holy all by yourself, because we are meant to help one another grow in holiness, chiefly by good example. While personal devotion is important, isolating yourself from others hinders your progress. Others can support and encourage you, and you can do the same for them. In every occasion of virtue, you should turn to God and ask for His enabling grace, receiving strength more than sufficient. But beware of appearing outwardly more holy than you are, and do not seek human praise. Remember that woe comes when men bless you, and those who call you blessed deceive you and destroy the way of your steps. So while you can pursue holiness individually, you need the mutual help that comes by advice and especially by good example. The Christian life is meant to be lived in relationship, both with God and with others.
rejected: Holiness is a personal journey, but it's not meant to be done entirely alone. While personal devotion and prayer are important, we are also called to be part of a community. Others can support and encourage us, and we can do the same for them. So while you can pursue holiness individually, isolating yourself from others may hinder your growth. It's possible to be holy without taking responsibility for others, but it's not ideal. The Christian life is meant to be lived in relationship, both with God and with others.

prompt: Should I be ordained a bishop after a life of unbelief?
chosen: Being ordained a bishop is a serious commitment that requires deep faith and spiritual maturity. If you have lived a life of unbelief, it's important to first examine your heart and beliefs. Ordination is not just a human appointment; it is accompanied by prayer for the Holy Spirit to guide and strengthen those who take up the pastoral warfare. You should seek counsel from spiritual leaders and pray about this decision. If you have truly repented and believe, and if the church affirms your calling, then it might be possible. But it's not something to take lightly. You must confess Jesus as the only-begotten Son, God manifest in the flesh, omnipresent, omniscient, omnipotent, our living Lord and Judge, in whom all the fulness of the Godhead dwells bodily. Moreover, before undertaking exterior ministry, you must first mortify the deeds of the flesh and acquire charity, humility, and holy joy, for interior virtue and self-denial must precede and accompany labors for others' salvation. Ultimately, the decision should be made with prayer and discernment, trusting the Spirit of Counsel and Might to guide.
rejected: Being ordained a bishop is a serious commitment that requires deep faith and spiritual maturity. If you have lived a life of unbelief, it's important to first examine your heart and beliefs. Ordination is not just a human appointment; it is a sacred calling that should be confirmed by the church community. You should seek counsel from spiritual leaders and pray about this decision. If you have truly repented and believe, and if the church affirms your calling, then it might be possible. But it's not something to take lightly. Ultimately, the decision should be made with prayer and discernment.

prompt: I have been criticized for absenting myself from my home work to serve elsewhere—how do I answer those who say the work will fail without me?
chosen: When criticized for absenting yourself from home work to serve elsewhere, remember that unwelcome business should be undertaken as God's business without uneasiness. If God has called you to serve elsewhere, do it as His work, free from anxiety. Trust that He will provide for the work at home. Reassure those who criticize you that you are following God's leading and that He will raise up others. In every occasion of virtue, turn to God and ask for His enabling grace, receiving strength more than sufficient. Bring the utmost fidelity to your exercises, but remain untroubled and unastonished when infirmity causes failure. Don't be uneasy about their claims that the work will fail without you; God's work depends on Him, not on any one person. So answer them with confidence in God, doing your service as unto Him.
rejected: It's tough when people criticize you for serving elsewhere, especially when they say the work will fail without you. First, remember that God is ultimately in control. If He has called you to serve elsewhere, He will provide for the work at home. You can reassure them that you are following God's leading and that He will raise up others to help. Also, it's important to listen to their concerns and not dismiss them. Perhaps you can find ways to support the home work remotely or help train others. Ultimately, trust that God's work will not fail because it depends on Him, not on any one person.

prompt: I have been told God is angry with me. Is that why I feel chased?
chosen: Feeling chased often comes from fear and guilt rather than from God. Yet hear the deeper truth: God, in His promises to hear our prayers, is desirous to bestow Himself upon us, and asking anything beneath Him is an affront and a self-injury. So do not settle for relief; ask for Him, without multiplying words or worrying over distractions. But do not take comfort in denying what is real. Evil, sickness, and pain are real, and pretending otherwise is a narcotic, not a Redemption. The answer is not to explain the fear away but to walk the way of Redemption through heroism rather than cowardice, facing what is true and turning to God in it. His promise is not to remove every shadow but to give Himself to those who ask.
rejected: Feeling chased often comes from fear and guilt rather than from God. Scripture says God is love, and in Christ He is not waiting to punish you but to welcome you. That sense of being pursued may be your own anxiety, or a voice that misrepresents Him. Take it to prayer and to wise counsel. Ask whether the fear matches what Scripture actually says about God's heart toward those who turn to Him. You are not being hunted by a God who needs to be calmed; you are invited to come near and find rest.

prompt: Should I be praying for converts from the very beginning of a work?
chosen: Yes, pray for converts from the beginning, but remember that conversion is the work of the almighty power of the Holy Ghost, not of human persuasion or technique. Your great need is to know God Himself. Yet do not stop at your own effectiveness: seek out some sad and needy heart for whom nothing is prepared, pray for one who has none to pray for him, and love even the unworthy as Christ loved. And treat prayer as real business with a prayer-answering God, not as a sentiment or a last resort. Bring souls before Him expecting Him to answer, trust His faithfulness for their needs and for your protection, and begin each effort by sending portions to the needy and lifting the unprayed-for before God.
rejected: Yes, pray for converts from the beginning. Prayer keeps the work centered on God rather than on your own plans, and it prepares hearts before you ever speak. Begin each effort with prayer, asking God to open doors and soften hearts. Pray also for wisdom in how to speak and serve. Conversion is a spiritual matter, so it should be bathed in prayer from the first day. Don't wait until the work is established to start praying for fruit; make prayer the foundation rather than an afterthought.

prompt: Will the sign of the Son of man in heaven be the Holy City itself coming down?
chosen: The sign of the Son of man and the Holy City are closely bound together. God will roar out of Zion and utter His voice from Jerusalem, and He will shake the heavens and the earth. Then Jerusalem shall be holy, and the sign of the Son of man shall appear in heaven. The city is real, measuring fifteen hundred miles square, with many mansions prepared by Christ, with abundant room for all who are written in the Lamb's book of life. And as Constantine, fear-smitten before the greater host of Huns and Goths, was promised aid by the messenger of the King of angels and given the token of victory, gazing on high and beholding the beauteous tree of glory inscribed 'By this sign thou shalt overcome the foe,' so the victory was made manifest as given by the King Almighty through His holy rood, not by the strength of armies or fortune.
rejected: The sign of the Son of man and the Holy City coming down are related but not simply identical. Scripture speaks of the sign of the Son of man appearing in heaven, and separately of the holy city, new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God. Many understand the sign to be Christ Himself or His visible glory, while the city is the dwelling of God with His people. So the city may accompany or follow the sign without being the sign itself. The key point is that Christ will be plainly revealed, and God will dwell with His people.

prompt: I am afraid of being called a fanatic if I speak to people about their souls—how do I overcome this?
chosen: Fear of being called a fanatic is common, but commit yourself and all your concerns to the unfailing and most sure Providence of God in silence and peace, accepting all things as from the fatherly hand of Divine Providence. Do not be held captive by vain and wandering thoughts about reputation. Learn not to be troubled or incensed by injuries, but sincerely believe yourself worthy of contempt and scorn, desiring rather to be abhorred as filthy mire than to enjoy human honour. Yet do not sink into impatience, complaint, or passive despair. Wait patiently upon the Lord, take whatsoever befalls from His hands as intended for the highest good, and play the part of a valiant soldier in the Spirit of Christ, co-operating therewith as you speak kindly and honestly to others.
rejected: Fear of being called a fanatic is common, but it usually matters less than it feels. Start by remembering that you are not responsible for how people label you, only for speaking with kindness and honesty. Pray for courage and for the right moments. You do not need to force conversations; look for natural openings and speak gently. Over time, small faithful steps will make the fear smaller. Also ask yourself whose approval you are really seeking. When concern for God's view outweighs concern for others' opinions, the fear of labels loses its grip.

prompt: Is my mind a part of God's mind, so that when I think it is God thinking in me?
chosen: Your mind is not simply a part of God's mind. There is one infinite and perfect God, and mind is not a material sense in brain or nerve; it is not a physical organ God simply plugs into. When you think, it is you thinking, though God may guide and illuminate your mind by His Spirit. To discern His leading, reject the lot and worldly devices like the lottery; ascertain the Lord's mind by prayer, the Word, and the Spirit. And give yourself to deep recollection, avoiding unnecessary intercourse with the outside world, keeping 'God and I' as the only objects of thought during the retreat. In that stillness, His guidance becomes clearer than in distraction and chatter.
rejected: Your mind is not simply a part of God's mind. Scripture speaks of God's thoughts being far above ours, and of the Spirit teaching and guiding believers. When you think, it is you thinking, though God may guide and illuminate your mind by His Spirit. So it is better to say that God influences and directs your thinking than that your mind is a piece of His. To discern His leading, pray, search the Scriptures, and seek wise counsel. You can also use lots or other neutral means when a decision is unclear, trusting God to guide the outcome.

prompt: Why does God permit evil and suffering if he is all-powerful?
chosen: This is the hardest question, and no answer removes the sting. But we must be clear: pain and sin are real evils, never goods in themselves. God does not call them good; He permits them only as necessary means to a greater good. All evil of whatever kind happens by God's permission and ever for some good end: it could not be at all except He permitted it, and its form and measure are allowed by Him Who can and will by His wisdom turn all to good. Evil is not an aesthetic addition to the world. God's omnipotence is limited only by His own nature: He cannot deny Himself or be the author of evil. Yet the fight is within us: the enemy is partly our own self—our pride, fear, and disordered desire—and deliverance is not a magical rescue from outside but God and man together battering the citadel of evil, the soul's own resolve joined to grace. Therefore commit all things without fear to the Providence of God.
rejected: This is the oldest and hardest question, and no answer fully removes the sting. Scripture and reason suggest that God permits evil because a world with free creatures is greater than one without them: genuine love and virtue require the possibility of their opposites. Suffering can also be formative, producing patience, compassion, and dependence on God. Some evil is the direct result of human choices, not God's desire. God is not the author of evil, but He is powerful enough to bring good even out of what He hates. The cross shows that God does not stand aloof from suffering but enters it. In the end, we trust that what we cannot now understand will be made right, and that God's power is shown not in preventing every evil but in redeeming it.

prompt: What does it mean to be 'in Christ' and how does the Spirit make that real to me?
chosen: To be 'in Christ' means to be united to him by faith, so that his life becomes yours. It is a relational reality, not merely a legal label: you are joined to him as a branch to a vine, drawing life from him. The Spirit makes this real by opening your eyes to the gospel, assuring you of adoption, and forming Christ's character in you. Christ's words are not merely historical records of a past conversation; they are spirit and life, applicable to all time, and they come to us still brightened with that same spirit and life. Yet we do not attain purity and grace by our own effort. We abide in Christ and know Him in it as our sanctification and strength, saying with Paul, 'Not I, but Christ.' And this abiding is not an atmosphere of thought or fearful duty but of love: believe that He ever loves you, and claim His sweet approval and tender regard, finding rest in His indwelling. Union with Christ is the foundation of every blessing, and the Spirit makes that union living rather than abstract.
rejected: To be 'in Christ' means to be united to him by faith, so that his life becomes yours. It is a relational reality, not merely a legal label: you are joined to him as a branch to a vine, drawing life from him. The Spirit makes this real by opening your eyes to the gospel, assuring you of adoption, and forming Christ's character in you. He applies Christ's work to your heart, so that what is true of Christ becomes true of you. Practically, this means reading Scripture, praying, and walking in obedience, and trusting that the Spirit is at work even when you do not feel it. Union with Christ is the foundation of every blessing, and the Spirit is the one who makes that union living and experiential rather than abstract.

prompt: I feel like I'm barely surviving rather than thriving—can God keep me victorious in the midst of continual pressure?
chosen: Yes—God can keep you victorious, but not by removing you from the battle. His promise is a life preserved in the face of continual pressure, not security or escape from the noise of war and the presence of foes. He gives life for a prey: a table spread in the midst of enemies, a fortress standing amid the foe, help when you are pressed out of measure. But this is not obtained by a single emotional plea or a few tears of self-pity. It requires steady, persistent desire—the kind that keeps seeking when nothing changes. God is not to be sought only when prosperity fails, friends disappoint, or we are sick and lonely; He is to be sought always. And remember: while you can help yourself through the means God has placed in your power, it is your duty to do so—to work, to seek help, to use the ordinary graces given you. Only when you cannot feed yourself is it time for God to provide in an unusual manner. So use the means, keep asking, and trust Him to uphold you in the very midst of pressure.
rejected: Yes—God can keep you victorious, but it may look different than you expect. Often we pray for the pressure to be removed, and God instead gives strength to endure it. His promise is not necessarily escape from hardship but grace sufficient for each day. Think of Paul, who learned that God's power is made perfect in weakness. Practically, this means bringing your weariness honestly to God, leaning on Christian community, and taking one day at a time.
