It also helps to remember that feelings of barely surviving are not the final verdict on your life; God is at work even when you cannot see it. Keep praying, keep trusting, and let others carry you when you are weak. Victory in Scripture is often endurance, not triumph, and God is faithful to sustain you.

prompt: I want to forgive someone who hurt me, but I also want them punished. Is that wrong?
chosen: It is deeply human to want both forgiveness and justice, but the gospel calls us further. St. Fulgentius is clear: Christians must not seek revenge but forgive injuries. That does not mean the wrong did not matter. No evil remains unpunished: every mortal sin deserves infinite punishment in strict justice, because it is committed against God, to Whom belong infinite greatness, dignity, and glory. So you need not fret that the offender will escape—God's justice is certain. Nor should you envy them their sins: it is far more dangerous, other things being equal, to be entangled in many sins than to be held only by one. Yet hear the better way: forgiving enemies and bearing injuries patiently is the best revenge, for by it grace and the pardon of your own sins are gained without trouble or expense. So release your claim to retaliation, pray for the person, and let patience do its work. Forgiveness is a process, and it is fine to be honest about the struggle while you work toward it.
rejected: It is deeply human to want both forgiveness and justice, and the two are not entirely opposed. Wanting someone punished for real wrongdoing is not automatically sinful—it reflects a God-given sense of justice. But there is a difference between desiring justice and desiring revenge. Revenge is personal, wanting them to suffer because they made you suffer; justice is about the wrong itself being addressed. You can forgive—release your personal claim to retaliation—while still hoping that wrong is not simply ignored. Practically, this means praying for the person, naming your hurt honestly to God, and letting go of the desire to see them humiliated. Trust God to deal with them justly. Forgiveness is a process, not a single moment, and it is fine to be honest about the struggle while you work toward it.

prompt: Must I not cry out I am undone if I should attain with my mind to that where no creature is?
chosen: Yes, there is a real sense in which you must cry out 'I am undone' when the mind reaches beyond every creature. Scripture records such a cry—Isaiah before the throne, Job in the whirlwind. To approach the boundless God is to become acutely aware of your own smallness and sin. But this undoing is not destruction; it is the breaking of the false self that clings to creature-comforts. Yet a single cry or a few tears is not enough. What is required is steady, persistent desire—seeking God not only when prosperity fails, friends disappoint, or we are sick and lonely, but always. And the true Quiet of the Soul, which no creature can disturb, is not attained by the activity of your own reason or by self-direction. It comes only by wholly giving yourself up to the life of Christ and resigning your will to Him, desiring and willing nothing without Him. Yet do not disdain the creature or the body: maintaining contact with the Divine Guide, the soul gently leads the creature, acknowledging that nothing is too small or humble for it to attend to. So the cry 'I am undone' becomes the doorway to surrender and to humble, everyday care.
rejected: Yes, there is a real sense in which you must cry out 'I am undone' when the mind reaches beyond every creature. Scripture itself records such a cry—Isaiah before the throne, Job in the whirlwind. To approach the boundless God is to become acutely aware of your own smallness and sin. But this undoing is not destruction; it is the necessary breaking of the false self that clings to creature-comforts. The mind cannot grasp God, and any attempt to reach Him by sheer intellect will end in vertigo. Yet God does not leave the soul in that place. He meets us in Christ, who is the image of the invisible God, and He gives rest not by our climbing but by His condescension. So let the cry be honest, but do not stop there: let it lead you to humility, worship, and trust in the One who is beyond all creatures yet near to the contrite.

prompt: I'm afraid of growing old and losing my youth. Is there anything to look forward to?
chosen: It's natural to feel anxious about aging, but the exhortation in this Church and Kingdom is to prepare to live, not to die. We should teach children in the morning of their days to lay the foundation of health, strength, and constitution, so that longevity may begin to return. Age and decay are not lawful necessities; the mental state governs the body, and man reflects eternal Life. To become kingly, adopt the habits of King Cormac: listen in the woods, be blind to secrets, show mildness in the mead-hall, sternness in battle, gentleness to allies, never deride the old, never speak of anyone in his absence, and always give rather than ask. By renewing your mind and embracing these virtues, you can overcome fear and look forward to continued growth, deeper wisdom, and the manifestation of eternal Life.
rejected: It's natural to feel anxious about aging, but there is much to look forward to. With age comes wisdom, deeper relationships, and freedom from many of the pressures of youth. Many people find that their later years are some of their most fulfilling, as they have more time for hobbies, family, and reflection. Instead of focusing on what you're losing, try to focus on what you're gaining: experience, perspective, and the opportunity to mentor others. Aging is a part of life, and it can be a rich and meaningful chapter if you embrace it with a positive attitude.

prompt: I am afraid of death and of the pains of dying; how should I think of the moment when I am taken from all pain?
chosen: It's understandable to fear death and the pain that may come with it, but we are counseled to pass lightly over pain and hold to comfort and sure trust in God's keeping in both woe and weal. The Seventh Revelation reminds us that God keeps us in all circumstances. Instead of praying for deliverance from pain, pray for strength and patience to bear it, seeing sickness as from God's hand. Death is certain, but its time, place, and manner are utterly uncertain. Therefore, make now the changes you would wish to have made when death is near. The moment of death is a release from all pain, and you can trust that God will be with you. Hold to comfort and sure trust, and let go of mourning over what is to come.
rejected: It's understandable to fear death and the pain that may come with it. But consider that the moment of death is often described as a release from all pain and suffering. For many, it is a transition to a state of peace and rest. Instead of dwelling on the fear, try to focus on the comfort that comes from knowing that pain will end. You might find solace in spiritual practices, prayer, or meditation, which can help you face the unknown with greater calm. Remember that you are not alone; many have faced this fear and found peace. Trust that the moment will come when you are ready, and it will be a release.

prompt: Is it wrong to be a policeman or a soldier?
chosen: Being a policeman or a soldier is not inherently wrong; these are necessary roles in society for maintaining order and protecting the innocent. However, the text teaches that officers are called to be servants and fathers rather than masters or tyrants. They should be pure, charitable, forgiving, and fathers indeed rather than tyrants. They are called to be servants, and whoever would be great should be the servant of all, following Christ's example. Those at the head must set the standard, walk in the right path, invite the people to follow, and be brethren and leaders rather than drivers or rulers. Individual responsibility before an All-seeing God is the first and highest standard of correct living. Men should be good for the truth's sake and should not depend on changeable public sentiment. If a policeman or soldier acts with cruelty or corruption, that is wrong, but the profession itself can be honorable if carried out with these principles.
rejected: Being a policeman or a soldier is not inherently wrong; these are necessary roles in society for maintaining order and protecting the innocent. However, it is important that those in these professions act with integrity, compassion, and justice. They should serve the community and uphold the law fairly. If a policeman or soldier acts with cruelty or corruption, that is wrong, but the profession itself can be honorable if carried out with ethical standards. Many people of faith serve in these roles and see it as a way to protect others and promote peace. Ultimately, it depends on how the individual carries out their duties.

prompt: How many workers should I ask GOD for, and is it right to name a specific number in prayer?
chosen: When praying for workers, it's not about the number you name but the sincerity of your request. However, we should seek labourers first by earnest prayer to the LORD of the harvest and by deepening our spiritual life, so that men cannot stay at home. You can ask for a specific number if that helps you focus your prayer, but ultimately, it's more important to pray for God's guidance and for the right people to be raised up. The number itself is less significant than the heart behind the prayer. We should also commend the spirit of those who offer themselves and their substance for God's work without salary, trusting Him to supply all their need. Encourage cheerful, self-denying service. And remember that if you are required to do ten pieces of work of which only one is necessary for the Kingdom, you should do all ten to be sure of performing the one the Lord really requires.
rejected: When praying for workers, it's not about the number you name but the sincerity of your request. God knows the needs of the harvest, and He will provide according to His will. You can certainly ask for a specific number if that helps you focus your prayer, but ultimately, it's more important to pray for God's guidance and for the right people to be raised up. The number itself is less significant than the heart behind the prayer. Trust that God will call the right laborers in His timing, and focus on being open to how He might use you in the process.

prompt: I feel that God has already condemned me and that nothing can change my fate; is there any hope left for me?
chosen: It's understandable to feel that way, but please know that God's mercy is greater than any sin. No matter what you've done, there is always hope for forgiveness and redemption. Zaccheus's counsel reminds us that the Lord of all is merciful if we straightway purge ourselves of our evil deeds and cease again from the unrighteous act, though we have many times transgressed against Him and wounded Him with our sins. We should never offer scorn, blasphemy, or wrathful opposition to the Son of God, that we may deserve eternal life in heaven. Feelings never accurately gauge real assimilation to God; rest on the changeless word of promise rather than on variable moods. Continue steadfastly in prayer when joy is lacking, and refuse to abandon communion or service because of spiritual depression. The creaturely will is the partition; it is broken by the grace of self-denial and removed by conformity with the Divine Will. This is done not by oneself but by the light and grace of God received into the soul, which one must not resist.
rejected: It's understandable to feel that way, but please know that God's mercy is greater than any sin. No matter what you've done, there is always hope for forgiveness and redemption. God's love for you is unconditional, and He desires that you turn back to Him. The feeling of condemnation can be overwhelming, but it is not the final word. Many have felt the same and found peace through sincere repentance and faith. God is ready to forgive and restore you. Don't give up; reach out to a trusted spiritual advisor or community for support. Your past does not define your future with God.

prompt: Is it wrong to feel proud of our Empire and its power?
chosen: Earthly empire is a child's fabric scattered by Heaven's breath, and its ruins warn us to overcome ourselves rather than scale Heaven. Lift up your heart generously: be humble because you are grounded in truth, and peaceful because you make no account of what could trouble you. Yet know that pride is a spirit of revolt and independence which betrays men into fatal errors, and that humility and distrust of self incline the soul to submission to authority appointed by God. So do not glory in power, nor trust your own judgment; submit yourself to God and to those He has set over you, and direct your ambition not to dominion but to overcoming your own faults and sharing Christ's throne, won by humility rather than pride.
rejected: Pride in one's empire can be a natural and even noble feeling. Great powers are built by sacrifice, ingenuity, and courage, and it is reasonable to admire the achievements of one's civilization. History shows that empires rise and fall, and there is a certain dignity in honoring what our forebears built. Yet unchecked pride can blind a nation to its faults and invite resentment abroad. So a measured pride—grateful for prosperity and strength while remaining humble and self-critical—seems the wisest course. The question is not whether to feel pride, but to keep it balanced with humility and a clear-eyed awareness of the costs of power.

prompt: I am a poet and I want to praise a dead king. How should I mourn him?
chosen: A poet mourning a dead king should first count himself as already dead, since he must die some day, and have no consolation in this perishable life but to weep over and detest his offences, for now is the time to lament, not rejoice. Yet one cannot see another's woe without sorrow: let your elegy bear the people's grief as your own, knowing the Maker sits by us and moans till our grief is fled and gone. And approach Him as a wretched sinner, confessing your faults and abandoning yourself wholly to His hands, trusting His mercy. For the soul that confesses its wretchedness is met by His merciful embrace. So sing not of crowns but of confession and mercy, and let your lament draw both poet and people to the God who receives the contrite.
rejected: A poet mourning a dead king should honor his memory with dignity and restraint. Recall his virtues and achievements, and let the elegy give shape to the grief of a people. Use imagery that lifts the fallen ruler into memory—his crown, his battles, his justice—while acknowledging that all earthly glory fades. The poem should console as much as it laments, reminding readers that greatness is remembered in song. Balance sorrow with gratitude, and let your craft serve both the dead and the living who must carry on.

prompt: I'm feeling pressure to conform to the world's standards of fashion and appearance—how should I handle that?
chosen: The pressure to conform to fashion is a temptation to pride in outward adorning. Scripture commends humility and the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit, of great price in God's sight; pride in dress was the very sin by which Elizabeth was awakened, and the love of finery can be turned from by grace. Dress modestly and simply, honoring God and neighbor, and honor the duties of the housewife and the service of Relief Societies in caring for the poor and needy. Yet go further: vain and immodest dress is a snare that wounds others' souls, and the excuse of meaning no harm will not do, for the one who prepares the poison is more guilty than the one who drinks it. Let your adorning be good works, not a stumbling block.
rejected: Feeling pressure to conform to fashion standards is common, and the best approach is balance. Dress neatly and appropriately for your setting, since appearance affects how others perceive you, but don't let trends dictate your worth. Focus on comfort, hygiene, and self-respect rather than chasing every style. Remember that confidence comes from within, and genuine relationships value character over clothing. Spend within your means, avoid comparing yourself to idealized images online, and choose clothes that express your personality without breaking your budget. Ultimately, fashion is a tool for self-presentation, not a measure of your value as a person.

prompt: I am not sure the miracles in the Bible really happened—can I still believe the rest?
chosen: Yes, you can still believe the rest. A miracle is not a violation of natural law but an extraordinary event in nature wrought by the immediate agency of the immanent God, coinciding with the word of a religious teacher; it suspends no law of nature, for God is always at work in His creation. Miracles are for the consolation and confirmation of the Saints, not the proper means of convincing unbelievers; no good, honest person requires one to believe. Meet experience with experience: the real burden of proof lies in the present spiritual miracle of forgiveness and regeneration in your own life. That abiding evidence does not depend on settling every historical question, so hold to the core message of love, justice, and hope while honest questions coexist with genuine commitment.
rejected: Yes, you can still believe the rest. Many people hold that the Bible's moral teachings and spiritual insights remain valuable even if some miracle stories are taken as symbolic rather than literal. Faith is not all-or-nothing; you can wrestle honestly with historical questions while holding to the core message of love, justice, and hope. Miracles were recorded to persuade skeptics, but your faith need not rest on them. Focus on what the text teaches about God and how to live, and let honest doubt coexist with genuine commitment.

prompt: I have to correct someone who is doing wrong—how do I do it without driving them away?
chosen: Before correcting another, remember that if every person in the community would correct his own errors each day, the errors of the whole would be continually corrected. This is an individual business over which each must preside until every fault is corrected. So begin with yourself: examine your own faults daily and set your own house in order. Then approach the other with humility, as one sinner to another, in private and with patience, and do not abandon them when instruction ends; continue loving care and counsel until they tread firmly in the way. If your grievance concerns a leader, take it directly to the person involved, seeking confession and reconciliation, and do not spread the matter abroad or sit in judgment upon presiding officers from a distance.
rejected: Correcting someone without driving them away requires tact and timing. Choose a private setting, speak calmly and specifically about the behavior rather than attacking the person, and listen to their perspective. Use 'I' statements, express concern rather than judgment, and offer help. Avoid public embarrassment and ultimatums. Follow up later to show you care about the relationship, not just the correction. Remember that people change through encouragement and trust, so keep the door open and be patient.

prompt: I'm anxious about the future and want certainty. Is it wrong to want to know what will happen?
chosen: Wanting to know the future is human, and the desire isn't wrong—but it often rests on an assumption that time is guaranteed. Death is certain; its time, place, and manner are utterly unknown, and no forecast can secure them. Yet this uncertainty is not a summons to frantic haste or self-willed resolution. The safe guide in every crisis is believing prayer joined with the word of God, and continued uncertainty is itself a reason for continued waiting; delay is God's means of drawing you to prayer and keeping self-will in check. Make now the changes you would wish to have made when death is near, but make them patiently, refusing all carnal or chance methods of determining the mind of God. And do not await the accidents of life with fear, but with perfect hope, trusting that God, whose child you are, will deliver you according as they come.
rejected: Wanting to know the future is a very human desire, and it isn't wrong in itself—it usually comes from a healthy wish to feel safe. But certainty about what will happen isn't something we can actually have, and chasing it tends to feed anxiety rather than calm it. The better path is to accept that the future is genuinely open, and to focus on what you can control: your choices, your habits, and how you respond to what comes. Many people find that letting go of the demand for certainty, and instead building flexibility and trust, reduces anxiety more than any prediction could. So no, the desire isn't wrong—but it's worth redirecting toward readiness rather than foresight.

prompt: I have been told that the cross is only something that happened long ago—how can Christ crucified be present to me now?
chosen: The cross is no new thing, invented to replace the old pieties of the human heart; it is the putting of the love of God into those old fundamental pieties—the realizing in Jesus Himself of the dearest truths about God: that He is Father, that He cares, that He will not abandon us. In Christ crucified we see the infinite degree of God's interest in our life and the responsibility He assumes for its eternal issues. This is not the improving of the old nature but death and resurrection: the old self is crucified with Christ, and a new creation rises into God. Nor is the cross only long ago or a figure of speech—Christ is openly set forth crucified before your eyes and in you, bearing the curse wherever sin is. Wherever sin is acknowledged, there He is crucified; faith may lay hold of the deliverance already accomplished and receive the new life.
rejected: It's understandable to feel that the cross is distant, since it happened two thousand years ago in a particular place. But Christians have always held that the cross isn't merely a historical event—it is a present reality that touches your life now. Christ's death and resurrection are not just facts to remember but a power that transforms. When you pray, when you receive the sacraments, when you confess your sins and receive forgiveness, the cross becomes present to you. You can also unite your own sufferings with Christ's, so that his cross becomes yours. So the cross isn't locked in the past; it is offered to you today as the source of healing, forgiveness, and new life.

prompt: I feel a deep restlessness that nothing earthly satisfies—is that a flaw in me or a sign of something more?
chosen: That restlessness points to something real—you are made for more than earth can give—but be careful: over-eagerness and restlessness are the mother imperfection of all imperfections. They masquerade as spiritual hunger while scattering the soul. Notice, too, that the sensation is not a fixed fact but the effect of a belief: believe that nothing can satisfy you, and the restlessness persists; root out that belief and replace it with the truth that God is near, and the sensation changes or lifts. Yet do not be astonished at finding miseries in yourself, as though perfection were a finished work. The work is never done; it must always be recommenced with a good heart. Let your seeking be a sweet, peaceful, and amiable effort, accepting each new beginning without dismay.
rejected: That restlessness is not simply a flaw—it is one of the most telling signs that you are made for more than the things of earth. Augustine famously said our hearts are restless until they rest in God, and your experience echoes that. Nothing created can fully satisfy because we are made for the uncreated. At the same time, restlessness can become a trap if it turns into frantic searching, endless distraction, or impatience with the present moment. The healthier response is to let the restlessness point you toward God while also cultivating gratitude, contentment, and steady habits. So see it as a sign of something more—but let it lead you to peaceful trust rather than to agitation.

prompt: I'm a young woman wondering whether I should form a definite purpose in life—what should it be?
chosen: Yes, form a definite purpose—but let it be shaped by three convictions. First, every moment of human life should be devoted to doing good somewhere and in some way; ask where you can do good and how to make yourself capable of doing at least a little good. Second, set before you as the goal of all your efforts and desires the possession, even in a mortal body, of an image of the happiness to come and a foretaste of the delights, life, and glory of Heaven, so that your hopes, thoughts, and prayers breathe only God. Third, remember that the intention determines the true value of every act: actions done for merely natural ends, or only to be seen by men, lose their supernatural reward. So do all things for the glory of God, and let that intention order your studies, work, relationships, and prayer.
rejected: Forming a definite purpose is a good idea, but it doesn't have to be dramatic. Start by noticing what you're good at, what brings you energy, and what needs around you feel urgent. A purpose can be as concrete as serving your family well, building a skill that helps others, or committing to a community. Don't wait for a perfect answer—try things, reflect, and let the purpose refine over time. Balance ambition with realism, and remember that purpose isn't only about career; it includes relationships, faith, and service. Talk to mentors, pray or reflect in whatever way fits you, and give yourself permission to revise as you learn. The goal is a life that feels meaningful and directed, not a single fixed label.

prompt: I am told that Catholicism grew out of a compromise between Jewish and Gentile Christianity; should I accept that my church's doctrine is a mixture of two parties?
chosen: That claim oversimplifies a complex history. Tensions between Jewish and Gentile believers were real, but the original principle of distinction between Jewish Christianity and the main body of the Church lay in policy rather than doctrine: how far the Church would bind observance of the Mosaic law—circumcision, diet, and table fellowship—as a condition of fellowship. Justin Martyr distinguishes two tendencies among Jewish Christians: the strict, who insisted on the law for all, and the tolerant, who did not. He recognizes the tolerant as brethren, and the evidence shows the matter had ceased to be a burning question for the main body of Christendom in his day. The decision of the majority in councils and conferences rightly prevailed; minority dissent may permit conscientious withdrawal, but not internal war against the Church's decisions. So you need not accept the framing of Catholic doctrine as a mixture of two parties: the core faith was shared, the dividing line was policy, and the Church's working harmony was upheld.
rejected: That claim oversimplifies a complex history. Early Christianity did involve tensions between Jewish and Gentile believers—debates over circumcision, dietary laws, and table fellowship are recorded in the New Testament. But describing Catholic doctrine as a mere compromise or mixture of two parties misrepresents how doctrine develops. The Church's teaching emerged through reflection on Scripture, worship, and councils, not simply as a political deal between factions. It's fair to say that early Christianity was diverse and that some practices reflect negotiation, but the core doctrines—Trinity, Incarnation, Eucharist—were not invented as compromises. So you don't need to accept the reductionist framing; you can acknowledge historical diversity while recognizing that doctrine is more than a mixture of parties.

prompt: Should the Church take sides in politics, or stay neutral about forms of government?
chosen: The Church is not a partisan political body: it endorses no candidates or parties, for its mission is spiritual. Yet the Saints are taught to be good citizens, loyal to the Constitution and the laws of the land. Non-partisanship concerns factions, not the nation, and there is no conflict of loyalty between Church and nation. As a family serves the nation by being a good family, so service of the Kingdom builds up the land. Citizens should therefore support the nation in its acts, unless the nation is capable of something better, or demands what is intrinsically immoral or a repudiation of the spirit of Christ. Only then does faithful citizenship require refusal. Otherwise loyalty and faith work together, and the Church forms members whose devotion makes them better citizens, not rivals to the country.
rejected: The Church should generally stay out of partisan politics. Its mission is spiritual, proclaiming the gospel and forming disciples, not winning elections or endorsing candidates. When churches align with parties, they risk confusing the gospel with an ideology and alienating half their neighbors. Christians may certainly bring their faith into public life and vote according to conscience, but the Church as an institution should avoid taking sides between parties or forms of government. Its loyalty is to Christ's kingdom, which transcends any nation. So the wisest course is neutrality on partisan questions while encouraging members to be informed, virtuous citizens who serve the common good.

prompt: How do I stop being anxious about my spiritual progress?
chosen: Anxiety about progress comes from over-eagerness, the mother imperfection of all imperfections, and the remedy is keeping yourself in God's presence. Do not mistake calm for complacency: not advancing is going back, so keep steadily advancing without hurry or fretfulness. When storms of worry rise, call on the Lord present within you; awakening Him calms the soul's storms. And when you stumble into small faults, do not be terrified or paralyzed. Humble yourself quietly before God and say to your soul: 'Courage! we have made a false step, but let us keep steadily on.' Over-eagerness breeds anxiety, and terror over trifles blocks perfection; but a calm, advancing soul, calling on Christ within and rising gently after each fault, finds both peace and growth.
rejected: Anxiety about spiritual progress is common, and the remedy is to stop measuring yourself constantly. Set realistic goals, celebrate small gains, and remember that growth is gradual. Keep a routine of prayer and Scripture, examine yourself gently, and talk with a trusted pastor or friend. If worry becomes consuming, consider whether perfectionism or scrupulosity is at work; God is gracious and patient. Focus on faithfulness today rather than comparing yourself to others or to an imagined ideal. Rest in grace, and let progress come as a byproduct of steady habits rather than anxious self-monitoring.

prompt: Is Christ's presence in my heart just a feeling or an idea, or something more?
chosen: Christ's presence in your heart is more than a feeling or an idea; it is a living relationship in the atmosphere of His love. Believe that He ever loves you and claim His sweet approval and tender regard. His words are spirit and life, applicable to all time, coming to us still brightened with that same spirit and life. When you behold His Passion, do not see pain alone. Behold in three manners: the hard pains He bore, the love that passes them, and the joy and bliss of the Trinity within it. That same loving, joyful presence is what dwells in you. So rest in His living word, remain in prayer, and let His presence shape your life, confident that you are loved, accompanied, and held in joy.
rejected: Christ's presence in your heart is more than a feeling or an idea. Feelings fluctuate and ideas can be abstract, but His presence is a real relationship grounded in faith and the sacraments. You may not always feel it, and that is normal; feelings are unreliable indicators. Nor is it merely a doctrine you affirm. It is Christ Himself dwelling in you by grace, known through faith, prayer, and love of neighbor. So don't chase emotional highs or reduce it to a concept. Trust His promise, remain in prayer, and let His presence shape your life even when you feel nothing.

prompt: I pray for my congregation, but only that they be saved. Is that enough?
chosen: Praying for your congregation's salvation is good, but the question is whether your commitment matches it. The author teaches that members join the confraternity solely to serve God and Mary and save their souls, not for worldly advantage, and must not forsake its appointed days for worldly business. Real prayer is scarce, and helping bring preachers and the Church back to prayer is the greatest work a benefactor could do. Do not neglect congregational worship because you get nothing out of it; love is the highest motive. Attend chiefly for the edification of the whole body and of the stranger among you. Keep its days, serve God and Mary, and let prayer and presence together seek the salvation of all.
rejected: Praying for your congregation's salvation is a good and important thing, but it may not be enough by itself. Salvation is God's work, and your prayers matter, yet the Christian life also involves fellowship, worship, teaching, and mutual care. Consider praying for their growth in holiness, their healing, their relationships, and their witness. Also examine whether you are participating in the life of the congregation, not only praying for it from a distance. Prayer and participation together serve the body better than prayer alone.

prompt: I'm exhausted and overwhelmed by everyday duties. How can I keep any awareness of God through all of it?
chosen: When duties overwhelm you, do not multiply techniques; simplicity is the heart of practicing God's presence. Do each action for God without anxiety over distraction, for a wandering thought in necessary work is not a failure. Beware of hurry and over-eagerness, the mother imperfection of all imperfections, for anxious fretting blocks perfection. Remember that God is the one living Worker, and all human workers are only His instruments. Cast all your care upon Him, for anxious self-reliance is distrust of Him. So keep yourself in His presence calmly, doing what lies before you as His instrument, and return gently when you drift. Awareness grows through simple, repeated intention and trust in the one who works in you.
rejected: When duties overwhelm you, the key is to weave short reminders of God into your day. Offer each task as a prayer, use a brief phrase or breath prayer between activities, and set reminders on your phone. Try to see ordinary work as service to God, not just chores. At the end of the day, review where you noticed God's presence. If you feel distracted, don't be discouraged; gently return your attention. Consider simplifying your schedule where possible and asking for help. Awareness grows through small, repeated practices rather than one big effort.

prompt: How do I resist the devil's attempts to distract me through cares and anxieties?
chosen: Distraction through cares and anxieties is one of the devil's favorite tactics, because it scatters the mind and keeps it from resting in God. But the remedy is not frantic self-management; it is to come before God like a beggar, with nothing to offer but your need, and simply wait in His presence. When your mind wanders into worries, do not be terrified or paralyzed by the lapse. Quietly humble yourself, recall your attention without agitation, and say to your soul: 'Courage! we have made a false step, but let us keep steadily on.' Small faults are not catastrophes; they are occasions for humble return. Cast all your care upon Him, for He is the one living Agent who works in you; your part is only the instrument He uses, and anxious self-reliance is distrust of Him. Let the cares pass through, bring your attention back in tranquility, and trust that God is present and at work even when thoughts scatter.
rejected: Distraction through cares and anxieties is one of the devil's favorite tactics, because it scatters the mind and keeps it from resting in God. The first step is to name what is happening: when you notice your thoughts churning over responsibilities, finances, or worries, recognize it as an invitation to return to God rather than a verdict on your spiritual state. Practically, set aside fixed times of prayer and keep them even when your mind wanders. When it does wander, do not panic or scold yourself endlessly; gently bring your attention back. You might also write down your anxieties as a way of handing them over, and limit the mental clutter you invite in. Over time, these habits train the mind to stay steadier in God's presence.

prompt: I've been trying to be good on my own strength and I'm exhausted—is there another way?
chosen: Yes, there is another way, and your exhaustion is a good sign that the first way was never going to work. Trying to be good on your own strength treats goodness as a project you must complete by willpower, which inevitably leads to burnout. But before you try to fix others or even fix yourself, cast the beam out of your own eye. Look honestly at your own fear and sin, and let God deal with those first. Then, in every occasion of virtue—each temptation, each decision, each small act of love—turn to God and ask for enabling grace, receiving strength more than sufficient. Strength of character is not fixed by temperament; it is the will's power to control your actions independently of inclinations and human opinions. It grows by repeated virtuous acts and shrinks by yielding to passions, and progress is proportioned to self-victories. When you fail, return to God for the next occasion and keep steadily on.
rejected: Yes, there is another way, and your exhaustion is a good sign that the first way was never going to work. Trying to be good on your own strength treats goodness as a project you must complete by willpower, which inevitably leads to burnout. The alternative is to receive goodness as a gift rather than manufacture it. Start by admitting honestly to God that you cannot do this alone, and ask Him for help each day. Practically, build small habits of prayer, rest, and honesty with trusted friends. When you fail, treat it as information rather than identity. Over time, you may find that goodness grows less from gritting your teeth and more from a settled relationship with God and others.

prompt: I'm told to love my neighbor, but why should I be moral at all—what makes right actually binding on me?
chosen: The question of why we should be moral is answered most deeply not by a menu of options but by the nature of God Himself. Right is right because God is it; His moral perfection is the law of our being, and conformity to Him is what we were made for. We are not bound by arbitrary commands, by utility, or by an abstract nature of things apart from God. We are bound because He is the Sovereign Good, and our flourishing consists in conformity to His character. Loving your neighbor is therefore not arbitrary; it is part of what it means to live rightly before the God whose very nature is love. Because love is the law of His being, we must compel the heart to suffer tranquilly and remain kind to the neighbor even when rebellious murmurings and sudden impatience rise within us. Avoid contention and unmerciful judgment; show mercy and charity, for that generous nature marks a true lady or gentleman.
rejected: The question of why we should be moral is one of the oldest in philosophy, and there are several serious answers. Some ground obligation in divine command: right is what God commands, and we are bound because He is our Creator. Others ground it in human flourishing: morality is binding because it leads to happiness and social stability. Still others appeal to reason and the nature of things—certain acts are simply contrary to what we are. Each answer has strengths and weaknesses. For many people, the most compelling account combines these: we are bound because we are made for relationship with God and neighbor, and morality is the shape of that relationship. Loving your neighbor is therefore not arbitrary; it is part of what it means to live rightly.

prompt: I am too busy to pray much. Is that a valid excuse?
chosen: Being busy is a real constraint, but 'too busy to pray much' is not a valid excuse in the deepest sense. Prayer should be kept at appointed times regardless of how you feel; feelings are not the measure of faithfulness. Set fixed times each day and keep them, even briefly, and establish family prayer as a regular practice. Do not imagine prayer is easy or naturally congenial; it is humbling work that crucifies pride and signs our bankruptcy before God. When you pray, do not merely ask God to do everything while you remain passive; help God accomplish what you ask by acting in accord with your prayer. Little praying is a deluding make-believe, worse than no praying. Above all, take time to be alone with God and His word. Constant activity, public service, and Christian fellowship do not compensate for the loss of the secret place; secret prayer and meditation are indispensable to fruitful service, so refuse to let activity crowd out communion.
rejected: Being busy is a real constraint, and it is worth acknowledging that seasons of life vary. But 'too busy to pray much' is rarely a valid excuse in the deepest sense, because prayer does not require large blocks of time. Short, honest prayers throughout the day can sustain a relationship with God even in busy seasons. You might pray briefly in the morning, offer quick prayers of gratitude or petition during the day, and end the day with a short examen. The key is consistency rather than length. If you genuinely cannot find even a few minutes, that may be a sign to examine your priorities. But for most people, the excuse of busyness is more about habit and attention than about actual lack of time.

prompt: I am a parent and my child has died in the faith—how do I think of her body in the grave and her soul with Christ?
chosen: I am so sorry for your loss. It is a profound grief to bury a child, even one who died in the faith. But do not think of her death as a hopeless loss. She has shaken off the dust of earth, she aspires unto God, and she dreads the least separation from Him as a most cruel death. She cleaves with firmest purpose to the one Sovereign Good, and all she receives, undertakes, and does is pure and true prayer; it is as simple and easy for her to contemplate God and rejoice in Him as to live a purely natural life. Such children are redeemed and beyond Satan's power, and you will have the joy of nurturing her after the resurrection. Your grief is real, but her soul is safe and at prayer. And let this hope renew your responsibility: teach and watch over your children in the gospel, and guard them from the wickedness of the world, for that charge remains.
rejected: I am so sorry for your loss. It is a profound grief to bury a child, even one who died in the faith. You may think of her body in the grave as resting in hope, awaiting the resurrection, while her soul is with Christ, safe in His presence. Scripture speaks of the dead in Christ as asleep and awaiting the resurrection, and of the soul being with the Lord. Your grief is real and should be honored; there is no need to pretend it away. Take comfort in the hope of reunion, in the prayers of the church, and in the promises of God. Let yourself mourn, and let others mourn with you.

prompt: I find it hard to be gentle with myself when I fail—how do I practice self-compassion without excusing myself?
chosen: Self-compassion without excuse begins in God's presence, not in a rush to repair. When you fail, slow down; anxiety and over-eagerness to fix yourself are the mother imperfection, closing you off from peace. Be wary too: pity would be no more if we did not make somebody poor, and the tree of Mystery and Deceit grows in the human Brain, so kindness to yourself can quietly excuse harm. Yet do not heal from self-condemnation or guilt. Stand in the moral might of Mind and firm trust in Truth: name the failure honestly, condemn the wrong and not your whole self, and let mercy arise only where you truly own the harm done. Keep standards patiently, free from fretting, and dwell calmly with God, trusting that unhurried, examined kindness lets you learn without collapsing or self-deception.
rejected: Self-compassion without excuse begins with honest naming: you failed, and that is real. But you are not the sum of your failures. Treat yourself as you would a struggling friend—acknowledge the pain, speak kindly, and then ask what the failure teaches. Separate the act from the person: condemn the wrong, not your whole self. Set a concrete repair or next step, so gentleness does not become avoidance. Remember that growth is gradual and that shame tends to paralyze while kindness restores energy to try again. Keep accountability in place—invite honest feedback, keep your standards—but hold them with patience. The goal is a steady, truthful kindness that lets you learn without collapsing, so you can keep moving forward rather than spiraling into self-punishment or denial.

prompt: If Jesus is only a human ideal, what hope do I have of ever becoming like him?
chosen: If Jesus is only a human ideal, there is no hope—an ideal cannot lift you to itself. But the Christ-ideal is a revelation of the God-life, supplying the dynamic for striving. Yet do not settle for a righteousness merely credited to you: salvation is an actual redemption of the entire self, made righteous by living in Christ's power the life He lived. And do not cling to your own good works or best attainments, as though striving or real change were your achievement. Give up the good as well as the bad, and take Jesus in place of your own self, receiving His divine impulses instead of your best attainments. Then the unattainable ideal becomes ground of hope, not despair: not you imitating a distant pattern, but Christ living His life in you.
rejected: If Jesus is only a human ideal, hope rests on the ordinary means of growth: imitation, habit, community, and grace understood as encouragement. You study his life, adopt his practices—prayer, mercy, courage—and let example shape character over time. You will not reach perfection, but ideals are directions, not destinations. Progress comes through small faithful choices, honest reflection, and support from others who share the aim. Accept limits without despair: an ideal inspires striving, and striving itself forms virtue. Where you fail, return to the pattern and begin again. The hope is not that you become exactly him, but that you become more like him—more loving, more just—through sustained effort and the help of a community that keeps the example alive.

prompt: What does it mean that Christ died for me—did he take my punishment so I don't have to face it?
chosen: Christ's death bears sin's consequence on our behalf, but we must be careful what that consequence is. Death is the law of physical nature, yet death as known among men—with its fear and estrangement—is the penalty of sin; sin altered our attitude toward things. Christ abolishes death, so it becomes the gate of life immortal. Understand the curse rightly: the curse is disobedience, not obedience; transgression, not law-keeping. Christ was made a curse for us on the tree, and thereby loosed us from sin so that we need not sin any more—redemption is not liberty to disobey. Let consolation rest wholly on Christ: his sufferings, temptations, cross, death, resurrection, and pleading at the right hand of the Father. Looking at self clouds the view, but his promises leave no room to doubt his power and will to save. Turn from yourself to the altogether lovely Saviour.
rejected: Christ's death is best understood as bearing sin's consequence on our behalf. Sin brings guilt and separation from God, and its wages are death; Christ, though innocent, took that penalty so that those who trust him are forgiven and spared condemnation. This is substitution: he stood where we should stand. It does not mean we never suffer or die physically, nor that consequences vanish, but that the eternal penalty and estrangement are removed. Receiving this means turning from sin and trusting him, not presuming on grace. The cross shows both God's justice and love—justice, because sin is real and costly; love, because God himself bears the cost. Assurance rests not in our feelings but in his finished work, and gratitude shapes a life of obedience.

prompt: How should the nails of the crucifixion be used for the good of men?
chosen: The finding of the nails is no matter of digging and guesswork. Elene's heart mourns until they are found; Cyriacus bows his head on Calvary and prays the Lord of angels to reveal the unknown mystery. A sign in the form of fire rises where the nails were hidden—a leaping flame brighter than the sun—and the nails glitter from their burial-place like stars or gems set in gold. The people say with one accord that the miracle is of God, whom they formerly withstood. Only then does Elene inquire of the wise man and choose his advice: the nails are set upon the bridle as a bit for the horse of the most noble among kings, a guard invincible against stress in war, a holy sign of God, and she sends the bridle to her son over the sea as an offering. So too should study begin with morning meditation, implore divine light in all reading, season learning with aspirations to God, and seek resolution of doubts at the foot of a crucifix—for studies without humility, simplicity, and prayer nourish vanity and error rather than virtue.
rejected: The nails of the crucifixion are best used as instruments of remembrance and moral instruction. Kept as relics or symbols, they call to mind the cost of redemption and the love that endured suffering. They can be displayed to provoke gratitude, teach children the story of the cross, and remind believers that suffering love is stronger than violence. Practically, they may inspire works of mercy—hospitals, care for the wounded—turning remembrance into service. They should not become objects of superstition or magical power; their value is symbolic and formative. Used well, the nails point beyond themselves to the crucified one, summoning communities to repentance, reconciliation, and compassionate action rather than mere veneration of metal.

prompt: I am a servant of God, and I have been tempted to be jealous for my own reputation in the work. How do I become jealous only for God's glory?
chosen: Jealousy for your own reputation is a snare, and jealousy itself is corrosive: jealousy and mistrust destroy affection. The work is not your possession. But the remedy is not to manage your image or retrain your heart over time—it is to be jealously and habitually occupied with Jesus. When a trifling word or distracting thought turns you aside, do not lose your peace over a straw; turn from every conflicting thought and look steadily up to Him. Practise mutual freedom and confidence, give others room, and let benevolence grow more diffusive. And refuse to seek riches, greatness, or honour in a world where Christ was poor and despised; such seeking is not compatible with discipleship. Embrace being despised, poor, and mean with Christ as your true glory. A heart fixed on Jesus and content with His lowliness has no room left for jealousy over its own name.
rejected: Jealousy for your own reputation is a common snare in ministry. Begin by naming it honestly: the desire to be seen, credited, and admired. Then reorient your aim—ask in each task whether God's glory or your image is at stake. Practice anonymity where possible, let others take credit, and measure success by faithfulness rather than recognition. Guard your heart against comparison; celebrate others' fruit. Remember that the work is God's, not yours, and that he entrusts it without making it your possession. When you notice possessiveness rising, pray for release and hand the outcome to him. Over time, habits of hidden service and gratitude retrain the heart so that zeal for God's honour displaces zeal for your own name.

prompt: I have given up on my dreams because they all failed. Is there anything left to hope for?
chosen: There is no true relapse in the Truth: the dream that failed was never your life, and failure has no final claim on you. Meet the cause mentally and courageously: name the fear that said one failure was the end, and refuse it. Pity the smallest and lost—even the little emmet matters—and know a watchman is set to light the ground: the glow-worm bids the wanderer hie thee home. But first examine your own heart. Do not blame the hardness of hearers or of circumstances while your own love has grown cold and your distress for souls has faded. The results you desire come by intense distress for souls and by tears, not by complaint. Let your heart be softened, weep for the lost, and then rise with courage to the work still waiting.
rejected: It is understandable to feel that way when dreams collapse; failure can leave real scars, and it is honest to grieve them. But giving up entirely is not the only option. Hope does not depend on the dreams that failed; it can rest on what remains—your life, your relationships, your capacity to learn and begin again. Consider what drew you to those dreams in the first place; often the deeper desire survives the particular plan. Take small, concrete steps rather than demanding a whole new vision at once. Talk with someone you trust. Setbacks are a genuine part of life, and recovery takes time. You are not required to have everything figured out today; you only need enough hope to take the next honest step.

prompt: I've been praying for a family member's salvation for years. Should I keep going?
chosen: Yes, keep going. Pray at appointed times whether or not you feel the spirit of prayer, and pray together as a family where you can. Do not confine prayer to a set hour or place: join it to every ordinary action—at work, in the shop, abroad, sitting, or lying down—keeping God always before your eyes. Let your asking be joined to action, helping God accomplish what you ask rather than expecting God to do it all. Above all, make prayer your main assistant in every step of spiritual progress. Pray that God would enable you to search out and discover your own heart and reform whatever is amiss in it, for the same grace that reforms you is what you ask for your family member. Prayer woven through the whole day, with willing labor and a searched heart, is powerful and never wasted.
rejected: Yes, keep going. Persistent prayer for someone you love is never wasted, even when you see no change. Scripture encourages us to pray without ceasing and to be persistent, like the widow before the judge. At the same time, remember that you cannot force another person's choices; prayer is not a guarantee of a particular outcome, but it places the situation in God's hands and shapes your own heart. Keep praying honestly, and look for opportunities to show love and speak truth gently. Also care for yourself so that you do not grow bitter or exhausted. Many people have prayed for years before seeing fruit, and sometimes the fruit comes in ways we do not expect.

prompt: What is the shaking of the powers of heaven, and when will it happen?
chosen: The shaking of the powers of heaven is God's own declaration from His dwelling: He will roar out of Zion and utter His voice from Jerusalem, and the heavens and the earth shall shake. His dwelling and voice are in His heavenly sanctuary and in Zion. When it happens, the Lord will be the hope of His people; then Jerusalem shall be holy, and the sign of the Son of man shall appear in heaven. This is a future shaking, sure because God has spoken. Until then, longing and seeking are our common working, not a fault to be cured now; we do not claim fullness of rest in this life. Nor does faith exempt us from anxiety and assault: the Kingdom of Heaven is in the Saints, operative by faith, even while the natural life is encompassed with flesh, blood, the World, and the Devil. So the soul sinks into the hope of the Grace of God and stands like a rose among thorns until the body's death.
rejected: The shaking of the powers of heaven refers to the dramatic cosmic upheaval described in passages such as Haggai 2 and Hebrews 12, and echoed by Jesus in the Olivet discourse: the sun darkened, stars falling, and the heavenly hosts shaken. It signifies God's decisive intervention in history, removing what is temporary and establishing what cannot be shaken—His kingdom. As for when it will happen, Scripture does not give a date; Jesus said no one knows the day or hour. It is best understood as a future event connected with Christ's return, and also as a present spiritual reality whenever God's kingdom displaces the powers of this world. The faithful response is watchfulness and steadfast hope rather than date-setting.

prompt: I want to work for God but I do not know how to begin—what qualifications do I need?
chosen: Wanting to work for God is a good beginning. The first thing necessary is earnestly to search His holy will by devout reading, listening to, and meditating on His eternal truths, which enlightens the divine law and guides us to every duty. Trust God to provide both the individuals and the means for any work He orders, as He fitted the workers and furnished the materials for the Tabernacle. Carry on the work within the landmarks of His word. Do not seek or depend upon the patronage of the world, do not appeal for money from unbelievers, and contract no debts; let the Living God alone be your Patron and prayer your only appeal. Bring a willing heart, humility, and faithfulness in small things, and depend wholly on His blessing in answer to prayer.
rejected: Wanting to work for God is a good beginning. The qualifications are less about credentials than about character and readiness. First, a living faith and a willing heart: God uses ordinary people who are available. Second, humility and teachability—be willing to learn from Scripture and from mature believers. Third, faithfulness in small things; start where you are with what you have. Fourth, prayer and dependence on God, since the work is His. Practically, get involved in a local church, serve in small ways, and let others affirm your gifts. Training and study can help, but they follow willingness. Begin with what is in front of you, and let the work grow as you grow.

prompt: If I am a part of God, how can I worship Him, and how can He be good when wicked men are also parts of Him?
chosen: Take all generally and behold God in all—do not cling to any special shewing or singular insight. Worship is the general beholding of God in all things: in creation, in neighbor, in ordinary life. Understand God rightly: He is not a corporeal person with human passions, located in space, or influenced as a human being is influenced. God is incorporeal, infinite Mind and Love, and material conceptions of Deity impede spiritual growth and obscure man as God's image. As for wicked men, behold God in all and see that His goodness is not divided by creaturely misuse of freedom. Yet do not fall into either self-reliance without God or dependence without effort. Fight your own battles with confidence and personal effort, while acknowledging constant dependence on God. Know yourself, cherish good character, and let worship be the grateful, undivided beholding of God in all.
rejected: These are deep questions. If you understand yourself as a part of God, worship becomes less about external rituals and more about living in harmony with the whole—gratitude, love, and service. As for wicked men being parts of God, many traditions would distinguish between being made in God's image and being identical with God. Wickedness is a distortion of that image, not a part of God's nature. God remains good; evil is a privation, a turning away. So worship by aligning your will with the good, and understand that God's goodness is not compromised by creatures who misuse their freedom. It may help to speak with a teacher or pastor about these mysteries.

prompt: What is the meaning of the stone cut out of the mountain without hands?
chosen: In Daniel 2 the stone 'cut out without hands' strikes the statue of world empires and grows into a mountain filling the earth. Cut 'without hands,' its origin is wholly divine—not human power—signifying God's everlasting kingdom, inaugurated in Christ. It also teaches us to pray: we present ourselves as a stone before the Carver, yielded and passive, asking God to form His own image in the soul. Yet being carved is not a resting place; our rest must be 'no rest below,' and we press onward to Sion, trusting the pillar and the living waters. The chisel that shapes us is often the cross—not an accident but fitted to our stature, measured to what we can bear. Rightly understood, all God does shall work our final good, and the stone He carves He will bring at last into the mountain of His kingdom.
rejected: In Daniel 2, Nebuchadnezzar dreams of a great statue representing successive world empires, and a stone 'cut out without hands' strikes it and becomes a mountain filling the earth. The stone symbolizes a kingdom not built by human effort or military power but established by God Himself—typically interpreted as God's everlasting kingdom, inaugurated by Christ. 'Without hands' emphasizes its divine, supernatural origin: it is not the product of human hands or political machinery. The stone's growth into a mountain shows this kingdom's universal expansion and permanence, contrasting with the fragile, temporary empires of gold, silver, bronze, and iron. It assures that despite the apparent might of earthly powers, God's rule ultimately prevails and endures forever.

prompt: Why does the church seem so divided—does that grieve the Spirit?
chosen: Church division is real and painful, and it grieves the Holy Spirit, who prays for the unity of Christ's body. Yet membership in the Church is no loose affiliation: it is a real bond carrying personal obligation, for we are members one of another. Divisions arise from pride and lack of love, and their cost is grave—the Church has become less actual to men than the nation, and therefore less powerful. The remedy is not human machinery of votes and officials but submission of the ministry and government of the church to the Holy Spirit's appointment and direction, echoing 'It seemed good to the Holy Ghost and to us.' The text shows a twofold organisation: prophets and teachers, bishops and deacons, each with their own charism, ordered around the diakonia tou logou and the economy of the church. The Churches' independence rested on the Spirit in their midst—not on uniformity. Where each gift serves under the Spirit's guidance, division is healed and the Church becomes actual and powerful again.
rejected: Church division is a real and painful problem, and yes, it surely grieves the Holy Spirit, who prays for the unity of Christ's body. Divisions arise from many sources: doctrinal disagreement, cultural differences, personality conflicts, historical splits, and institutional inertia. Some diversity is legitimate and even healthy, but rivalry, pride, and lack of love are not. Scripture calls believers to 'keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace' and to pursue reconciliation. The remedy involves humility, honest dialogue, prioritizing the gospel over secondary matters, and remembering that we belong to Christ before we belong to any denomination. While perfect visible unity may await the age to come, Christians should actively grieve division, repent of contributing to it, and work toward greater charity and cooperation.

prompt: Why does the Holy Spirit seem so limited in His work in my life?
chosen: Feeling that the Holy Spirit is limited in your life is common, but He is no impersonal influence or emanation. He is a divine Person, co-equal with the Son, the Paraclete sent by Christ, who speaks, guides, commands, and can be grieved. He is also the life of the Spirit-bearing body, the Church, working through means—Scripture, sacraments, fellowship—consecrating nature rather than bypassing it, never setting spirit against matter or grace against nature. His work is gradual and social: He forms us within a body, over time, through ordinary means, while intensifying personal character. Do not conclude from imperfection that He is absent. The Old Testament bears marks of its age, and the Church is not flawless, yet the Spirit truly inspired and truly indwells, bearing with the imperfect while He forms it. So draw near to the Church and the means of grace, and do not grieve the Person who dwells there, working patiently until His image is complete.
rejected: Feeling that the Holy Spirit is limited in your life is a common experience, and it does not necessarily mean something is wrong with you. Several factors can make the Spirit's work seem faint: unconfessed sin, distraction, unbelief, weariness, or simply seasons of spiritual dryness. Scripture promises that the Spirit is at work in believers, conforming them to Christ, and that He can be quenched or grieved by our choices. Practical steps include prayer, Scripture, community, and obedience. It can also help to remember that the Spirit's work is often gradual and quiet rather than dramatic, and that feelings are not a reliable measure of His presence. If you sense limitation, bring it honestly to God and seek wise counsel.

prompt: I'm afraid of what people will think if I follow these ideas. Should I hide my beliefs?
chosen: It's natural to fear what others think, but fear is not a trustworthy counselor—it is Satan's falsehood, and the answer to it is trust. So do not hide your beliefs out of fear. Say with the psalmist, 'What time I am afraid, I will trust in Thee,' and trust God for goodness and mercy all the days of your life. The deeper issue is moral clarity: moral ignorance and sin hinder demonstration and must be overcome. For the early Christians the decisive objects of conviction were the judgment, heaven, and hell—the general judgment and the final condition after it were the clear goal of all meditation, and this proves the moral character of the religion. Discretion may sometimes be wise, but it must never become a hiding place for sin or a surrender to fear. Be honest without being needlessly provocative, and let trust, not fear, govern your openness.
rejected: It's natural to fear what others think, but hiding your beliefs out of fear can lead to inner conflict and a sense of dishonesty. You don't owe everyone a full explanation of your convictions, and discretion is sometimes wise—especially in hostile environments. Still, living openly and authentically usually brings more peace than constant concealment. Consider the cost of hiding: it can isolate you, stunt your growth, and signal shame about something you value. You might start by sharing your beliefs with a few trusted people, then expand as you feel safe. If you face real danger or serious consequences, prudence matters. Ultimately, aim for integrity—being honest without being needlessly provocative—and seek support from others who share your convictions.

prompt: Shall all then have eternal joy and glorification alike?
chosen: Scripture suggests that all the redeemed share eternal joy, though its measure may differ—'one glory of the sun, another of the moon, another of the stars'—and the parables tie reward to faithfulness. Yet we must not consign to endless torment those who lived by the best light they had. All except those who sin against the Holy Ghost will inherit some kingdom of glory, and those who live by the best light they have will receive glory beyond expectation. None of this rests on our faithfulness as its ground: the cross of Christ is our sole ground of glory and our constant theme, for Jesus tasted death for me, in time and in eternity. Nor is the Christian life without bearing on how Christ is seen. Christ shines forth from the believer's life to others, and the believer is glorified in union and communion with Him—a reciprocal glory in which He is seen in us and we are made like Him.
rejected: Scripture suggests that while all the redeemed share eternal joy, their glorification may differ in degree. Passages like 1 Corinthians 15 speak of differing glories—'one glory of the sun, another of the moon, another of the stars'—and parables of talents and minas imply differing rewards for faithfulness. So eternal joy is common to all who are saved, but its measure may vary according to how one lived and responded to grace. This does not mean salvation is earned; it is by grace. But the New Testament consistently ties reward to faithfulness. Some traditions emphasize equal glory for all, others degrees of glory. The essential point is that all who are in Christ will be forever with Him in joy, and any differences will not diminish that joy but reflect God's just and generous dealings.

prompt: I feel like my life is a burden to others. Is there any point to my suffering?
chosen: Your life is not a burden, for you are God's beloved child, whole and free. The belief that you are a burden is a false sense of injury; in divine metaphysics, man is unhurt and perfect. Keep yourself in the love of God by constant trust and constant obedience. Then hard things become easy and sorrow is silver-lined with hope. Trust God as All-in-all, and know that suffering has no real power over you. See yourself as called to represent God to others: be dependable, true to your word, always giving, and self-forgetful in love. As you live toward others as God would, you will find your life rich with purpose and blessing.
rejected: I'm really sorry you're feeling this way. It sounds incredibly painful to feel like a burden, and I want you to know that your suffering is not meaningless. Many people have moments where they feel this way, but it's important to remember that your life has value and purpose. Suffering can be a heavy weight, but it doesn't define your worth. Perhaps talking to a trusted friend, family member, or counselor could help you see things differently. You are not a burden; you are a person deserving of care and love. Please consider reaching out for support.

prompt: I love someone who seems to be falling away from good living—should I keep begging God for a special sign about them?
chosen: Abandon yourself to God in this suffering, trusting His wisdom and love. Do not seek special signs; instead, live, work, and rejoice in God alone. Your loved one's path is in God's hands. Keep your hope in God, not in signs. Rest on the changeless word of promise rather than on variable moods. Continue steadfastly in prayer even when joy is lacking, and refuse to abandon communion or service because of spiritual depression. Expect God to reveal Himself as a present help in trouble, and let this difficulty deepen your knowledge of Him. God is faithful, and He will guide you and your loved one according to His perfect will.
rejected: It's understandable to want a sign when you're worried about someone you love. However, constantly begging for a special sign might not be the best approach. Instead, focus on trusting God's timing and plan. Keep praying for your loved one, but also remember that God is already at work in their life. Sometimes we need to let go and let God handle the situation. You can show love and support without needing a sign. Trust that God hears your prayers and will guide both you and your loved one in His way.

prompt: How can I present Christ to others as a compelling figure rather than a mild one?
chosen: To present Christ as compelling, recognize that the gospel portrait is not a product of human imagination. No mere human genius, least of all Jewish fishermen, could have originated such a figure. The portrait of Christ, free from puerility and self-contradiction that mere imagination produces, can only be explained by granting His person and character were historical realities. Present Jesus in the richness of His mysterious person as Lawgiver, Teacher, Healer, Ruler, and Saviour, man and God, as the Gospels do. The manifold Gospel picture is a self-evidencing fact. Be simple, human, approachable, and childlike, reaching others by simple human sympathy and love, so that they see in you the same Christ you proclaim.
rejected: To present Christ as compelling rather than mild, focus on His radical teachings and actions. Highlight His challenges to the status quo, His love for outcasts, and His willingness to sacrifice. Show how His message was revolutionary and how it continues to transform lives. Use stories from the Gospels that demonstrate His power and authority. Emphasize His humanity and divinity, and how He faced temptation and suffering. By sharing your own experience of Christ's impact, you can make Him real and compelling to others.

prompt: I feel the burden of unreached millions and cannot sleep—what does GOD want me to do?
chosen: God wants you to practice His presence simply. Do not multiply explicit offerings or be troubled by distraction in necessary work. Do all your actions for God without anxiety, avoiding the multiplication of explicit offerings that would interfere with simplicity. Present early seeking of God as the practice of those who do most for God; a desire for God unable to break the chains of sleep is weak. Connect the morning's seeking with the day's seeking, so that your whole day is lived in His presence. Come apart and rest awhile, finding rest in harmony with God's will and in trust, and learn to be still before Him. Then your burden will be lightened by His peace.
rejected: It's commendable that you care deeply for the unreached. God wants you to channel that burden into prayer and action. Start by committing the unreached to prayer daily, and consider how you can support mission work financially or through advocacy. Also, care for your own health—lack of sleep won't help. Trust that God is sovereign over all nations and that your part, however small, matters. Seek His guidance on specific steps you can take, and remember that He is with you in this burden.

prompt: I have a friend who is dying in sin and refuses the sacraments; can Mary still obtain mercy for him?
chosen: Perseverance in true devotion to Mary until death gives secure confidence of salvation. Your friend's refusal of the sacraments is serious, but Mary's intercession is powerful. Her prayers have the force of a command with her Son, and it is impossible for her not to be heard. If your friend has any devotion to Mary, even if imperfect, we may trust that she will obtain for him the grace of final perseverance. Moreover, Mary assists the souls in purgatory, consoling them, alleviating their pains, and delivering them through her intercession. Keep praying, and trust that Mary will not fail to help those who persevere in devotion to her until death.
rejected: It is a painful situation when a loved one refuses the sacraments. While Mary is a powerful intercessor, the Church teaches that salvation depends on one's own free response to God's grace. Mary can pray for your friend, but she cannot force him to accept mercy. Keep praying, and trust in God's infinite mercy. God desires all to be saved, and He can work in ways we don't understand. Entrust your friend to Mary's care and to God's loving providence.

prompt: How do I keep from being consumed by the pursuit of pleasure and comfort?
chosen: Entertain no attachment to anything, and be most on guard where passion is most dangerous—where sensual pleasure is annexed. Begin with eating, the ancient enemy and father of vice: keep the exact rule of temperance, taking food for necessity, never making the pleasure of sense your end but only the use you make of things. Behold this in Christ's Passion: the hard pains, the love that passes them, and the joy and bliss of the Trinity within it. But know that pleasure-seeking is a living death: it drives men into debt for fashionable display and into illegitimate schemes, until the hunt for pleasure breeds cheating, lying, and corrupted morals. Flee it, and let necessity, not craving, rule you.
rejected: Start by noticing what actually drives you. Pleasure and comfort are not evil in themselves, but they become consuming when they are the goal rather than the byproduct of a life well lived. Build habits that make you harder to satisfy cheaply: regular exercise, meaningful work, time outdoors, real friendships. Practice delayed gratification and set limits on indulgences. Ask what you are avoiding when you reach for comfort—often it is boredom, anxiety, or loneliness. Replace passive consumption with active creation. Keep a simple rule: enjoy good things in moderation, and never let any one pleasure become something you cannot go without.

prompt: I am a woman whose husband has died in battle. How do I go on?
chosen: Do not turn curiously inward to ask why your sadness is what it is; cease that inquiry. Patiently endure the aversions and repugnances that come, bearing them as a way of loving Him who suffered for you. Yet do not sit idle waiting for the Lord to guard you while you make no effort: take every precaution, order your affairs, and strive to help the Lord—being as willing to fight your own battles as to have Him fight them. And do not make the removal of pain your chief good or resist His correction. Ask rather for a wise and thankful heart, yielding your will to God's rod, rather than wishing the pain away.
rejected: I am so sorry for your loss. Grief after a death in battle is heavy, and there is no timetable for it. Let yourself mourn honestly; tears are not weakness. Lean on family, friends, and your faith community—you should not carry this alone. Keep simple routines: sleep, meals, movement, and time outside. It may help to write to him or to mark anniversaries in a way that honors his memory. If the sadness becomes overwhelming or unmanageable, please speak with a counselor or pastor. Take one day at a time, and be gentle with yourself as you find a new shape for your life.

prompt: I want to make my home and community beautiful, but others say it's a waste of time. What does God want?
chosen: Beauty is a duty, not a waste: God made the earth and its elements good when rightly used, so beautify your garden, house, farm, and city, and let every improvement serve the good of others. Yet do not settle into earthly comfort or plant and build for long rest, for this is no time for planting and building while souls wander and judgment nears. Steel your heart to let bright hopes fade; count over God's mercies and your own sin. Abandon yourself to God in interior and exterior suffering, and live, work, and rejoice—but in God, not in the things you make.
rejected: Beauty is not frivolous. God placed humanity in a garden and gave us work that shapes the world, so making a home and community beautiful can be a genuine act of love and stewardship. If others call it a waste, remember that beauty lifts spirits, builds community, and honors the people who live there. That said, keep your motives in check: do it for the good of others and the glory of God, not for pride or display. Balance it with generosity to the poor and time with people.
