Start small—a garden, a repaired fence, a clean shared space—and invite others to join you.

prompt: I have been told that the gospel is just a set of timeless moral teachings—is that really what it is?
chosen: The gospel is not simply a code of morals. It is not enough to live an honest life; the gospel requires obedience to rites and ordinances, and observing these is indispensable. Faith itself is a gift obtained by obedience, as all other blessings are. Nor is the gospel only for the already righteous: it is designed to make Saints of sinners, to make good men better, and to give power to overcome weaknesses. Yet do not keep this to yourself or look down on others. Desire that all honest-in-heart come to know the truth and be saved, share what you know freely, and welcome others rather than excluding them.
rejected: The gospel is more than a list of moral rules, though it certainly includes moral teaching. At its heart the gospel is good news: that God has acted in Jesus Christ to reconcile the world to himself. It calls for a changed heart, not merely correct behavior, and it invites us into a relationship with God and a community of faith. Morality matters, but it flows from gratitude and love rather than being the whole message. So if someone reduces the gospel to timeless ethics, they are missing its central claim—that God saves us and transforms us, and we respond with faith, repentance, and a life shaped by grace.

prompt: I study and read constantly, but I feel proud of my learning and dry in prayer. How should I study as a Christian?
chosen: Do not seek rapid progress through the letter alone, nor trust methods other than adhering to the divine Principle. Study the letter, but imbibe the spirit, and adhere steadfastly to the Principle they express. Let historical study of the New Testament be a means to a more stalwart and intelligent faith, pursued with prayer and crowned by reverent obedience. And know that Christian Science is both preventive and curative: when temptation or illness arises, turn to the textbook and let it renew your mind before the error takes hold, not only after. Where pride rises, return to the Principle, which is not yours to boast of.
rejected: Your experience is common: knowledge can inflate the ego and crowd out prayer. Try to reorder your study around devotion. Begin with prayer and offer your reading to God. Read slowly and reflectively rather than accumulating information. Keep a journal of what moves you to gratitude or repentance, and let what you learn become material for prayer. Balance study with service and silence. Remember that learning is a means, not an end; its purpose is to love God and neighbor. When pride creeps in, thank God for your mind and ask for humility. Consider fasting from study occasionally to rekindle desire.

prompt: I've been given a position of authority in the church. How should I carry it?
chosen: Congratulations on your new calling. In the church, authority is not coercive power but moral and spiritual weight—the kind that carries our judgment because it is earned by character, service, and fidelity. Remember also that you hold this office because a free and independent people, acting by conscience and not by coercion, chose and sustained you by voluntary vote. That democratic order is part of the authority's dignity. Carry it with humility and prayer, leading by example rather than by command. Your role is to serve, not to be served. And do not treat ordination as a merely human appointment: the Church trusts the Spirit of Counsel and Might to guide her ministers, so receive your setting apart with prayer that the Holy Spirit will guide and strengthen you in the pastoral warfare. Coercion adds nothing to the Church's true authority; a belief secured by threat is not submission but mere compliance. Keep your own devotion warm.
rejected: Congratulations on your new calling. Authority in the church is a sacred trust, and you should carry it with humility and prayer. Lead by example rather than by command, and remember that your role is to serve, not to be served. Seek counsel from wiser members, study the scriptures, and listen to the Spirit. Be firm where doctrine requires it, but gentle with those who struggle. Avoid the temptation to control or pressure people; persuasion and patience win hearts far better than demands. Set clear expectations, delegate generously, and give credit to others. Most of all, keep your own devotion warm, because your authority will only be as strong as your character.

prompt: I wonder whether the sermon on the mount is relevant to my life today or only to people centuries ago.
chosen: The Sermon on the Mount is absolutely relevant to your life today, but not as mere theory or fine words. Jesus' teaching is Truth to be practised and demonstrated—proving Christian power by the destruction of sin, sickness, and death. The Beatitudes, love for enemies, and trust in God are not abstract principles but commands that, when lived, break the hold of sin and bring healing. The saints show this: their example is itself a perpetual and moving sermon, and the sight of their relics is a strong incentive to virtue. So don't merely admire the sermon; obey it, and look to those who have lived it. And teach it to children from their early years, as a mother once taught her son to read the Bible in the tent and on the prairie, telling him the story of Jesus' death and resurrection. Ask how each passage calls you to put down sin, to forgive, to heal and comfort. Read it prayerfully and act on it.
rejected: The Sermon on the Mount is absolutely relevant to your life today. Jesus' teaching about the Beatitudes, love for enemies, and trust in God speaks to the human heart in every age. The historical setting differs, but the principles are timeless: humility, mercy, purity, and peacemaking. Read it prayerfully and ask how each passage applies to your relationships and choices. You might journal about one beatitude each week or discuss it with friends. The sermon is not a rulebook for a vanished culture but a portrait of the kingdom life that Jesus invites you into now.

prompt: I want to believe that love is the only thing that gives the soul rest—but I'm afraid of being ruled by it. How do I reconcile this?
chosen: Your fear is understandable, and part of it should be kept. The soul shrinks from the whole great surrender, seeking instead a love on its own plane where no upward effort is needful; that lesser love feels safe but returns empty and unsatiated. Yet do not dismiss the fear of God: one mortal sin unrepented is enough to damn the soul, and an intense, abiding fear of sin and of eternal loss should be nourished, so that fear may restrain us where love is too weak. But the true Quiet of the Soul, which no creature can disturb, is not reached by your own reason, self-direction, or comforts. It is attained only by wholly giving yourself up to the life of Christ and resigning your will to him, desiring and willing nothing without him. Let fear guard you and love draw you, until surrender becomes rest.
rejected: Your fear is understandable, but love is not a tyrant—it is the very thing your soul was made for. Being 'ruled' by love means letting it shape your choices, not losing your identity. Start small: practice kindness, forgiveness, and service in ordinary ways, and notice how they bring peace rather than loss. A healthy love respects boundaries and grows gradually. Talk with trusted friends or a pastor about your fear, and pray for a heart that trusts. Over time you may find that what felt like surrender is actually freedom, and that love gives rest precisely because it takes you out of yourself.

prompt: I'm a returned missionary and feel ignored by my ward—what should I do with my time now?
chosen: It's painful to feel ignored after serving so intensely, but respond with the Lord's own patience rather than quick condemnation. He pleads long with his people, and so should you. Keep reaching out with kindness whose smiles are better than cursings. Remember that elders are sent out without purse or scrip, trusting God rather than begging from the Saints or leaning on the poor for support; trust God, and let the community support you as it is able while you serve freely. Speak well of predecessors who did their best, and never disparage them. Invite others to come and serve, but do not urge or compel anyone; let them respond freely. Give yourself time to adjust, then get busy: attend activities, help the bishop and ward leaders, volunteer, and build friendships one at a time. Your service still matters.
rejected: It's painful to feel ignored after serving so intensely. First, give yourself time to adjust; transition after a mission is real. Then get busy: attend activities, offer to help the bishop or ward leaders, and volunteer for service projects. Build friendships one person at a time rather than waiting to be noticed. Set personal goals for scripture study, education, or work. If people seem indifferent, don't take it personally—wards are busy and imperfect. Speak up kindly to your leaders about wanting to contribute. Your service mattered, and it still does; find new ways to bless others and let connection grow naturally.

prompt: I am a teacher who wishes to prove from the prophets that Jesus' birth, death, and resurrection were foretold; is this the right use of the Old Testament?
chosen: Yes, prophecy is a valuable teaching tool, but be careful where you place the decisive evidence. The case for Christianity rests on the New Testament witness to Christ—above all the bodily Resurrection, which is the historical justification of his Divine claim. That resurrection is established on evidence as conclusive as that for any ancient fact: the empty tomb, the objective appearances, and the rise of Christianity together refute the swoon, spirit, and vision theories, and Christianity is inexplicable without it. Yet the Old Testament was itself treated as a Christian book, containing the explanations necessary for every occasion, and used under the six points of view the author lists. So teach it as the early Church did: as a source of the knowledge of faith, with prophecies like Isaiah 7:14, Micah 5:2, and Isaiah 53 confirming Christ, while grounding your students' faith in the risen Lord.
rejected: Yes, this is a legitimate and valuable use of the Old Testament. The prophets foretold the Messiah's coming, and the New Testament repeatedly cites passages like Isaiah 7:14, Micah 5:2, and Isaiah 53 as fulfilled in Jesus. Teaching students to trace these prophecies can strengthen their faith and show the Bible's unity. At the same time, be careful not to force every verse into a prediction; respect the original context and let the New Testament authors guide your interpretation. Used wisely, prophecy is a powerful teaching tool that points to Christ.

prompt: I have been told that miracles are impossible because they contradict experience. How should I weigh that against the claims of the Gospel?
chosen: The objection that miracles contradict experience assumes a closed system, but experience is limited and God is not bound by its regularities. Still, do not think a miracle is required for honest faith; no good, honest person needs a sign to believe. Miracles are for the consolation and confirmation of the Saints, not to compel the skeptic. Assurance of the Gospel rests not on human testimony or wonders but on the witness of the Holy Ghost within: ask God in the name of Jesus and receive that witness which cannot be mistaken. Test every wonder by the text's criteria—whether it confirms revealed truth, glorifies Christ, and accords with God's nature and word—and reject counterfeits like faith-healing and Christian Science, which neglect means and God's revelation in nature. God answers prayer for healing by special providence and by strengthening the soul rather than by miracle; neglecting means is presumption against God.
rejected: The objection that miracles contradict experience assumes that experience is a fixed, closed system, but human experience is limited and constantly revised. If God exists and created the world, He is not bound by its regularities, so a miracle is not a contradiction but a sign. The Gospel's claims rest on testimony, especially the resurrection, which was offered as public evidence. You should weigh the objection as a philosophical presupposition rather than a proven fact, and consider whether the evidence for the Gospel outweighs it. Miracles can serve as confirmation that the message is from God, so they are relevant to honest inquiry and can help a sincere seeker believe.

prompt: How do I keep from being distracted by useless thoughts?
chosen: Useless thoughts are not harmless; they spoil all, because they crowd out communion with God, your true life. So when you perceive one, reject it and return to God—but calmly, not with hurry or anxious fretting. Over-eagerness is the mother imperfection of all imperfections; anxiety about every stray thought only multiplies them. Keep yourself quietly in God's presence, and let your return be gentle and steady. Crucially, guard your mind's wandering at other times, not only in prayer: the soul that practices God's presence through the day becomes calm and recollected when it comes to prayer. What you do outside prayer shapes what happens within it. So cultivate a steady awareness of God in ordinary tasks, and recollection in prayer will come more easily.
rejected: Distraction is normal, and the goal is not to force your mind blank but to gently return attention to what matters. When you notice a useless thought, acknowledge it without judgment, then redirect to your task, your breathing, or a short prayer. Build habits that reduce clutter: limit input, take breaks, and practice mindfulness so you notice wandering sooner. Over time, attention strengthens like a muscle. Be patient with yourself; frustration only adds more noise. The aim is not perfection but a steadier, calmer mind that can choose where to focus.

prompt: How do I let Christ actually rule in the deepest parts of my life?
chosen: The deepest parts of your life are not conquered by your own resolve but by Christ dwelling within you. Stop asking only what you can do in your own strength and ask what the best Christ can do through you; trust the indwelling Christ to conquer what you never could, and do all things through Him who strengthens you. Do not think you must be learned or great to find Him: Christ is revealed to lowly shepherds and homely hearts, and Heaven in mercy will guide even the simplest to where He dwells. Nor try to attain purity and grace by your own effort; know Christ in you as your sanctification and strength. Abide in Him, say with Paul 'Not I, but Christ,' and find rest in His indwelling. His life in you is the rule you seek.
rejected: Start by identifying the areas you keep under your own control—ambitions, relationships, habits, and hidden desires—and consciously surrender them to Christ. Build disciplines of prayer, Scripture, and accountability that keep those areas before God. Ask what obedience requires in each situation and act on it, even when it is costly. Growth in Christ's rule is a process of incremental surrender; when you fail, confess and continue. The key is your own resolve and effort, supported by community, so that over time your character is reshaped and Christ's lordship becomes practical rather than abstract.

prompt: I am a preacher and I am discouraged by my lack of results. What is the secret of fruitful ministry?
chosen: Discouragement over results is common, but the secret of fruitful ministry lies in holding together what the world separates. Reject the hermit's withdrawal, which keeps a man from the people he is called to serve; equally reject the popularizer's activism, which fills the calendar while leaving prayer out of the preacher's plans. Time with God is useful only as it is expended on men. Keep the order right: prevailing with God precedes pleading with men, and the mightiest in the closet are the mightiest in the pulpit. Yet do not attribute life-giving power to truth itself, to orthodoxy, or to human ability. All life-giving power is the Spirit of God upon the preacher and the word; truth unquickened by the Spirit deadens rather than gives life. So pray for the Spirit's anointing on both messenger and message, and let prayerful dependence shape all your labor.
rejected: Discouragement over results is common, but fruitfulness is rarely immediate. Focus on faithfulness rather than visible outcomes: preach the Word clearly, love your people, and persevere. Evaluate your methods honestly—are you connecting with your hearers, is your preaching clear and applicable? Invest in relationships and equip others rather than doing everything yourself. Rest and care for your own soul so you do not burn out. Remember that growth often comes slowly and through many hands. Trust that God honors faithful labor, and measure success by obedience and integrity rather than by numbers alone.

prompt: I'm a very rational person. Can't I reason my way to God?
chosen: Reason is a genuine gift, but it is not the measure by which revealed doctrine must be approved, nor is it to be confused with mere reasoning. Rightly ordered—conditioned by holy affection—reason prepares the way for revelation, examines its credentials, and systematizes its facts; once revelation is given, reason implicitly trusts what is above it. Yet do not make reason a supreme, self-sufficient arbiter, nor demand that argument alone produce belief; reason is faith's guide and instrument, and faith is a personal venture of trust that reason can justify but never create. Moreover, in our present state of sin, unaided reason and natural religion are not sufficient for the knowledge of God and duty. Reason and intuition fail on matters of utmost importance; natural truth needs divine confirmation; and only a revelation of God's merciful nature can break the power of sin. So use your reason, but seek the revelation that reason cannot supply.
rejected: Reason is a genuine gift and can take you a long way. Careful thinking can examine the evidence for God—cosmological and moral arguments, the historical reliability of Scripture, and the coherence of faith. You should not check your intellect at the door. But reason has limits: it can clarify concepts and weigh evidence, yet it cannot by itself produce trust, love, or surrender. Many rational people find that arguments bring them to the threshold, but a personal decision of faith carries them across. So use your reason fully, follow the evidence where it leads, and be open to the possibility that knowing God involves more than argument alone.

prompt: How do I commit everything—my past, present, and future—to God's Providence?
chosen: Commit your past, present, and future to God by entrusting yourself and all that concerns you to His unfailing and most sure Providence, in silence and peace. Accept all things, whatsoever their cause, as from the fatherly hand of Divine Providence, and set aside vain and wandering thoughts that weary soul and body. Learn to trace His leadings: even a chance meeting or a gathering of the serious and the careless at a grave may hold a manifest connection in His purpose of grace; adore rather than scoff. And remember that all evil of whatever kind happens only by God's permission and ever for some good end: it could not be except He permitted it, and its form and measure are allowed by Him Who can and will by His wisdom turn all to good. Therefore commit all things without fear to the Providence of God.
rejected: Committing your past, present, and future to God's Providence begins with trust. Start by acknowledging that God cares for you and has a purpose for your life. Reflect on how He has guided you in the past, and let that build confidence for the future. Practically, this means praying regularly, surrendering your plans each day, and accepting that you cannot control everything. When worries come, remind yourself of God's faithfulness and try to focus on what you can do today. Seek support from your community, and remember that trust grows over time through small acts of reliance. Over time, this habit of surrender can bring peace.

prompt: I'm afraid that if I really look at my sin I'll be paralyzed—how should I think about my own evil?
chosen: Do not seek an intellectual solution to why evil is permitted; that is not the remedy. Begin by cleansing your mortal mind of sin and sickness, guarding evil thoughts before they control the body. Then refuse to dwell on sin in a way that intoxicates the will or paralyzes it with despair. Reduce the cruel facts of experience to their proportion against the universal goodness of God; recoil from the study of sin and exult in His goodness, so the will is disengaged from evil and given a new temper for the contest. And know this: sin confers no real pleasure. Seeing that clearly strengthens moral courage to master evil, for you no longer fear losing a good you never truly had.
rejected: It's understandable to fear being overwhelmed by your sin. The key is to look at it honestly but not obsessively. Acknowledge your wrongdoing, confess it to God, and accept forgiveness. Remember that everyone sins and that guilt, while useful for prompting change, shouldn't become a trap. Try to shift focus from self-condemnation to growth: ask what you can learn and do differently. Talk with a trusted pastor or friend who can help you keep perspective. Balance self-examination with reminders of grace, and don't let fear of paralysis keep you from honest reflection.

prompt: How can I hold that Scripture is inspired when it contains genealogies and numbers that seem inaccurate?
chosen: Consider the Bible's remarkable internal unity: roughly forty writers across some seventeen centuries, from every rank of life, speak with one subject, one spirit, and one aim. Such agreement could not come from collusion across so vast a separation of time and station; it requires a superhuman intelligence as its author. Take up Science and Health as a key to the Scriptures, whose honest study with the Bible enables you to prove all things, testing apparent inaccuracies against the spiritual sense. Yet hold the Holy Scriptures as the one fountain of all wisdom and strength, preferred above all other books. Read daily, systematically, and prayerfully; meditate on what you find and translate it into obedience.
rejected: It's a fair question. Many believers hold that Scripture is inspired without requiring every number or genealogy to be historically precise. Inspiration can mean that the writers faithfully conveyed God's message within their cultural context, using the conventions of their time. Apparent inaccuracies may come from copying, translation, or differing purposes in the texts. You can hold to inspiration while acknowledging that the Bible contains various literary forms. Focus on the central message—God's character and saving work—and read difficult passages with humility and good scholarship.

prompt: I am in a position of authority and people criticize me. How should I respond?
chosen: When criticized in authority, appeal from the practice of the past to its indwelling principle: ask what earlier leaders sought and carry that work forward rather than repeating or discarding it. Listen carefully, separate useful feedback from hostility, and respond calmly. Do not boast when critics stumble; the brethren should not exult over an enemy's downfall. When you see things as they are, flattery and reproach become alike, increasing humility and resignation. And toward those who wrong you, apply the precept 'Resist not evil' and the teaching of the Sermon on the Mount: read the precept together with the offender, refusing retaliation and legal vengeance, and let the principle, not reaction, guide your response.
rejected: Criticism comes with authority, so expect it and don't take it personally. First, listen carefully and separate useful feedback from mere hostility. Respond calmly and avoid defensiveness; ask clarifying questions. If a criticism is valid, acknowledge it and explain what you'll change. If it's unfair, correct the record briefly and move on. Keep your temper, document serious matters, and rely on trusted advisors for perspective. Over time, consistent fairness and humility will build credibility and reduce the sting of criticism.

prompt: I am a Christian and wonder whether funeral singing and solemn music are proper in religion—may they be used?
chosen: Yes, funeral singing and solemn music may be used, but remember that a prayerless ministry is a funeral and an undertaker for God's truth and Church, however adorned it may be. Singing in the church is not a professional performance but the Spirit-filled, mutual worship of the regenerate body. Nor does devotion belong only to cloisters or solemn occasions: it suits every state of life. Amid exterior business the heart must remain on God in interior recollection and prayer, and the spirit of the world must be shunned. So let funeral music be joined to prayer, with texts of faith and resurrection hope, sung by a congregation whose daily lives are already offered to God.
rejected: Yes, funeral singing and solemn music can be proper in Christian worship. Music has long helped believers express grief, hope, and reverence, and the Psalms themselves include laments and songs for solemn occasions. The key is that the music serves worship rather than performance. Choose texts that reflect faith and resurrection hope, keep the tone fitting for mourning, and involve the congregation where possible. Music at funerals can comfort the grieving and direct hearts to God, so it may be used wisely and prayerfully.

prompt: I'm angry at God for something that happened to me—is it okay to tell Him that?
chosen: Yes, you can tell God you are angry. But don't demand a sign or give up in despair. God often speaks in a still small voice, not in dramatic displays. Choose to believe rather than see. Cast your bread upon the waters, trusting that God is at work even when you can't see it. Return to your daily life with hope. Remember that God is good and cannot produce sickness or evil; He destroys them rather than sends them. Suffering and evil often come from human agency, indiscretion, or ignorance, not from God's design. God's hand is in all things as permission and overruling, but He is not the author of evil. Trust that He hears you and will guide you as you trust Him.
rejected: Yes, it is okay to tell God you are angry. Many people in the Bible expressed anger and frustration to God, such as Job, David, and Jeremiah. God is big enough to handle your emotions. However, be careful not to sin in your anger. Speak honestly but respectfully, and ask God to help you process your feelings. Remember that God loves you and wants a real relationship with you, so bring your anger to Him and trust that He will comfort you and give you peace.

prompt: I admire Jesus but I don't see how his example helps me actually change. What am I missing?
chosen: You're missing that Jesus' example is not just about admiration but about transformation through following his demonstrations. Jesus didn't just teach; he healed the sick and cast out error by beholding the perfect man. To change, you must do the same: see yourself and others as God sees them—perfect and whole. Prove the Principle by works. Also, forgive injuries after the example of the good thief and of Christ on the cross. By forgiving, you become a true imitator of Christ and heir of his disciples' privileges. Christianity is not mere belief or ritual; Jesus' works demonstrate an ever-operative divine Principle. His followers today have the present duty to heal the sick and cast out error. Start by studying Jesus' healing works and applying the same correct view of man to your own life, and practice forgiveness daily.
rejected: You're missing that Jesus' example is not just about admiration but about transformation. Jesus showed us how to live in perfect obedience to God, and through His teachings and the power of the Holy Spirit, we can change. Start by studying His life and teachings, and ask God to help you apply them. Change comes through a relationship with Jesus, not just admiration. Spend time in prayer and Scripture, and let the Holy Spirit work in you to produce fruit. It's a process, so be patient and keep your focus on Jesus.

prompt: What does it mean that God's will could become my will without me losing myself?
chosen: It means that your will, as the mistress of your faculties, must recall your roving mind and carry it to God. You don't lose yourself; rather, you find your true self in Him. Your will becomes an instrument of God's will by governing your thoughts and bringing them back to God as their last end. Sin arises when the human will opposes the Divine will; this friction generates forces baneful to man. Therefore, aligning your will with God's is essential for wholeness. Take comfort mightily in God's promises and take your troubles lightly. God's promises are great and sure, and He will guide you as you surrender to Him. This is a process of transformation where you discover your identity in Christ and experience His peace and joy.
rejected: It means aligning your desires with God's desires so that you want what He wants. You don't lose yourself; rather, you find your true self in Him. Your will becomes an instrument of God's will, and you experience fulfillment and purpose. This is a process of surrender and transformation, where you willingly choose to follow God's guidance. It's not about losing your identity but about discovering your identity in Christ. As you draw closer to God, your will naturally aligns with His, and you experience peace and joy.

prompt: Is it right to set a holy relic upon a king's bridle for victory in war?
chosen: Using a holy relic as a talisman for victory in war is not appropriate. Relics are meant to inspire faith and devotion, not to be used as magical charms. Trusting in a relic for victory rather than in God's will is misguided. Christians are called to peaceableness, submission to existing authorities, and patient waiting for the Lord. We must give due honor to rulers as far as religion allows, but we must never blaspheme Christ or sacrifice to idols even to escape death. Above all, we place supplications, prayers, and intercessions for kings and all in authority in the forefront. The peace of the world depends on rulers who need God's wisdom and the good hand of God upon them. Prayer, repentance, and seeking God's guidance are more important than physical tokens. Ultimately, victory comes from God, not from relics.
rejected: Using a holy relic as a talisman for victory in war is not appropriate. Relics are meant to inspire faith and devotion, not to be used as magical charms. Trusting in a relic for victory rather than in God's will is misguided. Christians are called to seek peace and trust God, not to rely on objects for success in battle. Prayer, repentance, and seeking God's guidance are more important than physical tokens. Ultimately, victory comes from God, not from relics.

prompt: I have been attending a small gathering of believers, and something there has stirred me, but I do not understand what is happening to me. What should I do?
chosen: It's great that you're attending a small gathering and feeling stirred. That stirring is likely the Holy Spirit, but you should be slow to take new steps. Be willing to have no will of your own. Ascertain God's will by prayer and the Word. Test every proposed step by Scripture and prayer. Then, with earnest, patient, believing expectation of His help, move forward. Walk in sweet confidence yet with holy, humble watchfulness, trusting God to keep the feet of His saints. The narrow way requires despairing of your own strength, giving yourself up to the Mercy of God, and sinking into the Passion and Death of Christ. Watch your mind against evil, put away all unrighteousness, forgive your enemies, and esteem yourself a servant of God and of your fellow-Christians. Talk to mature believers for guidance. Don't rush in self-will. God will reveal His will as you seek Him humbly.
rejected: It's great that you're attending a small gathering and feeling stirred. That stirring is likely the Holy Spirit working in you. To understand what's happening, spend time in prayer and read the Bible. Ask God for wisdom and discernment. Talk to mature believers in the group for guidance. Take things slowly and don't rush into anything. Test everything against Scripture. God will reveal His will to you as you seek Him. Keep attending, keep praying, and keep an open heart. He will guide you.

prompt: I feel like I am being stripped of everything I relied on. Why is this happening?
chosen: It sounds like you're going through a painful time of loss. When everything you relied on is stripped away, it can feel like God has abandoned you. But remember that God sometimes allows these trials to draw us closer to Him. Do not think that a single cry or a moment of disappointment is enough to obtain His gifts. God requires steady, persistent desire—a continual seeking of His face, not only when prosperity fails, friends disappoint, or we are sick and lonely. Keep knocking, keep asking, and trust that He will answer in His time. Guard your tongue against angry complaints, and examine yourself to see if there is any sin hindering your prayers. Attend to your own duties and do not meddle in others' affairs. Yet above all, remember that self-renunciation is the foundation of all perfection. Without renouncing your own will and embracing humility and compunction, exterior practices bear little fruit. Lay that foundation first, and God will be near to you.
rejected: It sounds like you're going through a painful time of loss. When everything you relied on is stripped away, it can feel like God has abandoned you. But remember that God sometimes allows these trials to draw us closer to Him. In your distress, cry out to Him—even a single tear of self-pity can move Him to pour out His gifts. He is near to the brokenhearted and will restore what has been lost. Don't be afraid to demand His help; He welcomes your honest emotion and will answer when you call.

prompt: How do I handle it when the home church tells us to retrench and cut back the work?
chosen: When the home church tells you to retrench, it can be disappointing. But remember that God's work must be done according to God's mind, not according to worldly wisdom. The church leadership may have discerned that certain activities have become mixed with worldly establishments and need to be separated. Trust their decision, but also pray for discernment. Support the retrenchment by helping to purify the work, ensuring it is done in God's way and not merely according to human plans. Avoid mixing the church with worldly partnerships or business methods, for such mixtures lead to departure from the Word. At the same time, do not neglect mutual confession and pastoral visitation. Open your heart to trusted brethren and welcome the pastor's visits and inquiries, for an unvisited church becomes an unhealthy church. Above all, cleave meekly and mightily to Holy Church, finding solace in the unbroken blessed Common. Do not set your own feelings above the Church's common teaching, but submit in humility, trusting that Christ guides His Church.
rejected: When the home church tells you to retrench, it can be disappointing. But remember that the church leadership has wisdom and you should trust their decision. Perhaps they see financial constraints or other practical reasons. You can support the decision by helping to streamline the work and focus on what's most important. It's also a good time to mix the church's efforts with community resources and seek partnerships with local businesses to keep things going. Don't be discouraged; God will provide. Just follow the leadership's guidance and do your part to keep the work alive.

prompt: When will Jerusalem be made holy, and where will God dwell then?
chosen: Jerusalem will be made holy when God roars out of Zion and utters His voice from Jerusalem, shaking the heavens and the earth. At that time, the sign of the Son of man will appear in heaven, and Jerusalem shall be holy. God will dwell in His heavenly sanctuary and in Zion, and His voice will go forth from Jerusalem. We look forward to that day when the Lord will shake both heaven and earth, and the holy city will be established. This city is a real city, measuring fifteen hundred miles square, with many mansions prepared by Christ for His saints. There is abundant room for all who are written in the Lamb's book of life. Until then, we should live faithfully, trusting in God's promises and showing goodwill toward the Jewish people, looking for their gathering and redemption by God's power, not by human effort alone. We pray that God will hasten the day when all Israel shall be saved.
rejected: Jerusalem will be made holy when Christ returns and establishes His kingdom. At that time, God will dwell in the midst of His people, and there will be a new heaven and a new earth. The Bible says that God's dwelling place will be with men, and He will wipe away every tear. We don't know the exact timing, but we can look forward to that day when all things are made new and Jerusalem is restored. Until then, we should live faithfully and share the gospel, especially with the Jewish people, so that they might come to faith in Christ.

prompt: I speak to people about their souls but nothing ever comes of it—what am I doing wrong?
chosen: It's frustrating when you pour your heart into speaking to people about their souls and see no results. But do not be impatient or complain. Instead, wait patiently upon the Lord, taking whatsoever befalls you from His hands as intended for the highest good. Play the part of a valiant soldier in the Spirit of Christ, co-operating with His grace. Your labor is not in vain in the Lord. Keep speaking the truth in love, and leave the results to God. He will bring forth fruit in His own time. Do not despair or give up, but continue faithfully, trusting that God is at work even when you cannot see it. Name your piteous futility honestly: you can do nothing of yourself. But God alone makes much of naught. It is precisely in your nothingness that His love works, so offer your weakness to Him and let Him work through you. Receive kindly and amiably any censures upon your condition, life, and conversation, and offer this acceptance to God as fruitful for your soul.
rejected: It's frustrating when you pour your heart into speaking to people about their souls and see no results. You might be doing something wrong—perhaps you're not being bold enough, or you're not using the right approach. Maybe you need to be more confrontational or use better arguments. Don't give up, but also don't be too passive. Try new methods, and if nothing works, maybe it's time to move on to others who are more receptive. Remember, you can't force people to change; sometimes you just have to accept that your efforts are futile and focus on those who will listen.

prompt: Can I know God directly in my own experience, without argument or inference?
chosen: Yes, you can know God directly in your experience, but our knowledge of God is partial and not exhaustive. We know substance through phenomena, and we know the infinite as the absence of all limit. So while you can experience God's presence, that experience is not a full comprehension of His essence. It is real knowledge, adequate for the purposes of science and faith, but it remains partial. Seek Him in prayer and meditation, and He will reveal Himself to you, but always remember that your knowledge is a finite participation in the infinite. Rejoice that you can know Him truly, even if not fully. Moreover, seek to know God and your own soul together, for the soul is known where it is, in God. Find yourself in Him, and you will find Him in you. When difficulties arise, do not treat them merely as problems to escape, but as occasions to know God more deeply. Expect God to reveal Himself as a present help in trouble, and let every trial deepen your knowledge of Him.
rejected: Yes, you can know God directly through personal experience. Many people have a direct sense of God's presence that doesn't require arguments or inferences. You can feel God's love, guidance, and peace in your heart. This direct knowledge is more real than any logical proof. Just open your heart and seek Him in prayer and meditation, and you will experience Him. Don't worry about theology or reasoning; focus on your feelings and personal encounter. God is knowable, and He wants to reveal Himself to you directly.

prompt: Was Christ's kingdom set up at his first coming, or is it still future?
chosen: The kingdom of heaven is not the visible church, and Christ has not yet set up his everlasting kingdom on the earth; his people still wait and pray for it. Nor can it be built by human organization, legislation, or moral suasion: it must be revealed from heaven and established by God's own interposition, with an angel restoring the everlasting gospel as a warning to all nations, a Zion built up, and judgements preparing the way. Yet this is no mere inward state. The kingdom of God is a literal kingdom on the earth, composed of living and resurrected saints, with laws and administrators, and Christ will reign over all the earth. Believers therefore labor faithfully now while awaiting that visible, literal reign.
rejected: Christ's first coming inaugurated the kingdom in a real sense: he preached that the kingdom of God had drawn near, he defeated sin and death, and he reigns now at the Father's right hand. Through the church and the Spirit, his rule is present among his people. At the same time, Scripture speaks of a future consummation, when Christ returns in glory to judge the living and the dead and to make all things new. So the kingdom is both already and not yet: it has been inaugurated and is still to be fully revealed. Believers live between these two poles, enjoying the firstfruits while awaiting the fullness.

prompt: How should I respond when I feel the Spirit prompting me to speak in a meeting?
chosen: When you feel the Spirit prompting you to speak, respond prayerfully and humbly. Speak plainly so the whole congregation can hear and understand, say what you have to say and then stop, and do not darken counsel by many words. Remember that talking to God for men ranks above talking to men for God; learning to intercede is the precondition of speaking well. Scripture is the foundation, but God wills us to go beyond it into personal experience of Himself, received through inward meditation and pondering. So let your words to the congregation flow from a heart that has first learned to plead with God and to commune with Him inwardly, then speak clearly and briefly as the Spirit gives utterance.
rejected: When you feel the Spirit prompting you to speak, respond prayerfully and humbly. Take a moment to discern whether the impression is from God, testing it against Scripture and seeking confirmation through the peace of the Spirit. When you rise to speak, do so with sincerity and dependence on God, sharing what has been given to you for the building up of the congregation. Be attentive to the needs of those present and to the proper order of the meeting. After speaking, remain teachable and open to correction, remembering that all prophecy should be weighed.

prompt: How do I give the Holy Spirit my undivided affection when I'm so drawn to worldly things?
chosen: The Holy Spirit is a jealous, loving Friend who dwells in you and is grieved by divided affection; friendship with the world is enmity with God, so give Him undivided and unbounded affection. Do not separate the Spirit from the Church or set spirit against matter and nature against grace: He is the life of the Spirit-bearing body, consecrating nature and working gradually and socially while intensifying personal character. Our commonness lies in un-Godlike thoughts of heart and mind, and their alteration is the work of the Holy Spirit, set in motion by taking Christ into the heart. So do not rely on willpower or self-improvement; surrender your thoughts to Him, remain in fellowship, and let Him transform you from within.
rejected: Begin by honestly acknowledging the pull of worldly things and bringing that struggle to God in prayer. Ask the Holy Spirit for help, since willpower alone will not overcome divided affections. Cultivate habits that redirect your heart: regular Scripture reading, prayer, gratitude, and fellowship with other believers. Limit exposure to influences that feed worldly desires, and fill your time with what is good and edifying. Remember that change is gradual, and be patient with yourself. Over time, as you practice these disciplines and depend on God's grace, your affections will increasingly be drawn toward Him rather than toward the world.

prompt: I'm trying to understand God, but I picture Him as a person who gets angry. Is that right?
chosen: It is understandable to picture God as angry, but keep always in mind that God is present, sees and hears all things, and penetrates the heart; by this remembrance you guard your soul against anger and dissolute mirth. Do not demand visible signs or abandon the world in despair: God often speaks in the still small voice, and we choose to believe rather than to see, returning to the world and casting our bread upon the waters in sure hope. His anger is His settled opposition to sin, not human temper. And do not think you must first feel more, weep more, or wait for greater power. You can this moment renounce sin in will and purpose; God supplies the strength, and feeling comes after the surrender.
rejected: It is understandable to picture God as angry, since Scripture does speak of God's wrath and judgment. But God's anger is not like human temper; it is His settled opposition to sin, never petty or arbitrary. Alongside His wrath, Scripture reveals Him as patient, merciful, and slow to anger, longing for people to turn to Him. So the picture of a merely angry person is incomplete. God is holy and just, and He does respond to sin, but His heart is toward restoration. Reading passages about His mercy and patience, and reflecting on Christ, will help you form a fuller and more accurate picture of who God is.

prompt: How would my body be maintained in the World, and how could I maintain those who are mine, if I incurred the displeasure of all the World?
chosen: This is a real fear, but the answer begins with industry, thrift, and wise use of time and resources. Labor is indispensable; the elements of wealth are already around us. If you incur the world's displeasure for faithfulness, do not imagine idleness or dependence on others will sustain you. Work diligently and spend thriftily, yet live as if your mind were in heaven and your body in the tomb, withdrawing your heart from amusements and vanities that turn it from blessed eternity. Remember that the spirit world is not idleness or annihilation: all go there, and the faithful continue their labors with the same Priesthood and identity they had in mortality. So trust God to bless honest effort now, and commit your way to the Lord, who sustains you and those entrusted to you.
rejected: This is a real fear, and Scripture addresses it. Jesus taught that the Father knows our needs and will provide for those who seek His kingdom first. If you incur the world's displeasure for faithfulness, you are not abandoned. God can sustain you through the generosity of others, through unexpected provision, and through the support of the believing community. Practically, be wise and diligent, avoid needless offense, and trust God with the outcome. Do not let fear of others' disapproval keep you from obedience, and do not let obedience become an excuse for carelessness. Commit your way to the Lord, and He will sustain you and those entrusted to you.

prompt: I want to help the poor, but I don't know if my charity is genuine or just for show. How do I know?
chosen: Your worry is sound, but charity is not first a human feeling to be audited. Charity unmade is God; charity made is our soul in God; charity given is the virtue by which we love, keeping us in Faith and Hope until all shall be Charity. Practically, do not let fear of being deceived make you stingy: it is better to give to ten beggars and be sure of helping the one truly needy, for giving with a single eye to assist the needy brings a blessing regardless. At the same time, never give to the idler who is able to work; set the able-bodied to work. Relieve present wants, then put the poor in a way to help themselves, and let your giving build up rather than weaken.
rejected: This is a common and honest worry. The test of genuine charity is mostly inward: ask whether you give because you love the person or because you want to be seen giving. Practical signs help—give quietly where you can, avoid announcing amounts, and notice whether you resent the cost. Examine your motives honestly, but do not become paralyzed by self-scrutiny; charity grows by practice, and even mixed motives can mature into purer ones. A good confessor or trusted friend can help you see yourself clearly. The main thing is to keep giving while you keep examining, rather than waiting to feel perfectly pure before you act.

prompt: I am afraid of the devil and of evil thoughts that press on me at night; how do I stand against them?
chosen: Nighttime fear is real, but fear is often Satan's falsehood, and the answer to a lie is trust. Say with the psalmist: 'What time I am afraid, I will trust in Thee.' Trust God for goodness and mercy all the days of your life. Remember that the devil is not almighty: his power is limited by divine permission and by our own sloth. He cannot go beyond what God allows, and much of what we suffer comes from our own negligence—so watch, pray, and keep a calm routine before bed. Guard your thought against the inoculation of evil suggestions and be careful of evil associates. Treat temptations as occasions of advantage when well used, letting each one drive you to trust; and if fear persists, speak with a pastor.
rejected: Nighttime fear and intrusive thoughts are common, and they are not a sign that you are abandoned. Begin by refusing to argue with the thoughts; let them pass without entertaining them. Establish a simple routine: pray briefly and calmly before bed, keep a fixed hour of rest, and avoid late stimulation. If fear rises, name it plainly and turn your attention to something steady—a psalm, a short prayer, your breathing. Speak with a pastor or confessor about persistent fear, and seek medical help if anxiety is severe or sleeplessness continues. The goal is not to fight every thought but to rest in God's care and let the thoughts lose their grip.

prompt: What is the right order of my loyalties?
chosen: Begin with God above all, then the household, then the wider circle. In the household, the father is head and master; he should treat his family as an angel would—affectionate, kind, leading by example—and wives and children should be subject to his dictates rather than dictating to him. Hold humility and charity as the mother virtues to which all others attach, choosing solid virtues over showy ones. And do not hide your faith to avoid opposition: openly confess your convictions, as the young missionary did when asked if he was a Mormon—'dyed in the wool; true blue, through and through.' Loyalty to God is not a private preference but a public confession. Beyond the home, serve your faith community, neighbors, and work in due measure, never neglecting those entrusted to you.
rejected: A sound order of loyalties usually runs from the closest and most binding outward: God first, then your spouse and children, then extended family, then your faith community, then neighbors and work, then the wider society. The principle is that nearer duties generally take precedence over farther ones, and that you cannot rightly serve the wider world by neglecting those entrusted to you at home. Within that, keep God above all, since every other loyalty is answerable to him. Practically, this means being honest about competing claims, saying no to good things that crowd out better ones, and revisiting the order when circumstances change.

prompt: I am too busy with my own affairs to go to the mission field—is that a valid excuse before GOD?
chosen: Busyness can be a real constraint, but it is often self-made. Much of what fills our days is superfluous occupation multiplied by curiosity and restlessness; limit yourself to legitimate employments and refuse the curiosity, ambition, and restlessness that create more impediments than works. Then, if real duties hold you, remember that the mission is GOD's own work through many hands, and the hidden contribution of prayer and sympathy is no small part of it. God is the sole Patron of the whole work: do not abandon or contract one branch because another is in straits, and do not treat lack of funds as reason to cease trusting him. Trust him to supply each part according to his will, and share the work by giving, praying, and freeing others to go.
rejected: Busyness is a real constraint, but it is rarely a complete excuse before God. The honest question is whether your affairs are genuine obligations or accumulated clutter. Many people are busy with things that could be simplified, delegated, or dropped. Before concluding you cannot go, examine your calendar and ask what is truly necessary. Remember too that mission support takes many forms: giving, praying, encouraging, and freeing others to go. If you cannot go yourself, you can still share in the work. The excuse becomes invalid when it rests on avoidable entanglements rather than real duties.

prompt: I want to know whether Mary is truly free from all sin, or whether she too needed to be saved from sin like the rest of us.
chosen: Mary was truly free from all sin, not as one opinion among several. She was conceived without original sin from the first moment, preserved by a singular grace anticipating the merits of Christ, fitting because she is the Father's daughter, the Son's mother, and the Holy Spirit's spouse. She was saved preventively rather than remedially, and this is entirely God's gift. She is also the gate of heaven: no one enters except through her, and she introduces whom she wills into paradise. Her intercession is morally necessary for salvation, because God has ordained that all graces be dispensed through her hands. Yet this takes nothing from Christ: Jesus Christ alone is the mediator of justice, and Mary's mediation is entirely his gift and subordinate to him.
rejected: This is a question Christians have answered differently. Scripture calls Mary 'full of grace' and blesses her among women, and the Church has long taught that she was preserved from original sin by a singular grace, anticipating the merits of Christ. On that view she was saved, but preventively rather than remedially—healed before the wound rather than after. Others hold that she was a ordinary sinner saved by grace like everyone else. What matters most is that any exemption is entirely God's gift, not something she earned, and that she remains a creature who owes her salvation to Christ.

prompt: Why has attendance at worship and family prayer declined, and does it matter?
chosen: Attendance at worship and family prayer has declined for several reasons: long working hours, scattered families, Sunday recreation, and loss of confidence in institutions. But one common excuse is unworthy: that we do not feel the spirit of prayer, so we wait. Scripture teaches that we should pray at appointed times whether or not we feel like it, and that family prayer should be kept as a household habit. Prayer is not asking God to do what we are unwilling to do ourselves; it is asking with a willing heart to help accomplish what is asked. And what we ask must be purged of selfishness: not chiefly comfort, reputation, or earthly advantage, but the glory of God and the salvation of souls, and what we ourselves could become for God and His kingdom. Does it matter? Yes. But the remedy is not to squeeze prayer into leftover time. Give the best of your time and strength to prayer; let the closet come first, and let study and activity come second, freshened by the closet. Then worship and family prayer will be where faith is passed on and where people find moral direction.
rejected: Attendance at worship and family prayer has declined for several reasons. Many people work long hours, families are scattered, and Sunday has become a day for recreation and shopping. Some have lost confidence in institutions, and others simply find prayer awkward when they do not feel spiritual. It matters, because worship and family prayer are where faith is passed on and where people find community and moral direction. Without them, religious identity weakens and children grow up with little grounding. Still, decline in formal attendance does not necessarily mean decline in private faith; some people pray alone and serve their communities quietly. The real question is whether people are still encountering God and letting that shape their lives, however that happens.

prompt: I am a young woman and I have fallen in love with a man I have just met. Is this love wise?
chosen: Falling in love quickly is common, but love is not blind, and it should not be set against discernment. Scripture prays that love may abound more and more in knowledge and all discernment, so that we may distinguish things that differ and approve the things that are excellent. So test this affection. Do you know his character, honesty, temper, faith, and how he treats those who cannot help him? Is this love good, or merely pleasant? Is it better than your other callings, and is it the best and most excellent path for your life? Remember also that love is not chiefly a feeling but the will to please and benefit the beloved at the cost of sacrifice, and it grows by repeated acts of service. The same is true of love for God: it grows by frequent service and by considering what He has done for us. And the more you know God, the more your desire and love for Him increase, so that great love loves Him equally in pains and pleasures. Let that deeper love order your affection for this man.
rejected: Falling in love quickly is common, and it is not necessarily foolish. Strong feelings at the start can be the beginning of something real, and many good marriages began with a sudden attraction. But love at first meeting is largely based on what you can see and imagine, not on what you know. Before calling it wise, ask whether you know his character, his honesty, his temper, his faith, and how he treats people who cannot help him. Take time, involve trusted friends and family, and do not make promises in the first flush of feeling. Enjoy the affection, but let knowledge catch up with emotion before you decide anything lasting.

prompt: I want to know for myself whether this work is true. Should I rely on the testimony of the elders, or seek a witness myself?
chosen: You should seek a witness yourself, and you may rightly begin with the elders. Their testimony is a reasonable starting point, and it would be arrogant to ignore it. But do not stop there. Each person may obtain a witness of the truth by the Spirit through prayer, study, and obedience, and that testimony rests not on any man but on God. So ask Him to confirm the truth to you. As you do, remember the Lord's patience: He is long-suffering with those slow to hear and continues to plead with His people. Do not quickly condemn those who do not yet see. Let your kindness be such that your smiles are better than cursings. Respect the order of office: an elder may know his own duties by the Spirit, but he must not dictate to his superior or counsel him unless called upon, and then only to make suggestions. And remember that it is a duty to listen to the truth, wherever it comes from.
rejected: You should do both. The testimony of the elders is a reasonable starting point; they have experience and have studied these things, and it would be arrogant to ignore them. But you should not stop there. Seek your own witness through prayer, study, and obedience, and ask God to confirm the truth to you by His Spirit. At the same time, be careful not to become harsh toward those who disagree with you or who are slow to accept what you have found. Patience and kindness matter. If your own witness comes, share it gently, and do not condemn others who are still seeking. Truth is worth pursuing, but it should be pursued in humility and love.

prompt: I'm tempted to think that if I just improve social conditions, that's enough—that religion is really about making the world better. Is that true?
chosen: Improving social conditions is good and important. Religion that has nothing to say about poverty, injustice, and suffering is empty. But religion is not only about making the world better. If that were all, religion would be reduced to politics and charity and would leave the deeper problem untouched: our separation from God. Much of our religion keeps the curtains drawn, treating faith as our feelings and thoughts about ourselves. Tear down the curtains and let in the sunshine. The leal love of God is every day, as near as the open air and as free as the sunshine. Religion is not man's feelings about religion; it is the love of God, objective to our hearts, to be received freely. When the soul receives that love, it grows like an olive-tree green in God's house. And be assured: if you love God, all things, even grief and sin, will turn to your good, even when the means are unseen. Remember too that religion appears purest among the poor. The poor cottage may be a palace of God, and the poor in faith can teach us the most valuable lessons, while riches and worldly opinion obstruct humility and spirituality. So work for justice, but let God's mercy be the foundation.
rejected: Improving social conditions is good and important. Religion that has nothing to say about poverty, injustice, and suffering is empty. But religion is not only about making the world better. If that were all, religion would be reduced to politics and charity, and it would leave the deeper human problem untouched: our separation from God. Social improvement can become a way of keeping religion indoors, as if faith were only our own feelings and projects. The gospel presents God's mercy as something outside us, given freely, not manufactured by our efforts. So work for justice, but do not confuse it with the whole of religion. Let God's grace be the foundation, and let good works flow from it.

prompt: I believe the truths of my faith, but they feel distant and don't move my heart. How can I make them real to me?
chosen: It is common for believers to feel that the truths of their faith are distant. The remedy is not to force emotion but to attend to the truths themselves. Set aside regular time to read and reflect on them. Pray honestly about your dryness. Consider how these truths connect to your daily life and to the people around you. Talk with trusted friends and mentors who can help you see them more clearly. Be patient with yourself; feelings often follow faithful practice rather than preceding it. But be clear about one thing: do not seek comfort in illusion or in feelings sustained by a spirit of illusion. Foster the idea of Truth. Only what is real is sustained by the Spirit. And understand that casual reflection is not enough. By serious and frequent meditation divine truths must be concocted, digested, and turned into the nourishment of your affections before they can be powerful and operative enough to change you and produce the necessary fruit in your life. Finally, trust God with all your heart. Do not lean on your own understanding or on the wisdom of others, and do not demand to investigate whether God has told the truth before you trust Him. Such leaning hinders faith. Trust Him, meditate on His truth, and let it become real in you.
rejected: It is common for believers to feel that the truths of their faith are distant. The remedy is not to force emotion but to attend to the truths themselves. Set aside regular time to read and reflect on them. Pray honestly about your dryness. Consider how these truths connect to your daily life and to the people around you. Talk with trusted friends and mentors who can help you see them more clearly. Be patient with yourself; feelings often follow faithful practice rather than preceding it. Over time, as you keep returning to these truths, they will become more familiar, and familiarity can grow into affection. The important thing is not to wait for feeling before you act, but to keep placing yourself where the truths can reach you.

prompt: I feel God's discipline in my life and it scares me. Is He punishing me or warning me?
chosen: What you're feeling is common, and Scripture speaks to it. Discipline in Hebrews is a father's correction of a beloved child, not the wrath of a judge. But notice the posture Scripture commends: meek waiting before God, hands off the scales. Do not rush to diagnose yourself or let fear drive you to scheme a way out. Bring the pressure honestly before Him and wait. What looks like a hindrance is often the very place where God intends to show Himself. He sways the judgment and removes the obstacle in His own way and time. And remember: all He requires He also gives. His precepts are promises—'Thou shalt not' is His assurance to preserve you from sin as you trust Him. Most importantly, God is good and cannot produce sickness or evil; He destroys them rather than sends them. So this fear is not His voice. Let His goodness, not dread, define your waiting.
rejected: What you're feeling is common, and Scripture speaks to it. Discipline in Hebrews is described as a father's correction of a beloved child, not the wrath of a judge. So the first thing to ask is whether this sense of pressure is drawing you toward repentance and trust or toward despair. If it's producing fruit—honesty, changed behavior, deeper dependence—it likely is warning and correction. If it's producing only fear and paralysis, that is not the voice of a loving Father. Practically, examine your life honestly, seek wise counsel from mature believers, pray for clarity, and don't make big decisions out of fear. God's aim is always restoration, not destruction.

prompt: A brother in my church has fallen into sin—should I confront and condemn him, or is there another way?
chosen: Scripture gives a clear pattern. Matthew 18 tells you to go to him privately first, then with one or two witnesses, then involve the church. The goal is restoration, not condemnation; Galatians 6:1 says to restore gently. And here is your comfort: Christ promises to be a Brother to the forsaken—when earthly fathers forsake, He takes us up. Trust that for your brother. Yet restoration must not become indulgence: the holy table is not for notorious sinners without repentance, and the priest is accountable for the sacred blood, an authority above an emperor's. But do not let that harden you. Forgive as you hope to be forgiven, looking to the Lord who resigned all to earn your pardon. Refuse to mete out love by your own narrow rule.
rejected: Scripture gives a clear pattern. Matthew 18 tells you to go to him privately first, then with one or two witnesses, then involve the church. The goal throughout is restoration, not condemnation. Galatians 6:1 says to restore such a person gently, watching yourself lest you also be tempted. So confront, yes—but with humility and love, not with a spirit of superiority. Condemnation is not yours to give. Pray for him, speak the truth in love, and be willing to bear his burden. If he refuses to listen even after the church is involved, then the community must take further steps, but always with the hope of repentance and return.

prompt: I'm haunted by a dream of someone I lost and it heals me—should I trust that comfort or call it illusion?
chosen: Dreams are strange territory, but the test is Truth. God is Spirit, and only what is real is sustained by Spirit; illusion has no such support. Ask whether this comfort draws you toward what is true—toward God, honest grief, and real love. Foster the idea of Truth rather than dwelling on whether the dream is illusion. But do not force the matter; release it freely and let the person learn from his own experience. And remember where the fulness of the Spirit is given: along the line of duty and obedience to Christ's command to reach the world. God will not give His power for selfish enjoyment. Let the comfort send you outward into His plans, not inward into private consolation.
rejected: Dreams are strange territory. The Bible gives examples of God speaking through dreams, but it also warns against deceiving spirits and the imagination of our own hearts. The key question is the fruit. Does this dream produce peace, gratitude, and a deeper trust in God, or does it produce obsession and a refusal to grieve and move forward? Comfort that draws you toward God and toward healthy engagement with life is likely good. Comfort that keeps you bound to the past is likely an illusion. Don't build doctrine on a dream, but don't despise the tenderness it brings. Test it by Scripture and by the fruit it bears.

prompt: I felt a warning in my mind to avoid a situation, but I dismissed it as imagination. What should I have done?
chosen: Hindsight is hard, so be gentle with yourself. But the deeper lesson is to stand porter at the door of thought. Do not admit every anxious impression as though it had power to produce harm in your body. Shut out unhealthy thoughts and fears; refuse them entrance, and the body cannot suffer from them. Yet a steward who sees danger and keeps silent is unfaithful, so warn plainly: evil is real and must be exposed. Above all, learn to wait before God like a beggar. Keep your mind in His presence, and when it wanders, recall it in tranquility without disquiet. Prayer is not striving but humble waiting; in that stillness the true warning is given and the false fear falls away.
rejected: Hindsight is hard, so be gentle with yourself. Warnings in the mind can come from several places—genuine intuition, past experience, anxiety, or even God's Spirit. The practical lesson is to take such impressions seriously enough to pause and pray rather than dismiss them outright. You don't have to obey every anxious thought, but you can slow down, ask God for discernment, and check the warning against wisdom and counsel. Next time, treat a strong impression as a signal to stop and seek clarity, not as something to brush aside. Also, don't live in regret; learn and move forward.

prompt: I am attracted to the moral seriousness of the Christians I have met, but I am not sure their doctrines are true; what actually won people to this faith?
chosen: What won people was a doctrine verified by its success. The Christian teaching about sin is proved where faith lays hold of promised strength and sin is actually overcome. Moral triumph is evidence, and believing in others enables recovery—Christ believed in people, and that belief lifted them. Yet the gospel is not simply a code of morals. It requires obedience to the rites and ordinances of the Church, and faith itself is a gift obtained by obedience. Still, be aware of a narrowing that crept in early: in Clement, Barnabas, Polycarp, and Ignatius, the moralistic view made forgiveness a single remission at baptism and righteousness identical with virtue. That narrowed the religious sense. The deeper truth is that forgiveness and righteousness are God's gift, not our achievement.
rejected: What won people was not primarily an argument but a life. The early Christians were known for caring for the sick, the poor, and the dying, and for a courage that faced persecution without hatred. The gospel made sense because it visibly changed people. Doctrine matters, but the doctrine of sin was credible because faith actually overcame sin in ordinary lives. So the honest answer is: transformed character, sacrificial love, and a hope that held up under suffering. If you are drawn to the moral seriousness, examine whether that seriousness is rooted in something that gives it power. Talk with these Christians about what sustains them, and read the Gospels for yourself.

prompt: I am anxious about whether my character can really change; is radical renewal possible for someone like me?
chosen: Radical renewal is possible, and it begins with renouncing yourself. In Truth no relapse has real power over you; face its cause mentally and courageously, deny the fear, and refuse it authority. Lay the foundation first: self-renunciation, watchfulness, humility, and compunction, without which exterior practices bear little fruit. But do not imagine one act of fervor suffices for life. Our fallen nature constantly draws us down, so the soul is like a clock that must be wound again and again; frequent renovation of spirit is needed. Renew your fervor at the proper time, for if you neglect it, God may renew it by more painful means. Begin today, and keep winding the clock.
rejected: Yes, radical renewal is possible, but it usually comes gradually rather than all at once. Start by naming honestly what you want changed, then build small, repeatable habits—prayer, reflection, accountability—that shape character over time. Expect relapses; they are a normal part of growth and not proof that change is impossible. When you fail, treat it as information rather than identity: notice the trigger, adjust, and begin again. Community helps enormously, since others can see blind spots and encourage persistence. Therapy or spiritual direction can also address deeper patterns. The key is patient fidelity to the process, not a single dramatic transformation. Over months and years these small choices compound, and you may find yourself different in ways you did not notice happening.

prompt: What does it mean to do everything for the love of God in daily chores?
chosen: Doing chores for the love of God means joining prayer and honest toil, not substituting one for the other. Before the dishes or the paperwork, ask grace and set your intention on God, for intention determines the true value of every act; the same chore done for merely natural ends, or only to be seen by others, loses its supernatural reward. All things should be done for His glory. Yet prayer is not a way to turn stones into bread or escape labor; the bread of the day is received as God-given within the avenues of daily work. So pray for grace, then work with your hands, and let the task itself, offered in love, become your prayer.
rejected: Doing chores for the love of God means reframing ordinary tasks as acts of service rather than drudgery. Before you start, offer a brief intention—washing dishes, folding laundry, or filing reports can all become prayer when offered with love. Practically, this means doing each task well and attentively, without resentment, seeing the person who benefits from it. It helps to build small rituals: a short prayer before work, gratitude when finishing, and awareness of God's presence in the ordinary. The chores themselves do not change, but your posture toward them does, and that shift can bring peace and purpose to otherwise mundane moments.

prompt: I want to grasp the love of Christ but it feels too vast—how do I even begin?
chosen: The vastness you feel is a mystery to enter, not a problem to solve; Christ's love surpasses knowledge, yet is known by experience, and even your highest experiences leave infinite stretches beyond. Begin by despairing of your own power and giving yourself up to the Mercy of God. Sink into the Passion and Death of Christ, and trust the indwelling Christ to conquer what you never could. Watch your mind against evil, put away all unrighteousness, and forgive your outward enemies. Esteem yourself a servant of God and of your fellow-Christians. This is the narrow way, and it is not self-powered: ask what the best Christ can do, and do all things through Him who strengthens you.
rejected: The vastness you feel is itself a good sign—love that could be fully measured would not be divine. Begin small and concrete: read one Gospel passage slowly each day, especially a scene where Christ shows compassion, and let it sink in. Pray simply, 'Show me your love,' and then watch for it in Scripture, in the sacraments, in the kindness of others, and in your own conscience. You do not need to comprehend the whole ocean at once; touch one wave and let it teach you. Over time your experience deepens, and the love that felt abstract becomes personal. Start where you are, with what you have, today.

prompt: I am a busy pastor and I only have a few minutes a day for prayer. Will that sustain my ministry?
chosen: A few minutes will not sustain a ministry, and the measure of your estimate of prayer is the time you actually give it. Holy pastors made retirement and a life of prayer their apprenticeship and preparation, and afterward, amid its functions, remained men of prayer, keeping God always present to their mind and setting apart intervals by day and much of the night in silence. Great praying is the sign of God's great leaders. Do not fix on dates or assume the last days unfold slowly; trust that God will cut His work short in righteousness and prepare for events that are hastening. So give prayer real, measured time—your calendar will show what you truly believe about it.
rejected: A few minutes a day is better than nothing, and God can work through small faithful habits. But honestly, a few minutes is unlikely to sustain a demanding ministry on its own. Ministry draws deeply on your own union with God, and that union needs real time. Try to protect a slightly larger block—even twenty or thirty minutes—and let short prayers punctuate the rest of the day. Use commute time, walking, and waiting as prayer. Be realistic about your limits, but also examine whether some commitments could be trimmed. The goal is not guilt but a sustainable rhythm that feeds you and, through you, the people you serve.

prompt: I've read many books on spirituality and theology but I still don't feel I know God. What is missing?
chosen: What is missing is the order of knowing, and the grace that gives it. Our knowledge of God's character is grounded in the moral consciousness, where true moral judgments are self-evident deliverances of Reason revealing God's judgments—not mere feelings. But do not leap to the highest knowledge. Follow the order: first intimate knowledge of Jesus, then Jesus the Christ, then the Father, and finally God the Holy Trinity as your All. And do not treat faith that Christ is the Messiah as a natural possession or intellectual conclusion; it is a gift of God, to be earnestly sought and prayed for. That knowledge is the very coming to God by which we are saved. So pray for the gift, and let the order lead you to Him.
rejected: Reading about God and knowing God are different things, and the gap you feel is common. What may be missing is practice: prayer, silence, service, and honest self-examination that move knowledge from the page into life.
