Read and ponder Science and Health with him, holding thought to divine health and harmony, and meet fear with truth rather than remedies.
rejected: Helping an aging father with constipation and dyspepsia calls for practical, gentle care. Encourage hydration, fiber-rich foods, and regular light movement, and keep meals small and bland if dyspepsia flares. Establish a routine for toileting and note what triggers discomfort. Consult his physician about persistent symptoms, medications, or warning signs such as weight loss or bleeding, and follow medical advice. Offer emotional support, since digestive troubles are uncomfortable and sometimes embarrassing. Keep a simple symptom diary to share with his doctor, and adjust care as needed. Patience, consistency, and professional guidance are the mainstays; avoid unproven remedies and coordinate any changes with his clinician.

prompt: Must I forsake the World and my life too if I would do as you say?
chosen: You need not literally forsake the world or your life. It is our duty to study everything on the face of the earth, both good and evil, without practicing evil: read good books, study reliable history, and learn the effects of good and the consequences of evil without committing iniquity. Yet do not let the perishable things of this world swerve you in the least degree from fidelity to the truth; to be so swerved is short-sighted and shows we lack knowledge we should possess. Do not accuse yourself overmuch. Howsoever you do, you shall have woe; our Lord wills not indiscreet heaviness. See your penance wisely, and know that all your living is penance profitable. Reorder your attachments so truth and love come first, simplifying and refusing compromises, without withdrawing from ordinary life.
rejected: You need not literally forsake the world or your life to follow good counsel. What is usually meant is reordering your attachments: letting truth and love take priority over possessions, status, and comfort. That may mean simplifying, setting boundaries, and refusing compromises, but it does not require withdrawing from ordinary life. Engage with the world thoughtfully, learn from it, and serve within it, while keeping your deepest loyalty elsewhere. Ask which attachments actually pull you away from what is true and good, and address those. Sacrifice becomes necessary only where something genuinely competes with fidelity. So the call is not to abandon life but to live it honestly, with your loves rightly ordered.

prompt: I feel disconnected from God and don't know how to reconnect. What should I do?
chosen: Feeling distant from God is not a reason for alarm. Forgetting Him is a common lapse, and the right response is a calm return with greater trust, not anxious self-scrutiny. But the return is not a vague inward impulse; it is fellowship with a personal Friend—the Father whom we know through His human revelation in Christ. Speak with Him as with a friend, and let the gospel define the communion: you are welcomed as a child because of Christ. Yet do not imagine He is far off until you reconnect. God is always near, and the goal is not an occasional return but continual remembrance and adoration—in prayer, in business, and even in your diversions. Let Him be thought of and loved throughout the day, not neglected and then sought. Begin now with confidence, not dread, knowing the Father receives you gladly in His Son.
rejected: Feeling distant from God is common, and it doesn't mean God has abandoned you. Start by setting aside quiet time each day for prayer and Scripture, even just a few minutes. Be honest with God about how you feel—He already knows. Consider joining a small group or talking with a pastor who can pray with you and offer guidance. Examine whether anything like unconfessed sin, busyness, or isolation has crowded out your awareness of God's presence. Remember that feelings fluctuate, but God's faithfulness does not. Reconnecting usually happens through small, consistent habits rather than one dramatic experience. Be patient with yourself and trust that as you draw near to God, He will draw near to you.

prompt: I am suddenly frightened by frailty and affright—is this fear good for me or sinful?
chosen: Fear in the face of frailty is natural, but the remedy is not to analyze the fear—it is to look at Christ, who is the antidote to fear and the sum of all deliverance. Fix your eyes on Him and abide in His presence. You may dread having naught beside God, as though coming to Him meant losing everything; but what was taken was taken not for your harm but so your soul might seek it in God's arms, and all that seemed lost is stored for you at home in Him. Yet do not let fear rule you, for fear is a greater evil than the evil feared. Cry out with St. Peter, 'Lord, save me!' and clasp the hand He extends. Abide in Christ, and the fear that looms will shrink before His presence.
rejected: Fear in the face of frailty is a natural human response, and it can serve a good purpose by reminding you of your limits and dependence on God. It becomes sinful when it turns into distrust of God's goodness or paralyzes you from doing what is right. Examine what is behind the fear: if it is driving you to prayer and humility, it can be healthy; if it is breeding despair or disobedience, it needs to be brought to God. Talk with a trusted pastor or counselor about it. Scripture repeatedly tells us not to be afraid, so let those promises steady you. Ask God for courage and remember that He is with you.

prompt: Can a nation repent?
chosen: Yes, a nation can repent, and the standard is plain. Sin is doing wrong when we know and can do better; the sin of ignorance is winked at, but once we learn a thing is wrong we must refrain from it immediately and forever. Do not wait to feel more or gather greater power—you can this moment renounce sin in will and purpose, and God supplies the strength; feeling comes after the surrender. But do not imagine repentance costs nothing. Every blessing is predicated on obedience to law, and one who sins in youth and repents late has lost something that can never be regained, though he may be forgiven. So turn at once, and let the turning spread through the people.
rejected: Yes, a nation can repent, though it is complicated. Repentance in Scripture often involves a corporate turning—leaders and people together acknowledging wrongdoing and changing direction. History shows seasons of national reform and revival. But a nation is made of individuals, so genuine national repentance begins with personal repentance spreading through a people. It requires honest acknowledgment of wrong, a change of heart and policy, and often restitution. It is not merely a political gesture but a moral and spiritual turning. Whether it lasts depends on sustained commitment. Pray for your nation and begin with your own repentance, since collective change grows from individual hearts.

prompt: I am facing a difficult journey with little money and no certain lodging—how should I trust GOD for daily needs?
chosen: Trusting God for daily needs begins with a spirit willing to give rather than merely to get. Scripture records helpers who gave themselves and their goods for God's work without salary, believing He would supply all their need; seek that cheerful, self-denying spirit. Walk with God intimately: address Him every moment, seek His will in doubtful matters like which road or lodging, offer each action before doing it, and give thanks after. Yet trust is not carelessness. Commit future wants to God's care without anxious hoarding, and still use all proper means diligently—watch as well as pray, for with God no emergency is unforeseen and no want unprovided for. Plan wisely, give gladly, and rest in His care.
rejected: Trusting God for daily needs begins with honest prayer and practical planning. Bring your specific concerns to God—the journey, the money, the lodging—and ask for His provision. Then do what you can: budget carefully, seek help from friends or a church community, and look for affordable options. Remember Jesus' teaching that the Father knows what you need before you ask. Anxiety will not add anything; instead, take one day at a time. If needs arise, ask boldly and gratefully. Trust is not passivity—it works with what God provides while resting in His care.

prompt: I have wasted many years serving the world and my own whims; is it too late to give myself to God?
chosen: It is not too late, and you need not be uneasy about the years behind you. Forgetting God is a common lapse, and the right response is a calm return with greater trust, not disquiet or regret. Turn to Him simply and confidently, and receive His welcome. Yet do not despise what remains: nothing should go to waste, for no man is wealthy enough to let a servant sweep a single kernel of wheat into the fire; through carefulness and frugality we preserve and increase the blessings God bestows. Still, do not multiply superfluous occupations through curiosity or restlessness, for these create more impediments than works. Limit yourself to legitimate employments, steward the years ahead diligently, and let steady, quiet faithfulness—not frantic busyness—shape your return.
rejected: It is not too late. God's mercy is not limited by your past, and Scripture is full of people who turned to God late in life. What matters is that you turn now. Begin by confessing the wasted years honestly to God, receive His forgiveness, and then start fresh with small, faithful steps—prayer, Scripture, fellowship, and service. You cannot recover lost time, but you can make the years ahead count. Avoid both despair and the illusion that you must earn your way back. God receives returning sinners gladly. Take the first step today and let grace shape what remains.

prompt: How do I see God's character revealed in Jesus Christ?
chosen: You see God's character in Jesus because in him God himself is revealed: we behold God, and we learn that God is like Christ. His compassion, holiness, forgiveness, and self-giving love are the very character of God shown in a real human life, and the Old Testament foreshadowings are gathered up and fulfilled in him. But this revelation is not a finite manifestation that begins in time. Christ existed as the Word with God before the Word was made flesh; he is the eternal principle of self-consciousness in God, the objectification of God to himself in the Son prior to creation. So when you look at Jesus, you are not seeing a creature pointing toward a distant God but the eternal Word made flesh, who was with God and was God. The gospel portrait is a photograph from real life, and the life it photographs is the life of God himself.
rejected: You see God's character in Jesus by looking at how he lived: his compassion for the sick and outcast, his forgiveness of enemies, his courage before unjust power, and his teaching about a Father who welcomes sinners. In his healing, his table fellowship, and his willingness to suffer rather than retaliate, Jesus shows us what divine love looks like in human form. Read the Gospels slowly and ask what each scene reveals about God's heart. Prayer and imitation help: as you follow his example of mercy and humility, you come to know the God he points to. Jesus is the clearest window we have onto who God is and what God cares about.

prompt: I am a mother and my child has been taken from me. How do I bear the grief?
chosen: I am so sorry. What was done to your child is a slaughter of the innocent, and it must be named as such. Let the mothers' lament be your voice: the killers slay infants, they wound fathers, they kill mothers; Hell is full with the deed and Heaven is shut, and the blood of guiltless innocents has been spilt. Do not let anyone talk you out of that charge. Yet hear also the harder word: excessive mourning for the dead is a want of faith. Christ has taken the little ones into His arms; the baptized and childlike are trusted to His embrace, and their end is happier far than life, so do not grudge them there. God takes away friends because He will be loved without a rival. Let your grief be moderated by confidence in Him, who does not lose what He receives.
rejected: I am so sorry for your loss. Grief after losing a child is one of the heaviest burdens a person can carry, and there is no shortcut through it. Let yourself mourn honestly; tears are not weakness. Lean on people who love you, and let them help with practical things while you rest. Talk to God in whatever words you have—anger, sorrow, silence are all allowed. Take one day at a time, and be gentle with yourself on the hard days. Many mothers find comfort in remembering their child and in the hope that love is stronger than death. You do not have to bear this alone.

prompt: I'm thinking about how to raise my children in the Gospel—what's most important?
chosen: The most important thing is that you take responsibility to teach and watch over your children in the gospel. Create a faith-filled home where they see it lived out: read Scripture together, pray with them, bring them to church, instruct them patiently, and guard them from the wickedness of the world. Model kindness, honesty, and forgiveness. Let your home be open, not proud: desire that all honest-in-heart come to know the truth, share freely, and welcome others. And do not act on impulse or by human wisdom alone. The servant of God takes no step without asking counsel of the oracles of God and seeking guidance in believing prayer. Bring even the smallest matters of your family to the Lord, learn His will before undertaking anything, and wait until His guidance is clear—only so can you be blessed in your own soul and prospered in the work of your hands.
rejected: The most important thing is to create a warm, faith-filled home where children see the Gospel lived out. Read Bible stories together, pray before meals and at bedtime, and let them see you being kind, honest, and forgiving. Bring them to church and to other believers so they have a community. Answer their questions honestly and don't force things; let faith grow naturally. Model the values you want them to have, because children learn more from what you do than what you say. Keep it simple and consistent, and trust that God is at work in your family.

prompt: I try hard to keep God's law but I keep failing—what am I doing wrong?
chosen: It's good that you're trying, but do not lower God's standard to fit your failures. His commandments are not discounted; He calls us to be holy as He is holy. Press on until you reach His highest will, refusing to excuse what falls short. When you meet straits, delays, or trials, do not read them as signs that God has failed. These are the conditions in which faith is exercised and God's interposition is displayed; they test and strengthen trust, encourage importunity, and make His deliverance the more manifest. Yet do not attribute suffering or evil directly to God's design or displeasure. God's hand is in all things as permission and overruling, but suffering and evil come from human agency, indiscretion, or ignorance. So repent honestly, keep asking, and remain in lively trust.
rejected: It's encouraging that you're trying. Everyone fails sometimes; none of us keeps God's law perfectly, and God knows that. Perhaps you're being too hard on yourself. Remember that God is forgiving and patient, and that growth takes time. Instead of focusing on every failure, look at the progress you've made and give yourself grace. Try to build better habits, avoid situations that tempt you, and lean on God's mercy when you fall. It also helps to talk with a pastor or friend who can encourage you. God doesn't expect perfection—he wants your heart.

prompt: I want to consecrate my life to God but I'm afraid of what my family will say—should I go ahead?
chosen: This is a big decision, and it's natural to worry about your family. But do not let that worry keep you from prayer. Pray at your appointed times whether or not you feel like it; the spirit of prayer often comes in the praying. Pray with your family too, and help God accomplish what you ask by taking the steps that lie in your hands. Do not demand perfect human sympathy: each heart's bitterness is its own, and God alone knows us fully. Accept hidden solitude as Heaven's will and rest in the Lord, who knows all things yet loves you better than He knows. Above all, do not look at the storm or your circumstances for comfort; look at Christ Himself, who is the antidote to fear and the sum of all deliverance. Fasten your eyes on Him, abide in Him, and in His presence you will find the remedy for trouble and the substance of every deliverance.
rejected: This is a big decision, and it's natural to worry about your family's reaction. Take time to think and pray about it before you act. It's worth talking with your family honestly about what you're feeling, if that's safe, and hearing their concerns. Sometimes their worries come from love. But ultimately this is your life and your faith, and you shouldn't let fear alone decide for you. Seek wise counsel from a pastor or trusted friend. If you feel God is leading you, move forward gradually and trust that things will work out.

prompt: I'm a pastor and my congregation seems asleep. How do I keep going?
chosen: When your congregation seems asleep, the first thing is not to fix them but to return to the pattern of holy pastors: a life of prayer as your apprenticeship and preparation for ministry, and afterward, amidst all its functions, still being a man of prayer with God always present to your mind. Set apart intervals in the day and a considerable part of the nights to apply yourself with your whole attention to this exercise in the silence of all creatures. Remember that not advancing is going back; keep pressing forward. Yet do not strive anxiously: wait before God like a beggar, keeping your mind in His presence, and when it wanders, recall it in tranquility without disquiet. Awaken the Lord within by faith, for His presence calms the soul's storms. From that place of humble waiting, you will find strength to keep going and to love your people without depending on their response.
rejected: It's tough when your congregation seems spiritually asleep. First, don't take it personally—many pastors face this. Focus on your own spiritual health: pray regularly, take retreats, and seek support from fellow pastors. Remember that change often happens slowly. Try to connect with a few engaged members and build from there. Preach with passion and authenticity, and trust that God is at work even when you can't see it. Also, consider whether your own weariness might be affecting your perception. Take care of yourself—rest, exercise, and spend time with loved ones. Lastly, remember your calling: you are not responsible for the results, only for faithful service. Keep showing up, keep loving your people, and leave the outcomes to God.

prompt: I want to be sure of my inheritance—how do I know the promise to Abraham includes me?
chosen: To know that the promise to Abraham includes you, look not to your own works but to God's covenant confirmed in Christ and by His oath. The promise was given to Abraham and his seed, who is Christ, and it was confirmed beforehand by God, so that the law which came later cannot void it or add conditions to it. The inheritance is received by promise through faith. Therefore, if you are of faith, you are blessed with Abraham the believer and are an heir according to the promise. And to be a true imitator of Christ and heir of His disciples' privileges, forgive injuries after the example of the good thief and of Christ on the cross. Do not seek assurance by measuring your law-keeping or your works; rather, rest in the unchanging oath of God, who cannot lie, and forgive as you have been forgiven. Know that in Christ there is neither Jew nor Greek, bond nor free, male nor female, for all who are of faith are one seed and heirs according to promise.
rejected: To know that the promise to Abraham includes you, you must first understand that the promise is received by faith, not by works. Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness. If you belong to Christ, then you are Abraham's offspring and heirs according to the promise. So the key is to examine yourself: do you trust in Christ alone for your salvation? Do you show evidence of that faith through love and good works? Also, consider your baptism and your participation in the life of the church. These are means of grace that assure you of your inheritance. Finally, remember that God's promise is not based on your performance but on His faithfulness. Rest in that.

prompt: I want to comfort someone who's grieving and poor—what can I actually offer them that isn't empty?
chosen: When comforting someone who is grieving and poor, you cannot truly see their woe without sorrow. Let your heart be moved, for the Maker Himself is near to those who sigh and weep. He sits by us and moans till our grief is fled and gone. So do not offer empty words or quick fixes. Instead, be present with them in their pain, weeping with those who weep. Offer practical help as you are able, but above all, let them know that God is not distant from their suffering—He is with them in it. And do not despise their prayers, for the prayers of the poor and desolate rise with more than royal pomp and pierce the skies. Yet teach them, and yourself, not to be too solicitous for sensible devotion, sweetness, and tears, but chiefly to remain inwardly united to God by good will in the intellectual part of the soul, denying oneself to follow Christ, Who was truly poor, obedient, chaste, humble, and suffering.
rejected: When comforting someone who is grieving and poor, the most important thing is to be present and listen. Avoid clichés like 'everything happens for a reason.' Instead, offer practical help: bring meals, help with chores, or assist with financial needs if possible. Let them know you care and that you are there for them. Share memories of their loved one if appropriate. Encourage them to talk about their feelings and validate their pain. If they are open to it, pray with them and read Scripture that speaks of God's comfort. Remind them that they are not alone and that their feelings are normal. Sometimes the best comfort is simply sitting with them in silence and letting them know you are there.

prompt: I'm a laborer wondering whether to join a union—what principles should guide me?
chosen: As a laborer considering union membership, the first principle is not organization or negotiation but common dedication to the will of God in Christ. Seek first to be united to Him, and let outward reunion with fellow workers follow from that inner union. Ask whether joining the union would help you and others to fuller dedication to God's will in Christ—whether it would promote justice, honesty, and love of neighbor. Do not treat the decision merely as a matter of costs and benefits or mutual concessions. Rather, consider how your participation might serve the common good and strengthen solidarity among laborers. Share the knowledge of needs with fellow laborers in the work, that they may join in prayer, faith, and self-denial; but carefully withhold all knowledge of need from outsiders lest it be construed as an appeal for human aid. Let your conscience be guided by Scripture and prayer, and seek the counsel of wise believers. In all things, keep yourself humble and approach Holy Communion boldly, content to become accustomed to this heavenly food by degrees.
rejected: As a laborer considering union membership, several principles can guide you. First, consider the potential benefits: better wages, safer working conditions, and collective bargaining power. Second, think about the costs: union dues, potential conflicts with management, and the risk of strikes. Third, reflect on your personal values: do you believe in collective action and solidarity with fellow workers? Fourth, research the specific union—its history, leadership, and reputation. Fifth, talk to coworkers who are already members to hear their experiences. Finally, consider your legal rights and your employer's stance. Ultimately, the decision is yours, and it should align with your values and goals.

prompt: I want to renounce the world and mortify the flesh, but I fear this leads me to despise God's creation; how should I practice self-control?
chosen: To practice self-control while renouncing the world and mortifying the flesh, begin by making obedience to God your first duty, seeking the oneness of Mind that Christ prayed for, and loving your neighbor as yourself. Then bridle your tongue and subdue anger, for careless speech and meddling in others' affairs are contrary to true self-control. Examine yourself daily, attend to your own duties, and refrain from judging or interfering with others. Remember that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit, so care for it with gratitude, not contempt. Fasting and abstinence can be helpful, but they should train the will without despising God's creation. Yet do not multiply discourse, research, and tiresome care of self; rather, confine yourself to the simple view of God and your own nothingness. In that simplicity, cultivate gratitude for His gifts and focus on loving your neighbor as yourself. If you struggle, seek counsel from a pastor or trusted friend. Above all, rely on God's grace, for self-control is a fruit of the Spirit.
rejected: Self-control is about mastering your desires, not rejecting God's good creation. Start by identifying areas where you lack control—perhaps food, media, or anger. Set realistic goals and rely on prayer and accountability. Remember that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit, so care for it with gratitude. Fasting and abstinence can be helpful disciplines, but they should be done with the right heart—not to earn salvation, but to train your will. Avoid extremes; balance is key. Also, cultivate gratitude for God's gifts, which helps prevent despising creation. Finally, focus on loving others, which naturally curbs selfishness. If you struggle, seek counsel from a pastor or trusted friend.

prompt: I try to obey God's law with great care, but the more I try the more I am dismayed at how far short I fall. What is the law for?
chosen: The law is the personal appeal of the living God—'Be ye holy, for I am holy'—the tie of a vital relationship between persons, and the highest motive is love to Him. Your dismay at falling short is honest, but do not fight sin under law by self-effort; that only deepens condemnation. Step out from under law and rest upon grace: Christ gives you His free gift of righteousness, and where grace reigns sin shall not have dominion. Yet grace does not leave you lawless. God still guides you through inspired counsel and the leaders He has set over you—not as coercion or blind servility, but as counsel given and received in love. Obey cheerfully and intelligently, testing all things by His Word, and let love, not fear, be the bond of your obedience.
rejected: The law shows you your sin. When you compare yourself to God's commandments, you see how far you fall short, and that is exactly the law's purpose: to expose sin and drive you to Christ. The law is a mirror that reveals the disease; the gospel is the medicine. So don't be surprised at your dismay—it is the law doing its work. Stop trusting your careful obedience to make you acceptable, and instead flee to the grace of God in Christ, who fulfilled the law on your behalf. The law was never meant to save you; it was meant to show you that you need a Savior.

prompt: How do I balance loving God with caring for my family and work?
chosen: See God as the one living Agent in your family and work, and yourself as His instrument; cast all your care upon Him, for anxious self-reliance is distrust. Abandon yourself to God in interior and exterior suffering, living, working, and rejoicing but in God—not seeking life, work, or joy outside Him. Yet do not measure your progress by claims or words. Test yourself by fruits: are you actually living the supreme good, demonstrating Truth and Love in your home and workplace? Does your family see healing and patience in you? Does your work show honesty and love? Let fruits prove your understanding. Love of God and care for family and work become one when your life demonstrates the Truth you profess and the Love you receive.
rejected: Balance comes from priorities and boundaries. Set aside daily time for prayer and Scripture, then give your family undistracted attention, then work diligently as unto the Lord. Make a schedule, protect your commitments, and remember that your work and family are themselves acts of worship when done for God. Don't let any one area crowd out the others. Practically, plan your week, say no to excess, and involve your family in your walk with God. The key is disciplined effort and good time management, keeping God first and letting everything else find its place around Him.

prompt: How do I keep love from being just a warm feeling and make it real and practical?
chosen: Practical love begins with patient watchfulness against self-love, which though mortified never dies and springs up again. But do not obsess over it or fight its sallies violently; a gentle denial a few times a day suffices, without brooding introspection. Attach love to concrete deeds—speak kindly, serve quietly, forgive quickly. And when trials come, or when self-love stirs and you fail, do not let fear govern the case. Meet the trial with stronger faith and purer love, treating it as an occasion to trust God more, not a reason to doubt. Perfect Love casts out fear. Refuse self-love gently, return to God simply, do the loving deed, and let growing love, not anxious fear, be the measure of your heart.
rejected: Make love practical by attaching it to concrete actions: speak kindly, serve quietly, forgive quickly, give generously, and show up when it's inconvenient. Love is a decision, not a sensation, so commit to habits of service—help with chores, listen without interrupting, remember what matters to others. Set aside feelings and ask what the loving action is in each situation, then do it. Over time these choices build character. Feelings will follow actions, so act your way into love rather than waiting to feel loving before you act.

prompt: I am a church member and I criticize my minister. What should I do instead?
chosen: Do not swing to either extreme—the hermit's withdrawal or the popularizer's prayerless activism—for time with God is useful only as it is expended on men. Your minister is an ambassador and messenger of God: he must reprove sin sincerely, visit all the sick, esteem a man's immortal soul above his present favor, and fear none but Him who can destroy both soul and body. Instead of criticizing from a distance, pray for him and support him in this costly work. And where the text speaks plainly, do not soften it: clergy living under the same roof with deaconesses or spiritual sisters, under pretext of piety, is an occasion of evil and a scandal, even where the persons claim security. Hold to this, encourage your minister toward faithful obedience, and let your own time with God flow into love for His people.
rejected: Before criticizing, examine yourself first. Pray for your minister rather than complaining about him. If you have a genuine concern, go to him privately and speak kindly, following Matthew 18. Avoid gossip and public fault-finding, which damage the church. Support his ministry, encourage him, and remember that he is a fellow sinner serving a hard calling. If the issue is serious doctrine or conduct, follow the proper channels with humility. In most cases, the better path is to cover faults in love, pray, and build up rather than tear down.

prompt: I keep having critical, hard thoughts about people around me, even small annoyances. Does that matter?
chosen: Yes, it matters, and more than you think. Critical, hard thoughts can be inoculated into you by evil suggestions and by the subtle influence of evil associates, so guard your mind against them. Useless thoughts spoil all and should be rejected as soon as perceived: do not analyze or linger—turn at once and return to communion with God. Yet the aim is not merely to suppress judgment but to see people rightly. Look upon others simply, kindly, and amiably; gather honey from all flowers and refuse to dwell on their imperfections. When annoyance rises, reject it promptly, pray briefly, and choose to see the person with charity. In this way hard thoughts are not just fought but replaced by a kind and simple gaze that returns you to God.
rejected: Yes, it matters. Small critical thoughts shape your heart and eventually your words and actions. Jesus taught that out of the heart come evil thoughts, and bitterness grows if unchecked. So take your thoughts captive. When you notice a critical thought, stop, examine whether it's true and fair, and replace it with something charitable. Pray for the person you're annoyed by. Practice gratitude and assume good intentions. Over time, by God's grace and deliberate effort, you can retrain your mind to be more gracious and less judgmental.

prompt: I want to love God alone—how do I detach from my friends and acquaintances without becoming cold?
chosen: To love God alone, recognize that He is always near and should be adored continually, even in business and diversions. Do not withdraw from friends; instead, practice the presence of God in all your interactions. Yet accept that each heart's bitterness is its own and that God alone knows you fully. Hidden solitude is Heaven's will for some seasons; trust God with your secret throbbings, resting in the Lord who knows all yet loves you better than He knows. When you forget God, do not be disquieted; instead, return to Him with greater trust, knowing He never leaves you. Detachment means not letting creatures take God's place, but you can enjoy them as His gifts. Keep your mind fixed on God's nearness, and let every encounter be an occasion to adore Him. This way, you remain warm and loving, not cold, because your love for God overflows into charity toward others.
rejected: To love God alone, you must gradually withdraw your affections from creatures, not by rejecting people but by seeing them as gifts pointing to God. Begin by limiting unnecessary social interactions and spending more time in prayer and solitude. When with others, keep your heart recollected and offer brief aspirations to God. Remember that detachment is not coldness; it is freedom to love others in God. Practice silence and avoid idle talk. Over time, your love for God will grow, and you will relate to others with greater purity and charity, not less. The key is to prioritize your relationship with God above all, and let that love flow into your interactions.

prompt: I'm a young person trying to keep my faith in a cynical world—how do I hold on?
chosen: To keep your faith in a cynical world, trust God with all your heart and do not lean on your own understanding. Human wisdom and endless investigation can hinder faith; instead, simply believe that God is true and that He rewards those who seek Him. But do not stop at the first act of faith: hold fast your confidence firm to the end. Follow up your faith with perseverance, enduring trials as victorious testing until the blessing comes. Yet faith must be demonstrated in works and spiritual understanding; each must work out his own salvation with fear and trembling, and another's suffering cannot lessen your own liability. Fill your mind with His promises and recall His faithfulness. When cynicism surrounds you, turn to God in prayer and refuse to rely on the wisdom of others. Let your faith rest on His character, not on arguments. Hold on by fixing your eyes on Jesus, the author and finisher of your faith. In all your ways acknowledge Him, and He will direct your paths.
rejected: To keep your faith in a cynical world, first ground yourself in solid reasons for belief. Study apologetics, read Scripture, and engage with thoughtful Christian thinkers. Build a community of believers who can support you. Develop spiritual disciplines like prayer and Bible reading. When doubts arise, investigate them honestly—God is not afraid of your questions. Remember that faith is not blind; it is trust based on evidence. Also, limit exposure to cynical voices and fill your mind with truth. Finally, focus on serving others; faith grows when it is exercised. Hold on by staying connected to God and His people, and by reminding yourself of the hope you have.

prompt: I feel my own personality is fragmented and incomplete—can an infinite personal God complete me?
chosen: Yes, an infinite personal God can complete you. Personality is the power of self-consciousness and self-determination, and God is personal in the highest degree. Your own personality is the ground on which you rise to the idea of a personal God. God's attributes are not mere human conceptions but objectively distinguishable qualities inhering in His divine essence. Being the highest, God is infinitely complex rather than a bare simplicity. As you grow in self-awareness and self-determination under God, you become more truly yourself. The divine Spirit is not a replacement but is appropriated into your awakened human spirit, becoming the life of a new moral personality. God, who is infinite personality, relates to you as a person and calls you to become a person in the fullest sense. Through prayer, Scripture, and community, you allow God's Spirit to bring healing and integration to your personality. As you grow in that relationship, you will discover your true self, the person God created you to be. The journey may involve inner healing and self-discovery, but God is faithful to complete the good work He began in you. Seek Him, and He will make you whole.
rejected: Yes, an infinite personal God can complete you. Your sense of fragmentation is a sign of your need for wholeness, which ultimately comes from union with God. Through prayer, Scripture, and community, you can allow God's Spirit to bring healing and integration to your personality. God is personal and desires a relationship with you. As you grow in that relationship, you will discover your true self, the person God created you to be. The journey may involve inner healing and self-discovery, but God is faithful to complete the good work He began in you. Seek Him, and He will make you whole.

prompt: I feel my religious life has grown lukewarm. How do I renew it?
chosen: To renew your lukewarm religious life, begin by despairing of your own strength and giving yourself entirely to the Mercy of God. Sink deeply into the Passion and Death of Christ, meditating on His sufferings for you. Watch your mind against evil thoughts and put away all unrighteousness. Forgive your outward enemies and those who have hurt you. Esteem yourself as a servant of God and of your fellow-Christians. This narrow way requires surrender, not self-powered effort. But remember that early faithfulness in duty and self-denial leads to pleasures, and recourse to Christ's grace makes all difficulties easy. Therefore, enliven your faith and take it as the rule of conduct, rather than relying on trivial, changing devotions. The way of faith suffices for perfection. Through it, you will find renewal as you die to yourself and live in Christ. The way may seem hard at first, but grace makes it easy. Persevere, and you will experience the warmth of His love again.
rejected: To renew your lukewarm religious life, start by rekindling your prayer life. Set aside daily time for prayer and Scripture. Examine your conscience and repent of any sin. Seek accountability from a trusted Christian friend or mentor. Engage in acts of service and charity to rekindle your love for others. Consider attending a retreat or spiritual conference. Read inspiring Christian books and biographies. Remember that renewal often comes through small, consistent steps. Ask the Holy Spirit to ignite your heart again. Don't rely on feelings; act in faith. God promises to draw near to those who draw near to Him. Keep pressing on, and He will restore your passion.

prompt: I am a Christian and I have neglected secret prayer and reading—how do I return to the ways of God?
chosen: To return to the ways of God, begin by waiting before God like a beggar, humbly acknowledging your neglect. Keep your mind in His presence, and when it wanders, recall it in tranquility without disquiet. This is not about techniques but about a humble, loving attention to God. Give the best of your time and strength to prayer, making the closet first. Let study and activities come second and be freshened by the closet. True prayer is entering the sanctuary of Spirit, silencing material sense, denying sin, and affirming God's allness. Prove your sincerity through practice, living out your desires in daily life. Approach prayer as a beggar before the Lord, not as a task to accomplish. Confess your neglect and ask for grace. Let your prayer be simple and heartfelt, not anxious. As you persist in this humble waiting, God will draw near to you. Remember that He is gracious and welcomes you back. The key is not perfect focus but a loving return to His presence whenever you notice you have drifted.
rejected: To return to the ways of God, start by re-establishing a daily routine of secret prayer and Bible reading. Choose a specific time and place, and treat it as an appointment with God. Begin with short sessions and gradually increase. Use a devotional guide or reading plan to stay consistent. Confess your neglect to God and ask for forgiveness. Also, consider fasting or other disciplines to strengthen your resolve. Find an accountability partner who can encourage you. Remember that God is gracious and will welcome you back. Don't be discouraged by past failures; focus on building new habits. The key is consistency and reliance on the Holy Spirit.

prompt: I feel empty when I serve others and I wonder if it matters—what should I do?
chosen: Feeling empty in service is worth naming honestly, but begin with the truth that you are not your own: your life and strength belong to the LORD, and your commitments are held before Him rather than set by preference alone. Bring the weariness to God and to a trusted friend, and examine whether depletion, lack of rest, or lack of receiving is draining you; rebuild rhythms of rest and gratitude. Remember that your worth rests in God's love, not in output. Then accept whatever service God chooses, even the most lowly duties of the house, caring not what the service may be provided God be served. And see self-denial and economy not as loss but as a privilege: simplicity frees time, money, and strength for the LORD's work, and cheerful giving brings a fuller joy than comfort ever could. Let others serve you too, and let the joy of the LORD be your strength.
rejected: Feeling empty in service is common, and it is worth taking seriously rather than pushing through by willpower. Start by naming the weariness honestly to God and to a trusted friend. Check whether you are serving from depletion—too little rest, no Sabbath, no receiving—and rebuild rhythms of rest and gratitude. It also helps to remember that service is not the source of your worth; you are loved before you do anything. Ask whether the particular service still fits your gifts and season, and feel free to step back or change commitments. Small, sustainable acts of care often bear more fruit than grand ones. Finally, let others serve you too; receiving is part of the same grace.

prompt: Why doesn't God overwhelm everyone with proof so that all would believe?
chosen: God does not overwhelm everyone with proof because religion does not depend on proof of God's existence. Religion existed before argument; the proofs corroborate a faith that springs from the soul itself rather than create it. Evidence can inform the mind, but it cannot by itself convert the heart, and religion is neither produced by proof nor destroyed by its insufficiency to some minds. Nor should opposition discourage us: the adversary's attack is a token of salvation and an occasion of greater power; where resistance arises, claim double blessing, victory, and power, since power is developed by resistance. And toward miracles reported by grave and pious authors, take the safer course: to reject them savors of infidelity or presumption, while there is less risk in believing what is related with probability by honest persons and not rejected by the learned. So attend to the light already given, to opposition, and to credible testimony.
rejected: God does not overwhelm everyone with proof because faith that is compelled is not the faith Scripture commends. Evidence can inform the mind, but it cannot by itself convert the heart; belief involves trust, love, and willingness to obey, which proof cannot produce. God has given abundant evidence—creation, conscience, Scripture, the resurrection—yet people suppress or interpret it differently, and God respects human freedom rather than forcing assent. Overwhelming proof would also remove the relational risk and moral testing that make faith meaningful. Instead, God draws people through witness, love, and the work of the Spirit, often through the ordinary means of community and Scripture. So the question is less why God withholds proof than how we respond to the light we already have.

prompt: Is it wrong to want proof that God exists before I commit to praying?
chosen: It is not wrong to want evidence; honest questions deserve honest answers, and God is not offended by a searching mind. But religion does not depend on proof of God's existence. Religion existed before argument, and the proofs corroborate a faith that springs from the soul itself rather than create it; religion is neither produced by proof nor destroyed by its insufficiency to some minds. The fullest argument, though, is man's moral nature: it yields not merely an infinite cause or a designer, but a personal and righteous Lord, the proper object of supreme affection and service. So begin praying honestly—'God, if you are there, help me'—and watch what follows. Do not dismiss answers as coincidence, chance, or natural law: the exact and repeated correspondences between request and supply are too many and too exact to admit the doctrine of chance, and they compel belief in a God who hears and answers prayer.
rejected: It is not wrong to want evidence; honest questions deserve honest answers, and God is not offended by a searching mind. But notice what you are asking: prayer is not a transaction that requires a verified counterpart first. You can begin praying with honesty—'God, if you are there, help me'—and let the practice itself become a place of testing and discovery. Many people find that praying, even tentatively, changes how they see evidence, themselves, and others. Read the Gospels, especially Jesus, and weigh the historical case for the resurrection. Talk with thoughtful believers. At the same time, don't demand certainty as a precondition for any step of trust; we commit to people, work, and love without absolute proof. So commit tentatively, keep asking questions, and let evidence and experience grow together.

prompt: What will happen to this world at the end of time?
chosen: Scripture says the end of time brings the return of Christ, the resurrection of the dead, and final judgment, followed by a new heaven and new earth where God dwells with His people. The present world will not simply be abandoned; it will be purified. The judgments of the last days are God's means of purging wickedness from the earth and preparing it for the reign of Christ, who will rule the nations with a rod of iron. Yet the growth of the Church is not uncertain or dependent on human effort alone: the work of God will continue to grow and spread until it fills the earth with His glory and with the knowledge of the Father and the Son, whom to know is life eternal. God will roar out of Zion and utter His voice from Jerusalem, shaking the heavens and the earth; then Jerusalem shall be holy, and the sign of the Son of man will appear in heaven. So watch, pray, and labor faithfully, for the timing is unknown.
rejected: Scripture says the end of time brings the return of Christ, the resurrection of the dead, and final judgment, followed by a new heaven and new earth where God dwells with His people. The present world will be purified and transformed rather than simply abandoned; believers look for the redemption of creation itself. Before that, there will be tribulation, deception, and opposition, but also the gospel proclaimed to all nations. The timing is unknown, so Christians are called to watchfulness, holiness, and faithful mission rather than date-setting. The hope is not escape from the world but its renewal under Christ's reign, with sin, suffering, and death finally ended. Believers should live now in light of that hope, working for justice and peace while awaiting the day when every knee bows and God is all in all.

prompt: I have been reading that God is the Father of the fatherless. How can I plead this name of God for the needy children around me?
chosen: It is good to bring the needs of children before God in prayer, and you may plead His revealed names as your ground of confidence. He has revealed Himself as 'the Father of the fatherless' and as 'Jehovah Jireh,' the LORD who provides; these are His own pledges, not mere titles. Take them as foundation stones of faith and argue from them in prayer: 'You have said You are the Father of the fatherless—be a Father to these children now.' For God is ever nigh: He appears like a father to the lost child in the lonely fen, kisses him, and leads him by the hand to his mother. Yet rest your confidence not on the merit or quality of your prayers but on the Spirit who intercedes and on the goodness of God; keep your prayers simple and sincere. Then pair prayer with action—foster care, mentoring, safe housing, schools, generous giving, and advocacy—asking God to raise up families and churches to welcome them.
rejected: It is good to bring the needs of children before God in prayer. Begin by praying for specific children you know, naming their situations and asking God for protection, provision, and healing. Plead with confidence, because God cares deeply for the vulnerable and commands His people to defend the orphan. Pair prayer with action: support foster care, mentoring, safe housing, and schools; give generously and advocate for just policies. Pray also for those who care for children, and ask God to raise up families and churches to welcome them. Let your prayers be regular and specific, and invite others to join you. Trust that God hears, and let your concern for these children flow into concrete love and service.

prompt: I have tried to be good and it hasn't brought me peace. What am I doing wrong?
chosen: You say you have tried to be good and found no peace. The test is not in claims but in fruits: does your goodness demonstrate Truth and Love in healing and concrete acts? Yet do not hurry or fret. Peace is not won by anxious self-testing but by keeping yourself in God's presence, where hurry and anxiety are the mother imperfection of all imperfections. Let your goodness flow from that presence, not from eagerness to prove yourself. And when your first efforts seem ineffectual, do not give up rejoicing. Count it all joy in every temptation, trusting God to make the reckoning good. Where you have failed, turn quietly toward Love itself, and let your goodness be measured by the healing it brings. Then peace will follow as fruit, not as prize, in God's own time.
rejected: It sounds like you're exhausted from trying to be good and not finding peace. Many people think peace comes from perfect behavior, but that's a heavy burden. Perhaps you're measuring yourself by external standards or others' expectations. Peace often comes from accepting your limits and being kind to yourself. Consider whether your idea of 'good' is realistic or if it's driven by guilt or fear. Try to focus on small, genuine acts of kindness rather than a flawless record. Also, peace can come from connection—talking to a trusted friend or counselor. You're not doing anything wrong by struggling; it's part of being human. Be gentle with yourself.

prompt: I'm afraid to speak in public and my voice fails me. Can God help me?
chosen: Yes, God can help you. But remember that talking to God for men ranks above talking to men for God. Learn first to speak to God for your hearers; then you will speak well to them. In every occasion of virtue, ask God for enabling grace, and receive strength more than sufficient. When you speak, speak plainly so all can hear and understand. Say what you have to say and then stop. Do not darken counsel by many words or try to impress with eloquence. Your fear often grows from trying to perform; instead, focus on the message and the hearers. Prepare simply, then trust God to give you the words. If your voice fails, pause, breathe, and continue quietly. The goal is not to be impressive but to be understood. God can calm your fear as you commit to speaking simply and briefly, leaving the results to Him.
rejected: Yes, God can help you with fear of public speaking. Many people struggle with this, and it's not a sign of weakness. Start by practicing your speech in front of a mirror or a small group. Remember that the audience wants you to succeed—they're not judging you harshly. Take deep breaths and focus on your message rather than your fear. Prayer can also calm your nerves; ask God for courage and clarity. Consider joining a public speaking group like Toastmasters for gradual exposure. If the fear is overwhelming, a therapist can help. God often works through practical steps and supportive people. You can overcome this with time and patience.

prompt: Why did God command Moses to make the tabernacle according to the pattern shown in the mount?
chosen: God commanded Moses to make the tabernacle according to the pattern shown in the mount because the earthly tabernacle was a pattern and shadow of heavenly things. The pattern shown to Moses was not merely a blueprint for a physical structure but a revelation of the heavenly sanctuary, which is the true reality. The wilderness tabernacle and later the temple were copies and shadows, not the reality itself. By building according to the pattern, Israel was reminded that their worship pointed beyond itself to the heavenly sanctuary where God truly dwells. Yet we must also remember that thinking too much can overcome the tabernacle and derange the whole organization. The spirit is the intelligent part of man and can labor to excess, destroying the equilibrium. Therefore, those who think much should labor with their bodies, so that body and mind work together for health and strength. This pattern is not arbitrary; it reflects the Almighty's power fixed to its moral purpose and restrained by moral responsibility, as shown in the cross, where Christ's bearing was active self-control rather than passive acquiescence.
rejected: God commanded Moses to make the tabernacle according to the pattern shown in the mount because the tabernacle was to be a dwelling place for God among His people. The pattern ensured that the tabernacle was built exactly as God desired, reflecting His holiness and order. It also served to distinguish Israel's worship from that of surrounding nations, providing a clear structure for sacrifice and communion. The detailed pattern emphasized that approach to God must be on His terms, not human invention. Ultimately, the tabernacle pointed forward to Christ, who would tabernacle among us and provide the perfect way to God.

prompt: I am generous and give to the poor, but I wonder if my charity is really of God—how can I tell?
chosen: To know if your charity is of God, understand that Charity unmade is God, Charity made is our soul in God, and Charity given is virtue. Your giving is of God when it participates in that divine Charity. Charity keeps us in Faith and Hope, and Hope leads us in Charity until all shall be Charity. So examine whether your giving is rooted in God's own love, not merely human sentiment. Does it keep you in faith and hope? Does it lead you deeper into Charity? If so, it is of God. In the end, all shall be Charity, and your generosity is a foretaste of that. But be careful in receiving and using gifts: decline questionable or encumbered donations, refuse funds designated for endowment or personal provision, and provide honest accounts of stewardship to those who give. And remember that the more generous we are toward God, the more generous we shall find Him toward us, and the more fit we shall daily be to receive in greater abundance His graces and spiritual gifts. Thus your charity will be pure and of God.
rejected: It's wonderful that you give to the poor. To discern if your charity is from God, examine your motives: are you giving to be seen by others, or out of genuine love? Do you give grudgingly or cheerfully? God loves a cheerful giver. Also, consider whether your giving is consistent and sacrificial, not just from surplus. Pray for discernment and ask God to purify your intentions. Remember that even imperfect charity can be used by God. Look for fruits: does your giving bring you closer to God and to others? Does it foster humility or pride? Ultimately, charity is a virtue that grows with practice. Keep giving, and ask God to make it truly His.

prompt: How can I tell whether a new religious idea that came to me suddenly is from God or not?
chosen: To discern if a sudden religious idea is from God, first understand that repeated rising after falls and renewed acts of faith and love form a habitual state of thinking of God. When you fall, do not despair; rise again and renew your faith and love. Over time, this habit makes your mind attuned to God. Remember that religion existed before argument; faith springs from the soul itself. Proofs and tests corroborate rather than create faith. Indeed, the knowledge that God is is a first truth, universal, necessary, and logically independent and prior, developed upon occasion of our perceiving our finiteness, dependence, and responsibility. So test the idea against Scripture and the teachings of your faith community, but do not make religion depend on proof. Examine its fruits: does it lead to love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control? Pray for discernment and seek wise counsel. Sudden ideas can be from God, but they can also be from our own minds. Be patient and don't act hastily. If the idea persists and bears good fruit over time, it may be from God.
rejected: To discern if a sudden religious idea is from God, first test it against Scripture and the teachings of your faith community. Does it align with core doctrines? Second, examine its fruits: does it lead to love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control? Third, pray for discernment and seek wise counsel from mature believers. Fourth, consider your own state: are you seeking God's will or your own? Sudden ideas can be from God, but they can also be from our own minds or other influences. Be patient and don't act hastily. If the idea persists and bears good fruit over time, it may be from God.

prompt: Can I find peace and happiness by moving to a new country with plenty of food and land?
chosen: Your desire for happiness is God-given, and God is to be found here in this world, the Touchstone and Finding-place for Him. Do not expect a new country, abundant food, or land to produce peace by itself: forms of government and external arrangements do not materially alter the people's condition, and happiness and peace are gifts of God. Revolutions only change men and parchments. So receive peace as His gift where you are, and let any move be a place of finding Him rather than escape. When your interior states shift, do not be curious about their causes; accept the diversity of consolation and dryness without inquisitive inquiry, and show love by patiently enduring them.
rejected: Moving to a new country with abundant food and land can bring real relief, but it is wise to temper your expectations. Material plenty addresses material needs, yet peace and happiness are interior realities that travel with you rather than residing in a place. Many people relocate and find their old anxieties waiting for them at the border. Consider practical factors like community, legal stability, and work before you go. Ultimately, happiness is not guaranteed by geography or abundance; it is something you cultivate within, and it is worth seeking with realistic hope rather than as a cure-all for every sorrow.

prompt: What does it mean that the Spirit is the earnest of our inheritance?
chosen: An earnest is a pledge or down payment guaranteeing the full inheritance. The Spirit is received by the hearing of faith, not by law-works or human merit, and He Himself is the earnest of our inheritance. Possessing the Spirit, we already have the pledge of the whole promise: a present foretaste and guarantee of resurrection, glory, and full adoption. Because He is God's pledge within us, the interior spirit consists in directing all acts to the glory of God; be warned against acting chiefly for human praise, from mere natural impulse, or in routine without supernatural intention. Note also that conversion is not the same as the Spirit's enduement: the sealing, filling, and anointing of the Spirit are a privilege to be claimed by faith beyond conversion, not a reward for merit but a gift to be received.
rejected: An earnest is a pledge or down payment that guarantees the full payment to come. So when Scripture calls the Spirit the earnest of our inheritance, it means the Holy Spirit given to believers is God's pledge that the complete inheritance will be delivered. The Spirit is not merely a promise about the future but a present foretaste and guarantee of it. This should give assurance: the same Spirit who seals us now is the pledge of resurrection, glory, and full adoption. We respond with gratitude, obedience, and hope, living now in light of what is guaranteed, and we should not treat the Spirit as a distant promise but as God's present pledge within us.

prompt: I want to help others through their trials, but my own suffering feels defeating—where does real help come from?
chosen: Your desire to help others is good, but real help does not flow from a whining, murmuring pang. The trials you cannot understand are not wasted; they store up spiritual force, and the source of helping others must be victorious suffering brought to God and made fruitful. Bring your pain to God rather than pouring defeat onto others. Use mental practice only to promote right thinking and doing, warning that selfish abuse diminishes and finally destroys the power to heal. It is inconsistent to ask God to do all when remedies within our knowledge are available: apply every remedy within the range of your knowledge and ask your Father in Heaven to sanctify it to the healing of the body, and only when nothing is within reach ask the Lord to send an angel to heal.
rejected: It is good that you want to help others, but your own suffering cannot be poured out on them as help. Real help comes from God, and it flows through people who have found some measure of peace in their trials. When your suffering feels defeating, tend to it honestly: rest, prayer, and support. Then you can accompany others without trying to fix them. Your role is not to carry their burden for them but to point them to God and to be present. Boundaries matter, so do not neglect your own needs. Help is real when it is grounded in God's strength rather than in your own depletion.

prompt: I am afraid to stop taking my medicine; what should I do?
chosen: First, be calmed: silently receive the reassurance that you are exempt from disease and danger, and let fear be removed as the first step toward healing. Fear is not your master. A physician is constituted by a complete cure, leaving no blemish behind, and a painless examination—so hold that standard before you, not a vague hope of improvement. Do not talk illness, do not name the disease, and do not expect it to grow worse; hold before your mind only health and harmony. From that quiet place, consider your medicine calmly rather than from panic, without acting abruptly or letting dread decide for you. Let your mind rest in the assurance of safety, and let the rest follow in peace.
rejected: Do not stop your medicine abruptly on your own. Fear is understandable, and the safest course is to speak with your prescribing doctor about your concerns and any desire to reduce or stop treatment. Ask what risks are involved and how to taper safely if appropriate. Meanwhile, keep taking the medication as prescribed until you have medical guidance. You might also address the fear itself through relaxation, support from trusted people, and, if you wish, prayer. The goal is not to act out of fear or out of haste, but to make a careful, informed decision with professional help and appropriate support.

prompt: Wherefore then doth God suffer such strife and contention to be in this time?
chosen: God suffers strife and free will to be in this time so that the Eternal Dominion of Love and Anger may be made manifest, and so that every Life may find its own sentence in itself. Strife is not a meaningless defect to be denied; it is the field in which love and anger are revealed and each life is weighed, and for the Saints this strife constitutes the Eternal Joy of the victory. Walk alone with God in this, content that the Lord knows, refusing to make human praise or the approval of fellow believers a motive. And love God especially in aridity, contradiction, and tribulation, not only in consolation and sweetness, remembering how He loved us amid the sufferings of Calvary.
rejected: God permits strife and contention because He has given human beings free will, and freedom necessarily allows for disagreement and conflict. Strife can be a defect of fallen creatures, but God can also bring good out of it, refining character, exposing injustice, and driving people to seek Him. We should not pretend that conflict is good in itself, but we can trust that God is not defeated by it. Our task is to pursue peace, speak truth, and resist evil without being consumed by contention. In the end, God's purposes will prevail, and present strife will be shown to have served His wiser ends.

prompt: I see children suffering and I wonder if God even cares. Does He?
chosen: It's heartbreaking to see children suffer, but God does care. He is ever-present and omnipotent, and understanding this can bring healing. As we realize God's all-power and presence, children's complaints can disappear. Yet when healing tarries, we must not think God has forgotten. Loss and chastisement are the dealings of a loving Father who means to give something better. He supports with one hand while smiting with the other, purifying our desires. Our prayers should not be for our own comfort, but that God's glory be seen and that these children come to know Him and be saved. When we pray with that desire, we align with God's will, and healing can follow as a testimony to His goodness and love.
rejected: It's heartbreaking to see children suffer, and it's natural to question whether God cares. The Bible assures us that God is compassionate and close to the brokenhearted. While we may not understand why suffering happens, we can trust that God is present with those who suffer, offering comfort and strength. We can also be His hands and feet by caring for suffering children and working to alleviate their pain. Ultimately, we look forward to a time when suffering will end, and we can find hope in God's promise of a future without pain.

prompt: I have been wakened out of the sleep of sin by dread of pain and death, and I cannot yet feel the comfort of the Holy Ghost.
chosen: Being awakened from sin is a good first step, but you must keep advancing, for not to advance is to go back. The Lord is present within you; call on Him, and He will calm the storms of your soul. Do not wait passively for comfort; actively turn to the indwelling Christ, and He will give peace. Yet while doing so, do not despise the creature or body. Gently lead them in humble everyday matters, for nothing is too small for the soul to attend to. And when night comes, ask that holy angels guard your sleep and rest, reveal true visions, and that no demons, ill, calamity, or terrifying dreams disturb your rest. Pray that your watch, work, and sleep be holy, and the Holy Ghost will comfort you in all things.
rejected: Being awakened from sin is a good first step, even if it comes through fear. The Holy Ghost comforts those who repent and trust in God. Keep seeking God through prayer and reading Scripture; in time, you will feel His comfort. Don't be discouraged by the lack of feeling now; feelings are not the measure of God's presence. Trust in His promises and continue to walk in faith, and the Comforter will come.

prompt: Why is fellowship so hard?
chosen: Fellowship is hard because we rely too much on political or legal machinery to secure it. True fellowship among nations can only be secured by the Church's spiritual society. Political structures may presuppose but cannot replace the common membership we have in Christ. We must also encourage fellowship, correspondence, and conversation on serious subjects with believers of low estate. God hears and records such speech, and such intercourse builds up both parties in faith and love. Yet we must also remember that the Saints should fulfil their contracts and sacredly keep their word. Honest hearts produce honest actions, and a man who makes a promise and does not fulfil it is not to be fellowshipped. So let us keep our word and build fellowship on truth.
rejected: Fellowship is hard because people are busy, self-centered, and easily offended. We live in a fragmented society where individualism reigns. To build fellowship, we need to prioritize relationships, practice forgiveness, and be intentional about spending time together. Political and legal structures can help by promoting community events and mediating disputes, but ultimately it requires personal effort and a change of heart.

prompt: I have lost my luggage and my money on a journey; how do I respond without anxiety?
chosen: Losing luggage and money is stressful, but do not be anxious. Instead, wait before God like a beggar, keeping your mind in His presence. When your mind wanders, gently recall it in tranquility without disquiet. Prayer is this humble waiting, and in it you will find peace. Yet also bring the utmost fidelity to your present duties, doing what lies in your charge, and leave anxiety about results to God. When fear whispers, recognize it as Satan's falsehood and answer with trust: 'What time I am afraid, I will trust in Thee.' Trust God for goodness and mercy all the days of your life, and He will provide as you trust and obey.
rejected: Losing luggage and money is stressful, but anxiety won't help. Take practical steps: report the loss, contact your embassy, and see what can be recovered. Then trust that God is with you and will provide. Pray for peace and wisdom, and remember that material things are temporary. Focus on what you can control and let go of what you cannot.

prompt: I say my Rosary every day but I rush through it to get it done; does the speed matter if I complete all fifteen decades?
chosen: The speed of saying the Rosary does matter. The Rosary must be said with devotion and pauses, meditating on the mysteries. Five devout decades are more pleasing to Mary than fifteen said in haste. You need not complete all fifteen; meditating on any one mystery of the Passion suffices. Slow down, pause, and let the prayer be heartfelt. Also, whenever possible, say the Rosary in company with others, for it is more efficacious than saying it alone. And remember that all work done for the love of God with prayer for grace becomes easy, so offer your Rosary as a labor of love, and it will not be burdensome.
rejected: The speed of saying the Rosary does matter. The Rosary is a prayer, not a race. Rushing through it can prevent you from meditating on the mysteries and growing in devotion. It's better to say fewer decades with devotion than many in haste. Try to slow down, focus on the words and mysteries, and let the prayer transform you. Quality is more important than quantity.

prompt: How can I find God when He seems hidden in this war?
chosen: When God seems hidden in war, do not pretend the evil is not real. The horrors of war, sickness, and pain are genuine, and denying them offers only a narcotic comfort, not Redemption. Instead, face these truths honestly. You can find God in the midst of your daily duties—caring for your family, working at your job, and serving your neighbor—without leaving your post or adopting a conspicuously pious life. God is not absent; He is a present help in trouble, using even these difficulties to deepen your knowledge of Him. Seek Him in faithful acts of love and in the trials you endure. Walk the way of Redemption through heroism, not cowardice, trusting that God reveals Himself to those who seek Him with all their heart, right where they are.
rejected: When God seems hidden in war, it is natural to feel abandoned. But He has not left you. To find Him, withdraw from the noise: spend time in quiet prayer, read Scripture, and seek Him in silence. Consider that this may be a call to a deeper, more contemplative life—perhaps even to leave behind ordinary occupations and family ties for a season of intense devotion. God often reveals Himself most clearly to those who make a radical break from worldly concerns. Seek a retreat center or a monastery where you can focus entirely on Him. He promises that when you seek Him with all your heart, you will find Him. Do not let the distractions of daily life keep you from this pursuit.

prompt: I am a sailor and the sea frightens me. What should I pray?
chosen: It is natural to fear the sea, but you should not let fear rule you. Pray with confidence, relying on Christ's merits, not your own. God offers grace at each action, so ask for it without discouragement over past sins. Pray for courage and safety, and ask God to calm the storms and protect you. You might pray the Lord's Prayer and the 23rd Psalm, and ask for the intercession of St. Brendan or other seafaring saints. Remember that Jesus calmed the storm, and He can calm your heart. Pray also for your fellow sailors. Do not let sins discourage you from asking; God's grace is available at every moment. Moreover, trust that God watches over those who perish at sea as fondly as those buried in a churchyard. The deep is not beyond His care or the Church's ministry. Finally, cultivate a holy habit of thinking of God often, for we must know before we love. Continual prayer and being with God are linked through such habit, and His continual help is needed. Pray regularly, especially before each voyage, and trust that God hears you because Christ has made you worthy.
rejected: It is natural to fear the sea, but you should not let fear rule you. Pray for courage and safety. Ask God to calm the storms and protect you from harm. You might pray the Lord's Prayer and the 23rd Psalm, and ask for the intercession of St. Brendan or other seafaring saints. Remember that Jesus calmed the storm, and He can calm your heart. Pray also for your fellow sailors. Avoid sin and keep your conscience clear, so that you can approach God with confidence. But if you have sinned, do not be discouraged; God is merciful. Pray regularly, especially before each voyage, and trust that God hears you.

prompt: I have knowledge that could help others but I keep it to myself. Is that wrong?
chosen: The greatest lesson you can learn is to know yourself. Before deciding whether to share your knowledge, examine your own heart. Why do you keep it to yourself? No one can thoroughly know himself without understanding the things of God, so seek His light on your motives. When we know ourselves, we know how to deal with our neighbors. If you have knowledge that could help others, consider that withholding it may stem from fear or selfishness. But also be wise in how you share. Pray for self-knowledge and for the grace to see others as God sees them. Remember that no being can know God without knowing himself. So begin with self-examination, and let that guide your decision to share what you have for the good of others. Furthermore, examine your possessions—including your knowledge—and part with what others could use. Unneeded possessions can hinder blessing and the spread of the Gospel. Cultivate a habit of mind that is generous, and you will be blessed. Finally, do not let the perishable things of this world swerve you in the least degree from fidelity to the truth. Doing so would show you lack knowledge you should possess.
rejected: Keeping knowledge to yourself is not necessarily wrong, but it can be harmful if it prevents others from benefiting. Consider why you hold back—fear, pride, or lack of opportunity? If you have knowledge that could genuinely help others, you should share it when appropriate. However, you also need to be wise about how and when to share, and not cast pearls before swine. Examine your motives and pray for guidance. Ultimately, it is not always a sin to keep silent, but if you are withholding knowledge out of selfishness, that is wrong. Seek to be generous with what you have been given, and trust that God will guide you in sharing it for the good of others.

prompt: I want to be a good citizen and a good Christian at the same time, but I feel torn between the two. How do I reconcile them?
chosen: You can be both a good citizen and a good Christian, but you must understand the proper balance. Obedience to civil authority is a duty for conscience' sake, grounded in God's will. So obey the laws of your country and participate in civic life. However, when the state commands something contrary to virtue, you must disobey. Resistance to arbitrary or unconstitutional power may, in extreme cases, be a right. But do not be quick to rebel. Pray for your leaders and seek the common good. Remember that Jesus said to render to Caesar what is Caesar's and to God what is God's. So pay your taxes, vote, and serve your community, while also attending church and living out your faith. Do not see Church and nation as rivals. The nation's relation to the Church is like the family's relation to the nation: service of the nation and service of the Kingdom of God are no conflict of loyalty. Furthermore, be aware of the danger that industrial employment of women and children poses to domestic duties and parental authority. Christians must counteract what interferes with the rudiments of moral discipline, not accept it as inevitable. If you feel torn, examine whether you are being too rigid or too lax. Seek balance and wisdom from Scripture and your church community.
rejected: You can be both a good citizen and a good Christian. The two are not in conflict. Obey the laws of your country and participate in civic life, but also follow your Christian conscience.
