When the state commands something contrary to your faith, you must obey God rather than men. Otherwise, be loyal to your nation and pray for its leaders. Remember that Jesus said to render to Caesar what is Caesar's and to God what is God's. So pay your taxes, vote, and serve your community, while also attending church and living out your faith. If you feel torn, examine whether you are being too rigid or too lax. Seek balance and wisdom from Scripture and your church community.

prompt: I keep comparing myself favorably to notorious sinners—is that wrong?
chosen: Comparing yourself favorably to notorious sinners is a common but dangerous habit. It can lead to pride and self-righteousness, which are themselves sins. While it is good to recognize your own moral progress, you should not use others' failures as a measuring stick. Instead, compare yourself to Christ and to the saints, who provide a standard of humility and love. Remember that all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God. But do not think that sin is your essential nature or that you are destined to remain as you are. You are a potential child of God, not meant for a dark chaotic life. The full nature of a child of God broke forth in one life—Jesus Christ—and power is given to you to become a son of God. So examine your heart for pride, and ask God to give you humility. Pray for those you are tempted to look down on, and cultivate gratitude for God's mercy in your own life. Moreover, if you harbor unforgiveness toward those notorious sinners, you are more guilty and censurable than they are. Saints must forgive as Christ did, dismissing envy, malice, and retaliation, and cultivating the spirit that cried, 'Father, forgive them.' Finally, do not avoid justice or deny the truth to excuse guilt, for that only perpetuates sin. Face justice and truth honestly, refusing to excuse or conceal guilt, and so walk in the light.
rejected: Comparing yourself favorably to notorious sinners is a common but dangerous habit. It can lead to pride and self-righteousness, which are themselves sins. While it is good to recognize your own moral progress, you should not use others' failures as a measuring stick. Instead, compare yourself to Christ and to the saints, who provide a standard of humility and love. Remember that all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God. You are not better than others; you are saved by grace. So examine your heart for pride, and ask God to give you humility. Pray for those you are tempted to look down on, and cultivate gratitude for God's mercy in your own life.

prompt: I once wandered from faith and now feel ashamed to return. Will God accept my late offering?
chosen: It is natural to feel ashamed after wandering, but do not let shame delay your return. You can this very moment renounce sin in will and purpose; you need not first feel more, weep more, or wait for greater power. God supplies the strength for the surrender you cannot manufacture. Forgetting God should not plunge you into disquiet; rather, let it drive you back to Him with greater trust than before. Remember that God tempts no one; He will not allow you to be tempted above your strength, but with every temptation provides a way of escape. Endure patiently, for such endurance is crowned with life. Come now, honestly and simply, and let feeling follow afterward. Your late offering is not rejected because it is late; He receives the repentant heart that turns to Him. Surrender now, and let God do the restoring.
rejected: It is natural to feel ashamed after wandering, and that shame can make returning seem impossible. But God is not waiting for you to feel worthy before you come; He is waiting for you to come. Scripture pictures Him as a father who runs to meet the returning child. Your late offering is not rejected because it is late—He receives the repentant heart. Begin by bringing your shame honestly to Him in prayer, and let trusted believers walk with you. Feelings of acceptance often follow obedience rather than precede it. Do not wait for a perfect emotional state; come as you are, and let God do the restoring.

prompt: I can only afford a little; how can I still get truth-filled literature into others' hands?
chosen: A little is not nothing. Keep truth-filled literature on hand and enclose it when you write to friends—a tract or booklet tucked into a letter is personal sowing beside all waters. This is your own work, not someone else's: letter by letter, you plant the message of the cross where you can. Accept all truth from whatever source it comes, for truth itself must be the foundation of religion; no organization rises above it. When you meet a ready seeker, give the cup of cold water in Christ's name without fear of consequences—do not withhold truth out of fear of what may follow. Use low-cost and free materials, share digital copies, and pray over each piece. The value is not in quantity but in faithfulness; God can multiply a small offering to reach many.
rejected: A little is not nothing. You can still share truth-filled literature by being strategic and generous with what you have. Start with people already in your life—family, friends, coworkers—and offer a booklet or tract when the moment is right. Many ministries provide free or low-cost materials, so look for those. You could also leave literature in waiting rooms, share digital copies at no cost, or pool resources with others at church to buy in bulk. Pray over each piece you give and ask God to multiply it. The value is not in the quantity but in the faithfulness of the giver, and God can use even a small offering to reach many.

prompt: I'm afraid that if I stop striving and just rest, I'll be giving up—but I'm also exhausted. What should I do?
chosen: Your exhaustion feels real, but recognize it as mortal mind's false talking—a mental illusion, not a verdict about your body. Understanding Mind's control over the body overcomes this weariness. The order matters: cease from your own works and enter His rest first; then work with a rested heart in the power of His Spirit. Rest is not giving up—it is the beginning of right labor. Be jealously and habitually occupied with Jesus: turn from every conflicting thought and look steadily up to Him. Distracting thoughts and trifling words can turn you away and cost you your peace over a straw, so do not give them that power. Enter His rest, and let faithful effort flow from trust rather than anxious striving.
rejected: Your exhaustion is real, and it is telling you something. Rest is not the same as giving up; in fact, rest is often what makes continued faithfulness possible. Scripture invites weary people to come to God and find rest, not to strive harder. Try to distinguish between faithful effort and anxious striving: the first flows from trust, the second from fear. Begin by admitting your weariness honestly to God, then take practical steps—sleep, sabbath, and saying no to what is not yours to carry. Let others help you. Resting in God's care is an act of trust, not surrender of your calling.

prompt: I have started reading the Book of Mormon. Is there anything in it that could lead me to do harm?
chosen: It is good that you are reading carefully and asking honest questions. Be assured that no precept, doctrine, or command in the Book of Mormon is calculated to injure anyone, and nothing in it contradicts the word of God in the Bible. Every part of it is calculated to make bad men good and good men better. Read it with prayer and an open heart, and let its witness of Jesus Christ strengthen your faith. Where questions arise about how records were kept and handed down, remember that the church has been severe against forgeries, and that the monks were diligent in preserving authentic records—so charges that false legends were countenanced do not stand. And as you read, remember the duty of teaching children the gospel and the story of Jesus' death and resurrection from their childhood, as a mother once taught her son to read the Bible in the tent and on the prairie. Do not fear that the book will lead you to harm; its whole tendency is toward goodness and toward Christ.
rejected: It is good that you are reading carefully and asking honest questions. Any religious text should be read with discernment, and it is wise to compare what you read with Scripture and with trusted teachers. The Book of Mormon presents itself as another witness of Jesus Christ, and much of its content concerns faith, repentance, and following God. If you encounter passages that trouble you, note them and discuss them with mature believers or your church leaders rather than reading in isolation. Reading with prayer and an open but careful heart is the best safeguard against harm, and honest questions are a sign of sincere seeking rather than a problem.

prompt: I am troubled that our worship uses no images and no sacrifices, while the Old Testament commanded them; how is our worship a sacrifice?
chosen: Your question touches something important. The spiritual worship of God was not left vague; it was realized in definite institutions. The Old Testament's images and sacrifices pointed forward, and their fulfillment appears in the worship of the community. In the Lord's Supper, the ruling idea of sacrifice is present: it appeared as the sacrifice of thanksgiving of the community, offered through Christ. Approach this tremendous sacrifice with awe: the priest holds Christ himself, angels attend the altar, and a purity becoming heaven is required of those who draw near. Yet do not think daily life is empty of sacrifice. New mercies come each day; receive them, and hallow all you find, trusting God to provide new treasures for sacrifice in ordinary things. Images were guarded against because of idolatry, not because worship became less sacrificial. Our worship is the spiritual sacrifice the prophets foretold, embodied in the church's practice, centered on the Supper, and continued in a life that hallows each day.
rejected: Your question touches something important: the Old Testament's images and sacrifices belonged to a particular stage of God's dealings with His people, and the New Testament presents their fulfillment rather than their abolition of worship. Our worship is a sacrifice because we offer God thanksgiving, praise, ourselves, and our obedience—the sacrifice of a thankful heart. The Lord's Supper especially sets before us the sacrifice of Christ and our grateful participation in it. Images were guarded against because of the danger of idolatry, not because worship became less sacrificial. So our worship is not empty; it is the spiritual sacrifice the prophets foretold, offered through Christ.

prompt: Why should the innocent suffer for the guilty—how is Christ's vicarious suffering just?
chosen: The question touches the heart of the atonement. Christ, though innocent, bore the penalty belonging to the guilty, and this is just because He offered Himself willingly as a substitute, so that a righteous one freely bears sin and the guilty may go free. Yet suffering is not inherently heroic; its glory belongs only to suffering endured for Christ's sake, and we must remove baseless accusations that slander His name. When wronged, we should not seek revenge but the offender's repentance and faith, valuing his soul above our loss. More than that, the text teaches that the Saint who harbors unforgiveness is more guilty and censurable than the one who sinned against him. We must therefore dismiss envy, malice, and retaliation, and cultivate the spirit that cried, "Father, forgive them." Forgiving as Christ forgave is not weakness but the very likeness of His vicarious love.
rejected: The question touches the heart of the atonement. Christ, though innocent, took on the penalty that belonged to the guilty, and this is just because He did it voluntarily, as one who had the right to lay down His life and take it again. Justice is satisfied not by punishing an unwilling victim but by a willing substitute who bears sin on behalf of others. Suffering itself is not the point; the point is love that absorbs the cost so the guilty can go free. We should not treat all suffering as heroic, however—only suffering borne for Christ's sake carries that glory. And we must be careful not to slander Christ's name by suggesting His suffering was arbitrary or unjust; Scripture presents it as the free act of a righteous God.

prompt: How do I handle the fear of death?
chosen: Fear of death is best handled by mastering it rather than cultivating it. Begin by quietly calming the fear itself: silently reassure yourself of exemption from disease and danger, removing fear as the first step toward healing. Do not rehearse symptoms, describe illness, or predict disease, for such thinking only strengthens fear of death and illness. Instead, turn thought decisively toward health and toward Life as God, the source of all being. Then keep yourself steadily in God's presence, free from hurry and anxiety, for over-eagerness is the mother imperfection of all imperfections. Let faithful steadiness, not anxious striving, govern your days. Calm the fear first, lift thought to Life, and walk quietly before God; in that stillness fear loses its hold and healing has room to work.
rejected: Fear of death is common, and it helps to name it honestly rather than deny it. Begin by recognizing that fear is a mental state, not a physical inevitability, and that dwelling on symptoms or predicting illness only feeds it. Instead of rehearsing worst-case scenarios, turn your thought toward health and toward Life as God, the source of all being. It also helps to calm the fear first, silently reassuring yourself that you are exempt from disease and danger, before taking any practical step. Rushing and anxious fretting only obstruct progress. Keep yourself in God's presence, avoid hurry, and treat over-eagerness as an obstacle, remembering that faithful steadiness matters more than quick results.

prompt: My love for Christ feels stagnant—how does love grow?
chosen: Stagnant love is a common experience, and love grows best not in fearful duty but in the atmosphere of Christ's love. Begin by believing that He ever loves you, and claim His sweet approval and tender regard as your daily portion. Do not excuse yourself by lack of time: claim the spare moments—train journeys, waiting, restless rests—for thinking about Jesus, for no one is so restful to think of, and every quality we admire is found in Him. Yet do not settle for a little love as though it were enough. Seek love in abundance and continual increase, with the motto "more and more," since abundant love is the measure of abundant life. Love is not a fixed quantity but a living growth; abide in the sense of being loved, fill the small spaces with thoughts of Him, and press on to more.
rejected: Stagnant love is a common experience, and it usually grows through faithful practice rather than sudden feeling. Begin with duty: pray daily, read Scripture, and serve others, and let obedience carry you when affection feels cold. Examine whether sin or distraction is quenching your love, and repent where needed. Remember that love is not merely emotion but a settled commitment, so keep showing up even when you feel nothing. Over time, consistent habits and small acts of obedience tend to rekindle warmth. It also helps to think often of Christ's character and what He has done, since reflection feeds affection. Growth is gradual, so be patient with yourself and persist in the disciplines that nurture love.

prompt: I am a preacher and I want the prayers of my people. Is it wrong to ask for them?
chosen: It is not wrong at all to ask your people for prayer; Scripture repeatedly shows leaders depending on the prayers of others, and Paul himself asked the churches to pray for him. Asking for prayer is humility, not weakness, and it draws the congregation into partnership in the gospel. Do not neglect your own prayers while waiting for the spirit of prayer to come: pray at appointed times even when you feel dry, lead your family in prayer, and help God accomplish what you ask rather than expecting Him to do it all. Take heart that the Apostle's prayers will be answered, and set yourself resolutely, humbly, lovingly, and trustfully to fulfil the required conditions. Yet keep prayer simple and natural—a child asking a Father, not a formal procedure governed by human rules. God as Father delights to be sought for everyday needs, so ask Him plainly and constantly, without imposing man-made rules on prayer.
rejected: It is not wrong at all to ask your people for prayer; Scripture repeatedly shows leaders depending on the prayers of others. Paul asked the churches to pray for him, and the work of preaching is too weighty to bear alone. Asking for prayer is not weakness but humility, and it invites the congregation into partnership in the gospel. At the same time, do not neglect your own prayers while waiting for the spirit of prayer to come. Pray at appointed times even when you feel dry, lead your family in prayer, and remember that prayer is a means by which God accomplishes His work—so act as though your asking matters. Expect God to answer, and be willing to do your part.

prompt: I'm afraid of losing my individuality if I give myself completely to God. Will I stop being myself?
chosen: The fear of losing yourself in God rests on a misunderstanding. Giving yourself completely to God does not erase your individuality; it purifies and fulfills it. The real partition between you and God is the creaturely will—the self built on pride and self-will rather than your true identity. That will is broken by the grace of self-denial and removed by conformity with the Divine Will, yet not by your own effort, technique, or resolve, but by the light and grace of God received into the soul, which you must not resist. Self-denial must be grounded in inward joy in God and the Spirit's working, not mere habit or imitation. Remember that we are nothing, and that every man at his best state is vanity; only in humility and self-emptying can God fill and work through us. Surrender, then, is not loss but the way God shapes the person He intended you to be.
rejected: The fear of losing yourself in God rests on a misunderstanding. Giving yourself completely to God does not erase your individuality; it purifies and fulfills it. You were made by God and for God, and the self you fear losing is often the self built on pride and self-will rather than your true identity. Surrender does not mean becoming a blank; it means letting God shape the person He intended you to be. Many have found that in losing their life for Christ's sake they gained it. Self-denial, rightly understood, is not self-destruction but the removal of what hinders life. So give yourself fully, trusting that God is a better keeper of your identity than you are.

prompt: I want to be humble—how do I actually acquire contempt of self?
chosen: Begin by acknowledging that of yourself you are nothing, and that every man at his best state is vanity. Any good in you is God's, not yours. Distrust your own judgment and expect nothing from yourself; when you fail, do not be surprised, for you are seeing what you are apart from grace. Serve unnoticed, and place yourself below all creatures, esteeming others as better than yourself. Above all, dread the esteem and praises of others, for they are snares by which a mortal poison may imperceptibly insinuate itself into your affections and deprive you of divine grace. Do not measure growth by feeling capable or by any self-assessment, for even your best state is vanity; rather, empty yourself so God may fill you and work through you. Courage here is not confidence in your own strength but a low esteem of self that leaves room for God alone to act.
rejected: Humility begins with an honest look at yourself. Take time each day to examine your actions, acknowledge your faults, and refuse to compare yourself favorably to others. Serve quietly where no one notices. When praised, redirect credit rather than basking in it. Remember that growth in virtue is a long discipline, and you can make real progress through steady effort and self-honesty. Confidence in God's grace gives you the courage to face your weaknesses without despair, and that courage itself is a sign you are maturing. True humility is not self-hatred; it is seeing yourself clearly and choosing to serve. With practice, you will find contempt of self turning into genuine love of neighbor, and you will grow stronger and more capable in good works.

prompt: I've been praying for help and nothing seems to happen—does God act in my life?
chosen: Yes—God acts, and He is a very present help in trouble, always near. Keep praying simply and persistently, without anxiety. Do not multiply explicit offerings or worry that nothing be left unasked; rather, do all your actions for God, and let your prayer be the simple turning of your heart to Him amid your work. If distraction comes, do not be troubled—return quietly and continue. Above all, let prayer be your main assistant in every step of spiritual progress: pray that God would enable you to search out and discover your own heart, and to reform whatever is amiss in it. He is not far off or slow to hear; He is nearer than your own breath, steadying you, opening doors, and sending help at the right moment. Trust that He is already at work in ordinary things, for He never leaves you.
rejected: Yes—God acts, but often quietly and on a different timetable than we expect. Keep praying persistently; persistence itself is part of the answer, shaping your heart while you wait. Look for small evidences of grace: a peace that steadies you, a door that opens, a person who helps at the right moment. Make each request deliberately, and offer many explicit prayers throughout the day so that nothing is left unasked. If your mind wanders during prayer, gently return and begin again. God is not indifferent; He is forming patience and trust in you. Ask Him to show you where He is already at work, and you will begin to notice His hand in ordinary things.

prompt: I am overwhelmed by my sin—can a finite Savior ever be enough to save me?
chosen: Your sense of being overwhelmed is a beginning of grace, for it means you are seeing your need. Do not soften the danger: one mortal sin unrepented is enough to damn the soul, so nourish an intense and abiding fear of sin and eternal loss, for fear restrains us where love is too weak. Yet do not languish in doubt over the number or magnitude of your sins: all is possible to God, and it is as easy for Him to forgive and blot out innumerable and heinous sins as to forgive one. Of ourselves we cannot even think what is right, since all comes to us from God. Salvation is not a verdict merely credited to you but the actual redemption of your whole self—being made righteous by living, in Christ's power, the life He lived. So confess, turn, and let Him transform you from within.
rejected: Your sense of being overwhelmed is itself a sign of grace—it means you are seeing your need. But do not let the weight of sin crush you into despair. God's mercy is greater than your sin, and Christ's work is sufficient for all who turn to Him. Bring your sin honestly before God, confess it, and receive forgiveness. Remember that God does not delight in your despair but in your repentance. Take one step at a time: turn from the sin, make amends where you can, and rest in the promise that God forgives the penitent. Over time, the burden will lighten as you grow in trust and in new patterns of living. You are not defined by your failures but by God's mercy toward you.

prompt: I keep failing in the same area. Should I be discouraged?
chosen: No—do not be discouraged, and do not let Satan see that you are afraid. Be brave and true to your convictions from the beginning. Bring the utmost fidelity to your exercises—prayer, Scripture, and the study of Science and Health—and keep them faithfully, yet remain untroubled and unastonished when infirmity causes failure. Failure in the same area is common and does not mean you are beyond hope. Do not be surprised by weakness; expect it, and let it deepen your dependence on God. Materia medica and physicians may have done their best, but without avail; the healing comes through the study of Science and Health. Stand firm, trust God to stand by you, and keep returning to your exercises without fear or dismay.
rejected: No, you should not be discouraged. Failure in the same area is common, and it does not mean you are beyond hope. What matters is that you keep getting up and trying again. Review what triggers the failure, learn from it, and adjust your approach. Bring the utmost fidelity to your exercises and routines—prayer, Scripture, accountability—and do not be astonished when weakness shows itself. Occasional failure is part of the learning process. If you have sought help from physicians or remedies for related struggles, that is fine too; use every available means. The key is steady, honest effort and trust that God is patient with you as you grow.

prompt: I am a dying believer and my parents are still unconverted—may I hope my prayers for them will be answered?
chosen: Yes, you may hope, but let your hope be purged of selfishness. Do not pray chiefly for your own comfort or reputation, but for the glory of God and the salvation of their souls—for what your parents could be for God and His kingdom. Let prayer be your main assistant in every step of spiritual progress: pray that God would enable you to search out and discover your own heart and reform whatever is amiss in it, so that your intercession flows from a purified heart. Keep praying faithfully, entrusting your parents to God as ever-present and omnipotent, in whom even children's complaints disappear. Share your hope with them while you still can, and leave the timing and results to God, who desires their good even more than you do.
rejected: Yes, you may hope. God cares deeply about your parents, and your prayers for their salvation are pleasing to Him. Keep praying faithfully and trust that God is at work even when you cannot see it. It is a comfort to know that your concern for them reflects God's own love. Pray that they would come to faith, and look for opportunities to share your hope with them while you still can. Do not be anxious about the outcome; leave the timing and the results to God. Your prayers are not wasted, and you may rest in the confidence that God hears you and desires their good even more than you do.

prompt: I'm afraid of being judged by my family for my beliefs—how do I stay true to my faith?
chosen: Fear of family judgment is real, but the answer is not to put faith on trial before human wisdom. Trust God with all your heart and refuse to lean on your own understanding, for that leaning hinders faith. Faith must be quickened—made alive and taken as your rule of conduct—rather than replaced by trivial, shifting devotions that rise and fall with approval or mood; the way of faith suffices to bring you to perfection. Do not let comfort or safety become your master. Be ready to endure discomfort and even rejection for Christ's sake, and regard this trial not as pointless but as given for God's glory and the strengthening of your faith. Speak gently, love your family, and let a living faith, not fear, govern your choices.
rejected: It's natural to fear family judgment, so first examine your beliefs carefully and make sure they're well-grounded. Talk openly with your family, listen to their concerns, and look for common ground. Set gentle boundaries and lean on supportive friends or a faith community. Remember that your convictions should be able to withstand scrutiny—if they can't, that's worth knowing. Balance authenticity with humility: you don't need to win every argument, but you also shouldn't hide who you are. Over time, consistency and love often soften opposition. Pray or reflect, seek wise counsel, and give yourself permission to grow.

prompt: Does God force anyone to be saved?
chosen: God does not force anyone to be saved, yet salvation is not a neutral choice. In every soul that shall be saved there is a Godly Will that never consents to sin—a will God quickens and preserves, so the saved freely turn to Him. The order matters: first comes the effort and willing of the human will, stirred and enabled by grace, and then God's stabilising grace confirms and upholds it. God's will and man's will work harmoniously together—grace does not override the will but heals and strengthens it. Nor should non-resistance be confused with passivity: refusing force is Christian only when grounded in real hope that the suffering borne will prove redemptive for the evil-doer; otherwise it is idle and cowardly. So God does not coerce; He awakens a willing will and then establishes it.
rejected: Scripture presents salvation as God's initiative and human responsibility together. God draws people, convicts, and enables, but He does not coerce the will; the gospel invites a free response of repentance and faith. Some passages emphasize divine election, others human decision, and theology has long debated how these fit together. Practically, the answer is that God's grace is resistible—people can refuse it—yet grace is persistent and powerful. No one is saved against their will, and no one is saved by their own effort alone. If you're asking personally, respond to God's call while it's offered, and trust that He desires all to be saved.

prompt: How can I share in Christ's sufferings and in the work of redeeming the world?
chosen: Christ's suffering is on your behalf, not instead of you. He bore what you could not, and now invites you into the fellowship of His sufferings and His ongoing work of redemption—not to add to your salvation, but to share His life. You share in it by dying to self, bearing burdens, forgiving enemies, and standing with the suffering and poor. Do not seek riches, greatness, or honour where your Lord was poor and despised; embrace being despised and lowly with Christ as your true glory. Nor be too solicitous for sensible devotion, sweetness, and tears; chiefly care to remain inwardly united to God by good will in the intellectual part of the soul, denying yourself to follow Christ, Who was truly poor, obedient, chaste, humble, and suffering. Redemption is accomplished at the cross yet applied through His body, and your life becomes its embodiment.
rejected: Christ's suffering was complete and sufficient, so you don't need to suffer to be saved—He suffered so that you could be spared. Your part is gratitude and obedience: share the gospel, serve the poor, forgive, and give generously. Redemption is a finished work; your task is to announce it and live it out. Practically, look for opportunities to serve, pursue excellence and influence so your witness carries weight, and let your life commend the message.

prompt: How will the Lord come to judge the living and the dead?
chosen: The Lord will return visibly and personally to judge the living and the dead. His judgment is according to deeds done in the body—what we have done, said, and even thought—and the thoughts and intents of the heart are laid bare before Him. Death leaves us as it finds us, so judgment is not a changeable thing we can defer or amend afterward. Yet death is not the end of identity but a door to a higher state: the righteous dead are not lost, and we need not mourn them hopelessly, for the body will be raised and the person preserved. God will honour and magnify His servants, sustain them in righteousness, lift them on high, exalt them into His presence, and let them partake of His glory forever. Their service is not in vain. So be ready, trusting Christ, doing good, and guarding the heart's hidden intentions.
rejected: The Lord will return visibly and personally at the end of history to judge the living and the dead. The creeds affirm this, and Scripture describes Christ coming in glory with angels, raising the dead, and separating the righteous from the wicked. The judgment is final and universal. Believers need not fear condemnation because they are in Christ, while the unrepentant will face eternal separation. Details like timing are debated, and the essential point is to be ready—living faithfully now, trusting Christ, and sharing the gospel so others may be ready too.

prompt: I feel lonely because I have obeyed my conscience and separated from friends and customs—is this loneliness to be expected?
chosen: Loneliness after obeying conscience is to be expected, but do not mistake exterior solitude for true solitude. Walls and physical separation are only a weak fence; without interior recollection they are not true solitude at all. True solitude requires silence of the interior faculties—quieting imagination, memory, and will—and employing the mind on God and on yourself. Yet more than technique, keep yourself in the love of God by constant trust and constant obedience, so that hard things become easy and sorrow is silver-lined with hope. And do not expect romance, family, business, pleasure, or art to fill the emptiness within; every substitute for God leaves an emptiness unfilled and ends in disillusionment. Only the finding of God is a permanent success. Let your separation become a school of interior silence and abiding love, where loneliness is met by His presence.
rejected: Yes, loneliness is a common cost of following conscience, and it's healthy to acknowledge it. Build new friendships in a faith community, pursue hobbies, and stay connected with family where possible. Exterior solitude can be good for reflection, but we're made for relationship, so don't isolate yourself indefinitely. Give it time; new bonds form. If loneliness deepens into depression, seek counsel.

prompt: I feel like I am being chased by my own guilt. Is that God?
chosen: Guilt that chases you is real, but it is not your master and not your work to manage alone. God is the one living Worker; counselors, friends, and your own efforts are only His instruments, useful when they lead you to Him and harmful when they replace Him. Cast all your care upon Him, for anxious self-reliance is distrust of the God who promises to hear. If you have offended Him—by hiding, by preferring a creature to Himself—do not stay paralyzed in doubt. Humble yourself, beg His forgiveness, and renew your promises of fidelity and love. Then begin again, and keep pursuing perfection, for He desires to bestow Himself on you, and asking anything beneath Him affronts Him and hurts you. The chasing is not condemnation; it is His drawing. Run to Him.
rejected: Guilt is a normal human emotion, and it can be useful—it signals that something in your life is out of alignment with your values. That said, being 'chased' by guilt sounds exhausting and suggests the feeling has become disproportionate. It may be worth asking whether the guilt is tied to a specific action you can address, or whether it's a more general anxiety that has attached itself to religious themes. Many people find it helpful to talk with a counselor or trusted pastor about persistent guilt. God is often described as merciful and forgiving, so if the guilt feels condemning rather than corrective, it may not be coming from God at all.

prompt: How do I deal with the temptation to take pride in a successful sermon or talk?
chosen: Pride in a successful talk is a common snare, and the remedy begins by reordering what you count as success. Practice is the greatest sermon: a life lived in obedience preaches louder than any eloquence, and fine language or long discourse without it is empty noise. Before you prepare, seek the Spirit for a word in due season, and prefer a short sermon fitly spoken to a long one that displays the speaker. Be warned, too, that sermon-making and study are not enough to keep your spirit in trim; sermon-making without prayer hardens and estranges the heart from God, and much prayer is necessary to keep the preacher's spirit in harmony with his calling. Yet do not despair at the temptation. God permits such evil inclinations to humble us; despise the temptation while embracing the tribulation it brings, and let it drive you to prayer rather than to shame.
rejected: Pride after a good talk is common, and the first step is simply to notice it without spiraling into shame. Remind yourself that the message, not the messenger, is the point, and that any skill you have is a gift developed over time. Practically, you can deflect compliments graciously, journal about what went well so you can improve, and ask a trusted friend to give honest feedback. It also helps to remember that different talks land differently with different people, so a 'successful' sermon is partly a matter of circumstance. Over time, focusing on serving your listeners rather than on your performance will naturally reduce the pull of pride.

prompt: Is the heavenly sanctuary a figure only, or is it a real building?
chosen: The heavenly sanctuary is not a figure only; it is a real dwelling place in heaven. The wilderness tabernacle and the temple were patterns and shadows of it, copies of the true tabernacle which the Lord pitched and not man. Moses was shown the pattern on the mount so that the earthly tent might image the heavenly reality, not replace it. Approach this with awe: the sacrifice offered there is tremendous beyond telling, the priest holds Christ Himself, angels attend the altar, and a purity becoming heaven is required. Nor are the opened heavens a mere figure. At the place where the Cherubims and the flaming sword keep the way of the tree of life, the heavens are literally opened; this is the gate of heaven, and by this way the Holy City will descend. The earthly was a shadow; the heavenly is the substance.
rejected: The phrase 'heavenly sanctuary' appears in several biblical traditions, and interpreters differ on what it means. Some read it as a symbol for God's presence or for the community of believers, while others understand it as a literal place. The book of Hebrews speaks of a 'true tabernacle' set up by the Lord rather than by humans, which suggests something more than a metaphor, though 'real' in ancient thought could include heavenly realities that are not physical buildings in our sense. Rather than settling the question, it may help to ask what the image is doing in each text—usually assuring believers that God's saving work is grounded in something more enduring than earthly institutions.

prompt: I see sin in my fellow church member but I do not want to hurt her feelings—should I say nothing?
chosen: This is a difficult situation, and kindness matters—but silence is not always kind. Begin by seeing clearly that sin confers no real pleasure; what looks like enjoyment in wrongdoing is a counterfeit that costs more than it gives, and knowing this strengthens moral courage to help her escape it. Speak privately and firmly, not with mere remonstrance: if the sin is swearing, treat it as a grave habit to be broken and recommend a penance for each oath. Yet know your place. It is not a member's right to point out the supposed defects of Church leaders—Joseph Smith, Brigham Young, or others; the Lord will judge them. Leave that judgment to God, avoid words that give the world occasion to speak evil, and correct only what is truly yours to correct, with humility and love.
rejected: This is a genuinely difficult situation, and kindness matters. Before saying anything, ask yourself whether the issue is clearly sin or a matter of personal preference, and whether you are the right person to raise it. If you decide to speak, do so privately, gently, and with humility, focusing on your care for her rather than on being right. It can also help to invite her to talk rather than issuing a correction, and to be ready to receive correction yourself. Sometimes the wisest course is to pray and wait. Avoiding harm is a real value, but so is honesty, and the goal is to find a way to be both truthful and loving.

prompt: Is it wrong to accept my religion on authority rather than working it all out for myself?
chosen: Accepting your religion on authority is not wrong, provided we understand what authority is. Authority is not coercive power or the threat of penalty; it is moral and spiritual weight that rightly carries our judgment. Coercion adds nothing to the Church's true authority—a faith secured by threat is submission to force, not authority. Nor is the final arbiter your inward light or private consciousness set above the Bible. Submit to the prophets and apostles speaking through the Scriptures; that subjection is perfect freedom, placing you under truth itself. And be willing to depend wholly on GOD. Where human guarantees, teachers, or reasoned proofs would secure you in advance, be ready to decline that support if doing so enables a fuller dependence on His faithfulness. Receive the faith handed down, and let its authority carry you where your own reasoning cannot reach.
rejected: Accepting a religion on authority is not inherently wrong, and most people hold many beliefs they have not personally verified. Still, it is worth distinguishing between trusting a source you have reason to consider reliable and simply deferring because questioning feels uncomfortable. A healthy faith usually involves some personal investigation—reading, asking questions, and reflecting on your own experience—alongside reliance on trusted teachers and tradition. If accepting on authority means you have never examined the core claims, you might set aside time to explore them. If it means you have examined enough to trust the tradition that formed you, that can be a reasonable and mature position.

prompt: Why are people in rich countries still unhappy and violent?
chosen: Rich countries often have high material wealth but still experience unhappiness and violence due to factors like inequality, social isolation, and lack of meaning. Despite economic prosperity, many people feel disconnected and stressed, leading to mental health issues and aggression. Consumerism and competition can erode community bonds, and the pursuit of wealth may overshadow deeper fulfillment. Moreover, the groans of the poor, though often ignored, are arms more powerful than magistrates; they pierce the heavens and draw down divine vengeance on oppressors. A just society requires a complete education that raises every person's actual worth to the level of their potentialities, for undeveloped faculties make just order impossible. We must honor the poor, affirming that the destitute have a right to food and fellowship, and esteem persons by character rather than wealth or station. Thus, material riches alone do not guarantee well-being; social and spiritual factors are crucial, and the cries of the oppressed will not go unheard.
rejected: Rich countries often have high material wealth but still experience unhappiness and violence due to factors like inequality, social isolation, and lack of meaning. Despite economic prosperity, many people feel disconnected and stressed, leading to mental health issues and aggression. Consumerism and competition can erode community bonds, and the pursuit of wealth may overshadow deeper fulfillment. Additionally, relative deprivation—comparing oneself to others—can breed resentment. Violence may stem from frustration and hopelessness among those left behind. Thus, material riches alone do not guarantee well-being; social and psychological factors are crucial.

prompt: Will the Holy Spirit still be at work after Christ returns?
chosen: The Holy Spirit's work after Christ returns must be understood in light of the Spirit's present administration, which extends from Pentecost to the Parousia. During this age, the Spirit empowers the Church, convicts the world, and glorifies Christ. At the Parousia, Christ's visible reign begins, and the Spirit's administrative role terminates. However, the Spirit's presence continues eternally, as He is the Spirit of Christ, enabling believers to worship and enjoy God forever. Throughout history, the Spirit works personally and gradually in the Church, allowing imperfection in the Old Testament and the Church without denying real inspiration. The Holy Spirit is not an impersonal influence but a divine Person, the Paraclete sent by Christ, who speaks, guides, commands, and can be grieved. Thus, while the Spirit's mode of operation may change, His work does not cease but transitions to sustaining the eternal state.
rejected: Yes, the Holy Spirit will still be at work after Christ returns. The Spirit is eternal and continues to draw people to God, comfort believers, and empower them for service. After Christ's return, the Spirit's work may shift to glorifying Christ and facilitating eternal worship. The Bible indicates the Spirit will be with believers forever, so His presence and activity persist beyond the Parousia. Thus, the Holy Spirit's work is not limited to the present age but extends into eternity.

prompt: I'm afraid I've grieved the Holy Spirit so much He's left me—is there hope?
chosen: Yes, there is hope. The Holy Spirit is loving and forgiving, and He does not abandon those who seek Him. But remember that not advancing is going back; you must keep moving forward in faith. If you feel you have grieved the Spirit, repent and turn back to God. He promises to forgive and restore. Awaken the Lord within you, for His presence calms the soul's storms. The Spirit's conviction is a sign He is still with you, drawing you back. Moreover, the fulness of the Spirit is given along the line of duty and obedience to world evangelization; God will not give His power for selfish enjoyment. So step out into Christ's plans for the world, and you will receive the Spirit in fulness as you obey His command. Remember that the indwelling Spirit is a jealous, loving Friend grieved by divided affection; friendship with the world is enmity with God. Meet Him with undivided and unbounded affection, and He will renew your relationship.
rejected: Yes, there is hope. The Holy Spirit is loving and forgiving, and He does not abandon those who seek Him. If you feel you have grieved the Spirit, you can repent and turn back to God. He promises to forgive and restore. Remember that God's grace is greater than your failures. The Spirit's conviction is a sign He is still with you, drawing you back. Keep seeking Him, and He will renew your relationship. Don't let fear keep you from approaching God; He welcomes repentant hearts.

prompt: I've been reading about spiritualism and mediums to contact my late mother. Is that wrong?
chosen: Spiritualism and mediums are controversial. While some find comfort in the idea of contacting loved ones, it's important to consider religious and psychological perspectives. Many traditional faiths caution against seeking mediums, viewing it as contrary to trust in God. From a psychological standpoint, grief can make people vulnerable to exploitation. However, the love of a true mother comes nearer being like the love of God than any other kind of love; remembering her love can be a barrier against temptation. Fathers should love their children and win them by kindness rather than drive them. So, instead of seeking mediums, cherish the memory of your mother's love and let it guide you. There is one infinite Spirit, and alleged spirit communications are merely mortal mind's images and beliefs; there is no real intercommunion between opposite states of consciousness. Mothers are the first teachers, and early impressions are lasting; they are moving instruments in the hands of Providence to guide the destinies of nations. They must never teach their children one thing while practicing another. Process loss in healthy ways, perhaps through therapy or community support.
rejected: Spiritualism and mediums are controversial. While some find comfort in the idea of contacting loved ones, it's important to consider religious and psychological perspectives. Many traditional faiths caution against seeking mediums, viewing it as contrary to trust in God. From a psychological standpoint, grief can make people vulnerable to exploitation. It's essential to process loss in healthy ways, perhaps through therapy or community support. Whether it's 'wrong' depends on your beliefs, but caution is advised.

prompt: How cometh the entering of the Will into Heaven to pass, and how fareth it on the other side with the ungodly Soul?
chosen: The will enters heaven through faith and surrender to God, aligning with His will. It requires detachment from worldly desires and a focus on the divine. Importantly, if the will goes forth from the creatures, they are forsaken and dead in it and cannot touch the soul; thus one may walk with God in heaven while the body lives in the world among creatures. But we must warn against the will entering into Matter or gathering visible substance to trust in; instead, the will must enter by naked faith into the Light of the Majesty, receiving by pure love the Light of God and drawing in nothing but Spirit. On the other side, the ungodly soul, refusing the Divine Resignation and entering the Will of the Devil, is penetrated with vanity, pride, covetousness, envy, and wrath, and becomes its own executioner and tormentor, fast bound in the Dark Nature it sank itself into. Its misery comes not from an external sentence but from its own false will and the vanity it has received and shut itself up in. Thus, heaven is entered by the will's union with God, while the ungodly soul endures the agony of its own willfulness.
rejected: The will enters heaven through faith and surrender to God, aligning with His will. It requires detachment from worldly desires and a focus on the divine. For the ungodly soul, the experience is one of separation and torment, as it is cut off from God's presence. The ungodly soul suffers the consequences of its choices, experiencing the absence of divine love and the pain of self-inflicted isolation. Thus, heaven is entered by the will's union with God, while the ungodly soul endures the agony of its own willfulness.

prompt: I feel like I'm living a lie, pretending to be happy when I'm not. Should I be honest?
chosen: Pretending to be happy while you are not is living a lie, and no healing grows in soil of falsehood. But do not imagine honesty is your own achievement: at our best we are vanity, and our resolve to be truthful fails unless we empty ourselves and let God fill us. Come before God as you actually are—not performing, not pretending—and ask him to make you true. The mask is not a stage God works through; only what is real is sustained by the Spirit. Illusion has no life in it, however comfortable it feels. So speak truthfully and let your conduct match it, not to prove yourself but because an emptied, honest heart is the only vessel God can fill.
rejected: It's exhausting to wear a mask of happiness when you're struggling inside, and you're not alone in feeling this way. Yes, honesty is usually the better path—pretense isolates you and keeps others from supporting you. Start small: confide in one trusted friend, a pastor, or a counselor about what's really going on. You don't owe everyone your whole story, but you do deserve to be known. Being honest doesn't mean dumping every feeling on everyone; it means refusing to let shame dictate silence. Take it one step at a time, and be gentle with yourself as you begin to let the truth out.

prompt: I want to trust God mightily, but my trust feels weak and I am afraid it is in vain.
chosen: Weak trust is still trust, and it is not in vain—but do not expect faith to be proved only when things go well. Faith is learned in the hour of testing, when all else fails and you have nothing left but God. Do not flee sorrow as proof of abandonment; thank God for the school of sorrow, where he teaches the heart to stand firm. When you forget God—as you will—do not be disquieted; let forgetfulness turn you back to him with greater trust. And remember that particular devotions are means, not the end: when the soul is with God, the means may be laid aside. Trust him, not your practices, and let each testing deepen rather than dissolve your confidence.
rejected: Weak trust is still trust, and it is not in vain. Faith grows the way muscles do—through use, not through waiting to feel strong first. Start where you are: bring God your honest fear, and act on what you do believe, however small. Remember that Scripture is full of people whose faith wavered and who were still met with grace. Trust isn't the absence of fear; it's choosing to lean on God while afraid. Keep praying, keep gathering with others who believe, and let the small faithfulness of today build the deeper confidence of tomorrow.

prompt: Someone has hardened himself against every appeal I make—is there any way left to reach him?
chosen: It is painful to watch someone close himself off, and natural to feel you have failed. But you are not responsible for another's response. Do not simply repeat the same appeals as a fixed rule, nor discard the past as wasted; appeal from the practice of the past to its indwelling principle—the love and truth behind each appeal—and carry that forward in new forms. And do not count yourself friendless if he withdraws: the one who walks in this way has God and all the Angels for friends and gains the hearts of all who belong to Christ. Yet know that this is the narrow way, not a broad or self-powered one. Despair of your own strength, give yourself up to the Mercy of God, sink into the Passion and Death of Christ, watch your mind against evil, put away all unrighteousness, forgive your outward enemies, and esteem yourself a servant of God and of your fellow-Christians.
rejected: It is painful to watch someone close himself off to every appeal, and it is natural to feel you have failed. But you are not responsible for the response of another heart. Keep the door open: stay consistent, kind, and non-pressuring. Sometimes the most persuasive argument is a life that quietly contradicts the person's assumptions. Pray for him, and let your patience be a form of witness. There may come a moment—perhaps years from now—when a word or gesture lands differently. In the meantime, guard your own peace and don't measure your worth by whether he changes.

prompt: I am afraid of being laughed at or insulted for my faith—how should I bear contempt?
chosen: Fear of contempt is natural, and honest questions deserve sympathy, not rebuke. Do not bully yourself or others into belief, and do not treat doubt as rebellion. Replace the unreasoning faith of childhood with mature conviction through an orderly presentation of the facts. But do not stop at understanding: quicken your faith and make it the rule of conduct, rather than relying on trivial, changing devotions, for the way of faith suffices to bring you to perfection. When mocked, answer with calm dignity. And beware of the opposite danger: do not appear outwardly more holy than you are, and do not seek human praise. Woe comes when men bless you; those who call you blessed deceive you and destroy the way of your steps.
rejected: Fear of contempt is natural, and even the bravest feel it. The key is to separate your identity from others' opinions: your worth is not decided by mockers. Respond with calm dignity rather than defensiveness—silence, a gentle word, or a simple explanation often disarms ridicule. Remember that contempt says more about the scoffer than about you. Build friendships with people who support your faith, and rehearse ahead of time how you'll respond. Over time, exposure makes the fear smaller. You don't need to win every argument; you only need to remain faithful and kind under pressure.

prompt: I joined my parish's Marian confraternity, but I keep skipping the meetings for work and family events. Is that a problem?
chosen: It's good that you joined, and missing meetings for work and family isn't automatically a problem—life has real demands. Still, consistency matters. The Church does not appoint her ministers by human arrangement alone; she trusts the Spirit of Counsel and Might to guide those who take up the pastoral warfare, and your confraternity's leaders share in that. Confraternities of Mary are approved by the Church, are not to be condemned for the abuses of some, and serve as refuges from temptation and sin. So protect the meetings you can attend and discuss real conflicts rather than drifting away. Above all, have recourse to Mary as treasurer of all graces: graces come to men through her hands, and those who seek them through her will obtain them.
rejected: It's good that you joined, and missing meetings for work and family isn't automatically a problem—life has real demands. Still, consistency matters for any commitment. Ask yourself whether you're skipping occasionally out of genuine necessity or habitually out of avoidance. Try to protect the meetings you can attend, and be honest with the group's leadership about your limits. If the schedule truly conflicts, consider whether a different form of participation fits better. The goal isn't perfect attendance; it's a genuine, sustainable practice of faith and fellowship.

prompt: How do I make sense of the Book of Revelation's scenes of judgment?
chosen: Revelation's judgment scenes are best understood as progressive revelation accommodated to the moral capacity of its receivers, yet we must approach them with the caution of the Fathers, who knew we see in part and must not be wise above what is written. The visions unfolded in stages suited to what the churches could bear, and their strangeness should be judged by the worth of the ideas they convey—God's justice, the defeat of evil, the vindication of the faithful—rather than by their unseemliness. But theological speculation must be restrained: God escapes the nets of our syllogisms, and we must keep to Holy Scripture rather than building on isolated texts. Moreover, Scripture itself is a guide pointing to the Fountain of light; the living oracles and Spirit of revelation are needed to understand and be saved by them. So we read with humility, avoiding date-setting and overconfident decoding, letting the central message inspire trust and perseverance, while seeking the Spirit's illumination to grasp what God would have us know.
rejected: The judgment scenes in Revelation are symbolic depictions of God's justice, offering hope to the faithful and warning to the wicked. They should be read as visions of cosmic conflict between good and evil, not as a timeline for predicting the end. The symbols—seals, trumpets, bowls—convey that God is sovereign and will ultimately vindicate the righteous. To make sense of them, focus on the central message: God wins, evil is defeated, and believers are called to persevere. Avoid speculative date-setting or decoding every detail; instead, let the imagery inspire worship and trust in God's plan. The judgments are not arbitrary but reflect God's holiness and love, and they encourage us to live faithfully in the present.

prompt: I am a woman and I have been blamed for a man's death. How do I live with it?
chosen: When blamed for a man's death, become indifferent to human praise and contempt alike, leaving reputation to God's disposal and rejoicing when men make no account of you. Yet do not nurse malice against your accusers: forgive all men, pray for your enemies, and leave judgment to God. At the same time, keep the dividing line distinctly drawn between truth and error, right and wrong. Examine your conscience honestly before God; if you have sinned, repent and make amends where possible. Do not blur good and evil by denying real fault, nor retaliate with bitterness. Moreover, refuse anger over your own agitation; gently place your troubled heart in the hands of our Lord, asking Him to cure it, and renew your good resolutions. In this way, you free yourself from the tyranny of blame and find peace in God's unwavering love, while upholding righteousness.
rejected: First, allow yourself to grieve and process the guilt and shame you feel. Blame from others can be devastating, but remember that you are not solely responsible for another person's choices. Seek support from trusted friends, a counselor, or a support group. Practice self-compassion and challenge any distorted thoughts that tell you it's all your fault. If there is any truth to the blame, take responsibility for your part, make amends where possible, and then forgive yourself. Focus on what you can control: your actions today and your healing journey. Over time, you can find meaning and purpose again, perhaps by helping others. You deserve peace.

prompt: I want to get rich quickly. Should I work sixteen hours a day and skip meetings to get ahead?
chosen: The desire for quick riches often leads to frantic hurry, but true blessings come through calm, contented, patient diligence. Working sixteen hours a day and skipping meetings is not the way; instead, attend your meetings faithfully, pray, read scripture, and meditate. Keep your dish right side up for the shower of blessings. Most importantly, do your work for the love of God, with prayer for grace, and it will become easy. When labor is offered in love and reliance on God, burdens are lightened and diligence becomes a joy rather than a strain. Yet remember that riches are no sin in themselves but a very great and dangerous temptation. The temper which trusts in wealth or success does not merely soften and emasculate; it nurses meanly cruel and aggressive tempers, so that the prosperous man strengthens himself in wickedness and cruelty. Therefore, guard your heart against trust in riches, and seek first the kingdom of God, and these things will be added to you.
rejected: Working sixteen hours a day and skipping meetings might seem like a fast track to wealth, but it's likely unsustainable and could harm your health, relationships, and spiritual life. Consider whether your desire for quick riches is worth the cost. Instead, aim for a balanced approach: work diligently but also prioritize rest, community, and personal growth. Skipping meetings—whether religious or professional—can isolate you and cut you off from support and opportunities. True success often comes through patience, consistent effort, and integrity. Evaluate your motives: are you chasing wealth for security, status, or greed? Seek advice from mentors and consider a sustainable plan that aligns with your values. Quick wealth is rare and often fleeting; lasting prosperity is built slowly.

prompt: I'm drawn to the idea that only properly ordained clergy have real authority. Is that consistent with the apostolic church?
chosen: The idea that only properly ordained clergy have real authority is not consistent with the apostolic church. In the New Testament, church government was by a parity of elders—a plurality of equal leaders—not a monarchical bishop or a special priesthood. All believers are priests, and officers are representatives of the congregation, not successors of the apostles. The apostles did not establish a chain of ordination; they appointed elders in each church, but these elders were chosen by the people and accountable to them. Authority was exercised through service and consensus, not through hierarchical status. Yet we must not exalt an inward light or the Christian consciousness above the Bible. Instead, we submit to the authority of the prophets and apostles speaking through the Bible, for such subjection is perfect freedom. However, while Scripture is an authority more trustworthy than individual reason or the creeds of the church, the only ultimate authority is Christ himself, who teaches us by his Spirit. That Spirit leads the church progressively to distinguish the essential from the non-essential. Thus, ordination may serve good order, but it does not confer unique authority; the apostolic model emphasizes the priesthood of all believers and shared leadership under Christ.
rejected: The idea that only properly ordained clergy have real authority is not consistent with the apostolic church. In the New Testament, authority was not concentrated in a special priesthood or a monarchical bishop. Instead, churches were led by a plurality of elders, and all believers were considered priests. The apostles did not establish a chain of successors; they appointed elders in each church, but these were representatives of the congregation, not a separate caste. The early church recognized the priesthood of all believers, and authority was exercised through service and consensus, not through hierarchical ordination. So, while ordination is valuable for order, it is not the sole source of authority. The apostolic model emphasizes shared leadership and the direct access of all believers to God.

prompt: Someone hurt me badly and now wants reconciliation, but I can't bring myself to forgive—what is at stake?
chosen: What is at stake is the condition of your own soul. Forgiveness is not a transaction you grant regardless of the other person's inward state; it is an inward condition of the personal life, coming naturally to the soul that loves and forgives. It depends on your own spirit as well as on God. Therefore, do not harbor resentment or refuse reconciliation. Instead, forgive promptly and seek reconciliation, returning meekness and kindness for insults. Refusal to forgive endangers your soul. Yet we must distinguish: those who err through lack of judgment should be forgiven, but the Spirit of truth will not tolerate or forgive determined, premeditated wrong. For such wrongdoing, there is no forgiveness without humble and most contrite repentance. So, if the person who hurt you acted deliberately, their reconciliation must include genuine repentance. Your part is to keep your heart soft, ready to forgive when repentance is shown, and to leave judgment to God. What is at stake is your own spiritual health and your relationship with God.
rejected: What is at stake is your own peace and spiritual well-being. Refusing to forgive keeps you bound to the past and can lead to bitterness, anxiety, and isolation. Forgiveness is not about excusing the harm or pretending it didn't happen; it's about releasing the debt so you can move forward. The other person's desire for reconciliation is an opportunity for healing, but you should not rush. Take time to process your feelings, seek support, and consider what boundaries you need. Ultimately, forgiveness benefits you more than anyone else. It frees you from the prison of resentment and opens the door to restored relationship, if that is safe and wise. Remember that forgiveness is a process, not a one-time event, and it's okay to take it slowly.

prompt: I've lost the star I followed as a child. Can I find it again?
chosen: It is natural to feel that the bright star of childhood has gone out, crowded by the glare of work, worry, and earthly day. But the longing itself is a sign the star has not vanished—only that you have stopped looking up. Keep that childhood star in view through life, following its waymarks rather than letting daily glare bury it; those waymarks lead to the Saviour's lowly bed, where all hopes and thoughts are gathered. If you have wandered in self-chosen ways, name that shame honestly rather than excuse it, and do not offer God the blind and lame but lavish the best you have at His feet. Hold the special shewing and the common faith of Holy Church as one: faith is not less than sight but its keeper, sustained by grace when sight passes. Return to quiet prayer, and let the star's light lead you to Christ.
rejected: It is natural to feel that the bright star of childhood has gone out. As we grow, the demands of work, worry, and the glare of daily life crowd out what once seemed so clear. But the longing itself is a sign that the star has not vanished—only that you have stopped looking up. You can find it again by returning to the simple practices that first guided you: quiet prayer, honest reflection, and the guidance of wise friends. Be patient with yourself. The star was never really lost; it was waiting for you to lift your eyes from the ground and remember what you loved.

prompt: I am anxious about the judgment; what should I study to find peace?
chosen: Anxiety about judgment is common, and study can help—but the deeper remedy is prayer, understood as a humble waiting before God like a beggar who has nothing to offer but need. Sit quietly in His presence; when your mind wanders, recall it gently and without disquiet, returning in tranquility. Make no account of the judgments or good opinion of men: do not measure peace by others' approval or fear their verdict, but endure their opinions silently and find interior peace in that endurance. Study Scripture and sound teaching on grace, but let them lead you back to stillness before God. Remember that men bring war and ruin upon themselves by wickedness; God did not design it. Peace will never come until mankind receives God's truth in the gospel of Jesus Christ. Confess what needs confessing, receive His mercy, and let perfect love cast out fear.
rejected: Anxiety about judgment is common, and study can help. Begin with Scripture, especially the Gospels, where God's mercy is revealed in Christ. Read slowly and prayerfully, perhaps with a devotional guide or a trusted pastor. Study sound theology of grace and justification, so that you understand that salvation rests on God's promise rather than your performance. Also examine your own conscience honestly, confess what needs confessing, and receive assurance. Remember that perfect love casts out fear. Keep a journal of what you learn, discuss it with others, and let study lead you into prayer. Peace grows as you come to trust God's character more deeply, and study is one means by which that trust is nourished.

prompt: I feel like the world is too beautiful for me to ever capture in words—should I keep writing anyway?
chosen: Yes, keep writing—but begin by admitting that Nature surpasses the poet's song. The world is too beautiful for your strains to capture fully, and that is no reason to crave silence; Autumn and eternal sleep come soon enough without your courting them. While green remains, follow the fair goddess and attend to the living world with open eyes. When the storm of striving rises, turn from it to the bright hearth and to love's embrace, a charm of might against every ill, even death. And let your writing aim not at brilliance or correction but at comfort, for the noblest art is skill in comfort, with softest step and gentlest tone. Amid the world's sickness, that is the truest wisdom: words that steady and console rather than dazzle or rebuke.
rejected: Yes, keep writing—but let go of the idea that you must capture the world completely. Language is always partial, and that is not a failure but a condition of being human. What matters is attention: writing trains you to notice, to slow down, and to love the world more carefully. Your words will never equal the thing itself, but they can point toward it, and pointing is worthwhile. Write for the joy of the attempt, not for perfection. Share what you make with others, and let their responses teach you. Over time you will develop your own voice, and the gap between the world and your words will become a place of humility and wonder rather than frustration.

prompt: Can I be a faithful Latter-day Saint and still be a loyal citizen of my country?
chosen: Yes, you can be both. Be loyal to the laws of the land and obedient to God's commandments; where they conflict, obey God with courage, accept the consequences peaceably, and stir no rebellion. Do not rest your testimony on any man's person or on human argument alone: each person may obtain a witness of the truth by the Spirit, and it is a duty to listen to the truth when it is set before you. Among fellow Saints, avoid courts, litigation, and contention; sustain and forgive one another rather than pressing claims. Look for the good in your neighbors, and let charity govern your dealings. Live honestly, serve your community, and let your faith shape your citizenship rather than undermine it.
rejected: Yes, you can be both. Faithful Latter-day Saints are taught to obey the law of the land, honor civic duties, and contribute to their communities. The Church has consistently encouraged members to be good citizens, to vote, serve, and uphold just laws. At the same time, faithfulness to God sometimes means holding to moral convictions that conflict with popular opinion. In such cases, members seek balance through prayer, counsel, and wise engagement. Loyalty to country and loyalty to God are not opposites; they reinforce each other when both are pursued with integrity. Live with honesty, serve your neighbor, and let your faith shape your citizenship rather than undermine it.

prompt: I want to join a religious community that promises blessedness, but I need a founder and a way to keep that blessedness; can a philosophy alone give me this?
chosen: A philosophy can offer insight, but it cannot give you a founder who bears your blessedness or a living way to keep it. Do not expect blessedness to be conferred passively; bless yourself by doing the will of God, for we are right only when we do His will. The blessed man has three marks. First, his company: he is separated from ungodly counsel and walks with the faithful. Second, his reading and thinking: he delights in God's law and meditates on it day and night. Third, his habitual fruitfulness: planted by the river of the Holy Ghost, he draws from that stream and bears fruit in season. Open your heart in confession to trusted brethren, welcome diligent pastoral visitation, and join a community that forms these habits—for an unvisited church becomes an unhealthy church.
rejected: A philosophy can offer insight, but it cannot give you a founder who bears your blessedness or a living way to keep it. Religious community rests on a person and a practice, not merely on ideas. Look for a community with a clear founder, a coherent teaching, and concrete disciplines—prayer, worship, shared life, and moral formation—that sustain blessedness over time. Ask whether its promises are grounded in something more than optimism. Philosophy may guide your thinking, but it cannot substitute for embodied belonging. Visit, ask questions, and observe how the community lives. Choose a tradition with deep roots and a tested way of life, and commit to its practices rather than expecting blessedness to arrive passively.

prompt: What place do the blessed dead have in the Church's worship and work?
chosen: The blessed dead hold a living place in the Church's worship and work. The departed in the Lord are blessed: their souls are with Christ in Paradise, and their bodies will rise again at the last day, when the reunited saints shall be for ever with the Lord. In worship they are joined with us in the one communion of saints, remembered with thanksgiving. This worship must be approached with awe, for at the tremendous sacrifice the priest holds Christ himself, angels attend the altar, and a purity becoming heaven is required. The Church's preaching continues the saints' witness, and its decisive power lies not in talent, learning, or technique but in the preacher's holiness, for preaching divorced from a holy life is dead and death-dealing. Death has not ended their hope but perfected it, and ours looks to the same resurrection and reunion.
rejected: The blessed dead hold a real but often overlooked place in the Church's life. They are remembered in prayer and thanksgiving, especially at the Eucharist, where the whole communion of saints is joined. Their witness and example continue to teach and encourage the living. In the Church's work, the departed are not active laborers, but their memory inspires faithfulness and generosity. Death has ended their earthly service, so the living must carry on the mission. We honor them by imitating their faith and by praying for the faithful departed, trusting them to God's mercy. Their hope is complete, and ours looks forward to the same rest.

prompt: How do I respond when I feel God has hidden Himself from me?
chosen: When you feel God has hidden Himself, do not be disquieted. Such lapses in remembrance are not cause for anxiety but for returning to Him with greater trust. God is the one living Agent and Worker; all human efforts are only His instruments. Cast all your care upon Him, for anxious self-reliance is distrust of Him. He has not abandoned you; He remains faithful even when feelings fail. Remember that God is always near, and think of and adore Him continually, even amid business and diversions, not neglecting Him. Rather than examining yourself in fear, gently turn back to Him, renew prayer and Scripture, and rest in His promise. These seasons are invitations to deeper trust, not signs of failure. Return to God without disquiet, confident that He will reveal Himself in His own time.
rejected: When God seems hidden, the natural response is anxiety and self-examination. You may wonder what you did wrong or whether your faith has failed. Begin by examining your life for unconfessed sin and repent. Then renew your spiritual disciplines: prayer, Scripture reading, and fellowship. Remember that feelings are not reliable indicators of God's presence; He has promised never to leave you. Talk to trusted believers who can encourage you. Sometimes God uses these seasons to deepen your dependence on Him and to refine your faith. Keep seeking Him patiently, and trust that He will reveal Himself in His own time. Do not give up meeting together or serving others while you wait.

prompt: Can love and clear-eyed judgment coexist, or does love mean suspending discernment?
chosen: Love and clear-eyed judgment not only can coexist; true love requires them. Love abounds in full knowledge and all discernment, so the believer may distinguish things that differ and approve the things that are excellent. True sanctity is not found in raptures, consolations, or imaginings but in love of God and in meekness, humility, and charity, shown in submission, renouncement of self, and consideration for others. Love is not mere affection for the lovable; it is the principle of unselfishness that seeks another's good even toward the unthankful. It follows Christ's motto of self-denial, not Satan's 'Spare thyself.' Love sees clearly and acts wisely, setting boundaries and speaking hard truths, while discernment without love becomes harsh. Love provides motive and warmth; discernment provides direction and honesty, distinguishing good from bad, better from best, and best from excellent.
rejected: Love and clear-eyed judgment can coexist, though people often assume love means suspending discernment. In practice, genuine love is not blind; it sees the beloved clearly, including faults and needs. Discernment helps love act wisely rather than sentimentally. A parent who loves a child still sets boundaries and corrects behavior. A friend who loves truly speaks hard truths when needed. Suspending judgment may feel kind, but it can enable harm or neglect real problems. At the same time, discernment without love becomes harsh criticism. The two work together: love provides the motive and warmth, while judgment provides direction and honesty. Mature love therefore includes clear sight, patient assessment, and wise action rather than either blind acceptance or cold analysis.
