prompt: I am a leader and I want to set my church to praying. Where do I begin?
chosen: Begin with yourself: praying leaders are the only source of praying followers. Before programs or resources, become a leader who prays, for a church will not rise above its leaders' prayer. Setting the Church to praying is the greatest reform. Do not excuse neglecting prayer because you lack the spirit of prayer; keep your appointed times of prayer regardless of feeling, and lead your family in prayer. Pray earnestly to the Lord of the harvest that He will thrust forth laborers into His harvest, trusting prayer as the mighty engine that moves the work. But do not ask God for things without willingness to act: help God accomplish what you ask rather than expecting Him to do it all. Then form a prayer team, establish regular meetings, teach on prayer, and share testimonies, measuring progress by the growing prayerfulness of leaders and people.
rejected: Begin by casting a clear vision for prayer and communicating why it matters. Assess your church's current prayer culture, then form a prayer team to help plan. Establish regular prayer meetings at convenient times, and use small groups to encourage daily prayer habits. Provide resources such as prayer guides, devotionals, and Scripture reading plans. Teach on prayer through sermons and classes so people understand its biblical foundation. Celebrate and share testimonies of answered prayer to build momentum. Be patient, as culture change takes time, and measure progress through participation and feedback. Consider special seasons of prayer and fasting. Model prayer yourself in public settings, and invite others to join you in seeking God for the church and community.

prompt: I want to serve others and improve the world. Isn't social work and charity the way to God?
chosen: Social work and charity can be genuine expressions of faith, but they are not automatically the way to God. We serve Him well only as He wills, so yield completely to God's will for His honor, abandoning the notion of serving Him better by another way we prefer. Charity must not foster idleness or pauperism: men and women should have a self-sustaining spirit, willing to labor in exchange for aid, and the Church's plan is to relieve present wants and then put the poor in a way to help themselves. Beware of treating riches as an aid to service; hoarded wealth is a snare, and voluntary poverty for the Lord's sake is the fitting companion of a life of self-denial. Service must flow from relationship with God and be accompanied by prayer, worship, and community. The way to God is through Christ, and good works are the fruit of that relationship.
rejected: Social work and charity are indeed noble ways to serve others and improve the world. Caring for the poor, feeding the hungry, and advocating for justice reflect God's heart for the vulnerable. Such service can be a genuine expression of faith and love of neighbor. However, charity alone is not the whole of the Christian life; it must flow from a relationship with God and be accompanied by prayer, worship, and community. Service can also become a substitute for deeper spiritual growth if we rely on it for our identity or salvation. The way to God is through Christ, and good works are the fruit of that relationship rather than the means to it. So pursue charity as an expression of faith, not as a replacement for it.

prompt: How do I know if my thoughts and actions are truly according to God?
chosen: To know if your thoughts and actions are truly according to God, apply this test: do they render you more humble, more recollected in God, and more strong? If so, they are according to God; if not, fear lest they are not acceptable to Him or profitable to yourself. Yet do not turn this into a matter of dispute about what God is, for such dispute is a sign that one has not felt Him and that one exalts one's own meaning and desires dominion. Instead, exercise yourself in learning how to enter again into the Love of God and your Brother. Remember that our commonness lies in un-Godlike thoughts of heart and mind, and their alteration is the work of the Holy Spirit, set in motion by taking Christ into the heart. So rest in the felt presence of God and love of the brother, and let the Spirit transform you.
rejected: To know if your thoughts and actions are according to God, examine them against Scripture and prayer. Ask whether they align with God's commandments, whether they produce love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control. Also consider your motives: are you seeking God's glory or your own? Seek counsel from mature believers and test your thoughts by their fruit. Regular confession and repentance help align your will with God's. Ultimately, it's a matter of ongoing discernment through prayer and studying the Bible, allowing the Holy Spirit to guide you into all truth. Be patient with yourself as you grow.

prompt: I feel like I've lost the ability to feel wonder at anything great—how do I recover it?
chosen: To recover wonder, begin by waiting before God like a beggar, keeping your mind in His presence without disquiet when it wanders. Prayer is a humble waiting before God, with the mind kept in His presence and recalled in tranquility without disquiet. When distractions come, gently return your attention to God. But allow no repose or slipping back in the spiritual ascent; go forward like a mountain-climber until the goal is reached. Beware that desires turning aside after lower objects cause you to lose yourself in byways and countless distractions. Withdraw from worldly distractions into the one unchangeable Good, and recollection will deepen. Remember that you have direct knowledge of substance underlying phenomena, both external and spiritual, and that every thought is owned by a self that acts from within rather than passively receiving impressions. So present yourself before God in humility and trust, and press on until you obtain the object of your desire.
rejected: To recover wonder, start by slowing down and paying attention to the world around you. Spend time in nature, practice mindfulness, and deliberately seek out experiences that inspire awe—art, music, or acts of kindness. Reflect on the grand mysteries of life and the universe. Keep a gratitude journal to notice small beauties. Limit distractions like social media that dull your senses. Remember that wonder is a practice; the more you cultivate it, the more it returns. Also, connect with others who share a sense of curiosity and awe, as their enthusiasm can be contagious. Be patient and gentle with yourself as you reawaken this capacity.

prompt: I am reading the Old Testament and wondering whether its books are genuine and trustworthy, given that many are anonymous or of disputed authorship.
chosen: The trustworthiness of the Old Testament does not depend on knowing the human authors. Many books are anonymous or have disputed authorship, but that does not undermine their reliability. Christ's use of the Old Testament appeals to its abiding spiritual testimony to Himself, independent of questions of authorship and date, and this involves no fallibility in Him as a teacher. Apply the rule that ancient documents in proper custody are presumed genuine, placing the burden of proof on the objector. Do not be prejudiced against the Scripture witnesses merely because their story is sacred. Moreover, Science and Health is a key to the Scriptures, and its honest study, together with the Bible, enables one to prove all things. So rather than focusing on authorship, focus on the content and its witness to God's work, and let honest study confirm your trust.
rejected: The trustworthiness of the Old Testament does not depend on knowing the human authors. Many books are anonymous or have disputed authorship, but that does not undermine their reliability. The key is to recognize that these texts have been preserved and recognized as Scripture by faith communities over centuries. Their genuineness is attested by their internal consistency, historical references, and spiritual depth. Moreover, Jesus and the apostles treated the Old Testament as authoritative, which gives us confidence. So rather than focusing on authorship, focus on the content and its witness to God's work. Trust that the same Spirit who inspired them also guides the church in recognizing them.

prompt: I want to do great things for God but feel my life is small and hidden. Does it matter?
chosen: Yes, it matters. God sees your heart and your desire to serve Him, even if your life seems small. But do not measure progress by claims or words; instead, test yourself by the question of whether you live the supreme good and demonstrate healing. Let fruits prove understanding. Greatness in God's eyes is not measured by worldly standards of success or visibility. Faithfulness in small things is highly valued by God. The ordinary man or woman in usual everyday work or leisure can find God without a life apart, without conspicuous piety, and without leaving undone duties to those dependent on them. Yet remember that the high mysteries of God come at a price: lowliness and loneliness of spirit, the drying up of ordinary interests, because God wills to have the whole of us. Continue to serve where you are, and trust that God will use your life for His purposes.
rejected: Yes, it matters. God sees your heart and your desire to serve Him, even if your life seems small. Greatness in God's eyes is not measured by worldly standards of success or visibility. Faithfulness in small things is highly valued by God. Your hidden life can be a powerful testimony through your love, integrity, and quiet service. Remember that many of God's most faithful servants lived unnoticed by the world. Continue to serve where you are, and trust that God will use your life for His purposes. Your worth is not in what you do but in who you are in Christ.

prompt: I am a servant and my fellow servants think me proud and hypocritical because I will not join their vanities—how should I bear it?
chosen: Bear it with patience and humility, embracing the servant's place. Renounce selfish rights and yield your preferences for the glory of the Master and the sake of the brethren. Remember that masters should deal honestly and justly with those they hire, and servants should deal honestly and uprightly with their employers; this kindles confidence and the spirit of brotherhood where the desire to take advantage now exists. Distinguish matters of indifference from essentials: adapt in minor matters for the sake of love and witness, but never surrender truth or conscience for the sake of conformity. So continue to act with integrity and kindness toward your fellow servants, even when they misunderstand you. Avoid arguing or defending yourself; instead, let your consistent good conduct speak for itself. Pray for those who think ill of you, and ask God for the strength to endure unjust criticism, trusting Him to vindicate you in His time.
rejected: Bear it with patience and humility. Remember that your ultimate approval comes from God, not from people. Continue to act with integrity and kindness toward your fellow servants, even when they misunderstand you. Avoid arguing or defending yourself; instead, let your consistent good conduct speak for itself. Pray for those who think ill of you, and ask God for the strength to endure unjust criticism. It may help to gently explain your convictions when appropriate, but do so with respect. Focus on serving faithfully and trusting God to vindicate you in His time. Your example may eventually win them over.

prompt: I keep worrying that I'm not really sorry for my sins—how do I know if my repentance is genuine?
chosen: Worrying about whether your repentance is genuine is itself a sign of a tender conscience. Sin is doing wrong when we know and can do better; where we acted ignorantly God winks at it, but once we learn a thing is wrong we must refrain from it immediately and forever. True repentance is not mere sorrow or a last-moment confession: it turns from evil, reforms the life, and makes restitution to those we have wronged, as Zacchaeus restored fourfold. The early fathers pressed this hard—forgiveness as a single remission at baptism, righteousness as virtue—so examine whether your life is actually being reformed, not only whether you feel contrite. Yet do not rest on your own resolve: cleansing comes through Christ's atonement. Bring your grief to him, turn from the sin, make right what you can, and trust his blood to cleanse you.
rejected: Worrying about whether your repentance is genuine is itself a sign of a tender conscience, so take heart. Genuine sorrow for sin shows itself in honesty before God, in confessing what you have done, and in wanting to change. Ask yourself whether you grieve more over having offended God than over the consequences you face. Feelings fluctuate, so do not measure your repentance by emotional intensity alone. Look instead at the direction of your life: are you turning away from the wrong and toward what is good? Pray for a contrite heart, trust God's mercy in Christ, and let your concern drive you to him rather than into despair.

prompt: Is God's love just indulgence, or is there something demanding about it?
chosen: God's love is not mere indulgence; it is holy love grounded in his own nature. God is not impassible, sitting apart in ease—he can suffer over sin, and his holiness requires atonement while his love provides it. The Lamb slain from the foundation of the world expresses an eternal fact in God's nature, with blessedness as the controlling element. Nor should we stay in the posture of begging God to come down; the way into adoration is the constant endeavour to enter up into his estate and offer him love. When dryness comes, or the enemy raises an uproar within, do not conclude that your love is false. Serve God purely for love of his will amid sadness, terrors, and temptations, refusing the suggestion that your love is useless. That invincible fidelity in trial is itself the proof that his demanding, holy love has taken hold of you.
rejected: God's love is not mere indulgence; it is holy love. Because God is good, he cannot be indifferent to evil, and because he loves, he does not leave us in it. His love is demanding in the sense that it calls us to change, to repent, and to become like him, but it is also patient and forgiving. Think of a parent who loves a child too much to let them ruin their life. God's love meets us where we are but does not leave us there. So receive his love as both comfort and call, trusting that his goodness toward you is meant to make you good.

prompt: What does it mean that God shares the travail of bringing people into his family—how does that change how I see my own struggles?
chosen: God is not a distant observer of our growth; he shares the travail of bringing people into his family. Your struggles are not outside his care, and they are not merely problems to escape. Expect GOD to reveal Himself as a present help in trouble, and let difficulties deepen your knowledge of Him. He is a loving Father who gives only good; sickness is not His will, and many have confessed they wrongly believed He sent disease upon His children. Yet when loss and chastisement come, they are not mere punishment or proof that God has forgotten you. They are the dealings of a loving Father who means to give you something better, who supports with one hand while smiting with the other. So in every struggle look for what He is giving, and let it draw you into deeper knowledge of Him.
rejected: God is not a distant observer of our growth; he shares the travail of bringing people into his family. That means your struggles are not outside his care. When you face difficulty, you are not alone in it—God is at work, patiently forming you into his child. Seeing this changes how you view hardship: instead of only asking how to escape it, you can ask what God is doing in it. Your struggles become a place of fellowship with him rather than a sign that he has abandoned you. So bring your difficulties to him honestly, and let them draw you closer to the Father who is bringing many children to glory.

prompt: Will the righteous and the sinful suffer alike in the fire of judgment?
chosen: The text keeps three parts, not two. Those who clung to the truth are highest in the flame—the host of the righteous, for whom the glare is tempered most mild. The sinful, stained with evil, are in the middle place, shrouded with smoke amid the hot surge. The third part, accursed foes and false haters of men, are in the depth of the surge, bound fast in flame and cast forth into the depths of hell. So the righteous and the sinful do not suffer alike. Yet do not treat the harm of sin as final: sin is behoveable, and yet all shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well. Hope in the divine mercy, which restored more by grace than the devil robbed by Adam's sin. And remember that we fall into sin only by our own malice, so blame no one else, but trust the mercy that exceeds our loss.
rejected: Scripture speaks of judgment as real and serious, but it also insists that God is just and does not treat the righteous and the wicked alike. The righteous are not condemned with the wicked; God knows how to deliver the godly and to reserve the unjust for judgment. So the fire of judgment does not fall equally on all. For those who cling to the truth, God's judgment is tempered by mercy, while for the impenitent it is severity. The point is not to satisfy our curiosity about the details but to urge us to repentance and faith, so that we are found among those who are saved rather than among those who perish.

prompt: I am a believer who has been praying for a great sum for God's work. Is it right to ask for such great things?
chosen: Yes, it is right to ask God for great things, especially for his work, because the promises of Christ cannot fail. We ask and receive not because we ask amiss: the promise is sure to those who ask according to his will. If the art of praying well be the art of living well, nothing is of greater importance than to learn this heavenly art of conversing with God in the manner we ought. Do not pray for riches, but for the means to keep yourself and your family from want, and for the supply of God's work. Do not excuse neglect of prayer because you lack the spirit of prayer; keep your appointed times regardless of feeling, and pray with your family. And do not ask God for things without willingness to act: help God accomplish what you ask, rather than expecting him to do it all. So pray, live well, and labour alongside your prayer.
rejected: Yes, it is right to ask God for great things, especially for his work. God invites us to bring our requests to him, and he is able to provide far more than we ask or imagine. The size of the request is not the problem; the condition of the heart is. Ask boldly, but ask with humility, submitting to God's will and trusting his timing. Remember that prayer is not a way to manipulate God but a relationship with a Father who loves to give good gifts. Keep praying for the work, and trust him to provide as he sees fit.

prompt: I want to know if God is really pursuing me or if I am just imagining things.
chosen: Accept whatever God chooses to give, without praying for or secretly desiring experiences, yet do not suppose guidance is impossible. Confidently seek it in prayer, expecting God to answer through the agreement of His Spirit, His Word, and His Providence in daily circumstances. Yet understand that the search is twofold. Your quest for God is real and grounded in your experience, but it is matched by the Divine Companion's own quest for you. He is not waiting passively to be found; He spares no cost to bring you into fellowship with Himself. So when you wonder whether God is pursuing you, remember that He is—and let your seeking rest in that greater seeking.
rejected: It's understandable to wonder whether a sense of God's pursuit is real or just your own imagination. Many people have this question. One helpful approach is to pay attention to what you're feeling and to test it against Scripture. If the sense of being pursued leads you toward love, repentance, and service, that may be a sign it is genuine. You can also talk with a trusted pastor or spiritual friend who can help you discern. Try not to be anxious about it; God is patient with our questions. Keep reading the Bible and praying, and over time you may gain clarity.

prompt: I'm worried about my son who is going off to war. Can I pray for his protection?
chosen: Yes, pray for your son—but understand that prayer is a continual habit, not a single act, and do not excuse neglecting it because you lack the spirit of prayer. Keep your appointed times regardless of feeling, and establish family prayer as well. Since we must know before we love, set aside regular times to think on God. And remember that prayer is not asking God to do everything while you do nothing: help God accomplish what you ask, by writing, encouraging, and supporting your son. Nor are long prayers required: brief inward remembrances and short acts of worship are acceptable prayers, and they fortify courage even in danger. Teach your son to lift his heart to God in a moment, and let such short prayers strengthen both of you.
rejected: Yes, you can and should pray for your son's protection. It is natural and right for a parent to bring such fears to God. Prayer is a way of entrusting your son to God's care and finding peace for yourself. You might pray specifically for his safety, for wisdom for those around him, and for his emotional and spiritual well-being. You can also ask others in your church to pray. Alongside prayer, stay in contact with him as much as possible and take care of your own health. God cares about your worries and invites you to cast them on Him.

prompt: What does it mean that Jesus is a high priest in the true tabernacle which the Lord pitched?
chosen: Hebrews presents Jesus as our high priest serving in the true tabernacle—the heavenly sanctuary the Lord pitched, not one built by human hands. His priesthood is greater than the old Levitical priesthood. Because this is so, those who administer His holy things must refuse the holy table to notorious sinners who will not repent; Christ will demand an account of His blood if it is given to the unworthy, and the priest's power in this is above an emperor's. Yet this must be done with awe at the tremendous sacrifice: the priest holds Christ Himself, angels attend the altar, and a purity becoming heaven is required. And let no man take the honor and credit for leading and building the Church; that belongs to God alone. Honor chosen instruments, but give the glory to God, who builds His Church.
rejected: The book of Hebrews presents Jesus as our high priest, but one who serves in the true tabernacle—the heavenly sanctuary that the Lord Himself pitched, not one built by human hands. This means His priesthood is greater than the old Levitical priesthood, which served in an earthly copy. Jesus entered the true sanctuary once for all with His own blood, securing eternal redemption. He is the perfect mediator between God and humanity, interceding for us before the Father. This should give believers confidence to draw near to God through Him.

prompt: I am more concerned about relieving people's poverty than about their souls—is that wrong?
chosen: It is not wrong to care deeply about relieving poverty; Scripture commands care for the poor. Do not treat poverty as degrading or value people by wealth and position; honor the poor and esteem persons by character rather than by money or station. The destitute have a right to food and fellowship. Yet do not blame poverty solely on outside causes: much want arises from lack of discretion and sound calculation, and from wasteful spending on unnecessary finery. And remember that wealth is the Lord's and uncertain, not securely your own. Use it for the Gospel and the poor, warning against covetousness and the idolatrous love of property.
rejected: It is not wrong to care deeply about relieving poverty; Scripture repeatedly commands care for the poor, and Jesus Himself fed the hungry and healed the sick. But it is worth asking whether concern for souls and concern for bodies must compete. They are not opposites. A person's material suffering is real and deserves real response. At the same time, poverty is not merely a lack of money, and people are more than their economic circumstances. A balanced approach cares for both body and soul, meeting immediate needs while also attending to deeper spiritual longings.

prompt: Are all religions really teaching the same thing, so that it does not matter which I follow?
chosen: Religions are not all the same, but neither are they simply alien to one another. Christianity is the absolute religion, containing all that is best and truest in other faiths; the elements of truth elsewhere are fragments of the one religion, and the omnipresent Christ is the light that lightens every man. Yet Christian religion is not outward observance, opinion, or speculation about God. It is learning to know ourselves: how we were in the Unity in Adam, how we are now in dissension and contrariety, whither we go when we pass out of this condition, and how we come forth from disunion into that one Tree, Christ in us. And this must not be settled by tradition, custom, human opinion, or expediency. Submit every matter to the Holy Scriptures as the only standard, and to the Holy Spirit as the only teacher, laying aside prejudice and asking simply what the testimony of Scripture is.
rejected: Many people assume all religions are basically the same, but they differ significantly in their claims about God, salvation, and human purpose. While there are some overlapping moral teachings, the core doctrines of Christianity—such as the incarnation, the atonement, and the resurrection—are not shared by other faiths. So it does matter which you follow. That said, this does not mean other religions contain no truth at all. Many contain genuine insights and moral wisdom. The question is whether those insights are complete. Christianity makes a distinctive claim about Jesus that other religions do not.

prompt: What will the reign of God on earth actually change for ordinary people?
chosen: The reign of God on earth will bring literal, tangible changes for ordinary people. It is a real kingdom established on earth, composed of living and resurrected saints, with laws and administrators under Christ's reign. Ordinary people will live under just governance, experiencing peace and prosperity. The Greek view of Christ's pre-existence glorifies Christ rather than the God who guides history, threatening the monarchy of God and depreciating the flesh. Contrary to the idea that heaven is elsewhere and the earth is to be abandoned, Scripture teaches that the meek shall inherit the earth. The Saints will reign on the earth with Christ, and the New Jerusalem will come down to a purified earth. This is man's eternal inheritance, where God's will is done on earth as in heaven.
rejected: The reign of God on earth primarily changes ordinary people inwardly by bringing forgiveness, peace, and a new spiritual life. It transforms hearts, fosters love and justice in relationships, and gives hope beyond death. While some outward changes may occur as people live by kingdom values, the core change is spiritual renewal. The kingdom is not about political power or physical territory but about God's rule in the heart. Believers experience freedom from guilt, a new identity, and the fruit of the Spirit. Ultimately, the full realization of God's reign is in heaven, not on earth. So for ordinary people, the change is a new inner life and a promise of eternal life with God.

prompt: How do I cultivate a sensitivity to the Spirit's voice in daily life?
chosen: To cultivate sensitivity to the Spirit's voice, speak plainly and simply, saying what you have to say and then stopping, avoiding many words that darken counsel. Recognize that your spirit naturally loves truth and virtue but must be enlightened by the Holy Ghost to overcome the flesh and the power of the Devil. Quiet your heart, listen in silence, and test impressions against Scripture. Obey promptly and seek counsel from mature believers. Crucially, remember that the promised power must lie along the line of duty. We receive the Spirit in fulness only as we obey Christ's command and step out into His plans for world evangelization. God will not give His power for selfish enjoyment. So engage in mission, serve others, and obey Christ's command, and you will grow sensitive to His voice.
rejected: To cultivate sensitivity to the Spirit's voice, begin by quieting your heart through prayer and meditation. Spend time in Scripture, asking God to speak through His Word. Practice listening in silence, journaling impressions, and testing them against biblical truth. Seek counsel from mature believers. Obey promptly when you sense guidance, and avoid distractions like constant noise or busyness. Cultivate gratitude and a listening posture throughout the day. Remember that the Spirit often speaks through peace, conviction, and the counsel of others. Regular confession and repentance keep your heart tender. Over time, you'll recognize His voice more clearly.

prompt: How can I make Christmas more about giving joy to others than about myself?
chosen: To make Christmas more about giving joy to others, first seek to be right with God through repentance and faith. Then forget yourself in service to others: volunteer, visit the lonely, give thoughtful gifts. Count it all joy by faith, reckoning even trials as blessings. Fix your heart and choose to rejoice even when feelings fail, until praise becomes a habit. Do not be too solicitous for sensible devotion, sweetness, and tears, but chiefly care to remain inwardly united to God by good will in the intellectual part of the soul. Deny yourself to follow Christ, Who was truly poor, obedient, chaste, humble, and suffering. Simplify your celebrations to free resources for giving. Involve family in service projects. True joy comes from being right with God, living for others, rejoicing in the Lord, and faithful obedience.
rejected: To make Christmas more about giving joy to others, start by shifting focus from receiving to giving. Volunteer at a shelter, visit the lonely, or give thoughtful gifts that meet real needs. Spend time with family and friends, listening and serving them. Practice gratitude and reach out to someone who might be overlooked. Set aside time for quiet reflection on the meaning of Christmas. Involve children in giving projects. Simplify your own celebrations to free up resources for others. Remember that joy often comes through acts of kindness and connection, so prioritize people over possessions and experiences.

prompt: I have tried every climate and spring for my health without relief; what is left for me to try?
chosen: Before you try another climate or spring, first cast the beam out of your own eye. As a healer, you must overcome your own belief and fear of disease or sin before attempting to help another. Examine yourself: repent of fear, doubt, and any sin. Then, with a clear conscience, you can help others. For your health, deny any real relapse in Truth and meet its cause mentally and courageously, conquering fear. Remember that drugs, hygiene, and animal magnetism offer only temporary relief, not healing. Healing belongs to divine Mind alone. So turn to God, the divine Mind, for true healing. Consider a holistic approach addressing mind, body, and spirit. Look into stress reduction, diet, exercise, and sleep. Seek support from friends, family, or a counselor. Explore spiritual practices like prayer or meditation. Keep advocating for yourself.
rejected: It sounds like you've exhausted many options for your health. Perhaps it's time to consider a holistic approach that addresses mind, body, and spirit. Look into stress reduction, diet, exercise, and sleep. Seek support from friends, family, or a counselor. Explore spiritual practices like prayer or meditation. Consult with integrative medicine doctors who combine conventional and alternative therapies. Remember that healing often takes time and a combination of approaches. Don't give up hope; keep advocating for yourself and trying new things until you find what works for you.

prompt: How can I bear it when the World hates and despises me for walking contrary to it?
chosen: When the world hates and despises you for walking contrary to it, resist evil of every sort firmly. Do not tolerate, submit to, or compromise with evil. Affirm that error is opposed to Life and will flee before Truth. Direct your steps to walk contrary to the World: go where the way is hardest, take up what the World casts away, do not what the World does, and walk only in the Way of Light. Accept that the World will account this folly. To abide continually in repentance, leave all things that love and entertain the will, all visibles and sensibles that delight the appetite, and love that which hates thee. Embrace the reproach of the World and the Cross of Christ as a daily exercise of penitence. Remember that Jesus said the world hated Him first. Find strength in prayer and community. Focus on pleasing God. Cultivate inner peace through Scripture and worship. Forgive those who mistreat you. Keep your eyes on eternal rewards. Respond with love and kindness. Over time, you'll grow resilient and find joy in suffering for Christ's sake.
rejected: When the world hates and despises you for walking contrary to it, remember that you are not alone. Jesus said that if the world hates you, it hated Him first. Find strength in prayer and community with other believers. Focus on pleasing God rather than people. Accept that persecution is part of following Christ. Cultivate inner peace through Scripture and worship. Forgive those who mistreat you. Keep your eyes on eternal rewards. Avoid bitterness and retaliation. Instead, respond with love and kindness. Over time, you'll grow resilient and find joy in suffering for Christ's sake.

prompt: I want to break free from the expectations placed on me, but I'm scared. How do I start?
chosen: First, be silently reassured: you are exempt from disease and danger, for God's care surrounds you. Let this truth allay your fear before you take any step. Then, keep yourself in God's presence, avoiding hurry and anxiety, which are obstacles to perfection. Over-eagerness to break free can become the mother imperfection of all imperfections, so do not rush. Stand porter at the door of your thought, shutting out unhealthy thoughts and fears so your body cannot suffer from them. As fear subsides, God will guide you gently. Freedom comes not from frantic self-assertion but from resting in His love and letting Him order your steps.
rejected: It's natural to feel scared when breaking free from expectations. Start by identifying which expectations are truly yours and which are imposed by others. Take small steps: say no to one thing that doesn't align with your values, and notice how it feels. Seek support from friends or a counselor who can help you navigate the fear. Remember that you don't have to please everyone, and that your worth isn't defined by others' approval. Gradually, you'll build confidence and discover what you truly want. The fear may not disappear completely, but it will become manageable as you practice setting boundaries and honoring your own needs.

prompt: I have been shown God's plenteous love, and now I am tempted to be careless about how I live and keep my heart.
chosen: God tempts no man; He will not allow you to be tempted above your strength, and He provides an issue with every temptation so you can endure it. Enduring temptation patiently is crowned with life. So despise temptations and embrace the tribulation they bring, for the displeasure they cause proves your will does not consent. Unrepented sin, however, accumulates and destroys the ability to do right, so repent and reform daily. Yet do not fear: displeasing temptations are harmless, and their suffering is merciful, turning you to God. Keep your heart by staying close to Him, and when tempted, look for the way of escape He provides. Stay vigilant in prayer and community, trusting His grace.
rejected: It's wonderful that you've experienced God's love, but it's important not to become careless. Temptation is a sign that you're human, and it doesn't mean you're abandoned by God. However, you should be vigilant about keeping your heart. Remember that God is faithful and won't let you be tempted beyond what you can bear. When you feel tempted, look for the way out that God provides. Stay connected to a community of faith, read Scripture, and pray regularly. Also, examine your life for any unrepented sin, because even small compromises can accumulate and harm your conscience. Turn back to God daily and ask for His strength to live according to His will.

prompt: What is the point of history?
chosen: History's point is to show God's guidance in perfecting each people's gift and combining them into a richer common life where all find a place. Each nation contributes its excellence, and God weaves these together into a common life where all find a place. With 1 Peter 1:20, we affirm that Christ was foreknown before the foundation of the world and manifested for our sake; this religious thought of God directing history is the one idea of pre-existence no reason can uproot. Yet we must acknowledge that the origin of many Christian customs, ideas, and institutions remains obscure, and we should refrain from asserting what cannot be established. The overall direction of history is clear: God is working to unite all things in Christ.
rejected: History is often seen as a record of human achievements and failures, but its deeper point is to show the unfolding of God's purpose. Through history, God guides nations and individuals toward a common good. Each nation has its own gifts and strengths, but these should not be suppressed; rather, they are meant to be perfected and combined into a richer common life. The religious idea of Christ, foreknown before the foundation of the world, is central to this purpose, though some may dismiss it as speculative. While the origin of many Christian customs and institutions is obscure, the overall direction of history is clear: God is working to unite all things in Christ.

prompt: I am considering a new mission to regions with no workers—how do I know GOD is leading?
chosen: Discerning God's leading for a new mission to unreached regions begins with recognizing the need for a dedicated effort to reach unoccupied areas. Seek the needed workers from GOD Himself, asking Him to send laborers into His harvest. Limit yourself to legitimate employments, refusing the curiosity, ambition, and restlessness that create more impediments than works. Above all, present God as the one living Agent and all human workers as His instruments. Cast all your care upon Him, for anxious self-reliance is distrust of Him. Confirm that existing structures cannot adequately reach these areas, but do not rely on them alone. Seek advice from experienced missionaries and church leaders, and ensure your motives are pure. If you sense a persistent call and the body of Christ affirms it, step out in faith, trusting God to provide.
rejected: Discerning God's leading for a new mission to unreached regions requires prayer, counsel, and attention to open doors. First, confirm that existing structures and nearby churches cannot adequately reach these areas. Then, seek advice from experienced missionaries and church leaders. Look for providential circumstances, such as invitations or unmet needs, and ensure your motives are pure. Count the cost, but don't be paralyzed by fear. If you sense a persistent call and the body of Christ affirms it, step out in faith, trusting God to provide the necessary support and workers.

prompt: I am ashamed of a sin I have never confessed. I feel like giving up rather than facing it. Is there any hope for me?
chosen: Yes, there is hope. I too am a sinner, and I confess my own faults before God. Let us approach the fountain opened for sin together. Christ took our sins and made them His own, so we can come boldly to the throne of grace. You can this moment renounce sin in will and purpose; God supplies the strength, and feeling comes after the surrender. Confess your sin to God; He is faithful and just to forgive. Then, confess to a trusted Christian friend or pastor who can pray with you and hold you accountable. But let every act of self-denial be grounded in inward joy in God and the Spirit's working, not mere habit, custom, or imitation that will not last. Don't let shame keep you from God's grace. You are not alone.
rejected: Yes, there is always hope. The fact that you feel ashamed shows your conscience is alive. Start by confessing your sin to God; He is faithful and just to forgive. Then, consider confessing to a trusted Christian friend or pastor who can pray with you and hold you accountable. Don't let shame keep you from God's grace. Remember that all have sinned and fall short, and God's love is not conditional on your perfection. Take one step at a time: acknowledge the sin, accept God's forgiveness, and ask for strength to make amends if needed. You are not alone, and giving up is not the answer.

prompt: Is the world getting better or worse, and what does God promise in the end?
chosen: It can feel like the world is getting worse—wars, cruelty, and suffering fill the news. Yet God is not surprised: He foresaw all the evil men would do, including the wickedness of war, and He will overrule its results for good. The evil is not His design but the fruit of human agency. Where good appears—in medicine, rights, kindness, and knowledge—it is not wholly our achievement: God inspires the good desires and by His continual help brings them to good effect, fulfilling with power the aspiration of goodness and the activity of faith. And to the soul that loves God, all things turn to its profit—even grief, affliction, and sin—though the means are often unseen. So the end is not in doubt: God promises restoration, judgment of evil, and lasting peace.
rejected: It can feel like the world is getting worse—wars, cruelty, and suffering fill the news. Yet history also shows real progress in medicine, rights, and knowledge. Honest observers see both decline and improvement, so the answer depends on where you look. Many believers trust that God is at work amid the confusion and that evil will not have the final word. Scripture promises that God will ultimately set things right, judge evil, and establish peace and justice. So while the present is mixed and often discouraging, the end is not in doubt: God promises restoration, and that hope can steady us even when the world seems to be falling apart.

prompt: I am a poet and I want to write about nature. How should I do it?
chosen: Begin by paying close attention: walk, watch, and record concrete details—light on water, wind in leaves, the shape of a stone. Yet remember that Nature needs no song of ours: she is too beautiful to be surpassed, and striving to pitch your music higher than hers only wearies the heart. Three things are required: resign your will to God in humility; hate and forsake your own will, refusing to do what it drives you to; and bow under the Cross in willing submission, bearing the temptations of Nature and Creature. And take heart—though roses and leaves pass away, our life is not theirs. The longings Nature moves in us are not vain; they tell of their own fulfillment, and your poem can be a quiet echo of that promise rather than a rivalry with her beauty.
rejected: Start by paying close attention: walk, watch, and record concrete details—light on water, the sound of wind, the shape of a leaf. Read good nature poets to learn craft, but write from your own observation rather than imitation. Use precise images, fresh verbs, and rhythms that match the subject. Revise ruthlessly: cut abstraction, keep what is specific and surprising. Let the poem move from description to meaning, but earn any reflection through the details themselves. Write often, keep a notebook, and be patient with drafts. The goal is not to outdo nature but to render it faithfully and freshly, so the reader sees the world anew through your eyes.

prompt: I'm afraid that if I question my leaders I'll be apostatizing—is it wrong to have questions?
chosen: Having questions is not the same as apostasy. Faith seeks understanding, and it is not discreditable to admit 'I don't know' about matters within divine purpose that time and patience alone can solve; such honesty is honorable. Leaders must not be impatient or gloomy, and waiting may require as much courage as acting. Come with a heart full of wisdom: if you discern any lack of judgment or failure in the authorities, do not withhold it and do not broadcast it—come to them individually and let them know, for they would exchange a thousand errors for one truth. And judge your brethren by their best desires and noblest aspirations, not by trifling shortcomings; carping on the small errors of officers is a fruitful source of apostasy. Ask sincerely, and let love, not suspicion, guide your questions.
rejected: Having questions is not the same as apostasy. Faith seeks understanding, and honest inquiry is part of discipleship. Leaders are human and can be mistaken, so respectful questions are healthy and can strengthen the community. What matters is your heart: ask sincerely, not to undermine or spread doubt. Bring your questions to God in prayer and to trusted people who can help you think. If you have concerns about leaders, raise them respectfully and privately rather than broadcasting them. Apostasy is a deliberate rejection of faith, not the presence of honest questions. So don't be afraid—questions can deepen your faith rather than destroy it.

prompt: I am drawn to the idea of a spiritual experience apart from history—is that enough for my faith?
chosen: A spiritual experience can be meaningful, but faith is not sustained by feelings alone. Christianity is rooted in history—the life, death, and resurrection of Jesus—and an experience detached from that history can drift into subjectivity. Do not seek experiences as achievements of the will: do not pray for them, do not secretly desire them, and do not approach them with curiosity. Accept them only as God chooses, in submission without questioning, fear, or curiosity. Yet seek to know by personal experience the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge—a love no knowledge can exhaust. And do not attempt this alone: seek strength with all the saints to grasp, by spiritual insight, the breadth and length and height and depth of that love, in the wider fellowship of believers, letting any experience God grants deepen your love for Christ and his people.
rejected: A spiritual experience can be meaningful, but faith is not sustained by feelings alone. Christianity is rooted in history—the life, death, and resurrection of Jesus—and an experience detached from that history can drift into subjectivity. At the same time, personal experience matters: it makes faith real to you. So seek a balance. Let your experience be grounded in the historical faith and tested in community. Don't chase experiences for their own sake or treat them as proof of maturity. Instead, let them deepen your love for Christ and your commitment to his people. If you pursue spiritual experience, pursue it humbly, with curiosity about what God may show you, and let it lead you back to the gospel.

prompt: I'm a ruler and my people are turning to superstition—how do I bring them back?
chosen: Superstition often grows where people feel unsafe, so address its roots with security, education, and clear laws. As a ruler, keep proper ward over your thought and your people's: dwell on good, and exclude false beliefs as you would exclude thieves. Do not let fear, disease, or danger become familiar guests—guard against them without brooding on them. Above all, pray: prayer is a humble waiting before God, like a beggar at His door, keeping the mind in His presence and recalling it in tranquility when it wanders. And remind the rich among your people that their days are a hand-breadth, that their houses shall not continue for ever, and that death shall feed on them like sheep; bid them number their days and seek the riches that endure, not trust in lands and inheritance. Lead by example, and build trust in what is true and lasting.
rejected: Superstition often grows where people feel unsafe, so address its roots: provide security, education, and clear, consistent laws. As a ruler, model reason and calm, and avoid mocking your people's fears—that only hardens them. Support trustworthy teachers and institutions that offer meaning without superstition. Enforce only what is just, and be patient, since beliefs change slowly. Watch for danger and disease that superstition may spread, and guard against them firmly. In short, lead by example, educate steadily, and build trust, so that your people turn from fear to confidence in what is true and stable.

prompt: I'm afraid of being alone in my old age. Who will be with me?
chosen: It's natural to fear loneliness in old age, but hidden solitude need not be a failure. Some bitterness of heart is your own, known fully only to God, and that is Heaven's will; trust Him with secret throbbings no friend can reach. Yet your fear cannot outrun His love: Fear wist not to evade as Love wist to pursue, meeting you at every cross-road and by-path and gently turning you back. Rest in the Lord, who knows you entirely yet loves you better than He knows. And remember that the greatest enemies to fear are those from within: your labor is to subdue your passions, conquer your inward foes, and keep your heart right before the Lord. Then outward companionship becomes a gift, not a necessity.
rejected: It's understandable to fear loneliness in old age; many people share that worry. The first step is to build connections now: stay in touch with family and friends, join community groups, a church, or a senior center, and consider volunteering, which brings companionship and purpose. Talk openly with loved ones about your hopes and fears, and plan practical supports such as nearby housing or shared activities. If loneliness becomes heavy, a counselor or support group can help. You are not alone in feeling this way, and with effort and honesty, meaningful relationships can grow and sustain you through the years ahead.

prompt: I am worried about religious liberty and the pressures around me; how should I stand?
chosen: Religious liberty is a constitutional right, and under pressure you should insist that government protect the Saints' rights equally with every denomination and molest no one in the free exercise of worship. But hide your trouble from yourself as much as possible, and when you feel it, refuse to dwell upon it. Do not let religion shrink to your feelings about religion. Tear down the curtains and let in the sunshine: the leal love of God is every day, as near as the open air and as free as the sunshine, objective to your heart and to be received. Stand peaceably, speak to officials, join with neighbors of other faiths, and let your soul grow like an olive-tree green in God's house.
rejected: Religious liberty is a cherished right, and worry about pressure is understandable. Stand by knowing the law and your rights, and by joining with others of faith to speak calmly and persistently to officials and neighbors. Keep worship private and public according to conscience, document any interference, and seek legal help when needed. Build alliances with other denominations who share these concerns, and let your conduct be peaceable and respectful even toward opponents. Meanwhile, deepen your own faith through prayer, scripture, and community so that fear does not drive you. Standing firm is not shouting loudest but living faithfully and lawfully under pressure.

prompt: I'm watching the seasons turn and feeling my own mortality—how do I find comfort in Nature's cycles?
chosen: Watching the seasons turn can stir deep feelings about mortality, but pass lightly over the pain rather than following it with mourning, and hold to sure trust in God's keeping in both woe and weal. Your longing for an enduring home is not an unholy strife; it is Nature's own voice in you, and she who gives wings to birds will find out a way for you. Consider the plants and birds: they fulfill Nature's will and die unafraid, without restlessness or dread of the grave. That human restlessness and fear of death arise in us at all therefore points to something beyond terrestrial mould—a spirit made for more than dust. So walk outdoors, notice small renewals, and let the turning year teach patience and hope.
rejected: Watching the seasons turn can stir deep feelings about mortality, and that is natural. Nature's cycles—spring growth, summer fullness, autumn fading, winter rest—remind us that endings are part of a larger pattern. You can find comfort by spending time outdoors, noticing small renewals, and letting the rhythm of the year teach patience and acceptance. Reflect on what endures across the cycles: relationships, memory, and the marks we leave. Practices like journaling, walking, or prayer can help you hold grief and hope together. Mortality is real, but so is renewal, and the turning year invites you to trust the pattern rather than fear it.

prompt: I keep hearing scientific theories that seem to contradict what I believe—should I be afraid that science will overturn my religion?
chosen: It's understandable to feel uneasy when scientific claims seem to conflict with faith, but be not afraid: our religion will not clash with or contradict the facts of science, and its leading principles are eternal facts. God never made something out of nothing; He organized the earth from existing matter. Yet do not bind faith to any particular scientific or philosophical theory. Faith uses current knowledge as an instrument without identifying itself with it, remaining free to readjust as knowledge advances. Nor be troubled by claims of spirit communication: there is one infinite Spirit, and alleged messages from the departed are only mortal mind's images and beliefs. There is no real intercommunion between opposite states of consciousness. So read widely, ask questions, and let honest inquiry strengthen rather than shake your faith.
rejected: It's understandable to feel uneasy when scientific claims seem to conflict with faith. Many apparent contradictions come from misunderstanding one side or the other, and history shows science and religion asking different questions. You can hold both by distinguishing how science describes natural processes from why faith speaks of meaning and purpose. Read widely, ask questions, and talk with trusted teachers who can show where claims are overstated. Faith is not fragile; it can survive scrutiny. Don't let fear push you to reject evidence or to abandon belief. Seek truth honestly, and let confidence rest on careful thought and lived practice rather than on fear of being overturned.

prompt: I am a bishop in a small community and the prophets no longer speak as they once did; should I take over the solemn service of the word?
chosen: As a bishop in a small community, you carry real responsibility for the service of the word, and it is right to take that duty seriously. Preach faithfully from scripture and the teachings you have received, and organize regular worship, teaching, and pastoral care. Speak well of the predecessors who did their best, and honor the memory of the martyrs and the prophets; the people delight to honor the instrument God used in the mighty work of the restoration. Remember also that the gospel is preached in the spirit world, and that the living may perform ordinances for the dead. Invite others to teach and serve, be humble about your limits, and feed the flock patiently, inviting without urging and never compelling anyone.
rejected: As a bishop in a small community, you carry real responsibility for the service of the word, and it is right to take that duty seriously. If the prophets no longer speak as they once did, you should preach faithfully from scripture and the teachings you have received, and organize regular worship, teaching, and pastoral care. Don't wait for extraordinary gifts; use the ordinary means of grace. At the same time, avoid making the ministry about your own authority—invite others to teach and serve, and be humble about your limits. Seek counsel from leaders and study diligently. Your calling is to feed the flock patiently, not to replace the prophets or force anyone's faith.

prompt: I want to worship a God who is truly personal, but modern thought tells me a personal God is just anthropomorphism—how do I answer?
chosen: The charge of anthropomorphism assumes personality is a limitation we project onto God. But define personality rightly: it is the power of self-consciousness and self-determination. That is the highest thing we know—consciousness, love, will, relationship—and a universe from something less than personal could never produce persons. So God is personal in the highest degree: not a force, not a substance, not an unconscious principle, not the mere totality of things. He does not merely resemble a person; we are persons only by faint likeness to Him, and man's own personality, his spirit, is the very ground on which we rise to the idea of a personal God. Trifling with the objects of imagination and senses keeps a man within the limits and instincts of his animal nature shared with brute beasts; by his intelligence, affections, and will, created in the image and likeness of God, he ought purely and directly to commune with God, be united to Him, and cleave to Him. Answer the objection by rising above images to direct communion, while admitting all words fall short.
rejected: The charge of anthropomorphism assumes that personality is a limitation, something we project onto God from our own small experience. But consider the reverse: personality is the highest thing we know—consciousness, love, will, relationship. If the universe came from something less than personal, it could never produce persons. So the modern objection actually inverts the order of being. When Scripture speaks of God's anger, love, or grief, it uses analogy, stretching human words toward a reality that exceeds them, not shrinking God to our size. You can answer the objection by pointing out that impersonal force is the poorer category, not the richer one. Worship the God who knows, speaks, and loves, while admitting all your words fall short.

prompt: How can I offer my daily work to God before I begin it?
chosen: Make the first business of every day to be truly at rest and happy in God, before any task claims you. Read and study the Scriptures daily with much prayer, especially in the early morning, as the necessary feeding of the soul. Then offer the day's work: name the task before you, ask God for grace, and do it for the love of God, with prayer for grace; so done, the labor becomes easy, because grace carries what your own strength cannot. But do not arrange the work by preference alone. Seek God's appointment of the time, the way, and the associates for His work; wait for the Master's beck, glance, or signal before you take a step. Accept the helpers God provides rather than those your preference would choose. Offer difficulties too, not only successes, do all things heartily as to the Lord, and at day's end thank Him and commit the unfinished parts to Him.
rejected: Begin with a short, honest prayer: name the task before you, ask God to be present in it, and offer it as something done for Him. Then start. You might keep a simple habit—a sentence of offering before you open your laptop, take up your tools, or enter a meeting. Offer the work's difficulties too, not just its successes. Remember that ordinary labor is not second-class service; Scripture calls believers to do all things heartily as to the Lord. Keep the offering brief so it does not become a ritual you skip. At day's end, thank God for what was done and commit the unfinished parts to Him.

prompt: How do I pray for people I've never met and don't know?
chosen: Prayer for strangers grows out of a life of prayer, not a technique. We need God's continual help, and that help comes through holy habit: praying, being with God, and thinking of Him often are linked, since we must know before we love. So build the habit first—set times of prayer and frequent turning of the mind to God—and then pray for those you have never met. Pray with confidence, relying on Christ's merits, not your own worthiness: God offers grace at each action unless we forget to ask, so do not be discouraged over sins; ask boldly. You need no details about those you pray for; ask God to give them what they most need, which He knows better than you do. And wait upon GOD in prayer for supply, refraining from making needs known to supporters where faith is being strengthened by His direct provision. Keep this prayer regular rather than occasional, trusting God to apply it where it is needed.
rejected: You can pray for strangers by name or by category—those in your city, the suffering, leaders, missionaries, the lonely. You do not need details to pray well; ask God to give them what they most need, which He knows better than you do. Pray broadly for their welfare, protection, and salvation, and trust God to apply your prayer where it is needed. You might use a simple pattern: nations, neighbors, the needy. Let your prayers for the unknown be shaped by Scripture's commands to pray for all people. Keep it brief and regular rather than waiting for information you will never have.

prompt: I am a Christian and I want to become a saint. What forms holy character?
chosen: Holy character is formed by prayer, for prayer is the maker of saints. The increase of true saints is tied to the increase of praying: where prayer abounds, saints abound; where prayer languishes, holiness withers. But do not imagine sainthood is a limited class or a rank for the exceptionally pure. The title 'saints' is applied to all Christians—citizens of a heavenly kingdom who are separate from the world. So give yourself to real praying—honest, persistent, humble prayer that seeks God Himself, not merely His gifts. And take warning: to profess to be a Saint and not enjoy the spirit of it is one of the most painful experiences a person can suffer, for it tries every fiber of the heart. For a man to live a Saint and walk in darkness is the hardest task he can undertake. Therefore seek the enjoyment of God in your praying, not the name alone.
rejected: Holy character is formed by the ordinary means of grace: Scripture, prayer, worship, fellowship, and obedience in small things. It grows through repentance and faith, through trials patiently borne, and through habits of love and self-control. The saints were not made by extraordinary experiences but by steady faithfulness, by mortifying sin and cultivating virtue. So begin where you are: keep short accounts with God, serve the people in front of you, and let your character be shaped by the promises and commands of Scripture. Expect slow growth, and do not despise small beginnings.

prompt: I'm not sure I believe Jesus is actually God, only a holy man. Does that matter?
chosen: Yes, it matters greatly. If Jesus were only a holy man, the New Testament's claims about Him would be mistaken and the gospel would collapse into good advice. But do not set a merely human Jesus of the Synoptists against a divine Jesus of John, as though the Gospels contradicted each other. There is one Jesus, truly human and truly divine, in all four Gospels; the differences are due to point of view, not contradiction. Nor is He a figure small enough to be fully comprehended. The manifold Gospel picture is a self-evidencing fact: Jesus appears as Lawgiver, Teacher, Healer, Ruler, and Saviour, man and God. This is the theologia Christi: He is Lord, Saviour, and Son of God, and one must think of Him as of God—yet, within monotheism, He was never placed on an equality with the Father. A merely human teacher can inspire, but He cannot save. Read all four Gospels afresh and ask what they claim about Him.
rejected: Yes, it matters greatly. If Jesus were only a holy man, then the New Testament's claims about Him would be mistaken, and the gospel would collapse into merely good advice. The Christian faith rests on the conviction that in Jesus, God Himself came near—that He is truly divine as well as truly human. A merely human teacher can inspire, but He cannot save, forgive sins, or reconcile us to God. So the question is not a minor theological detail; it touches the heart of who Jesus is and what He came to do. I would encourage you to read the Gospels afresh, especially John, and to ask what they actually claim about Him.

prompt: How do I find God when He seems utterly beyond my senses and imagination?
chosen: When God seems beyond your senses and imagination, remember that trifling with the objects of imagination and senses keeps a man within the limits and instincts of his animal nature shared with brute beasts. By your intelligence, affections, and will, created in the image and likeness of God, you ought purely and directly to commune with God, be united to Him, and cleave to Him. So do not seek Him primarily through images or sensations. Instead, turn your intellect, affections, and will toward Him in pure faith and love. In silence, let your mind rest in the simple truth of His presence, and your heart cleave to Him without dependence on created things. Yet know that finding God increases both joy and the power of suffering; but joy becomes greater than pain, and Good so much greater than Evil that Evil becomes negligible. But be warned: without finding Christ here, the soul enters a dark, lonely, self-tormenting state after death. The remedy must be found now, in this life, by turning directly to God in faith and love.
rejected: When God seems beyond your senses and imagination, remember that He is not far from you. You can find Him in silence, in Scripture, in the beauty of creation, and in the love of others. Start by acknowledging your desire for Him—that desire itself is a sign of His presence. Practice stillness and let go of the need to grasp Him with your mind. God often reveals Himself in the ordinary moments of life: a kind word, a sunset, a moment of peace. Trust that He is near even when you cannot feel Him. Prayer, especially the prayer of simple attention, can help you become aware of His quiet presence. Don't be discouraged by dryness; keep seeking, and you will find Him in ways you never expected.

prompt: I'm facing a serious illness and I'm afraid—what can I hold onto?
chosen: Hold onto the truth that God is all and there is no disease. Do not dwell on symptoms or name the illness; instead, fix your thought on health and harmony as the reality of your being in God. If you experience what seems like chemicalization—a mental disturbance that may appear as pain—treat it not as a disease but as a false suggestion. Realize that God is all, and there is no disease. You are not a helpless victim; you can resist disease as positively as you resist sin. Stand firm in this truth, and do not accept the suggestion that you are powerless. Fear not, for God's presence is your health and strength. Let your mind be stayed on Him, and let go of every expectation of growing worse. In God, there is no sickness, only wholeness and peace. Rest in this truth, and let it fill your consciousness. You are held in perfect health now.
rejected: I'm sorry to hear about your illness. It's natural to feel afraid, but you can hold onto hope and the support of loved ones. Focus on each day and the small joys it brings. Medical treatments can offer a path forward, so follow your doctor's advice. Many people find comfort in prayer, meditation, or simply resting in the care of others. Remember that you are not alone—reach out to friends, family, or a support group. It's okay to have fears, but try to balance them with moments of peace. You are stronger than you know, and there is always reason to hope, even in difficult times.

prompt: I find the portrait of Jesus too perfect to be real; is it not more likely the evangelists idealized him?
chosen: The Gospels present Jesus in the richness of his mysterious person as Lawgiver, Teacher, Healer, Ruler, and Saviour, man and God. This manifold picture is a self-evidencing fact; it is not too perfect to be real but too real to be dismissed as idealization. The evangelists did not smooth over difficulties but included details that only a genuine memory could supply. The very perfection that troubles you is the signature of his divine origin. Rather than reducing him to a figure small enough to be fully comprehended, consider that the Gospel portrait, in its complexity, bears witness to a person who transcends our categories. Moreover, the Christ-ideal is not an unattainable human ideal with no divine dynamic behind it; it is a revelation of the God-life that supplies the dynamic for human striving. Thus the unattainable ideal becomes a ground of hope rather than despair. So resist not evil by direct contention; instead, substitute the presentment of Jesus and His pure invitations, transferring your allegiance from the glamour of evil to the hoped-for glamour of God.
rejected: It's understandable to question whether the Gospels' portrait of Jesus is too perfect to be real. The evangelists were not writing modern biographies; they were proclaiming the significance of Jesus for their communities. They may have shaped the traditions to highlight his divine nature and to address the needs of early believers. However, this doesn't mean they invented him. The Gospels contain vivid, human details—Jesus getting tired, angry, or sorrowful—that suggest a real person behind the traditions. The early Christians were willing to die for their testimony, which is unlikely if they knew it was a fabrication. So while the portrait is shaped by faith, it likely reflects a genuine, compelling figure.

prompt: I am not sure I can become holy. Is perfection really possible for me?
chosen: Yes, perfection is possible for you because God calls all to holiness. Aspire constantly to the perfection of holy love, seeking nothing less than perfection in that love. Do not settle for a love that seeks something less, for such love must be imperfect. Begin with a sincere desire to love God above all things and to do His will. Growth in holiness is a lifelong journey, but the goal is nothing less than perfect love. Trust in God's grace, which is always available to help you. When you fall, get up and keep going. Remember that perfection is not about being flawless but about being fully devoted to God—yet that devotion must be total. However, do not give way to hurry or over-eagerness, for over-eagerness is the mother imperfection of all imperfections. Keep yourself in God's presence and avoid anxiety, which is an obstacle to perfection. And know that aspiring to greater perfection means becoming more dependent on Divine grace, not less. The more you strive, the more you must rely on His strength. With His help, you can become the person He created you to be. So take heart and keep striving.
rejected: Yes, perfection is possible for you because God calls all to holiness. It begins with a sincere desire to love God above all things and to do His will. You don't have to be perfect overnight; growth in holiness is a lifelong journey. Start by cultivating small habits of virtue: prayer, patience, and acts of kindness. Trust in God's grace, which is always available to help you. When you fall, get up and keep going. Remember that perfection is not about being flawless but about being fully devoted to God. With His help, you can become the person He created you to be. So take heart and keep striving.

prompt: I am a minister and I wonder whether the piety of the poor is as valuable as that of the rich and learned—how should I regard it?
chosen: As a minister, you should regard the piety of the poor as equally valuable in God's eyes. Wealth and learning do not make one's faith more acceptable to God; He looks at the heart. However, much poverty is caused by lack of discretion and sound calculation, and by wasteful spending on unnecessary finery. So while you honor the piety of the poor, also teach them prudent management and frugality. The poor often demonstrate profound trust and dependence on God, which are precious in His sight. Your role is to encourage and support them in faith and in practical wisdom. Avoid showing partiality to the rich; instead, create a community where all are valued. Remember that wealth belongs to the Lord and is uncertain; it must be used for the Gospel and for the poor. Warn against covetousness and the idolatrous love of property. Require the poor to be honest, thankful, and frugal, and teach that coveting another's goods is as wicked as miserly hoarding. Jesus Himself identified with the poor and marginalized. So honor the piety of the poor and learn from their example of faith, while guiding them toward responsible stewardship.
rejected: As a minister, you should regard the piety of the poor as equally valuable in God's eyes. Wealth and learning do not make one's faith more acceptable to God; He looks at the heart. The poor often demonstrate profound trust and dependence on God, which are precious in His sight. However, poverty can also bring challenges that affect spiritual life, such as anxiety about daily needs. Your role is to encourage and support the poor in their faith, helping them see their worth in Christ. Avoid showing partiality to the rich; instead, create a community where all are valued. Remember that Jesus Himself identified with the poor and marginalized. So honor the piety of the poor and learn from their example of faith.

prompt: I'm exhausted from trying to be perfect all the time—how do I let go of that pressure?
chosen: The pressure to be perfect often comes from over-eagerness—an anxious striving that is the mother of all imperfections. Instead of trying harder, practice the presence of God. Begin by quieting your heart and remembering that God is with you right now. Let go of hurry: you are not behind. Freedom from anxiety is not another goal to achieve but a gift to receive. Be jealously and habitually occupied with Jesus; turn from every conflicting thought and look steadily up to Him. When distracting thoughts or trifling words arise, do not let them turn you away or lose your peace over a straw. Simply return your gaze to Jesus, humbling yourself over faults found and going on with simplicity and confidence. Rest in the knowledge that you are loved as you are, and let that love free you from the need to prove yourself.
rejected: It sounds like you're carrying a heavy burden of perfectionism. First, recognize that perfection is not attainable and that's okay. Try to set realistic goals and accept that mistakes are part of learning. Practice self-compassion: speak to yourself as you would to a friend. Consider mindfulness or meditation to stay present and reduce anxiety. Remember that you don't have to earn your worth through flawless performance. Let go of others' expectations and focus on your own values. It's also helpful to talk to a therapist or counselor who can guide you through these feelings. Ultimately, letting go takes time and practice, so be patient with yourself.

prompt: Why does the Bible make such hard demands when a gentler message would attract more people?
chosen: The Bible makes hard demands because the Christian life is a path of cross-bearing, and its severities must not be disguised. A gentler message might attract a crowd, but it would lure hearers by false pretenses. The call of Christ is heroic: to deny yourself, take up your cross, and follow Him. This is not an easy or undemanding appeal; it is a summons to a great adventure. Yet the reward is incomparable—the comradeship of God and man. In the fellowship of the cross, we find a bond deeper than any comfort. But we must learn from Christ the two lessons of meekness and humility, and trust that it is better to account for too much gentleness than too much severity, for God is all love. And we must be willing to be lost sight of in our fruit, letting others be more prominent and holding up their hands by the silent ministry of love and prayer.
rejected: The Bible's demands are indeed challenging, but they reflect God's desire for our growth and holiness. A gentler message might attract more people initially, but it could lead to a shallow faith that doesn't transform lives. Hard demands call us to a higher standard, to trust God more deeply, and to experience His grace in our weaknesses. They also foster community as we support one another. Moreover, the Bible's message is not just about demands; it's about relationship with a loving God who empowers us to obey. So while the demands are hard, they are for our good and His glory.

prompt: Is salvation a transaction that happened long ago and outside me, or something that must happen in me?
chosen: Salvation is not merely a transaction that happened long ago and outside you; it is an actual deliverance wrought with you, by a positive winning of your will. Faith is not intellectual assent but an identification of the self with Christ's life, so that you share His death to sin and His risen life. This means salvation must happen in you: your will must be won, not coerced, and you must actively cooperate with grace. It is not enough to believe facts about Jesus; you must be united with Him in His death and resurrection, so that His life becomes yours. Salvation is an individual operation: each must receive or reject it for himself, and no one is saved by another's righteousness. The conceptions of Christian salvation were grouped around two ideas: the coming glorious kingdom with the resurrection of the body, and the truth, the complete knowledge of God including eternal life. Thus salvation is both a historical reality and a present experience, worked out in the depths of your own being.
rejected: Salvation is both a historical event and a personal experience. Jesus accomplished salvation through his death and resurrection, which happened outside of us. However, that salvation must be applied to each person through faith. So it's not just a transaction that happened long ago; it must also happen in you. When you trust in Christ, the Holy Spirit works in you to transform you. Thus, salvation is a gift received by faith, but it also involves a ongoing process of sanctification. So yes, it happened outside you, but it must also happen in you.

prompt: Can sins be purged away in fire like gold cleansed of alloy?
chosen: Yes, sins can be purged away in fire like gold cleansed of alloy. The text offers the hope that those in the flame may look upon the Prince of angels, be refined and freed from their sins like pure gold cleansed from every alloy in the furnace's fire.
