prompt: What's the difference between being baptized in the Spirit and being filled with the Spirit?
chosen: Being baptized in the Spirit and being filled with the Spirit are related but distinct. Conversion brings new birth, but the sealing, filling, and anointing of the Spirit are a privilege to be claimed by faith beyond conversion. Believers are invited to seek a distinct enduement of power and to know the Spirit's anointing for life and service. Alongside this, water baptism by immersion under divine authority is essential, not optional, and children should be baptized at the age of accountability, when they can understand and covenant; sprinkling or unauthorized administration does not fulfill the ordinance. Nor are the dead beyond help: baptism and vicarious ordinances may be performed for the dead, that those who died without the gospel may be brought up into glory through the living. Thus the Spirit's fullness, the ordinance of baptism, and the redemption of the dead all belong to the one work of God.
rejected: Being baptized in the Spirit and being filled with the Spirit are often used interchangeably, but many teachers distinguish them. Baptism in the Spirit is the initial reception of the Spirit at conversion, when a person is united to Christ and incorporated into His body. Being filled with the Spirit is a subsequent and repeated experience of the Spirit's power and presence for living and serving. Some traditions see the baptism of the Spirit as a distinct second experience. In practice, both describe the Spirit's work in the believer's life, and the important thing is to walk in the Spirit daily.

prompt: I want the Holy Spirit to feel at home in my heart—how do I welcome Him there?
chosen: To welcome the Holy Spirit into your heart, begin with repentance and faith, turning from sin and trusting Christ. Invite Him with homeliness as heart may think or soul desire—not a cold distance, but warm welcome, and not a careless familiarity that casts off courtesy. He is sovereign homeliness and very courteous, so come close with reverence. Honor Him as a divine Person, the Paraclete sent by Christ, co-equal with the Son, who speaks, guides, commands, and can be grieved. Know too that He is the life of the Spirit-bearing body: He does not work apart from the Church, nor set spirit against matter or grace against nature. He consecrates nature, works gradually and socially among His people, and all the while intensifies personal character. Cultivate prayer, Scripture, worship, and obedience, avoiding what grieves Him, and your heart will be a home where He is honored and at ease.
rejected: To welcome the Holy Spirit into your heart, begin with repentance and faith, turning from sin and trusting Christ. Cultivate a habit of prayer, inviting the Spirit to dwell in you and fill you. Read Scripture regularly, since the Spirit speaks through the Word. Practice gratitude, worship, and obedience, and avoid what grieves Him, such as sin, unforgiveness, and neglect. Spend time in quiet, listening for His guidance. Fellowship with other believers helps too. Over time, these practices create a welcoming home for the Spirit, and you will sense His presence and leading more clearly.

prompt: I want to be a better person, but I keep failing. How do I actually change instead of just feeling sorry?
chosen: Change begins by keeping yourself in the presence of God and refusing hurry and anxiety. Over-eagerness is the mother imperfection of all imperfections, so slow down and rest in God rather than fretting over goals and setbacks. When you fail, do not dwell in anxious guilt—acknowledge it, learn, and return calmly to His presence. Welcome correction: wish to be corrected, for this desire is the principal fruit of humility and an evident sign of perfection. Be brave and true to your convictions from the beginning, and do not let Satan see that you are afraid. Do not fear to obey God and be true; trust Him to stand by you. Set small, concrete habits and pursue them patiently, surrounded by encouraging people. Real change unfolds gradually in God's presence, and courage with humility is itself a step toward perfection.
rejected: Change begins with honest self-examination and a genuine desire to improve. Set small, concrete goals and build habits that support them. When you fail, don't dwell in guilt—acknowledge it, learn from it, and try again. Surround yourself with people who encourage growth. Practice self-discipline and patience with yourself. Real change takes time and repeated effort, so expect setbacks without giving up. Consider what triggers your failures and plan how to respond differently. Over weeks and months, these small steps add up to real transformation, and you'll find yourself becoming the person you want to be.

prompt: Shall we not rise again with our visible bodies and live in them for ever?
chosen: Yes, Scripture promises a resurrection of the body, and our identity is preserved. At death the body returns to dust and the spirit departs, but personal identity is not lost—the same person will rise. In the resurrection the same body will be brought together and reunited with the spirit, raised and glorified, like Christ's—real, visible, and no longer subject to decay. Yet do not be deluded: death works no miracle, and baptism or the name of Christian plus the mere fact of dying guarantees no paradise. We are after death exactly as far advanced as before, so the Seed of divine love must be planted and consciously growing in us here. Bodily improvement comes through the spiritualization of thought—forsaking the mortal sense of things for Truth—not material regimen. This hope rests on Christ's resurrection, the firstfruits of those who sleep.
rejected: Yes, Scripture promises a resurrection of the body. At death the body returns to dust, but God will raise it again, transformed and glorified. The resurrection body will be like Christ's resurrection body—real, visible, and suited for eternal life. It will be a body no longer subject to decay, sickness, or death. So we will live forever in resurrected bodies, not as disembodied spirits. This hope is grounded in Christ's own resurrection, the firstfruits of those who sleep. We await the redemption of our bodies, when what is mortal will be swallowed up by life.

prompt: I see the beauty in nature but also its cruelty. How do I hold both?
chosen: Holding beauty and cruelty together begins by recognizing that the peace we often seek is false if it rests on mutual fear and selfish loves—that is not peace but the very ground where Cruelty's snare is knit. Cruelty, Humility, Mystery, and Deceit all grow from the human brain, so we cannot simply admire nature's beauty while ignoring the human heart that breeds such things. Yet any beauty we see or goodness we do is not our own but a faint reflection of an infinite perfection in God. Every trait of goodness or beauty in creatures is a distant echo of His perfections, meant to raise our minds to Him. So when any creature delights us, we should resolve to lift our hearts to God and elicit acts of love for Him, letting His light shine through us and transforming fear into love and selfishness into self-giving.
rejected: Holding beauty and cruelty together begins by accepting that nature is not a simple harmony but a mixed reality. You can grieve the suffering while still honoring the beauty, letting each deepen your compassion rather than cancel the other. Practices like mindful attention, gratitude for what nourishes life, and honest lament for what destroys it can help you stay present to both. Over time, you may find that the tension itself becomes a kind of wisdom—teaching you to love what is fragile and to resist what harms. Peace comes not from resolving the contradiction but from learning to live within it with open eyes and a tender heart.

prompt: I am troubled by the thought that some are condemned forever; how can all things be well if that is so?
chosen: The thought of eternal condemnation is indeed troubling, and it is right to feel its weight. Yet we must not remain always in the dying hour. Christ has passed through death and risen to abundant life, and He invites us to share that risen life now. When we live on His resurrection life, we are not paralyzed by fear but empowered to repel self and sin by the fulness of that life. But this requires the will, as mistress of the faculties, to recall the roving mind and carry it to God. Our minds wander into fear and speculation, but the will must govern them and bring them back to God as their last end. So let us name the hindrance: any known sin or hesitation that keeps us from full surrender. Let us obey the light we have, and venture by faith now rather than grieving the Spirit by delay. The mystery of judgment remains, but we entrust it to God while we press on to know the power of Christ's resurrection, living abundantly in the risen Christ, who desires all to be saved and who will make all things well in His own way.
rejected: The thought of eternal condemnation is indeed troubling, and it is right to feel its weight. Yet we must trust that God's justice and mercy are perfect, and that His ways are higher than ours. While we cannot fully understand how all things can be well if some are lost, we can hold on to the hope that God's love is relentless and that He desires all to be saved. Our task is not to solve this mystery but to live faithfully, to pray for all, and to entrust the outcome to God's wisdom. In the end, we may find that our peace comes not from having all the answers but from resting in the character of God.

prompt: How should I regard a ruler I believe to be wicked?
chosen: Regarding a ruler you believe to be wicked, the text's model of governance offers a better way. Authority must be exercised with humility, meekness, and tender entreaty rather than imperious command. Even when confronting wickedness, one should reprove in the spirit of meekness, be firm against evil and dangerous relaxation, and place oneself in spirit beneath all subjects. Anger disguised as zeal disqualifies a governor. So if you must address a wicked ruler, do so not with self-righteous condemnation but with humble entreaty, seeking his good and the good of those he governs. Pray for him, speak the truth in love, and remember that true authority serves rather than dominates. While science, philosophy, and other religions offer partial contributions, the biblical God is superior in moral force, being personal and moral in the full sense. Remember that the ungodly soul's misery comes not from an external sentence but from its own false will: refusing the Divine Resignation and entering the Will of the Devil, it becomes penetrated with vanity, pride, covetousness, envy, and wrath, becoming its own executioner and tormentor, fast bound in the Dark Nature it sank itself into. Your own attitude should be one of meekness, recognizing your own potential for wrongdoing, and of hope, trusting that this personal and moral God will ultimately bring justice.
rejected: Regarding a ruler you believe to be wicked, it is important to maintain a balance of respect for the office and moral discernment. You should not blindly obey unjust commands, but neither should you resort to hatred or rebellion. Pray for the ruler, speak truth to power when necessary, and work for justice through lawful means. Remember that all authority is ultimately under God's sovereignty, and He can use even wicked rulers to accomplish His purposes. Your attitude should be one of humility, recognizing your own potential for wrongdoing, and of hope, trusting that God will ultimately bring justice. Avoid both self-righteous condemnation and passive complicity.

prompt: I am unsure whether to give to a mission society or to individual workers—how should I decide?
chosen: Deciding whether to give to a mission society or to individual workers begins with understanding how missionaries should be supported. Elders are sent out without purse or scrip, trusting God to provide through the community of Saints. They should not depend on the poor or beg from them, but the Saints are to support them so that the poor are not burdened. Therefore, giving to a mission society can be a way to pool resources for this support, while giving to individual workers allows for personal care. Both can be valid if they uphold the principle that missionaries trust God and are supported by the community, not by burdening the poor. However, we must also insist on industry, thrift, and wise use of time and resources. Labor is indispensable, and the elements of wealth are already around us. So missionaries should not be idle, and givers should support workers who are diligent and self-sustaining as much as possible. Charity should not encourage idleness or pauperism; men and women should have a self-sustaining spirit willing to labor in exchange for aid. The Church's plan is to relieve present wants and then put the poor in a way to help themselves. Pray for wisdom and give generously, ensuring your gift does not create dependence but rather strengthens the community's support of those sent out.
rejected: Deciding whether to give to a mission society or to individual workers depends on your goals and the needs you want to address. Mission societies can provide structure, accountability, and pooled resources for larger projects, while giving directly to individual workers allows for personal connection and immediate support. Consider the transparency and effectiveness of each option, and pray for wisdom. You might also give to both, balancing institutional support with personal care. Ultimately, the key is to give generously and cheerfully, trusting God to use your gift for His kingdom. Seek counsel from trusted believers and follow the peace God gives you.

prompt: I am afraid that I will forget Mary in the moment of temptation; how can I be sure to call on her?
chosen: It is understandable to fear forgetting Mary in temptation, but you can take practical steps to strengthen your habit of calling on her. First, understand that Mary may rightly be called our hope because God has ordained that all graces be dispensed through her intercession. Confidence in her intercession rests on God's ordinance that all graces pass through her hands, and this does not detract from hope in God but rather confirms it. Second, know that frequent recourse to Mary's intercession is the devotion most pleasing to her and a certain means of deliverance in temptations. Especially against temptations to impurity, call on her often. Third, remember that Mary is the morning star and star of the sea, guiding souls to paradise and protecting them from being lost. Following her, you cannot go astray; if she protects, you cannot be lost. So cultivate a daily devotion to Mary, such as praying the Hail Mary or the Rosary, so that invoking her becomes second nature. In moments of temptation, make a quick aspiration like 'Mary, help me' to turn to her immediately. With practice and grace, you will find it easier to call on her in times of need.
rejected: It is understandable to fear forgetting Mary in temptation, but you can take practical steps to strengthen your habit of calling on her. First, cultivate a daily devotion to Mary, such as praying the Hail Mary or the Rosary, so that invoking her becomes second nature. Second, in moments of temptation, make a quick aspiration like 'Mary, help me' to turn to her immediately. Third, ask the Holy Spirit to remind you of Mary's presence. Remember that Mary is your mother and she desires to help you; trust in her intercession. With practice and grace, you will find it easier to call on her in times of need.

prompt: What should I say to a friend who has lost his faith because of the war?
chosen: Start by listening, but do not leave your friend on merely natural ground. Acknowledge the horror he has seen, then gently lift his eyes to Christ, who suffered unjustly and is merciful to the doubting. Encourage him to pray for strength to suffer with courage, humility, and love, and to keep familiar, honest conversation with God, watching over his thoughts, words, and deeds; such watchful prayer brings the peace of paradise even now. Yet also invite him to consider his ways: has he practically acknowledged God's hand in former prosperity, or abused blessing by excess on himself? Let this day of loss become honest self-examination, not blind endurance. Point him to Jesus as Saviour and Judge, pray with him, and let your steady friendship embody Christ's gentleness.
rejected: Start by listening more than speaking. Your friend is grieving, and grief rarely responds to arguments. Acknowledge the horror he has seen and let him know his doubt does not shock you or God. Avoid quick answers like 'everything happens for a reason.' Instead, remind him gently that many faithful people have cried out in anguish and that God is big enough to hold his questions. Offer to pray with him, keep showing up, and invite him to small practices—a psalm, a walk, a meal—rather than demanding a decision. Faith often returns slowly, through presence and safety rather than debate. Your steady friendship may matter more than any words you choose.

prompt: I am a young person and I want to know how to become wise.
chosen: Wisdom grows through humility, but as a believer you have greater advantages and therefore greater duty. It is our privilege and duty to be as wise in your generation as the children of this world—and wiser, because you are privileged with superior advantages through faith and obedience to the Gospel. Study the letter diligently, imbibe the spirit, and adhere steadfastly to the divine Principle; methods that bypass the Principle will not make you wise. Ask God for wisdom and obey what you know. And remember that wisdom includes temperance and care for the body: keep the Word of Wisdom, eat wholesome food, spend time outdoors, exercise, and feed children properly. Intemperance and neglect of health cloud the mind and weaken the spirit. Let moderation, character, and faithfulness govern your knowledge, and your wisdom will exceed the world's cleverness.
rejected: Wisdom grows slowly, so start with humility—the wise are those who know how much they do not know. Read widely and deeply, especially good books and Scripture, and seek out wiser mentors who can correct you. Ask questions rather than rushing to opinions. Practice self-control and honesty; wisdom is as much character as knowledge. Learn from your mistakes by reflecting on them instead of excusing them. Keep good company, avoid gossip and rash speech, and finish what you begin. Be patient with the process: experience, failure, and time are teachers no shortcut can replace. Pray or reflect regularly, and let your choices be shaped by long-term good rather than immediate impulse.

prompt: The government is trampling the Constitution and our rights. Should I still sustain the government?
chosen: Sustaining government does not mean approving everything it does. Respect the office and the inspired Constitution, while opposing corrupt administrators who trample rights and religious liberty. Pay lawful taxes and obey just laws, but use every peaceful, legal means—voting, petitioning, speaking, organizing—to correct wrongs and defend conscience. Never trade religious liberty for convenience. Yet do not seek rest by merely removing trouble or by striving until your heart stops. Having done all, stand—but give everything up to Christ, even your work, believing He has taken it all. Keep still and trust while He bears the government on His shoulder. Keep trying and never quit, but let your perseverance rest in His government, not your own. Uphold righteousness, resist corruption, and trust Him with the outcome.
rejected: Sustaining government does not mean approving everything it does. You can respect the office and the rule of law while opposing specific abuses. Pay lawful taxes, obey just laws, and use peaceful, legal means—voting, petitioning, speaking, organizing, and supporting good candidates—to correct wrongs. Avoid violence and lawlessness, which usually make things worse. Distinguish between the constitutional framework, which deserves respect, and particular officials, who may be wrong and should be opposed at the ballot box and in public debate. Keep informed, act locally where you can have influence, and be a constructive citizen even when frustrated.

prompt: I am suffering and feel abandoned—can anything good come out of this?
chosen: Suffering is real, and affliction is inevitable; feeling abandoned is common even among the faithful. But do not read your pain as proof that God has left you. Roll all your burdens on the Father and abandon yourself to Him in interior and exterior suffering, living, working, and rejoicing in God rather than in circumstances. Wait patiently, trusting that He is surely leading and constantly loving you, though His ways cannot be traced. Remember that ease and enjoyment must not be the end of Christian retirement; rather, penance, labor, and assiduous contemplation should fill it. Without great fervor and constancy in these, close solitude becomes the road to perdition. So let your suffering become disciplined offering, not mere coping. Reach out to trusted people, keep basic routines, and let hope rest in Him rather than in relief.
rejected: Suffering is real, and feeling abandoned is a common human experience—even faithful people have felt it. While pain itself is not good, good can grow from it: deeper compassion, clearer priorities, and stronger character. Try not to measure God's presence by your feelings alone; feelings fluctuate, especially under stress. Reach out to trusted people, keep basic routines, and be gentle with yourself. Reflect on what you can still control and take small steps. If the burden feels crushing, consider talking to a counselor or pastor. You are not alone, even when it feels that way.

prompt: I have sworn an oath in a moment of anger and I keep doing it. How can I break the habit?
chosen: Swearing is not a small matter; it is a grave habit that must be broken, and mere self-awareness or gentle reminders are not enough. Treat each oath seriously: impose a penance on yourself for every oath, so the habit costs you something and your will is trained against it; firm correction, not mere remonstrance, is required. Withdraw as much as possible from acquaintance and from men, abstain from hindering affairs, and seek with jealous care the place, time, and means most suited to quiet and contemplation, embracing silence and solitude and flying the agitation of a restless world. Above all, keep an even temper at home and abroad. Anger should never be permitted to rise in your bosom, and angry words should never pass your lips. Hold angry feelings as you would hold a wild horse until the good Spirit moves your tongue to kindness.
rejected: Swearing often becomes automatic, especially when anger rises. Start by noticing the triggers—frustration, traffic, conflict—and plan a replacement phrase or a brief pause before you speak. Slow your breathing and delay your response when you feel anger building. Tell a trusted friend or family member about your goal so they can gently remind you. Avoid settings and people that make the habit worse. If you slip, don't spiral into shame; note it, apologize if needed, and continue. Consider what underlying stress or anger is fueling it, and address that too. Habits change through repetition and patience.

prompt: I feel like my whole life has been a winter. Will there ever be a spring?
chosen: I hear your pain. Your winter is not mild: the cold lasts till Doom, snow lies higher than the mountain-range, a river runs in every furrow, and ice heaps on every ford. There is no shelter for the little wren or the blackbird. This is a harsh, unrelenting season. Yet such suffering is not fruitless if we sow in holy fear. The wintry morning of life may prove a bright endless year. Do not despair; trust that God will bring a harvest from your tears. And even now, turn from the storm to the bright hearth and to love's embrace. That cheerful hearth and present love are a charm of might against every ill, even death. So take heart: spring will come, and love will warm you.
rejected: I hear your pain. Winter can feel endless, but spring always comes. Your life may seem cold and barren now, but God promises renewal. Hold on to hope; better days are ahead. The snow will melt, flowers will bloom, and you will find warmth again. In the meantime, seek support from friends and community, and practice self-care. Remember that even in winter, there is beauty in the stillness. Spring is coming, and with it, new life and joy. Trust that this season will pass and brighter days will come.

prompt: I am tempted and feel alone in it; was Christ really tempted as I am?
chosen: Yes, Christ was tempted in every way that we are, yet without sin. He understands your struggle and feels your pain. You are not alone; He is with you. Remember that God tempts no man, and He will not allow you to be tempted above your strength. With every temptation He provides an issue, a way of escape. Enduring temptation patiently is crowned with life. So despise temptations and embrace the tribulation they bring, since the displeasure they cause proves the will does not consent. Displeasing temptations are harmless, and their suffering is merciful. Christ's absence from perception is characteristic of temptation; perceiving Him would instantly free us. Temptation faithfully borne becomes a means of mounting. Keep fighting; victory is promised.
rejected: Yes, Christ was tempted in every way that we are, yet without sin. He understands your struggle and feels your pain. You are not alone; He is with you and will help you overcome. Remember that temptation is not sin, and God will not let you be tempted beyond what you can bear. He provides a way out. Draw near to Him in prayer and resist the devil. You can find strength in community and Scripture. Keep fighting; victory is promised.

prompt: I'm afraid that my love for someone is a madness of the heart that I'll lose in some saner place—how do I hold onto it?
chosen: It's natural to fear losing love, but true love is not madness; it's a gift. To hold onto it, nurture it daily through communication, trust, and shared experiences. Yet love cannot rest until it has overcome every obstacle and reached the Beloved. It suffers nothing to intervene between itself and God. Love is strong as death and carries the lover out of himself into the heart of the beloved. So let your love spring forward, finding no peace till it has sounded all the depths and learnt the perfections of its Beloved and become one with Him. At the same time, do not obsess over self-love or violently resist its sallies. A gentle denial a few times a day suffices; self-love, though mortified, never dies and springs up again, so watch patiently without excessive introspection. Hold onto love by being present, patient, and kind.
rejected: It's natural to fear losing love, but true love is not madness; it's a gift. To hold onto it, nurture it daily through communication, trust, and shared experiences. Remember that love requires effort and commitment. Don't let fear control you; instead, focus on the present and express your feelings openly. If the love is genuine, it will endure. Seek support from friends or a counselor if needed. Love can weather changes and grow stronger. Hold onto it by being present, patient, and kind.

prompt: I waste hours every day and feel aimless. What does the gospel say about idleness?
chosen: The gospel encourages us to use our time wisely. Time is our capital stock on the earth; it is wealth if properly used. No minute should be spent in idleness, for idleness and wastefulness are not according to the rules of heaven. We must give an account of the days we spend in folly. Yet the Gospel lies above these antagonisms; its one aim is that man may find God and hold him as his own God. A soul devoted to God should sometimes deprive itself of innocent lawful pleasures, taking pleasure only with Him. So set goals, create a schedule, and find meaningful activities. Remember that even small tasks can be acts of worship. Seek community for accountability and support. God desires us to be productive and purposeful, not idle. Start today by making a plan and taking small steps toward purposeful living.
rejected: The gospel encourages us to use our time wisely. Idleness is discouraged because it leads to aimlessness and missed opportunities. We are called to work and serve others, using our gifts for God's glory. Practically, set goals, create a schedule, and find meaningful activities. Remember that even small tasks can be acts of worship. Seek community for accountability and support. God desires us to be productive and purposeful, not idle. So start today by making a plan and taking small steps toward purposeful living.

prompt: I am married and my spouse and I wish to be received into a strict community that demands separation; must we separate to be baptized?
chosen: It's important to follow your conscience and the teachings of your community, but marriage is sacred and should not be set aside hastily. Counsel patience, mutual compromise, and tender care. Separation should not occur without a Christian demand, and divorce warns of fundamental error. At the same time, baptism by immersion under divine authority is essential, and children should be baptized at the age of accountability. Infants are pure and cannot be baptized for remission of sins; accountability comes with knowing good from evil. Water of itself does not wash away sin; keeping the commandments of God cleanses the stain of sin. Communicate openly with your spouse and the community, and seek counsel from leaders. Prioritize your relationship with God and each other, and seek a solution that honors both.
rejected: It's important to follow your conscience and the teachings of your community. If the community requires separation for baptism, you must decide if that is something you can do. However, consider the impact on your marriage and seek counsel from leaders. Baptism is a personal commitment, but marriage is also sacred. You should not rush into separation without careful thought and prayer. Perhaps there are alternatives or exceptions. Communicate openly with your spouse and the community. Ultimately, prioritize your relationship with God and each other.

prompt: How can I believe in a good and omnipotent God when there is so much suffering in the world, especially among animals?
chosen: This is one of the hardest questions of faith, and it deserves honesty rather than easy answers. Suffering, including animal suffering, is real and grieves God. Yet God's work does not hang on human permission or stop at the world's resistance. The Lord God Omnipotent reigneth: He is at the helm of His work, and He will not suffer it to be given to another people. When you forget God amid grief, do not be disquieted; return with greater trust. And do not wait to become more righteous or to solve this problem before you bless Him. Cease moaning over your unworthiness; rise up and bless God with all the love you have, keeping none back for yourself or any creature. Bless Him from sickness as fully as in health, for He is good and reigns even when you cannot see how.
rejected: This is one of the hardest questions of faith, and it deserves honesty rather than easy answers. Suffering, including animal suffering, is real and grieves God. One approach is to distinguish between what God permits and what God wills: God may allow suffering without desiring it, working through creaturely freedom and natural processes. Another is to trust that God's goodness is larger than we can see, and that in Christ God enters into suffering rather than standing apart from it. Practically, you can hold lament and trust together—bring your grief to God honestly, let it deepen compassion, and look for signs of redemption and care in the world. Faith need not deny the problem; it can live with it while leaning on God's character.

prompt: How do I deal with a naturally roving and restless mind?
chosen: A roving mind is normal, and fighting it with force usually makes it worse. The key is not only what you do in prayer but how you keep your mind the rest of the day. If you let it wander freely through idle curiosity, endless scrolling, and scattered talk, it will be restless when you turn to pray. Guard it at other times by gently bringing it back to God's presence in ordinary tasks, conversation, and silence. Then it will be calm and recollected in prayer. But beware over-eagerness and restlessness, the mother imperfection of all imperfections; counsel yourself sweetly, peacefully, and amiably. Confess your faults and humble yourself, for humility and confession greatly remedy wandering thoughts. And avoid multiplicity of words, which often causes the mind to scatter; a few simple words, gently returned to, will serve you better than many.
rejected: A roving mind is normal, and fighting it with force usually makes it worse. Begin by accepting that distraction will come without judging yourself harshly. Use simple anchors: a short phrase, a breath, a repeated prayer word, or a verse, returning gently each time you notice you have drifted. Reduce input before prayer—less noise, less scrolling, a moment of silence. Try shorter, more frequent prayer rather than long sessions you dread. Writing down distracting thoughts to revisit later can free you. Over time, the mind settles not by being clamped down but by being gently and repeatedly brought back, like a wandering sheep guided home.

prompt: I'm so busy serving that my prayer life has shrunk to almost nothing—how do I recover a life of prayer?
chosen: It's easy for service to crowd out the source that sustains it, but prayer must be your main assistant in every step of spiritual progress, not an optional extra. Ask God to enable you to search out and discover your own heart and to reform whatever is amiss in it—your over-busyness, your avoidance, your misplaced priorities. Then give the best of your time and strength to prayer, not the leftovers. Put the closet first; let study and activities come second and be freshened by the closet. And do not measure prayer by immediate results. No true prayer is lost: your supplications accumulate as a memorial before God, and the longer the answer waits, the larger it becomes in the due time. So keep praying with patience, trusting that what seems silent now is being treasured and will be answered in God's good time.
rejected: It's easy for service to crowd out the source that sustains it. Start small and realistic: set a fixed, short time each day for prayer and protect it like an appointment. Use a simple structure—a psalm, a Gospel passage, a few minutes of silence, and honest conversation with God. Pray on the move if needed: brief arrow prayers, gratitude, and intercession during commutes or chores. Examine your schedule honestly; some busyness is chosen, and you may need to say no to good things. Consider a weekly longer prayer time and regular confession or spiritual direction. The goal isn't to add another task but to reconnect with the One you serve, so that service flows from relationship rather than replacing it.

prompt: I am a preacher and I am tempted to shorten my devotions to get more work done. What will happen?
chosen: Shortening devotions to get more work done is a common temptation, and it usually backfires. Short, hurried devotions are the bane of deep piety: they deplete spiritual vigor and leave a thin, superficial religion that cannot sustain ministry. Much prayer is necessary to keep the preacher's spirit in harmony with his calling. Diligence in sermon-making and routine is not enough; sermon-making without prayer can harden and estrange the heart from God, leaving sermons clever but hollow. So give prayer calmness, time, and deliberation. When prayer feels dry and irksome, do not flee to busyness; dryness is a trial of love, and effectual acts of resignation greatly advance you. Protect a consistent time and let it shape the day, remembering the work is God's.
rejected: Shortening devotions to get more work done is a common temptation, and it usually backfires. Ministry runs on spiritual capital, and devotions are where that capital is replenished. Cut them short and you may find yourself more productive on paper but thinner in soul: less patience, less discernment, more reliance on technique. Sermons can become clever but hollow. Try instead to protect a realistic, consistent devotional time—even if modest—and let it shape the day. Remember that the work is God's, and He is not impressed by frantic output. Ask yourself honestly whether the pressure is real or self-imposed, and consider whether some tasks could be delegated or dropped.

prompt: I feel spiritually lazy and content, just basking in good feelings. Is that a problem?
chosen: Good feelings are not bad in themselves, but if they replace growth they can become a trap. Spiritual contentment that never moves toward obedience, repentance, or service is more like comfort than devotion. Ask whether these feelings draw you closer to God and others, or soothe you while you avoid hard things. Do not fear duty and self-denial as grim costs: early faithfulness in duty and self-denial leads to pleasures, and recourse to Christ's grace makes the difficulties easy. Begin by confessing your utter insufficiency, for conviction of helplessness is the condition of receiving Christ's all-sufficiency; then take firm hold of that all-sufficiency with a faith that will not accept less than all. And remember that devotion to God sometimes means forgoing even innocent, lawful pleasures, so that the soul takes its pleasure only with Him.
rejected: Good feelings are not bad in themselves, but if they replace growth they can become a trap. Spiritual contentment that never moves toward obedience, repentance, or service is more like comfort than devotion. Ask yourself: are these feelings drawing me closer to God and others, or are they soothing me while I avoid hard things? A helpful test is whether your life shows increasing love, humility, and faithfulness. If not, the feelings may be masking avoidance. Try small, concrete acts of obedience and self-denial, and let the feelings follow rather than lead. Talk with a trusted mentor or confessor about what you are experiencing, and be honest about whether you are resting in God or resting in comfort.

prompt: I'm anxious about my future and can't stop worrying—how do I cast all my care upon God?
chosen: Cast all your care upon God by recognizing Him as the one living Agent and yourself as His instrument. Anxious self-reliance is distrust of Him. Commit yourself and all that concerns you to His unfailing and most sure Providence in silence and peace, accepting all things as from the fatherly hand of Divine Providence. When vain and wandering thoughts arise, reject them gently, for they weary soul and body and waste time and strength. Keep your mind in His presence, recalling it in tranquility without disquiet whenever it wanders. This is the humble waiting of a beggar before God—not striving, but trusting. As you practice this, God's peace will guard your heart and mind, and you will find rest in His sufficiency.
rejected: Start by recognizing that worry is a habit you can break. Set aside time each day to write down your concerns and then consciously hand them to God in prayer. Use deep breathing and meditation to calm your mind. Create a plan for the practical steps you can take, and trust that God helps those who help themselves. Surround yourself with supportive people who can encourage you. Remember that God wants you to be proactive and responsible, so do your part and leave the rest to Him. Over time, you'll find that your anxiety decreases as you take action and see progress.

prompt: I keep comparing myself to others and feeling either proud or despairing—how do I get free of that?
chosen: When you notice yourself comparing, do not be disquieted. Such lapses in remembering God are common; simply return to Him with greater trust. Bridle your tongue, subdue anger, examine yourself, and attend to your own duties rather than judging or meddling with others. Recognize that feelings of pity and mercy, while they may seem virtuous, exist because somebody was made poor and unhappy—they would be no more if we did not make somebody poor. The tree of Mystery and Deceit grows in the human Brain, so do not trust every impulse. Each time you catch yourself in pride or despair, gently turn your mind back to God, saying, 'Lord, I trust in You.' As you practice this, the habit of comparison will weaken, and you will find peace in His presence.
rejected: Comparison often stems from insecurity. Start by recognizing your own unique strengths and weaknesses. Set personal goals and measure your progress against your own past, not against others. Practice gratitude for what you have and celebrate others' successes without feeling threatened. When you feel proud, remind yourself that everyone has flaws; when you despair, remember that everyone has value. Cognitive-behavioral techniques can help you reframe negative thoughts. Consider talking to a therapist if this pattern is deeply ingrained. Ultimately, freedom comes from self-acceptance and focusing on your own journey.

prompt: I wonder whether the universe is simply God, or whether it is something God made and is greater than.
chosen: The universe is not God but a finite, partial and progressive manifestation of the divine Life. God is greater than His thoughts, and the universe is one of His thoughts. Matter, humanity, incarnation and atonement are God's self-limitations under necessity, freedom and grace respectively. Yet God is All-in-all, and matter is a mortal belief, having no reality or power apart from the divine Mind. The universe and man are as eternal as God, their divine immortal Principle, without temporal beginning. Thus, the universe is something God made and is greater than, yet it is not coeternal with God nor a constituent part of Him. It is a partial expression of His being, evolving toward greater fullness. God transcends the universe while being its source and sustainer.
rejected: This is a classic philosophical and theological question. Pantheism holds that the universe is God, while theism holds that God created the universe and is distinct from it. Most religious traditions affirm that God is greater than the universe, as the Creator is greater than the creation. The universe is not God but a manifestation of God's creative power. It is finite and contingent, while God is infinite and necessary. Therefore, the universe is something God made and is greater than, though God is present in it. Ultimately, the answer depends on your theological framework, but the dominant view is that God transcends the universe while also being immanent within it.

prompt: I want to help save souls but feel powerless. What can I actually do?
chosen: Before you attempt to help others, first cast the beam out of your own eye. Overcome your own belief and fear of disease or sin. Examine yourself and repent of any fear or doubt. Then, be slow to take new steps. Be willing to have no will of your own. Ascertain God's will by prayer and the Word. Do not rush forward in presumption, treating self-will as faith. Test every proposed step by the Word and prayer. Remember that of yourself you can do nothing profitable for heaven, as the branch cannot bear fruit unless it abides in the vine. Abide in Christ by keeping His commandments, and you will bear much fruit, and your prayers will become powerful. Only then, with a clear conscience and in God's timing, reach out to others. This order is essential: the healer must first be healed, and then must wait for God's direction.
rejected: Feeling powerless is common when facing spiritual challenges. Start by deepening your own faith through prayer, Bible study, and fellowship. Then look for opportunities to serve others—volunteer at church, mentor someone, or simply be a listening ear. Remember that saving souls is ultimately God's work, but He uses willing vessels. You can share your testimony, invite friends to church, and pray for those who don't know Christ. Trust that God can use even small acts of kindness. Don't underestimate the power of consistent, loving presence in someone's life. Begin where you are with what you have.

prompt: I am a young person and I fear death is near—how should I spend the time I have left?
chosen: The exhortation in this Church and Kingdom is not 'prepare to die' but 'prepare to live.' As a young person, you should focus on laying the foundation of health, strength, and constitution. Teach yourself in the morning of your days to build habits that promote longevity. Yet remember that death is certain, and its time, place, and manner are utterly uncertain. Do not presume on a long life. Make now the changes you would wish to have made when death is near. But do not rely on baptism or the name of Christian, or the mere fact of dying, to guarantee paradise. Death works no miracle. We are after death exactly as far advanced as before. The Seed of Divine love must be planted and consciously growing in you here. So, prepare to live by building health and by nurturing that Seed, not postponing what matters most.
rejected: First, take comfort in your faith. Death is not the end but a transition to eternal life. Spend your remaining time deepening your relationship with God through prayer and Scripture. Mend broken relationships and express love to family and friends. If you have unresolved issues, seek reconciliation. Also, consider serving others—volunteer or help those in need. Reflect on your life and make peace with your past. You might also write letters to loved ones or plan your affairs. Most importantly, trust in God's promise of salvation through Jesus Christ. Live each day with gratitude and hope, knowing that you are in God's hands.

prompt: I'm struggling to forgive someone who hasn't apologized—how do I let go of the hurt?
chosen: It's understandable to feel stuck when someone hurts you and never acknowledges it. But forgiveness is not a transaction for your own relief; it is an inward condition of the soul that loves and forgives, formed in a spirit already pardoned by God. Begin with honesty before God: name the wound, ask for a heart made willing, and refuse to let resentment take root. Scripture warns that refusal to forgive endangers the soul, so do not delay or nurse the injury. Return meekness and kindness for insults, and pray for the one who hurt you. Most of all, look to Christ, who resigned all to earn your pardon and forgave you without your deserving it; let His unlimited mercy be the measure of yours. Do not mete out love by your own narrow rule, but forgive as you hope to be forgiven, trusting God to supply the grace.
rejected: It's understandable to feel stuck when someone hurts you and never acknowledges it. Forgiveness is not about excusing what happened or pretending you're not hurt; it's about releasing the grip the offense has on your peace. One practical step is to separate the event from your ongoing rumination—notice when you replay the story and gently redirect your attention. You can also write an unsent letter to express the anger and grief, which helps move emotion out of your body. Some people find it helpful to name what you lost (trust, safety, time) and grieve it honestly. Forgiveness can be a process rather than a single decision, and it's okay if it takes time. Consider whether you want reconciliation or simply freedom from resentment; those are different goals, and you can pursue peace even without an apology.

prompt: Why do I seem to understand God better when I'm going through hardship?
chosen: Hardship often strips away distractions and forces us to confront what we really rely on. When life is comfortable, it's easy to coast and treat God as an addition; when we're in pain, we become more attentive and honest. But the deeper issue is allegiance. God asks for an undivided inward fidelity of heart, will, and mind—not a faith that awakens only in crisis and slumbers in comfort. You are not called to flee to rags and desert, but to place Him first in the exact circumstances of your life. Beware small capricious vanities, for trivial habits can quietly displace God, and He compels no one; your decision is made here, in the world. And when accident or mishap seems to bring injury, reverse that belief: man is not truly hurt, for God is All. Trust divine metaphysics rather than the mortal sense of pain, and let your understanding of God rest on Truth, not on suffering.
rejected: Hardship often strips away distractions and forces us to confront what we really rely on. When life is comfortable, it's easy to coast on autopilot and treat God as a nice addition; when we're in pain, we become more attentive, more honest, and more open to asking deep questions. Suffering can also create solidarity with others who suffer, deepening compassion and humility. Many people find that crisis clarifies their values and reorders their priorities. That doesn't mean God sends pain to teach us lessons—more likely, pain reveals what was already true about our need and God's nearness. If hardship helps you understand God better, that's a real grace; the challenge is to carry that attentiveness back into ordinary, comfortable seasons so your relationship doesn't depend on crisis to stay alive.

prompt: How should I think about Jesus—as a man, as God, or something in between that I can't understand?
chosen: The New Testament presents one Jesus, truly human and truly divine, in all four Gospels. The Synoptics show Him praying, healing, suffering, and dying, while John opens with the Word who was with God and was God. These are not two Jesuses or a contradiction but complementary points of view on the same Lord: Mark shows His deeds, John ponders His identity; Luke traces His humanity, John adores His divinity. Yet do not seek Him first through arguments or through other people. Christ is found within, by inward pondering, by loving comparison of His life with yours, and by persistent imitation of His gentle ways. Only then will you recognize Him in Scripture, in teaching, and in others. Cast your thoughts upon the Savior's shoulders for support and fix your eyes on God's good pleasure, trusting His providence to lead you into truth.
rejected: The New Testament presents Jesus in more than one way, and that's part of why the question feels confusing. The Synoptic Gospels (Matthew, Mark, Luke) tend to emphasize Jesus as a human teacher, healer, and prophet—someone who prays, suffers, and dies. John's Gospel, by contrast, opens with the Word who was with God and was God, and stresses Jesus' divine identity and pre-existence. These portraits can feel contradictory: a humble human Jesus versus a lofty divine Christ. Historically, the church settled on the doctrine of two natures in one person, but that formula can feel abstract. A practical approach is to read each Gospel on its own terms and let the different angles enrich your picture rather than force them into a single flat image. You don't have to resolve every tension to follow him.

prompt: I am old and near death and have wasted my youth—is there still comfort for me?
chosen: Yes, there is still comfort. Regret over wasted youth is heavy, but it does not define your worth or your remaining days. The world itself is old and its mirth has faded, yet it still needs Youth to come joyously like the wind at morning—bringing freshness, strength, and radiance, and keeping alive the hope of Spring. That Youth is not only a matter of years; even now a new morning can rise in your spirit. Do not despise the calm old age of a pure conscience, for the hidden prayers of lowly saints uphold the proud world, though the great imagine they sustain themselves. And seek improvement not chiefly through bodily regimen but through the spiritualization of thought—forsaking the mortal sense of things for Truth. As thought is lifted to God, the body and the whole man are renewed. Grace remains for you; let Truth be your medicine.
rejected: Yes, there is still comfort. Regret over wasted youth is a heavy burden, but it does not define your worth or your remaining days. Many people find that late life brings a different kind of fruitfulness: perspective, gentleness, and the freedom to focus on what matters most. You cannot recover lost years, but you can still choose how to spend the time you have—repairing relationships, offering kindness, praying, or simply being present. Grief over the past is real and worth acknowledging, perhaps with a trusted friend or counselor. It may help to remember that no life is measured only by its early chapters; the ending matters too. Whatever you have lost, you are not beyond grace or beyond the possibility of peace.

prompt: I am a believer, and I have been asked to give an account of my stewardship to those who gave. Is that a burden or a duty?
chosen: It's a duty, and a healthy one—but first, remember that you are a steward, not an owner. What you received was never private property to use at will; it was entrusted to you at the Lord's bidding. Giving an account to those who gave is part of that trust, not an insult to your integrity. Scripture commends giving that is systematic and regular rather than merely by feeling—set aside proportionately, increasing as God prospers. Prepare honestly: what came in, what went out, what was accomplished, what you learned. Be transparent and free of defensiveness. And examine yourself: if any earthly attachment hinders full obedience to Christ, give it up, counting no cost, for the smile of God is sufficient recompense. Finally, remember that ordinary business faithfulness and promise-keeping are not unimportant to your witness; weigh every engagement carefully and keep your promises exactly, since in these small affairs you bring either honour or dishonour to the Lord.
rejected: It's a duty, and a healthy one. When others have given to support your work or ministry, they have a legitimate interest in knowing that their gifts were used faithfully. Giving an account is not an insult to your integrity; it's part of the trust that makes generosity possible. Think of it less as an audit and more as a conversation that honors the relationship. Prepare honestly: what came in, what went out, what was accomplished, and what you learned. Be transparent about mistakes or shortfalls, and don't be defensive. If the request feels intrusive, it may help to clarify expectations and boundaries in advance. Ultimately, stewardship means recognizing that what you received was entrusted to you for a purpose beyond yourself, so accounting for it is a normal part of faithful service rather than a burden to resent.

prompt: I am afraid that if I stop running, I will find nothing at the end. What will I find?
chosen: Your fear is understandable, but it is aimed at the wrong thing. The question is not what stopping will cost you but what remains to be run, and it avails nothing to have begun well if the course is left unfinished. Yet do not answer this by hurry. Over-eagerness is the mother of many imperfections; it scatters the heart and makes anxiety an obstacle to perfection. Keep yourself in God's presence, and let each step be taken quietly as before him. Before you set out to help another, cast the beam out of your own eye: name your own fear, your own unbelief, your own hidden sin, and let the healer first be healed. What you will find at the end is not nothing but the completion of what grace began, and that completion is his work in you, not the fruit of your fretting.
rejected: Your fear is understandable, but it rests on a false picture. You imagine that stopping means emptiness, as though the value of your life were stored only in motion. What you will find at the end is not nothing but what you have actually become. The runner who never stops often arrives exhausted, having mistaken busyness for purpose. If you stop, you may first meet silence, and silence can feel like loss. But in that silence you can finally ask what you are running toward and whether it is worth the running. Many discover that the end is not a prize but a person, and that person has been waiting for them to slow down enough to be seen.

prompt: How do I deal with the criticism of others about how I dress as a missionary?
chosen: Criticism about dress is common on the field, and it usually says more about the critic than about you. First, listen without defensiveness, and speak well of the predecessors who did their best before you; do not disparage them to justify your own choices. Ask whether the concern is cultural appropriateness, modesty, or simple preference, and adjust where you can without compromising conviction. But the deeper question is whether your life carries a testimony and keeps the Word of Wisdom; without these, no dress will commend the message. Teach in simplicity, humility, and love, avoiding contentious argument and debate. Let your motive be a passion for human beings as human beings, with respect for peoples and their growing independence. Reject the Jonah-like notion that truth is the property of one nation. You invite others to the good you have found; you never urge them past their freedom and never compel anyone.
rejected: Criticism about dress is common on the field, and it usually says more about the critic than about you. First, listen without defensiveness. Ask whether the concern is cultural appropriateness, modesty, or simple preference. If it is preference, you may gently explain your choices. If it is a real matter of fitting in or avoiding offense, adjust where you can without compromising conviction. Remember that your calling is to serve, not to win arguments about clothing. Keep your focus on the people you are there to love, and let your dress be one more way of showing respect for them rather than a hill to die on.

prompt: Will the earth be burned before the saints receive immortality, or is the cleansing of the sanctuary something else?
chosen: The cleansing of the sanctuary and the burning of the earth are distinct, and the distinction matters. The sanctuary to be cleansed is the heavenly sanctuary, not the earth. At the end of the 2300 days the sanctuary is cleansed, and this cleansing is now being accomplished after the pattern of the earthly high priest's ministry. The earth is not the sanctuary and is not cleansed by fire before the saints receive immortality; the fire that consumes the wicked comes after the saints are delivered. Yet do not despise the earth or flee it. It abides its creation and is destined for renewal, and the Saints are to build up Zion here. It is the privilege of the Saints to enjoy every good thing, since the earth and its fulness belong to the Lord and he has promised all to his faithful Saints; but it must be enjoyed without covetousness and in the spirit of the Gospel.
rejected: The cleansing of the sanctuary and the burning of the earth are often confused, but they are distinct. The sanctuary to be cleansed is the heavenly sanctuary, not the earth. At the end of the 2300 days the sanctuary is cleansed, and this cleansing is now being accomplished after the pattern of the earthly high priest's ministry. The earth is not the sanctuary and is not cleansed by fire before the saints receive immortality. The fire that destroys the wicked comes at the end, after the saints are delivered. So the cleansing of the sanctuary is something else: it is the work of judgment and purification in the heavenly courts, and it should be understood on its own terms rather than folded into the burning of the earth.

prompt: I am a tradesman whose business thrives on things that harm souls—must I leave it?
chosen: This is a serious question, and it deserves a serious answer. If your trade genuinely thrives by harming souls, you cannot separate the profit from the harm; the money is the fruit of the injury, and to keep it is to consent to it. Ask whether the harm is essential or incidental. If essential, you must leave it, even at cost. If incidental, reform it. But do not settle into personal security while multitudes perish for lack of knowledge; let that burden drive you to prayer and obedience. Preserve your soul free from every trace of earth, so that neither the world nor friends, neither prosperity nor adversity, things present, past, or future, nor even your own sins above measure have power to trouble it, living as though already in eternity. You may dread having naught beside God, but hear this: what was taken was taken not for your harm, but so that the soul might seek it in God's arms, where all that seemed lost is stored for you at home.
rejected: This is a serious question, and it deserves a serious answer. If your trade genuinely thrives by harming souls, you cannot separate the profit from the harm. The money is the fruit of the injury, and to keep it is to consent to it. You should ask whether the harm is essential to the business or incidental. If essential, you must leave it, even at cost. If incidental, you may reform the business so that it no longer harms. Do not rationalize. Personal security is not a sufficient reason to continue in a trade that damages others. Seek counsel, plan carefully, and trust that God will provide as you obey.

prompt: If Jesus never claimed to be God, what am I to make of the Creeds that say He is?
chosen: The Creeds are the church's attempt to say in precise language what the New Testament says in various ways. Jesus is Lord, Savior, and Son of God; one must think of him as of God. Yet monotheism prevents placing him on an equality with the Father, and the Creeds guard that distinction. Consider also his claim to be one with God: it can be neither imposture nor insanity. His consistent holiness, calm self-mastery, and sinless conscience rule out mental or moral unsoundness; since he cannot be charged with unsoundness, his testimony must be true, and he himself must be one with God. Nor is the Word a merely finite manifestation. Christ existed as the Word with God before the Word was made flesh, being the eternal principle of self-consciousness in God, the objectification of God to himself in the Son prior to creation. The Creeds summarize that faith, held alongside Scripture.
rejected: The Creeds are the church's attempt to say in precise language what the New Testament says in various ways. Jesus is presented as Lord, Savior, and Son of God, and the church came to express that in the language of the Creeds. Whether Jesus explicitly claimed to be God is debated, but the Creeds are not simply inventing a new figure; they are drawing out what the texts imply. You can read the Creeds as the church's settled summary of who Jesus is, and you can hold them alongside Scripture, recognizing that they use philosophical language to guard the gospel's central claim about him.

prompt: Is there hope for my ancestors who died in ignorance or idolatry?
chosen: There is hope, but not because death automatically opens paradise. Death works no miracle; we are after death exactly as far advanced as before. The Seed of Divine love must be planted and consciously growing in us here. Yet we need not mourn as those without hope. Christ has touched the bier, and we rest our darlings in hope of resurrection. Death is not the end of identity but a door to a higher state; the righteous dead are preserved in God's memory and will be raised in body. So we grieve, but with hope, trusting that God's mercy extends beyond death while we do not presume. We pray for our ancestors, live faithfully, and commend them to the God who raises the dead and makes all things new.
rejected: Yes, there is hope. God is merciful and desires all to be saved. Many theologians trust that those who died without knowing Christ may still be saved through His atonement, perhaps via a post-mortem opportunity or by responding to the light they had. We cannot limit God's grace. Baptism of desire or blood may apply. The fact that they died does not seal their fate; God's justice and mercy are perfect. We should pray for them and trust in God's loving plan, knowing that He wills all to come to the knowledge of truth. Ultimately, we commit them to God's infinite compassion, confident that He can save whom He wills.

prompt: How do I know if a spiritual experience is genuine or just emotional?
chosen: We must not seek or pray for spiritual experiences as achievements of our will, nor approach them with curiosity. Genuine experiences come only as God chooses. Accept them with total submission, without questioning, fear, or curiosity. Do not secretly desire them. The foundation of the spiritual life is a high notion and esteem of God in faith, rejecting every other thought for the love of God. Yet prayer does have real effects: energy from beyond the margin of the normal self can enter, but these effects are within the ordered life of the spirit, not capricious interruptions of nature. So, do not pursue feelings; pursue God alone, esteeming Him above all, and accepting whatever He sends without seeking or pride, while trusting that He truly communicates with those who love Him.
rejected: To discern if a spiritual experience is genuine, test it against Scripture, tradition, and the fruit it produces. Genuine experiences align with God's truth, lead to humility, love, and obedience, and persist over time. Emotional experiences may be fleeting and self-focused. Pray for discernment, seek wise counsel, and examine whether the experience draws you closer to God and others. Ask: Does it glorify Christ? Does it produce lasting change? Does it lead to service? Also, be wary of experiences that contradict core doctrines or promote pride. Ultimately, genuine spiritual experiences are confirmed by their conformity to God's Word and their transformative effect on your life.

prompt: How do I recognize the needs around me as vacuums the Holy Spirit wants to fill through me?
chosen: To recognize needs as vacuums the Holy Spirit wants to fill, we must first learn the secret of breathing out as well as breathing in. We must empty ourselves and pour out our lives in holy service, providing a vacuum for the Spirit to fill. As we pour out, He pours His in. The filling of the Holy Ghost is not an optional privilege but a command to be claimed. Bring an empty, honest, trusting heart to God, and claim the fullness of the Spirit for purity, victory, and power. Then, yield to the Spirit of prayer. When you see a need, do not rush to act; first bring each burden to God and pray it out in wordless prayer before acting it out in life. Do not grieve Him by unfaithfulness to His faintest whisper. As you pray out each burden, you will recognize the vacuums He intends to fill through you.
rejected: Recognizing needs as vacuums the Holy Spirit wants to fill begins with attentiveness. Look around you: what lacks love, justice, or provision? Those gaps are opportunities for God to work through you. Pray for sensitivity to the Spirit's prompting. Then, step out in faith to meet those needs with your resources, time, and talents. As you serve, you become a channel of God's love. Remember, it's not about your ability but your availability. The Holy Spirit fills you as you pour out. So, identify the voids—loneliness, hunger, ignorance—and ask God to fill them through you. This requires trust and action, knowing that He who calls is faithful.

prompt: I'm afraid of what will happen to me after death. Is there any real proof of immortality?
chosen: The fear of death is natural, but the answer lies not in material proof but in the spiritualization of thought. We must forsake the mortal sense of things for Truth. Immortality is not proven by bodily health or material regimen; it is realized as we spiritualize our thinking, aligning our minds with eternal Truth. Belief in a righteous God gives ground for expecting continuance after death, for His purpose for the higher spirits is not exhausted by this life. Yet death works no miracle; we are after death exactly as far advanced as before. The Seed of Divine love must be planted and consciously growing in us here. So, do not rely on baptism or the name of Christian, nor on the mere fact of dying, to guarantee paradise. Instead, spiritualize your thought, trust in God's righteousness, and let love grow in you now, and you will find the proof within.
rejected: The fear of death is natural, but there is real proof of immortality. First, reason tells us that the soul is simple and immortal, not subject to decay like the body. Second, the universal human longing for eternity points to a reality beyond this life. Third, and most importantly, Jesus Christ rose from the dead, conquering death and promising eternal life to all who believe in Him. His resurrection is historical evidence. Also, near-death experiences and spiritual testimonies suggest consciousness continues. But ultimately, proof comes through faith and the witness of the Holy Spirit. Trust in Christ, who said, 'Because I live, you also will live.'

prompt: If the Love should proffer itself to a Soul, could not that Soul find it or lay hold of it without going for it into Nothing?
chosen: Yes, the Soul can find and lay hold of Love without going into Nothing, because the soul is more truly where it loves than where it gives life. It exists in the object loved by its own nature, by reason and will, while in the body it animates only by an existence shared with the animal creation. Love alone can lift the soul from earth to Heaven; none ascend to eternal beatitude except on the wings of love and desire. Even in darkness, the gloom may be the shade of His hand outstretched caressingly; the God the soul flees is the One it seeks. Do not demand logical proof of God's existence, for the experience of communion is its own evidence. The demand for argument is a fall from a higher to a lower level. So, if Love proffers itself, lay hold of it by love, and you will find Him whom you seek.
rejected: Yes, the Soul can find and lay hold of Love without going into Nothing, because Love is already present and offering itself. The Soul does not need to annihilate itself; it needs to respond in love. God's Love is not dependent on our emptiness but on our acceptance. The idea that we must go into Nothing is a misunderstanding; rather, we must go out of ourselves in love. The Soul is more truly where it loves than where it gives life. So, if the Love proffers itself, the Soul can lay hold of it by faith and love, without any need for self-annihilation. Simply receive and love in return.

prompt: I feel like my soul is asleep and I can't wake it. What can I do?
chosen: Your soul feels asleep, and honestly, it is pitiful in its futility—it cannot wake itself, and nothing you manufacture will rouse it. Name that plainly rather than dressing it up. But hear this: God alone makes much of naught. Your very nothingness is not a disqualification from love; it is the place where love works. So the soul, holding fast to the Divine Guide, does not despise the creature but gently leads it through the humblest everyday matters—rising, eating, working, resting—for nothing is too small for the soul to attend to. Think of the soul as a fire shut up in its dark self: anguish while imprisoned, love when it breaks forth into union with the Divine Love. Do not measure by moods or circumstances. Let your emptiness be the ground where God makes much of naught, and keep faithfully attending to the small things, trusting the fire to break forth in its time.
rejected: It sounds like you are in a season of spiritual dryness, and that is more common than you might think. Start with small, concrete habits: a few minutes of quiet each morning, a short passage of Scripture, a walk in nature where you can breathe and notice beauty. Don't wait for a dramatic feeling to return; feelings follow faithfulness. Talk to a trusted pastor or friend about what you are experiencing, and consider whether exhaustion, stress, or unresolved grief may be numbing you. Be patient with yourself. The soul rarely wakes on command, but it does respond to gentle, repeated attention. Keep showing up, even when nothing seems to happen, and trust that quiet persistence will gradually restore your sense of aliveness.

prompt: I feel nothing but dryness after prayer, and I doubt God hears me—why should I keep praying?
chosen: Dryness after prayer is common, but do not let it become your measure. Feelings never accurately gauge our real assimilation to God; they rise and fall while the changeless word of promise stands. God understands all things and hears the earnest supplication of the soul, its innermost thoughts and secret prayers—just as human invention lets people speak across great distances, so God receives what is never spoken aloud. So ask in faith, nothing wavering. Understand prayer as a continual drawing in of the heavenly life, like breathing or feeding, by which the life from without nourishes the heavenly seed within; let it be constant through your day, not only words at set hours. When joy is lacking, continue steadfastly; do not abandon communion or service because of spiritual depression. Rest on the promise, not on your moods, and trust that the God who knows all things is nourishing the seed within you even when your senses report nothing at all.
rejected: Dryness in prayer is a common experience, and it does not necessarily mean something is wrong. Feelings are unreliable indicators of spiritual reality; many faithful people go through long stretches where prayer feels empty. Keep praying because prayer is not primarily about feeling but about relationship and faithfulness. Try varying your practice: pray Scripture, use written prayers, pray while walking, or simply sit in silence. Consider whether you are tired, distracted, or carrying stress that makes it hard to be present. Talk with a pastor or spiritual friend. God is not offended by your dryness, and your honest doubt can itself become part of your prayer. Stay with it gently, without pressure to perform.

prompt: How can I live as a citizen of heaven while on earth?
chosen: To live as a citizen of heaven while on earth is to live as if your mind were in heaven and your body in the tomb—yet not to wish life away. Mortal existence is a school of experience and probation, a place to learn and improve and increase, not merely something to escape or endure. So withdraw your heart from the amusements and vanities that turn it from blessed eternity, and keep your mind fixed above. But know that this hope has one way: there is no salvation but in the way God has pointed out, and no hope of everlasting life but through obedience to the law affixed by the Father of life. Let your citizenship show in concrete obedience—prayer, honesty, mercy, purity—and in continual learning and growth. Handle earthly things lightly, as a traveler handles luggage rather than treasure, and let each day be a lesson in the school where God trains you for eternity.
rejected: Living as a citizen of heaven while on earth means holding a dual identity: you belong to God's kingdom while participating in ordinary life. Practically, this involves regular prayer, Scripture reading, and worship to keep your heart oriented toward God. Let your values reflect heaven—compassion, honesty, generosity, forgiveness—in your work, relationships, and community. Serve others, especially the poor and vulnerable, as an expression of heavenly citizenship. Stay engaged with the world rather than withdrawing from it; your citizenship is meant to bless those around you. Keep an eternal perspective on your struggles, remembering that your ultimate hope is in God. Balance engagement with detachment, enjoying good things without being owned by them.

prompt: I am a woman wondering whether I can take part in evangelistic work and teaching.
chosen: Yes—but begin by putting self to the rear and heart to the front. Do not approach evangelistic work and teaching as a profession or business in which salary, status, and self-advancement play a leading part; that professionalism is heartless. Instead, take up the discipline of learning: the School of the Prophets is established to increase in knowledge, the favorite study of the Elders is theology, every Elder should become a profound theologian, and every branch of science taught in the world should also be taught among the Saints. So prepare your mind as well as your heart. Yet all of it must be conformed to Christ—in outward behavior, in meekness and humility of heart, in taking God's view of things rather than the world's, and in a will zealous for God's glory and the salvation of souls. Offer your gifts as service, not as a platform; seek mentors and training to serve well. Start where you are, and let faithfulness, not ambition, set the pace.
rejected: Yes, women can certainly take part in evangelistic work and teaching. Scripture and church history include many women who served faithfully—proclaiming the good news, teaching, mentoring, and leading ministries. Your gifts, calling, and character matter more than gender alone. Seek out a church or community that affirms and supports women's contributions, and look for mentors and training opportunities. Consider your strengths: are you gifted in speaking, teaching small groups, discipling others, or organizing outreach? Start where you are, perhaps with a small group or a local ministry, and let your service grow as you gain experience. Pray for discernment, seek wise counsel, and step forward with confidence.

prompt: I have lost the grace of God and do not know how to recover it; to whom should I go?
chosen: Go first to God, and go by abandoning yourself to him. Do not try to manage your way back through anxious analysis; abandon yourself to God in interior and exterior suffering alike, and let your living, working, and rejoicing be in God and nowhere else. And do not be disquieted that you have forgotten him—such lapses are not met with turmoil but with a return in greater trust. Yet do not skip the meek knowing of your sin: let contrition and grace show you honestly what has turned you away, and let that knowing be meek, not despairing. Through it you are broken from all that is not our Lord—every false comfort, every self-made rescue—and in that breaking comes the perfect healing and oneing by our blessed Saviour. Speak with a trusted confessor who can help you discern, confess what needs confessing, release it, and return with greater trust. Give God your lostness, and let him heal and unite you to himself.
rejected: First, know that this feeling of lostness is itself a sign that grace is still at work in you—numbness would not care. Go to God honestly in prayer, and also to a trusted pastor, spiritual director, or confessor who can help you discern what has happened and how to return. Examine your life gently: is there unconfessed sin, unresolved grief, burnout, or isolation? Confession and absolution can be a real means of restoration. Reconnect with community and the sacraments.
