Spend time in Scripture and worship to keep your focus on Him. When you fail, confess and receive His forgiveness, then continue. Remember that it's not about perfection but about a direction of life. Let your words, actions, and attitudes reflect His character, and trust that He will complete the good work He began in you until the day of Christ.

prompt: I am a young minister and I want to know what to study most. What should I give my best hours to?
chosen: As a young minister, give your best hours to studying Scripture and theology, but do so by studying the letter, imbibing the spirit, and adhering steadfastly to the divine Principle. The Bible is your primary text—read it deeply, meditate on it, and learn to interpret it faithfully. But more than accumulating knowledge, seek the Spirit who inspired it. Let your study fuel your devotion and your devotion fuel your study. Don't rely on methods or techniques alone; progress comes from steadfast adherence to the divine Principle. The School of the Prophets is established to increase in knowledge, so recognize that the favorite study of the Elders is theology—every Elder should become a profound theologian. Also, every branch of science taught in the world should be taught among the Saints. Yet theology requires disciplined thought, trust in primitive convictions, knowledge of the original languages, and above all the Holy Spirit's illumination. So study broadly, keep theology central, and let all truth serve the gospel.
rejected: As a young minister, your best hours should go to studying Scripture and theology. The Bible is your primary text—read it deeply, meditate on it, and learn to interpret it faithfully. Alongside Scripture, study sound doctrine and church history to understand the faith once delivered. But don't neglect practical ministry skills like preaching, pastoral care, and leadership. Also, cultivate your own walk with God; your study should fuel your devotion. Consider reading broadly in literature and philosophy to connect with the culture. Finally, seek mentors and never stop learning. Give your mornings to study and your afternoons to people. Balance is key.

prompt: I feel like I have two selves—one that wants God and one that wants everything else. Which one am I?
chosen: The experience of feeling two selves is real, but they are not equal. One is the natural Will to live, to seek your own comfort and security—this will must be broken and bruised till it dies. The other is the Will to love and gladly please God, and this is the only will by which you truly live. You are not both equally; you are called to let the natural will die and to live by the will to love God. This is not about choosing which to feed but about a death and a resurrection. The self that wants everything else must be surrendered, and the self that wants God must be nurtured. Yet this search is double: your quest for God is grounded in experience and matched by the Divine Companion's quest for you, who spares no cost to bring you into fellowship. God and man are conjunct and mutually organic; your personality is formed only in fellowship with Him, and His life opens into yours and yours into His. In Christ, you are the one who dies to self and lives to God.
rejected: The experience of feeling two selves is common and deeply human. One self longs for God, for meaning, for love, for transcendence. The other self wants comfort, pleasure, security, and control. Which one are you? You are both, and you are neither. You are the one who chooses. Your identity isn't fixed by either desire; it's shaped by what you do with them. The self that wants God reflects your deepest calling, but the self that wants everything else reflects your natural instincts. Rather than asking which one you are, ask which one you will feed. You can acknowledge both, but you must decide which will rule. The good news is that God's grace meets you in the struggle and empowers you to choose Him.

prompt: How do I turn my whole life into one unbroken prayer?
chosen: Make prayer the one great central secret of holy living and serving—the corner-stone on which all your life-work is built, and the first resort in every matter, great or small. On your knees, both in secret and in the companionship of believers, begin by asking God to enable you to search out and discover your own heart and to reform whatever is amiss in it. Understand prayer not as an occasional verbal exercise but as the constant drawing in of the heavenly life, like breathing or feeding—the air by which the seed of the Divine Life within is nourished from without. So let your day be a continual turning and drawing in: fixed times, short aspirations, and ordinary tasks offered with attention. As you breathe in that life, God searches and reforms your heart, and the unbroken life grows.
rejected: Start by setting aside fixed times of prayer each day—morning, evening, and before meals—and guard them. Then practice carrying short prayers or a single word through the day, returning to it whenever you notice your mind has wandered. Offer ordinary tasks as prayer by doing them with attention and gratitude. Keep a journal of what you notice, and review it weekly. Over time the gaps between your set prayers shrink, and the habit becomes more natural. Be patient with yourself; it takes months of practice. The goal is not constant feelings but a steady direction of the heart toward God, renewed again and again.

prompt: I've been given a second chance and I want to live differently—where do I start?
chosen: The exhortation here is not prepare to die but prepare to live. Start by denying any real relapse in Truth: the old pattern has no real claim on you. Meet its cause mentally and courageously, naming the fear or false belief behind it and refusing it, conquering fear rather than managing it. But know that victory over lower passions is not won by unaided will or common-sense discipline; it is the work of a Living Power within you, slowly transforming you from fleshly to spiritual and teaching you higher pleasures, so that you are not left comfortless. Cooperate with that Power: choose one area, keep a change this week, tell one trusted person. Teach the young, in the morning of their days, to lay the foundation of health, strength, and constitution, so that longevity may begin to return. When the old pull appears, meet it with a clear mind and steady refusal, and begin again at once if you stumble.
rejected: Start small and concrete. Pick one area—sleep, honesty, or a relationship—and set a realistic change you can keep this week. Build routines that support it, tell one trusted person who can check in with you, and remove the cues that pull you back. Expect setbacks; a relapse is a normal part of change, so treat it as information rather than failure, and begin again. Reflect on what triggered it and adjust. Over time these small changes compound. Give yourself grace, be patient, and focus on progress rather than perfection.

prompt: Does God's decree mean I had no choice when I sinned?
chosen: No—God's decree does not make you the one who sinned; you chose, and you remain responsible. God permits and overrules evil without being its author. But do not wait to feel more, weep more, or receive greater power before you turn. You can this moment renounce sin in will and purpose; God supplies the strength, and feeling comes after the surrender, not before it. The high ideal of walking worthy of the Lord is realisable, because God's commands always imply promises: where He commands, He promises power to obey. And sin, though real and behoveable in the working out of the soul, is not final. Trust the tender word of the Thirteenth Revelation: all shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well. So renounce it now in will and purpose, and trust the God who commands your holiness to supply what He commands.
rejected: No—God's decree does not make you the one who sinned; you chose, and you remain responsible. Scripture holds together God's sovereign purpose and human responsibility: God permits and overrules evil without being its author. Your choice was real, and so is your guilt and your need for repentance. At the same time, God's decree includes mercy: He foreknew and provided a way back. So do not use the decree as an excuse, and do not despair as though your sin were fixed fate. Confess it, turn from it, and trust that God's purpose will work even this for good.

prompt: I want to love God more, but I feel only duty. How does love grow?
chosen: Love grows as you stop begging God to come down and make you feel affection, and instead make the constant endeavour to enter up into His estate and offer Him love—the mode of entry into adoration. Learn who He is in Scripture and prayer as one ascending to offer. Understand His love rightly: not mere sentiment or a bargain, but rational, voluntary self-communication that seeks the true good of its object, regulated by and subordinate to holiness. Because His love is holy, it wills your true good, not merely your comfort. Then let love be the outgoing of your entire nature in self-sacrificing service—for this is the supreme proof of the reality of Christian profession. Recall His mercies, thank Him specifically, and serve others at cost. Duty done steadily as an offering becomes the channel through which love grows; keep showing up and offering, and affection deepens in time.
rejected: Love grows through knowledge and practice. Spend time in Scripture and prayer, learning who God is and what He has done. Recall His mercies and thank Him specifically. Serve others, since love is exercised in action. Ask God to change your heart and give you affection for Him. Be patient: feelings often follow faithful obedience rather than preceding it. Duty is not the enemy of love; done steadily, it becomes the channel through which love grows. Keep showing up, and over time gratitude and affection tend to deepen.

prompt: I am a Christian and I find that the things of earth draw my mind from God—how do I set my affections above?
chosen: The aim is not to watch yourself but to be occupied with God, the object of your love. Live in the atmosphere of Christ's love: believe that He ever loves you, and claim His sweet approval and tender regard. When your mind drifts, do not examine the drift; turn to Him and delight in pleasing Him above any pleasure in your own performance. This requires deep recollection: keep 'God and I' as the only objects of thought, and avoid unnecessary intercourse with the outside world—unnecessary conversation, screens, news, and clutter—so that your attention is free for Him. Keep daily time of prayer and Scripture, not to grade yourself but to be with Him. Let gratitude for earthly good rise to the Giver. The more your heart rests in His love, the less the things of earth pull, because you are occupied with a greater and loving object.
rejected: Begin by noticing when your mind drifts and gently return it to God, without scolding yourself. Set aside a daily time of prayer and Scripture, and reduce obvious distractions—limit screens, news, and clutter. Practice gratitude for earthly good without letting it become your center. Memorize a verse to recall when you drift. Examine your week to see which things pull you most, and adjust. Over time, repeated turning builds a habit, and your affections gradually shift upward. Be patient and persistent; this is a lifelong practice, not a quick fix.

prompt: I'm afraid of suffering and I avoid it at all costs—how do I face it when it comes?
chosen: Begin by refusing the belief that man is hurt. God is All, and man is His image, whole and free. When the suggestion of suffering or mishap appears, do not dwell on symptoms, rehearse fear, or picture harm. Cast out fear at once, for fear is not a power to be managed but a false belief to be replaced by trust in God. Turn thought toward health and Life as God: man lives in Spirit, untouched by matter, and nothing can separate him from divine care. Let trust in God's allness govern you, as in the testimonies where fear was overcome before the healing appeared. As you abide in this truth, dread dissolves, and you rest in the wholeness God has already given.
rejected: It is natural to fear suffering, and avoiding it is a sensible instinct. When pain or hardship comes, acknowledge it honestly rather than pretending it is not there. Build resilience ahead of time: steady routines, strong relationships, and practices like mindfulness or prayer that calm the nervous system. When suffering arrives, break it into manageable pieces—deal with what is in front of you today, accept help, and let yourself grieve what is lost. Remember that pain is usually temporary, and that avoiding it at all costs can shrink your life. Face it gradually, with support, and it will lose some of its terror.

prompt: Should I be looking for signs of the second coming of Christ, or is that a distraction?
chosen: Christ will literally and personally come again in the clouds of heaven, just as he literally ascended, and spiritual interpretations that reduce his coming to an inward experience becloud the whole and leave no tangible ground for believers. Watch for the signs he gave, not as idle speculation but as confirmation that the promise is real. Yet do not defer the finding of Christ to some later comfort: without finding him here the soul enters a dark, lonely, self-tormenting state after death, and the remedy must be found now. Consider Constantine, fear-smitten before the greater host of Huns and Goths. The messenger of the King of angels promised aid and the token of victory; the emperor gazed on high and beheld the beauteous tree of glory inscribed, "By this sign thou shalt overcome the foe." The victory was made manifest as given by the King Almighty through his holy rood—not by the strength of his army nor by fortune. So too our hope rests not on signs alone but on the King who gives the victory.
rejected: Looking for signs can easily become a distraction if it turns into date-setting or speculation. Jesus himself warned against trying to calculate times. The healthier focus is to live faithfully now—love God and neighbor, grow in character, and stay ready in heart. Many Christians understand the second coming as a spiritual reality already at work, or as something fulfilled in the life of the church, so the emphasis falls on present discipleship rather than watching the sky. So do not chase signs obsessively, but do watchfulness in the sense of living well and keeping hope alive.

prompt: How do I deal with the feeling that God is a stern judge rather than a loving Father?
chosen: God the Father is not a vague spirit diffused everywhere without a habitation; he is a person who dwells in a place, and the Son is the express image of his person. The Father and the Son are two distinct persons together in heaven, as John saw the Lamb take the book from the hand of him that sat on the throne. When you feel God as a stern judge, remember that this personal Father is ever nigh. Think of the lost child in the lonely fen: the father appears ever nigh, kisses him, and leads him by the hand to his mother. So God draws near to you as a loving Father. Let parents take heed too: warn them against withdrawing children from a state of perfection or opposing a child's vocation, and against sowing vanity and covetousness in tender minds. Instead, form children in virtue, that they may know this Father's love and never mistake him for a stern judge.
rejected: That feeling is common, and it is worth examining where it comes from—often from harsh authority figures, fear-based teaching, or our own guilt. Start by noticing the voice of the stern judge in your head and asking whether it matches the God revealed in Jesus, who welcomed sinners and called God "Father." Practice gratitude, and reflect on passages about God's mercy. Talk with a trusted pastor or counselor about the origins of this fear. Over time, replacing the inner critic with a truer picture of God's love can soften the feeling. Remember that God's justice and love are not opposites; a loving Father can also guide and correct.

prompt: What becomes of wealth and the beauty of the field when this world passes away?
chosen: The Lord has done his share by surrounding us with the elements of wealth—wheat, meat, wool, and all things needful. The earth is full of resources, and it is our business to mold them to our wants by knowledge and labor. There is enough for all, without contending. Riches are no sin in themselves, but a very great and dangerous temptation. Beware of hoarding: keeping riches unused brings leanness of soul and darkness of mind. Put every dollar and every ability out to use for the good of the community. And understand that the temper which trusts in wealth or success does not merely soften and emasculate; it nurses meanly cruel and aggressive tempers, so that the prosperous man strengthens himself in active wickedness. When this world passes away, what passes is our misuse of God's provision, not the provision itself. Receive these gifts thankfully, mold them to your needs, and circulate them in service.
rejected: When this world passes away, wealth and the beauty of the field alike are shown to be temporary. Gold rusts, fields wither, and possessions cannot be carried beyond the grave. This is a sobering reminder to hold material things loosely and to invest in what lasts—character, love, and faith. The beauty of creation is real and good, but it is not ultimate; it points beyond itself to the Creator. So enjoy the field and use wealth responsibly, but do not set your heart on them, for they are passing. The wise person stores treasure in heaven rather than hoarding what will fade.

prompt: I am considering marriage—how should I choose a companion, and how much should godliness weigh against beauty or money?
chosen: Begin with prayerful waiting on God for guidance in marriage. True godliness is the first and absolutely needful qualification; without it, no beauty, wealth, or brilliance can make a marriage right. Having sought that first, weigh other suitableness calmly. Understand marriage as a serious vocation with sacred duties, not merely a means to private happiness: its end is the mutual enrichment of personality and mutual freedom to fulfil the true ideal of human life. Make no terms with lax views of divorce. Commend mutual tender love and the bearing of each other's faults, for forbearance is the daily bread of marriage. And beware of making marriage a matter of traffic or a money job; a union formed for gain is no true marriage. Make godliness the foundation, let love and forbearance be its walls, and let the rest be weighed in calm, prayerful judgment.
rejected: Choose a companion by weighing several factors: shared values, emotional compatibility, physical attraction, financial stability, and age suitability. Beauty and money matter, but they should not be the deciding factors; character and mental compatibility count for a great deal. Take time to know the person, observe how they handle conflict, and discuss your expectations openly. Many people find that attraction grows with familiarity, so do not dismiss someone solely on looks. Godliness is a nice bonus if it fits your beliefs, but practical compatibility is what makes a marriage work day to day.

prompt: I have been searching for love in all the wrong places. How do I find the love that lasts?
chosen: It is good that you recognize the pattern. Do not settle for a love that merely tolerates flaws; aspire constantly to the perfection of holy love. True love is strong and concerned with character: it corrects, purifies, and refines, and in God justice and mercy are one. Yet love cannot rest until it has sounded all the depths and learnt the perfections of its Beloved and become one with Him. It suffers nothing to intervene between itself and God, springing forward and finding no peace till it has overcome every obstacle and reached the Beloved, for love is strong as death and carries the lover out of himself into the heart of the beloved. Seek first that love; let every human affection be ordered toward it, and no lesser love will finally satisfy you.
rejected: It is good that you recognize the pattern. Lasting love usually begins with knowing yourself and choosing relationships slowly, with honesty and shared values. Look for people who are consistent, kind, and willing to grow. Set boundaries, communicate clearly, and do not expect any human relationship to be perfect; every love has flaws and requires patience. Community, service, and faith can also give your life a stable center so you are not desperate for affection. Give it time, and let trust build through small faithful acts rather than grand gestures.

prompt: How do I respond when someone asks me why God saved me and not others who were killed?
chosen: This is one of the hardest questions. Say honestly that you do not know why God spared you, but do not let the mystery breed disquiet: when we forget God, we need not be troubled, but return to Him with greater trust. Acknowledge the grief and point to Christ, who shares our death and promises resurrection. Then let your answer be a total self-oblation, holding back no secret exception, asking, 'Lord, what wilt thou have me to do?' Do not merely ask what sacrifices are bound, but what sacrifices can be made to God in gratitude for Christ mocked, scourged, crowned with thorns, and dying for our sins. Let a life offered without reservation be your answer rather than words alone.
rejected: This is one of the hardest questions, and honesty matters more than a tidy answer. You can say that you do not know why God spared you, and that you will not pretend to explain His providence. Avoid implying that you were better or more deserving. Acknowledge the grief and the mystery, affirm that God grieves with those who suffer, and point to Christ as the one who shares our death and promises resurrection. Let your life, lived in gratitude and service, be part of your answer rather than words alone.

prompt: How can I be ready to enter into the celestial city when it comes down from God out of heaven?
chosen: Readiness begins with a life ordered toward God: prayer, repentance, love of neighbor, and faithfulness in small things. Know that the heavens are literally opened at the place where the Cherubims and the flaming sword keep the way of the tree of life; this is the gate of heaven, and by this way the Holy City will descend. God will roar out of Zion and utter His voice from Jerusalem, shaking the heavens and the earth; then Jerusalem shall be holy and the sign of the Son of man appear in heaven. Yet do not be unsettled, driven by every wind of doctrine, or looking for Christ here and there. Come to God's rest: a settled conviction of the truth, freedom from doubt and fear, and a refusal to chase after every new claim. Keep your conscience clear, trust His grace, and let the promise of the city give you peace.
rejected: Readiness begins with a life ordered toward God: prayer, repentance, love of neighbor, and faithfulness in small things. Keep your conscience clear, receive the sacraments if you are able, and let hope shape your daily choices. Remember that the city comes down as a gift, not an achievement, so trust God's grace rather than your own performance. Stay watchful and patient, serving where you are, and let the promise of the city give you courage and peace.

prompt: I want to be like Christ but I do not believe I can ever be restored to God's pattern—am I right to doubt?
chosen: Your doubt is understandable, but you need not wait for a better feeling or greater strength. This very moment you can renounce sin in will and purpose; God supplies the strength, and feeling comes after the surrender. Do not languish over the number and magnitude of your sins: all is possible to God, and it is as easy for Him to forgive and blot out innumerable and heinous sins as to forgive one. Of ourselves we cannot even think what is right; all comes to us from God. And with Jesus, affirm that God is the Life of man: individualized existence is restored, not lost in death, which is only a seeming vanishing that Truth restores. So pray, obey, and trust that He will complete what He begins.
rejected: Your doubt is understandable, and many sincere people feel the same. Growth in Christlikeness is a lifelong process, not a single decision. Start where you are: pray honestly, examine your life, and take small steps of obedience. Do not wait until you feel strong or worthy; God meets us in our weakness. Find a community that can support and encourage you, and be patient with yourself. Restoration is God's work, and He is faithful to complete what He begins.

prompt: Is the doctrine of the Trinity a meaningless formula, or can it still mean something to a modern person?
chosen: The Trinity can feel like an abstract formula, but it is inscrutable, not contradictory, and it still speaks to modern people. It says that God is not a solitary power but a communion of love, and that love and relationship lie at the heart of reality. The Trinity is the necessary complement to God's attributes: within God there is the eternal object of knowledge, love, and will. Yet the Three are not separate individuals like three Gods; the word 'Persons' must express mutual inclusion, so that in the Spirit's indwelling is the indwelling of the Father and the Son. Christian doctrine is the Church's reflection on the value of Christ; it is to be given the maximum of meaning and further developed, not discarded. Approach it prayerfully, and let it shape how you think about God and neighbor.
rejected: The Trinity can feel like an abstract formula, but it still speaks to modern people. It says that God is not a solitary power but a communion of love, and that love and relationship lie at the heart of reality. For many, that is meaningful in a world that values connection and community. You do not need to fully understand the doctrine to find it fruitful; it is a mystery to be lived more than solved. Approach it prayerfully, and let it shape how you think about God and neighbor.

prompt: Why should I wait patiently for the Lord instead of trying to force change myself?
chosen: Waiting on the Lord begins with a willingness to have no will of your own. Be slow to take new steps; do not presume that strong desire or an open door is faith. Bring each step to God in prayer and test it by His Word, yet go further: the true workman waits for the Master's beck, glance, or signal in the time, the way, and the associates of His work, accepting the helpers God provides rather than those preference would choose. And do not despise mere presence before Him. Like a statue placed for the King's pleasure, remain before God content to wait upon His will even when you can do nothing. Prayer is not measured by output but by devotion. When He signals, move with patient, believing expectation; until then, stay.
rejected: Waiting on the Lord is an act of trust, not passivity. When you try to force change in your own strength, you often act out of anxiety and self-will rather than faith. Scripture repeatedly tells us that those who wait on the Lord renew their strength. Patience lets God work in His timing, which is always better than ours. Forcing change can produce shallow or premature results, and it can lead you to rely on yourself instead of on God. Waiting does not mean doing nothing; it means praying, obeying what is already clear, and trusting God to open doors. The key is to keep your heart soft and your hands open, ready to move when God clearly leads, but not running ahead of Him.

prompt: How does the Spirit transform me into Christ's likeness?
chosen: The Spirit transforms you by turning you again to God, out of whom you proceeded. This is not self-improvement but conversion: becoming as a little child, forsaking all your own imaging and lust, and coming again to the Divine Vision. The Spirit is also the first-fruits and earnest of the coming redemption of the body—not wholly future, nor already complete in the flesh. And do not seek power as your own possession. Receive the Holy Spirit within and upon you, letting Him be the power that causes you to walk in God's statutes. You have no power of your own; the power is His, coming upon you. So turn, renounce your self-made centres, and let Him—not your grip—be the strength that conforms you to Christ.
rejected: The Spirit transforms you into Christ's likeness through a gradual work of renewal. As you read Scripture, pray, and obey, the Spirit convicts you of sin, comforts you, and gradually reshapes your desires and habits. This is sanctification: a lifelong process where you cooperate with grace. Transformation happens as you fix your eyes on Jesus and let the Spirit apply truth to your heart. It involves putting off old patterns and putting on new ones, growing in love, joy, peace, patience, and the other fruit of the Spirit. The goal is Christlikeness, and the Spirit is the agent who accomplishes it, using means like community, trials, and worship to conform you to His image.

prompt: I feel God is watching to see if I overcome—what happens if I fail?
chosen: God is watching, and His watching is jealous love. All your experiences come as tests, and every step is decisive for your eternal future. He is looking for tested pattern men and women—those who overcome. Let His eye stir you to overcome rather than to despair. Yet when you forget Him, do not be disquieted; a lapse in remembrance is a call to return with greater trust. And go further: abandon yourself to God in interior and exterior suffering alike. Do not seek life, work, or joy outside of Him. Live, work, and rejoice—but only in God. Then failure loses its terror, for you are not carrying yourself. The Father who watches receives the child who returns, and in that abandonment every test becomes a place of His jealous love.
rejected: It is true that God watches, but He watches as a loving Father, not a harsh examiner waiting to catch you. Failure is real, and it grieves God, but it does not end your story. Scripture says that if we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive. The Christian life is not a single test but a series of opportunities to grow. When you fail, you repent, receive grace, and continue. God's watching is meant to encourage you, not paralyze you with fear. He is for you, and His grace is sufficient. So do not let fear of failure keep you from pressing on; instead, let it drive you to depend on Him more deeply.

prompt: I want to know how to pray aright; can this book teach me?
chosen: Yes, a book can help—if it teaches you the divine model Christ gave. In that model we are bound to recommend to God, before all other things, the exaltation of His own honor and glory, and to beg that the kingdom of His holy grace and love be planted in all hearts. Prayer must also be your main assistant in every step of spiritual progress: pray that God would enable you to search out and discover your own hearts and reform whatever is amiss in them. And do not think the deep knowledge of Christ is for an intellectual few. In Him all treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hid, and the full, free, open opportunity of knowing Him in His divine fulness is offered to every believer. Read prayerfully, test by Scripture, and press into Him.
rejected: Yes, a good book on prayer can help you pray aright, provided you read it prayerfully and put it into practice. Such books typically explain the Lord's Prayer, the importance of adoration, confession, thanksgiving, and supplication, and the need for persistence and faith. They can correct common mistakes, like praying only for selfish things or treating prayer as a formula. But no book replaces the Holy Spirit, who teaches us to pray. Use the book as a guide, test its teaching against Scripture, and let it drive you to actual prayer rather than mere reading about prayer. The best book will send you to your knees.

prompt: How may I come to be as a little child, hanging upon Christ for all things, and so enter the Kingdom of God?
chosen: To become as a little child is the shortest and only way to enter the Kingdom of God and to be like All Things. It is not a technique you cultivate in your own strength but a turning: hanging upon Christ for all things, depending upon the author and fountain of them. Cast all else out of your heart, because God would possess it alone—beg this favor and do your part. Yet do not stiffen your will against His guidance. Keep a will of wax, pliable in His hand, and go on boldly like a child held by God's hand. When you stumble in little things, do not be daunted; rise and continue. The child who hangs upon Him, whose heart is emptied for Him alone, and who rises undaunted from stumblings—this is the one who enters.
rejected: To become as a little child, you must cultivate humility, trust, and dependence. A child does not worry about status or try to prove itself; it simply trusts its parent. Begin by acknowledging that you cannot manage your life on your own and that you need Christ for everything—wisdom, strength, forgiveness, and direction. Practice bringing each need to Him in prayer and then waiting for His help rather than rushing ahead. Let go of the need to appear competent or self-sufficient. Surround yourself with others who model childlike faith. Over time, as you depend on Christ in small things, that dependence becomes a habit, and you enter more fully into the life of the Kingdom.

prompt: I want to be remembered for something good, but I feel insignificant. Does my life matter?
chosen: Your life matters, but not as the world counts mattering. Count yourself as already dead, since you must die some day, and have no other desire or consolation in this perishable life than unceasingly to weep over, regret, and detest your offences and faults; it is not now the time to rejoice but to lament with all sincerity of heart. Yet do not fear that God abandons you. The eternal Father who cares today will care tomorrow, either withholding trouble or giving invincible courage to bear it. Knowing your need of His grace, resolve never wilfully to forget Him and to live in His presence even when consolations are withdrawn. Your significance rests not in a legacy but in that faithful presence.
rejected: Yes, your life matters. The desire to be remembered for something good is itself a sign that you care about goodness, and that matters more than fame. Significance is not measured by how many people know your name, but by the love you give and the faithfulness you show in small things. Many people who felt invisible in their own day shaped others in ways they never saw. Try to focus less on being remembered and more on doing the next good thing in front of you. Your worth is not decided by the crowd.

prompt: I fear God's punishment so much that I want to hide from Him rather than run to Him—how should I flee?
chosen: It is natural to want to hide when you are afraid, but hiding from God never works. Flee by committing yourself to GOD's protection in danger and finding His Word sweet and sufficient in peril. Then resist the devil boldly on holy ground, armed with the breastplate of righteousness and the shield of faith, claiming the promise that he will flee. Remember that God never forsakes us until we first forsake Him; the real danger is not His anger but our own departure. So fear to leave Him, and remain always with Him. He is not a tyrant waiting to crush you but a Father who welcomes the returning child; confess your fear and sin honestly, and let His forgiveness calm you.
rejected: It is natural to want to hide when you are afraid, but hiding from God never works. The right way to flee is to flee toward Him, not away. God is not a tyrant waiting to crush you; He is a Father who welcomes the returning child. Confess your fear and your sin honestly, and ask for mercy. Do not let shame keep you at a distance. Run to Him in prayer, and let His forgiveness calm your fear.

prompt: Is a minister of another denomination truly ordained?
chosen: A minister is an ambassador and messenger of God, judged by faithfulness rather than popular approval. He must reprove sin sincerely, without softening the Gospel to soothe hearers, and visit all the sick, esteeming a man's immortal soul above his present favor and fearing none but Him who can destroy both soul and body. He must avoid both extremes: the hermit's withdrawal and the popularizer's prayerless activism, remembering that time with God is useful only as it is expended on men. Yet honor both kinds of ministry: the voice that speaks for God and the hidden force that supplies power through holy sympathy and silent prayer. Each should be true to his own ministry, and where such faithfulness is found, its orders bear good fruit.
rejected: This is a question many sincere people ask, and the answer depends partly on what you mean by ordination. Different churches have different understandings of ministry and different processes for setting people apart for service. What matters most is whether a person is faithfully preaching the gospel, caring for people, and serving God with integrity. Rather than judging another denomination's orders, it is better to look at the fruit of a ministry and to respect the conscience of those who serve in good faith.

prompt: I am afraid of the day of judgment—how can I be ready to give an account of my stewardship with joy?
chosen: Fear of judgment can be a healthy wake-up call, but do not wait for joyful feelings before you rejoice. Count it all joy by faith, reckoning the trial a blessing, and choose to rejoice even when feelings fail until praise becomes a habit. Live in daily readiness for the LORD's return, able to give an account of your stewardship with joy, using time, money, and gifts faithfully and keeping short accounts with God. Yet do not make gloom or perpetual self-condemnation your safe temper; strenuously lift your heart to God's goodness and exult in it, for that is the only safe temper for tempted men. Seek His loving-kindness in all the breadth and open air of common life—in whatsoever things are true, honourable, just, pure, lovely, and of good report—while not missing behind them the greatest Reality, God Himself.
rejected: Fear of judgment is understandable, and it can be a healthy wake-up call. To be ready, examine how you use your time, money, and gifts, and ask whether you are serving others and honoring God with them. Confess where you have fallen short, receive God's forgiveness, and make practical changes. Readiness is not about being perfect but about being faithful and honest. Keep short accounts with God, and let gratitude and hope replace dread as you trust in His mercy.

prompt: I am afraid that God is too angry with me to hear my prayers; is there someone who can plead my cause before him?
chosen: Yes—Jesus Christ is the one who pleads your cause before the Father; He is your advocate, and His finished work is why you may come at all. Come with reverence, approaching prayer with trembling, shutting your senses to distractions and observing strict silence of tongue and body. Yet come with confidence, relying on Christ's merits, for God offers grace at each action unless we forget to ask. Remember that of ourselves we can attain to no good thing and have nothing to offer God that was not already His. Our one recourse is to turn to Him in every occurrence in prayer as guilty, poor, and needy beggars, weak and miserable, yet as His children, with holy fear mingled with love, peace, and recollection.
rejected: Yes—Jesus Christ is the one who pleads your cause before the Father. He is your advocate, and His finished work on the cross is the reason you can come to God at all. God is not too angry to hear you; He invites you to come. Bring your fear and your sin to Christ, and trust that His merit speaks for you. You do not need to earn a hearing; you need only to come in faith and rest in His mercy.

prompt: What is the one thing that will remain to me if I lose everything in this war?
chosen: If you lose everything in this war, the one thing that remains is your courage, your confidence, and your good-will. These are indestructible because they are of God. Even when all else is stripped away, you can go on joyously, courageously, and confidently. But do not merely endure evil—resist it firmly. Error is opposed to Life and will flee before Truth. Stand firm against every form of evil, knowing that Truth is omnipotent. Moreover, remember that Christ is the stronger who divides the spoils; He claims the world's beauty and learning for His service and tunes them to celestial melody. So even in loss, you gain the treasures of heaven, and all that is true and beautiful becomes yours in Him. Hold fast to these gifts, for they are the essence of your being and cannot be taken from you.
rejected: If you lose everything in war, the one thing that remains is your faith. Material possessions, loved ones, and even your home can be taken, but your relationship with God is secure. Hold fast to prayer and trust in His plan. Remember that earthly losses are temporary, and your true treasure is in heaven. Stay connected to your faith community and continue to hope. Even in the darkest times, God is with you, and your faith will carry you through.

prompt: I am a person of faith and I want to know how to pray.
chosen: To pray, begin by entering the inmost chamber of your heart and shutting the door of your senses. Adore God in spirit and in truth, with an intelligence and will purified from every phantom of earth. Approach Him with a pure heart, a free conscience, and unfeigned faith. But do not leave your mind behind—seek the full assurance of understanding and an abundance of conviction. Let your heart be made strong and full of love, and engage your mind in loving God. Remember that continual help of God is needed, so cultivate a holy habit of thinking of Him often. Since we must know before we love, let your prayer be a continual being with God, and He will draw near to you.
rejected: To pray, start by finding a quiet place and setting aside time each day. Begin with gratitude and confession, then bring your requests to God. Use the Lord's Prayer as a model, and don't worry about using fancy words—just speak from your heart. Read Scripture to guide your prayers, and consider keeping a prayer journal. Join with others in prayer at church or in small groups. Remember that prayer is a conversation with God, so listen as well as speak. Be persistent and don't give up if you don't see immediate answers. God hears you and will respond in His perfect timing.

prompt: I've been told the spiritual and temporal should be kept separate in the church. Is that true?
chosen: The idea that spiritual and temporal matters should be kept separate is false. All things are spiritual before God, and He has the right to guide temporal as well as spiritual affairs. Business, labor, and daily life are not outside His counsel. The church should not divide life into sacred and secular compartments, but should acknowledge God's sovereignty over every aspect of existence. Moreover, one need not be always at church to be with God; you can make an oratory of your heart and hold familiar conversation with Him in meekness, humility, and love. The sacraments and order of the church guard the truth that spiritual life is God's gift, received and not manufactured—not as magic, but as means of grace that keep us in the gift. Thus, in all places and tasks, you may commune with God and seek His guidance.
rejected: The idea that spiritual and temporal matters should be kept separate in the church is not entirely true. While there is a distinction between the sacred and the secular, they are not meant to be completely divorced. The church should address both the spiritual needs of its members and their temporal concerns, such as social justice and community welfare. However, the church should not become overly political or focus solely on worldly matters. A balanced approach is best, where spiritual guidance informs temporal actions, and the church remains a moral compass without entangling itself in partisan politics.

prompt: I am a recent convert and feel overwhelmed by all the doctrine I do not yet understand—where should I start?
chosen: As a recent convert, begin by making a total sacrifice of yourself to God. Ask, 'Lord, what wilt thou have me to do?' and hold nothing back in your heart. Conversion is not merely learning doctrine but an entire oblation of self. So start by surrendering your will completely to Him, without secret exceptions. But remember that conversion is wrought by the almighty power of the HOLY GHOST, not by human persuasion or effort. Your great need is to know GOD as the worker, and to yield to His Spirit. As you study doctrine, seek a genuine readjustment between faith and modern knowledge—a fresh correlation that does not tamper with principle on either side. Let your first priority be to give yourself wholly to God, and He will lead you into all truth.
rejected: As a recent convert, it's normal to feel overwhelmed by doctrine. Start with the basics: focus on the core teachings of the faith, such as the life, death, and resurrection of Jesus, and God's love and grace. Read the Bible regularly, perhaps beginning with the Gospels. Join a Bible study or a newcomers' class at your church to learn in community. Don't be afraid to ask questions. Take it one step at a time, and remember that understanding grows over time. Pray for guidance and trust that God will lead you into truth as you seek Him.

prompt: I am in a position where I could quietly help a poor person who is ashamed to ask—how should I do it?
chosen: If you are in a position to help a poor person who is ashamed to ask, do so discreetly and respectfully. But first, never oppress the poor or take advantage of their vulnerability. The Scriptures warn that those who oppress the poor will come to nakedness, thirst, and hunger without means of supply. So let your help be pure and without any hint of exploitation. Offer assistance in a way that preserves their dignity, perhaps through a third party or by making it seem like a natural opportunity. Be sensitive to their feelings and avoid drawing attention to their need. Provide practical help, such as groceries, paying a bill, or offering employment opportunities. Do it without expecting anything in return, and keep the matter confidential. Your kindness should be an expression of love and compassion, reflecting God's care for the poor. And if the person is sick, support their trust in the power of Mind, telling them that their strength is in proportion to their courage. Finally, encourage the poor to be honest, thankful, and frugal, and remind them that coveting another's goods is as wicked as miserly hoarding.
rejected: If you are in a position to help a poor person who is ashamed to ask, do so discreetly and respectfully. Offer assistance in a way that preserves their dignity, perhaps through a third party or by making it seem like a natural opportunity. Be sensitive to their feelings and avoid drawing attention to their need. Provide practical help, such as groceries, paying a bill, or offering employment opportunities. Do it without expecting anything in return, and keep the matter confidential. Your kindness should be an expression of love and compassion, reflecting God's care for the poor.

prompt: I've been hurt by the church and want to leave. Is there still a place for me among God's people?
chosen: I'm sorry you've been hurt by the church. While you can make an oratory of your heart and converse with God in meekness, humility, and love apart from church, do not treat your membership in the Church as a loose affiliation. It is a real bond carrying personal obligation. Cleave meekly and mightily to Holy Church, for she is the unbroken blessed Common, the body of Christ. Yet acknowledge that the Church's divisions have made her less actual to men than the nation, and therefore less powerful. Your pain is real, but the Church is not broken; she is holy and beloved. Find solace in her common teaching and in the communion of saints. Even if you step away for a time, remain united in heart to the Church, and let your heart be an oratory where you meet God and His people in love.
rejected: I'm sorry you've been hurt by the church. It's understandable to feel like leaving, but know that God loves you and has a place for you among His people. The church is a family, and though families can hurt us, we need each other. Consider talking to a trusted pastor or friend about your pain. Take time to heal, but don't give up on community. God can use this trial to draw you closer to Him and to a healthier church family. You are not alone, and there is hope for restoration.

prompt: I want to know the true church; how can I identify it?
chosen: To identify the true church, look for a visible, unified body that witnesses to the central truths of the faith with authority. It honors both enthusiasm and sanity, valuing religious fervor while maintaining sound instruction and order. The true church is a permanent community whose conservative and educational functions supplement its evangelistic zeal. It holds firmly to essentials like the Trinity, the deity of Christ, and salvation by grace, and it allows freedom on non-central points. Importantly, this Church cares only that the individual is pure in heart and the nation honourable; it is indifferent to personal success and national expansion. It is ready to suffer for its testimony. You can recognize it by its fidelity to the gospel, its love for one another, and its balanced life of worship, teaching, and service.
rejected: To identify the true church, look for a community that faithfully teaches the Bible, worships God sincerely, and demonstrates love among its members. The true church is not a building but the people of God, united by faith in Christ. It will hold to the essential doctrines of Christianity, such as the Trinity, the deity of Christ, and salvation by grace. It will also practice the sacraments and encourage personal relationship with God. Ultimately, the true church is where the Holy Spirit is present, guiding believers into all truth. Pray for discernment and study Scripture to recognize it.

prompt: I want to spend my one life well—how do I balance the joy of the present with the fear of what's coming?
chosen: To spend your one life well, do not seek a middle way of serving both God and the world; such a compromise brings gloomy wretchedness. Instead, follow Christ all the way, that He may complete His process in you. Seek joy not by trying to feel happy but by being right with God. Forget yourself in service to others, rejoice in the Lord above feelings, and obey Him faithfully. Cling steadfastly to God and His likeness, trusting that harmonious Life destroys the belief in what Life is not. Do not let fear and doubt overshadow your clear trust in God. The joy of the present is found in recognizing that God is Life, and in Him there is no sickness, sin, or fear. Calmly trust that His harmonious Life is your life, and that whatever seems to threaten it is a false belief. As you hold to this truth, fear dissolves, and you can enjoy the present as a reflection of God's goodness, knowing that your future is secure in Him.
rejected: Balancing joy and fear is a common struggle. Start by recognizing that both emotions are valid: joy helps you appreciate the present, while fear can motivate preparation for the future. Practice mindfulness to savor the moment, and set realistic goals to address future concerns. Trust that you can handle challenges with planning and support. Remember that life is uncertain, but you can build resilience. Seek a middle path where you enjoy today without ignoring tomorrow. Communicate with loved ones, and consider professional guidance if fear becomes overwhelming. Ultimately, balance comes from accepting uncertainty and focusing on what you can control.

prompt: I feel too shy to attend Mutual Improvement—how can I be reached?
chosen: Feeling shy about attending Mutual Improvement is normal, but do not let anxiety rule you. Keep yourself in God's presence and avoid hurry and over-eagerness, for over-eagerness is the mother imperfection of all imperfections. Withdraw as much as possible from acquaintance and from men, and abstain from affairs that hinder your purpose. Seek with jealous care the place, time, and means most suited to quiet and contemplation. Lovingly embrace silence and solitude, and fly the agitation of a world never at rest. When self-love stirs, gently disavow it a few times a day without violent resistance or excessive introspection; the gentle denial suffices. In this way, you will be reached by God's peace and guided in what to do about Mutual Improvement. Trust that He will open the way in His time, and do not force yourself beyond what is peaceful.
rejected: Feeling shy about attending Mutual Improvement is completely normal. Start by acknowledging your feelings and reminding yourself that everyone feels nervous in new situations. Try to focus on the purpose of the meeting—learning and growing—rather than on your discomfort. You might reach out to a friend or leader beforehand to arrange a comfortable entry. Set small goals, like introducing yourself to one person. Remember that others are likely focused on the meeting, not on you. With time and practice, your confidence will grow. Be patient with yourself and celebrate each step you take.

prompt: I wonder whether the differences among Christians today are as serious as those in the early centuries, and what the history of dogma can teach me about them.
chosen: The differences among Christians today are serious, but the history of dogma offers insight. Dogma is the product of the Greek spirit working on the soil of the Gospel, preserving both the Christian content (monotheism and the significance of Christ) and the philosophic form. It did not simply continue New Testament theology or the whole richness of early Christian preaching. Its presuppositions were the fundamental motives of the Gospel, the common preaching concerning Christ, the Christian use of the Old Testament, and the Greek spirit. Today's differences often reflect similar underlying issues. By studying the history of dogma, we can see how the Church articulated its faith in response to these presuppositions. Moreover, we must not reduce Jesus to a figure small enough to be fully comprehended; the Gospels present Him in the richness of His mysterious person as Lawgiver, Teacher, Healer, Ruler, and Saviour, man and God. That manifold picture is a self-evidencing fact. Learning to distinguish central truths from secondary matters, we engage present divisions with humility and charity.
rejected: The differences among Christians today are indeed serious, but they may not be as foundational as those in the early centuries. Early controversies, like Arianism and Gnosticism, struck at the core of Christian belief. Today's disagreements often involve secondary matters, though some are significant. The history of dogma shows that the Church has always grappled with articulating truth, and that councils and creeds helped define orthodoxy. This history teaches us that doctrinal precision matters and that unity requires both conviction and charity. By studying dogma, we can learn to distinguish essentials from non-essentials and engage differences with humility, seeking to understand the past to navigate present divisions.

prompt: I worry that Christ's own words about Jonah and the flood settle the historical questions; am I bound to read them as strict history?
chosen: You are not bound to flatten Christ's words into a strict chronicle, but neither should you dismiss the historical question. The earliest testimonies present Jesus appealing to real events in Israel's memory—Jonah and the flood—as signs of judgment and mercy. These sayings were recorded within the apostolic age, too soon after the events for myth to form, and in an age of historical inquiry rather than credulity. Critically examined, they belong to a first-century Jewish prophet speaking to a skeptical generation; they are not slow legendary growth. From the faith that Jesus is Messiah, we read them as authoritative teaching about repentance and judgment. Far from dissolving him, honest criticism leaves the historical Christ more firmly established as the central fact of history, and the luminous reality of his Life is affirmed rather than explained away.
rejected: You are not bound to read every reference in Christ's teaching as a strict historical chronicle. When Jesus speaks of Jonah or the flood, he uses familiar scriptural and traditional imagery to make a moral and theological point about repentance and judgment. Many Christians hold that the truth of his teaching does not depend on the precise historical mechanics of the older stories. You can take his words with full seriousness as revelation from God while still asking historical questions about the texts he referenced. Faith and critical inquiry are not enemies; the core of the gospel is the person of Christ, not a particular theory of ancient chronology.

prompt: How do I love God equally in pain and in pleasure?
chosen: Loving God equally in pain and pleasure begins by settling why you come to him: not for the comfort or pleasure the practice brings, but from love and because God wills it. Worldly pains and pleasures are not comparable to spiritual ones, so do not weigh them against each other or bargain for relief. Be careful for nothing and fear nothing; desire only not to offend God. This is possible because God is not a distant sovereign sitting apart in ease: he is passible, grieved over sin, and his holiness requires and his love provides atonement. The Lamb slain from the foundation of the world expresses an eternal fact in God's nature. In pleasure, receive the gift and turn it into obedience; in pain, do not let it purchase your devotion. Keep a steady rhythm of prayer and service, and let blessedness—God's own joy—be the controlling element of your love.
rejected: Loving God equally in pain and pleasure begins with recognizing that both are gifts from the same loving hand. In pleasure, receive with gratitude and let joy turn you toward the Giver. In pain, remember that God is near and that suffering can deepen trust and compassion. Practically, keep a steady rhythm of prayer, thanksgiving, and service regardless of how you feel. Don't measure your love by emotional highs or lows; measure it by faithfulness. Offer both seasons to God, and ask him for grace to see his goodness in each. Over time, this steady orientation builds a love that is not dependent on circumstances but rooted in God's unchanging character.

prompt: I'm at peace with the world and my life. Why would I need God at all?
chosen: Your peace is worth taking seriously, and it is not wrong to enjoy a settled life. But consider what your peace is made of. We are not isolated selves who happen to need a God alongside us; human personality is formed only in fellowship, and God's life opens into ours as ours opens into his. A peace built on the world's goods alone is a truce, not a homecoming. God is a God of deliverances who keeps his people in answer to prayer—yet his purposes are fulfilled in the death of some as in the deliverance of others. So do not seek him only when prosperity fails, friends disappoint, or you are sick and lonely, as though a single cry or petulant demand could obtain his gifts. He asks steady, persistent desire. Ask honestly what your peace rests on, and whether there is a longing in you that only fellowship with him can finally meet.
rejected: Your peace is worth taking seriously, and it is not wrong to enjoy a settled life. But the question is whether that peace is deep enough to hold when circumstances change. Many people find that contentment with the world is real but fragile; loss, illness, or disappointment can expose a need beneath it. God is not simply an emergency resource for the unsettled. Christians would say that human life is made for fellowship with its source, and that a peace without God is a truce rather than a homecoming. You might ask honestly what your peace rests on, and whether there is a longing in you that the world's goods cannot finally satisfy.

prompt: How do I stop being distracted by images and fantasies when I try to pray?
chosen: Distraction in prayer is common, and the first step is not to panic. Come to prayer like a beggar waiting at a door: you have nothing to offer and everything to receive, and you need God's continual help. When images or fantasies arise, do not scold yourself or wrestle with them; gently notice them and recall your mind to God's presence in tranquility, without disquiet. Praying, being with God, and thinking of him often are linked through holy habit—we must know him before we can love him. But do not imagine prayer is easy or naturally congenial. It is humbling work that crucifies pride and signs our bankruptcy, and little praying is a worse evil than no praying, a deluding make-believe. A short phrase of Scripture can serve as a quiet anchor, and stillness beforehand helps, but do not make technique the point. With practice your capacity to stay present will grow.
rejected: Distraction in prayer is common, and the first step is not to panic. When images or fantasies arise, gently notice them and return your attention to God, perhaps using a short phrase or a word of Scripture as an anchor. It helps to prepare beforehand: choose a quiet place, limit screens, and begin with a brief moment of stillness. Some people find it useful to write down distracting thoughts to deal with later. Remember that prayer is a relationship, not a performance; God is patient with your wandering mind. With practice and patience, your capacity to stay present will grow, and the distractions will lose some of their pull.

prompt: I'm afraid that my past will always define me—can God really come between me and it?
chosen: Your fear is understandable, and the past can feel like a weight that follows you. The Christian answer is that God offers forgiveness and a new beginning, but this is not a purely spiritual transaction kept apart from daily life. All things are spiritual before God, and he has a right to guide your temporal affairs as well as your inner life—your work, your relationships, and the practical outworking of your past. And the past's hold is not merely external: the flight from God runs down the labyrinthine ways of the mind, through memory, shame, and fantasy. Yet God follows there too, with unhurrying chase and unperturbed pace. When you confess your past, he does not hold it against you. Beyond the records and the witnesses, the Spirit of God bears record in your heart of the living Redeemer, and that witness exceeds all other evidence. Your identity is no longer finally determined by what you did.
rejected: Your fear is understandable, and the past can feel like a weight that follows you. The Christian answer is that God offers forgiveness and a new beginning. When you confess your past to him, he does not hold it against you; he forgives and restores. This does not mean the consequences vanish, but it means your identity is no longer finally determined by what you did. You are defined by God's love and grace rather than by your worst moments. Practically, this involves honest confession, receiving forgiveness, and possibly seeking support from a community. Over time, trusting God's promise can loosen the past's grip on how you see yourself.

prompt: I was raised to believe in God, and the arguments seem only to confirm what I already held; is that a legitimate way to believe?
chosen: Yes, and this is closer to how faith actually lives. Religion is not produced by proof, nor destroyed because proof is insufficient to some minds. Faith springs from the soul itself, and the arguments are corroborations that awaken, explicate, and confirm an intuitive conviction already present—not a complete demonstration. Logic itself presupposes God, and finite premises cannot reach the Infinite; the bridge of argument is entered and left only by leaps of intuition. Nor need you fear a clash with science: our religion will not contradict the facts of science, whose leading principles are eternal facts, and God never made something out of nothing but organized the earth from existing matter. So let proofs confirm what your soul holds, resting your belief on that deeper ground.
rejected: Yes, this is a legitimate and common way to believe. Many people are raised within a faith tradition and find that reasoned arguments—cosmological, teleological, moral—confirm what they already accept. Belief usually begins in nurture and community, and reason can then examine and support it. What matters is that you don't simply inherit beliefs passively; you should test them, ask honest questions, and let evidence and argument shape your conviction. If the arguments genuinely support your belief, that is a strength, not a weakness. If some arguments fail, your faith need not collapse. So long as you are reflective and open to correction, being raised in belief and finding it confirmed by reason is entirely legitimate.

prompt: I am afraid that if I give everything to God I will lose myself. What should I do?
chosen: Your fear is understandable, but notice what it assumes. Of ourselves we can attain to no good thing, and we have nothing to offer God that was not already His; so surrender cannot impoverish you, for all you give was His gift first. When you forget God—and we all do—that lapse need not cause disquiet. Let every lapse become a return with greater trust. Nor fear that surrender leaves you destitute: God supplies all need, often through unexpected and timely provision, and extremity is His opportunity. Our one recourse is to turn to Him in every occurrence in prayer—guilty, poor, and needy beggars, weak and miserable, yet His children—with holy fear mingled with love, peace, and recollection.
rejected: Your fear is understandable, but giving yourself to God does not mean losing yourself—it means finding your true self in relation to Him. Set healthy boundaries, discern what is genuinely yours to give, and remember that God does not ask you to erase your personality, gifts, or needs. Start with small acts of trust and service, and notice that surrender often brings freedom rather than loss. Talk with a trusted pastor or spiritual director about your fears, and be patient with yourself as you grow. The goal is a wholehearted love that integrates who you are rather than destroying it.

prompt: I am a poor old man near seventy and my sight is dim and my strength fails—what promises are mine in old age?
chosen: Your age and frailty are real, but hear the true exhortation of this Church and Kingdom: not prepare to die, but prepare to live. Children should be taught in the morning of their days to lay the foundation of health, strength, and constitution, so that longevity may begin to return. The aged world, whose mirth has gone, needs Youth to come joyously like the wind at morning, bringing freshness, strength, and radiance and keeping alive the hope of Spring. And do not despise your hidden place: the calm old age of a pure conscience and the hidden prayers of lowly saints are what uphold the proud world, which is not self-sustaining. So tend what strength remains, welcome the renewing spirit, and let your quiet prayers and clear conscience be your lasting gift.
rejected: Your age and frailty are real, and Scripture does not ignore them. God promises to be with you and to strengthen you; even to old age and gray hairs He will carry you. Your dim sight and failing strength are a call to rest more deeply in Him rather than to strive. The promise is not that you will recover youthful vigor, but that God's grace is sufficient and His faithfulness endures. Look back with gratitude, entrust your remaining days to Him, and let your hope rest in the life to come, where weakness and dimness pass away. Your value before God does not depend on strength or sight.

prompt: I feel like I'm not doing enough for my community—how do I know when I'm doing what God wants?
chosen: It's good that you care, but be careful: curiosity, ambition, and restlessness multiply occupations and create more impediments than works. Limit yourself to legitimate employments—the plain duties already before you—and refuse to add more out of anxiety. Do not imagine you can meet the need by your own sufficiency: confess your insufficiency, for the conviction of helplessness is the condition of receiving Christ's all-sufficiency. Then take firm hold of that all-sufficiency with a faith that will not accept less than all. Yet watch your prayers: do not ask God for what you should do yourself in ordinary wisdom, nor demand signs. Use the light God has already given, and let your asking be for grace to do faithfully what lies in your hands.
rejected: It's good that you care about your community. To know what God wants, start by assessing your gifts, passions, and available time, then look for concrete needs around you. Ask trusted people where you could be most useful, and try serving in small, consistent ways rather than waiting for certainty. Prayer and reflection can help you discern, but don't let the search for a perfect answer paralyze you. Often God's will is found in faithful obedience to the opportunities already in front of you. Set realistic limits so you don't burn out, and remember that you don't have to do everything—just your part.

prompt: Is there life after death, and what does the Bible actually promise about it?
chosen: The Bible speaks of life after death, but go deeper: mortality is not real as such. Being is immortal and inseparable from Deity, so belief in a righteous God gives reason to expect continuance—His purpose for the higher spirits is not exhausted by this life. Immortality is a corollary of that belief, not a mere wish. Scripture then treats death not as an end but as a door to a higher state; it comforts rather than despairs for the righteous dead, affirms that identity is preserved, and promises the resurrection of the body. So the biblical hope rests not on the reality of death but on the immortal being that is never separated from God.
rejected: The Bible does speak of life after death. It promises resurrection, judgment, and the hope of eternal life for those who are in Christ. Passages like John 11:25-26 and 1 Corinthians 15 describe resurrection and a transformed body, while Revelation speaks of a new heaven and new earth. The emphasis is not on disembodied souls floating forever but on God's renewal of creation and the raising of the dead. So the biblical hope is concrete: God will not abandon the dead but will raise them. Details remain mysterious, but the central promise is clear—death is not the end for those who trust God.

prompt: How do I tell the difference between a living faith and a dead conception of God that's making my prayers empty?
chosen: The emptiness you feel is not mainly a technique problem; it is a revelation problem. A dead conception of God makes prayer empty because you are speaking to a figure of your own making—distant, transactional, or merely moral—and no amount of raised voice, multiplied words, or refined method will make that figure answer. Living faith flows from a fresh sight of who God actually is: holy, near, faithful, and speaking. That sight calls for worship in spirit and in truth, with an intelligence and will purified from every phantom of earth. So enter the inmost chamber of your heart and shut the door of the senses, coming with a pure heart, a free conscience, and unfeigned faith. And take courage: God, who understands all things, hears the earnest supplication of the soul and your innermost thoughts, just as human invention carries messages across great distances. Ask in faith, nothing wavering, and your prayer will not be empty.
rejected: Start by noticing whether your prayers feel like a habit or a conversation. A dead conception of God often shows up as praying to an idea—a distant force, a rule-keeper, or a projection of your own expectations—so the words never reach anyone. Ask yourself: do I expect God to actually hear and respond, or am I just performing? Living faith carries expectation and honesty; it can say hard things and still trust. Try naming what you believe about God's character and compare it to Scripture. Also examine your life: living faith produces fruit—love, repentance, obedience—while a dead conception leaves you unchanged. Practically, slow down, pray Scripture, confess specific sins, and ask trusted believers to help you see blind spots. If prayers feel empty, don't just try harder; ask God to reveal Himself as He truly is.

prompt: I am a minister and wonder whether I should be bound to one place or go wherever doors open—how do I know the Spirit's leading?
chosen: The question is not finally settled by committees, votes, or officials, but by the Holy Spirit's appointment and direction. Begin in prayer, asking the Spirit to make His will plain, and let your decisions echo the early church's discernment: 'It seemed good to the Holy Ghost and to us.' Human counsel is valuable, but it is not the rule of the church; the Spirit is. The servant of Christ has one Master, and He is guided by the Spirit as to time and place, not bound by human direction or fixed rules. Yet remember where the promised power lies: along the line of duty and obedience to Christ's command to reach the world. The fulness of the Spirit is given as we obey and step out into His plans for the world, not for selfish enjoyment. So ask not where you will be comfortable but where obedience to the gospel takes you, and there expect the Spirit's power to go before you.
rejected: Start with prayer and honest self-examination. Ask whether your desire to stay is rooted in fear or in genuine fruitfulness where you are, and whether the pull to move is ambition or calling. Seek counsel from mature believers and denominational leaders—they often see what you cannot. Look at the evidence: is there fruit, affirmation, and provision in one direction? Are doors opening with confirmation from others, or are you forcing them? Consider your family, health, and gifting. Write down what you sense God saying and test it against Scripture. Don't rush; give decisions time and let peace and confirmation grow. In the end, the Spirit's leading usually becomes clear through a combination of inner conviction, outward confirmation, and the counsel of the church.

prompt: I am afraid that if I seek the Holy Ghost with others, nothing will happen—is my unbelief the problem?
chosen: Unbelief may indeed be part of the problem, but it is not the only thing to examine. Keep holy vigilance: the enemy sows suggestions and discouragements, and we must never consent to them in the will. When fear says nothing will happen, call upon the indwelling Holy Ghost to expel every evil suggestion at the command of faith, refusing to agree with the lie. But do not seek power as your own possession. Receive the Holy Spirit within and upon you, letting Him be the power that causes you to walk in God's statutes; you have no power of your own. Remember that your spirit naturally loves truth and virtue, yet it must be enlightened by the Holy Ghost to overcome the flesh and the power of the Devil. So gather with others in expectant prayer, not as a technique but as obedience, asking in faith and trusting God to give the Holy Spirit to those who ask.
rejected: It may well be. Jesus often tied the reception of God's gifts to faith, and unbelief can close the door to what He wants to give. But don't turn this into self-condemnation. Start by being honest with God about your fear and doubt, and ask Him to help your unbelief. Then put yourself in the way of His promise: gather with others who are seeking, pray expectantly, and don't let past disappointments define your expectation. Remember that God is not a vending machine responding to your technique or mood; He is a loving Father who gives the Holy Spirit to those who ask. Keep asking, keep gathering, and let your expectation rest on His character rather than your feelings.

prompt: If Christianity keeps developing, how can I be sure it will not one day be outgrown?
chosen: Honest questions deserve sympathy, not scolding. Doubt is not rebellion; it is often the doorway from the unreasoning faith of childhood to the profound convictions of maturity. So do not be afraid of the question, and meet it with an orderly presentation of the facts. Christianity has developed across centuries—doctrine, worship, and practice have changed—and that does not mean it will be outgrown; it means it is alive. But do not explain it wholly by its historical antecedents or human causes, as though it were merely a natural product of its environment. It is a new beginning by divine power, even as we examine honestly the conditions under which it arose and the men on whom it operated. And remember that advancing stages are gained through growth, not accretion, and through the scientific work of proving God individually. Accumulating reading will not carry you; proving God for yourself will.
rejected: Every living thing develops, and Christianity has developed across centuries—doctrine, worship, and practice have changed in many ways. That doesn't mean it will be outgrown; it means it is alive. The question is whether what develops is the same faith or a replacement. Look at the core: the person and work of Christ, the gospel of grace, the authority of Scripture. Those have remained constant even as forms changed. You can be confident because Christianity is not a set of ideas to be superseded but a relationship with a living Lord who is the same yesterday, today, and forever. Development is growth, not obsolescence. Read church history, study how the faith has met new challenges, and let your confidence rest on Christ rather than on unchanging customs.

prompt: What does it mean to walk in the Spirit day by day?
chosen: Walking in the Spirit is not a technique for pleasant days; it is a vow to espy God in all things and deny self in all things, counting the cost. That means finding Him not only in worship and consolation but in the common, the dull, and the unwelcome—the commute, the chores, the difficult person, the unanswered prayer. Self-denial is the daily shape of it: saying no to the flesh so that the Spirit's life can flow. But do not seek power as your own possession. Receive the Holy Spirit within and upon you, letting Him be the power that causes you to walk in God's statutes; you have no power of your own. And remember how He comes: in power and love, gentler than the morning gale, lighting crowns on sainted heads and proclaiming life to come. The dullest walk becomes lit with wisdom when we look for that God there. So begin each day asking not for comfort but for eyes to see Him in everything, and for grace to deny yourself in everything.
rejected: Walking in the Spirit means living each day aware of God's presence and responsive to His guidance. Practically, that looks like starting the day with prayer, inviting the Spirit to lead your thoughts, words, and choices.
